MasterZoo invests over $130,000 in website upgrade, mobile app development
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:42:35 EEST
00:42:35 KST

Ukrainian pet store chain MasterZoo has launched an upgraded online store at masterzoo.ua and its first mobile app, investing $100,000 in the website upgrade and more than $30,000 in app development, the company’s press service told Interfax-Ukraine.
"We are investing in building a digital ecosystem that will meet pet owners' varied needs, from regular purchases to discovering new products and getting professional advice. At the same time, we recognize the specifics of pet retail. In some categories, pet owners need to see products in person, try clothing or accessories on their pets, or receive in-person consultations. Our task is therefore not to pit online against offline, but to combine their advantages and create a seamless customer experience. For us, investment in technology is a strategic investment in MasterZoo's future," MasterZoo CEO Oksana Kyrychenko said.
The new platform offers product recommendations based on a pet's species and breed, expanded customer account features, an auto-subscription service offering a 10% discount on repeat orders, and other personalized offers. The upgraded platform lists more than 18,000 SKUs from over 350 brands. The mobile app is available for download from the App Store and Google Play.
The chain is developing an omnichannel model in which physical pet stores and digital services complement each other. Its more than 200 stores in 40 cities are gradually becoming part of its e-commerce infrastructure, serving as pickup and product reservation points. In the future, some stores are expected to function as "dark stores" for picking and dispatching online orders through postal operators or MasterZoo's own delivery service.
MasterZoo aims to make shopping convenient and personalized regardless of how customers interact with the brand. Online sales accounted for an average of 15% of the company's total sales in 2024, rising to 18% in 2025 and reaching 25% in 2026.
Company data show that customers increasingly combine online and offline channels. One in three to four buyers of dry pet food already uses multiple sales channels. The average online order value is 2.5 times the average purchase value at physical stores, while the lifetime value (LTV) of omnichannel customers is almost four times that of customers who shop exclusively at physical locations.
Pickup plays an important role in this model, accounting for about 35% of all MasterZoo online orders. More than 40% of pickup orders are placed in Kyiv. Kharkiv, Lviv, Dnipro and Odesa follow in terms of order volume.
"We see the habits of Ukrainian pet owners changing. Online shopping is becoming increasingly common not only in major cities but also in smaller communities. The share of orders from outside regional centers has increased from 26.4% to 29.7%, while the number of orders delivered by MasterZoo's own courier service has nearly tripled in a year, rising 182%. Delivery preferences also vary by location. In smaller communities, Nova Poshta handles about 80% of orders, compared with 39% in Kyiv. That is why our goal is not simply to develop an online store, but to create a flexible system that allows every customer to choose the most convenient way to shop and receive products, regardless of where they live," MasterZoo e-commerce director Alisa Dashevska said.
MasterZoo, operated by Petmaster LLC, is Ukraine's largest pet retail chain, with more than 200 stores in 40 cities and 19 grooming salons in seven cities. The chain has opened 15 new stores in 2026, including in Pryluky and Kamianets-Podilskyi, where it had not previously operated. MasterZoo is part of the Ukrainian family-owned Suziria Group. Its range includes more than 18,000 SKUs from over 350 brands.
According to Opendatabot, Petmaster LLC's revenue increased by 18.81% to UAH 2.282 billion in 2025, while net profit fell by 24% to UAH 6.256 million from UAH 8.234 million in 2024.

A lifesaving medication is not behind the drop in U.S. overdose deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:33:50 UTC

A lifesaving medication is not behind the drop in U.S. overdose deaths
New research suggests the use of naloxone, which reverses opioid overdoses, also fell
Drug overdose deaths unexpectedly took a nosedive in the United States a few years ago. But it doesn’t appear to be due to more people being revived than before.
At the peak in mid-2023, there were around 111,000 drug overdose deaths per year in the United States. By the end of 2025, the number had fallen to under 71,000 per year, and researchers are still piecing together why. One theory: The wider availability of naloxone, a medication that reverses opioid overdoses, made it possible to revive more people than before.
But a study of U.S. emergency medical services agencies found that emergency medical responses for nonfatal overdoses dropped along with deaths, and the use of naloxone also declined. That suggests that fewer overdoses overall occurred, not that naloxone stopped deaths more often, researchers report October 21 in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
“Naloxone still saves lives every day,” says Michael Barnett, a health services researcher at Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I. “But it doesn’t look like the reason for the sudden turn” in overdose deaths.
State policies, community distribution programs and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s approval of the nasal spray version of naloxone as an over-the counter drug have expanded access.
Barnett and colleagues analyzed nearly 186 million emergency medical service activations — an ambulance or other EMS response after a 911 call — nationwide that occurred from May 2020 through December 2025. Of 2.5 million responses for nonfatal drug overdoses, 40.5 percent involved opioids.
From May of 2023 onward, EMS activations for nonfatal opioid overdoses fell on average by about 6,000, or around 33 percent, below what was expected. Total administrations of naloxone dropped as well, by around 4,700 on average, or 21 percent below what was expected. The study suggests that naloxone was not used more often than before by bystanders prior to the EMS response, but did not include data on cases when a bystander provided naloxone and no one called 911.
Additional possibilities to explain the steep drop in overdose deaths — which followed a three-decade increase — include changes to the illicit opioid supply or with the population of people at risk for overdoses. “My own read is that a disruption in the fentanyl supply best explains how sudden and widespread the turn was,” Barnett says. “Underneath it, the population at risk has probably been shrinking for years.”
But “a supply-driven decline can reverse,” Barnett says, noting that the decline in overdose deaths slowed in 2025. Traffickers can adapt “by finding new chemical sources or turning to more potent synthetic opioids.”

Kazakhstan-EU trade tops $26 billion as investment ties deepen
Bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and the European Union reached $26.4 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 3% year-on-year, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Kazakh Foreign Ministry.
The Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Ardak Zebeshev, met with the Ambassador of the European Union to the Republic of Kazakhstan, Aleška Simkić, in Astana.
The parties discussed the implementation of agreements reached during the official visit of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, to Brussels, as well as prospects for expanding trade, economic, investment, and transport cooperation.
“The European Union remains Kazakhstan’s largest trade and investment partner. In 2025, bilateral trade exceeded USD 45 billion, while cumulative investment from EU countries since 2005 has surpassed USD 200 billion. Our priorities remain unchanged: trade and investment, transport connectivity, energy, the green and digital transitions, critical raw materials, environmental protection and climate action,” said Ardak Zebeshev.
In January–July 2026, bilateral trade rose 3% year on year to USD 26.4 billion, compared with USD 25.6 billion in 2025. Kazakhstan’s exports to EU countries increased by 5.9% to USD 20.8 billion, while imports from the EU declined by 6.5% to USD 5.6 billion.
The Deputy Minister outlined measures to improve the investment climate and mitigate administrative risks. Investors have access to investment agreements, tax and customs incentives, state in-kind grants and opportunities offered by special economic zones. Investment protection and support are ensured by the Investment Ombudsman, a dedicated investment prosecutor, the National Digital Investment Platform and the “green corridor” mechanism.
The parties also discussed the Global Gateway Investment Hub, launched by the European Commission to facilitate investment projects in partner countries. The Kazakh side emphasised that the mechanism’s practical value would depend on its ability to help move projects from the conceptual stage to implementation.
Another key topic was the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, one of Kazakhstan’s strategic priorities. The Kazakh side welcomed the signing, with EU support, of loan agreements with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and the European Investment Bank (EIB), including agreements aimed at modernising the Port of Aktau and developing sustainable transport infrastructure in Kazakhstan.
Following the meeting, the parties agreed to maintain close cooperation to advance joint projects.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan is strengthening the Middle Corridor role as President Tokayev advances Caspian cooperation.

'Lefty and proud': Spain's Sánchez hits back at Argentina's Milei in Madrid

Javier Milei has again attacked Pedro Sánchez during a visit to Madrid, where he will meet Isabel Díaz Ayuso. Sánchez replied on X, defending his left-wing stance in a fresh war of words between the two leaders.
Argentine President Javier Milei lashed out at Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez once again during a visit to Madrid on Wednesday, calling him a "disgraceful dictator" and urging that the Socialists be removed from power "by force".
Sánchez responded with a video on X defending his left-wing politics against Milei's derogatory use of the word "lefty".
"If raising pensions, increasing the minimum wage or defending the right to abortion means being a lefty, I am a lefty," the Spanish prime minister said, concluding: "Yes, I am a lefty, and proud of it."
He also swapped his official portrait on social media for a profile picture bearing the slogan "Lefty and proud" against a red background.
Sánchez's Socialist Party (PSOE) joined in, hanging a banner at its headquarters on Madrid's Calle Ferraz to greet the Argentine leader. It reads: "The lefties, men and women, welcome you to Spain".
Relations between the two leaders have been strained since May 2024, when Milei, speaking at a rally organised by the far-right Vox party in Madrid, accused Sánchez's wife of corruption. Spain responded by withdrawing its ambassador from Buenos Aires, sparking a diplomatic crisis between the two countries.
Milei is due to meet Isabel Díaz Ayuso, president of the Madrid region and one of the leading figures in the conservative People's Party (PP), Spain's main opposition party, at 17:00 on Wednesday. It will not be their first encounter: in June 2024, at the height of the diplomatic row, Ayuso awarded him the International Medal of the Community of Madrid.
No photo with Feijóo or Abascal
Whether because of diary clashes or political caution, with the general election on 29 November only weeks away, neither PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo nor Vox leader Santiago Abascal will meet Milei publicly or be photographed with him. Milei and Feijóo have never held a formal meeting, crossing paths only briefly at a handful of public events.
Abascal, by contrast, knows Milei well. Both appeared at Vox's Europa Viva 24 rally at Madrid's Palacio de Vistalegre arena, which brought together leading figures of the international hard right, including France's Marine Le Pen, Hungary's Viktor Orbán, Chile's José Antonio Kast and Portugal's André Ventura.
Vox has since joined Orbán's Patriots for Europe group in the European Parliament.
Clashes in La Coruña over Abascal rally
Although he will not be pictured with Milei, Abascal still found himself at the centre of tensions on Wednesday in A Coruña, in the north-western region of Galicia, where he was giving a speech.
A protest organised by the Socialist Youth, the PSOE's youth wing, together with members of Galiza Nova, the youth wing of the Galician nationalist BNG, began peacefully. Demonstrators chanted "They shall not pass", the anti-fascist slogan made famous during the Spanish Civil War.
But tensions boiled over as the event ended, with eggs and other objects thrown at the police cordon.
Abascal described the protest as "coercion" and said Galicia remained a "thorn in the side" for Vox, calling on supporters to mobilise in the name of "freedom".
He also attacked Sánchez, branding him a "traitor" and a "careerist" over the government's handling of the situation in Ceuta, the Spanish enclave on the North African coast bordering Morocco. Abascal confirmed there would be no photo with Milei, saying the two would instead meet in private.

From dust to dirt: Australians to become compost after death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:29:04 KST

From dust to dirt: Australians to become compost after death
Residents of New South Wales, Australia could soon have the option to make a final contribution to their garden upon death, after the state’s parliament approved turning human remains into compost as an alternative to burial and cremation.
The bill, introduced by Independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich, cleared the upper house on Wednesday after passing the lower house unanimously last week. It now awaits assent, with a minimum two-year wait before going into force.
Known as ‘terramation’ or natural organic reduction, a body is placed in a vessel with wood chips, straw, and other plant material. Microbes break down the remains, producing material that can eventually nourish trees and gardens.
US operator Recompose says its process takes 8-12 weeks, including a curing period. Remaining bones are mechanically ground down and mixed back in, and artificial implants are removed.
Under the NSW bill, families can take the resulting compost home to nourish a memorial tree or garden, or arrange for it to be placed elsewhere. However, choosing to become garden material remains a personal decision; operators are barred from turning a deceased person’s remains into compost against their written wishes.
Supporters of the method say the method uses less land and energy than conventional burial and cremation and could ease the financial and environmental burden of dying.
“We are running out of burial space [and] that space can cost as much as $50,000 [Australian dollars],” Greenwich told ABC in June. He predicted that composting will become cheaper than cremation, although local prices have yet to be established.
Not everyone is pleased with the proposal. NSW Premier Chris Minns said in June that he felt “a bit weird about it.” Catholic Weekly columnist Michael Cook described it as a “bizarre solution to saving the planet,” arguing that composting conflicts with religious respect for the human body.
Similar human composting practices have already been approved in several US states and part of Germany. England and Wales are considering rules that could eventually allow it.

Su-30 fighter jet crashes in Russia
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed in the Kaliningrad region during a scheduled training flight, the Russian Defense Ministry said.

Nuclear collaboration completes its mission

Nuclear collaboration completes its mission
Cross-industry programme set up to safeguard skills has concluded its work
The UK Alpha Resilience and Capability (ARC) Programme has formally closed.
It leaves a positive legacy of technical products, standards, knowledge, teamwork, and lasting relationships.
Since it began, the programme has united organisations from the civil and defence nuclear sectors.
Its aims were to tackle common challenges, boost resilience and capability, and speed up the sharing of knowledge and expertise across the sector.
By working together, partners found ways to create shared solutions, creating greater benefits than if each organisation worked alone.
Its success was built on the commitment and expertise of partner organisations including:
- Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ)
- Nuclear Decommissioning Authority (NDA)
- AWE Nuclear Security Technologies
- Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR)
- Sellafield Ltd
- Ministry of Defence (MoD)
- UK National Nuclear Laboratory (UKNNL)
- Nuclear Restoration Services (NRS)
- Nuclear Transport Solutions (NTS)
They provided expert knowledge, resources, and leadership. This helped create solutions that improve capability throughout the UK nuclear industry.
The programme’s biggest success may be the strong professional networks and the culture of collaboration now found across the sector.
Investments and interventions from all organisations involved helped the programme deliver a portfolio of products. They included standards, frameworks, training solutions, and Communities of Practice to support current and future Alpha programmes.
Key achievements included:
- Development of sector-wide engineering standards and guidance, de-risking our national programmes
- Delivery of the non-active Glovebox Training Facility, accelerating capability development
- Development of collaborative platforms and digital knowledge-sharing tools, building resilience across the sector
Dale McQueen, UK ARC Programme senior sponsor, said:
  ARC has shown the power of enterprise-wide collaboration.
By bringing together expertise from across the UK nuclear sector, the programme has delivered solutions that no single organisation could have achieved alone.
The legacy of ARC includes not just its products and standards. It also involves the relationships, knowledge-sharing communities, and collaborative behaviours that will keep strengthening the sector for years.
Scott Bazley, programme manager for the UK ARC Programme said:
  ARC has shown what’s possible when civil and defence organisations unite for a common goal.
In the last six years, we have provided standards, guidance, collaboration tools, and lasting networks. These will keep adding value even after the programme ends.
Most importantly, ARC has built a culture of collaboration and trust. This strong foundation supports future cross-sector initiatives.
Richard Gibson, vice president for legacy sites at UKNNL, said:
  We are proud to have been a key partner to ARC since its inception in 2020.
It’s a ground-breaking partnership between civil and defence nuclear groups for the UK’s alpha missions.
It has provided real benefits, such as shared engineering standards and strong Communities of Practice and knowledge management.

Russian authorities have released 74-year-old U.S. national Stephen Hubbard, who in October 2024 was sentenced by the Moscow City Court to six years and 10 months in prison on charges of “participating as a mercenary in an armed conflict on the side of Ukraine.” The release became known during the Oct. 21 meeting between Vladimir Putin and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff.

This past August, Russia released 32-year-old U.S. citizen Robert Gilman, a former Marine who had been in custody since January 2022. Vladimir Putin approved his pardon “for humanitarian reasons.” U.S. President Donald Trump stressed at the time that Moscow had released Gilman unilaterally: “Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place.” The released American returned to the U.S.
Gilman had been taken off a Russian train in Voronezh, allegedly over drunken and disorderly conduct. At the police station, according to the investigation, he kicked a police officer in the leg. A criminal case was opened against Gilman for assaulting a public official, and he was subsequently sentenced to 4.5 years in a general-security penal colony. Gilman was later handed two more sentences for allegedly assaulting employees of the Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN). In total, the American was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

Indian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:26:25 UTC
00:26:25 KST

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

The Kremlin wants Russian media to call attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ‘Putin strikes.’ The inspiration? Stalin.
Russia’s Presidential Administration has ordered state and Kremlin-aligned media outlets to begin writing about “Putin strikes” on Ukraine, two employees at such outlets told Meduza.
The Presidential Administration’s political bloc sent loyalist media recommendations advising them to report that “the effectiveness and efficiency of Russia’s strikes far exceed what the Ukrainian military has achieved.”
“Our ballistic weapons have performed flawlessly. The Ukrainian regime has lost its most important production and storage sites, where cruise missiles and drones, along with their components, were assembled and stored. ‘Putin strikes’ are far larger in scale and more effective than enemy attacks. We are shutting down the militants’ missile programs, which helps keep Russia’s regions secure,” the guidance document says.
Headlines, comments from servicemen, and articles using the phrase “Putin strikes” indeed appeared this week in major Russian media outlets.
For example, the Russian news website Gazeta.ru published an article with the following subheadline:
“SVO” veteran Konovalov: “Putin strikes” deprive the Ukrainian military of the ability to fight.
The outlet cites Vitaly Konovalov, head of the Association of Veterans of the Russia-Ukraine War in Stavropol Krai, who says the strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure are allegedly aimed at undermining supplies to the Ukrainian military. Notably, Konovalov himself never uses the phrase “Putin strikes.” It appears in the connecting phrases and generalizations added by propagandists.
Novye Izvestia published an article titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Left Without Electricity and Weapons.” Rosbalt used the phrase in the headline of a news item titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Losing Logistics Hubs, Substations, and Vessels.” It also appears in headlines and articles from Fedpress. Segodnia.ru writes about a “series of “Putin strikes.”” The phrase has even appeared in pro-government Instagram accounts.
A political consultant who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc said directly linking Putin to the strikes on Ukraine is meant to try to boost the president’s approval ratings.
According to polls by the Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), Putin’s approval rating fell from 75% in July to 71% in early October, while trust in him fell from 74% to 70% over the same period.
“In this case, [the idea is to raise the ratings] among the pro-war, ultra-patriotic segment of society, who need to be shown some successes from the war. To the question “What has been accomplished?” [at the front], the suggested answer is “Putin strikes,” by analogy with the “Stalinist strikes,”” the consultant said.
During Joseph Stalin’s rule, the term “Ten Stalinist Strikes” referred to 10 major Soviet army operations during World War II.
The source told Meduza that it is hard to assess how effective the appearance of “Putin strikes” in the press has been: “Maybe it will have some effect on the older segment [of society].”
Speaking at a press conference in Bishkek on September 1, following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, Vladimir Putin said he had ordered the Russian military to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. “They’re striking our people, so they’ll get a response,” he added.
In mid-October, discussing the Russian army’s strikes on Ukraine, Putin said:
They took the first step. We started responding. Now they’re whining about energy facilities too, and about other targets, including data centers and so on. They started it. They shouldn’t have started it.

Five bullets and a broken promise: Israel's forgotten political assassination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:25:23 UTC
00:25:23 KST

On the evening of January 12, 1981, a security guard outside Jerusalem's Holyland Hotel heard gunfire. Looking toward the entrance, he saw a military jeep speeding away against the direction of traffic. Nearby, inside a bullet-riddled Peugeot 504, Israeli lawmaker Hamad Abu Rabia lay dead. He had been struck by five bullets. 
The killing made him the first serving member of Israel's Knesset to be assassinated. The motive was extraordinary: Abu Rabia had refused to surrender his parliamentary seat under a political rotation agreement, and the men responsible for his murder were the sons of the politician who stood to replace him.
Abu Rabia's life had begun far from the corridors of the Knesset. Born in 1929 in a Bedouin tent near Tel Malhata, in what is now the southern Negev between Arad and Dimona, he attended elementary school in Beersheba and later studied in Hebron. At just 18, he became sheikh of the Abu Rabia tribe and worked to expand educational opportunities for its children. In the 1973 election, he headed the Arab List for Bedouins and Villagers, becoming the first Bedouin elected to Israel's parliament when the eighth Knesset convened in 1974. His election was celebrated with a gathering of some 2,000 guests at his tribe's encampment. Among those attending were senior politician Yigal Allon and Druze lawmaker Jaber Muadi, who would later become his political rival.
Abu Rabia's early parliamentary career was closely tied to the political representation of Israel's Bedouin population. His faction joined the Labor Alignment before breaking away and eventually becoming part of the United Arab List, a small Arab party affiliated with the Alignment, then led by Shimon Peres. In the 1977 election, the United Arab List won just one seat, prompting its three senior figures to agree to share it through a rotation arrangement. Saif al-Din al-Zoubi, a former mayor of Nazareth, served first, resigning after approximately two years. Abu Rabia replaced him in April 1979, with Muadi, from the northern Druze village of Yarka, next in line.
But when Abu Rabia's allotted time expired, he refused to step aside. His decision was not simply a dispute over political status. Following the peace treaty with Egypt, Israel planned new military airfields in the Negev to replace installations in Sinai, raising concerns over the displacement of Bedouin communities and the expropriation of their land. Abu Rabia argued that he needed to remain in parliament to defend his community's interests. "I must continue being a member of the Knesset to protect the Bedouins," he explained at the time. Muadi, however, insisted that the rotation agreement obligated Abu Rabia to resign. He pursued the matter through parliamentary channels and the courts, but efforts to compel the resignation failed.
The dispute grew increasingly bitter. In the months before his murder, Abu Rabia feared for his safety and was occasionally accompanied by armed bodyguards. He also carried a pistol, which was found in his possession after the assassination. On January 12, he spent the day at the Knesset, briefly speaking with Labor politicians Shimon Peres and Moshe Shahal before driving to the Holyland Hotel in Jerusalem's Bayit Vegan neighborhood, where lawmakers frequently stayed during parliamentary sessions. At approximately 8:30 p.m., attackers waiting near the hotel opened fire as he arrived, killing him inside his car before escaping in a jeep.
Muadi initially denied any connection to the killing. He acknowledged that he and Abu Rabia had quarreled but maintained that they had reconciled. Asked whether he knew who might have murdered his colleague, he replied: "How could I know? It hurts me very much." As suspicion increasingly focused on his family, Muadi rejected suggestions that he had been involved. "Would I kill a man just to get into the Knesset?" he asked, according to contemporary reporting in Yedioth Ahronoth. He nevertheless continued to criticize Abu Rabia for breaking their agreement, saying the murdered lawmaker had sworn on the Quran to honor it. Muadi acknowledged telling him that God would take revenge on him and his children, but insisted the remark had not been a threat.
Police arrested six suspects, several of them members of Muadi's family. Investigators established that three of his sons had traveled to Jerusalem and waited near the Holyland Hotel for Abu Rabia to arrive. According to the reconstruction presented during the investigation, Saif Muadi fired the fatal shots before fleeing with his brothers. In January 1982, all three brothers were convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. The court accepted the prosecution's account that they had acted to secure their father's place in the Knesset, regarding Abu Rabia's refusal to honor the agreement as an affront to their family's honor. In 1984, however, the Supreme Court overturned the murder conviction of the third brother, Dahash Muadi, who had served as deputy commander of Nablus Prison. He was released after being acquitted of murder, although he had been convicted of other offenses.
The assassination also had an immediate political consequence. Muadi took Abu Rabia's place in the Knesset just days after the killing, in a swearing-in ceremony held under heavy security. He remained in parliament until the ninth Knesset was dissolved about six months later but did not regain his seat in the subsequent election. Throughout the investigation and trial, he maintained that he had no involvement in the murder, despite acknowledging the bitter dispute with Abu Rabia and the exchanges that had preceded it.
The two convicted brothers remained imprisoned until January 10, 1991, when President Chaim Herzog granted them pardons following sustained political pressure from members of the Druze community. Their release was celebrated in Yarka with a large gathering. According to reports from the time, 130 sheep were slaughtered and half a ton of baklava and other sweets were served to guests welcoming the brothers home.

Denmark guarantees $113 million loan for Ukrainian defense company Fire Point

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:25:03 UTC
00:25:03 KST

Denmark will guarantee a 750 million Danish kroner ($113 million) loan to the Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, the Danish government announced on Oct. 21.
The guarantee highlights Denmark’s role in helping Ukraine expand defense production beyond its borders as Russian attacks threaten domestic manufacturing and supply chains.
The loan is backed by the Danish state as Russia’s war against Ukraine prevents the company from borrowing on ordinary terms in Denmark. The funding will be channeled through Denmark’s Export and Investment Fund (EIFO).
"Denmark strongly supports the Ukrainians’ fight for freedom," Business and Industry Minister Martin Lidegaard said. He added that hosting a Ukrainian defense company in Denmark would bring "knowledge and production, as well as partnerships" that could strengthen Ukraine, Denmark’s defense industry and a more independent Europe.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said locating Ukrainian defense production outside Ukraine would make it more resilient to Russian attacks.
"When Denmark supports the Ukrainian defense industry, the combat power of Ukraine’s defense increases," Bruus said. He added that production outside Ukraine would provide safer supply chains for critical defense equipment and technologies while creating opportunities for cooperation between Fire Point, Denmark’s Defense Ministry, and Danish companies.
Denmark announced in September 2025 that Fire Point would establish production of fuel for long-range missiles on Danish soil. The facility is expected to become operational by the end of 2027.
Fire Point is also expanding its European defense partnerships. In August 2026, the company signed agreements with more than a dozen European defense companies to integrate radar, guidance and other technologies into its Freyja missile defense project. The project aims to provide Ukraine with a domestic alternative to the U.S.-made Patriot air defense system.
EIFO CEO Peder Lundqvist said the fund is currently involved in almost 40 projects supporting Ukraine and cooperation between Ukrainian and Danish companies.
"The financing of Fire Point is a concrete example of how these efforts can be put into practice," Lundqvist stated.

Rare 700-year-old Quran manuscript to be auctioned in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:24:52 UTC
00:24:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Rare 700-year-old Quran manuscript to be auctioned in London
A rare Quran manuscript page dating back more than 700 years to medieval Baghdad is set to go under the hammer at Christie's in London next month, with an estimated value of between £50,000 and £70,000.
The elaborately decorated folio, believed to have been produced around 1310 during the Ilkhanid period, features verses from the Quran written in gold and surrounded by intricate Islamic ornamentation.
The manuscript will be offered as part of Christie's Art of the Islamic and Indian Worlds auction on 12 November, which will feature more than 230 historical objects, including manuscripts, ceramics, paintings, metalwork and textiles.
According to Christie's, the page contains the opening three verses of Surah al-Humazah, the Quran's 104th chapter, written in four lines of gold muhaqqaq script, a distinctive style of Arabic calligraphy associated with monumental manuscripts.
The lettering is outlined in gold, silver and black ink, while individual verses are separated by decorative rosettes featuring gold and multiple colours.
The chapter heading appears in black Kufic script outlined in gold, surrounded by an elaborate panel of interlacing arabesque patterns and a decorated marginal medallion.
Measuring approximately 57.7 by 42.6 centimetres, the unusually large folio reflects the importance attached to the production of luxury Qurans under the Ilkhanids, the Mongol dynasty that ruled much of Iran and Iraq between the 13th and 14th centuries.
The manuscript's illumination, or decorative artwork, has been attributed to Muhammad ibn Aybak ibn Abdullah, regarded as one of the leading manuscript illuminators working in Baghdad during the early 14th century.
Ibn Aybak is associated with two monumental Qurans produced for the Ilkhanid royal court, one probably commissioned for Sultan Ghazan, who ruled from 1295 to 1304, and another for his successor, Sultan Uljaytu.
Both rulers belonged to the Mongol dynasty that emerged following the conquests of Genghis Khan's descendants, with Ghazan's conversion to Islam helping consolidate the religion's position within the Ilkhanid state.
The period witnessed significant developments in Islamic manuscript production, particularly in Baghdad, where calligraphers and illuminators developed elaborate styles combining Arabic lettering with colourful decorative motifs.
Christie's says the manuscript closely resembles pages associated with Ibn Aybak's royal commissions, although the identity of the calligrapher responsible for its lettering remains uncertain.
The auction house notes that the decorative style incorporates Chinese-inspired details, reflecting artistic exchanges across the territories once connected by the Mongol Empire.
A comparable folio held by the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha is believed to have originated from the same manuscript, offering further evidence of the artistic traditions associated with Ibn Aybak's workshop.
The page's known ownership history is limited, with Christie's listing it as having belonged to a private collection in the UK, reportedly by 1971.
Its appearance at auction highlights the continuing international market for historic Islamic manuscripts, particularly examples associated with major centres of medieval Islamic scholarship and artistic production.
Christie's November sale will also include works from across the Islamic world and Indian subcontinent, with objects representing artistic traditions stretching from North Africa and Spain to Central Asia.
The auction is scheduled for 12 November in London, following a public exhibition running from 7 to 11 November.

Ukraine’s top war charity names only way to save $25,000 to $4 million each time cheap Russian jet-powered drone is shot down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:19:43 UTC
00:19:43 KST

Intercepting a jet-powered Geran can cost anywhere from $2,000 to $4 million depending on the weapon used. Cheap interceptor drones are the only option that keeps air defense affordable, the foundation of Ukrainian top war volunteer Serhii Sternenko said on Telegram.
Russia’s jet Gerans now carry every characteristic of a small cruise missile, and Russians keep raising their speed in answer to each Ukrainian countermeasure. Former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi has framed the shift bluntly: an expensive Cold War missile has become a cheap weapon fired in bulk, and the drone is now “a missile in all but name,” affordable to any side, not only wealthy countries.
Sternenko heads a charitable foundation that has purchased 291,502 FPV drones, which have helped Ukraine’s military down more than 12,954 aerial targets. Also, has advised the team of former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Three ways to kill a jet Geran, and what each costs
The foundation laid out the price of each method:
- Aircraft (F-16, MiG-29, Su-27, Mirage 2000): $25,000 to $1.2 million per kill. Effective, but the stock of missiles is critically low, and some air-to-air types are no longer being replenished.
- Surface-to-air and shoulder-fired systems (IRIS-T, NASAMS, Vampire, Avenger): about $30,000 to $4 million. Good for shielding key sites, but a missile capable of reaching a jet Geran at 6 to 7 kilometers costs $0.5 million to $4 million.
- Interceptor drones (makers undisclosed): from $2,000. Cheap, with trained operators ready, but not yet scalable.
Why the cheapest option is the one that matters
No single tool is enough, the foundation stresses. Downing jet Gerans still needs aircraft, small aviation and missile systems together, but it is the interceptors that make the defense affordable, taking out the cheaper Shaheds and saving costly missiles for targets nothing else can reach.
The foundation says it has found a way to counter drones that already match small cruise missiles, working with Ukrainian manufacturers, without disclosing details. The method is far cheaper than other ways of downing jet Gerans and significantly strengthens air defense, it says, as part of a wider Ukrainian push to field interceptor drones fast enough to catch Russia’s fastest weapons.

Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:19:14 UTC
00:19:14 KST

You can’t hold antimatter in your hand or even in a regular laboratory apparatus. As soon as antimatter meets matter, the two tend to annihilate each other. This makes studying antimatter tricky. But now physicists have managed to trap a single subatomic particle of the stuff for months at a time in a way that allows them to study its quantum states.
Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way.
Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron—the antimatter counterpart of the electron.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them,” says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters.
The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. “Every time they bang into something, there’s a chance of annihilation, but it doesn’t always happen,” Gabrielse says. “If they make it to the end, they get popped out.”
Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. “If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls,” Gabrielse says.
This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a month—and could let them do so indefinitely.
The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron’s magnetic moment—basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron’s spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state.
Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. “We’re looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment,” Gabrielse says. That’s the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.
Just after the Big Bang, scientists think there were roughly equal amounts of the two. Most of the matter and antimatter must have annihilated, but a small excess of matter was somehow left over to seed the stars and planets we see. The magnetic moment measurement is just one of many realms where physicists are seeking differences between matter and antimatter to account for this profound discrepancy.
“Turn every particle to its antiparticle, look at physics through a mirror (flipping left and right) and press the ‘rewind button’ to reverse the flow of time,” says Roni Harnik, a theoretical physicist at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Batavia, Ill., who was not involved in the project. “Our most basic theories say that physics stays the same.”
If it turns out things are different—that the positron, for instance, has a different magnetic moment than the electron—then we’d have a hint about how matter won out.
“This is an exciting development,” Harnik says, “that will enable us to test a basic symmetry.”

African health ministers to hold Ebola crisis talks as Nigeria confirms first case

African health ministers will hold crisis talks on Ebola as Nigeria becomes the fourth country to confirm a case. The patient is now in isolation, while her contacts, including her spouse, a Swiss national, are being monitored.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for urgent action to contain the growing Ebola outbreak and is convening African health ministers to coordinate the response, as Nigeria becomes the latest country to confirm a case.
The outbreak began in Congo and has so far also spread to Kenya and Uganda; the latter said it has no cases at the moment. Such geographic spread across Central, Eastern and Western Africa demands urgent, coordinated action, Africa CDC said.
“Ebola is crossing borders. Our response must move faster, with stronger coordination, greater solidarity and decisive political leadership,” said Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa CDC in a press release.
“We have the expertise and the capacity on this continent. We must mobilise them together to stop this outbreak and save lives,” he added.
On Tuesday, Nigeria reported its first case, linked to a traveller from Uganda who arrived there earlier this month.
Uganda, which declared itself Ebola-free in July after recording 20 cases, has denied claims that Nigeria’s first case originated there.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement on X. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases."
Nigerian authorities said they were tracing 44 contacts.
The patient, who entered Nigeria on 5 October, was initially treated for malaria but failed to recover, arousing suspicion among the attending physicians, Odianosen Ehiakhamen, an assistant director at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control, local media reported. The patient is now in isolation and receiving medical care.
Ehiakhamen said the contacts are mostly healthcare workers, along with the patient’s spouse, a Swiss national.
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or via contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May and 9,552 confirmed cases.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccine or specific treatment exists, although trials are underway in Congo.
The risk of importation into Europe from the outbreak areas remains very low, according to the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).
“While sporadic importations cannot be excluded, the probability of multiple independent importations is very low, even in a pessimistic scenario whereby incidence continues to rise in the affected regions,” the Center wrote on its website.

JD Vance snubs Netanyahu as MAGA divisions over Israel deepen

Trump had offered Netanyahu his "Complete and Total Endorsement" the previous day, praising the Israeli leader's partnership with Washington against Iran and declaring that he would never let Israelis down.
Vance's refusal comes as Netanyahu faces growing political opposition at home and international condemnation over Israel's genocide in Gaza, which has severely damaged the country's international standing.
Netanyahu has also become an increasingly toxic political figure in the US, where Israel's genocide in Gaza and the war against Iran have severely eroded longstanding public support for the country.
An October Chicago Council survey found American favourability towards Israel at its lowest level since polling began in 1978, while Pew Research found that 60% of Americans viewed Israel unfavourably and 59% lacked confidence in Netanyahu.

It also exposes differences within Trump's political movement over the extent of American support for Israel, particularly following the US-Israeli war against Iran.
While traditional Republican figures remain strongly supportive of Israel, influential voices within the MAGA movement have increasingly questioned whether Washington's military commitments serve American interests.

Vance, who maintains close ties with Carlson, has sought to navigate these divisions while preserving his standing within Trump's administration.
In June, he criticised members of Netanyahu's government for opposing Trump's attempts to negotiate an end to the Iran conflict.
The following month, Vance accused elements of the Israeli government of attempting to manipulate American public opinion to prolong the war.
"There are some people within their system that we know beyond a shadow of a doubt are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely," he told Joe Rogan.
He has also argued that American foreign policy must not become subordinate to Israel's priorities, while maintaining that Israel remains an important US ally.
The tensions have complicated Vance's relationship with some influential Republican donors and pro-Israel organisations.
In August, he attended a Republican Jewish Coalition gathering in Las Vegas, seeking to reassure members concerned about his foreign policy positions and his association with Carlson.
His refusal to endorse Netanyahu is particularly significant given his widely discussed ambitions to succeed Trump as the Republican presidential candidate in 2028.
During the same interview with Halperin, Vance said he believed Trump would endorse him if he decided to run, although he acknowledged that the two had not discussed the matter.
The vice president's decision to distance himself from Israel's election therefore comes as he faces the challenge of maintaining Trump's support while appealing to competing factions within the Republican Party.
His explanation that he avoids foreign elections is also complicated by his previous endorsement of Hungary's Viktor Orban, whom he actively supported during an unsuccessful re-election campaign earlier this year.
For Netanyahu, the absence of Vance's endorsement adds another dimension to an increasingly difficult election campaign.
Opinion polls have suggested that Netanyahu's governing coalition could struggle to secure the 61 parliamentary seats needed to retain power, with opposition parties seeking to capitalise on public dissatisfaction with his leadership.
Netanyahu also remains subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, further complicating his international standing.
Trump's endorsement demonstrates that Netanyahu retains powerful supporters in Washington, despite previous tensions between the two leaders over Iran and regional diplomacy.
Vance's position, however, reflects the increasingly contested nature of American support for Netanyahu within the Republican movement.
Although his refusal does not amount to an outright rejection of the Israeli prime minister, it illustrates the competing pressures facing a potential successor to Trump as MAGA debates the future direction of US foreign policy.

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: Xi Jinping's new Long March
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:18:29 CST
00:18:29 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- On the banks of the Yudu River in east China, a choir sang of soldiers leaving home more than nine decades ago. Beside the singers, eight large red Chinese characters proclaimed: "May the spirit of the Long March shine forever."
In October 1934, some 86,000 Red Army soldiers crossed the river, little knowing that they were embarking on a grueling 12,500-kilometer journey, which American journalist Edgar Snow hailed as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times." In October 1936, three main Red Army forces converged in northwestern China, marking the end of the Long March.
As China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victorious conclusion this year, visitors have traveled to the mountainous county of Yudu in Jiangxi Province to see where it all began.
Yudu's visitors number in the millions each year. Among those who have made the trip is Chinese President Xi Jinping.
During his visit in May 2019, Xi laid a floral basket at a Long March departure monument, went to the river crossing used by Red Army soldiers and met their descendants.
"I have come here to let people across the country know that the Party has not forgotten its original aspiration," said Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission.
"We must build on the past, pack our bags and set out again," he said.
CARRY THE BATON FORWARD
The Long March was a strategic shift. In 1934, the fledgling CPC was forced to abandon its main base in the provinces of Jiangxi and Fujian after failing to repel the Kuomintang regime's fifth encirclement and suppression campaign.
The maneuver took the Red Army across nearly 100 rivers and more than 40 towering mountains, and through marshland known as a "death zone." The troops fought more than 600 battles. Many lost their lives along the way.
Far in the northwest, Xi's father, Xi Zhongxun, and his comrades Liu Zhidan and Xie Zichang established the Shaanxi-Gansu revolutionary base. The existence of the base was an important factor in Mao Zedong's decision to make it the Long March's final destination.
After the Long March, the Party established a firm foothold in northern Shaanxi, with Yan'an as its headquarters for more than a decade. From there, it grew in strength, led the Chinese people in fighting against Japanese invasion and eventually overthrew the Kuomintang regime.
Growing up in such a revolutionary family, Xi developed a deep connection to the Long March and the region. He was not yet 16 when he left Beijing for a village in Yan'an, where he spent seven years living and working alongside farmers. There, he joined the Party, became the village Party chief, forged close ties with local people, and made a commitment to serving the people through public office.
Yan'an, the Chinese revolution's foothold after the Long March and its springboard for national victory, was thus the starting point of Xi's political journey.
"Whenever I went to Yan'an in those years, I felt a deep sense of reverence and excitement," Xi recalled.
As a young man, Xi was deeply fascinated by the history of the Long March. In the 1980s, he was acquainted with writer Wang Yuanjian, who devoted himself to chronicling the Red Army's heroism. Wang had interviewed many Long March veterans. As he recounted their stories, Xi would pull a notebook from his pocket and carefully take notes, Wang's wife recalled in an article.
In 1996, while serving as Fujian's deputy Party secretary, Xi joined a 1,000-person torch relay marking the Long March's 60th anniversary. He set off at the front alongside an 82-year-old Red Army veteran.
In 2006, as Party secretary of Zhejiang, Xi visited a photo exhibition marking the 70th anniversary of the Long March. He described the Long March as both an extraordinary test of the human spirit and will, and a journey in pursuit of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
Since taking the top office in late 2012, Xi has retraced the Long March routes on visits across the country: from Yudu, where the Central Red Army assembled and set out, to Quanzhou, where soldiers fought the bloody Battle of the Xiangjiang River; Zunyi, the site of a decisive turning point; and Jiangtaibu, where Red Army forces joined up at the end of the Long March.
At museums, Xi studied artifacts and asked questions. At monuments, he paid tribute to revolutionary martyrs by presenting flower baskets and bowing. He also instructed authorities to recover and properly bury soldiers' remains and build memorial facilities.
On one visit, he paused before a painting of Chen Shuxiang, whose division served as the Red Army's rear guard. Captured after covering the main force's river crossing, Chen refused to surrender and died after tearing open his abdominal wound.
Xi asked how the Red Army had broken through encirclement and held together despite devastating losses, then offered his answer: the power of conviction.
For generations of Chinese leaders, the Long March is not just a military campaign, but a metaphor for the ongoing task of transforming China.
In 1949, more than a decade after the Long March ended, the People's Republic was founded. Earlier that year, with victory in sight, Mao said that winning the revolution "would be only the first step of the Long March." The journey of building a new China had just begun.
It significantly gained pace with the launch of the reform and opening up in 1978. Deng Xiaoping, a Long March veteran, proposed a three-step strategy for China's modernization, which was later elaborated as follows: meet the people's basic needs of food and clothing by 1990, achieve moderate prosperity by the end of the 20th century, and basically attain modernization by the middle of the 21st century. This modernization drive came to be known as the new Long March.
"The Long March of our generation is to attain the 'two centenary goals' and realize the Chinese Dream -- the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," Xi said.
The two goals refer to achieving moderate prosperity in all respects by the Party's centenary in 2021 and building a great modern socialist country in all respects by the centenary of the People's Republic around the middle of the century.
In 2017, Xi brought forward the timetable for basically achieving modernization under Deng's three-step strategy by 15 years to 2035.
"Every generation must undertake its own Long March," Xi said.
BRAVE THROUGH ALL ODDS
When the Long March began, the Red Army faced an enemy superior in both numbers and weaponry. Kuomintang forces pursued it from behind and blocked the routes ahead, seeking to encircle and destroy it. Breaking through meant fighting for every chance of survival.
In the winter of 1934, the struggle reached a critical point at the Xiangjiang River. Under heavy bombardment, Red Army troops fought their way toward the crossing points. By the time the army broke through, its ranks had dwindled from some 86,000 at the start of the march to just over 30,000.
The new Long March Xi is leading would test the Party's resolve against a different set of challenges. When he was elected the Party's top leader in 2012, China had become the world's second-largest economy and largest manufacturer after more than three decades of rapid economic growth.
That transformation also brought new challenges. China needed to sustain its economic momentum while narrowing regional disparities, tackling corruption, eradicating absolute poverty, and easing mounting environmental pressures. Meanwhile, the international community's expectations for China were rising.
Talking about "today's Long March," Xi said that although the conditions and tasks differ greatly, it remains "a pioneering, arduous and complex undertaking."
The modernization drive Xi now leads is unprecedented in human history. A population exceeding 1.4 billion is collectively advancing toward modernity on a scale surpassing the combined populations of existing developed nations. His goal is common prosperity for all, encompassing both material wealth and cultural-ethical advancement. Harmony between humanity and nature is emphasized. China also pursues rejuvenation through peaceful development.
None of these is easy.
Xi believes that overcoming the risks and challenges on the new journey requires the same revolutionary will forged during the Long March. "No matter how great the difficulties, think of the Red Army's Long March, and think of the bloody battle at the Xiangjiang River," he said.
He put forward a series of visionary strategies to ensure the march proceeds in the right direction. These include an extensive reform package -- the most comprehensive in history -- that gives the market a "decisive" role in allocating resources while making sure the government better fulfills its role. He promises broader market access for foreign investors. Since 2013, the number of pilot free trade zones in China has expanded from one to the current total of 23.
He put forward a new development philosophy that places greater emphasis on innovation, coordination, green development, openness and shared benefits. All these echo the important experience drawn from the Long March -- acting on one's own initiative, seeking truth from facts, and proceeding from reality.
More recently, Xi introduced "new quality productive forces" -- his term for growth driven by technological advances and industrial upgrading. Like his predecessors during the Long March, Xi leads from the front, demonstrating his strategic vision and decisiveness.
Upon visiting an automobile factory years ago, he called for a shift from conventional fuel-powered vehicles to new-energy vehicles, identifying the transition as the future of China's auto industry. Over a decade ago, Xi urged China's top scientists to pay attention to a "robot revolution" that could reshape global manufacturing, emphasizing the need for China to strengthen its robotics capabilities and compete for a larger share of the market.
During the Long March, the Red Army fought the enemy with outdated weapons. Today, the challenge is different: keeping pace with the scientific revolution and the explosion of technological innovation. As the pressure of overseas technology restrictions and trade barriers rises, Xi directs the country to strengthen independent innovation and the resilience of industrial and supply chains, and ensure both development and security.
He spearheaded a campaign to build China into a sci-tech powerhouse, elevating the country to the world's forefront in fields such as artificial intelligence, quantum technology and new energy.
From carrier rockets to nuclear submarines, China has named some of its major technological achievements after the Long March, honoring a history of self-reliance and perseverance while inspiring new technological advances.
In 2014, Xi led high-ranking generals to Gutian in Fujian, where a 1929 Red Army meeting established the principle of the Party's absolute leadership over the army, to reinforce that principle. He initiated a sweeping military reform, laying the groundwork for achieving the goals for the centenary of the People's Liberation Army in 2027 and building world-class armed forces.
The new Long March is progressing steadily with significant results. From 2012 to 2025, China's GDP grew from about 54 trillion yuan to more than 140 trillion yuan, while per capita GDP rose from just over 6,000 to nearly 14,000 U.S. dollars. The country has built a complete industrial system covering all industrial categories in the United Nations classification.
China's economy remains the largest engine of global growth, accounting for roughly one-third of the increase in global output in recent years, according to data from the Chinese government and international institutes. China's technology and cultural influence are also increasingly viewed positively around the world.
A global survey released by the Pew Research Center in July found that views of China had improved in many countries in recent years. For the first time, China was viewed more favorably than the United States in a majority of the countries surveyed.
Yet, as the 2035 modernization target draws closer, Xi has warned against complacency. "There are still many 'snowy mountains' and 'grasslands' for us to cross," Xi said.
Meeting those challenges hinges above all on strengthening the Party's leadership. The historical parallel is explicit. The Long March helped form a new central leadership with Mao at its core and opened a period in which the Party increasingly found its own answers to the problems the Chinese revolution faced.
"After the Long March, the Party and the Red Army were stronger, not weaker," Xi said. "This is because they had found the right path and the theory to guide them."
In the new era, the Party established Xi's core position on the Party Central Committee and in the Party as a whole and established the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
Lu Yi, a professor at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee, said navigating the challenges of the new Long March requires sound strategic direction from the Party's leadership, unity within the CPC and across the country, as well as discipline, commitment and dedication among all Party members.
"This is how the steel was tempered," said Yuri Tavrovsky, a Russian expert on China. "The dramatic events of 1934-1936 brought to the fore and strengthened the CPC's finest qualities, enabling it to unite a divided country and build a great one."
ALL FOR THE PEOPLE
In his masterpiece "Red Star Over China," first published in 1937, Snow recorded a Red Army soldier's simple explanation of what he and his comrades were fighting for: "Here everybody fights to help the poor, and to save China."
Lu, the Party school professor, said that the history of the Red Army's epic march is also a history of the deep bonds between the army and the people, and of how the Party relied on the very people it sought to serve.
In Yudu, residents took down doors and dismantled beds to build makeshift bridges that carried the Red Army across the river. Along the Long March, local people supplied them with food, served as guides and sheltered the wounded.
"Back then, we relied on the people at every turn. We relied on them for food, and to fight our battles we had to mobilize them and rely on their support. Without them, we could not have accomplished anything," said Xi's father, Xi Zhongxun, when recalling his early revolutionary years.
That reliance on the people remains central to Xi's approach to governance. He has stressed that the Party must work for the people and draw on their wisdom and initiative, grounding its policies in their needs and experience.
Xi called on officials to draw inspiration from the Long March spirit and better understand the Party's original mission, which is "to seek happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation."
He once recounted the story of "half a quilt." During the Long March, three Red Army soldiers slept at a villager's home, where the family lacked adequate bedding. Before leaving, they cut their only quilt in half and gave one half to the family to help them keep warm.
When Xi took the top office, the Party had been in power for more than six decades, and some of its members had increasingly strayed from the traditions forged during the revolutionary years.
Xi condemned some officials for being so brazen in their misconduct, including cronyism, factionalism, dangling official posts and feigned compliance -- practices that alienated the Party from the people.
Xi warned that unchecked corruption could spell the end of both the Party and the state. He soon introduced a code of conduct known as the eight-point rules to curb official extravagance. He launched the largest anti-corruption drive in the Party's history, which has seen millions of people investigated for disciplinary violations. He also led improvements to the internal Party regulatory framework and established supervision commissions, all to "confine power to an institutional cage."
Earlier this year, Xi initiated a Party-wide study campaign, prodding Party members to fix their mindset regarding governance performance. A key target is to stamp out the tendency among some officials to sacrifice public well-being in seeking to polish their performance records.
"Ultimately, the Long March succeeded because the Party and the Red Army stood together with the people, maintained a close bond with the people, and shared weal and woe with the people. This is also a fundamental guarantee that enables us to overcome all difficulties and dangers," Xi said.
Sustaining that bond means understanding what people hope for and acting on their most urgent concerns.
Xi spearheaded an unprecedented poverty alleviation campaign that lifted nearly 100 million rural residents out of absolute poverty over eight years. Since the start of reform and opening up in 1978, over 70 percent of the world's poverty reduction has been attributed to China.
Xi used Long March metaphors for the tough battle against poverty. "Just as Liupan Mountain was the last high peak the Red Army had to cross during the Long March, lifting all people out of poverty is the final summit we must overcome to build a moderately prosperous society in all respects," he said.
Xi's anti-poverty war was vast in scale but granular in its approach, reaching into individual households to identify what kept them poor. Aid was tailored accordingly -- fostering industries suited to local conditions and relocating villagers out of inhospitable places. Over eight years, more than 3 million cadres were sent to villages to work on the frontline of fighting extreme poverty.
As in the Long March, some never lived to see the victory: more than 1,800 Party members and officials died in the line of duty. Xi has described the willingness to make sacrifices for the country and its people, whatever the hardship, as central to the spirit of the Long March.
The snow-capped mountains and grasslands that the Red Army had to surmount on foot are now linked by highways and railways. China has built the world's largest expressway and high-speed railway networks, which have brought agricultural products out of remote villages to boost income for local residents.
Ecological restoration is another feat. China has become the country with the largest and fastest increase in forest area worldwide. At the foot of the mountains along the Long March routes, ordinary visitors today may encounter giant pandas and other wild animals. Photovoltaic and wind power installations rise from the grasslands. Kerosene lamps that herders once provided to the Red Army are now mostly seen in museums.
The country has also built the world's largest education, social security and health-care systems. Life expectancy reached 79.25 years in 2025. China now ranks among the best in upper-middle-income countries on major health indicators.
The Long March China pursues today requires no less effort than the historic Long March, British scholar Martin Jacques said.
"It's a complicated challenge, but there's so much possibility and so much potential in that. And the rewards will be enormous," he said.
ECHO ACROSS THE WORLD
The international community, according to Xi, increasingly believes that the Long March was one of the key events that shaped world history in the 20th century, regarding it as an epic of ideals, devotion, willpower, and bravery whose inspirational power has transcended time and borders.
In the 1930s, Snow anticipated that someone would one day write the full epic of the Long March. In the decades since, many people have retraced its path, sought out survivors and written their own accounts. Among the best-known was American journalist Harrison Salisbury, who in his 1985 book "The Long March: The Untold Story" described the Long March as "sui generis," with its heroism firing the dreams of a huge nation and setting it moving toward a destiny no man can yet divine.
Kenyan military officer Felix Gitaari Njage, among more than 100 officers from over 80 countries and regions who were studying in China, visited sites along the Long March routes this summer. He said the Long March spirit is a precious asset for the world, offering lessons for military personnel across nations.
"Its underlying spirit offers countries of the Global South strategic wisdom and intellectual strength for achieving unity and self-reliance and overcoming adversity," he said.
The Long March continues to draw interest from scholars in both developed and developing countries. They believe China's success in the new Long March would benefit people beyond its borders as well as its own population.
In 2013, Xi put forward the vision of a "community with a shared future for humanity." The vision, together with the initiatives he later proposed on global development, security, civilization and governance, set out China's proposals and solutions to tackle shared challenges in a world marked by wealth gaps, conflicts, mistrust, unilateralism and bullying.
In September, at the BRICS summit in India, Xi urged the grouping to take the lead in promoting innovation, peace and stability, exchanges between civilizations, and reform of global governance.
Kirill Babaev, director of the Institute of China and Modern Asia at the Russian Academy of Sciences, interpreted China's message as a call for other major countries to join a "new Long March" toward an international order based on equality and mutual respect. Its outcome, in his assessment, would matter to all humanity, not only to China.
Keith Bennett, vice chairman of Britain's 48 Group, has drawn a similar connection between revolutionary memory and international cooperation. Writing in "China Today" in July, he said that the spirit of the Long March now finds expression in projects such as the Belt and Road Initiative, which connects countries through infrastructure, trade and development.
The Long March, he wrote, remains a guiding force in tackling difficult and complex tasks, overcoming development bottlenecks, and pressing ahead with long-term national goals.
For countries that look to China's experience, its efforts to combine development with security, shift toward cleaner energy, and advocate common prosperity may offer insights into addressing challenges such as climate change, public health emergencies, food and energy insecurity, and inequality.
The Long March stands as a powerful testament to the boundless strength of the human spirit once awakened, said Professor Lu. "It offers confidence to developing countries and hope to all humanity, affirming that even in a world rife with uncertainties, there are still forces steadfastly defending justice and striving toward a brighter future," he said.
The horizon stretches far ahead. The first of China's "two centenary goals" has been achieved. The second, tied to the People's Republic's centenary in 2049, still lies ahead.
"Today, we are closer, more confident, and more capable than ever of reaching the goal of rejuvenating the Chinese nation," Xi said.
"We will strive to safeguard world peace and development as we pursue our own development," he added. ■
