News Analysis: Israeli incursions complicate security outlook in S. Syria
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:18:16 CST
00:18:16 KST

by Hummam Sheikh Ali
DAMASCUS, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Israeli forces advanced into the northern countryside of Quneitra province in southern Syria on Tuesday with seven military vehicles and two tanks before taking up positions near the former governorate headquarters, Syrian state TV Al-Ikhbariya reported.
The move was the latest in a series of Israeli military operations in southern Syria since the fall of the former Syrian government in December 2024.
Syrian analysts said that repeated Israeli military incursions into southern Syria could gradually establish a lasting security reality, complicating Damascus' efforts to restore sovereignty and stability.
POST-ASSAD INCURSIONS
Following the fall of Bashar al-Assad's government in December 2024, Israeli forces deployed near Quneitra and established positions within the demilitarized zone, a United Nations-monitored buffer area established under the 1974 disengagement agreement to separate Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan Heights.
Israel subsequently expanded its presence within the zone, taking control of the Syrian side of Mount Hermon, the highest point in Syria, and establishing multiple military outposts on the mountain.
From these positions, Israeli forces have periodically conducted raids deeper into southern Syria to seize weapons and arrest individuals reportedly linked to groups like Hamas.
Damascus views these incursions as violations of Syrian sovereignty and the 1974 disengagement agreement. Israel, by contrast, has treated the agreement as no longer binding following the collapse of the Assad government.
Syria reportedly seeks to use the 1974 disengagement agreement as the basis for a new security arrangement with Israel, while Israel appears to extend beyond the restoration of the pre-existing arrangements.
SECURITY CONCERNS, STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES
Mohammad Nader al-Omari, a political researcher and analyst, said Israel's operations reflected both tactical security considerations and longer-term strategic objectives.
Israel had cited concerns about potential cross-border attacks by armed factions or individuals, he said, adding that Israel is also seeking to establish new facts on the ground by expanding buffer zones, altering the security landscape and strengthening its position in any future negotiations with Damascus.
Such moves could allow Israel to seek security arrangements different from those established under the 1974 disengagement agreement, al-Omari said.
"The strategic objectives cannot be discussed separately from the tactical objectives," he said, arguing that immediate security measures could serve broader political and territorial goals.
Maher Ihsan, a journalist and political analyst, said that Israel had taken advantage of the security vacuum that followed the collapse of the former Syrian government to expand its military presence in the south.
Ihsan said maintaining positions inside Syrian territory could increase the distance between Israeli territory and potential security threats. The disparity in military capabilities also gave Israel greater operational freedom, he added.
CIVILIAN LIFE UNDER PRESSURE
The incursions could gradually reshape everyday life in southern Syria, the analysts said.
Al-Omari said temporary checkpoints, road closures, detentions and movement restrictions could disrupt commerce, prevent residents from reaching their workplaces and undermine livelihoods in communities still recovering from years of conflict.
He warned that prolonged insecurity could also prompt some families to leave their communities in search of safer living conditions and more reliable sources of income.
Ihsan said repeated, short-duration operations could gradually normalize the presence of Israeli forces in local communities. The recurring pattern of military vehicles entering villages, establishing checkpoints, detaining residents and later withdrawing could make such activity increasingly familiar to local communities, he said.
For al-Omari, the civilian impact also carries wider political implications, as continued insecurity could weaken public confidence in the authorities' ability to restore stability and exercise effective control over the country's territory.
DIPLOMATIC IMPASSE, UNCERTAIN FUTURE
The continued incursions have also raised questions about the prospects for security understandings between Syria and Israel.
Al-Omari said the 1974 disengagement agreement remained a viable foundation for negotiations, but argued that Israel had little incentive to return to arrangements that would require it to withdraw from areas entered since December 2024.
He described Damascus' diplomatic options as limited, particularly in the absence of stronger international pressure to halt the incursions.
Ihsan was also skeptical about the immediate prospects for an agreement. Given Israel's operational freedom in southern Syria, he said, it might see little advantage in accepting restrictions under a negotiated arrangement.
The two analysts, however, differed in their assessments of how the situation might develop.
Al-Omari warned that continued territorial advances could eventually provoke localized resistance or draw Syria into a wider regional confrontation, particularly if tensions elsewhere in the Middle East intensify.
Ihsan considered a broader military confrontation less likely, arguing that Israel would probably continue to make incremental advances, establish additional positions, and respond forcefully to any localized challenges. ■

Moscow and Beijing could seal major gas pipeline deal by year-end – Russian deputy PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:18:06 UTC
00:18:06 KST

Moscow and Beijing could seal major gas pipeline deal by year-end – Russian deputy PM
Russia and China could finalize agreements on a major new gas pipeline by the end of the year, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said on Wednesday, in a potential breakthrough that would significantly expand Moscow’s energy exports to Asia.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of talks between Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his Chinese counterpart Li Qiang in St. Petersburg, Novak said the planned Power of Baikal pipeline was among the issues discussed.
“Our companies – Gazprom and China National Petroleum Corporation – are negotiating a second route for gas supplies from Russia to the People’s Republic of China,” he said. “We are waiting for our companies to complete commercial negotiations and hope they will reach the relevant agreements by the end of the year.”
Li arrived in St. Petersburg on Tuesday for the regular meeting of the Russian and Chinese heads of government.
Russia already supplies gas to China through the Power of Siberia, a more than 3,000-kilometer pipeline launched in 2019. It carries gas from the Chayandinskoye field in Yakutia and the Kovyktinskoye field in Irkutsk Region through Russia’s Far East and across the border near Blagoveshchensk, connecting to a Chinese network extending toward Shanghai. Its annual export capacity is 38 billion cubic meters (bcm), with deliveries reaching 38.8 bcm in 2025.
The planned Power of Baikal, previously known as Power of Siberia 2, would open a major new energy corridor. The roughly 2,600-kilometer pipeline is designed to deliver up to 50 bcm annually from Russia’s Arctic gas fields on the Yamal Peninsula to China via Mongolia, including the Soyuz Vostok transit pipeline.
Unlike Power of Siberia, which draws gas from eastern Siberia, the new route would tap western Siberian reserves that previously supplied Europe, giving Moscow a major new outlet for gas following the collapse of much of its European market. Novak said the project was renamed Power of Baikal to distinguish it from the existing pipeline and reflect its planned route along the southern shore of Lake Baikal. The precise route remains subject to final commercial agreements.
Together, the two pipelines would give Russia a combined nominal export capacity of around 88 bcm annually to China – roughly 80% of the 110 bcm combined capacity of Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2, built to supply Russian gas to Europe via the Baltic Sea.
Gazprom and CNPC signed a legally binding memorandum on the project in September 2025, envisaging deliveries of 50 bcm annually over 30 years. A final supply contract, however, was not signed. Pricing is a key sticking point, with media reports suggesting Beijing is seeking rates close to Russia’s domestic prices, while Moscow has pushed for more commercially favorable terms. President Vladimir Putin said last year that pricing would follow a market-based formula similar to that used for European supplies, stressing that there would be “no charity” on either side.
The expansion comes as Russia accelerates its energy pivot toward Asia in light of Western sanctions and EU efforts to phase out Russian supplies. Before the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, Europe was Russia’s largest pipeline gas market, with Gazprom providing around 40-45% of the bloc’s total gas imports. Deliveries subsequently plunged as Brussels pursued alternative suppliers and imposed successive sanctions on Russia.
Meanwhile, China has emerged as Russia’s largest pipeline gas customer, with Power of Siberia reaching its full contracted capacity and further export routes under development.
Unlike oil, which can be redirected by tanker, pipeline gas requires extensive infrastructure, making Power of Baikal a key project in Moscow’s efforts to replace lost European demand. Moscow has repeatedly accused Western governments of undermining European energy security through their sanctions policies.
The shift also follows the September 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines that previously brought Russian gas to Germany beneath the Baltic Sea. Novak said on Wednesday that Moscow remains ready to resume deliveries through the one Nord Stream pipeline string out of the four that remained undamaged.
“We have one of the four strings in working condition. If European consumers and politicians want it, supplies can, of course, be delivered through that line,” he said. The decision rests primarily with European countries, particularly Germany, where the pipeline terminates, Novak added. He said the three damaged strings could also be restored if demand and economic conditions justified repairs, suggesting it would not take long to bring them back to working order.
Russia has repeatedly offered to resume energy supplies to Europe, particularly in light of the disruptions to global markets caused by the Middle East crisis, but says its proposals have received no response from European governments.

EU should revive talks on broader China trade deal, top MEP says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:16:43 UTC
00:16:43 KST

As EU lawmakers prepare to visit Beijing, the European Parliament's trade chief is calling for a broader agreement that could revive elements of a frozen investment pact and address unfair Chinese trade practices across multiple industries.
The European Union should seek a broad trade agreement with China, potentially including investment, rather than continue negotiating over individual sectors, a senior European Parliament lawmaker said on Wednesday.
Bernd Lange, the German Socialist who chairs the Parliament's Trade Committee, made the call ahead of a visit to Beijing next week by 12 MEPs, as Brussels and China seek to ease mounting trade tensions.
The two sides reached a deal on hybrid cars on 9 October, but the EU views it as insufficient to address a trade imbalance that sees the bloc run a deficit of around €1 billion a day with China.
Brussels and Beijing previously negotiated a Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI), but the European Parliament froze its ratification in 2021 after China imposed retaliatory sanctions in response to EU measures over human rights abuses.
“It is necessary to have a more comprehensive agreement,” Lange told reporters. “I'm also in favour to have an agreement quite soon. Negotiation forever make no sense.”
Lange added that the discussion should include investments. Speaking of the CAI, he also said: “Perhaps it's useful to have a look at that, specifically regarding the investment part.”
Beyond cars, a wider threat to industry
Earlier this month, the European Commission announced a deal under which China agreed to halve its hybrid car exports to the EU over the next four years.
Under the agreement, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.
The deal was presented by the Commission as a "first phase" of the negotiation which will continue on a technical level until next political talks scheduled for March 2027.
But French liberal MEP Pascal Canfin, who will join Lange on the trip, warned that the EU needs to look beyond individual industries. He argued that the Commission's negotiations on behalf of the 27 member states should address broader unfair trade practices that threaten European manufacturers across multiple sectors.
“We are open for negotiation, sector per sector, but at the same time, we look at things that it is not a sectorial threat,” Canfin said. “It's the risk of horizontal unfair practices that would have a very detrimental impact on our industries.”
During their visit to China from 27 to 29 October, EU lawmakers will meet representatives of the Chinese Ministry of commerce and members of the National People’s Congress. They are also expected to hold meetings with high-tech business representatives in Hangzhou.
Lange highlighted other issues that should be covered by a future agreement with Beijing, including Chinese export restrictions — Beijing imposes strict licensing requirements on EU businesses seeking to export rare earths, essential to European industry — unfair subsidies in the chemicals and machinery sectors, and a 20% price surcharge on EU bids in public procurement.
The EU is walking a tightrope in its relations with Beijing, pushing for dialogue while simultaneously enforcing trade defence measures to protect its industry.
Last week, EU leaders gave the Commission a political mandate to introduce unilateral quotas to protect the chemicals and machinery sectors, given the urgency of the threats posed by Chinese competition.
However, some member states, such as Spain, favour a softer approach towards Beijing, keen to secure Chinese investment.

Home Office lifts deportation order for man, 62, who has lived in UK for 50 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:15:52 UTC
00:15:52 KST

The Home Office has lifted a deportation order handed to a 62-year-old man who has lived in Britain for 50 years after criticism of the department’s attempts to remove him to Barbados, a country he left as a child.
The Home Office wrote to Tony Hall on Tuesday to inform him that his deportation order had been revoked. His case had been highlighted in the Guardian a day earlier.
Hall had repeatedly tried to get the deportation order lifted, arguing that as the child of parents who emigrated to the Britain as part of the Windrush generation, he had the right to remain in the UK. He has no surviving relatives in Barbados and has not visited the country since arriving in London aged 12 to join his parents and five older sisters in 1976.
The Home Office had previously stated that he was liable for deportation because of a 2001 conviction for conspiracy to rob and having a firearm with intent. Police stopped Hall and his co-defendants before the robbery was committed. Hall spent eight years in prison.
Officials have been attempting to deport him since the end of his sentence in 2009. As a result of his precarious immigration status, he has been prohibited from working, renting somewhere to live, receiving benefits or receiving full access to NHS treatment.
Hall had argued that he should not continue to be punished as a result of a crime committed 25 years ago, and for which he had served prison time. The Home Office put him on a flight to Barbados in January 2010 in an attempt to deport him to the country of his birth, but he was returned to London on the same plane, arriving the next day. Officials in Barbados appear to have been unwilling to issue him with papers to enter because of the length of time he had been in the UK.
His lawyer, Naga Kandiah at MTC Solicitors, welcomed the decision but said: “The historical injustice at the heart of this case remains unresolved. For over 17 years, our client has endured fear, detention, relentless uncertainty, exclusion from work and housing, and ultimately destitution.
“The Home Office may revoke a deportation order, but it cannot give our client back 17 years of his life.”
Hall said the protracted period of limbo had been very difficult, and that he was relieved that he now had “the chance to live in the country I call home without fear”.
The Home Office indicated that the timing of the decision to lift the deportation was coincidental.
Clive Foster, the Windrush commissioner, the independent advocate for victims and families affected by the scandal, also intervened with the Home Office, arguing that a compassionate approach should be taken in Hall’s case.
Fiona Bawdon, the author of Will I Always Be British?, a recent study of people with precarious immigration status, said: “Either the government wants to do right by all of those it harmed or it doesn’t. What ministers fail to realise is that each time they treat someone in the way they treated Tony Hall, other Windrush victims – even those who’ve now had their citizenship confirmed – feel as if they could still be at risk, as if they are not really seen as British and this could be taken away from them again.”

Breadcrumb
'My image is mine': UK rapper IAMDDB slams Israel for stealing identity in AI video
UK rapper and singer IAMDDB has condemned the Israeli government for using an AI-generated likeness of her in a propaganda video promoting pro-Israel messaging, accusing it of stealing her identity without consent and declaring her solidarity with Palestinians amid Israel's genocide in Gaza.
In a statement on Tuesday, IAMDDB, whose real name is Diana Adelaide Rocha De Brito, denounced the unauthorised use of her image to promote a political narrative she firmly rejects, raising concerns about Israel's use of artificial intelligence to impersonate artists and exploit their identities for propaganda.
The video, published on the Israeli government's official X account, featured an AI-generated rapper bearing a striking resemblance to IAMDDB performing lyrics asserting Jewish historical ties to the region.
"Jews from Judea, it's in the damn name, same Hebrew letters, same culture, same prayers remain," the lyrics read.
"Berlin to Baghdad, Moscow to Fez, they said, 'Go back to where you came from,' We did."
The video drew criticism after US activist Rafael Shimunov spotted the resemblance and identified a promotional photograph of IAMDDB wearing a near-identical outfit to the AI-generated figure.
"There is nothing more funny than Israel stealing the identity of a British Angolan-Portuguese singer to create a fake Israeli in an AI video about indigeneity. Her name is IAMDDB," Shimunov wrote on X.
IAMDDB publicly confronted the Israeli government on Sunday, questioning why her likeness had been appropriated for a political message she had never endorsed.
"Hiya, yeah, so - why did you steal my identity for something I 100% did not consent to?" she wrote on X.
In a follow-up statement on Tuesday, the artist said she was seeking advice and exploring steps to protect her image, work and rights.
"I do not support genocide, the killing of innocent people, or the suffering of women, children and families," she wrote.
"My heart is with every innocent person experiencing loss, displacement and violence, especially the Palestinian people who have endured unimaginable suffering."
The video has since been deleted following the singer's criticism.
IAMDDB also addressed her previous performance in Israel, distancing herself from the country's actions and explaining that her understanding of the Palestinian struggle had changed.
She said she had not had "the awareness or understanding of the situation that I have today" when she performed there.
"Had I understood then what I understand now, I would have made a different decision. That performance should not be taken as an endorsement of any government's actions, past or present," she added.
"My image is mine. My voice is mine. My values are mine. FREE PALESTINE," she concluded.
Israel accused of stealing artist's identity for propaganda
The AI-generated video was created by Israeli-born director Eyal Be and circulated with the caption: "'GO BACK WHERE YOU CAME FROM!' We did," according to the Manchester Evening News.
The AI-generated likeness appears to have been modelled on a promotional photograph used in a January 2018 profile of IAMDDB published by a music news outlet.
In the original photograph, the singer wears clothing from Dutch brand BALR. and Calvin Klein, with the logos seemingly altered in the AI video to read "RALA." and "Calvin Kale".
The apparent appropriation of the singer's image has renewed scrutiny of Israel's use of AI-generated propaganda to promote its political narratives while its military campaign has devastated Gaza.
The Israeli government and senior officials have repeatedly faced criticism over their use of artificial intelligence, including content accused of mocking or trivialising Palestinian suffering amid Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
On Tuesday, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir released an AI-generated election campaign video depicting Gaza as a devastated ghost town in 2030.
The video mocked Palestinians who remain in the besieged territory while showcasing the destruction inflicted by Israel's military assault, turning the devastation of Palestinian communities into campaign material ahead of Israel's parliamentary elections next Tuesday.

Water sector to wait until 2027 for full details of Burnham’s overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:14:30 UTC
00:14:30 KST

LONDON — Water firms and campaigners are set to wait until next year to see the full details of Andy Burnham’s plans to overhaul the sector in England.
Britain’s new prime minister has promised greater “public control” of the water industry as a centerpiece of his domestic agenda, partly reversing a wave of privatization that began in the 1980s. Ministers are due to unveil more detail in a “10-year plan for Britain” that is currently expected in December.
However, while this 10-year plan will contain a high-level vision, priorities and principles for the industry’s future, much of the granular detail of how future ownership models will work in practice is only expected later, said two people with knowledge of the discussions.
Advertisement
Some of these key details will be laid out in Chancellor John Healey’s multi-year spending review at some point in 2027, added the two people, who were granted anonymity to discuss evolving policy. One said the spending review — a date for which has not been decided — was where the full details would be “nailed down.”
These include any fiscal implications for the Treasury, which could have to find billions of pounds if ministers decided to transfer privately-owned shares to the public purse.
This appears to mirror an approach Burnham has taken to policymaking for decades, first as a Cabinet minister and then mayor of Greater Manchester before he took over 10 Downing Street in July. He is known for setting out a broad direction which his officials can later use to pin down detailed policy, while also seeking buy-in from private industry.
With a general election due by summer 2029, however, any wait will compress the prime minister’s window to enact far-reaching reform before he goes back to the electorate.
‘£40 being added to every single water bill’
England’s privatized water firms also argue that uncertainty over the sector’s future is damaging investor confidence.
The industry trade association Water UK has said the entire industry risks being downgraded by the credit ratings agency Moody’s, which would add £40 to customers’ annual bills.
Advertisement
Water UK Chief Executive David Henderson urged the government to move ahead with reforms suggested last year by former Bank of England Deputy Governor Jon Cunliffe, before ministers decide the overall path of how the sector is owned.
The Cunliffe report “was given to the government 15 months ago and the credit rating agencies are watching,” Henderson told POLITICO. “If the government doesn’t pretty soon decide what it wants to do with that report, then we risk a downgrade, as Moody’s has indicated. And if there’s a downgrade, that would sadly see £40 being added to every single water bill across England and Wales. That’s the last thing anybody wants.”
He added: “We still have no idea how [a proposed] new regulator will look, what status it will have, what its duties will be, which parts of the Environment Agency will stay in the Environment Agency, and which parts will go into the new regulator. That is causing uncertainty … an important consideration for any investor.”
One government official insisted the 10-year plan would contain some finer details of plans to overhaul the water industry, though they accepted that fiscal implications were always dealt with in fiscal events such as the spending review.
Environment Secretary Angela Eagle is also due to bring a water bill to parliament before Christmas with separate policy, such as closing what Burnham has called “loopholes used to pay excessive bonuses” to water company executives. It will also contain scrutiny powers for regional mayors.
Burnham announced last month that the bill would lift a ban on the government owning more than 3% of shares in any English water firm. But he has also long made clear that he would not fully nationalize the industry, a move the government previously estimated would cost £100 billion for England and Wales together.
First Secretary of State Louise Haigh, one of Burnham’s most powerful allies in government, is leading three task forces including one on public control of water alongside housing, energy and transport.
Officials have been working through a “spectrum of options” for how public control in the water sector will look, a second government official said. They added that ministers are due to begin deciding which option — or combination of options — will be taken forward before the 10-year plan.

Poland’s abortion reforms would leave it among the EU’s most restrictive, even if signed into law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:13:29 UTC
00:13:29 KST

Poland’s parliament, Sejm, has voted to ease some of the country’s abortion restrictions, but the changes would leave its laws among the most restrictive in the European Union — and face an uphill battle to become law.
On Tuesday, 20 October, the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, passed amendments to the Criminal Code that would ease some penalties for people helping women access abortion care and restore access to abortion in cases of severe foetal abnormalities.
The vote marks a tentative step towards fulfilling Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s coalition pledge to restore reproductive rights, made nearly three years ago. But even if the legislation survives a likely presidential veto, it would fall well short of the coalition’s promise.
The changes would not introduce abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, a pledge made by Tusk’s Civic Coalition during the election campaign. Their passage into law is also uncertain: President Karol Nawrocki, who took office in 2025, has previously said that he would not support legislation easing abortion restrictions.
Under current law, anyone who terminates a pregnancy with a woman’s consent can face up to three years in prison. The same penalty applies to people who assist a woman in obtaining an abortion or encourage her to have one.
The proposed bill, backed by 217 parliamentarians, with 213 voting against and three abstaining, would exempt doctors, nurses and midwives from criminal liability when an abortion results from a medically necessary procedure intended to protect a pregnant woman’s health or life.
“It's time to end the punishment of all those who love, worry, and respect our choices,” Katarzyna Kotula, the government’s equality commissioner and a lawmaker from the Left, said on X.
Another bill, passed with 233 votes in favour, 203 against and one abstention, would again permit abortion in cases of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities or an incurable condition threatening the foetus’s life.
It would overturn the effect of a 2020 ruling by Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, which found abortion on the grounds of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities unconstitutional.
‘Incremental step forward’
Seeing these changes become law remains a challenge. Even if it passes the Senate, it will need Nawrocki’s signature. The president is aligned with the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, which oversaw a tightening of abortion restrictions five years ago.
Overriding a presidential veto would require a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, a threshold Tusk’s coalition does not have.
Despite that, such an “incremental step forward” shouldn't be understated “as it's the first time in many years now that there's been movement in the Polish Parliament,” Leah Hoctor, Senior Regional Director for Europe at the Center for Reproductive Rights, told Euronews. A similar attempt was unsuccessful in July 2024, after failing to secure the required majority.
However, even if the amendments become law, Poland would remain one of only two EU countries, alongside Malta, where abortion on request in early pregnancy is not legal.
“The legal changes that these bills represent are so narrow in scope that for most women who need abortion care, that care will remain illegal,” Hoctor said, adding that women would still be forced to travel to access care.
That would leave Poland out of step with much of Europe, where abortion on request in early pregnancy is legal in most countries and several governments have moved to reduce barriers to care and remove criminal penalties.
“Poland is an outlier in the European context,” she said. "Globally, Poland and the US are two of only four countries in the last 30 years to have removed a ground for legal abortion from their laws," she added.
Abortion in Poland is allowed when pregnancy threatens a woman's health or life or results from a criminal act, including rape or incest. Such a near-total abortion ban has been criticised by international human rights bodies.
The European Court of Human Rights has ruled against the country in several cases involving barriers to abortion access, while in 2024, following a three-year inquiry, the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women found that Poland’s abortion laws had resulted in grave and systematic violations of women’s rights and called for comprehensive legal reform.

Who is Stephen Hubbard, the American Putin just freed?

Unknown Publisher

Who is Stephen Hubbard, the American Putin just freed?
Vladimir Putin has released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had been convicted by a Russian court on mercenary charges. Putin announced the move at the start of his meeting with U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, saying Hubbard is already at Pulkovo Airport. He will likely leave Russia with Witkoff, who is expected to fly to Oslo later that evening.
Hubbard was officially released “as a goodwill gesture,” Kremlin press secretary Dmitry Peskov said, responding to a question from journalists about whether the U.S. had given Russia anyone in return. Donald Trump also said the release was unilateral and that Russia had not demanded anything in exchange “out of respect for President Trump.” The U.S. president added that he is now receiving apologetic phone calls from people who had previously demanded that Russia be hit with sanctions.
The Moscow City Court sentenced Hubbard, then 72, in October 2024. According to investigators, the American had lived in Ukraine since 2014 and joined the territorial defense forces in the Kharkiv region in February 2022. Russian forces captured him a month later and charged him with mercenary activity. Prosecutors had sought a seven-year sentence in a penal colony, but the court gave him six years and 10 months. The case was heard over two private hearings. Russian authorities claimed the American had pleaded guilty. Hubbard’s sister said in an interview that he had worked as an English teacher, held pro-Russian views, and did not know how to handle a weapon.
Hubbard was tortured in detention, said Ihor Chychko, a former Ukrainian prisoner of war who had been Hubbard’s cellmate before his sentencing. Chychko said Hubbard, like the Ukrainian servicemen held with him, was beaten, humiliated, and starved. “They constantly beat him, like any of us. They hit him with sticks, batons, and their feet. They set dogs on him, didn’t feed him, and made him crawl through the corridors,” he said. Hubbard himself told him he had also been tortured with electric shocks, according to Chychko.
Hubbard is the second U.S. citizen Russia has released recently. In August, Russia released Robert Gilman, 32, who had been serving a 10-year sentence on charges of attacking law enforcement officers. Gilman had been in custody since January 2022. His release was also officially presented as a goodwill gesture, though journalists called it “suspicious,” saying Moscow was likely trying to secure Trump’s support ahead of a possible resumption of talks with Kyiv.
Sixteen U.S. citizens are serving sentences in Russia, Russia’s Federal Penitentiary Service announced in September. Hubbard was the only one of them officially recognized by the State Department as “wrongfully detained.” The human rights organization Global Reach, which helps families of Americans held abroad, believes there are at least five more such wrongful cases. In August, a group of U.S. senators asked the State Department to grant the five that status. On the eve of Hubbard’s release, sources who spoke to ABC News reported that the Trump administration was negotiating a deal that could result in the release of several Americans from custody at once.

Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
- Published
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.
Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
'Roughly 70%' of internet
Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance, external" without specifying the reason.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. They used state-of-the art AI, made by OpenAI, to find the flaws.
OpenAI said in a blog post, external it was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
According to the firms, they had gone undetected for more than a decade.
"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.
It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.
The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note, external.
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning, external.
'Early attacks emerging'
"PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.
"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was, external "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".
The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

Kyiv’s Donors Expected Peace in 2027, but Russian Escalations Left 2026 Funding Unfulfilled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:11:00 UTC
00:11:00 KST

Each year since Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s donors have bet on peace the following year.
Each year, Moscow has proved them wrong.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
As of late 2026, Ukraine has been trying to work out how to counter jet-powered Russian drones, which have caused more civilian deaths and cost $1.5 billion in tax revenues by year-end, per the prime minister’s estimates. Moscow is also expanding the Alabuga-Volokno factory to raise Geran/Shahed drone production by 78%, according to Politico, even as the IMF reported that its economy grew only 1% this year.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko told Ukrinform that Russia may have enough resources to continue until 2028, and the Bank of Finland Institute for Emerging Economies (BOFIT) wrote a similar assessment: Russia can still sustain a full-scale war thanks to higher oil prices, despite weaker economic activity and a widening fiscal deficit.
“Even with the risks of continuing the war, there are no signs that the economy faces an immediate collapse into crisis,” it wrote in its latest Forecast for Russia for 2026-28.
Kyiv’s mission: two months to find almost $50 billion
The aid plans assume a happier ending in 2027, which isn’t the case in Ukraine.
In autumn 2026, the finance ministry received a bill from the defense ministry for an additional $27 billion to fund costlier warfare, and the treasury needed another $29 billion more for donor-backed social wages.
Putin Delays Trump’s Controversial Diesel Deal Delivery 1 or 2 Days
It had neither: In October, the government delayed $2.3 billion in development payments, and businesses went without value-added tax (VAT) refunds for a while.
Part of the problem also lies with Ukraine’s lawmakers, most of whom don’t see the worst of the war coming or the need to vote for reforms that will unlock the cash. The finance ministry has been sounding the alarm in finance for almost a year, since Ukraine signed the new $8.1 billion IMF program with benchmarks lawmakers must vote on.
The EU’s reform-tied Ukraine Facility also lists steps that parliament and the government have not adopted since 2025. The list deadlocked parliament from early 2026, as the government and lawmakers failed to agree until the treasury emptied. The EU, which had earlier accepted compromises, now refuses 2026 aid unless Ukraine implements the bills.
Now, Kyiv must find financing for 2026 and 2027 in under two months. The president and defense ministry team is negotiating weapons funding – one half of the financing – while the prime minister, finance ministry and central bank work on social spending, pensions and wounded businesses.
                                                                                                                                                                         (Chart by Olena Hrazhdan / Kyiv Post)                             
If lawmakers fail to vote for reforms, Ukraine may have nothing to pay for its survival and could resort to printing money and face protests.
“We will lose communications with international donors. The IMF program will be impossible to maintain with quantitative easing,” Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said at the tax committee meeting in September.
Ukraine printed money in 2022 and landed softly, but doing so again risks Argentinian or Venezuelan-style inflation.
If the IMF blocks a tranche over poor performance, Ukraine automatically loses the ability to attract aid from others, as the IMF’s green light signals that the country can be trusted. Defense needs make this funding a lifeline as Russia shows no desire to end the invasion.
But Ukraine’s delegation has options: reassure donors that the reforms have been voted on, and again negotiate the use of Russian assets.
To complete the mission, Kyiv must clear three quests: convince the IMF in Thailand, agree on funding with the EU, and push the Ukrainian parliament to do its one job.
Ukraine’s parliament and 2026 IMF Annual Meetings funding quests
For 2026, the EU told Ukraine it will receive the committed cash for its budget needs as parliament votes on the bills, a person familiar with the matter told Kyiv Post.
“In recent weeks, the IMF team has been in talks with various partners – primarily from the European Union – regarding the mobilization of additional funds to Ukraine. But Europeans gave a clear signal we need to fulfill the conditions necessary,” the person said.
Almost immediately after taking office, the new prime minister, Serhii Koretskiy, rushed to push through the reform decisions his predecessor, Yulia Svyrydenko, left undone.
Under Koretskiy, the government adopted six decisions that missed deadlines in 2025 and the first half of 2026. Eight Ukraine Facility steps and six of 12 Ukraine Support Loan conditions remain unmet, per the RRR4U monitoring, and President Volodymyr Zelensky still has not signed the digital-platform income tax bill, another IMF benchmark.
Finance Minister Marchenko did not attend the IMF’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand; instead, he kept a close eye on the lawmakers. When the state treasury became nearly empty, it partly worked: On the third attempt, they voted for an IMF benchmark scrapping the VAT exemption for parcels worth up to €150 ($174), and parliament began filling six of 11 Accounting Chamber seats.
                                                                                                                                                                         From left: IMF Alternate Executive Director Vladyslav Rashkovan, Deputy Minister of Finance Olha Zykova, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, National Bank of Ukraine Governor Andriy Pyshnyi and IMF European Department Director Mateusz Szczurek during a meeting on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. (Photo courtesy of Ukraine’s Ministry of Finance press service)                             
The mood was somber as delegations headed to Bangkok for the IMF Annual Meetings, but the last-minute vote reassured them.
“We came to Bangkok on a low, and we leave on a high. The Rada vote changed the mood. It showed once again that, against all odds, Ukraine continues to deliver on its reform agenda,” a well-informed source told Kyiv Post.
Before the meetings, the source was skeptical that the parties would arrive with any “significant headline announcements.”
Ukraine’s finance ministry is also happy.
“For our key partners, Ukraine’s performance is no longer in question. The discussion has now shifted to determining how to ensure and structure the necessary financing for 2027 in a sustainable and predictable manner,” Deputy Minister of Finance Olha Zykova told Kyiv Post.
                                                                                                                                                                         Ukraine’s finance ministry delegation at the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. From left: Deputy Ministers of Finance Yuriy Drahanchuk, Olha Zykova, Government Commissioner for Public Debt Management Yuriy Butsa and Finance Ministry press service staff. (Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Finance)                             
Kyiv Post still does not know whether Ukraine’s defense ministry shares that optimism. It did not answer Kyiv Post’s request on its $27 billion gap, but wrote that it freed up $354.5 million, 1.3% of the gap, by revising arms purchases.
Quest 2: Cash for 2027 and European partners
Immobilized Russian sovereign assets in the EU, amounting to €210 billion ($243.6 billion), remain key to Ukraine’s 2027 plan, despite earlier objections from Belgium.
Signed programs cover $20 billion for 2027, leaving $32.6 billion unfulfilled. Kyiv Post found that the EU has agreed to cover part of this, and Kyiv should find the rest elsewhere.
“Depending on the final size of the EU contribution to cover the budgetary needs in 2027, we calculate the residual amount to be covered by other donors in the range of $10-15 billion,” the second source participating in the discussions told Kyiv Post.
“It’s important to obtain those financing assurances, including from the EU, by the next IMF review scheduled by the end of the year,” the person added.
                                                                                                                                                                         (Chart by Olena Hrazhdan / Kyiv Post)                             
Kyiv Post was told that Kyiv’s allies are doing “a lot of work on [a] technical level” to secure Ukraine’s 2027 funding needs, with further details remaining undisclosed.
One potential option is a second Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) loan backed by Russia’s frozen sovereign assets.
“The European Commission is working on developing various options,” a person familiar with the matter told Kyiv Post.
Partners seem less willing to confiscate the principal of the frozen assets, according to the source. And with the US, which took part in the earlier ERA Loan, also showing less enthusiasm, another option could be a new EU-backed Ukraine Support Loan, the person added.
“They can find the resource if they have the political will and simultaneously Ukrainian authorities deliver their promises,” the person said.
Negotiations should turn to specific financing assurances by early December, Zykova told Kyiv Post.
“The focus is on finding the right combination of support from the EU and our non-EU G7+ partners, while safeguarding Ukraine’s debt sustainability,” she said.
The second IMF review is planned for November, when Ukraine will again report on whether Kyiv did its homework, and partners will face another checkpoint on whether they did theirs amid a looming increase in Russian escalations across Ukraine in the months to come.

Trump says AI data centres should pay ‘dividends’ in pre-midterm shift
US president has continued to support data centres in advance of midterms, despite growing opposition from Republicans.
United States President Donald Trump has said AI data centres should pay “dividends” to communities, in a shift before the midterm elections.
“If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend'” Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Wednesday.
The president’s comments come after he doubled down on his support for data centres, a stance seen as one of several political liabilities for Republicans in the run-up to the midterm election, as Trump’s approval rating has hit record lows.
Polls show dismal support for such centres amid concerns about the sprawling complexes’ water and energy use.
In the post, Trump advised companies that they could make the centres popular if they “pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend’.”
“I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck,” he said. “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!”
Several top Republican candidates have opposed data centres before the midterm polls, with the issue emerging as an area of rare bipartisan consensus in advance of the November 3 vote.
Republican Senate candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas, Mike Rogers in Michigan and John Husted in Ohio, have all called for more restrictions and oversight on the centres, in a reversal of earlier positions.
The issue featured prominently in a recent debate in Iowa, where Republican Senate Candidate Ashley Hinson said the local level should decide whether to build AI data centres.
Despite the shifting sentiment, Trump in late August issued an impassioned defence of data centres, decrying what he called “the anti-Data Center movement” as a gift to China.
“The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote at the time.
“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”
Trump has taken several measures to accelerate data centre development, including issuing an executive order last year that called for measures to fast-track permitting and environmental review. The order promised to use federal land for the “expeditious and orderly development of data centers”.
Trump has also backed a voluntary pledge by AI companies to cover the full cost of the electricity data centres use, but has avoided supporting legally binding federal restrictions.
A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans opposed establishing AI data centres in their areas.
An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll released on Wednesday identified a similar rate of disapproval, with 72 percent of respondents saying that they opposed building new data centres in their communities.

CERT-UA handles approximately 200 cyber incidents targeting Ukrainian citizens in first nine months of 2026 - Special Communications and Information Protection Service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:07:07 EEST
00:07:07 KST

CERT-UA, the national team for responding to cyber incidents, cyberattacks, and cyber threats, which operates under the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, recorded and processed approximately 200 cyber incidents targeting Ukrainian citizens between January and September 2026. For comparison, only 80 such incidents were recorded during the same period in 2025.
"However, this does not necessarily indicate an increase in the number of cyberattacks against citizens or an improvement in their effectiveness. These figures are significantly influenced by the fact that citizens have become more aware and are reaching out to us more frequently," noted Dmytro Pakholchenko, Director of the Cyber Defense Department at the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, in a brief interview with the Interfax-Ukraine news agency.
He pointed out that the primary cyber threats recorded against Ukrainian citizens included phishing campaigns aimed at stealing account credentials specifically for messaging platforms like Telegram and Signal, as well as other online services, along with the distribution of malicious software disguised as legitimate applications, documents, or software updates.
Overall, the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine has identified the primary cyber threats facing the country: cyber espionage, the distribution of malicious software, phishing campaigns, destructive cyberattacks, and the activities of financially motivated cybercriminal groups.
At the same time, key targets for these cyberattacks continue to be government agencies, local self-government bodies, institutions within the security and defense sector, energy industry enterprises, and other critical infrastructure facilities.
It is noted that malicious actors focus on disrupting the operation of information systems, stealing information and credentials, and gaining unauthorized access to information systems.

El Nino ‘wrecking ball’ could cause record Pacific temperature rise, UN says

El Nino ‘wrecking ball’ could cause record Pacific Ocean temperature rise, says UN
- The UN says a very strong El Nino could raise Pacific sea temperatures by 3.8C above normal from November to January, with peak effects in December.
- It may bring floods, droughts and extreme heat across Latin America, Africa, Asia and the Pacific, with risks to farming, water and health services.
- UN officials urged urgent preparation, warning that about 50 million people could face more hunger and major humanitarian harm.
AI generated
GENEVA – The El Nino weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels around the globe like a “wrecking ball” causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on Oct 21.
The new World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) seasonal outlook predicted the El Nino event would become extremely strong, with temperatures in the central Pacific rising about 3.8 deg C above normal between November and January, peaking around December.
“We have not seen in our records 3.8. We have seen around three in some record El Ninos before, with very substantive impacts across the world. So we are beyond that limit,” WMO secretary-general Celeste Saulo said.
El Nino is the warm phase of the naturally occurring El Nino-Southern Oscillation cycle – a climate pattern that influences weather around the world.
It tends to cause higher global temperatures and disrupt rainfall patterns across large regions, meaning drought in some areas and heavy rains in others.
It is a natural climate pattern, and is not caused by climate change. However, global warming can make El Ninos more intense.
El Nino-linked weather extremes could worsen pressure on housing, water, sanitation and health services, with flooding risks rising in southern Africa from November, the WMO said.
In South-east Asia, warmer conditions and a lack of rainfall could impact agriculture and water supplies, while Latin America could see increased rainfall, according to the WMO.
The WMO and the UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, Tom Fletcher, called for urgent action to get ready.
“This El Nino is the behemoth, it is a wrecking ball. It will tear through Latin America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and flood,” Fletcher said, warning of massive humanitarian consequences.
Some 50 million people could face increased hunger, he said. REUTERS

Name: Liz Truss’s Bank Job.
Age: Forthcoming.
Appearance: Etiquette dictates that you should never judge a book by its cover.
Yes, but do it anyway. It looks like a poster for one of those bad gangster films Danny Dyer used to make, featuring a shadowy set of tough guys – except, instead of Dyer front and centre, there’s Liz Truss.
So you’re saying this is a book – by Truss? Yes. The former prime minister’s new book is out next week. Its subtitle is A Short Book on How the Bank of England Broke the Bond Market and Brought Down the Government.
I have so many questions. Who wouldn’t? The response to her first book, Ten Years to Save the West, didn’t seem to guarantee that she’d get to publish a second.
OK, first: how short is short? Amazon states that the book comes in at just 99 pages. For reference, that’s about 13 times shorter than War and Peace, or three times shorter than the 2012 memoir by Tulisa from N-Dubz.
Next: who on earth is publishing this? That would be Free Speech Press, which says it is “dedicated to publishing books that challenge conventional thinking”. Its authors include Jennifer Arcuri, who you might remember as that woman who claimed she had an affair with Boris Johnson, and the guy who went viral for saying you can grow concrete.
Mike Graham? That’s him. Actually, this is an interesting link: Graham also owns UKLive, the YouTube channel that now hosts Truss’s show.
Is that still going? Sadly yes. And by the look of recent videos – which include “Why Britain’s political system is completely broken”, “Britain is becoming a LOW-TRUST society” and “Defund the BBC” – she’s still scratching around the US right’s favourite talking points in the hopes that someone will love her again.
What has been the response to the announcement? Are people excited? Well, when Truss announced Bank Job on X, just six days before its publication date, replies variously retitled it as “Bankrupt” and – inevitably – “Lettuce Job”.
I suppose we should ask what the book is actually about. It’s the same drum that Truss has been banging since her embarrassment as PM: the country is secretly run by the Bank of England, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility, with this unelected cartel ensuring that Britain will never change.
Still, at least it’s nice and short. Exactly – it’s a toilet book, in the sense that it will probably do in a pinch if you run out of Andrex.
One last question. Go ahead.
The book is about breaking the bond market, and bringing down the government, but … But wasn’t it Truss who did that? Yes, it was her.
Do say: “Liz Truss knows who broke the bond market.”
Don’t say: “Presumably because Liz Truss owns a mirror.”

UK approves drilling in controversial Jackdaw gas field, Trump hails ‘great news’
- Britain’s Labour government approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, calling it a “pragmatic” step to boost energy security and support homes and businesses.
- The move split opinion. Trump called it “great news”, while environmental groups said it was “climate vandalism” and would raise carbon emissions.
- Jackdaw is expected to lift gas output by about 6%, add £2.9 billion, create 27 jobs and protect 270 more, but it will not cut bills soon because prices follow world markets.
AI generated
LONDON - Britain’s Labour government announced plans on Oct 21 to start drilling in a controversial gas field in the North Sea, claiming the “pragmatic” move would boost energy security amid price shocks from the Iran war.
US President Donald Trump hailed the decision to approve the Jackdaw site, situated about 240km east of Aberdeen in Scotland, after a court ruling put its future in doubt.
Environmentalists said the approval would worsen carbon emissions, but industry groups and unions welcomed the project, which the government said would start supplying gas to homes and businesses within weeks.
In a post on his Truth social platform, Trump called the decision “great news for the wealth and prosperity of the United Kingdom and the wonderful region of Aberdeen”, where he owns a luxury golf resort.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his centre-left administration had made a “pragmatic” decision.
“At a time when people are really struggling, it’s right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” he said.
“We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come.”
The issue has divided the Labour Party, pitting its climate ambitions against pressure to increase domestic energy supplies and ease surging utility bills to help Britons with the cost of living.
Labour promised when returning to power in 2024 under former leader Keir Starmer not to issue any new oil and gas drilling licences as it sought to steer Britain away from fossil fuels towards cleaner renewable energy.
Supporters argue that neither Jackdaw, with its expected lifespan of 11 years, nor the Rosebank field – which mainly contains oil and lies west of the Shetland Islands and will be ruled on separately – are new fossil fuel sites.
The previous Conservative government approved drilling at Jackdaw, which already has the infrastructure in place, and at Rosebank before both sites became the subject of lengthy legal battles.
But a Scottish court ruled in early 2025 that the approvals failed to consider the carbon emissions the projects would indirectly generate, meaning both must reapply.
‘Vandalism’
The government said Jackdaw was expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6% at its peak and add an estimated £2.9 billion (S$4.9 billion) to the economy. The approval will create 27 new jobs and protect some 270 existing ones.
But energy minister Miatta Fahnbulleh conceded the new drilling will not immediately reduce energy bills, since gas and oil costs are determined by international market prices.
The government announced a new wealth fund designed to reinvest oil and gas revenues into the climate transition, a move seen as an attempt to appease left-wing Labour lawmakers unhappy at the imminent drilling.
The approval of Jackdaw was supported by all main parties except the left-wing Greens, whose leader Zack Polanski called the decision “climate vandalism”.
Friends of the Earth said it was a “huge blow” to Labour’s green credentials, while Greenpeace’s Ami McCarthy said: “True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates.”
Greg Jackson, chief executive officer of Octopus Energy, called it a “good energy policy” because Jackdaw will “replace 20 ships a year of imported gas, with cleaner British gas that pays tax here”.
Meanwhile, Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite labour union, also welcomed the approval, saying it gives Britain “a bit more time to create and fund a concrete plan for commensurate jobs” as the industry transitions to renewables.
Adura, the joint venture between Shell and Norway’s Equinor that is behind both projects, called for Rosebank to now also be approved and Trump said Britain should go “full blast” in extracting North Sea resources.
In interviews on Oct 21, Fahnbulleh said Rosebank – Britain’s largest remaining untapped oil field – was different to Jackdaw.
“One is a gas field that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oil field that is mainly for export,” she told the Guardian. AFP

Russian private carrier to launch direct flights to India
Russia’s Ural Airlines will start direct flights to Delhi next week, as it seeks to benefit from a spurt in business travel and tourism between the two countries.
The flights will operate from Ural Airlines’ base, Koltsovo Airport in Ekaterinburg, to New Delhi three days a week, on Tuesdays, Fridays, and Sundays, the airline told RT India.
The service will start on October 25.
“The decision to launch regular flights was driven by both commercial and strategic reasons,” the airline said, citing strong demand and the availability of a suitable fleet of Airbus aircraft.
Ekaterinburg is the largest transport and industrial hub in the Urals. Direct flights from the city will significantly slash travel time from the Urals and Siberia.
Russian Ambassador to India Denis Alipov recently said the number of airline services to India a week could soon jump nearly fivefold to 71 from the current 15.
“Siberian Airlines (S7) and Ural Airlines are actively working on the possibility of launching regular flights to Delhi from Novosibirsk and Ekaterinburg,” Alipov told RT.
“We are awaiting a response from our Indian partners,” the ambassador said.
S7 Airlines also told RT it is planning to launch a service between Novosibirsk and Delhi during the autumn-winter schedule. Tolmachevo Airport in Novosibirsk is a key hub for S7.
Officials in Tatarstan also previously indicated they are in talks with the East-West Group and Russian authorities about launching direct flights to India, including to its financial hub, Mumbai.
India and Russia are similarly boosting ties in the civil aviation sector. Two Indian domestic airlines have signed agreements on buying 85 Russian passenger aircraft, as Moscow and New Delhi move to expand cooperation in civil aviation and manufacturing.
The new services come amid an expected surge in activity in various sectors including tourism, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and food processing, information technology, engineering, and transport and logistics. India and Russia expect bilateral trade to hit $100 billion by 2030.

Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:02:15 UTC
00:02:15 KST

Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics, AI agents, and modular data centers, with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.
“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”
The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face—doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.
Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.
The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.
Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.
Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.
On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.
He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.
In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.

Oschadbank partners to provide EUR 2 mln in grants for women-owned businesses
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:01:52 EEST
00:01:52 KST

International partners in the Zhinoche Sprava (Women's Business) initiative launched by Oschadbank plan to provide approximately EUR 2 million in grants to support women-owned businesses, alongside preferential lending and training, Oschadbank board member responsible for micro, small and medium-sized businesses Natalia Butkova-Vitvitska said.
"Women's businesses are no longer a niche but a powerful driver of the economy. We see enormous potential and a readiness among women entrepreneurs to develop and scale up their businesses. Approximately 5,000 women will be able to participate in the initiative and receive business support. The comprehensive project includes a grant component worth approximately EUR 2 million," Butkova-Vitvitska said at the presentation of the initiative at OschadBusiness Hub in Kyiv.
The bank aims to help women entrepreneurs move from resilience to confident growth by combining financing with guarantees, grants, training and expert support, she said.
"We are sincerely grateful to our partners for their strong confidence in Oschadbank, as this synergy makes projects of this scale possible. For our part, we will contribute all the capabilities and instruments available to us," Butkova-Vitvitska said.
The initiative's partners include Prosper Global, the European Fund for Southeast Europe (EFSE), the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), German Sparkassenstiftung for International Cooperation (DSIK), and the Moving Forward programme, which provides grants and consulting to microenterprises and is funded by the German government and jointly implemented by GIZ and the National Development Institution (NUR).
Oschadbank is participating in the programme by providing preferential loans available to women-owned businesses, including startups, Butkova-Vitvitska said.
The EBRD is providing grant support of nearly UAH 80 million through cashback equivalent to 30% of a loan. Prosper Global offers cashback of up to 50% of a loan, while DSIK offers cashback of 30-50%. EFSE and Civitta Ukraine plan to provide business development training to 2,000 women, while GIZ and NUR offer grants under various programme categories, she said.
The programmes are scheduled to launch in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027, Butkova-Vitvitska said.
Women account for 43% of Oschadbank's micro, small and medium-sized business customers, according to the bank. In the first eight months of 2026, women accounted for 55% of all new customers in this segment, representing more than 10,000 new women entrepreneurs.

PRESS RELEASE 156
Spanish MFA organises ‘Literary Ibero-America’ exhibition to mark Madrid Summit
Promoted by the AECID, it brings together photographs of literary figures from the twenty-two countries that make up the Ibero-American Community of Nations 
The State Secretary for Ibero-America and the Caribbean and for Spanish around the World, Susana Sumelzo, visited the ‘Literary Ibero-America’ exhibition on Madrid’s Paseo de Recoletos, an initiative of the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID), which reports to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, celebrating the richness, diversity and vitality of literary creation across the twenty-two countries of the Ibero-American community.
The exhibition, which will be open from 21 October until 18 November on the Paseo de Recoletos and at the National Library of Spain, presents a selection of portraits taken by Daniel Mordzinski, regarded as one of the great visual chroniclers of Ibero-American literature, the result of several decades of work alongside writers from across the region.
A journey through the literary heritage of Ibero-America
The exhibition celebrates literature as one of Ibero-America’s most valuable shared cultural heritages. Through images that eschew the formality of official portraits, visitors can discover some of the most influential figures in Ibero-American literature, ranging from world-renowned authors such as Jorge Luis Borges and Gabriel García Márquez to talents who give voice to indigenous culture and reflect the region’s linguistic, cultural and social diversity.
The photographs invite visitors to explore a shared geographical landscape characterised by cultural exchanges, cross-fertilising influences and a long literary tradition that continues to renew itself and enrich the Ibero-American cultural sphere.
Culture to strengthen Ibero-American ties
The exhibition also helps to raise the public profile of the Madrid Ibero-American Summit and to bring the richness of a shared cultural heritage that transcends borders closer to the public.

Bulgaria to direct Ukraine aid towards non-lethal assistance
Government seeks to prioritise support for Bulgarians in Ukraine
Wednesday 21 October 2026 17:12
Wednesday, 21 October 2026, 17:12
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Bulgaria will direct its financial contribution to Ukraine under the European Peace Facility towards non-lethal assistance, the government said on Tuesday.
The government approved a position of “constructive abstention” from funding the purchase of new lethal weapons, while not blocking relevant European Union decisions.
Bulgaria will seek to ensure that its contribution is used as a priority in areas of Ukraine with ethnic Bulgarian communities, with options for doing so being discussed with the European Commission.
The European Peace Facility is funded by mandatory contributions from EU member states. Failure to meet existing commitments could result in interest charges and jeopardise reimbursement for assistance already provided, the government said.
“As a Black Sea country, Bulgaria has a strategic interest in ending hostilities in the immediate vicinity of its borders,” the government said in a statement.
It said focusing exclusively on non-military assistance would signal that Bulgaria supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity but rejects “the logic of endless military confrontation” and seeks to open diplomatic channels for negotiations.
