US congressional candidate Brad Lander freed after West Bank detention
Lander says dozens remain in Israeli custody after being detained while helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives.
United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander says he has been released from Israeli military custody with a warning after being detained alongside dozens of volunteers helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.
But several dozen others, including rabbis and international volunteers, remain in detention, according to Lander, who called for them to be released immediately.
“I’ve been released from IDF custody with a ‘warning,’ apparently because of my public profile,” Lander wrote on X. “I told them I wasn’t even a congressmember yet, just a nominee.”
Lander, a Jewish American and former New York City comptroller, was among approximately 80 volunteers detained by Israeli soldiers and police near the village of Nahalin, outside Bethlehem, according to the Israeli organisation Rabbis for Human Rights.
The group included American, Israeli, Palestinian, British and Canadian volunteers.
Beck Strober, a representative of the Protect the Harvest Coalition, which helped organize the olive harvest, told Al Jazeera that the group had been peacefully picking olives at the invitation of a Palestinian family for several hours when the Israeli army arrived.
“It was a nice, peaceful day,” he said. “There was no conflict. There was no settler violence. There was no violence of any kind.”
According to Strober, after a while, soldiers began checking the volunteers’ IDs, and soon after, issued an order declaring the area a closed military zone. They then detained the group, first in the field and later at a police station.
“To this moment, everyone’s still detained except for Brad Lander,” said Strober. “They very clearly told him that they allowed him to be released because he’s likely to be in Congress very soon.”
Anton Goodman, acting director for Rabbis for Human Rights, told Reuters that volunteers who were neither Israeli nor Palestinian citizens were expected to be transferred to an Israeli military base.
In a video posted on X from one of the buses, Lander said Israeli forces had detained the group after apparently being called to the area by settlement security personnel.
“We’ve been detained by the Israeli military for harvesting olives,” he said. “And let’s be clear, occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives is not a crime under any law.”
It’s not clear why the area was declared a closed military zone. Rabbis for Human Rights said they had no way of knowing about the order and had offered to leave voluntarily when they were told.
Lander said the volunteers had been taken away for processing but had not been told whether they were under arrest.
Lander, a vocal critic of Israel’s war on Gaza, is a former New York City mayoral candidate and an ally of Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He’s now running as the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th congressional district in the November 3 midterm elections.
Writing on X after his release, Lander said Palestinians face worse consequences every day.
“These detentions by the IDF are one more attempt to undermine Palestinians’ right to harvest their olive groves, travel on their roads, and live in their homes,” he wrote. “Yet one more element of escalating, and very clearly state-sponsored, ethnic cleansing.
Neither the Israeli government nor the US Embassy in Jerusalem immediately responded to a request for comment.
The volunteers had travelled to the West Bank to support Palestinian farmers during the annual olive harvest, amid a surge in settler violence, including several attacks in recent days targeting Palestinians and international observers.
Stober said Wednesday was the first time the Palestinian family had been able to access its own land since October 7, 2023 because violence in the area had made it too dangerous to return.
“The fact that Brad was thee, of course, made the situation more newsworthy, but we’ve been seeing this happen in the West Bank for years.”
On Friday, an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was beaten by Israeli settlers while covering the olive harvest. The following day, European diplomats and a French mayor were attacked by settlers during another harvest. Palestinians were also attacked in both incidents.
Israeli police said on Tuesday they had arrested 10 people in connection with the attacks.

Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashes in Kaliningrad Oblast during training exercises, Moscow says
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed during a scheduled training flight in Kaliningrad Oblast, a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea bordering Poland and Lithuania, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21.
Moscow has not elaborated on the reason for the plane crash. The Russian Defense Ministry said the crew ejected and evacuated by a ground search-and-rescue team, without disclosing whether they were injured.
The jet crashed near the town of Chernyakhovsk, about 90 kilometers (about 56 miles) east of Kaliningrad, according to the pro-Kremlin Mash Telegram channel. It said that both pilots were injured and were taken to a military hospital.
The Su-30 is a two-seat, multirole fighter for air-to-air and air-to-ground missions. Moscow said that the jet was not carrying any weapons at the time of the crash.
Russia has had multiple instances of a aircraft crashing during training exercises, including ones that led to the death of crew members aboard. In September, a Russian Tu-95 aircraft crashed in Russia's Amur Oblast during training, killing six crew members and injuring one, the Kremlin-controlled Interfax news agency said on Sept. 29, citing the Russian Defense Ministry.
The crash also occurred amid escalating tensions between Russia and NATO over Kaliningrad, prompting Lithuania's Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas to call for troops to be deployed to the country's border with the Russian exclave.

Feeding Our Tomorrow: how India’s women-led, sustainable farming is reaching Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:11:44 UTC
23:11:44 KST

At SIAL Paris 2026, the India Trade Promotion Organisation put sustainable agriculture, women’s empowerment and a changing relationship with Europe at the heart of India’s food story.
When Jawed Ashraf took to the stage at the opening of SIAL Paris 2026, in the presence of French Minister Anne Genevard and an international audience, he described an agricultural revolution taking place across India. Led by small farmers, he said, it rests on diversity, resilience, sustainability and greater self-sufficiency. These themes defined the India pavilion, which carried a simple title: “Feeding Our Tomorrow”.
As Chairman of the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), Ashraf led India’s presence as Partner Country at the exhibition, held at Paris Nord Villepinte from 17 to 21 October 2026. He knows the French capital well: he was India’s ambassador to France and Monaco from 2020 to 2024 and received the Commander de la Légion d’honneur for his service. More than 140 Indian exporters joined the pavilion, with live culinary masterclasses and a programme on plant protein, women-led agriculture and rice exports.
A farm sector built on sustainability
Ashraf described a shift towards more sustainable, climate-resilient farming, with less chemical use and better traceability. Drones, sensors, artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT) help farmers manage water, fertilisers and crop protection more efficiently, a growing advantage as extreme weather puts pressure on food production.
The stakes are global. Feeding a growing population amid climate pressure, trade disruption and inflation will demand change. India already produces grains, fruit, vegetables, dairy, meat and seafood for roughly one sixth of humanity, and Ashraf sees that capacity, paired with more sustainable methods, as part of the answer.
2026: the year of the woman farmer
The UN has designated 2026 the International Year of the Woman Farmer, and Ashraf used the occasion to highlight the role women play in India’s agricultural transformation. Many farmer/producer organisations are founded and run by women, raising household incomes and giving women greater independence and influence in their communities.
One of those women travelled to Paris. Priyanka Rhushikesh Mohite, from Nashik in Maharashtra, is a certified agricultural drone pilot. Her husband, an agricultural adviser, heard about a Government of India scheme training rural women to operate drones, the Namo Drone Didi Scheme. She applied, won a place and completed a month of training in Pune. She has flown since August 2024.
The practical gains are striking. Her drone sprays nano fertilisers and spreads seeds. Watering an acre once took a full day and around 200 litres of water. With the drone, she says, it takes seven to eight minutes and 10 litres.
Yet technology is only part of her story. “I am a simple housewife,” she says. Becoming a pilot has given her an identity of her own, respect in her community and the chance to encourage other women to follow. Before 2024, she could never have imagined travelling to Paris, and she thanked ITPO for the opportunity.
A trade deal with wider reach
A free trade agreement (FTA) reduces or removes customs duties on many traded goods and sets rules to ease cross-border commerce. The EU-India FTA was concluded in January 2026 and is expected to be signed by the end of the year. It builds on India’s arrangements with the UK and the European Free Trade Association, which have opened further opportunities for Indian food products through zero or reduced tariffs.
Ashraf believes the benefits could reach farmers and small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), provided they meet market requirements and reach European buyers. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has called the agreement the “mother of all deals”. Ashraf sees a partnership between economies representing around two billion people, with democracy and the rule of law as shared foundations.
Its reach extends well beyond food. According to Ashraf, India’s exports to Europe have grown by more than 100% in a decade, led by electronics, machinery, electrical goods and mobile phones. Future cooperation could span artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing equipment for data centres, clean energy, green mobility, biopharmaceuticals and critical minerals, alongside digital technology, defence, education and science. Energy security is a shared concern, and he sees nuclear power as one area for closer work.
He says trade between India and Europe has nearly doubled in a decade and that European investment in India has risen from 80 billion to 140 billion in four years. In France, bilateral goods trade stood at around €13.6 billion in 2025-26, and 38 CAC 40 companies operate in India.
“An FTA is an enabler,” Ashraf says. Exporters and trade agencies must now turn it into business.
From commodities to brands
For food exporters, that means thinking beyond volume and price. Ashraf wants more Indian products to build a recognisable presence in Europe, which requires understanding European standards, strengthening logistics and creating products that stand out on the shelf. At SIAL the emphasis was on packaged, ready-to-eat and premium foods, backed by traceability and geographical indication tags for products tied to particular places, such as Naga chilli and Mithila makhana, the edible seeds of the fox nut plant.
ITPO is also considering offices in several European cities, with Frankfurt, Paris, Milan and Rotterdam among the options.
Taking flight
Priyanka Rhushikesh Mohite’s journey to become a drone pilot is one example of what that change can look like. Her drone is a practical tool for farming. It has also given her a profession, a public voice and a reason to imagine new possibilities for other women in her community.
For India, the challenge now is to turn that kind of progress into something more widespread, while building a stronger presence for its food producers in European markets.

Russia is willing in principle to join new Ukraine peace talks in November, Kremlin says
MOSCOW, Oct 21 - Russian President Vladimir Putin told US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday that Moscow is willing in principle to resume talks next month with Ukraine and the US on ending the conflict in Ukraine, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
No such talks have taken place since February.
Ushakov said the proposed new round of talks should focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."
He said Witkoff had briefed Putin on his talks the previous day in Oslo, where the American met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, the Norwegian prime minister and the Finnish president.
Ushakov said Witkoff had "noted some new approaches, new points in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv, although they did not contain much that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis".
In talks lasting almost three hours, Putin and the US envoy also discussed the implementation of an October 9 deal between Putin and US President Donald Trump on supplies of Russian diesel to US and world markets, Ushakov added.
There was also discussion of the Iran crisis.
"Vladimir Putin emphasised that the potential for diplomacy is far from exhausted and that it is both possible and necessary to reach agreements with Tehran, which is our strategic partner," Ushakov said.
"Russia reaffirmed its readiness to continue facilitating the search for political and diplomatic solutions to the Iranian issue." REUTERS

What to Say When Someone Cuts in Line in Front of You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:05:54 UTC
23:05:54 KST

Wait a second. You’ve been standing in line for 20 minutes, famished and desperate to order one of the viral bagels that keep selling out—or for six hours outside a concert venue, determined to claim a spot at the barricade to see your favorite band.
And then someone strolls up and slips in line ahead of you. Apparently, the rest of you have been standing around for the ambiance.
How much of a sin are line-cutters committing? “You are ripping the fabric of society apart,” says Nick Leighton, an etiquette expert and co-host of the podcast Were You Raised by Wolves? Queue-jumpers have to live with that, he adds. “But worse, we have to live with you.”
Here’s exactly how to handle this maddening situation—including when and how best to speak up.
When to speak up about someone cutting in line
If a stranger jumping ahead of you feels strangely personal, Richard C. Larson, a professor emeritus of data, systems, and society at MIT who has studied queuing, understands why. “We only have a finite number of minutes of life on Earth,” he says. The cutter’s implied message: “A minute of my life is worth more than a minute of yours.”
Before you decide whether to confront the offender, think about what speaking up would accomplish. Are you trying to reclaim your turn or get revenge? Sometimes, the impulse is “to sort of let them know you think they’re a jerk,” says Ryan Martin, a professor of psychology and dean of the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences at the University of Wisconsin–Green Bay, known online as the Anger Professor because he studies strong emotions.
Martin would speak up to help someone recognize “that what they did wasn’t OK and that I wanted them to go to the back of the line,” he says. But he’d also consider: “What is going to allow me to have the kind of night I want to have?” If you spend the concert replaying a confrontation instead of singing your happy heart out, you’ve lost more than your place in line.
Leighton's gut check for situations like these is to ask yourself: Is this the hill you want to die on? “That’s always a good etiquette question,” he says.
Consider your safety, too. If the person seems hostile or you feel uneasy approaching them, you can ask staff for help or let the cut go. “Health and safety always trumps etiquette,” Leighton says.
What to say—if you do decide to say something
Marie Helweg-Larsen, a professor of psychology at Dickinson College who studies social norms, has explored what makes line-cutting so rage-inducing. For a 2008 study, she and a colleague surveyed U2 fans waiting for prime concert-floor spots, asking how they would react to hypothetical line-cutting scenarios.
Interestingly, fans reacted just as negatively to someone cutting behind them as ahead of them—even though their own place wasn’t affected. “You have to have people follow the rules,” she says, “or your investment into the line falls apart.” Helweg-Larsen’s co-author also heard fans invoke a higher authority when someone misbehaved: “Bono wouldn’t like that!”
You don’t need a rock star’s moral authority—or a grand speech—to point out where the line starts. Helweg-Larsen’s suggested opener: “Excuse me, but the line starts down there.” Aim for an “‘I’m just trying to be helpful’ kind of vibe,” she says.
That approach gives the person a chance to correct their mistake without having to defend their character. And you don’t have to believe it was an innocent oversight to deliver the message graciously. “Even if they’re doing it on purpose, you still need to use that tone,” Leighton says.
He’s been on the receiving end of a polite correction himself: At a deli, he once joined what he thought was the back of the line, only to discover he’d guessed wrong. He was happy for someone to point him in the right direction.
If you decide to speak up, do it promptly. “Your window of opportunity is short,” Leighton says. “As soon as it happens, that’s when you need to say something.” Waiting until you’ve spent five minutes glaring at the back of someone’s head won’t make the conversation any easier.
For a line that represents a serious investment of time, Martin suggests spelling that out: “Hey, I’m not sure you noticed, but there’s actually a really long line here, and people have been waiting all day.” You’ve identified the problem and given them an opening to say “Oops.”
Of course, some situations are murkier than a stranger breezing past the entire queue. Someone returning from a bathroom break is different from four friends arriving hours later to join the person who saved their places. Leighton is sympathetic to a water or restroom run. Holding spots all day for a last-minute entourage? “I don’t love that,” he says.
What to do if a line-cutter won’t move
Sometimes, your kind reminder won’t be met with the same level of helpfulness: They saw the line. They’re staying put. Now what?
If you feel comfortable continuing, Martin suggests a firmer follow-up: “I really think you should go back to the back of the line.” You’re making a direct request without adding an insult.
Larson advises skipping any confrontational nicknames or demands—like “What do you think you’re doing, bud?” You’re pointing someone toward the back of the line, not challenging them to a duel.
If the person still refuses to move, resist the urge to keep arguing. “We can’t control everybody,” Martin says. Continuing to push someone who’s already refused could lead to “a more significant confrontation.”
At a concert venue, amusement park, or other staffed location, you can ask an employee or security person to step in. “You can always appeal to a higher authority,” Leighton says. Whether they’ll enforce the rules is another question, but it’s an option worth trying when the cutting is particularly egregious.
If you decide to drop it, drop the parting shot, too. A sarcastic “Must be nice!” might feel irresistible, but Leighton advises against adding more rudeness to the encounter. “It will not achieve anything,” he says.
As Larson puts it, “A fight can ruin your whole day—or life.”

Iran tells US to prove it wants peace by lifting blockade
- Iran says the US must lift its naval blockade and show a “sincere desire” for peace before talks can restart, after a failed June deal on Hormuz, sanctions and oil funds.
- Talks are stuck as the US keeps pressure on Tehran, Trump threatens more strikes, and both sides fear renewed war without a clear US promise to de-escalate.
- Shipping attacks have pushed Brent above US$110 a barrel and raised fuel risks, while Iran warns of retaliation and Israel says it must “complete the elimination of the Iranian regime.”
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran said the US must lift its naval blockade and show it’s serious about ending the war diplomatically, as a deadlock over talks and growing threats from both sides fuel fears of a return to outright conflict.
“Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire on the part of the US to achieve a just and honourable solution to permanently end this conflict,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote in an op-ed in the Financial Times.
In an earlier interview with Iraqi media, Araghchi urged the US to return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding that was signed in June but quickly collapsed.
Under that deal, Iran agreed to re-open the Strait of Hormuz and the US was to lift the naval blockade, release frozen Iranian oil funds and remove sanctions.
“If they adhere to these conditions, they should know that the Strait will be fully opened, and after that, we will hold further rounds of negotiations until a final agreement is reached,” he said.
The US has shown little appetite to return to the June memorandum.
Since its collapse, Washington has ramped up economic pressure on Tehran and retrained its focus on Iran’s nuclear programme, widening the gulf between the two sides.
Brent oil rose above US$110 per barrel on Oct 21 as attacks on shipping in the Strait continued to disrupt traffic through the waterway.
US President Donald Trump has frequently dangled the threat of new strikes on Iran in recent weeks, suggesting he may restart bombing after the Nov 3 midterm elections.
That’s left talks deadlocked and has fuelled fears among Iranian leaders that, without a concrete guarantee from the US to de-escalate, Washington will re-enter negotiations with the intention of resuming military strikes.
Iranian officials have repeatedly spoken about the distrust between the two sides in recent days.
Both the June 2025 war and the current conflict were launched by Israel and the US in the middle of high-level talks between Tehran and Washington.
“Our nation today does not trust the United States and believes that if we negotiate, they will attack us again,” President Masoud Pezeshkian told Pakistan’s Army Chief Asim Munir, one of the main mediators between the two sides, during a visit to Tehran on Oct 20.
In comments made on Oct 21, Pezeshkian said that Iran and the US can “sit together and talk” when the US “recognises the rights of the Iranian people and stops bullying and aggression.”
“Given that the White House has shown no willingness to reach an understanding on the way forward, while also threatening more violence, there is little reason to expect progress now,” Araghchi wrote in his FT op-ed.
‘Finish the job’
Trump’s threats to resume air strikes on the Islamic Republic have prompted Iranian officials in turn to vow retaliation against infrastructure in Arab Gulf countries if they’re attacked.
US and Israeli strikes on Iran have killed thousands of Iranians, while dozens of people have been killed in Iranian drone and missile strikes on oil-rich US allies in the Persian Gulf.
The war created a crisis over fuel supply and prices as shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remains severely hindered by the tense stand-off.
“Unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job,” Trump said last week in his endorsement of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the upcoming Israeli elections.
Speculation about joint US-Israeli attack plans grew on Oct 20 after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel and met with Netanyahu.
“We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime,” the Israeli leader said in a speech at the opening of a university on Oct 20, according to a government statement.
“Because as long as it lives, even if it is battered, bruised, and beaten, it is so fanatical that it will try again to do what it did a year ago, which we stopped them from doing: producing nuclear bombs and rebuilding the axis.” BLOOMBERG

Sikorski signs motion to add Lviv Regional Council dpty Sheremeta to Poland’s list of personae non gratae
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:02:54 EEST
23:02:54 KST

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has signed a motion to include Sviatoslav Sheremeta, a deputy of Lviv Regional Council, on the list of individuals whose presence in Poland is considered undesirable.
Sikorski announced this in a post on the social network X on Wednesday.
"I have signed a motion to include Lviv Regional Council deputy S. Sheremeta on the list of persons undesirable in the Republic of Poland. He is a reenactor of the Waffen-SS 'Galicia' division and the initiator of a proposal to declare 2027 the 'Year of R. Shukhevych'—the commander of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) who issued orders for the expulsion and killing of Poles," the minister wrote.
As previously reported, on October 20, the Lviv Regional Council voted to designate 2027 as the "Year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, and Oleh Olzhych." This decision was approved by the Regional Council’s commission on culture, information policy, and promotion back on July 6 shortly after Karol Nawrocki (President of the Institute of National Remembrance in Poland) announced the decision to strip Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle. That move followed Zelenskyy’s decision to bestow the honorary title "Named After the Heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army" upon the Pivnich (North) Separate Special Operations Center of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. These events led to tensions in Ukrainian-Polish relations, though on October 17, Zelenskyy indicated that the situation had improved.
On October 20, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized Lviv Regional Council’s decision, noting that it aids Ukraine’s enemies, while Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that the move harms relations between the two countries. "Such a decision does not foster mutual trust between our peoples; on the contrary, it deepens divisions. It is essential that the Ukrainian authorities distance themselves from this position," he wrote.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine issued a statement emphasizing the importance of developing friendly bilateral relations with Poland and described Lviv Regional Council’s recent decision as counterproductive to ongoing efforts. "We believe that the recent decision by the Lviv Regional Council, which touches upon sensitive historical issues within our bilateral agenda, is counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations and resolving problematic issues, especially against the backdrop of full-scale Russian aggression and the unprecedented security threats facing both our nations and the region as a whole," the message reads.
Sheremeta also serves as the director of Dolya, a municipal enterprise under Lviv Regional Council tasked with locating the burial sites of participants in the national liberation struggle, as well as victims of wars, deportations, and political repression. The organization conducts search and exhumation operations, including within the territory of Poland.
In comments to the outlet Zakhid.net, Sheremeta stated that if he were to be barred from entering Poland, it would negatively impact the work of the Dolya memorial and search center. He also suggested that the recent statements by Polish politicians and government representatives might be linked to the discovery in the Polish border village of Łasków of the graves of Ukrainian civilians killed in 1944 by units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and the Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie).
"I cannot rule out that this is connected to our discovery of the graves of Ukrainian civilians in Łasków. This is how the Polish side reacts to the truth," Sheremeta added.
Earlier, the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory (UINP) reported that a Ukrainian expedition had uncovered the remains of more than 40 victims at an Orthodox cemetery in the village of Łasków, in Poland’s Lublin Voivodeship.

US citizen Hubbard freed in Russia is heading home — envoy
Unknown

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. US citizen Stephen Hubbard, who has been freed in Russia, is returning home, Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian President’s Special Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), announced.

Eight hearings postponed in a row: who is stalling the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors?
Kyiv • UNN
On October 21, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa was again unable to hold a hearing in the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors due to the continuation of the sick leave of the accused, Vitaliy Rusakov. The hearing scheduled for October 22 will also not take place. Thus, all three hearings scheduled for this week have been postponed.
On October 21, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa once again failed to continue hearing the case concerning medical negligence by doctors at the private Odrex clinic. One of the defendants, Vitalii Rusakov, did not appear in court and filed a motion to postpone the hearing due to the extension of his sick leave. The next hearing is scheduled for October 27, UNN reports.
Details
As a result, the court held none of the three hearings scheduled for the current week. Overall, in October, seven consecutive hearings have already failed to take place because of motions filed by the defense. The eighth hearing, scheduled for October 22, was canceled for the same reason.
According to UNN's sources familiar with the case, the participants in the proceedings expected Vitalii Rusakov to join the court hearing remotely via videoconference. However, this did not happen.
The case concerns criminal proceedings against surgeon Vitalii Rusakov and oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska, who have been charged under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker that caused grave consequences for a patient.
The case concerns the death of Odesa businessman Adnan Kivan, who died on October 27, 2024, while being treated for cancer at the private Odrex clinic. According to the investigation, after surgery, the doctors may have failed to prescribe the necessary antibacterial therapy to the patient and may have responded inadequately to postoperative complications. This could have led to the development of sepsis, which, against the background of the cancer, may have caused the businessman's death. The defendants do not admit their guilt. The court must provide the final assessment of their actions.
Reminder
The trial in the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors has been ongoing for almost a year. During this time, the proceedings have been accompanied by numerous motions from the defense, motions to recuse judges, and systematic postponements of hearings.
Systematic postponements create a risk that the statute of limitations will expire. Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine provides, in particular, for up to two years of imprisonment, while the statute of limitations for such an offense is three years. If the actions attributed to the doctors took place in October 2024, the relevant period may expire as early as autumn 2027 in the absence of statutory grounds for its suspension or interruption.

====================================================================================================

Extraversion is linked to faster relief from depressive symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

As patients receive inpatient treatment for depression, their personality traits often shift in tandem with their recovering mood, pointing to a deeply intertwined relationship between character and mental health. Individuals with higher average levels of neuroticism experience a slower recovery across a wide range of depressive symptoms, while those who lean toward extraversion or agreeableness tend to bounce back faster. These findings were recently published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
Mental health professionals classify human personality into five broad domains, often called the Big Five. Neuroticism involves a tendency to experience negative emotions like sadness and worry. Extraversion reflects how outgoing, enthusiastic, and socially engaged a person is. Openness describes a willingness to try new things and embrace novel ideas.
Agreeableness involves being cooperative, empathetic, and trusting. Finally, conscientiousness is characterized by being organized, reliable, and goal-oriented. Together, these traits shape how individuals perceive the world and interact with others.
Depression is a highly varied condition. Two people diagnosed with major depressive disorder might experience entirely different challenges. One might sleep too much and feel constantly guilty, while another might suffer from insomnia and a total loss of appetite. Standard therapies help many people, but about one third of patients do not see their symptoms improve.
Researchers want to know why some people respond well to therapy while others do not. Personality is a prime suspect in this investigation. Prior studies have established a strong link between personality dimensions and psychiatric conditions. Neuroticism is generally viewed as a risk factor for mental health struggles, whereas extraversion and conscientiousness are often seen as protective traits.
Mara Carlotta Berg and Maike Richter, along with senior authors Mitja Back and Nils Opel, led the new investigation. The team includes researchers from the University of Münster and Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin in Germany. They wanted to understand how personality and depression evolve together over time. They also wanted to look beyond total depression scores to see how specific symptoms respond to treatment in people with different personality profiles.
The research team recruited 334 psychiatric patients receiving care at a German university hospital. The participants had been diagnosed with affective or psychotic disorders, such as major depressive disorder or bipolar disorder. To be included in the analysis, patients needed to stay in the hospital for at least four weeks. This minimum duration allowed the research team to track their progress over a meaningful timeframe.
Patients completed digital questionnaires upon admission and then again roughly every two weeks. The final assessment took place shortly before they were discharged from the hospital. One questionnaire measured the severity of 21 different depressive symptoms experienced over the previous two weeks. This assessment included questions about mood, suicidal thoughts, and physical complaints.
A second questionnaire assessed the Big Five personality traits. The researchers opted for a very brief, 15-item version of a standard personality test. This shortened format reduced the burden on patients who were already dealing with severe mental health challenges. The research team then used statistical models to track how these scores shifted and interacted from admission to discharge.
The overall severity of depression dropped substantially across the study population as patients received inpatient care. Alongside this clinical improvement, the researchers observed coordinated shifts in how patients described their own personalities. Neuroticism scores went down over the course of the hospital stay. At the same time, scores for conscientiousness and extraversion went up.
The statistical models revealed a synchronized relationship between personality and mood. Patients who reported the steepest drops in neuroticism also experienced the largest reductions in their overall depression scores. The reverse was true for agreeableness, conscientiousness, and extraversion. For those three traits, greater increases over the course of treatment were tied to larger mood improvements.
The researchers then broke the depression data down to the level of individual symptoms. They wanted to see if a patient’s average personality profile during their stay influenced the speed of their recovery for specific issues. They found that higher average neuroticism was associated with slower improvement across 14 distinct symptoms.
These lingering issues spanned emotional problems like sadness, irritability, and suicidal thoughts, to physical complaints like insomnia, appetite loss, and somatic worries. The broad impact of neuroticism aligns with its reputation as a general vulnerability factor in mental health. Patients with high neuroticism often experience heightened emotional reactivity and persistent rumination, which might make these symptoms harder to shake.
Other personality traits were linked to faster recovery in specific areas. Patients with higher average extraversion saw quicker relief from seven symptoms, including work difficulty, indecisiveness, and pessimism. Higher average agreeableness mapped onto faster improvements in self-blame, guilt, and body image concerns. Openness was associated with a quicker return of sexual interest and a faster reduction in feelings of guilt.
Conscientiousness was the only trait that did not show these item-by-item associations with recovery speed. While conscientiousness increased overall as patients felt better, it did not seem to dictate the pace at which individual depressive symptoms faded. The researchers suspect that the benefits of conscientiousness might operate through broader behavioral habits that are not captured by specific symptom questions.
The study relies on observational data gathered during naturalistic treatment. Because patients received different types of therapy for varying lengths of time, the results cannot establish that personality directly caused the symptoms to change. The researchers note that the brief personality questionnaire used in the study has limited precision. The short test may have reduced the reliability of the measurements, particularly for the extraversion trait.
It is also difficult to separate true personality changes from a recovering mood. When people are deeply depressed, they often view themselves through a negative lens. The observed changes in personality traits might reflect enduring psychological growth. Alternatively, they might simply represent a return to the patient’s normal baseline as their depression lifts.
Future studies could track patients for months or years after discharge to see if the personality changes stick. Researchers could also use more comprehensive personality tests to confirm the symptom-specific findings. Understanding these patterns could eventually help mental health professionals design more personalized treatments.
Psychiatry is gradually moving toward precision medicine, where care is tailored to the individual rather than the diagnosis alone. If a clinician knows a patient has high neuroticism, they might anticipate a slower recovery and deploy targeted interventions earlier. These targeted interventions could focus specifically on emotion regulation or persistent rumination. Conversely, highly extraverted patients might benefit most from socially engaging group therapies.
The study, “Big Five personality dimensions and their association with depressive symptom severity over the treatment course,” was authored by Mara Carlotta Berg, Maike Richter, Marius Gruber, Janik Goltermann, Luise Victoria Claaß, Julian Herpertz, Ramona Leenings, Lara Gutfleisch, Jonathan Mathias Fasshauer, Michael Storck, Rogério Blitz, Udo Dannlowski, Mitja Back, and Nils Opel.

Military satellites could be refuelled in orbit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:00:44 BST
23:00:44 KST

Life extension of the in-service SKYNET 5 military communications satellites would use in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing technologies, and any requirement for future defence satellites to be capable of refuelling will be considered on a capability-by-capability basis, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Olly Glover, the Liberal Democrat member for Didcot and Wantage, asked whether the Secretary of State will set out whether future defence satellites will be required to be refuelled.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing was one of four prioritised sub-sectors in the UK’s National Space Strategy. As part of our Defence Investment Plan the life extension of the in-service SKYNET 5 military communications satellites, would utilise ISAM technologies. The Ministry of Defence continues to consider the potential benefits of emerging in-orbit servicing technologies, including satellite refuelling, which could enhance the resilience, flexibility and operational life of Defence space capabilities. Any requirement for future Defence satellites to be capable of refuelling would be considered on a capability-by-capability basis, taking account of operational requirements, technological maturity and value for money.”
A geostationary communications satellite spends most of its propellant on station keeping, nudging itself back into position against the pull of the sun and moon, and it dies when the tanks run dry even though the radios still work.
SKYNET 5 was launched between 2007 and 2012 and built by Airbus, carrying British secure military communications across most of the globe, and the fleet has already run well past its original design life. SKYNET 6A is under construction with Airbus for launch later this decade, and this publication reported when the contract was awarded, with the wider SKYNET Enduring Capability programme covering the ground segment and future spacecraft.

Peek into hidden worlds revealed by the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:31 UTC
23:00:31 KST

Peek into hidden worlds revealed by the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
Winners include ink droplets frozen in flight and what a molting tardigrade leaves behind
Nestled within a rebuilt inkjet printer, droplets of ink hang suspended above a page. Seen through a microscope, the droplets reveal how an inkjet printer produces crisp, uniform letters.
Ole Bielfeldt, a design student in Cologne, Germany, has been photographing the microscopic world since about 2021. His interest began as a quarantine hobby, when an old school microscope from his attic gave him a way to explore while stuck at home during the pandemic.
His printer image won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. To capture the winning photo, he built a custom rig that moved the paper instead of the printer’s ink nozzles, keeping the nozzles stationary and in focus.
The mini side of ‘macro’
Ole Bielfeldt created this custom rig to catch impossibly fast ink droplets midflight. The contraption is only a bit larger than his head. Swipe through to see what word the printer was spitting out ink to spell.
Bielfeldt estimates that the droplets traveled at nearly 20 meters per second — too fast for even his best slow-motion camera to resolve. To freeze their motion, Bielfeldt worked in darkness, illuminating the scene with a single brief flash. He instructed the printer to repeatedly spell out “macro,” a nod to his social media handle, macrofying.
Before this project, a printer was “like magic,” Bielfeldt says. Photographing its inner workings helped him understand how it operates.
Bielfeldt no longer takes the magic printers spit out for granted. “It’s so, so advanced technically, but at the same time it’s so, so common,” he says.
His photograph is one of 86 images recognized in this year’s competition, whose winners were announced October 21. Here are some of our other favorites.
Did you capture my jumping side?
This pollen-dusted jumping spider offers a close look at the bristling hairs and some of its eight eyes that are easy to miss with the naked eye.
John-Oliver Dum’s fascination with spiders began as a childhood fear. Dum says he suffered a particularly painful arachnid-inflicted bite when he was young. Several years ago, when he was inspired to study the movements of a curly hair tarantula (Tliltocatl albopilosus), Dum became passionate about capturing their beauty.
Preparations for his photographs can begin years before he submits them to a competition. His wife grows plants selected for their pollen, which Dum uses in his images.
“The biggest challenge was finding a spider like this on the right plants, with the right pollen attached to it, at exactly the right time of year and at exactly the right moment,” he says. “You need to understand not only the spider’s behavior, but also the surrounding insect and plant life and their seasonal rhythms.”
Dum hopes the photograph, which won second place, encourages viewers to look more closely, too. “We first have to see the beauty of this largely unknown world before we can truly understand what we may be destroying,” he says.
Seeing a mouse eye in a new way
It’s not a leaf and it’s not a flower. This cross section of a mouse eye is crisscrossed in fractals of blood vessels and tethered by the optic nerve.
Cell biologists Sinem Karaman and Satu Paavonsalo at the University of Helsinki visualize vascular networks, like blood vessels, to study how they work within tissues. The arrangement, Paavonsalo says, could even point to mechanisms underlying how these systems stop working in obesity and diabetes.
Paavonsalo says the duo set out to capture a mouse eye in 3-D, different from the flattened retinas typically used in her research. After meticulous mounting which required several attempts for an arrangement she was satisfied with, Paavonsalo still didn’t know for certain the image would turn out right.
“I had to hope that the sample was correctly positioned and that the staining was detected throughout the sample,” Paavonsalo says, which made her excitement upon seeing the image even more pronounced. The image won 19th place in the competition.
A tardigrade Easter egg
A water bear emerges from its shed cuticle, and oh! What’s that left behind? This egg will be protected by its mother’s discarded skin.
The tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is one of nature’s toughest creatures, able to survive space by going into a state of suspended animation. This species, emerging from its former skin, is only about two-and-a-half times as wide as a strand of hair. Evolutionary developmental biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas captured the image during his studies of these tiny wonders at the University of Montpellier in France.
In the tardigrade life cycle, “egg laying is closely synchronized with molting,” says Quiroga-Artigas. Tardigrades can lay up to about a dozen eggs at once, and the moment one sheds its old cuticle happens quickly enough that it’s easy to miss.
Snapping this image demanded painstaking mounting and imaging of many specimens. Quiroga-Artigas chose this particular one, which won 12th, because “the egg looks almost like a precious gem being left behind by its mother.”
The stretch of a slime mold
This slime mold (Hemitrichia sp.) was found in the heart of Brooklyn, N.Y., sprouting from a decaying log in Prospect Park. The image features the mold’s gelatinous fruiting bodies, which release spores as part of reproduction. To bring the delicate structures into sharp detail, Eric Epstein stacked 240 images.
First, Epstein searched local parks for slime molds to photograph, carefully cutting pieces of waterlogged wood free without disturbing his subjects. “In this liquidy state, any touch would demolish” the fruiting bodies, he says.
One species of slime mold closely mirrors the cosmic web of gas and dark matter connecting galaxies, which helps scientists to more accurately map the cosmos. Another species has fascinated researchers for its ability to pack a store of bacteria to feed the next generation, when it’s near death.
Epstein hopes the photograph hints “at [a] vast array of activity beyond our unaided perception.” The image won sixth place in the competition.
A brain full of stars
This cell could have become anything in the body. Through some scientific nudging, it burst into a brilliant neuron.
Clusters of nuclei, looking like flashpoints in an intricate web, were captured by undergraduate student Faith Fernandes and structural cell biologist James Glover at the University of California, Berkeley.
The image commemorates the team’s first attempt at crafting neurons from a particular kind of stem cell. “I was so instantly enamored with this piece that I made it my computer wallpaper as soon as it was taken,” Fernandes says.
The eruption of color depicts human induced pluripotent stem cells, which can become any type of cell in the body, that have developed into neurons. The neurotubules, which contribute to the structure of and transportation of intracellular molecules, appear blue. Orange indicates where the DNA is located.
The stem cells are created by reprogramming adult cells to a stage before the cell was locked into a path to become a specific type of cell. They are studied for their many potential applications in regenerative medicine.
Fernandes says she hopes that studying these cells will illuminate ways to address neurodegeneration in diseases such as Parkinson’s disease. Already, researchers have used these cells to regrow eye tissue, address premature aging in mouse studies and grow organs. The shot won an Image of Distinction title in the competition.

AI Guardrails Aren’t Stopping Criminal Hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

As AI adoption spreads among both malicious hackers and defenders, even relatively unsophisticated cybercriminals are incorporating agentic AI into their campaigns and getting around model safeguards, according to new details published on Wednesday about recent successful attacks by four different threat groups.
Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported groups—one that operates in Chinese, one in Spanish and English, one in Indonesian, and one in Russian. The former two exhibited sophisticated AI “harnesses,” the software that supports and guides a model to carry out tasks. The latter two showed less technical prowess, researchers found, but were still able to compromise multiple targets. All had left their AI infrastructure openly accessible on web servers, allowing the researchers to analyze their activity and which models they used—largely versions of Anthropic’s Claude as well as versions of the open-weight Deepseek models. All the actors devised ways to allow their campaigns to run autonomously over relatively long periods of time.
“You can leverage different models for different aspects in the operation. Model routing and selection is very important because it’s expensive and a lot of times would be overkill to use newer models,” says Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work. The researchers observed the attackers using both open- and closed-weight models; in almost all cases, they were using older versions rather than working with frontier models. Meyers notes that doing as much as possible with older models is common in legitimate AI usage, too, as costs mount.
The attackers also used multiple models to take advantage of differences in the guardrails meant to prevent people from using AI to carry out digital attacks.
“The models don't all have equivalent guardrails and protections, even from one company,” Meyers says. He adds about the sophistication of the hacking campaigns overall that “these attacks are not using new exploits or novel vulnerabilities. They’re really just taking advantage of the speed and the volume that you can use AI for in conducting these operations targeting the bulk of security hygiene issues in a lot of these environments—things that were preventable but weren’t prevented.”
The researchers found that all four threat actors circumvented AI safeguards, often by convincing a model that the activity was all legitimate and authorized, often for penetration testing or other security evaluation. One method used by many of the groups involves adding files to an agent’s working directory to try to show that tasks are approved and authorized. The attackers also used traditional jailbreaking methods, crafting prompts and narratives framing their hacking as authorized and benign, and proactively addressing potential questions or concerns the models might raise. The more sophisticated actors were typically more strategic in their world-building, while the less sophisticated actors sometimes resorted to more crude and aggressive prompts that tried to bully the models into accepting that the activity was legitimate.
The Chinese-speaking actor also used what's known as a “run time patch,” in this case a tool known as ClawGod, to add functionality on top of Claude Code and attempt to remove the “CYBER_RISK_INSTRUCTION” from the Claude Code system prompt, an instruction directing Claude Code to only participate in authorized security testing, not abusive or destructive hacking.
The actor that worked in Spanish and English targeted Argentine health care entities and successfully compromised at least 15 organizations. CrowdStrike researchers see evidence that the actor stole credentials and medical records from at least one of these victims. The actor special built a penetration testing harness, the kind an organization would use to test its own infrastructure, to find and fix vulnerabilities. Using models including Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Deepseek V4 Pro, the group set up a full infrastructure for autonomous attacks involving a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent to direct the steps of an attack and an “Executor” agent to carry them out.
The attacker working in Chinese also built penetration testing harnesses to guide Claude Code in reconnaissance and then autonomously attack once a human had selected a course of action. The researchers found that the actor successfully compromised government targets in both Brazil and Colombia and also targeted private organizations in Brazil and the United States in a range of sectors that include biotech, healthcare, food and beverage, retail, technology, and travel.
According to the researchers, the Chinese-speaking actor primarily relied on Claude Opus 4.8, but also used other models including Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Deepseek Chat. The actor accessed Claude through an AI proxy service based in China but set up multiple fallbacks to other AI tools if Claude was not available through the proxy.
Anthropic did not provide comment ahead of publication, and Deepseek did not immediately respond to WIRED's requests for comment.
The researchers say that both the Russian-speaking actor, which seems to have been focused on financially motivated “e-crime,” and the Indonesian-speaking actor (the least sophisticated of the four) used more basic, publicly available skills and harnesses to carry out their attacks. But both were still successful at compromising targets. This included multiple Indonesian government domains, a Bangladeshi government domain, and some private-sector targets, in the case of the Indonesian-speaking actor.
“What we are seeing is humans are doing some of the initial probing in these situations and then they’re engaging the AI for the hacking at scale,” CrowdStrike’s Meyers says. “I find it interesting that even with agentic attacks with all of these capabilities, we could still see that there’s a human behind it and what they’re up to.”

How a bizarre phrase became France's new protest slogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:59:31 UTC
22:59:31 KST

Breadcrumb
'Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres': How a bizarre phrase became France's new protest slogan
Across France, the phrase "Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres" has appeared on placards at demonstrations, posters and social media, becoming an unlikely rallying cry for a nationwide protest movement.
The phrase, which means "in the name of God, it's the darkness", makes little sense on its own, but has become a symbol of the generational divide between young protesters and the French authorities, as well as a way of mocking racial stereotypes held by police.
"Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres", which combines French and Arabic, appears to have originated on Snapchat, where someone attempted to join a private group of students organising protests and school blockades.
The message, sent under names including Mamadou and Abdellah and accompanied by Algerian flag emojis, used an awkward mixture of French slang and Arabic expressions commonly used by young people in France.
Students suspected the messages came from undercover police officers unsuccessfully attempting to infiltrate their protest groups by imitating the language of young French people.
Screenshots of the messages began circulating on social media in early October, and student protesters quickly adopted the phrase as a mocking slogan of resistance.
The slogan ridicules what protesters see as the authorities' racial stereotyping of young people, particularly those of Arab and African descent, and their failure to understand the generation leading the demonstrations.
"No young person talks like that," Sabrine Kharbach, a spokeswoman for a French student union, told The New York Times.
"Young people have reclaimed this phrase to point out that attempts to monitor and infiltrate their movements do not go unnoticed, and to assert their ability to organise in spite of them," she added.
Another student, Phèdre Quémener, said the phrase had become a national joke because it was "such a terrible impersonation of a young person".
"This is seen as an example of racism because it implies that the people who are going to vandalize property are Arab," she added.
Students across France have been protesting since September, demanding better conditions in schools and universities. The demonstrations have since grown into a wider movement involving parents, teachers, trade unions and other groups protesting against rising living costs and inequality.
The protesters are calling for smaller class sizes, more teachers, shorter school days and improvements to deteriorating school facilities.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across France over the weekend in the largest mobilisation since the protests began.
In response to the unrest, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu pledged on Tuesday that curfews would be imposed where necessary.
Protests have largely been peaceful, but some have descended into violence, with fires, looting and attacks on school buildings reported across the country.
According to government figures, at least 24 schools have been set alight or ransacked, while roughly 8,000 people have been arrested.
French police have responded forcefully to demonstrations, using tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters, many of whom are children. This response has further inflamed tensions.
France's police watchdog, the IGPN, is investigating at least 34 allegations of police misconduct since the protests began, including a case involving a 14-year-old boy who was severely injured by a tear-gas grenade fired at close range.
Rights group Amnesty International has condemned the police response and urged authorities to de-escalate tensions without the use of excessive force.
French police had already faced accusations of targeting Black and Arab young people before the recent outbreak of protests.
In June, Human Rights Watch reported that French police disproportionately targeted Black and Arab young people with fines, identity checks and searches.
The far right in France and beyond has sought to blame immigrant and Muslim students for the unrest, despite the protesters coming from a wide range of religious and ethnic backgrounds.
British far-right activist Tommy Robinson shared a video of riot police in Paris, blaming a "green/islamic unholy alliance" for supposedly destroying the French capital in a post on X.
However, the footage Robinson shared was not from the current protests and had been circulating online since 2022.
US President Donald Trump also weighed in on the unrest, claiming on his Truth Social platform that migrants had taken over France.
The slogan has since spread beyond France, appearing at demonstrations in Belgium, Germany and Italy, while Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg repeated it in a video expressing solidarity with the student movement.
"Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres" has become more than a viral joke, mocking far-right stereotypes of Muslims in France and the racial prejudices of the police, while serving as a rallying cry for a generation increasingly frustrated with the authorities.

Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow

Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
Russia is ready to resume three-way negotiations with the US and Ukraine to discuss security arrangements for when the conflict has ended, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
The announcement followed nearly three hours of talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Jared Kushner joined by video link after illness prevented him from traveling.
Ushakov said Putin told Witkoff that Moscow was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations in mid-November, with the main topic being a post-conflict security system for Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff indicated that Trump would welcome the proposal, the aide added.
The presidential aide noted that earlier attempts to restart trilateral talks were derailed by Kiev having carried out massive attacks on Moscow and other cities during Russia’s recent parliamentary elections. Polling stations were targeted on the main voting day, with election commission personnel killed.
However, the situation has since been “re-evaluated, taking into account the signals received from the Americans,” Ushakov said, adding that Putin had praised the mediation efforts of Trump, his administration, and special representatives in seeking mutually acceptable solutions.
The Russian president also presented an “objective picture of the situation along the line of contact, where Russian troops hold complete strategic initiative,” and noted that Moscow’s forces are conducting a “relentless offensive in all key areas” and effectively destroying military-industrial, energy, and logistics facilities in Ukraine.
Beyond Ukraine, the participants discussed the October diesel agreement, under which Washington eased sanctions on Russian fuel exports. Both sides said the deal served their interests and would help stabilize global fuel markets. Other joint economic projects are also approaching implementation, Ushakov added.
Russia, Ukraine and the US last held talks in Geneva in February, following two rounds in Abu Dhabi. Further negotiations, however, were put on hold after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, disrupting access to the UAE.
Ushakov told Russian media that Abu Dhabi was again being examined as a possible venue for renewed talks, noting that Putin has yet to choose the members of a future Russian delegation.
Asked by reporters whether the Ukraine conflict was approaching its end, Ushakov suggested it is “moving in that direction.”

How Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia are deepening defence ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:58:17 UTC
22:58:17 KST

How Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia are deepening defence ties
Experts say conflicts and uncertainty are accelerating efforts to strengthen regional military capacity.
Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia signed a deal on Wednesday to deepen their defence industry cooperation, reflecting a broader effort by countries in the region to widen their network of security partners amid the prolonged US-Israel war with Iran.
The four countries signed the memorandum of understanding in Doha, building on existing military projects through joint production, technology transfers and more closely integrated supply chains.
The initiative comes as the failure of the United States and Iran to reach a concrete peace agreement pushes countries in the region to diversify their defence partnerships and look beyond what experts described as an overreliance on Washington for their security. But they stress that closer cooperation does not mean abandoning long-standing alliances. Instead, the ambition is to gain greater control over their own security while strengthening pre-existing partnerships.
Arda Mevlutoglu, a defence industry analyst and managing director of Mergen Analytical Strategies, told Al Jazeera that the implications could extend well beyond the four participants.
“We may be witnessing the emergence of an interconnected network of defence and security arrangements extending from the Gulf to South and Southeast Asia, rather than a single formal alliance,” he said.
What would the agreement do?
In a statement, the Qatari Defence Ministry said the “Badr” Memorandum of Understanding “aims to foster cooperation in the field of defence manufacturing, enhance defence capabilities among the four countries, and promote collaboration in technical defence training, as well as in research and development areas, thereby contributing to the creation of solutions and industries worthy of the evolution of modern defences”.
Experts say that under the agreement, each country will bring its own resources or set of skills to the table. “Turkiye contributes technological expertise, systems integration and a mature defence industry; Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity, skilled workforces and sizeable domestic markets; and Qatar provides investment potential and demand,” said Mevlutoglu.
Together, the four nations could “establish integrated supply chains, allowing these countries to jointly develop, manufacture and sustain defence systems”, he told Al Jazeera.
Such arrangements could give buyers a larger role in producing and supporting their own equipment, while providing manufacturers with longer-term orders and investment. Albert Vidal, a research associate at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that Pakistan and Indonesia were both willing to purchase Turkish weapons and locate part of their production at home.
This could bring down costs for Turkish companies and bring jobs to Pakistan and Indonesia, while Qatar brings “financial depth”, he said.
Building on existing partnerships
Turkiye, home to one of the world’s most advanced defence sectors, already has military manufacturing ties with Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia separately. Qatar and Turkiye, for instance, signed a bilateral defence industry memorandum in October 2025.
But Vidal says that the new agreement, bringing together all four nations, points to a strategic calculation alongside an industrial one. Closer relationships could give more countries a stake in each other’s security. He pointed to Qatar’s investment in the Turkish defence industry over more than a decade and Ankara’s deployment of forces to Doha during the 2017 diplomatic crisis.
Pakistan’s existing naval manufacturing project with Turkiye, meanwhile, shows how weapons purchases can support domestic manufacturing. Of the four ships announced under the project, two are to be built in Istanbul and two at Karachi Shipyard.
Indonesia and Turkiye, meanwhile, are jointly building a tank.
“The rationale is to streamline these distinct defence export and joint production agreements under a more structured and resilient networked hub, rather than reinvent the wheel with each new defence agreement,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera.
Less dependence on Washington?
The US-Israeli war with Iran and recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have heightened regional security concerns, analysts say, while reported US weapons shortages may be adding urgency to efforts to strengthen pre-existing partners and bolster domestic arms-building capacity.
“Diversification is a major driver, particularly as recent conflicts have exposed vulnerabilities associated with dependence on foreign suppliers, technology restrictions and supply chain disruptions,” Mevlutoglu said.
But he cautioned against interpreting the memorandum as a break with Washington. “Qatar is unlikely to abandon its strategic relationship with Washington, while Turkiye seeks greater technological independence within NATO, not autonomy from it,” he said.
According to Bader Mousa Al-Saif, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme and an assistant professor at Kuwait University, the initiative reflects Gulf countries increasingly looking towards the Global South and fellow Muslim countries.
It also complements a separate effort to formalise military cooperation across the region, analysts say. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, establishing a mutual defence commitment. Ankara submitted the agreement to parliament for ratification on Wednesday, although deploying Turkish troops abroad would require separate parliamentary approval.
The Doha memorandum concerns industrial cooperation rather than a mutual defence pledge, but Mevlutoglu sees a connection between the two initiatives. “While Mecca focuses on collective deterrence and military cooperation, Doha could provide the industrial and technological foundations for such partnerships,” he said.

Israeli forces detained Democratic US congressional nominee Brad Lander, along with dozens of activists and Palestinian farmers, as they took part in the olive harvest in the occupied West Bank, an activist said.

She said the Israeli forces stopped the activists, placed them on buses and transferred them to a nearby illegal settlement. Their final destination and whereabouts remained unclear.
The group also included activists from a Jewish organisation based in New York City, Muslim added.

Attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their land in the occupied West Bank intensify during the olive harvest season.
The attacks include assaulting farmers, preventing them from accessing their land, stealing crops and damaging trees.
The olive harvest season, which began on October 9, has been marred by a surge in settler violence.
In the first week alone, 36 attacks struck 27 Palestinian villages, leaving one Palestinian dead and 99 wounded, while more than 1,430 trees and saplings, mostly olive, were destroyed and 40 vehicles vandalised.
The assault on the harvest is part of a broader pattern: since October 7, 2023, Israeli settlers and soldiers have destroyed 37,237 olive trees and attacked 7,154 Palestinians and their properties, methodically dismantling a way of life rooted in the land for generations.
Official Palestinian figures indicate that around 750,000 illegal Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, across 194 settlements and approximately 400 outposts.

Von der Leyen signals new EU trade measures against China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:55:32 UTC
22:55:32 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced plans for new trade measures aimed at addressing what she describes as unfair competition from China.
Speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday, von der Leyen said Chinese companies receive up to eight times as much state aid as comparable European companies, giving them an unfair competitive advantage.
“Our companies must be able to compete on fair terms globally. Let me take China as an example. In 2025, our trade deficit with China was one billion euros a day. That is not sustainable,” she said.
“Industrial overcapacity and unfair market practices distort competition, and our companies are paying the price,” von der Leyen added.
China was also discussed at last week’s EU summit in Brussels, where leaders from the 27 member states backed the European Commission’s efforts to seek results through dialogue with Beijing.
Those efforts have already produced agreements in some areas. In October, EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič reached an agreement on hybrid cars intended to reduce Chinese exports to the EU. The EU has also secured greater certainty for European companies seeking access to Chinese rare earth elements and magnets, which are important for manufacturing.
“Dialogue has delivered. It is an important first step, but one agreement cannot solve an overall structural imbalance,” von der Leyen said.
EU leaders also expressed support for taking action if negotiations with China fail to produce results, including the use of additional trade tools.
The EU already has defensive trade instruments that can be used if China, for example, suddenly floods the European market with large quantities of cheap goods. These measures include additional tariffs, which make imported Chinese products more expensive.
“The leaders of the EU countries gave a clear, positive signal of support for this last week. We are already working closely with the chemicals and machinery industries, which face growing concerns,” von der Leyen said.
The Commission also plans to introduce measures designed to make the EU less vulnerable to external pressure.
“We must reduce our vulnerabilities. In December, we will present a package that we call ‘Diversify EU’. It will help European companies diversify their supply chains,” von der Leyen said.
The Commission will also propose a new defensive trade instrument that would allow it to restrict access to the EU single market “immediately,” according to von der Leyen.
“Deterrence works when others know that we are ready to act,” she said.
Finally, the Commission plans to propose measures to strengthen solidarity between EU countries when trade pressure threatens a particular industry or member state.
“Economic threats are designed to divide us. Therefore, we will present a solidarity package so that no member state will stand alone against the pressure,” von der Leyen said.

The arrests come after a major political shift in Hungary. In the April election, Orbán and his Fidesz party lost to Péter Magyar and his Tisza party, which won a landslide victory.
Orbán and Fidesz emphasized national conservatism, criticism of the European Union and opposition to liberal values during their time in power.
Magyar also previously belonged to Fidesz but broke with the party in 2024. He subsequently helped bring Tisza to national prominence by campaigning against corruption, calling for democratic reforms and promising to rebuild Hungary’s strained relationship with the EU.
Magyar has repeatedly criticized prosecutors for moving too slowly in pursuing corruption cases.

Denmark guarantees 750 million kroner loan for Ukrainian rocket fuel factory in Vojens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:55:12 UTC
22:55:12 KST

Denmark will guarantee a loan worth 750 million kroner ($110 million) for a Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point to establish a rocket fuel factory in southern Jutland.
The Ministry of Industry, Business and Financial Affairs announced the state-backed guarantee in a press release, saying the support was necessary because the war in Ukraine makes it difficult for Fire Point to secure financing through conventional Danish lending arrangements.
The factory will be built in Vojens, near Skrydstrup Air Base. Production is now expected to begin in late 2027, a year later than originally planned.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh announced the delay in August, citing slower-than-expected construction.
Business Minister Martin Lidegaard said the project would strengthen Ukraine’s defense capabilities while supporting Denmark’s defense industry and European security.
Denmark invited Fire Point to establish production in the country in September 2025, becoming the first NATO member to welcome Ukrainian weapons manufacturing on its territory.
That same month, the Danish Parliament passed legislation allowing the defense minister to waive certain regulations for military projects considered nationally important.
Under the legislation, Fire Point can temporarily bypass more than 20 laws and regulations, including rules covering environmental protection, planning and nature conservation.
The company must eventually comply with the standard regulations governing such facilities.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said manufacturing military equipment outside Ukraine would help protect supply chains from Russian attacks.
He added that access to secure production facilities and critical defense technology was essential to Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
