E-scooter hospitalisations more than tripled since 2019
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

E-scooter and e-bike hospitalisations on the rise in Australia, report finds
In short:
A report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) has found e-scooter hospitalisations have more than tripled since 2019.
There were 4,089 hospitalisations involving e-scooter in the 2024-25 compared to 1,291 in 2019-20.
Two-thirds of those hospitalised in 2024-25 were male with largest increase in young boys aged between 12 and 15.
Teenage boys riding e-scooters drove a sharp rise in hospitalisations over the last five years, according to a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).
The number of boys aged 12 to 15 hospitalised following e-scooter falls saw a 15-fold increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25.
Boys in that cohort were four times more likely than girls to end up in hospital because of an e-scooter fall.
It also found hospitalisation rates increased for e-bike riders, but these data were harder to capture because of how these injuries were classified.
The report found e-scooter-related deaths increased over the last decade from seven in 2014/15 to 20 in 2024/25; however, the proportion of deaths was stable.
New codes introduced in July this year will help better differentiate between e-mobility devices such as e-scooters and e-bikes, the report said.
AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said the improved data will help better understand the risks surrounding e-mobility devices.
"Meaning these findings should not be interpreted as precise counts of injuries involving e-scooters or e-bikes alone," Ms Rek said.
"This report provides the first national view on this topic, while also highlighting where more data is needed."
What can improve safety?
E-bikes and e-scooters are now mainstream, with almost 1 million privately owned by Queenslanders, according to University of Queensland research.
Richard J Buning, who worked on the research, said improving safety was crucial given the growth.
"Every single year over the last five years, the growth in e-mobility device purchases has risen by 30 per cent," he said.
Dr Buning said unsafe devices such as over-powered e-bikes were among his chief concerns.
Last year, the federal government introduced stronger e-bike import standards similar to those in the European Union (EU), limiting access to unsafe devices.
"It's these unsafe, uncompliant, illegal devices that are creating much of the problems of people riding really fast on high-powered devices," Dr Buning said.
"But the safe, compliant devices, they don't provide more power than just a normal typical average fit person can provide."
Dr Buning highlighted Queensland as one jurisdiction in the country leading e-mobility device regulation.
People riding e-bikes in the state must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver's licence, including a learner licence.
Children aged between 12 and 17 (where 16- and 17-year-olds do not hold a driver's licence) will only be able to ride an e-bike or e-scooter with parental supervision.
Dr Buning disagreed with licensing e-bikes but praised the state's e-bike assurance scheme, which followed EU regulations.
It will mean from March 2027, all e-bikes in the state must have a compliance label to ride in public.
"So stopping those things from being sold and making sure that the public knows if they buy one of these devices that are uncompliant, they cannot legally ride it on the road," he said.
Dr Buning also suggested more targeted initiatives to better educate those who are riding unsafely, which was mostly younger people.
"Ideally we can get into schools and teach them how to ride a device safely. That's probably going to take out the majority of the problematic behaviour,"
he said.
"Because the vast majority of people that use e-bikes are actually much older, 70 per cent of e-mobility device users are over the age of 40.
"That highly visible behaviour may be obscuring public perception of an overall quite inclusive and sustainable transport mode."

====================================================================================================

Older adults tell the story of their lives differently, and it may not be a sign of decline, new psychology study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:00:44 UTC
22:00:44 KST

A new study published in Psychology and Aging indicates that having to switch between recalling different types of personal memories makes it harder for both young and older adults to follow instructions accurately. Beyond the mental effort of juggling changing rules, the findings suggest that older adults tend to include more general personal facts and fewer specific details than younger adults, whether they are recalling a one-time event or a recurring routine.
Autobiographical memory is the mental system that allows people to recollect their own life history. It encompasses two main kinds of information: episodic memory and personal semantic memory. Episodic memories are rich recollections of unique events tied to a specific time and place, such as a particular birthday dinner last month. Personal semantic memories are broader facts about one’s life that are not tied to a single episode, such as general self-knowledge. Falling between the two are memories of repeated events, like a weekly habit of cooking with a friend, which summarize many similar occasions while still carrying some sensory and contextual detail.
As people age, the balance between these forms of recall tends to change. A benchmark 2002 study of younger and older adults found that when asked to describe past life events, younger adults mostly shared specific details about what happened, where they were, and how they felt, whereas older adults shared fewer time-and-place details and favored general, factual knowledge.
“A typical example would be that if a young adult is telling you about their last birthday party, they are more likely to include specific contextual and perceptual details (such as the specific time and place, what clothes people wore at that party, or specific details about what they said),” senior author Louis Renoult, a professor of cognitive neuroscience and the postgraduate research director in the School of Psychology at the University of East Anglia, told PsyPost. “In contrast, when remembering the same event, older adults would typically provide more factual background knowledge about similar birthday parties or other celebrations they would have attended, or more general knowledge they have about the people involved, for example.”
This pattern raised questions about whether the shift toward general memories comes from changes in how memories are stored or from age-related declines in executive control, which is the set of mental skills used to manage goals, stay focused, and filter out irrelevant thoughts. A 2013 study explored this by changing how instructions were given while participants listened to musical clips, finding that younger adults adjusted how specific their memories were to match the rules, while older adults did not adjust their recall as much when task demands grew more complex.
To test how mental flexibility affects memory recall, another 2013 study of university students introduced a test requiring participants to rapidly alternate between recalling unique, one-time events and repeated routines. The students were less accurate at providing specific memories when they had to switch back and forth compared to when they followed a single rule at a time.
“In the field, people generally assume that the greater reliance on factual knowledge (and semantic memory) in aging would constitute a compensation, due to a less efficient episodic memory,” explained Renoult, who also recently discussed memory and aging on a podcast episode. “However, tests commonly used to assess semantic and episodic memory are rarely well matched in difficulty, and most tests of autobiographical memory focus on episodic memory only. Due to these issues, my research group has developed new memory tests to study semantic and episodic memory in parallel, in conditions where they are well matched experimentally to better understand memory changes as we get older.”
To examine whether mental switching places an extra burden on older adults during memory recall and how it interacts with the broader shift toward factual details, Renoult and his colleagues carried out the new study. The work was led by Greta Melega while she was completing her doctorate at the University of East Anglia; she is now a postdoctoral researcher at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin (“and also an elite European Ultimate Frisbee player (!),” Renoult noted).
The researchers recruited 45 younger adults and 45 older adults, all of whom were native English speakers without psychiatric or neurological conditions. After excluding participants who did not finish the study, had poor audio recordings, fell below a cognitive screening threshold, or did not pass an initial training check, the final sample included 37 older adults aged 60 to 85 and 37 younger adults aged 18 to 33.
The two age groups had similar levels of education and did not differ in self-reported symptoms of depression or anxiety, which the authors measured because mood can influence how specifically people recall the past. A subset of 30 younger and 30 older participants also completed standard tests of attention and working memory, showing no statistically significant differences between the age groups.
Participants completed an online memory task where they saw 21 neutral, easy-to-visualize cue words on a screen, one at a time. Depending on the prompt, they had up to one minute to think of either a specific memory (a unique event lasting less than a day, such as having “a good time at Jane’s party last month in London”) or a categoric memory (a repeated event that happened multiple times in a similar way, such as “When I go to Jane’s house, we usually cook together and watch a movie afterwards”).
Once a memory came to mind, they pressed a button and spoke aloud for up to two minutes to describe it in as much detail as possible. After each description, participants had five seconds per question to rate how vivid and emotional the memory was, whether they saw it through their own eyes or as an outside observer, and how long ago it took place.
The experiment was divided into two parts: a baseline block and a switching block. In the baseline block, participants followed one instruction at a time, recalling three specific memories in a row and three categoric memories in a row. In the 14-trial switching block, the instructions to recall specific or categoric memories changed unpredictably every two or three trials. This allowed the scientists to compare “switch trials,” where the rule had just changed from the previous prompt, with “remain trials,” where the rule stayed the same as the prompt right before it.
The research team evaluated the recorded narratives in two ways. First, they measured accuracy, defined as the percentage of memories that matched the prompt given on that trial. Second, for the memories that matched the instructions, the researchers broke the transcripts down to count the exact types of details produced: episodic details (specific sights, times, and feelings of a one-time event), repeated event details (context and sensory details of a recurring routine), semantic details (general facts and personal background knowledge), and other statements like repetitions. Because older adults spoke longer on average than younger adults (about 45 seconds versus 27 seconds) and produced more total details per memory (an average of 11.00 details compared to 7.41), the authors analyzed the proportion of each detail type rather than raw counts.
When looking at overall accuracy, both younger and older participants had a harder time following instructions when they had to juggle both rules in the switching block, dropping from 82 percent accuracy in the baseline block to 73 percent in the switching block. Within the switching block itself, accuracy did not differ between switch trials and remain trials, suggesting that the mental cost came from keeping two different rules in mind at once rather than the immediate act of switching from one trial to the next.
Older adults were not disproportionately harmed by the switching block compared to younger adults. Across the experiment, the two age groups were equally accurate when asked to recall specific, one-time events, with older adults succeeding on 81 percent of trials and younger adults on 80 percent. However, older adults were less accurate than younger adults when instructed to recall categoric, repeated events, matching the instructions 68 percent of the time compared to 81 percent for younger adults. When participants failed to provide a proper categoric memory, they most often defaulted to sharing general personal facts instead of an actual recurring event.
When the researchers examined how participants elaborated on their accurate memories, strong age differences appeared regardless of whether participants were in the baseline or switching block. Even when older adults successfully recalled a unique, one-time event, only 66 percent of the details they shared were specific episodic details, compared to 79 percent for younger adults. In turn, general semantic facts made up 18 percent of older adults’ descriptions of unique events, compared to 13 percent for younger adults.
A similar pattern emerged for categoric memories: older adults included a smaller proportion of on-target repeated event details than younger adults (48 percent versus 72 percent) and a much larger proportion of general semantic information across both blocks (40 to 42 percent for older adults, versus 15 to 24 percent for younger adults).
“As observed previously, older adults consistently produced more semantic (factual) details but less episodic (specific) elements than young adults,” Renoult said. “However, crucially, this was not only observed under specific (episodic) instructions, but also under categoric (semantic) instructions. This suggests that remembering the past using more factual knowledge is adaptive and meaningful to older adults, and not necessarily the result of a compensation, or of a general decline in their memory abilities.”
The study itself did not test what purpose, if any, this narrative style serves.
Increased task demands in the switching block also altered the makeup of memory details. Under categoric instructions, moving to the switching block reduced the proportion of target repeated event details from 67 percent to 54 percent across participants. The paper reports a similar shift under specific instructions, but its figures for that comparison duplicate those given elsewhere, so the size of that effect is uncertain.
The subjective ratings highlighted additional differences in how the two age groups experienced their memories. Even though older adults included proportionally fewer specific details in their stories, they rated their specific memories as more vivid than younger adults did (an average of 3.81 versus 3.53 on a 5-point scale) and rated their memories overall as more emotional (2.92 versus 2.46). Regarding the age of the memories, younger adults mostly drew from the past five years, especially the past year, whereas older adults recalled memories from more than 10 years ago on 39 percent of specific trials and 48 percent of categoric trials, compared to just 15 percent and 7 percent for younger adults.
“It is important to realize that, even though young and older adults remember their past differently (with different narrative style), in these studies participants of both age groups are able to follow the overall instructions and retrieve the relevant type of information in most trials (i.e., they produce the correct type of memory, even if with different amount of details),” Renoult noted. “Nonetheless, the results that we report in this study are consistent with previous findings from our group using different methods.”
Renoult also emphasized that differences in how older adults recount their past should not be mistaken for a broad loss of memory function. “Sometimes people have gloomy views of aging, but not all types of memory decline when we get older, as shown in studies such as ours: Semantic memory (general knowledge of the world) is well preserved in older adults (who sometimes outperform young adults in these tasks).”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study’s design and analysis plan were not preregistered. Because the baseline block was always completed before the switching block so participants could learn the rules, fatigue or the possibility that the easiest memories were used up first could have contributed to the drop in performance during the switching phase. The number of trials was also kept relatively small to prevent tiredness during online testing, which meant the authors could not separately test whether switching rules hurt one memory type more than the other.
In addition, the older adults in this sample performed just as well as the younger undergraduate students on standard cognitive tests of working memory and attention. Because executive control often declines with age, this high-performing group of older adults might not reflect the broader aging population, which could explain why they had no trouble finding specific memories when prompted. The participants were also predominantly female, and they were allowed to choose memories from any point in their lives; future studies could restrict recall to specific time periods and use standardized follow-up prompts to see if older adults can retrieve more specific sensory details when encouraged to do so.
Looking ahead, the research team plans to explore how the social context of a conversation shapes the way people recount their lives. “We are interested to investigate social elements that may influence memory retrieval in aging, such as with whom one is sharing their memories,” Renoult said. “One related bias in the literature is that older adults are typically interviewed by a young adult (e.g., a PhD student, or a research assistant). It is possible that, in such cases, older adults include more general knowledge to provide additional background information for someone of a different age group.”
The study, “Age-Related Differences in Autobiographical Memory Recall: Impact of Retrieval Mode Switching,” was authored by Greta Melega, Alice Bush, Tabitha James, Riccardo Sacripante, and Louis Renoult.

Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korea’s leader, said on Wednesday that by the end of October, the DPRK would deploy loudspeakers for anti-South Korean propaganda along the entire border. The move will lead to a further escalation of tensions along the heavily fortified border, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The publication notes that this development threatens one of the achievements of which the South Korean president’s administration was most proud. It concerns the suspension of South Korean broadcasts and the dismantling of fixed loudspeakers, carried out last year.
In a sharply worded statement released by the state news agency KCNA after visiting the border area, Kim said that North Korean tactical units were taking up new positions. “If the enemy’s provocative warning fire goes beyond its stated purpose and causes real harm to the security of our territory or our soldiers, our border troops will mercilessly destroy the armed bandits who have lost their minds,” she said.

This country aims to attract €18B in cleaner energy investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:00:17 UTC
22:00:17 KST

Kazakhstan aims to mobilise €18 billion in investment in cleaner energy through its just energy transition platform, QaJET, with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
The initiative targets renewable power and grid upgrades while addressing the impact on workers and coal-dependent communities.
Fossil fuels still supply around 85% of Kazakhstan’s electricity, according to LowCarbonPower. The country wants to expand renewable power, but that will also require upgrades to its electricity networks and support for workers in regions that depend on coal.
To help finance that shift, Kazakhstan aims to attract $20bn (€17.4bn) through QaJET, its just energy transition platform. Backed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the initiative brings together public and private investment.
The platform is already operational and is due to be officially launched at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, in November.
It supports Kazakhstan’s goal of carbon neutrality by 2060 and its commitment to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by up to 25% by 2030 compared with 1990 levels, subject to international support.
Kazakhstan’s Just Energy Transition platform QaJET
According to the platform’s investment breakdown, around half of the funding, approximately €8.7bn, is intended to support 10 GW of new renewable energy capacity by 2035.
A further quarter, around €4.35bn, is earmarked for integrating renewables into the power system and improving its reliability. The remaining quarter will support electrification in transport, industry and small and medium-sized enterprises, alongside upgrades to electricity networks and smart energy systems.
The platform is expected to reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions by more than 20 million tonnes, equivalent to around 7% of Kazakhstan’s energy-related emissions.
Projects already in the pipeline
QaJET already includes projects worth more than €1bn, including a major wind farm in the Zhambyl region and an electricity infrastructure upgrade in Almaty.
The Mirny wind farm, scheduled to enter operation in 2028, will have a capacity of 1 GW and include 150 turbines, alongside a battery energy storage system with a capacity of 600 MWh.
The project, developed by TotalEnergies and its Kazakh partners, is expected to generate around 4 TWh of renewable electricity annually. Its output will be sold to Kazakhstan’s state-owned Financial Settlement Centre for Renewable Energy under a 25-year agreement.
The project is expected to avoid up to 3.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year.
The second project focuses on modernising electricity distribution infrastructure in Almaty and the surrounding region. The EBRD is providing a loan of up to 102 bn tenge (€194m) to Alatau Zharyk Company, which serves around 50,000 commercial customers in Almaty and the surrounding region.
The funding will help the company install automated metering and remote-control equipment and upgrade its low- and medium-voltage distribution networks.
Investment opportunities
Beyond the projects already in the pipeline, Kazakhstan faces the challenge of modernising its existing energy infrastructure and preparing workers for the transition.
“We are a carbon-dependent country, with large combined heat and power plants and power stations. These facilities and the energy networks need to be modernised. Workers in the energy sector also need to be retrained as part of the energy transition,” said Saule Sabieva, Climate Policy Director at the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
The government is seeking support from international partners, including the European Union, the United Kingdom, the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Climate Investment Funds.
Ensuring a just energy transition
Moving away from coal also presents social and economic challenges, particularly in regions where employment and local economies depend heavily on conventional energy production.
Before major changes are made, QaJET’s partners are expected to assess the regions most exposed to the risks of decarbonisation and identify ways to ensure people have access to new economic opportunities.
“We are expecting these findings. After that, we will be able to assess our major infrastructure projects and calculate their costs for inclusion in the project portfolio,” Sabieva said.
She identified Karaganda, North Kazakhstan and East Kazakhstan regions as likely to face some of the greatest challenges.
More broadly, she said, the difficulties would affect regions where electricity is generated by large combined heat and power plants and major power stations.
Attracting renewable energy investment
The EBRD says Kazakhstan has many of the prerequisites for expanding renewable energy, including strong natural resources and a government seeking to improve the regulatory environment.
“Kazakhstan is blessed with the natural resources needed for renewable energy projects,” said Yerlan Ramazanov, the EBRD’s Deputy Head of Kazakhstan and Regional Head of Energy.
He pointed to regulatory changes, competitive auctions and long-term power purchase agreements as factors helping to attract investors.
These agreements provide greater predictability for developers and help lenders assess the risks associated with renewable energy projects.
Referring to the electricity buyer, Ramazanov said, “Over 11 years of experience, I would say that the agreements are being honoured and the off-taker is paying in full and on time.”
Renewable energy auction tariffs have also fallen since the system was introduced in 2018. Kazakhstan is developing domestic expertise, with local companies increasingly involved in building and operating renewable energy projects.
Remaining barriers
Despite progress, several obstacles remain. Ramazanov highlighted limitations in grid capacity and stability, as well as the challenge of balancing electricity supply as more renewable energy comes online.
The EBRD is already working with officials to develop the regulatory framework for battery storage and pumped-storage projects.
For investors, stable rules and a clear long-term outlook are essential. QaJET’s target of adding 10 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2035 could help provide that direction, setting out the scale of Kazakhstan’s ambitions.
With its renewable energy ambitions, growing project pipeline under QaJET and support from the EBRD, Kazakhstan is working to create new opportunities for investors to build a cleaner, more resilient energy system.

The Jet Training System programme is ongoing and no final procurement decisions have been made, according to an answer given in Parliament.

Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Jet Training System programme is ongoing and no final procurement decisions have been made.”
The Jet Training System will replace the Hawk T2 that trains fast jet pilots at RAF Valley, with the older Hawk T1 already retired and the T2 fleet running towards the end of the decade. A competition is expected, and Boeing, Saab and BAE Systems have offered the T-7A Red Hawk with local assembly in the United Kingdom, with Leonardo’s M-346 among the alternatives.
Ejection seats carry unusual weight in a British competition because Martin-Baker is a British company that has equipped almost every RAF type since the 1940s and holds a worldwide position built on that record. Choosing an airframe fitted with the American ACES 5 would move that work, and swapping a seat into an airframe designed around a different one is a design and certification exercise in its own right.
The T-7A’s escape system drew sustained criticism during American testing, with problems identified around the performance of the seat and canopy for pilots at the light end of the weight range and around the sequencing of the escape itself, and Boeing has worked through a series of modifications. Programme delays in the United States have pushed initial operating capability for the American air force to the end of the decade.
Martin-Baker’s Mk16 variants are fitted to Typhoon, the F-35 and the Hawk, which means an RAF trainer on a different seat would put student pilots through a different escape system from the one they meet on the front line.

Former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau on Wednesday accused US President Donald Trump’s administration of preventing her from traveling to Puerto Rico because of her activism against Israel’s war in Gaza, Anadolu reports.
“Milei can enter Spain to talk about cuts, but those of us who denounce genocide and defend human rights cannot enter the US, or other territories it has appropriated through colonialism,” Colau wrote on Instagram, referring to Argentine President Javier Milei’s visit to Spain.
Colau, a candidate for the left-wing Frente Amplio alliance in Spain’s forthcoming general election, criticized Trump’s immigration policies and accused him of disregarding Puerto Rico’s sovereignty.
“What a curious kind of freedom Trump defends,” she wrote, accusing the US president of deciding the fate of Puerto Rico’s residents and barring people who participated in a humanitarian aid flotilla to Gaza from traveling.
Colau vowed to continue opposing right-wing leaders, including Trump, Milei, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Spain’s Vox leader Santiago Abascal.
“Sooner rather than later, we will put an end to this reactionary wave,” she wrote, adding that she hoped to return to Puerto Rico.
Colau had planned to attend an event on local government in Puerto Rico but was denied travel authorization by US authorities, Spanish news outlet El Diario reported on Wednesday.
She told the newspaper that she believed the decision was politically motivated and linked to her participation in the Global Sumud Flotilla, which attempted to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza in October 2025.
“I went to Puerto Rico two years ago and had no problems,” she said.
READ: Spain’s National Court opens probe into Israeli military officials over Gaza flotilla interception
Colau described it as “extremely serious” that the Trump administration was “fortifying borders in an arbitrary, authoritarian and undemocratic manner.”
According to the newspaper, US authorities initially rejected her application under the Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA), which allows eligible foreign nationals to travel to the US without obtaining a visa.
Other members of her delegation received authorization without difficulty.
Colau subsequently sought an appointment at the US Embassy in Spain to request a review of the decision.
She said embassy officials questioned her about whether she had been arrested or had a criminal record, as well as whether she had traveled to Israel.
Colau told the officials that she had traveled to Israel as part of a peaceful humanitarian mission and had been detained by Israeli forces before being returned to Spain.
The embassy ultimately rejected her request, citing concerns that she intended to immigrate to the US, she told El Diario.
Colau disputed that explanation, maintaining that the decision was connected to her participation in the Gaza aid flotilla.
More than 400 activists, including Colau, were detained and held for four days. She subsequently accused Israeli forces of mistreating participants during their detention, alleging that they were subjected to insults, physical aggression, sleep deprivation and restrictions on access to water and medication.

Estonia to revoke draft dodgers' driver's licenses without court order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Estonia to revoke draft dodgers' driver's licenses without court order
Young people who repeatedly fail to attend a medical examination after being summoned by the Defense Resources Agency could face financial penalties and ultimately lose their driver's licenses.
Undergoing a medical assessment at the Defense Resources Agency (KRA) is a prerequisite for entering compulsory military service and no one can be called up without completing it. Attendance at the assessment is therefore mandatory for anyone who receives a summons.
Under the current rules, if someone repeatedly fails to appear after receiving a summons, the KRA can issue an order or impose a coercive fine. If these measures prove ineffective, the agency can apply to an administrative court to have the conscript's driving privileges suspended.
Starting next year, the procedure will change and the KRA will no longer need to seek permission from an administrative court to suspend a person's driving privileges. Instead, the agency will be able to make the decision itself if the conscript has repeatedly ignored summonses for a medical examination, has been warned of the consequences and has received the warning.
Krismar Rosin, a communications adviser at the Defense Resources Agency, told ERR that the change is primarily procedural and formal, eliminating the judicial review currently required before a suspension can be imposed.
"The aim is to save the courts time," Rosin added.
Anneli Vilu, spokesperson for Tallinn's administrative and circuit courts, noted that applications from the KRA to suspend driving privileges are treated as urgent by the courts and must be resolved immediately.
"However, courts can ask conscripts about their position regarding the KRA application and generally do," Vilu said.
According to Vilu, some people mistakenly believe that paying a coercive fine releases them from their obligation to appear before the medical commission, but this is not the case.
"If a conscript fails to appear before the medical commission, a coercive fine is imposed to compel the person to fulfill their obligation, not as a substitute for appearing before the commission," Vilu emphasized.
Rosin noted that even under the current system, when courts grant the agency permission to suspend driving privileges, they do not make a substantive decision but merely verify that the legal requirements for granting permission have been met.
"So, broadly speaking, the only change is that this preliminary review will be eliminated," Rosin added, referring to the changes taking effect next year.

Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:57:54 UTC
21:57:54 KST

Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
Poland does not have enough Patriot air defense missiles to hand over to Ukraine, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has said, urging other NATO members to supply Kiev with the scarce interceptors.
In an interview with the Polish Press Agency published on Monday, Sikorski warned of growing pressure on Western air defenses, citing the US-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran.
“Following the attacks on Iran, the shortage of interceptor missiles has indeed increased, and Russia is producing more missiles than we have interceptors to neutralize them. This is a real problem,” he said.
“There are NATO countries that still have such resources to contribute, but Poland is not one of them,” Sikorski said, adding that Warsaw “can only join the calls for countries possessing Patriot missiles to share them with Ukraine.”
The issue sparked a political scandal in Poland in July, when the government came under fire over the transfer of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine as part of a wider NATO-backed aid package. Opposition politicians accused Warsaw of sacrificing its own security to arm Kiev, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk insisted the deliveries would not compromise the country’s defenses.
Poland has emerged as one of the EU’s most rapidly militarizing nations, with defense spending reaching 4.7% of GDP. Warsaw has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers, pouring billions into military and other aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western arms shipments.
Yet Poland now faces delays in replenishing its own arsenal, with deliveries of US-made PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors pushed back as the war with Iran drains American weapons stocks, Polish General Ireneusz Nowak warned earlier this month.
Relations with Kiev have also soured over Ukraine’s honoring of Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) militants associated with the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) killed an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles. Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev continues to honor figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera.
Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky awarded a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.” Polish President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
The ammunition crunch is spreading across NATO. In July, the Netherlands said it had exhausted its capacity to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles from its own stocks, having already provided interceptors and helped assemble a complete Patriot system for Kiev.
Meanwhile, Kiev is facing a critical shortage of air defense ammunition as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian military and energy infrastructure. Moscow has said the attacks are in retaliation for Kiev’s continued strikes on Russian territory, including civilian targets and energy facilities.
Vladimir Zelensky has requested 300 Patriot interceptors from European backers and complained that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through a NATO-backed initiative. The White House has also delayed approving additional transfers as US President Donald Trump presses Ukraine to reach a negotiated settlement with Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly maintained that Western weapons deliveries prolong the conflict, obstruct peace efforts, and risk drawing NATO countries into a direct confrontation with Russia.

Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhürman has rejected a Greek Cypriot proposal linking U.N. administration of Maraş to direct EU trade through Mağusa port under the bloc’s control, saying the arrangement offers no balanced exchange.
Maraş, known internationally as Varosha, was closed off in 1974. Parts of the area reopened to visitors in 2020.
“This is not something I can accept,” Erhürman said during an Oct. 20 interview on Genç TV, outlining the proposal put forward by Greek Cypriot administration leader Nikos Christodoulides.
Erhürman stressed that Mağusa port, also known as Famagusta, was already operating.
The issue facing Turkish Cypriots was access to direct trade with the EU, rather than whether the port was open.
He said he had asked Christodoulides whether the proposal would bring the EU’s direct trade regulation into force and received a negative response.
Instead, trade would be permitted through the port because it would operate under EU control.
Erhürman questioned why direct trade should be tied to placing Maraş under U.N. administration, arguing that the terms were not balanced.
He also said the proposal repeated a formula presented to then-Turkish Cypriot President Mehmet Ali Talat in 2006 and rejected at the time.
“Twenty years have passed. It has been brought back as a new formula after 20 years,” he said.
Erhürman reiterated that Christodoulides had not provided him with a written 19-point proposal.
On broader Cyprus talks, Erhürman said negotiations must be aimed at reaching a settlement, explaining his decision not to attend a proposed three-way meeting in New York.
“I will not negotiate for the sake of negotiating,” he said.

CERT-UA handles 22.4% more cyber incidents in Jan-Sept 2026 year-on-year - State Special Communications Service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:57:12 EEST
21:57:12 KST

Ukraine's national Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-UA, operating under the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection, recorded and handled 4,800 cyber incidents in January-September 2026, up 22.4% from 3,900 in the same period last year.
"Government bodies, local authorities, security and defense sector institutions, critical infrastructure enterprises and commercial sector representatives were among the main targets of cyberattacks," Dmytro Pakholchenko, director of the Cyber Protection Department at the administration of the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, told Interfax-Ukraine in a blitz interview.
Incidents involving malicious code accounted for the largest share of cases, at 44.9%, followed by information gathering, including phishing, at 24.2%, he said.
"Incidents involving interference with or attempts to interfere with information systems, the distribution of malicious content and fraud were also recorded," Pakholchenko said.
The State Special Communications Service said attackers focused mainly on stealing credentials and information, gaining unauthorized access to information systems and maintaining a presence in compromised environments.
Compared with last year, attackers have been updating their malware tools and increasingly using legitimate software and web services to carry out cyberattacks, Pakholchenko said.
Another trend identified by the agency is the increasingly frequent use of techniques that induce users to execute malicious commands themselves, under the pretext of fixing technical problems or completing a verification procedure.
Emails containing malicious attachments and links also remain a concern, he said.
Earlier in October, the Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026 said Ukraine ranked third worldwide and first in Europe in the first half of 2026 among countries whose organizations and users were most frequently targeted by cyberattacks. In 2025, Ukraine ranked fifth globally and third in Europe.
According to the report, Ukraine accounted for 4.8% of victims worldwide, with only the United States and Israel ranking higher.
The Microsoft report also highlighted that Ukraine remains a major focus of activity by Russian state actors, accounting for 14% of their recorded activity.
The full text of the blitz interview with Dmytro Pakholchenko, director of the Cyber Protection Department at the administration of the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, will be published on the Interfax-Ukraine website.

Up to 12,000 North Koreans work under conditions of forced labor at Russia’s Alabuga drone plant, CSIS report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:57:07 UTC
21:57:07 KST

A factory in Russia’s Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, where Shahed-type attack drones are assembled, is using labor from victims of human trafficking, according to a report by Victor Cha of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and Joseph Kim of the George W. Bush Institute.
The authors said the drones are assembled by Russian teenagers, foreign workers from countries of the Global South, and citizens of North Korea.
Ukrainian intelligence estimates that as many as 12,000 North Koreans have been sent to Alabuga. They are paid around $2.50 an hour, with the regime of Kim Jong Un taking between 70% and 90% of their earnings.
Women ages 16 to 22 from Africa, Latin America, and Asia are recruited with promises of service-sector jobs paying salaries starting from $500 a month. After arriving, their passports are confiscated, and about 90% are sent to assemble drones, according to the report.
Students at Alabuga Polytech college are also put to work from the age of 15 under the guise of earning “work experience,” with shifts lasting as long as 12 hours.
The report’s authors write:
“North Korean laborers have their wages confiscated by the state that sent them. This is the definition of forced labor.”
The Alabuga factory is capable of producing more than 5,500 drones a month, according to the report. Ukrainian intelligence estimates that its workforce is planned to expand from about 1,000 people to 40,000.
The authors called on the U.S. Treasury Department to impose sanctions on companies and educational institutions involved in recruitment for the facility and urged Washington to establish a multilateral investigative group through the United Nations. In September, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), a group made up of the United States and allied countries, reported that as many as 25,000 North Koreans were working in Russian drone production. According to the group, the workers are registered as students in order to circumvent sanctions.

Emily Feng on the Uyghur fighters who helped topple Assad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:57:04 UTC
21:57:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Our Hearts Burned For Home: Emily Feng on the Uyghur fighters who fought Assad for a homeland of their own
How did a few thousand Uyghur hairdressers and farmers, shoe salesmen and writers, become part of an elite fighting troop, a pivotal force in overthrowing Syria's brutal dictator Bashar al-Assad?
That is the question at the centre of this remarkable, rarely-told story. Journalist Emily Feng had gone to cover the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire in December 2024, but instead made her way to Syria as Assad fell.
In 2025, she found Central Asian fighters everywhere she went. With the help of exiled Uyghur writer Abduweli Ayup, essential when the new regime banned her from interviewing them directly, they tracked down some five dozen fighters and families from a 20,000-strong Uyghur community that had made Syria home.
About 4,000 of them took up arms. But why would stateless people endure hardship and martyrdom for a country that was not their own?
The answer is that Syria was never the point. The history of this rebel movement is not straightforward. Feng's candid interviews shed light on their complicated, fractured story. Our Hearts Burned For Home: Uyghur militants in Syria’s Civil War is the result.
A revolution within a revolution
Their presence in Syria was almost accidental; a mix of China's crackdown after the 1990s protests and 2009 Ürümqi riots, geographical chance, and revenge.
Unwilling to live in what they called the prison of Xinjiang, they made their way, some via Afghanistan to Syria, not to save Syrians but to learn how to fight for Hotan and Kashgar.
With no Arabic and no war experience, they typically got three months of training and were sent straight to the front.
In Jisr al-Shughur, in houses emptied by war, they built a state within a state: schools, businesses, their own security, raising children for the next war.
"We are raising our own army," one commander tells Feng. They decorated classrooms with cardboard tanks and anti-aircraft rockets to "acclimatise" children to war.
Never losing sight of that goal, they avoided joining other rebel groups and insisted on fighting as Uyghurs. But ideologically, things got complicated and fractured.
From 2014, ISIS/ISIS-K tried to recruit Uyghurs for a global caliphate. Most Turkestan Independence Party (TIP) Uyghurs rejected it; they wanted a Uyghur state, not a caliphate. Those who joined ISIS were arrested and became enemies.
When East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) leader Abdul Haq in Afghanistan pressed them toward al-Qaeda and the Taliban, they split from the Afghan Uyghurs in 2018, swapped the black Islamist flag for the blue flag of East Turkestan, and recast themselves as nationalists.
As far as the new regime-in-waiting was concerned, it made them rather unreliable allies. In 2016-17 they refused to formally merge into Ahmed al-Sharaa’s Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS). Their goal was Xinjiang, not Syria, and joining HTS meant mission creep.
And yet they fought against the regime. Ferociously.
From neutral newcomers, they were dragged into the rebel independence fray in 2015, earning a fearsome reputation for holding the northern front against Russian bombardment for a decade.
They lived off savings brought from Xinjiang and weapons captured from regime forces. Forced to learn fast, they fashioned shoulder-launched rockets from scrap canisters and mixed their own explosives.
"War became free training," one says, for the future war with China.
Feng is compelling on the brutal reality of that training. The rebel regime was punishing and relentless as it hammered the motley band of volunteers into disciplined soldiers versed in intelligence, strategy and logistics.
Bilal, a former hairdresser, says, "Sometimes, I was so sad I cried.” Revenge pulled him through.
The book's heart is how they fought. After ten gruelling years of fighting hand-to-mouth, the book builds to its climax: Operation Deterrence of Aggression in November 2024.
Triggered by a regime strike that killed children in Ariha, the Uyghurs used a disused tunnel at Dadikh to penetrate Assad's stronghold.
Tragically, digging 500 metres short of their target, they pushed on regardless to break the line to Aleppo. Half their team was stuck with a jammed motorcycle in the tunnel, and one of their tanks was lost to a minefield.
But by November 30, thanks to a rebel-negotiated ceasefire with Russia, Aleppo finally fell. Days later, rebel troops stormed Damascus, and Uyghur fighters waving blue East Turkestan flags rolled into town, earning the respect of the new regime and a place in Syria’s independence struggle.
A new Syria, an uncertain future
It should have been triumphant. But it was hollow.
Feng captures the mood perfectly. They had fought tooth and nail for ten years, losing hundreds of kin. But this was not their war. They wept — not for Syria, but for home. They preferred to save their tears for Hotan or Kashgar one day.
What comes next is the book's most painful part. Where do 20,000 stateless Uyghurs fit in a new Syria when their loyalty lies 4,500 km away?
There are almost as many answers as there are Uyghurs.
Some Uyghur children feel no affinity with East Turkestan and want to become Syrian.
Others, with their long black beards and children who call Alawites and Christians "infidels," frighten locals and want to remain a state within a state independent of Syrian state institutions.
Neutrality, however, might have made them good wartime partners, but how could political independence work in the new Syria?
For many others, comfortable inertia has set in, and the debate over whether to settle or keep fighting for a liberated East Turkestan now dominates.
The new Syria is moving forward anyway, with or without the Uyghurs, and it has big decisions to make.
The TIP has been disbanded into the Syrian Army’s 84th Brigade, and Uyghur commanders have been given posts in the Defence Ministry.
Many hope for citizenship and schooling. But as one interviewee tells Feng: "I hope this exile does not last very long, because they will become more and more Syrian. I hope at the end, when we have our own land back, maybe they at least will still want to visit me in East Turkestan."
Debates about their future rumble on both inside Syria and among the exiled faithful marooned in Turkey.
Many of those in Turkey are de facto stateless after Ankara refused passports over their East Turkestan independence activism.
Living under a cloud of frequent threats of repatriation to China, Syria looks like the perfect place to raise children free to study the Quran and practise their faith.
Squeezed from all sides, the Uyghurs are threatened not only by Turkey but also by Beijing, determined to drag them back to the homeland.
Radicalised Syrian Uyghur fighters have been in China's sights for years, and the fear they might stir trouble in Xinjiang is never far from the surface.
One way for Beijing to solve that problem is to use them as a bargaining chip in Syria's desperate need for reconstruction. Rumours of such a deal abound, but Damascus has denied them for now.
What comes after victory?
Feng and Ayup have done something extraordinary in Our Hearts Burned For Home. This is not just a war story, but one of exile, ideology and what happens when a displaced people borrows another people’s revolution to train for their own.
Their story is not without controversy.
Some Uyghurs fear their militancy is justified, while others find it distasteful. They fear being tarred with the terrorist brush and thereby vindicating Beijing in its crackdown in the Uyghur region.
Feng was drawn to the sheer improbability of Assad's overthrow: some 30,000 rebels in fractious bands up against the Goliaths of Iran, Turkey and Russia. And winning.
In her conclusion, she hints their story might not be over: "What several thousand highly motivated, highly experienced Uyghur fighters can do may end up surprising us all. They have already surprised me."
The author is writing under a pseudonym to protect her identity

Elon Musk Ordered Ukraine Starlink Slowdown Despite Saying US Military Controls Limits, Says WSJ

- Category
- World
Elon Musk Ordered Ukraine Starlink Slowdown Despite Saying US Military Controls Limits, Says WSJ
Elon Musk personally ordered restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service used by Ukraine, on October 14, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 20.
The outlet disclosed the development, citing US officials and people familiar with the decision. According to the newspaper, Musk imposed speed limits on Ukrainian equipment connected to the satellite network, reportedly rendering some Ukrainian strike drones and aerial interceptors virtually unusable.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Journal's sources, Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the restrictions in a telephone conversation shortly after the slowdown became public. One person familiar with the situation also claimed the two discussed the matter before the restrictions were imposed. However, other US officials maintained that Musk acted independently and that Trump had not explicitly ordered punitive measures against Ukraine.
The restrictions reportedly triggered alarm in Kyiv and confusion within the Trump administration. According to the Journal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's warnings that the disruption could cost Ukrainian lives prompted an informal White House investigation into who authorized the decision.
SpaceX representatives also reportedly contacted White House officials to coordinate their understanding and public messaging about the restrictions.
Musk subsequently wrote on X that "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," according to the newspaper. Trump, meanwhile, denied knowing who was responsible for the slowdown and said he wanted to determine what had happened.
According to the Journal, some US officials maintained that Musk had acted unilaterally. Another person familiar with the matter claimed that he had consulted several senior administration officials, including Trump, before introducing the restrictions. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently denied that the administration had requested the slowdown.
The reported operational consequences extended to Ukrainian air defense. Michael Kofman of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told the Journal that Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones remained subject to a 160 km/h speed cap, while in practice reliable connectivity could be lost at speeds above roughly 130 km/h.
Zelenskyy separately said Ukraine does not use Starlink for strikes inside Russia, including attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. During an October 16 press conference in Brussels, he explained that Ukraine instead relies on the system to operate interceptor drones protecting civilians from Russian Shahed attacks.
"We do not use Starlink to attack or respond within the territory of the Russian Federation," Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated, according to Ukrinform. He added that Kyiv had previously asked SpaceX and the White House to provide such capabilities, indicating that they were not available to Ukrainian forces.
According to Zelenskyy, reducing Starlink connection speeds prevented Ukrainian interceptors from engaging some high-speed Russian Shahed-type drones. He described the restrictions as a dangerous surprise, explaining that certain Russian jet-powered drones were traveling at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour. Ukrainian units reportedly encountered severe connection limitations while attempting to intercept those threats.
SpaceX has not publicly explained the restrictions or responded to the Journal’s report that Musk personally ordered them.
The restrictions disrupted frontline drone units within hours of taking effect. Overnight on October 14, units of the 7th Air Assault Corps in the Huliaipole sector of the Zaporizhzhia region began losing drone connections for 10–20 seconds at speeds of roughly 110–120 km/h.
Medium-range strike drones, which must accelerate rapidly at launch, faced the greatest risk of failing to take off or complete their missions. Slowing down to stay connected left aircraft more exposed to Russian forces, and one drone unit in the sector canceled several missions that day as Ukraine's Defense Ministry began investigating the cause.

El Nino could be 'literally off the monitoring charts': UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:56:33 UTC
21:56:33 KST

Breadcrumb
El Nino could be 'literally off the monitoring charts', 'unprecedented in strength': UN
The El Nino weather phenomenon gripping the planet could be off the charts, the United Nations warned Wednesday, saying countries should take urgent action to prepare for the worst.
"The current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength. Literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades," Celeste Saulo, head of the UN's World Meteorological Organization, told a press conference in Geneva. "El Nino will peak towards the end of 2026, but its impacts will be felt long after that."
She said the WMO's latest global seasonal climate updates forecast that sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean—the epicentre of El Nino—may rise to 3.8C above average during November to January: way out of line with typical El Nino figures.
"This will have far-reaching consequences for weather patterns across the world," said Saulo.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN's weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
Saulo was joined by the UN aid chief Tom Fletcher.
"Today, we are issuing a joint call for urgent and coordinated anticipatory action... We cannot stop El Nino, but we can prevent many of its worst human consequences," she said.
Fletcher said El Nino was set to be a "wrecking ball" of extreme heat, droughts and floods in different parts of the world, triggering "massive humanitarian consequences".
"The damage will not stay in the countries in the immediate path of this El Nino," he warned. "It will create economic shocks for the global economy and drive further conflict, displacement, migration. I am sounding the alarm that the humanitarian system... cannot alone cope with a threat on this scale."
He called on countries, development banks and international financial institutions to get money moving "before that damage is done, not afterwards".
"The choice is clear: we can wait for disaster or we can invest in resilience. We cannot prevent El Nino but we can be serious about the challenges ahead," he added.
Fletcher said he had released $50 million to help 11 countries on the frontline, including Chad, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Somalia and South Sudan.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.

China launches satellite for low-inclination remote sensing net
A CERES-1S Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 am Beijing time on Wednesday from waters near east China's Shandong Province, delivering the Xiguang-4 01 satellite into a 541 km-altitude low Earth orbit, CGTN reports.
Xiguang-4 01 is the pilot satellite of the Wuyang Constellation, the world's first low-inclination remote sensing constellation. After entering orbit, Xiguang-4 01 will mainly provide commercial remote sensing services for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, South China, and low-latitude regions along the Maritime Silk Road. Its support functions will include natural resource monitoring, agricultural production, marine observation, ecological protection, flood and typhoon emergency response, disaster mitigation and urban governance.
Developed by Galactic Energy, the CERES-1 rocket model is China's first commercial rocket model capable of launching from both land and sea platforms. Wednesday's launch was the seventh sea launch mission of the CERES-1S carrier rocket. Since its maiden flight on September 5, 2023, the CERES-1S has maintained a 100% launch success rate.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Chinese scientists had successfully tested a domestic satellite internet system in the Arctic, establishing communication links between the Arctic Ocean, Antarctica, and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

Object that halted ship traffic off Helsinki identified as Soviet WWII torpedo
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:55:09 EEST
21:55:09 KST

A mysterious metal object discovered floating in the sea near Helsinki earlier this month has been identified as part of a Soviet naval torpedo dating from the Second World War, Finnish police confirmed on Tuesday. The Finnish Defence Forces have since destroyed the object, bringing the investigation to an end.
A fisherman spotted the cylindrical object on 3 October near Suomenlinna, an island fortress off Helsinki, in a shipping channel used by passenger ferries.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The discovery prompted a police operation involving the Finnish Border Guard and the Gulf of Finland Coast Guard, which temporarily closed the waterway while authorities recovered the object.
The metal cylinder measured 4.2 metres in length and 53.48 centimetres in diameter. Investigators initially considered whether it belonged to the machinery of an old shipwreck.
Police subsequently asked the Finnish Heritage Agency to examine the object. Working with maritime specialists, the agency identified it as the central section of what appears to have been a Soviet navy torpedo from the Second World War.
The torpedo's warhead and rear section were missing. Its central compartment contained tanks designed to hold compressed air, water and fuel.
Helsinki police confirmed that the object posed no danger when recovered and that investigators found no evidence of criminal activity.

Married couples can use double surnames from 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

Married couples can use double surnames from 2027
From January 1, 2027, married couples will once again be able to use a double surname in Switzerland. The government will bring this amendment to the Civil Code, which was passed by parliament, into force on that date.
From next year spouses will once again be able to use a double surname with or without a hyphen. However children will not be allowed this privilege.
Double surnames were allowed in Switzerland until an amendment to the Civil Code in 2013. From that year onwards, couples intending to marry had to choose a shared surname or retain their respective surnames. Only an unofficial “alliance name” was permitted. This refers to the unofficial double surname with a hyphen.
More
Why double surnames are stirring controversy in Switzerland
Under the amendments adopted by the government, people who are already married will be able to apply to the registry office for an official double surname from 2027 onwards. In future, the alliance name – which differs from the official surname – will no longer be included in passports or on identity cards.
However, a transitional period will continue to allow the alliance name to be recorded in identity documents to enable the authorities to make the necessary technical adjustments.
The governing Federal Council has not yet determined the duration of this transitional period. It will bring the relevant amendment to the Identification Documents Act into force in due course and announce the end of the period well in advance.

She told the BBC: “It really distresses me people can’t see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately.”
A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust said: “We are truly sorry that Ms Boardman was contacted in this way. Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her and discuss her diagnosis. This should not have happened, and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused.
“Appropriate action was taken following our investigation, which was carried out immediately after Ms Boardman raised her concern. While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously.
“We have reminded all our staff of their responsibility to protect patient confidentiality and that records must only ever be accessed for a legitimate work-related reason. We are also reviewing our policies and processes in light of the strengthened NHS England guidance on inappropriate access to patient information.
“We sincerely apologise to Ms Boardman for what happened and for the time she has had to wait for answers.”

New report points to widespread and systematic Israeli sexual violence against Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:52:26 UTC
21:52:26 KST

Content warning: This article contains descriptions of sexual violence and abuse that readers may find distressing.
Sexual violence against Palestinians has become part of a widespread and systematic pattern of abuse under Israeli occupation, with a new report laying out incidents of rape, genital torture, forced nudity and sexual humiliation across detention facilities, military operations and displacement sites.
The report in the British Medical Journal collates evidence from medical, humanitarian, and human rights organisations and examines the scale of the abuses to highlight the failure to secure accountability.
The report comes a few weeks after the third anniversary of the start of Israel’s genocidal war against Palestine that has killed more than 75,000 people and displaced millions in the devastated enclave of Gaza.
Sexual violence is part of a wider campaign of abuse that terrorises Palestinian communities and helps drive their forced displacement, according to Dr Nick Maynard, an Oxford-based consultant surgeon who has travelled to Gaza multiple times to provide medical care and co-author of the new report.
“It is important to understand that the evidence we have provided of sexual violence against Palestinians must not be considered as isolated incidents but a part of a widespread systematic pattern of severe physical and sexual abuse of Palestinians throughout the (occupied) West Bank and in Gaza,” Maynard tells TRT World.
“This behaviour is designed to break the will of the Palestinian people and clearly represents a fundamental and core part of their policy of forced displacement of Palestinian people and ethnic cleansing,” he adds.
In March 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinians was increasingly being used as a method of war.
It found that forced public stripping, sexual harassment and assault formed part of Israeli security forces’ standard operating procedures, with sexualised torture committed with explicit orders or implicit encouragement from senior civilian and military leadership.
The Commission documented a pattern of sexual violence, torture and other inhumane acts amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The evidence includes rape and sexual assault against Palestinian detainees, attacks targeting their genitals, threats of rape against detainees and their family members, and repeated strip searches conducted in degrading circumstances.
Life-altering injuries
The documented abuse against Palestinian detainees includes sexual violence and beatings that have left them with devastating and sometimes permanent injuries.
In one documented case, a Palestinian detainee suffered a rectal rupture requiring surgery and the formation of a stoma.
Other accounts describe detainees losing one or both testicles after beatings targeting their genitals.
The abuse has also extended beyond detention.
Palestinian men, women and children in Gaza were subjected to prolonged forced nudity during Israeli military operations, including being forced to walk naked in public.
Israeli soldiers also photographed and filmed Palestinian women’s underwear in homes they had raided, posting images online to humiliate them.
The UN’s 2026 report on conflict-related sexual violence verified sexual violence against 31 Palestinian men, women and children in Gaza and the occupied West Bank across 2023 to 2025.
Nine victims were subjected to rape or gang rape, in some cases repeatedly. The documented abuses included genital violence, forced nudity, threats of rape and invasive searches without apparent security justification.
Maynard, who has travelled to Gaza repeatedly since 2010, including on three occasions since October 7, 2023, says he witnessed appalling atrocities including mass casualties caused by bombings in densely populated civilian areas, with children among those killed.
During his work, Maynard collected detailed testimonies from two healthcare workers and one civilian who had been abducted and detained in Israeli prisons. Their accounts included descriptions of torture and sexual violence.
“I have worked in the hospitals with many patients who died because of the lack of resources, and clearly many of them would have survived if we had had adequate resources.”
“The lack of adequate medical resources, as a direct result of the direct targeting of healthcare facilities and the Israeli blockade stopping adequate aid and resources coming into Gaza, meant that patients suffering from trauma often were not able to get adequate medical care and support and this applied to those with trauma from sexual violence,” Maynard says.
“Those who were tortured and underwent sexual violence in Israeli detention centres and prisons were also denied medical care while in custody,” he adds.
Sexual violence drives fear and displacement
For Palestinians, sexual violence and threats have also shaped everyday life under occupation, including during military raids, at checkpoints and in displacement sites.
Reports document women being forced to undress in front of soldiers, subjected to sexual assault and threatened with rape, sometimes in front of their children.
Other accounts describe Israeli soldiers exposing their genitals to women and girls, while Palestinian women in the occupied West Bank have faced sexual harassment and threats from Israeli settlers.
In one study involving 39 displaced households in Area C of the occupied West Bank, more than 70 percent identified threats to women and children, particularly sexualised violence, as a decisive reason for leaving their homes.
The findings illustrate how sexual violence can contribute to an environment of coercion and displacement, alongside other forms of violence and intimidation faced by Palestinian communities.
Children are also among those affected.
In 2025, more than half of 165 Palestinian children aged 12 to 17 who had been detained by Israeli authorities reported witnessing or experiencing sexual violence in detention, including rape threats, forced stripping and genital assault, according to research cited in the BMJ article.
Underreporting and impunity
The scale of documented abuse is compounded by the barriers survivors face in reporting violence and obtaining care.
Fear of reprisals, shame, stigma, and distrust of complaint mechanisms can keep survivors from coming forward. Limited access for independent investigators also limits evidence collection and verification.
“We believe these abuses are greatly underreported for many reasons. Victims frequently refuse to report their injuries out of fear of further abuse and attacks on themselves and their families,” Maynard says.
“It is challenging to document the full extent of sexual violence as Israel has repeatedly refused to allow independent investigators to review what is going on,” he adds.
The accountability record is also troubling.
The UN Commission found that the Israeli civilian and military justice systems had failed to ensure accountability for sexual crimes against Palestinians.
Of 1,260 cases of offences by Israeli soldiers against Palestinians known to the military law enforcement system between 2017 and 2021, only 11 resulted in indictments.
Neve Gordon, professor of human rights and humanitarian law at Queen Mary University of London, said credible allegations required independent investigation, including into those who ordered or enabled the abuse.
Sexual violence can constitute a war crime and, where the legal requirements are met, a crime against humanity.
Establishing criminal responsibility requires investigators to examine individual incidents, preserve evidence and determine the roles of direct perpetrators and those in positions of command.
“The UN needs to be allowed to send in independent teams to investigate such reports of sexual violence and ensure not only that victims of this violence have access to all appropriate specialist medical care but also that perpetrators must be held accountable,” Maynard says.
“Western governments such as the UK government have an obligation under international law to prevent these violations and to make sure international humanitarian law is upheld.”
“These governments must do more to protect Palestinians and must insist on independent monitoring and investigation,” he adds.

Israel’s election may change its leader, but not Iran war policy

AI generated
DUBAI - Israel’s election next week may change its leader, but not its strategy: Iran will remain its chief adversary, military force will continue to be its preferred tool and Palestinian statehood a distant prospect, regional policymakers and analysts say.
That is because the strategic assumptions underpinning Israeli policy were hardened by the Oct 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israeli communities by Palestinian militant group Hamas and by the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
If anything, Israel could toughen its security policy, the analysts said, as victory for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with the backing of far-right coalition partners could embolden him to step up the war with Iran, tighten Israel’s grip on the occupied West Bank and push diplomacy further to the margins.
Israel’s security doctrine now rests on three pillars: breaking Iran, holding buffer zones beyond its borders and using force to deter enemies.
The real divide is one of degree rather than direction – how aggressively Israel fights its wars, how far it expands Jewish settlements in the West Bank and whether any leader opts for diplomacy, the analysts said.
From Tehran to Riyadh, the Oct 27 election is not seen as a potential turning point but as a test of whether the Middle East is settling into a long confrontation, where wars ebb and flow while the underlying conflicts are unresolved.
“If Netanyahu is elected, he’ll do whatever he thinks he wants to do,” said Aviv Bushinsky, a former adviser to Netanyahu. “Expansion of the settlements will continue. The wars against Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah will continue.”
“What you see now is what you’ll see after the election, maybe even more aggressively,” he said. “As long as Iran is in such a situation, it’s a waste of time talking about Palestine.”
Netanyahu said on Oct 18 that Israel must prioritise “prevention and offence over containment and defence”, including pre-emptive strikes to thwart emerging threats, while establishing Israel as a regional power and maximising its independence in armaments.
Why the course is unlikely to change
The election pits Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud and its ultra nationalist allies against an opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party.
Palestinian analyst Ghassan al-Khatib sees no prospect of a fundamental shift in policy towards the Palestinians, with Israeli political parties competing to project harder-line positions as public opinion moves further to the right.
“The substance of the policy remains the same: No to a Palestinian state and yes to further settlement expansion. On this, they are all in agreement,” he said.
A government led by Netanyahu’s opponents might seek to repair Israel’s international standing by curbing some settler violence or pursuing settlement expansion with less fanfare.
But such changes would be a shift in style rather than substance, al-Khatib said.
Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Center said Israel’s security establishment and much of its political class share a common strategic outlook, centred on confronting Iran, maintaining “forward defence” and preserving military deterrence, reducing the scope for big policy shifts.
Joost Hiltermann of the International Crisis Group, who has conducted research in the West Bank, said growing settler violence, mounting Palestinian frustration and the absence of a “political horizon” had created combustible conditions, where even a minor trigger could spark a wider uprising.
‘Venomous octopus’
Some regional policymakers ask whether Israel’s confrontation with Iran has become the organising principle of Middle East security, regardless of who wins the election.
US President Donald Trump’s praise of Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” has reinforced expectations that the Israeli leader will try to finish the campaign against Tehran if he retains power.
Netanyahu has made clear his ambitions extend beyond containing Iran to toppling its clerical rulers.
“Completing the task means toppling the terrorist regime in Iran, the head of the venomous octopus,” he said in a speech this week.
But military and political analysts question whether anything short of a US-Israeli ground invasion would force Tehran to abandon what it views as its core security interests in what it sees as an existential fight.
After surviving months of war, Iran may be betting it can outlast its opponents while continuing to exert pressure through regional allies.
“This is a quagmire,” Young said. “The Iranians can outlast Trump.”
Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza have been weakened, but the broader network of Iran-aligned groups has survived and the conflict could strengthen Tehran’s determination to pursue a nuclear deterrent, the analysts said.
For all the alarm Netanyahu causes in the Arab world, some Gulf leaders still see him as the Israeli politician most likely to keep Iran under pressure.
This creates a dilemma for them. They oppose what they view as his expansionist policies but want Iranian influence curbed.
“Netanyahu’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank, Syria and Lebanon are damaging,” said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Centre.
“As for Iran, a settlement is needed before the conflict escalates further. If Iran’s role is not curbed, the region could be heading toward 50 years of Iranian hegemony.” REUTERS
