UN warns world on course for 2.6 C warming this century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Current global commitments to cut greenhouse gas emissions fall far short of Paris Agreement goals, putting the world on track for 2.6 degrees Celsius of warming this century, the U.N. warned Wednesday.
The report by the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) highlights the gap between rhetoric and action on global warming and the challenge facing political leaders at November's COP31 climate summit.
Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6 C above preindustrial levels by 2100, the annual Emissions Gap Report said.
That would blow past the historic goal agreed to in Paris: keeping warming well below 2 C while striving for a safer 1.5 C. Any chance of meeting the 1.5 C target had been "lost" due to decades of insufficient climate action, the report said.
"The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5-C limit, and the consequences are already devastating," U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a statement launching the closely watched report.
"Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst," he added.
Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on par with record levels in 2024. The difference between the two years was insignificant, the report said.
Carbon emissions from burning coal, oil and gas – the main driver of climate change – rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.
Guterres said deep, immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts, but instead, emissions remain at record levels, and national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short.
Sticking with current policies would result in warming hitting 2.8 C, the report said.
Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree Celsius above 1.5 C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4 C relative to preindustrial times, and crossing 1.5 C is expected in a matter of years.
The G-20 accounts for three-fourths of global emissions, but Guterres said "all countries, especially the big emitters, must do more" to stop heating the planet.
This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than last year's due to the formal withdrawal of the U.S. from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, report co-author Anne Olhoff said.
Emissions growth slowed among the G-20, but the U.S. was a "major exception," the report added.
Among the world's top-six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the U.S., Indonesia and China and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.
But in terms of magnitude, the U.S. increase of 133 megatons of carbon dioxide equivalent "far exceeded" that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.
The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the U.N. climate summit in Antalya from Nov. 9-20.
The U.S. is the world's second-largest polluter, behind China. President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.
UNEP Executive Secretary Inger Andersen told reporters that no country was shielded from climate change, and impacts were being felt "on every nation on the planet, including the U.S."
The report details a scenario with a 50% chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5 C by 2100.
To get there, warming must peak around 1.8 C by 2050, and vast amounts of CO2 would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.
But this scenario assumes immediate emissions cuts of 6% annually until 2035 – nowhere near current projections.
"The main takeaway is simple – governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," Bill Hare, CEO of global policy institute Climate Analytics, said.
Some climate-vulnerable developing nations have accused bigger emitters of abandoning the Paris goals, and a showdown over the 1.5 C target is expected at COP31.
"This is a historic failure of political leadership. The science has been clear for decades, but governments have chosen delay over action. The consequences will be measured in lives lost, not just degrees of warming," Mohamed Adow, director of Kenya-based think tank Power Shift Africa, said.
Guterres agreed there was a climate "leadership gap" but said overshooting 1.5 C "is not surrender."

Student who stabbed housemate to death in Gloucestershire jailed for life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:50:55 UTC
21:50:55 KST

A university student who lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 28 years.
Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home in Filton, South Gloucestershire.
Bristol crown court heard Collins was stabbed repeatedly and Coughlan left him dying in an alleyway as he cycled away on his housemate’s bike.
Coughlan had denied murder and a trial was under way at Bristol crown court but he changed his plea to guilty on Tuesday.
Sentencing Coughlan on Wednesday, Mr Justice Linden said: “He [Collins] was caught totally unaware by you and was utterly defenceless.”
He dismissed Coughlan’s evidence in court that Collins had previously threatened him, describing Collins as a “gentle soul”.
The judge said no one would know why Coughlan killed Collins.
Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April this year after cycling home from University of the West of England (UWE) Bristol where he was studying robotics alongside his killer.
Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, told the jury: “This was a carefully planned and cold-blooded execution.”
Coughlan dumped the bike at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing in a pond, in carrier bags weighed down with bricks.
He returned to the house they shared at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends.
At around 2am, Coughlan dialled 999 claiming he had just found Collins’s body in the garden.
The attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house they shared, which Coughlan showed the attending police officers who initially treated him as a witness.
The defendant’s blood had been found on Collins’s bike, and analysis of his mobile phone matched the killer’s movements afterwards captured on CCTV.
Coughlan also had injuries to his hands, and he told people who saw him bleeding that he had been climbing trees and had fallen and hurt himself.
After the murder, Coughlan told a university friend he wanted to hold a memorial for his housemate.
Coughlan and Collins, originally from Swansea, were both final year students and lived together in a £300,000 three-bedroom house owned by the defendant.
The defendant is half Danish and grew up with his family in Cork, Ireland, before moving to Bristol to study robotics at the age of 19.
In a statement issued following Coughlan’s change of plea, Collins’s family said his death had “affected our family in a deep, profound, and lasting way”.
“As a family we have had to explain repeatedly to people what has happened,” they said. “Every time we do so it reinforces the pain of him having been killed so suddenly, and in such a senseless and brutal way.
“Our family has been sickened that Zack Coughlan pretended to help Jamie when in fact he is responsible for killing him.”

The minister said all government and private offices were required to implement a 50 percent "Work from Home" policy. ■

UOB also maintained its 2027 inflation forecast at 2 percent, within the government's projected range of 1.8 percent to 2.8 percent.
Kenanga Research likewise kept its inflation forecasts unchanged at 1.9 percent for 2026 and 2 percent for 2027, although it expects risks to remain tilted to the upside.

China Focus: China-initiated Luban Workshops empower global youth with practical skills
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:57 CST
21:48:57 KST

TIANJIN, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- At an automotive industrial park in north China's Tianjin Municipality, Egyptian students Abdelrahman Ayman Zaky and Adham Ayman are gaining hands-on experience in new energy vehicle (NEV) chassis systems alongside their Chinese peers.
Having acquired vocational skills at an Egyptian Luban Workshop, the two came to China to deepen their expertise. Adham, 20, hopes to improve his Chinese and vehicle maintenance skills before returning to Egypt to pursue a career as an automotive engineer.
Their experience highlights the mission of the China-initiated Luban Workshops, which over the past decade have equipped young people worldwide with useful skills, fostered local talent, and supported industrial development.
Named after Luban, an ancient Chinese craftsman and inventor who lived more than 2,500 years ago, the initiative draws on a longstanding Chinese tradition of craftsmanship and innovation.
Jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, Luban Workshops now offer vocational education and skills-training programs in 32 countries.
In Egypt, Luban Workshops are helping students like Adham translate classroom learning into engineering capabilities.
Mohamed Mostafa, a student at an Egyptian Luban Workshop now studying at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said hands-on practice has strengthened his ability to tackle real-world engineering challenges.
"In the EPIP (Engineering Practice and Innovation Project) classroom, we don't just work on simulated problems. We work on real-world engineering problems in teams, discussing solutions, refining our techniques and testing them again and again. We break down complex challenges to achieve the best results and meet engineering standards," Mostafa said.
He added that he has shared the approach with students in Egypt, where they have applied the same methods to develop their own projects.
The two Egyptian Luban Workshops have provided formal education to more than 3,100 people and skills training on over 4,000 occasions, creating new opportunities for industrial cooperation.
Wang Baolong, dean of the School of Mechanical Engineering at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said graduates trained in advanced technologies can meet the needs of local businesses, strengthening Chinese companies' confidence in investing in and establishing factories in Egypt while supporting local economic development.
An employment training base jointly established by the Egyptian Luban Workshops and the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone has provided young Egyptians with a direct pathway to employment.
"After receiving professional technical training, these young people can operate production equipment proficiently. They are exactly the kind of skilled workers that companies need," Wang added.
Beyond teaching technical skills, the workshops also help build local capacity for sustained vocational training. While setting up training centers and supplying advanced equipment, Chinese partners send teachers and technicians to train local instructors and arrange exchanges and learning opportunities in China.
In 2016, the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College and the Ayutthaya Technical College in Thailand jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system.
"We are not just cultivating talent for the local area, but leaving the whole system behind. Chinese standards and models are truly integrating into and promoting local development," said Mei Wentao, a staff member at the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College.
More than 100 Chinese companies in Thailand operate businesses ranging from NEV components to vehicle distribution. In August 2025, the China-Thailand automotive intelligent manufacturing industry-education integration community was established in Thailand. With a steady supply of skilled graduates, companies can recruit directly from schools, helping young Thai people find jobs more easily and quickly.
In Central Asia, the Tajik Luban Workshop is helping local young people explore new career opportunities. In nearly four years of operation, it has provided learning and training opportunities to more than 3,600 undergraduate and postgraduate students.
When Bakhtiyor Bozorzoda enrolled at the Tajik Technical University, he was uncertain about his chosen major in geodesy and cartography. Advanced surveying equipment, digital mapping technologies, and virtual simulation courses at the Tajik Luban Workshop helped him recognize the field's potential and develop a stronger interest in surveying.
During his studies, Bozorzoda gained hands-on experience with high-precision instruments and digital mapping technologies.
"I hope to continue my studies in China in the future, learn more advanced surveying technologies and contribute to infrastructure development in Tajikistan," he said.
Today, Luban Workshops have become a hallmark of China's international vocational education cooperation. Data from China's Ministry of Education show that the country has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, providing formal education to more than 30,000 students and non-degree training to over 160,000 people.
The Luban Workshops reflect a commitment to harmony, coexistence and the common good in Chinese cultural tradition. By responding to local needs, they help young people in different countries acquire skills that can benefit them throughout their careers, said Tian Xuejun, president of the China Education Association for International Exchange, at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, held in Tianjin from Oct. 15 to 17.
China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions.
As of the end of 2025, China's vocational education catalog covered 19 major categories, 97 subcategories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories.
China is continuing to strengthen its vocational education system to support the development of emerging industries and expand opportunities for people both at home and abroad. At the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, representatives from 45 countries jointly released the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards developed under China's leadership.
The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing lifelong education and training opportunities for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams through school-enterprise partnerships, and using artificial intelligence to drive reform in education and teaching. ■

ALMATY, Kazakhstan, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Russian tennis star Andrey Rublev joined 10 children with autism for a tennis session in Kazakhstan on Monday, as organizers of the ATP Almaty Open sought to promote inclusion through sport.
The event, organized by the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation in partnership with the Bulat Utemuratov Foundation, brought together Rublev and children from the foundation's Asyl Miras Autism Center at Almaty's Alatau Tennis Center.
Held on the sidelines of the ATP 250 tournament, the session featured adapted ball-and-racket exercises, accuracy drills and other activities designed to introduce the children to tennis in a relaxed environment.
"It was a great experience. First of all, it's always a pleasure to spend time with children. They teach you so much, and there's always something special about being part of that playful atmosphere," Rublev said.
The Russian, whose mother is a tennis coach, said he had grown up watching how coaches worked with young children.
"Every charitable initiative is incredibly meaningful, and everyone connects with it in their own way. But the most important thing is simply to do something good," he added.
The initiative forms part of the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation's efforts to encourage wider participation in the sport, which has undergone significant development in the country under federation president Bulat Utemuratov.
Ainur Karbozova, CEO of the Bulat Utemuratov Foundation, said sporting activities could help create a more inclusive environment for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
"It is particularly important to us that children with ASD have the opportunity to participate in all aspects of life, including sports," she said.
"Meetings like these help broaden the understanding of inclusion not only among children but also throughout society."
The initiative has previously attracted leading players including Novak Djokovic, Carlos Alcaraz, Elena Rybakina and Daniil Medvedev.
The Almaty Open, which runs through Sunday, is one of Kazakhstan's leading international tennis tournaments. ■

Malaysia's coral reefs at risk over climate change, says official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:37 CST
21:48:37 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Rising sea temperatures of up to 35 degrees Celsius have caused increased coral deaths and bleaching at six popular island destinations in Malaysia, a Malaysian official said on Tuesday.
Monitoring by the Fisheries Department at 32 islands in Malaysia's marine parks found serious environmental pressure and worsening reef health at six islands, Agriculture and Food Security Minister Mohamad Sabu told parliament.
"Monitoring found a drop in live coral cover and a higher rate of coral deaths after bleaching, caused by sea-surface temperatures reaching between 32 degrees Celsius and 35 degrees Celsius," he said.
Mohamad said coral reefs are important marine habitats, providing shelter and breeding grounds for sea life, while supporting the country's fisheries resources.
He said the ministry is carrying out a climate action plan for the fisheries sector for 2024 to 2030, which includes efforts to reduce the effects of climate change on coral reefs, adding that 4 million ringgit (980,000 U.S. dollars) has been allocated toward rehabilitation programs.
The government is also strengthening enforcement under the Fisheries Act 1985 against activities that damage coral reefs.
These include taking corals, dumping pollutants, destroying marine habitats and anchoring vessels in prohibited ways within marine parks and marine reserves without written permission. ■

====================================================================================================

Ruined by NATO, divided without Gaddafi: Can Libya’s new deal hold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:48:31 UTC
21:48:31 KST

Ruined by NATO, divided without Gaddafi: Can Libya’s new deal hold?
The long-awaited agreement between Libya’s rival factions was finally signed on August 30 under the auspices of the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL). On that day, the mission gathered the two negotiating delegations at its Tripoli headquarters to formalize the text ironed out during earlier rounds of talks in Rome and Tunis. UNSMIL invited foreign diplomats, media representatives, and Libyan delegations to the event, where UN Special Representative Hanna Tetteh hailed the accord in her opening remarks as “another important milestone in Libya’s journey toward stability and national unity.”
This, however, bore a resemblance to previous diplomatic milestones – most notably the 2015 Libyan Political Agreement (LPA) signed in Skhirat, Morocco. The LPA established the rules of the political game in the fractured country; rules to which none of the domestic political actors seem fully committed, yet from which none completely depart. In a sense, Skhirat remains the ultimate reference point for every subsequent UN roadmap in Libya.
In the vacuum left by the 2011 NATO intervention and the brutal murder of Muammar Gaddafi, Libya has seen a continuous parade of diplomatic accords. Yet the fundamental problem has never been a shortage of roadmaps, but rather their consolidation into nationally accepted political facts that elites cannot simply manipulate at will.
The August 30 agreement has two main parts. The first is restructuring the High National Elections Commission (HNEC), the agency in charge of organizing elections. In practice, this means replacing its leadership to settle disputes over appointments and regional representation. Although these changes were long delayed by regional quotas and political patronage stemming from the 2015 Skhirat agreement, rivals can still negotiate them with relative ease.
The 24-month timeline to hold elections was also established. However, the countdown is designed to govern the transition only once a single, unified executive authority and unified national institutions are established to oversee the voting process.
The second component concerns the central objective of UNSMIL’s latest roadmap: agreeing on viable election laws, an issue on which the UN has failed to make meaningful progress since the collapse of the planned 2021 elections.
Libya remains divided between rival power centers: the Government of National Unity (GNU), led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibah in Tripoli, the western part of the country, and the Libyan National Army (LNA) command in the east led by General Khalifa Haftar. These exist alongside two political institutions: the Tripoli-based High Council of state (HCS) and the eastern-based House of Representatives (HoR). To break the deadlock, UNSMIL established a smaller negotiating group known as the ‘Smaller Convening’, or the ‘4+4’. It brings together eight representatives from the GNU, Haftar’s military command, the HCS, and the HoR.
This mechanism directly mirrors the ill-fated 2021 Geneva process, Libyan Political Dialogue Framework, which ultimately hardened Libya’s institutional divide and brought the country closer to a permanent de facto partition than at any point since its formal unification in 1951. The UN Security Council issued a delayed presidential statement endorsing the deal, and thus repeating a familiar ritual that seems to elevates elite compromise over structural reform. Seeking to seize the political initiative, Speaker Aguila Saleh brought the 4+4 framework to the HoR floor for an immediate vote where it was approved by the majority of members.
The ‘4+4’ format developed alongside (and ultimately eclipsed) UNSMIL’s broader Structured Dialogue. Even before those conclusions were finalized, UNSMIL was already facilitating a parallel ‘Smaller Convening’ behind closed doors – the 4+4 was born. As Hanna Tetteh told the Security Council on June 18, the explicit goal of this smaller format was to bypass the paralysis between the legislative bodies and force an accord on the roadmap’s first two steps: reconstituting the elections commission’s board and resolving the contested electoral framework. Thus, the ‘4+4’ was a deliberate strategy to concentrate decision-making among the political and military figures deemed capable of enforcing an outcome.
After the HoR approved the agreement on September 14, the HCS formally rejected it on October 5, along with the related laws and decisions issued by the House, arguing that they bypassed the constitutional, legal and consensual frameworks governing the political process. In her October 14 briefing to the UN Security Council, Tetteh acknowledged this rejection but maintained that the agreement offers an actionable path to presidential and legislative elections under a single, unified executive authority within 24 months.
She also announced that UNSMIL would meet members of the 4+4 committee later this month to examine the possibility of establishing a broadly representative national mechanism under Article 5 of the agreement in consultation with the Security Council. This proposal implicitly acknowledges that the 4+4 mini-dialogue alone may not be sufficient to advance the roadmap.
Another significant development is the removal of Aguila Saleh as speaker of the HoR after 12 years in office. On October 7, the eastern-based parliament elected Al-Salhin Abdulnabi as his successor, ending Saleh’s long tenure amid growing discontent over his leadership. The change is particularly significant because Saleh had been accused of being a prominent obstacle to previous attempts to move Libya’s political process forward. Tetteh acknowledged the transition, expressing her appreciation to Saleh for “his leadership and engagement over his 12-year tenure of service.” Her emphasis on the change in parliamentary leadership is noteworthy: The departure of a figure long associated with resistance to political roadmaps could create new room for maneuver, although it does not by itself guarantee that the House will cooperate with the UN initiative or that the entrenched political divisions will be overcome.
Ultimately, the structural core of the August 30 agreement rests on a fundamental contradiction: 4+4 does not equal 1. Combining four delegates from Tripoli’s political-institutional structures, including representatives of the HCS, with four delegates representing the eastern power structure in Benghazi does not produce a unified state. Instead, it seems to function as a shared enterprise in which rival political elites, rather than competing to build a single nation, recognize that their mutual survival depends on dividing power and maintaining exclusive control over the state apparatus.
Setting a 24-month timetable neither offers a guarantee that elections will actually occur; instead, it grants entrenched factions another two years of status quo protection without imposing any penalty for non-compliance.
Still, the UN Security Council appeared to endorse the latest UNSMIL plan. Following Tetteh’s briefing on October 14, the Council reaffirmed its support for the agreement, despite concerns over its implementation and the High Council of State’s rejection.
By prioritizing elite consensus over an enforceable constitutional baseline, the international community risks continuing to repeat a flawed equation. Until UNSMIL and foreign powers break this cycle and align their strategy with the Libyan public’s demand for genuine democratic renewal, every new agreement risks becoming another monument to the status quo. In the end, the ‘4+4’ framework offers no viable fallback or alternative path forward if it fails.
Last week, the UNSC did not vote to extend UNSMIL’s mandate, which expires on October 31. However, this is largely a technicality, since the Council has already approved UNSMIL’s roadmap.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

VIENTIANE, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Lao government has officially released the results of the 2025 Population and Housing Census, revealing that the working-age population has grown to 65 percent of the country's total population, creating an opportunity to accelerate economic growth.
The findings, released Tuesday, show that Laos has an estimated combined resident and non-resident population of 7.55 million, including 7.24 million people living in the country and 313,766 Lao citizens residing abroad. Among the resident population, females account for 49.2 percent, while males make up 50.8 percent.
People aged 15-64 represent 65 percent of the resident population, offering Laos an opportunity to benefit from a demographic dividend through job creation, skills development, and investment in human capital.
In terms of education, the overall literacy rate for individuals aged six and above has risen to 83.6 percent.
For the first time, the census employed modern technologies, including electronic maps to define survey areas, digital devices for data collection through computer-assisted personal interviewing, and real-time data monitoring to improve efficiency and accuracy. ■

ZAGREB, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Croatian parliament on Wednesday rejected an opposition motion to remove Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic from office over the illegal dumping of hazardous waste in central Croatia.
Of the lawmakers present, 55 voted in favor of the motion, 79 voted against and two abstained. The motion failed to secure the 76 votes needed for approval in the 151-seat parliament.

The initial Europol report said much of the waste was imported from other European Union countries, namely Italy, Slovenia and Germany. An expert report found so-called "forever chemicals" and heavy metals downstream of the illegal landfill, and residents fear the waste is endangering their health.
Thousands of people rallied in Zagreb on Sept. 5 to demand an urgent cleanup of the site and an immediate ban on waste imports. ■

Interview: Spanish pottery hub seeks deeper ceramic ties with China, says mayor
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:23 CST
21:48:23 KST

MADRID, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Spain's historic pottery city of Talavera de la Reina is seeking to strengthen cultural and commercial ties with China through its participation in the Jingdezhen International Ceramic Fair, the city's mayor has said to Xinhua.
The fair is being held from Oct. 17 to 22 in Jingdezhen, in east China's Jiangxi Province, with five Spanish ceramic artists attending the event.
"We're very happy because this international fair is perhaps the most important one worldwide in terms of ceramics. The fact that we have 48 pieces from 18 workshops in Talavera is a challenge, and it is also a source of pride for me as mayor of this city," Jose Julian Gregorio Lopez, mayor of Talavera, told Xinhua on Tuesday.
Renowned for its ornate glazed pottery, Talavera has a centuries-old ceramic tradition that flourished in the 16th century. Its traditional ceramic-making processes were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019, alongside those of two Mexican communities.
The pieces selected for the exhibition feature a range of designs and techniques reflecting the diversity of contemporary Talavera pottery. According to the local council, participating artists were given complete freedom to choose works that best represent their artistic identities.
"The ceramics we have at the fair are contemporary, artistic but within the traditional ceramics of Talavera, so that our exhibition is very complete, and our ceramicists will be able to meet their counterparts from China and other countries at this major fair, and see how they work," said the mayor.
In 2025, Talavera hosted a touring exhibition of Dehua white porcelain, known internationally as "Blanc de Chine," from southeast China's Fujian Province. During the exhibition, Dehua officials expressed hopes of establishing sister-city ties with Talavera and expanding cooperation in ceramic craftsmanship, culture and trade.
Talavera's participation in Jingdezhen this year reflects the two-way nature of these exchanges, with Talavera now bringing its own ceramic heritage to Chinese audiences.
"We're doing this exhibition, but then we will also have exhibitions here in Talavera from China, showing their porcelain and their ceramics. It is a two-way street," said the mayor.
Beyond cultural exchanges, Talavera is also seeking to create new commercial opportunities for its ceramic artists and workshops in the Chinese market.
According to the local council, the works displayed at the fair will remain in China after the event, while Talavera will establish a permanent official sales point at the Jingdezhen Official Ceramic Flagship Store, providing a lasting platform for Spanish ceramic products in China. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: East China's Liangzhu offers Chinese wisdom for sustainable tourism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:22 CST
21:48:22 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A silver self-driving shuttle glided past golden rice fields on the outskirts of Hangzhou in east China's Zhejiang Province, linking several cultural landmarks, including the Liangzhu ruins, where an early regional state flourished over five millennia ago.
This route, launched earlier this month, points to a question facing many World Heritage sites: how to protect fragile ruins without turning them into isolated monuments, and how to let surrounding communities share in their value without putting the heritage at risk.
This year marks 90 years since the Liangzhu ruins were first discovered. From Oct. 18 to 20, the fourth Liangzhu Forum brought together officials, archaeologists and scholars from about 60 countries and regions in Hangzhou to discuss issues including advances in technologies for protecting and utilizing cultural relics and sustainable tourism.
"UNESCO believes that sustainable tourism can help safeguard cultural heritage by raising awareness of the importance of heritage for future generations, improving cultural understanding and strengthening local livelihoods," said Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO assistant director-general for culture, in his video speech.
"Liangzhu was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2019. Much of Liangzhu's ancient city layout and its water conservancy system lie beneath the surface, so non-specialist visitors may easily miss what makes the site remarkable," said Wang Shu, director of the Hangzhou Liangzhu Archaeological Site Administrative District Management Committee.
"If the public cannot see or understand it, the social value of the heritage cannot be fully realized. Our focus is on how to translate archaeological evidence into cultural experiences that the public can understand, participate in and share," Wang added.
Technology is helping make such translation possible. At the Liangzhu Museum, visitors can put on augmented reality glasses and watch a virtual exhibit appear to float out of its display case, revealing intricate carvings from every angle without touching the original.
In the virtual reality experience at the ruins, tourists can drift through ancient waterways on a bamboo raft, stand atop the palace to take in the city's grand layout, or walk into a virtual altar to witness a sacred ceremony firsthand.
"Just as tourism needs heritage, heritage also needs tourism," said Michael David Robinson, vice chair and non-executive director for culture, UK National Commission for UNESCO, adding that management plans and clear rules are needed to prevent excessive damage. "You have to ensure that the tourists understand how sensitive some of the archaeology is."
At many sites, conservation has focused on the ruins themselves and the museums built to tell their stories, while development in surrounding areas has followed a separate course. Residents may live alongside extraordinary cultural heritage yet have few opportunities to benefit from it.
Liangzhu's efforts have offered a window into China's practice regarding this global issue.
That effort now stretches across a 634-square-kilometer cultural corridor linking the Liangzhu ruins with the nearby Grand Canal, the world's oldest artificial waterway system and a UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2014, and with surrounding hills, waterways, woodlands and cultural institutions.
"Archaeology shows that over 5,000 years ago, Liangzhu was an early thriving regional state. Today, the same land is still buzzing with innovation and entrepreneurship," Wang said. "Liangzhu is using a corridor-style development approach to strike a balance between protection and growth."
"We have been trying to bring rural communities, urban centers and industry together to let culture benefit people," said Yao Huimin, deputy director of the Liangzhu Museum.
Driven by Liangzhu's cultural resources, the corridor has gathered more than 1,000 cultural enterprises above the designated size. In the first half of 2026, it added 50 such enterprises, with combined revenue exceeding 89.1 billion yuan (around 13.26 billion U.S. dollars), up 37 percent year on year.
Rather than simply restricting construction, Liangzhu has sought ways to turn protection into opportunity for its villages, which are home to residents who have lived on the heritage belt for generations.
In Xin'gang Village, idle land left by the closure of six furniture and brick factories in 2016 was transformed into a standard football pitch. This field quickly drew city dwellers to the countryside, hosting 12 corporate league matches in its first year.
This single move set off a chain reaction. Xin'gang has since built more sports venues, becoming a sports hub on Hangzhou's outskirts. The model is spreading across villages in Liangzhu, with softball, rugby, archery, tennis and pickleball centers now in use.
Raphael Callou Neves Barros, director general for culture, Organization of Ibero-American States, emphasized the need for continuous dialogue with local communities and to ensure tourism does not undermine the sustainability of culture and heritage.
The deeper value of sustainable tourism lies in what visitors take away and what they leave behind, Barros added. They take away not just a sightseeing experience, but an understanding of a civilization. And they leave behind not only short-term consumption, but a positive force supporting heritage protection, community development and the continuation of local culture.
"Heritage conservation does not end at the fence. Its true destination is people's hearts," said Liu Jiecheng, deputy director of Peking University's Institute for Cultural Innovation. ■

DPP's push for cross-Strait decoupling doomed to fail: mainland spokesperson
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:21 CST
21:48:21 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A mainland spokesperson on Wednesday said attempts by Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities to decouple the island's industries from the mainland market are doomed to fail.
Speaking at a regular press briefing, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said the DPP authorities had been desperately obstructing economic exchanges across the Taiwan Strait and catering to external forces.
According to official data, trade between the mainland and Taiwan totaled 301.2 billion U.S. dollars in the first nine months of this year, up 30.3 percent year on year. Mainland imports from Taiwan reached 216.3 billion U.S. dollars, an increase of 27.8 percent.
"These figures fully demonstrate that cross-Strait industrial and supply chains have become more resilient and that markets on both sides of the Strait will never be decoupled," Zhang said, adding that economic exchanges and shared development across the Strait are an unstoppable trend.
The spokesperson also responded to recent remarks by a Taiwan economic official regarding plans by the island's authorities to tighten controls on AI chip exports to the mainland and launch restriction measures that "correspond to U.S. ones."
She criticized the DPP authorities for disregarding the interests of Taiwan's industries and businesses, while following the United States in lockstep to pursue their own political interests, obstructing and restricting normal business operations.
"The mainland is committed to greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology," Zhang said. "External blockades have never been able to hold back our progress, and they will be even less able to do so in the future."
The Chinese mainland's AI core industry was estimated to have exceeded 1.2 trillion yuan in 2025. By the end of September, its smart computing power reached 2,592 EFLOPS, up 146 percent year on year -- EFLOPS refers to a unit measuring computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second.
Zhang warned that the DPP authorities' restriction measures would only benefit opportunists pursuing "Taiwan independence" at the expense of Taiwan's industries and ordinary people, as they are squandering the competitive strengths of the island's industries built through generations of hard work by professionals, entrepreneurs and researchers. ■

Kolkata stampede probe: SIT gets 3 months to uncover cause of tragedy

2026-10-21

21:48:09 KST

19 dead at Kolkata pandal, SIT tasked with probing tragedy and safety lapses
NEW DELHI: The West Bengal government, in consultation with the Calcutta High Court, has constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to probe the October 17 stampede at the Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata that claimed 19 lives and left 25 people injured.The SIT will investigate the circumstances leading to the incident and recommend measures to prevent similar tragedies. According to an official government notification, the panel must submit its final report to the state government within three months of the order.The committee will be chaired by retired Justice Anindita Roy Saraswati. Its members include the Principal Secretary of the Disaster Management and Civil Defence Department, the Director General and Inspector General of Police of the Special Task Force (STF), a police representative of at least Additional Director General rank, a Home and Hill Affairs Department representative of at least Joint Secretary rank, and a representative of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) based in Kolkata.Preliminary findings indicate that the victims sustained multiple traumatic injuries as the crowd surged towards the pandal’s exit during evening rain. The deceased included 13 women and six minors. The youngest victim was seven-year-old Aayansh Srivastava, who had travelled from Bihar with his family.The victims came from Kolkata, neighbouring districts and other parts of West Bengal. Among them were 14-year-old Sandip Bej from Purba Bardhaman, 13-year-old Pranjal Sarkar from Agarpara, and teenagers Priya Samaddar, 18, from New Barrackpore, Akriti Kumari, 17, from Bally, and Barnali Haldar, 17, and Tania Biswas, 18, from New Town.
Meanwhile, the Kolkata Fire Department has placed five Durga Puja pandals in South Kolkata under special scrutiny following the tragedy. The department has issued written instructions to the committees of Chetla, Tridhara, Deshapriya Park and Tollygunge Cultural, directing them to pay particular attention to entry and exit routes and implement additional fire safety measures.
The state government has announced compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a job for the family of each deceased victim. The Special Task Force has also begun an investigation to establish accountability for the incident.Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, along with the Chief Secretary, Home Secretary, Director General of Police and Commissioner of Police, is closely monitoring the situation.Hospitals have begun discharging injured survivors in phases. Fourteen patients were shifted to a private hospital off EM Bypass after initially receiving treatment at Medical College and Hospital and RG Kar Medical College and Hospital.

'Avoid airing anti-national content': Govt warns TV channels against inflammatory debates and AI misuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:48:06 UTC
21:48:06 KST

NEW DELHI: The ministry of information and broadcasting on Wednesday issued an advisory to satellite TV channels, asking them to avoid live coverage of anti-terror operations, exercise caution while broadcasting violent visuals and refrain from airing anti-national content.In its advisory, the ministry asked channels to strictly adhere to the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994."The ministry of information & broadcasting has observed instances of non-compliance with the provisions of the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, by various private satellite television channels," the ministry said."Instances of similar news/visuals broadcast on multiple channels on similar topics were observed during the meeting of IDC. Therefore, IDC recommended that all private satellite television channels be advised to strictly adhere to the statutory provisions governing content broadcast on television. The committee also emphasised that inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalized in telecast," it added.
The guidelines cover live coverage of anti-terror operations, violent visuals, crime reporting, natural disasters, the use of authentic maps of India, communal harmony and the protection of sexual assault victims' identities.On communal harmony and debate programmes, the ministry said channels must ensure that programmes, including live debates and panel discussions, "do not promote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudes".
Broadcasters have also been cautioned to exercise due care while using artificial intelligence, including generative AI, in programmes such as graphics and virtual news presentations.The ministry said AI tools "may be limited to assistive capacity" without compromising the "accuracy, authenticity, or sensitivity" of news content.The ministry further asked broadcasters to strengthen their editorial and content-review mechanisms and regularly sensitise and train personnel involved in news gathering, editing, production, transmission and telecast.The ministry said violations of these guidelines may invite action under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. The joint Japanese-US military exercise Keen Sword poses security risks to Russia’s Far Eastern borders, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a news briefing.
"Amid Japan’s current course toward remilitarization, this military activity, like many others, has lost its original, strictly defensive character as previously defined in Japanese legislation," she said.
"We have repeatedly conveyed to the Japanese side our serious concern over this trend, as such actions create additional security risks along Russia’s Far Eastern borders. In light of historical realities, these concerns are well founded," Zakharova concluded.
The joint US-Japanese military exercise Keen Sword is taking place in Japan and surrounding waters from October 19 to 29. It involves approximately 45,000 Japanese military personnel and 12,000 US troops.

Documents
Details
Timetables for operational low flying (OLF) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas (TTA) only. These are:
- LFA 7(T): central Wales
- LFA 14(T): northern Scotland
- LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England
When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.
Other low flying schedules
Related information
- Low flying military aircraft includes information about how to contact MOD about low flying in your area
- Military low flying includes detailed information about why we carry out low flying in the UK

How Israel's election could play out as polls forecast deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:47:39 UTC
21:47:39 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israel's election could play out as polls forecast deadlock
Israel could be heading towards another political crisis after its general election on 27 October, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, retired general Gadi Eisenkot, expected to secure a parliamentary majority.
With the two rival blocs neck and neck in the polls, the vote could trigger weeks of difficult coalition negotiations, leaving the country without a new government and potentially forcing another election.
The stakes are particularly high as Israel remains embroiled in regional conflicts, while deep divisions over military conscription, Palestinian statehood and the role of the far right threaten to complicate efforts to form a government.
Netanyahu's far-right bloc and Eisenkot's opposition coalition both face significant obstacles to securing the 61 seats needed to control the 120-member Knesset.
As Israel prepares to head to the polls on Tuesday, several scenarios could determine who governs the country next.
A Knesset majority
The simplest outcome would be for either the pro-Netanyahu group or Eisenkot's coalition to win more than 60 seats in the vote.
Current polling indicates that this is unlikely. An average of polls tracked by The New Arab over the past week shows that both sides are likely to fall short of a majority by around 10 seats.
Nevertheless, with a week to go before the vote, there is plenty of time for something dramatic to happen that alters the course of the race. US news reports suggest that Netanyahu and Trump have been discussing a renewed attack on Iran, while both leaders have escalated their rhetoric against Tehran in recent days. Few would be surprised if the two made a move against Iran if Netanyahu's position remains shaky ahead of election day.
That said, a majority doesn't necessarily ensure the quick formation of a government given the frictions among both coalitions.
While considered allies of Netanyahu, neither of the Haredi parties is guaranteed to go back into government with him given the continued tensions over the conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews. Shas and United Torah Judaism, which quit the coalition last year over the issue, will want commitments that religious Jews will remain exempt from military service before entering the next government.
Meanwhile, the Eisenkot coalition is united on its opposition to Netanyahu and a Palestinian state but little else. Its members range from the hardline ultranationalist Yisrael Beiteinu to the Democrats party led by Yair Golan. Golan, a former general, doesn't support a two-state solution but is against the annexation of the West Bank and supports negotiations with the Palestinians, putting him at odds with the rest of the coalition.
Coalition horse-trading
In the likely event that the vote produces a stalemate, it will fall to both sides to negotiate with other parties to expand their coalitions.
The Arab parties – which include the Joint List, an alliance of Palestinian parties spanning nationalist, secular and communist traditions, and the conservative Ra'am – are projected to win 14 seats between them, potentially leaving them holding the balance of power.
Between them, Ra'am's Mansour Abbas is most likely to do a deal to enter government with Eisenkot, in a repeat of his agreement with hardliner Naftali Bennett in 2021. There are potential roadblocks from within the coalition, with Yashar members opposing a deal with the party.
Assuming a deal can be done, including Ra'am in the coalition would only get Eisenkot so far. The party is expected to win only five seats, leaving him short of a majority.
That leaves the Joint List and the Haredi parties as potential pathways to government. Cooperating with the Joint List – which includes Sami Abu Shehadeh's nationalist Balad, Yousef Jabareen's left-wing Hadash and Ahmed Tibi's Ta'al – is scarcely thinkable, given the chasm that separates the two sides.
Alternatively, Eisenkot could look to enter talks with Shas and UTJ, which are projected to win 15-16 seats. That, theoretically, would get him over the line but would likely come with the cost of fracturing his existing coalition. Such a deal would require them to make a huge compromise over the draft – one which they are unlikely to swallow. Yisrael Beiteinu's Avigdor Lieberman is particularly hardline on this issue and has long refused to enter government with Shas or UTJ.
Minority government
Should negotiations stall, one side could decide to govern as a minority. This has never happened after an election in the country's history and would be a recipe for political instability.
It is also an option for Eisenkot if he can convince his coalition to make an informal arrangement with the Joint List. Jabareen said this month that he could agree to provide backing in the Knesset to an Eisenkot minority government if it means keeping Netanyahu out of power.
Such support would not necessarily require the Joint List to join the government or formally back it in every parliamentary vote. It could instead involve abstaining from confidence votes to allow a minority administration to take office.
But it's a big if. Jabareen has outlined conditions for the group's support, including commitments to combating spiralling crime in Arab communities and supporting a Palestinian state, the latter of which is anathema to every party in Eisenkot's coalition. Any arrangement would therefore depend on negotiations rather than unconditional or automatic backing.
National unity government
Given the potential for a post-election political crisis, speculation has increased in recent days about whether Netanyahu and Eisenkot could come together to form a unity administration and block the Kahanist right from staying in power.
Both leaders have flatly rejected the possibility of going into government with each other, though President Isaac Herzog is reportedly trying to bring them together.
Assuming the Likud leader were to cut ties with the extreme right, such an arrangement would still require the backing of most of Eisenkot's coalition, all of whom have staked out stridently anti-Netanyahu positions.
The record shows that such an administration is unlikely to last long. The most recent unity government - between Netanyahu and Benny Gantz in 2020 - barely lasted six months before it collapsed and new elections were called.
A new election
If all efforts to form a government fail, Israel could be forced to hold another election, raising the prospect of a return to the political paralysis of 2019 to 2021, when the country held four elections in just two years.
A prolonged deadlock in 2026 could prove even more destabilising, with the Israeli military engaged in conflicts on multiple fronts and social tensions continuing to rise.
With Trump threatening to relaunch the war on Iran next month and Israeli settler violence escalating across the occupied West Bank, a political vacuum could provide Netanyahu's Likud party and the increasingly powerful far right with an opportunity to advance their ambitions at home and abroad.

German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:47:04 UTC
21:47:04 KST

German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
A German sniper who deserted the Ukrainian military after failing to receive a promised payment has been detained by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), the agency announced on Wednesday.
In footage released by the agency, the man said he had served with German forces in Afghanistan between 2004 and 2010, took part in fighting in Somalia from 2006 to 2008, and later fought as a mercenary in Syria between 2008 and 2010.
The former Bundeswehr soldier said he then served as a sniper with Ukraine’s 25th Territorial Defense Battalion near Donetsk between 2016 and 2018, alongside fighters mainly from Britain and Georgia.
He later moved to Switzerland before returning to Ukraine in November 2025 to sign another three-year military contract the following month. The man said he held the rank of corporal and served as a sniper.
“After signing the contract, I was promised a payment of 100,000 hryvnias ($2,200). However, I did not receive this money and was forced to flee the Ukrainian armed forces,” he said in the testimony.
The FSB released copies of the German national’s military documents and contracts, with his identity concealed, as well as photographs showing him alongside other fighters. The agency said he could face criminal charges for mercenary activity under Russian law.
The detention comes a week after the FSB apprehended Swedish national Freddy Mikael Stalkrantz Lindholm in Russia’s Pskov Region. According to the agency, he crossed the border illegally to carry out sabotage and terrorist attacks on Russian military facilities, posing as a prospective recruit for the Russian Army.
Lindholm previously commanded a drone unit in Ukraine’s Aidar battalion, which Russia has designated a terrorist organization. He faces charges of illegally crossing the border, while investigators are considering additional charges related to terrorism and mercenary activity.
US investigators have also reportedly uncovered a scheme in which Mexican drug cartels sent their members to Ukraine to gain battlefield experience and paid officials close to Vladimir Zelensky for their “training,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on Tuesday.
Kiev has increasingly turned to foreign fighters as its military struggles with manpower shortages, draft evasion, and desertion. In March, then-Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov identified the recruitment of more foreigners as one of the measures aimed at tackling Ukraine’s mobilization crisis.
At least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have fought for Kiev since 2022, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova told the OSCE Forum for Security Co-operation earlier this month, saying most came from the US, UK, Canada, and Georgia.
Moscow has repeatedly pursued criminal cases against foreign fighters fighting for Kiev, including prosecutions in absentia, and has warned that mercenaries are not entitled to prisoner-of-war protections under the Geneva Conventions.

Israel condemns eastern Libyan parliament's policy flip, ratification of Turkey maritime deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:46:24 UTC
21:46:24 KST

Israel's Foreign Ministry released a statement on Wednesday condemning the Libyan House of Representatives (HoR) for ratifying a maritime jurisdiction memorandum with Turkey.
"Israel strongly condemns the decision of the Libyan House of Representatives to ratify the Maritime Jurisdiction Memorandum between Turkey and Libya. This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of our close allies in the region. Regretfully, once again, we see Turkey working to destabilize the eastern Mediterranean region," the ministry wrote on X/Twitter.
Egypt's Foreign Ministry also rejected the deal, saying in a statement that the ratification will have no legal impact on Cairo. The deal approved on Tuesday is part of a years-old dispute over competing claims to sea borders and energy exploration rights in the eastern Mediterranean.
The HoR is the legislative body representing eastern Libya, based out of Benghazi and Tobruk.
HoR backed the maritime deal with Turkey to "bring strategic economic, political, and national security advantages," according to two lawmakers who spoke with Reuters. The backing of the deal overturns a 2020 decision to cut political ties with Ankara.
Control of Libya is split between rival western and eastern administrations, with the east under Libyan National Army Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar. Turkey has in the past been a major backer of the internationally recognized Government of National Accord (GNA) in the west, succeeded by the Government of National Unity, which still holds de facto international recognition and rules from Tripoli.
'Some countries may be upset,' but Libya follows national interest
The maritime deal covering claims in the eastern Mediterranean had been agreed to by the GNA with Turkey in 2019, but was rejected by authorities in eastern Libya, as well as by Egypt and Greece, sparking a boycott.
Libyan lawmaker Tarek al-Jeroushi told Reuters the agreement would strengthen Libya's position as a political, military and economic partner to major powers.
"Some countries may be upset by this agreement, but what matters to us is our national interest," he said.
Lawmaker Aisha al-Tabalqi told Reuters the agreement was approved after specialized committees presented a full and detailed explanation of its provisions.
The parliament unanimously revoked two decisions issued in 2020: one rejecting the ratification of maritime and security memorandums signed by Libya's GNA and Turkey, and another cutting political relations with Ankara.
Greece on Tuesday rejected the decision, saying the deal was without legal effect.
James Genn contributed to this report.

currently "at the centre of a perfect storm", Maurizio Martina,

conflicts are causing for shipping, from the Strait of Hormuz to

FAO can play a key role.

principle: food and agricultural commodities should always
remain outside conflict".

Nvidia announces plug and play Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:43:49 UTC
21:43:49 KST

Nvidia announced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing.
The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said.
"The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week.
The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers.
Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analysts say a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million.
The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027.
Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated.
"What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said recently on a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up."

See one of the most iconic meteor showers at its peak this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:43:17 UTC
21:43:17 KST

Bright flashes of shooting stars are set to streak across the night sky this week as the Orionids meteor shower hits its peak—and if you’re lucky (and patient), you could spot dozens of these meteors.
NASA estimates stargazers might see three to six meteors per hour in suburban areas, with even more shooting stars likely to be seen in rural areas with less light pollution. Night owls can rejoice: the “prime viewing window” will occur after the moon sets around 3 A.M. over the nights of October 21 and October 22, NASA says.
The Orionids’ shooting stars are particularly fast and bright. They travel at around 41 miles per second, and the fastest ones can leave fiery trails of debris in their wake or even ignite into fireballs.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Meteor showers are the beautiful remains of debris trailing from comets and asteroids. As that debris hits our atmosphere, it burns up, creating the light shows we know as meteor showers and love to view. The Orionids gets their name from the constellation Orion because the shower seems to flow from that direction, but that’s not their true origin. These meteors were once part of Halley’s Comet.
The comet sheds rock, dust and ice as it shoots through the solar system. This iconic space rock is visible from Earth once every 75 to 76 years or so—it is famous for its brightness, appearing in historical records stretching back for millennia. Although we won’t see Halley’s again until 2061, the Orionids offer a glimpse of its leftovers.
If you can’t catch the Orionids, look out for a spooky full moon that’s traditionally called the “hunter’s moon” next week, on October 26. Plus, the Taurid meteor showers, which have been shooting across the sky since September, are set to peak next month: you can catch the Southern Taurids’ peak on November 4–5 and the Northern Taurids’ peak on November 11–12.

France Protests: How Fuel Prices, Student Anger are Driving Riots and Unrest

France Protests: How Fuel Prices, Student Anger are Driving Riots and Unrest

====================================================================================================

Why Europe's student protests signal a deeper education crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:40:03 UTC
21:40:03 KST

A wave of youth-led protests has swept across Europe, from France and Belgium to Spain, Portugal, Germany, Italy, Albania, and Greece, reflecting growing frustration among young people who feel the political establishment is increasingly ignoring their educational needs.
The protest in France began at the Saint-Exupéry high school in a Paris suburb before spreading to schools across the country.
French high school students and their peers across Europe have demanded better educational facilities, more teachers, smaller classes and adequate funding and learning resources.
While university students, trade unions, and other parts of French society have backed the protests and consider the demands legitimate, the demonstrations have also been marked by looting and violence, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to call on security forces to restore “calm and order”.
Emmanuel Dupuy, a French political scientist at the Catholic University of Lille, which has also witnessed these protests, says there is "a big difference" between earlier student protests and the violence that erupted over the weekend, when more than 3,000 stores were damaged or looted across France.
Videos also showed Limoges' historic town hall in flames.
While Dupuy describes the latest violent protests as riots, he sees student protests, from high schools to universities, as driven by legitimate demands over poor school conditions, from infrastructure to teacher shortages, and growing concerns about whether their education will help them secure jobs.
"The same sort of resentment" has become a powerful trend not only in France but also among young people in other European countries, the French professor tells TRT World
Beyond France, massive student protests erupted in Italy, with more than 400,000 people participating over the weekend, while similar protests against education budget cuts turned violent in Belgium.
“France reflects a wider European challenge affecting students, teachers and families,” Riyad Rogiest, a Ghent-based Belgian teacher, tells TRT World, referring to a growing education crisis across Europe.
This challenge is “particularly visible in schools serving socially disadvantaged communities”, where problems often accumulate, he adds.
“The anger we see in France is not simply about education budgets. It is also about young people who feel increasingly abandoned by the system.”
Education ‘falls victim’ to economics
Under Macron, a former Rothschild investment banker, the government has cut public spending, reduced corporate taxes and employer social contributions, and replaced the wealth tax with a narrower levy on property assets.
But France continues to face sluggish economic growth and mounting public debt, which reached 119.1 percent of GDP in the second quarter of 2026.
From the COVID-19 crisis to recent US-Europe tensions over NATO defence spending and ongoing escalations in the Strait of Hormuz, which have driven up energy prices, successive crises have put additional pressure on public finances, raising questions about governments' spending priorities, including investment in education.
These policies “have had some consequences and education is one of their victims,” Dupuy tells TRT World, referring to education spending cuts.
He says the current Macron government has not sufficiently considered the need to invest in education.
Dupuy also believes that the French education crisis extends beyond Macron’s governments.
“We haven't sufficiently invested in education over the last 20 years, and we're paying the price for that,” he says. “It has collapsed and is in very poor shape.”
While France and many developed European countries have long been admired by non-Western populations for their educational, economic and political standards, the current protests have shocked many international observers.
This international perception no longer reflects the realities on the ground in Europe, as "a sort of dream land" for non-European education "no longer exists in our countries," says Dupuy.
He also points to how the rise of AI has contributed to the decline of French education.
"New specialities like artificial intelligence are more linked to human resources, or management, which has never been a sort of French excellency," he says, noting that France has traditionally excelled in law and other social sciences.
Like France, other European countries also suffer from "the same reasons of shifting priorities" from education to sectors such as health, defence and AI, Dupuy adds.
"We didn't understand how low our investment was in education. But the situation is now so dire that there was an obligation to improve conditions for the sake of the new generation," he says.
‘Teachers are overwhelmed’
Among other measures, France's draft 2027 budget, which proposes eliminating 1,588 teaching posts in a country already facing overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages, has drawn criticism from teachers' unions amid growing student unrest.
In 2019, Macron's proposed pension reforms sparked widespread protests, adding to public anger after the Yellow Vest movement began in 2018 over fuel tax increases.
Despite continued opposition, Macron's government enacted a new pension reform in 2023, gradually raising the retirement age from 62 to 64, although the timetable was subsequently suspended until 2028.
But Macron’s position has been significantly weakened in recent years, as his decision to call snap elections in 2024 led to a divided parliament and further weakened his centrist allies. Since then, France has seen repeated changes of prime minister, with successive governments struggling to secure parliamentary support.
Amid growing protests, Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced plans to deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to schools facing shortages, a measure backed by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
But experts say this may not resolve the structural problems facing education systems in France and other European countries.
“We are facing a serious teacher shortage, while the teaching profession is becoming less attractive. Teachers are increasingly expected to be educators, psychologists, social workers, mediators and administrators simultaneously. Many experience exhaustion or burnout,” Rogiest says.
On the other hand, many young people carry frustrations from home into the classroom, as financial difficulties, family conflicts, parental separation, social media and a lack of emotional support deeply affect their behaviour and motivation, he adds.
These behavioural problems require additional meetings, administrative reports, and constant follow-up, leaving less time for teaching and personal interaction with students.
In Belgium, for example, new rules introduced in September 2026 require secondary schools, in principle, to organise supervision or alternative activities when lessons are cancelled.
Although limited exceptions exist, Rogiest says this creates additional organisational pressure on teachers.
He also notes that the current digital age makes his job difficult in certain ways, as students are increasingly influenced by social media and constant digital stimulation, which creates unrealistic teaching expectations.
“We expect teachers to solve society's problems inside the classroom, while giving them fewer resources and less time to build relationships with their students,” he says.
“This is neither fair to teachers nor beneficial to children.”
Future of European education
Europe has been facing not only rising inflation, which has increased the cost of living, but also growing political divisions between left-wing and far-right groups, both of which accuse mainstream politics of social and economic problems.
While worsening economic conditions hit classrooms, leading to various cuts in the educational sector, political divisions do not help countries meet the new generation’s demands, exposing deep social insecurity in the new digital age.
“European education has many strengths, but I am deeply concerned about its increasing focus on economic productivity rather than human development,” Rogiest says.
“Historically, we spoke about the humaniora: an educational tradition that sought to develop the whole human being, intellectually, morally, culturally and socially.”
But today, education is increasingly reduced to obtaining qualifications, entering the labour market, becoming economically productive, and paying taxes, he adds.
While earning a decent salary is important for a decent life, education must be much more than professional training, according to Rogiest.
“We should not only ask what profession our students will have, but what kind of human beings they will become.”
From this perspective, Rogiest says the future of European education depends on restoring its human dimension.
“We need smaller classes, better support for teachers, more investment in mental health and stronger cooperation between schools and families.”
While digital education and artificial intelligence offer enormous opportunities, young people “need guidance in developing concentration, discipline, empathy, responsibility and critical thinking,” he says.
Without these fundamental skills, modern technologies will help students little, he adds. This also requires restoring the dignity and attractiveness of the teaching profession.
“Education should not simply produce skilled workers for the economy,” Rogiest tells TRT World.
“It should develop responsible, compassionate and thoughtful human beings who can contribute positively to society. That is the educational vision Europe needs to rediscover.”
