Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:18:10 UTC
21:18:10 KST

Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
Iran’s nuclear enrichment has emerged as a major point of contention amid diplomatic push to end the war.
The renewed diplomatic push to end the United States-Israel war on Iran is facing headwinds as Tehran’s nuclear programme, which the two countries invoked to launch the war in February, has once again emerged as one of the biggest stumbling blocks in reaching a ceasefire.
Nearly eight months into the war, which has caused a global energy crisis, a deal to ensure a permanent ceasefire remains elusive. Moreover, the war has since spilled into a regional conflict, with Yemen emerging as its latest theatre.
The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz – a global oil chokepoint – was the focus of the June Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran.
The MoU had also stated that Iran “shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons”, but a comprehensive deal, including the nuclear issue, could not be thrashed out within the stipulated 60-day period. Analysts said that differing interpretations of the agreement clauses caused the MoU to fall apart.
Now the nuclear issue has once again emerged as the central point of contention, with Tehran insisting that uranium enrichment is a right guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
US President Donald Trump, on the other hand, has called for “zero uranium enrichment”. His ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on Sunday reiterated his pledge to topple the Iranian government, which he said is key to preventing it from developing nuclear weapons.
Earlier this week, US Vice President JD Vance appeared to offer concessions on the nuclear doctrine to reach a deal.
While Qatar and Pakistan are engaged in mediation efforts, how will they get the sides to agree on the nuclear enrichment issue?
What is Iran saying?
Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, who is also a key negotiator in the conflict, is currently in Tehran, where he met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday.
In the meeting, Rezaei said “even a particle of enriched uranium will not exit Iran at all,” according to comments carried by Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency, describing the material as a major national asset that would remain in the country for domestic use.
His response came amid media reports that the US wants Iran to transfer part of its enriched uranium out of the country. Trump has previously called for the removal of the enriched uranium stockpile from Iran.
Rezaei also said negotiations with the US would not begin until Washington fulfils trust-building measures, including meeting the latest conditions Iran has set.
Iran wants the US to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets as part of its latest terms to end the war. In return, Iran has promised to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Another Iranian lawmaker, Alaeddin Boroujerdi, also a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated that Iran is not seeking the production of nuclear weapons.
“Iran’s enrichment activities are unrelated to the US, and Washington should focus on fulfilling its own obligations regarding nuclear arms reduction,” he said.
Where does the US stand?
Addressing a Republican Party campaign rally earlier this week, Trump claimed that the US bombing had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities and that he would not allow Tehran to rebuild them.
“They cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told his supporters at a rally at Northern Kentucky University.
Vice President Vance said earlier this week that the US has “in some ways decisively won” the war on Iran and has destroyed the country’s nuclear programme.
He told a town hall hosted by CBS News that the US was now focused on ensuring that Iran makes a “long-term” and “verifiable commitment” not to rebuild its nuclear programme.
“Not over the administration of Donald Trump … but five years from now, could the Iranians rebuild that nuclear arsenal? Could they try to rebuild that enrichment capacity?” he asked.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that a decision to end the war finally rests with Trump. “The US will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to have a nuclear weapon. As long as President Trump is in office, they will not have a nuclear weapon,” he reiterated.
Last month, Vance told the Reuters news agency in an interview that Tehran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the war.
“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said.
“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” he added.
What the MoU says about Iran’s uranium programme
The MoU signed on June 17 left the future of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile to further negotiations, but identified downblending under international supervision of the International Atomic Energy Agency as the minimum approach to resolving the issue.
Downblending involves mixing highly enriched uranium with lower-enriched material, making it less suitable for rapid conversion into weapons-grade material.
The MoU left room for Iran to reduce the material’s enrichment domestically rather than surrender it. However, it did not specify the quantity to be downblended, a target enrichment level or a detailed implementation timetable.
“The two parties also agreed to discuss the issue of enrichment and other mutually agreed matters related to the Islamic Republic of Iran’s nuclear needs, based on a satisfactory framework being agreed upon in the final deal,” the MoU clause reads.
That final deal, of course, could not be reached as the MoU expired in mid-August.
The Trump administration invoked the imminent threat of Iran acquiring nuclear weapons to launch the war on February 28, 2026. On the first day of the war, US-Israel strikes killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had banned the development of nuclear weapons in a fatwa, or religious edict.
President Trump has often argued that Iran would use the nuclear weapon “within moments after getting it”, and then “the Middle East would be gone, Israel would be gone, and then hit Europe probably next.”
The US president has spoken out against Iran’s nuclear programme numerous times in the past.
As the war progressed over months, the US focus shifted gradually towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz as a base condition of the ongoing fighting.
Speaking in Alaska last week, Trump again falsely claimed that he had to start his war on Iran because, “[Iran was] two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon.”
In April, Trump had warned that “the enriched material, sometimes referred to as ‘Nuclear Dust,’ will be unearthed by the United States … and DESTROYED.” Later in the month, he told reporters on board Air Force One that the US would “go in with Iran, and we will take it together, and we will bring it back. 100 percent of it back to the United States.”
Mostafa Najafi, a foreign policy analyst based in Iran, noted that “despite [the US’s] insistence on nuclear negotiations and obtaining tangible concessions in this area, [Washington is] unwilling to offer significant concessions such as lifting sanctions.”
The US wants “to secure major concessions solely in exchange for lifting the blockade and releasing some of Iran’s assets”, he wrote in a post on X. “From Iran’s perspective, lifting the blockade and releasing assets is no longer a noteworthy concession for Tehran!”

Fire Point has received a Danish state guarantee for a $113 million loan
Kyiv • UNN
The financing will be provided through the Danish Export and Investment Fund.
Denmark will provide a state guarantee for a loan of 750 million Danish kroner (approximately $112 million) for the Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian drone and missile manufacturer Fire Point. Reuters reports this, citing the Danish government, according to UNN.
Details
As explained by the Danish government, the state guarantee is necessary because, due to the war in Ukraine, the company is unable to obtain financing in Denmark on normal market terms. The loan will be provided through the Danish Export and Investment Fund (EIFO).
According to Reuters, citing a statement by Danish Defence Minister Troels Lund Poulsen, locating production abroad enables Ukraine to protect supply chains from Russian attacks.
The Danish plant for producing rocket fuel is expected to begin operating by the end of 2027.
Let us remind you
As UNN reported, Fire Point is building a solid rocket fuel plant in the Danish town of Vojens in the south of the country, where FP-7 and FP-7.x missiles and boosters for Flamingo will be filled. This is the first case within NATO in which a member state has allowed a Ukrainian defence company to establish a production facility on its territory.
As Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh reported, the plant's total area will exceed 120,000 square metres, with a capacity ranging from 800 to more than 4,100 missiles per year, depending on demand. The construction process required a review of the regulations and expertise governing the construction of such large-scale facilities. In addition, the Danish authorities eliminated more than 20 legislative barriers overall.
During the war in Ukraine, the plant will operate to meet the needs of our Defence Forces; later, it is planned that the fuel will also be supplied to European partners.

Meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff thanked the Russian leader for releasing American teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom Washington considered wrongfully detained, while presenting proposals aimed at securing a ceasefire in Ukraine.
“You often describe President Trump as a humanist. But you are a humanist too, sir. I give you credit, express my respect and thank you again,” Witkoff said.
The praise came against a sharply different assessment from UN human rights monitors, who have documented escalating civilian suffering as Russia intensifies attacks across Ukraine.
The UN verified that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in Ukraine in September. In an update published Oct. 16, its monitoring mission said Russian attacks had continued to cause mass casualties into October, alongside renewed strikes on electricity and heating infrastructure as winter approaches.
Witkoff told Putin he had brought documents outlining possible approaches to a peace settlement and asked him to consider resuming negotiations involving the United States, Ukraine and Russia. He suggested that representatives of technical working groups could participate.
Putin Orders US Teacher’s Release as Witkoff Arrives for Talks
The envoy said there was a basis for moving toward a ceasefire and that he would brief Putin on discussions held in Oslo. He also asked to bring Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a participant in the diplomatic effort, into the meeting by telephone.
Witkoff urged Putin to discuss the next steps toward three-way negotiations even if no decision could be reached during Wednesday’s meeting.
Witkoff arrived in Russia from Norway, where he met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the meeting as positive, saying Witkoff would relay its outcomes to the Russian side.
Zelensky said on Tuesday that Ukraine and the US had agreed on a series of proposals to end the war during their meeting in Norway, including security guarantees for Kyiv.
He also confirmed that intelligence sharing with the US had resumed and said progress on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions could come within 48 hours.
Notably, hours after Zelensky met Witkoff in Oslo, US President Donald Trump said Ukraine “has to want to make a deal” to end Russia’s war, claiming Washington and Europe had spent “a fortune” on Kyiv and that Europe was tired of the conflict.
Trump also said the US had received “nothing back other than high diesel,” apparently defending his recent moves to ease pressure on Moscow.
Kyiv has repeatedly rejected claims that it is obstructing peace efforts, saying it has supported ceasefire proposals and initiatives from international partners.
Zelensky has offered a full ceasefire and proposed direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, while 51 countries signed a joint statement at the UN General Assembly in September urging Moscow to accept an immediate truce.
Russia has rejected such proposals, with Lavrov saying the Kremlin would not pause its war even during potential negotiations.
Tensions between Kyiv and Washington escalated on Oct. 9, when Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin as a Ukrainian delegation was holding peace talks with US officials in Miami.
Zelensky later said Ukrainian officials had been warned that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued striking Russian oil facilities.
The Trump administration also reportedly threatened to suspend the PURL mechanism, which enables European countries to purchase US weapons for Ukraine, including Patriot air defense interceptors.
Trump subsequently called for Ukraine to elect a new president, prompting Zelensky to insist that his removal was a decision for Ukrainians alone.
Kyiv proposed a 60-day ceasefire to allow elections, but Moscow rejected the proposal, offering only a one-day truce. Trump then announced an immediate energy ceasefire on Oct. 11, claiming both sides had agreed to it.
Ukraine signaled its willingness to observe the energy truce and refrained from striking Russian energy facilities, but Moscow continued attacking targets across Ukraine.
Meanwhile, restrictions on Starlink terminals and a week-long suspension of US intelligence sharing reportedly left Kyiv without allied warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks and vulnerable to attacks by jet-powered drones.

EU probes whether Booking.com is doing enough to tackle fake listings and phishing scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:12:34 UTC
21:12:34 KST

There is no fixed legal deadline for the investigation to conclude, but Booking.com can propose measures to address the European Commission's concerns.
The European Union has launched an investigation into online travel platform Booking.com on Wednesday over concerns that it has failed to adequately address fake listings and phishing scams.
EU authorities suspect the company has underestimated the impact of fraud and unlicensed accommodation on its platform and has not done enough to prevent users' data from being exploited by scammers.
"Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
The EU said it was also looking into whether the firm breached rules "because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users".
The probe marks the first investigation into Booking.com under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU's sweeping law regulating online platforms, including social media and digital marketplaces.
The DSA "sets clear responsibilities" and "we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously", Virkkunen added.
Booking.com pledges to cooperate
Booking.com said it was "cooperating fully" with the investigation, adding that "security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities".
"We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travellers and partners," it added.
Under the DSA, Booking.com could face fines of up to 6% of its global annual turnover if violations are confirmed.

Government websites shut down in Finland over critical security flaws
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:12:26 EEST
21:12:26 KST

Government websites across Finland have been taken offline after authorities identified two critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used by websites worldwide. The precautionary shutdowns began on Wednesday, disrupting government services, public institutions and other organisations.
The Finnish Government ICT Centre, Valtori, began restricting incoming public internet traffic at 12.45 pm local time to protect government systems against potential cyberattacks.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Finland's National Cyber Security Centre, which operates under the Finnish Transport and Communications Agency Traficom, classified both vulnerabilities as critical, assigning them a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.
The agency said there was no evidence that attackers had exploited the vulnerabilities, although the situation might change as information about the flaws becomes public.
Valtori stressed that the shutdowns were preventive measures rather than a response to a confirmed cyberattack or data breach. Internal government network traffic remains unaffected.
A software update addressing the vulnerabilities was scheduled for release at 5 pm Finnish time on Wednesday. Valtori said it would install the patches across the PHP applications it maintains and restore public access once security checks were complete.
The shutdowns have disrupted services across Finland. The National Land Survey of Finland experienced website outages, while Helsinki University reported disruptions linked to the security measures.
Finnish national broadcaster Yle also confirmed outages affecting several of its online services.
The interruptions extended beyond government agencies. The Finnish Film Foundation (SES) announced on Instagram that its website had been shut down.
Helsinki’s Messukeskus convention and exhibition centre also reported that its website, messukeskus.com, and event pages were temporarily unavailable. The centre said it expected services to resume at around 5 pm on Wednesday, once the necessary updates and security checks were completed.
Valtori director-general Hannu Naumanen told Finnish news agency STT that the shutdown process had begun shortly after 1 pm.
PHP supports websites, content management systems and online shopping platforms across the internet. The vulnerabilities therefore extend beyond Finland's government infrastructure.
The National Cyber Security Centre urged website administrators to install the security updates immediately after their release, prioritising systems accessible through the public internet.
Valtori said it would continue assessing affected services and restore connections once administrators had verified their security.

Politician who was intentionally hit by car loses both her legs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:10:14 UTC
21:10:14 KST

Australian politician who was intentionally hit by car loses both her legs
Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being hit by a car, her husband said on Wednesday, hailing her as a "fighter" despite critical injuries sustained in what police described as a targeted attack.
Haines, 65, is now in a stable condition at a Melbourne hospital days after being struck by a car on Monday near her office in the town of Wangaratta, which is just over 200 kilometers, or 120 miles, northeast of the Victoria state capital.
The incident has prompted soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare but where police have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse toward elected officials in recent years.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led tributes to Haines, an independent member of parliament and a passionate campaigner for transparency and against corruption. He has also acknowledged the need for Australians to turn down the temperature and embrace respectful disagreement over polarization.
Speaking at the hospital on Wednesday, Haines' husband of almost 40 years, Phil, said that after days in intensive care, surgeons had been forced to amputate both her legs.
"But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said, adding, "The two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind."
Haines' husband went on to describe her as "a very compassionate, caring, loving person" with a "huge" heart.
"Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," he said.
"Extremist views"
The man alleged to have wounded Haines in what police have called a "targeted" attack faced court for the first time earlier on Wednesday.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. He has also been charged with cultivating a cannabis plant and possession of the drug, according to court documents shared with AFP.
Nugent's initial hearing took place at a courthouse in Wangaratta, according to an AFP journalist at the scene. He didn't speak in court or apply for bail, and his next hearing is scheduled for Feb. 4.
In court, Nugent's lawyer Chirag Patel told Magistrate Allison Vaughan that his suffered from idiopathic transverse myelitis, a neurological condition, as well as a concussion. The lawyer didn't explain how Nugent had become concussed. Patel also said his client was suffering from potential mental health issues but had never been diagnosed with any mental health problem.
According to the Cleveland Clinic, idiopathic transverse myelitis is a rare condition that damages the spinal cord's protective myelin sheath and disrupts nerve signals between the brain and body, leading to rapid muscle weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder and bowel dysfunction.
The motive for the attack remains unknown, and authorities will not speculate while the investigation is ongoing. But police said Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical anti-government views.
"We're examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues," Victoria police commissioner Mike Bush told reporters. He said, however, that authorities had no intelligence on the suspect and hadn't seen anything to suggest he posed an immediate threat.
Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett pointed to a growing and concerning level of "extremist views" online, saying the incident was "what many had been dreading for some time."
World "more dangerous"
Helen Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.
The independent lawmaker was standing near the trunk of her car when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on Monday afternoon. Witnesses told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that they saw her pinned between the two vehicles.
Threats against Australian lawmakers and electorate offices doubled between 2021 and 2025, with 1,067 incidents reported to police last year.
Governor-General Sam Mostyn — King Charles III's official representative in Australia — said the nation was crying out for "decency" in the wake of the attack on Haines.
"Australians are yearning for kindness and care, and they're asking us why we've lost the great skill of disagreeing well," Mostyn said, speaking alongside Phil Haines.
Highlighting the tense climate, police in Western Australia charged a man late on Wednesday after he made threats and swung nunchucks at the office of state lawmaker Hannah Beazley, media said.
The incident has drawn comparisons to other acts of violence against elected officials elsewhere, most notably the killing of British lawmaker Jo Cox outside her office in 2016.
"It's a reminder that the world is a more dangerous and divided place than it was a generation ago," Prime Minister Albanese told ABC Melbourne radio.

Russia’s Novoshakhtinsk Oil Terminal Takes Heavy Damage as 8 of 12 Tanks Are Hit, Satellite Images Show
At least eight of the 12 large storage tanks at the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP) in Russia’s Rostov-on-Don were damaged following a drone attack on October 10, according to satellite imagery published by the OSINT monitoring channel Exilenova+.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The extent of the damage was revealed in a satellite image released by Exilenova+, providing further evidence of the impact of the strike on the facility, which handles petroleum exports and reportedly supplies fuel to Russian military forces.
The facility was targeted overnight on October 10, when drones struck the oil-loading terminal, triggering a large fire.
The Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP) operates an oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district, formerly known as Yug Rusi.
The facility handles the storage and transportation of petroleum products, including shipments destined for export, and reportedly provides fuel supplies to Russian military forces. Its annual handling capacity is estimated at between 2.5 million and 3.5 million metric tons.
Petroleum products arrive at the site by rail and road before being transferred to storage tanks and subsequently loaded onto vessels. The facility’s infrastructure includes pumping stations, pipelines, and specialized berthing equipment to support these operations.
The terminal is part of NZNP’s broader logistics network, which incorporates railway facilities and a dedicated tanker fleet. According to the company, the fleet comprises five river-sea tankers and three floating storage vessels.
The reported damage in Rostov-on-Don comes amid further drone attacks targeting Russian oil infrastructure, including a separate incident in the Tambov region.
On October 20, a fire broke out at the Nikolskoye oil pumping station following a suspected Ukrainian drone strike. The facility is connected to the infrastructure supporting the Druzhba oil pipeline network.

Ukraine Spots Mystery Russian Drone With Red-Starred Wings and Gasoline Engine
Russian forces have begun using a previously unidentified gasoline-powered drone resembling the Lancet loitering munition, according to information published on October 21.
Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported the development, citing Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technologies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"A new enemy drone has been spotted on the front. It resembles the Lancet in shape but has a gasoline engine. We are waiting for captured examples to study. Get in touch," Beskrestnov wrote on social media.
Beskrestnov later clarified that information about the drone's designation, manufacturer, and technical specifications had already emerged. However, he emphasized that these details remained unconfirmed and would not be disclosed yet.
The aircraft's most notable reported difference from the Lancet is its propulsion system. While the Russian Lancet uses an electric motor, the unidentified drone reportedly operates on gasoline. Internal combustion engines can provide greater endurance than battery-powered systems, although the new aircraft's actual range and flight duration remain unknown.
The Lancet is a Russian-made loitering munition developed by ZALA Aero Group. It is designed to strike artillery systems, armored vehicles, radar installations, and other battlefield targets. The system uses electric propulsion and is launched from a catapult, with variants carrying different warheads.
The appearance of the unidentified aircraft follows earlier Russian efforts to modify the Lancet family. In September 2025, Militarnyi reported that Russian forces had introduced an updated Lancet featuring a redesigned antenna system. The modification potentially affected the drone's communication capabilities, although Ukrainian forces continued intercepting the upgraded systems.
The rapid evolution of Russian drone designs reflects a broader pace of change that Ukrainian commanders and defense specialists have repeatedly warned about.
At a defense forum in Kyiv on September 25, military officials and industry figures cautioned that frontline technology can now shift within just several months. They called for faster innovation, wider use of artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, and engineering forecasts able to anticipate Russian developments six months to a year in advance.
Ukraine has leaned heavily on its own industry to keep pace, with domestically produced systems accounting for 95% of unmanned aerial vehicles procured for its Defense Forces.

Ukraine’s German Gepard Goes Six for Six Against Jet-Powered Aerial Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:08:04 UTC
21:08:04 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s German Gepard Goes Six for Six Against Jet-Powered Aerial Targets
A Ukrainian air defense crew operating a German-made Gepard self-propelled anti-aircraft system has destroyed six jet-powered aerial targets, demonstrating the continued role of Cold War-era weapons in countering modern airborne threats.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade released footage showing its Gepard crew conducting combat operations, including detecting incoming targets, tracking their movements, and engaging them with automatic cannons.
The brigade had previously reported that the same crew successfully intercepted six jet-powered aerial targets. It did not specify the exact types of aircraft or drones destroyed.
The Gepard is a German-developed self-propelled anti-aircraft system introduced into Bundeswehr service in 1976. Built on the Leopard 1 tank chassis, it was originally designed to protect ground forces against low-flying aircraft and helicopters.
The system carries two 35mm Oerlikon KDA automatic cannons, each capable of firing up to 550 rounds per minute, providing a combined maximum rate of 1,100 rounds per minute. Its effective engagement range against aerial targets is approximately four kilometers.
The Gepard also uses two radar systems—one for detecting airborne threats and another for tracking selected targets and supporting fire control. Its search radar can detect aerial objects at distances of approximately 15 kilometers.
Although initially developed to counter conventional aircraft, Gepard systems have become part of Ukraine’s defense against Russian drones and other aerial threats.
Earlier, a Ukrainian Gepard crew shot down 17 Russian attack drones during a single night of air defense operations in the Khmelnytskyi region, according to Ukraine’s Western Air Command on June 16.

Kazakhstan–Uzbekistan border crossing upgrade completion date revealed
Kazakhstan plans to complete the modernization of the Zhibek Zholy border crossing with Uzbekistan by the end of October, Finance Minister Madi Takiyev announced at a session of the Qurultay, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the minister, Kazakhstan has modernized nine border crossings over the past two years, with Zhibek Zholy set to become the tenth.
“We expect to complete the tenth border crossing this month. It is Zhibek Zholy, a pedestrian crossing on the border with Uzbekistan. What makes this project unique is that it has been funded through sponsorship rather than the state budget. Once completed, the crossing will be able to accommodate up to 70,000 pedestrians and 200 buses a day,” Takiyev said.
The minister also addressed the ongoing queues at the Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan border, explaining that growing passenger and freight traffic continues to put pressure on border crossings.
According to the Ministry of Finance, 650,000 vehicles crossed the country's border in the first nine months of 2026, an increase of nearly 20% compared with the same period last year.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan had announced plans to expand its international route network to 160, with Europe, China, India, the U.S., Türkiye, and Russia identified as priority destinations.

Russia Jailed a 74-Year-Old American Teacher as a “Mercenary”—Now Putin Wants Credit for Freeing Him
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has announced the release of 74-year-old American English teacher Stephen Hubbard, who spent more than four years in Russian custody after being captured in Ukraine and accused of fighting as a mercenary—allegations his defense lawyer disputed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Moscow Times on October 21, Putin announced Hubbard’s release during a meeting with US President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, in St. Petersburg. Putin said the American was already at Pulkovo Airport, preparing to return to the United States. Witkoff thanked Putin for the decision.
The announcement followed a personal request from Trump, who said on October 20 that he had raised Hubbard’s case with Putin and asked for his release.
Hubbard, an English teacher who previously spent approximately 25 years working in Japan, moved to Ukraine after living in Cyprus. He settled in Izium, Kharkiv region, with his Ukrainian partner and taught English online.
Russian forces captured him in April 2022, during their occupation of the city. Moscow subsequently accused Hubbard of joining Ukraine’s Territorial Defense Forces shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
Russian prosecutors alleged that he had signed a military contract in February 2022 and received a promise of at least $1,000 per month to fight for Ukraine. However, Hubbard’s defense lawyer disputed the allegations, maintaining that the American had neither participated in combat nor served in a Ukrainian military unit.
Despite those objections, a Moscow court sentenced Hubbard to six years and ten months in prison on mercenary charges in October 2024. Hubbard pleaded guilty during the proceedings, although his lawyer continued to deny that he had fought for Ukraine.
Former Ukrainian prisoners of war who were detained alongside Hubbard also reported that Russian personnel repeatedly abused him because of his American citizenship.
According to their accounts, Hubbard was beaten, forced to stand for extended periods, deprived of adequate food, and denied proper medical care. In January 2025, the US government formally designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, challenging the legitimacy of his imprisonment.

From surveillance to targeting: Israel's expanding use of AI against Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:07:24 UTC
21:07:24 KST

From detecting changes to Palestinian homes through satellite imagery to scanning faces at military checkpoints and identifying people for deadly strikes, Israel's expanding use of artificial intelligence is raising concerns about how automated technology is being used to control Palestinian lives.
In the occupied West Bank, AI-powered systems are helping Israeli authorities monitor land, buildings and movement, raising fears that the technology could facilitate demolitions and accelerate displacement.
In Gaza, investigations have documented accounts of AI-generated lists of suspected targets being used to inform military strikes, with Israeli intelligence officers describing approval processes that sometimes took just seconds.
"It's all apartheid automation," Mustafa Jarrar, professor of AI at Hamad Bin Khalifa University, told Anadolu.
"What is new now is that the AI is not only collecting and analysing, but also can make orders," he said.
Palestinian researcher Jalal Abukhater warned that the expanding surveillance systems were helping reinforce Israeli control.
"The pattern of behavior, the movement, the people you speak to, it's all monitored and going to one purpose: to aid the Israeli occupation in dominating and controlling this population," Abukhater, the policy manager for Palestinian digital rights organisation 7amleh, told Anadolu.
AI tool identifies changes to Palestinian land
A September 17 report by Al Jazeera highlighted ImiSight, an AI-powered tool used to identify changes to buildings and land, helping Israeli authorities detect structures they consider unauthorised and target them for enforcement.
Initially used in the Naqab desert, where Palestinian Israelis face restrictive building policies and demolitions, the technology has since been introduced in the occupied West Bank, raising concerns about the use of automated surveillance to expand Israeli control over Palestinian land.
Israeli media reported in January 2025, citing Israel Land Authority figures, that ImiSight had helped survey about 10,735 square kilometres in 2024.
The authority said it opened about 495 enforcement proceedings following detections by the system and inspections on the ground. Enforcement operations contributed to the eviction of thousands of Palestinian Israelis.
Jarrar explained that AI systems can compare satellite images taken at different times to detect changes to structures and flag them for further inspection, allowing authorities to identify buildings for potential enforcement action.
Researcher Abukhater said that before such systems were deployed, the process required officials to inspect sites in person before authorities sent forces and bulldozers to demolish structures.
“It would require, you know, human individuals going in to check and verifying,” Abukhater warned, adding that such technologies could accelerate demolitions and deepen Israeli control over Palestinian communities.
Demolitions accelerate amid restrictions
The technology's reported expansion comes amid rising demolitions of Palestinian structures in the occupied West Bank.
Across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, more than 1,100 structures had been demolished in 2026 by the time of UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)'s September reporting, displacing more than 1,500 Palestinians.
According to OCHA data, the annual average number of structures demolished by Israel in Area C over alleged lack of building permits rose about 80 percent, from 537 in 2010-2022 to 966 in 2023-2025.
Area C accounts for roughly 60 percent of the occupied West Bank and remains under full Israeli administrative and security control. Palestinians face severe restrictions on obtaining construction permits, leaving many structures vulnerable to demolition.
In April 2025, an Israel Land Authority enforcement unit was established to operate in the occupied West Bank, according to the UN.
Israeli rights group Peace Now described the move as a step towards annexation, while the UN warned it would intensify discriminatory building-permit enforcement and deepen Palestinian displacement.
In March 2025, ImiSight said its technology helped the authority identify unauthorised land use through satellite imagery, drones and aerial photography, reducing delays in enforcement.
“Years of AI-driven insights have transformed enforcement operations, reducing delays and enabling rapid, effective action in the field!” the company said in a blog post.
Abukhater estimated that the number of demolitions carried out since the introduction of these AI-supported systems has doubled.
"These entire systems are designed in a way to entrench the occupation, to empower the occupation with tools that could accelerate its actions against Palestinian communities," he added.
Facial recognition tracks Palestinians
Surveillance extends beyond land and buildings to the people living in the occupied territory.
In a May 2023 report, Amnesty International documented Israel's use of Red Wolf, a facial recognition system deployed at military checkpoints in Hebron.
Red Wolf scans Palestinians' faces without their consent and compares them with biometric databases to help determine whether they can pass through checkpoints.
Amnesty also documented the Blue Wolf smartphone application and Wolf Pack database, which Israeli forces use to collect and access information about Palestinians.
The organisation said the systems reinforced restrictions on freedom of movement, particularly in Hebron's H2 area, which remains under Israeli control.
It also documented extensive camera surveillance in occupied East Jerusalem, warning that facial recognition technology undermined privacy and discouraged political activity.
Abukhater said Palestinians were being photographed at both checkpoints and during military raids on homes.
"They just take a phone and take a photo of the person's face," he said, describing instances in which soldiers photographed Palestinians at checkpoints even when they did not present identification.
He also described nighttime raids in which soldiers photographed residents, including children.
"The soldiers have targets, and they are told that you should photograph 100 Palestinians a day," he added.
Abukhater said the information gathered could be used to build extensive profiles of Palestinians, including their movements, relationships and personal histories.
He described the wider system as "a big prison" and said Palestinians were subjected to surveillance that restricted their fundamental rights.
Jarrar said information from cameras, smartphones and vehicle identification systems could be combined to build detailed profiles of individuals.
He also said that Israeli forces hack Palestinians' private cameras.
"You identify human, you identify car … different kinds of objects," he said. "You monitor them all the time and so you identify targets."
He explained that AI could also detect unusual travel patterns, such as someone taking a different route between Ramallah and Nablus.
“AI will detect a new pattern and will quickly, basically click alarms,” he said.
From surveillance to military targeting
Alongside the system documented in the occupied West Bank, which primarily involves monitoring and surveillance, investigations into Israel’s military operations in Gaza have raised separate concerns about the use of AI-assisted targeting.
An April 2024 investigation by +972 Magazine and Local Call, based on interviews with six Israeli intelligence officers, reported that an AI system known as Lavender identified suspects as potential bombing targets, and flagged as many as 37,000 Palestinians during the early stages of the war.
One intelligence source described personnel acting as a "rubber stamp" for the system's recommendations, sometimes spending only about "20 seconds" reviewing a target before approving an attack.
Jarrar warned that such rapid approval processes could leave little room for meaningful scrutiny.
"It's all fully automated," he said of the process he described, calling it "machine killing, basically."
The investigation also identified a system known as Where's Daddy?, used to track suspected targets and determine when they entered their family homes. With the system, according to the award-winning NAZA documentary, a phrase as simple as “daddy’s home,” can trigger a bombing.
Jarrar said the wider use of such technologies should concern governments and researchers beyond the region.
"Israel is actually pushing and encouraging other countries to do the same," he said. "It's being a model."
Abukhater warned that the spread of such technologies could accelerate violations against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank as well.
"My concern is that these tools are accelerating the plans of ethnic cleansing, of entrenching the occupation, of solidifying the annexation of Palestinian territory in the occupied West Bank," he said.
Technology companies face scrutiny
The expanding use of surveillance technology has also raised questions about international companies providing digital services to Israeli security agencies.
Microsoft came under scrutiny in 2025 after The Guardian reported that an Israeli military intelligence unit used its Azure cloud platform to store recordings of Palestinian phone calls collected through surveillance in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
On September 25, 2025, Microsoft said a review had found evidence supporting elements of the reporting, including the use of Azure storage in the Netherlands and AI services.
The company disabled specified cloud-storage and AI services used by a unit within Israel's defence ministry, saying its terms prohibited mass surveillance of civilians.
"This is a direct complicity by private company actors with Israeli state actors who are directly violating rights," Abukhater said. "It's something that these companies should be held accountable for."
Jarrar also urged stronger international rules governing the use of AI in military operations.
"We need really a new international law regarding the use of AI in automated killing," he said.

God Save The Queens: New exhibition celebrates the women of punk and 50 years of She Punk history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:05:53 UTC
21:05:53 KST

There’s no denying the boys made a lot of noise. But foundationally, punk is female. A new exhibition opening in London celebrates the women of punk and to mark 50 years of She Punk, Euronews Culture picks five essential 70s female punk albums that every self-respecting fan should own.
Most people will tell you that punk rock kicked off in New York in 1976 when four rascals from Queens released their self-titled debut and gave the world the first punk anthem - 'Blitzkrieg Bop'.
The Ramones' hugely influential debut album celebrates its 50th anniversary this year, with many honouring punk's supposed Year Zero. However, Joey, Johnny, Dee Dee and Tommy didn't come out of nowhere, with several artists like The Stooges, The Velvet Underground and the New York Dolls considered as the music genre's forebearers – the artists who were punk, ie: rejected overproduction and mainstream arena rock, before the movement had a name.
Both a music genre and major cultural phenomenon leading to a subversive subculture expressing rebellion and an anti-establishment spirit through music, fashion and socio-political statements, the word 'punk' usually conjures certain names... Ramones, Dead Kennedys, Sex Pistols, The Clash, Gang of Four, The Damned, Bad Brains, Buzzcocks, Misfits, Black Flag, The Cramps...
The list goes on and there’s no denying the boys made a lot of noise. But foundationally, punk as music, punk as an anarchist mindset, punk as a counter-cultural ideology, is female.
Fearless artists like Patti Smith, Siouxsie Sioux, Nina Hagen, Poly Styrene, Viv Albertine, Debbie Harry, Linda Lunch and Poison Ivy shaped the punk movement in the 70s and were the driving force of a genre that was in fact a revolution. They shattered conventions, pushed boundaries, and tore down the expectations thrusted upon them. And one exhibition knows it.
This Friday marks the opening of "Up Yours! God Save The Queens" - a new multidisciplinary exhibition at London's Museum of Youth Culture which honours "50 years of She Punk!"
Curated by Lauren Estelle Jones, Celeste Bell and Vivien Goldman, "Up Yours! God Save The Queens" brings together rare archival material, unseen photography and contemporary artworks. The exhibit prioritises and celebrates the women who shaped punk culture and shows that the genre should never be reduced to just four rapscallions in Converse or a few safety pins on your jacket.
Because female punk artists and female-led bands have often slipped beneath the radar of certain (not all) music fans, Euronews Culture has put together a by no means exhaustive list of five essential 70s female punk albums that every self-respecting punk fan should own.
These are the albums from the trailblazers who paved the way for every female musician and female led-band that came after them, from Bikini Kill, Hole, L7 and PJ Harvey to Le Tigre, Sleater-Kinney, Yeah Yeah Yeahs and Amyl and the Sniffers.
Patti Smith - ‘Horses’ (1975)
Patti Smith’s debut album redefined the New York punk scene before it even had a name. A regular at Manhattan’s legendary venue CBGB, Smith's dreams of becoming a poet led her to the city's vibrant world of underground literature, art and music. 'Horses' established her as the “godmother of punk”; it's an eclectic and commanding declaration of artistic freedom, merging Beat lyricism with brash rock passion and the minimalist aesthetic of then-formative punk. Songs like 'Free Money' and 'Break It Up' are classics, as is her radical reworking of Them's 'Gloria'. Then there's 'Land', the 9-minute masterpiece which showed that Smith wasn't just a part of forming the punk movement; she was carving out a new space for female artists around the world. (On a side note, when are the Nobel Foundation going to give her the Nobel for Literature?)
Blondie - ‘Blondie’ (1976)
Debbie Harry was another CBGB regular alongside Patti Smith, and she too helped shape the New York scene. Her striking bleached-blond look was part of the visual language of punk, and even if Blondie leaned more towards new wave and pop sensibilities and found more mainstream success (especially with their 1978 classic 'Parallel Lines'), the band's first record had an unmistakable punk DIY energy to it. Kicking off with 'X Offender' (originally titled 'Sex Offender' but renamed because radio stations wouldn't play a song with such a provocative title), the album is a bold, foot-stomping gem which brought pop out of the 60s and shoved it into the 70s with a snarl.
X-Ray Spex - ‘Germfree Adolescents’ (1978)
Poly Styrene, the founder of UK band X-Ray Spex, is recognized as the first multiracial frontwoman of a punk band. She wore braces, made her Day-Glo rags, and sang anti-consumerist lyrics, upending every expectation of what a frontwoman could be. The band's debut album tackled feminism, identity politics, consumer society and not giving a shit about other people's opinions. As she screeches in the anthem 'Art-I-Ficial': “I am a poseur and I don’t care! I like to make people stare!” The album's highlight can be found on the reissue with the empowerment single 'Oh Bondage Up Yours!', with the chant "Some people think little girls should be seen and not heard, but I think 'Oh bondage, up yours! One, two, three, four!”. It became the prototypic British punk rallying cry but also a feminist statement that influenced many punk acts, including the 90s riot grrrl movement.
The Slits - ‘Cut’ (1979)
Another British gem, this time from the trio The Slits, who are not to be underestimated in how they too defined punk as feminist. The band boasted an unpolished style which fused punk rock, art pop and elements of dub and reggae, challenging both the music industry and societal norms. Their 1979 debut album is a defiant and raw collection of anarchic hits like the self-determination anthem 'Instant Hit' (later sampled by Lauryn Hill), 'Shoplifting', 'Newtown', and the classic 'Typical Girls' - a protest against female stereotypes. “Typical girls get upset too quickly / Typical girls can't control themselves / Typical girls are so confusing," incants singer Ari Up, before asking the question: "Who invented the typical girl?" The Slits defied preconceptions through humour, verve and a 'fuck you' spirit. Much like X-Ray Spex, their music would go on to influence countless other musicians and movements like riot grrrl and fourth-wave feminist punk music of the 2010s.
The Raincoats - ‘The Raincoats’ (1979)
Since the "Up Yours! God Save The Queens" exhibition is in London, we're sticking to the UK for our last pick. The first full-length album from the British foursome The Raincoats is perhaps best known for the ramshackle, off-kilter cover of the Kinks' hit song 'Lola', but the rest of the album is a ragged racket to treasure. It's dissonant, odd, features plenty of violins (courtesy of Vicky Aspinall), and is completely captivating. Bolstered by Ana da Silva and Gina Birch's vocals, as well as ex-Slits member Palmolive's drumwork, the anything-goes spirit present throughout the album is at the very heart of punk. The band used their songs to call out the establishment and address societal ills like rape culture and misogyny. If you're looking for a copy, seek out the 1993 reissue, which includes the single 'Fairytale in the Supermarket', and also check out their 1977 song 'No One’s Little Girl' (only released in 1982), featuring the lyrics: "I'm no one's little girl, oh no, I'm not / I'm not gonna be, cause I don't wanna be / I never shall be on your family tree..."
"Up Yours! God Save The Queens" opens on Friday 23 October at the Museum of Youth Culture in London and lasts until 22 November.

Tunisia toughens sentences for five convicted over 2023 Djerba synagogue attack
A Tunisian appeals court specialising in terrorism cases has increased prison sentences for five people convicted in connection with a deadly attack on the Ghriba synagogue on the island of Djerba in May 2023.
The ruling includes harsher sentences for the attacker's fiancée and another individual who provided him with accommodation, according to local media reports on Tuesday.
Both had their prison terms increased from eight to ten years and were fined 50,000 Tunisian dinars ($16,600) each.
The court also increased the sentence of a third defendant from two to six years in prison, while a fourth defendant was sentenced to six years.
A fifth defendant, who remains at large, was also sentenced to six years in prison.
The original verdicts were issued in February 2026 by a Tunisian court specialising in terrorism cases, with sentences ranging from an acquittal for one defendant to eight years in prison for others.
Two defendants had been detained on charges of involvement in murder and membership of a terrorist group, according to The New Arab.
The rulings relate to the May 2023 attack on the historic Ghriba synagogue, which took place during an annual Jewish pilgrimage that attracts worshippers from Tunisia and abroad.
The attack began when a member of Tunisia's National Guard killed a fellow security officer and seized his firearm before travelling towards the synagogue on a quad bike.
The gunman then opened fire near the synagogue, where hundreds of Jewish worshippers had gathered for the third day of the annual pilgrimage.
Five people were killed in the attack, including three security personnel and two visitors, before security forces shot dead the attacker.
The Ghriba synagogue, widely regarded as the oldest synagogue in Africa, was previously targeted in a suicide truck bombing in 2002 that killed 21 people.
The 2023 attack renewed security concerns surrounding the annual pilgrimage, one of the most important events for Tunisia's Jewish community.

School head: Failure is also something one needs to learn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:03:00 UTC
21:03:00 KST

School head: Failure is also something one needs to learn
Parents play a crucial role in shaping their children's self-esteem by providing unconditional support and helping them understand that failure is a natural part of learning, says school principal and trainer Cattre Hein.
"Parents are an incredibly important source of support for their children. A parent's role in supporting their child's self-esteem is to be a secure anchor. Parents need to reflect their child's worth back to them and that reflection should not change because of something bad the child has done or a mistake they have made. Nor should it change because of a bad grade at school, for example. A child is valuable and good enough no matter what and it is the parent's job to maintain that image at home. Our self-image begins at home," said school principal and trainer Cattre Hein.
A child's self-image can become more positive when we recognize their positive actions and efforts. "Working in a school, I see every day how easily children give up. What we want is for children to develop intrinsic motivation. Instead of simply telling a child 'good job,' we should praise the effort they have put in," Hein said.
If a child comes to help stack firewood, something they probably don't want to do, parents should acknowledge that the child came to help anyway and ask how they feel about the fact that their help made it possible to finish the job quickly.
"Similarly, we should recognize small achievements along the way. For example, we could praise a child for making an effort and asking their grandparents for advice, which helped them come up with a topic for their research project," Hein said.
According to Hein, everyone needs to experience failure. "Learning begins when things are difficult and we don't know how to do something. We should accept failure as a normal part of life. Some days everything goes really well, while on other days we can't seem to do anything right, everything goes wrong and nothing works out. But that doesn't make me a worse person. We all tend to give up very easily because failure is extremely uncomfortable. We also need to learn how to fail," Hein explained.
We should also learn to be more forgiving of ourselves. "Young children develop their sense of self through the feedback they receive from their families and at home, while teenagers get that feedback from their friends and social media. It's very easy to start feeling that you can't cope or that you're not good enough. But if we explain to young people how personal growth happens and they begin to understand it, they'll be better equipped to cope," the school principal said.

How to turn brown bananas into the best vegan bread of the bunch – recipe | Waste not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:02:18 UTC
21:02:18 KST

After nine years, I can’t believe I’ve never written a recipe for banana bread for this column, so it had better be a good one, especially after I picked up a huge bunch of brown bananas at the corner shop for next to nothing the other day. This is a vegan bread made with olive oil instead of butter and with the mashed bananas acting as a binder in place of eggs; I’ve also added some miso to boost the umami and overall satiety – the salt enhances the sugar, boosting the sweetness while rounding it off nicely. In the interest of biodiversity and flavour, I’ve used wholemeal spelt flour, but any will do.
Chocolate, spelt and miso banana bread
This has become our go-to banana bread at home because it has crazy levels of deliciousness. The recipe is inspired by a plant-based banana bread recipe I found on Laura Wright’s wonderful The First Mess website, and my tweaked version of her loaf uses extra-virgin olive oil and wholegrain flour for nutrition, flavour and biodiversity; I’ve also used miso instead of salt, to bump up the umami factor.
Makes 1 loaf
280g wholemeal spelt flour
  
1 tsp ground cinnamon
  
1 tsp baking powder
  
1 tsp bicarbonate of soda
  
150g dark chocolate chunks
  
150g walnut pieces

Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and grease and line a 1kg bread tin. Mix the flour, cinnamon, baking powder and bicarb in a large bowl. Set aside about seven pieces each of the chocolate and walnuts to decorate the loaf later, then stir the rest into the flour mix until well distributed. Peel five of the brown bananas and, in a second bowl, mash them with the maple syrup, olive oil, vanilla extract and miso. Add the banana mix to the bowl of dry ingredients, stirring until properly combined, then pour into the bread tin and level out the top. Peel the last brown banana, cut it in half lengthways and arrange on top of the dough with the reserved chocolate and walnut pieces. Bake for an hour, until just cooked through, then leave to cool before slicing.

Western forces behind India regime change talk – Modi party’s ideological parent
The ideological parent of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has slammed talk of regime change in the country in the wake of protests in Europe as a deliberate ploy by Western forces.
Citing recent political upheavals in neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal and the raging protests in France and Albania, the head of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), Mohan Bhagwat, said on Tuesday that such movements were fueled by forces pursuing vested interests inimical to the interests of the country.
“There are many powers in the world that want India to lose,” he said.
RSS, the world’s largest voluntary and Hindu nationalist organization, has between an estimated 4-6 million members across India.
“A storm has blown in from the West,” Bhagwat added. “India is their main target because India is progressing. Regime change will not happen in India.”
The row ignited when a leader of India’s Aam Aadmi Party, Prashant Bhushan, said at a press conference last week: “We want regime change… what is wrong in this?”
Uddhav Thackeray, a former Modi ally in the western Maharashtra state, also demanded “regime change” on Tuesday.
Their comments followed the massive protests by the opposition parties and the youth-led satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in the Indian capital earlier this month demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over millions of names being cut from the voter rolls following a nationwide revision exercise.
The commission has dismissed the charges that the voter roll revision was aimed at boosting the electoral prospects of the BJP.
The other opposition parties have not explicitly described the protests as an effort at toppling the Modi government.
“They claim that changing a regime will change the situation, but that has never really happened,” the RSS chief said at a rally. “Problems will remain, and protests are inevitable in a democracy.”
He added that the protests should be aimed at finding solutions.
The CJP’s protests have found resonance across the country, and police action against the protesters has triggered backlash.
The RSS chief slammed the “forces” exploiting social differences by injecting a sense of victimhood among communities. He urged political leaders, protesters, and administrators to refrain from pursuing a divisive agenda.

Ukrainian officials stole millions in drone deals – investigators
Ukrainian officials allegedly stole more than $5 million by purchasing over 5,000 drones for the military at inflated prices, according to anti-corruption investigators.
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), which exposed the alleged scheme last year, announced on Tuesday that they completed their investigation. The Western-backed agencies, which frequently target Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s inner-circle, put the losses at 254 million hryvnia ($5.65 million).
The alleged scheme operated from May to September 2023, after Ukraine’s State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection (SSSCIP) received $667 million to purchase drones for the military. Investigators say a department head at the agency, which oversees cybersecurity and secure government communications, rigged contracts for 5,100 drones, paying up to 90% above market prices.
Investigators froze assets believed to be proceeds of corruption, including more than $4 million held in overseas company accounts and 17 million hryvnia in Ukraine.
Ukrainian media previously identified all five suspects. The alleged ringleader is reportedly Vladimir Mokrenko, a former procurement chief at SSSCIP. His suspected civilian accomplice was identified as Lviv-based businessman Yury Volyan, reportedly the brother of a businesswoman who is a close acquaintance of Mokrenko.
The other suspects reportedly include another SSSCIP official and two private-sector representatives accused of participating in rigged tenders.
The drone procurement scheme coincided with the final months in office of then-SSSCIP chief Yury Shchigol and his deputy, Viktor Zhora, who were fired in November 2023 amid a separate corruption scandal uncovered by NABU. The two were implicated in an alleged scheme that operated from 2020 to 2022 and resulted in $1.72 million in overpayments for software and related services.
Zhora has also been identified by Ukrainian media as a defendant in a third NABU case involving officials from SSSCIP, the Ministry of Social Policy and the Pension Fund, accused of embezzling public funds through rigged software procurement.
Zelensky’s government has been rocked by a series of corruption scandals involving people close to him since November 2025, when NABU and SAPO accused businessman Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of the Ukrainian leader, of masterminding a $100 million kickback scheme involving state contracts in the energy sector.
Critics accuse Zelensky of presiding over a sprawling corruption network permeating his government, allegedly helping him maintain power and enriching those involved.
NABU’s latest high-profile investigation targeted an alleged protection racket involving scam call centers and officials from the Prosecutor General’s Office. Although he was not personally named as a suspect, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko left Ukraine before being dismissed by parliament last month, according to Ukrainian media. He has denied wrongdoing.

Early fluid intelligence linked to faster gray matter refinement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:00:40 UTC
21:00:40 KST

Early intelligence levels in children can predict the pace of their physical and functional brain development as they progress through adolescence. A large study found that children with higher cognitive abilities experience faster gray matter shrinkage and a more gradual maturation of white matter pathways. The findings were published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience.
During adolescence, the human brain undergoes immense physical and functional remodeling. Gray matter, which contains the main cell bodies of neurons, initially grows during childhood and then shrinks in a process of refinement known as synaptic pruning. At the same time, white matter, which acts as the communication cables connecting different brain regions, typically strengthens as protective sheaths of myelin wrap around nerve fibers.
As the brain physically changes, its functional networks also reorganize. The synchronization between different neural networks, measured while the brain is at rest, evolves to balance integration and specialization. Researchers wanted to understand how individual differences in early childhood intelligence relate to these long-term developmental trajectories.
Previous research on cognitive ability and brain maturation has often relied on cross-sectional data, taking a snapshot of a single moment in time. Longitudinal studies tracking the same individuals over many years have been relatively limited in size and scope. To address this gap, researchers Phoebe Thomson, Philip Shaw, and Divyangana Rakesh from King’s College London conducted a detailed investigation into how early intelligence tracks with multiple brain changes over time.
The investigators analyzed data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study. This is an ongoing, large study following thousands of children across the United States. For this analysis, the researchers reviewed data from 10,495 participants. The data spanned four time points, beginning when the children were around nine or ten years old and continuing into middle adolescence.
At the start of the study, participants completed a battery of tests to assess different facets of their general cognitive ability. The researchers separated these scores into three distinct categories. The first category was fluid cognition, which involves problem-solving, memory, and processing speed.
The second category was crystallized cognition, which measures accumulated knowledge, such as reading comprehension and vocabulary. The third metric was matrix reasoning, a specific type of visual and spatial abstract reasoning. Treating these abilities as separate constructs allowed the research team to see if different types of intelligence corresponded to different biological maturation patterns.
To measure brain development, the team examined three types of magnetic resonance imaging scans. Structural imaging provided data on the volume, surface area, and thickness of gray matter. Diffusion imaging tracked changes in white matter microstructure. Finally, resting-state functional imaging recorded how different functional networks in the brain communicated with one another.
Because family environment can influence both cognitive test scores and biological development, the researchers adjusted their mathematical models for household socioeconomic status. They also accounted for participant sex and the technical variations among different magnetic resonance imaging scanners used at different research sites.
The researchers first looked at gray matter structure across the whole brain. They found that baseline fluid cognition predicted how cortical surface area and volume changed over time. Specifically, teenagers who started with higher fluid cognition scores experienced a faster rate of gray matter contraction.
This faster decrease in gray matter volume and surface area was especially prominent in the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe is heavily involved in higher-order thinking and decision-making. These structural changes align with theories that children with higher cognitive abilities might undergo an accelerated period of neural refinement following childhood growth.
Cortical thickness, a different structural metric, did not show a statistically significant association with any of the cognitive measures. Crystallized cognition and matrix reasoning scores also did not relate to long-term changes in gray matter structure.
Next, the researchers examined white matter development using a metric known as fractional anisotropy. This metric evaluates how uniformly water molecules travel along neural pathways. Higher fractional anisotropy generally indicates thicker myelin sheathing and more tightly packed nerve fibers, which typically increase over the course of adolescence as brain regions become better connected.
The researchers found that early matrix reasoning scores predicted the rate of this white matter maturation. Children with higher matrix reasoning scores started with higher baseline white matter integrity, but they exhibited a slower, more protracted increase in fractional anisotropy over time. This pattern was visible in several major white matter tracts, including those connecting the frontal lobe to other areas.
Fluid and crystallized cognition did not show a statistically significant association with white matter development.
Finally, the team evaluated resting-state functional connectivity, measuring the communication strength between distinct brain networks. They focused on how often separate networks synchronized their activity. Early scores across all three cognitive measures predicted the trajectory of this between-network communication.
Children with lower baseline cognitive scores exhibited a longitudinal increase in connectivity between different functional networks. This general increase was absent in participants with higher initial cognitive scores. Instead, youth with higher intelligence scores showed a faster decrease in connectivity between certain networks that normally decouple during adolescence, such as those governing auditory processing and cognitive control.
When evaluating resting-state functional connectivity at a closer level, the team looked at exactly how specialized networks interact. They noticed that higher crystallized cognition and matrix reasoning scores were linked to a stronger separation between the default mode network, active during internal thought, and higher-order attention networks. Over the course of adolescence, these systems became more distinctly compartmentalized in youths with higher cognitive abilities.
This decoupling process is thought to help distinct brain networks operate more independently. The findings suggest that higher childhood intelligence might relate to an accelerated specialization of these functional networks.
The study provides an observational account of brain development and does not demonstrate that high cognitive ability directly causes these physical or functional changes. The findings could be influenced by shared underlying variables, such as genetics or environmental stimulation, which might independently shape both intelligence and brain maturation.
Because data from the final measurement time point was incomplete at the time of the analysis, the researchers primarily utilized linear models to chart developmental changes. Brain maturation often follows non-linear patterns, speeding up or slowing down at different ages. Future longitudinal tracking covering a wider age range could help map these physical changes with even greater precision.
The study, “Cognitive ability in childhood predicts adolescent structural and functional brain development: A longitudinal study,” was authored by Phoebe Thomson, Philip Shaw, and Divyangana Rakesh.

Submarine propulsion test facility decision due in 2028
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:00:32 BST
21:00:32 KST

SMITE2, a new submarine propulsion testing facility forming part of the wider Submarine Build Modernisation programme, is in its development phase, with dates for the start of construction and for completion to be agreed at a main investment decision point currently expected in 2028, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked when SMITE2 is scheduled to commence and to be completed.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “SMITE2, a new submarine propulsion testing facility and part of the wider Submarine Build Modernisation programme, is currently in the Development phase. Dates for key milestones, such as start of construction and completion, will be agreed as part of the main investment decision point, which is currently expected in 2028.”
Propulsion test facilities let engineers run a submarine’s power and drive train on land before any of it goes into a hull, shaking out the integration problems in a building where they can be reached with a crane. The alternative is finding them inside a pressure hull after the boat is closed up, which is where cost and schedule go in submarine programmes.
Submarine Build Modernisation is the programme rebuilding the industrial capacity behind the Dreadnought class and the SSN-AUKUS boats that follow, and the work covers facilities at Barrow-in-Furness, at Derby where Rolls-Royce builds the reactors, and across the supply chain. The department awarded BAE Systems £2.4 billion for Royal Navy submarine programmes earlier this year, and separate investment has gone into the Barrow site itself.
An investment decision in 2028 puts construction into the back end of the decade and completion some years after that, which places the facility alongside SSN-AUKUS, well after the Dreadnought build. The first Dreadnought boat is due in the early 2030s and is already building at Barrow, with the keel laid for the next generation missile submarine last year.
