Can We Eat Our Way Out Of An Ecological Disaster?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

When Rachel Bowman first tried to bring lionfish to restaurants and grocery stores in the Florida Keys in 2012, it was a hard sell. “We weren’t getting that much money for them, and it took a little convincing,” says the commercial lionfish hunter. That’s because the invasive lionfish—flamboyant enough that Bowman likens it to a Mardi Gras drag queen—wasn’t traditionally on the menu.
Native to the tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific, lionfish have infiltrated the western Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf of Mexico, where they have become a destructive invasive species ever since the first was recorded near Miami in 1985, likely after being released from the home aquarium trade. With few predators in these new habitats, a single fish can produce more than 2 million eggs a year. Studies have found that just one lionfish can reduce the replenishment of native fish populations on some reefs by nearly 80%.
In 2016, Bowman sold the first lionfish to Whole Foods in South Florida. “That was the ground-breaker,” she says, “because if Whole Foods is promoting something, then people know it’s good. We went from $2 per lb. to $10 per lb. pretty much overnight.” Now, 10 years later, through Keys Fisheries, her fish is sold in stores, and lionfish appears on restaurant menus throughout the area—and in doing so, millions of native reef fish have been saved from predation.
Bowman’s work is part of a growing trend that’s not just about introducing new dishes to the local food scene; creating a market for invasive species may also bring ecological benefits for the local environment.
Invasive species are considered one of the five most critical direct drivers of biodiversity loss, according to the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), whose most recent report in 2023 notes that the global economic toll of dealing with these species cost more than $423 billion in 2019. Once established, invasive species are often impossible to eradicate because they reproduce rapidly, spread across vast, interconnected environments, and often go unchecked until they are established. And the challenge of managing invasive species is particularly acute in the ocean, says Helen Roy, a professor at the U.K. Centre for Ecology & Hydrology and the University of Exeter and a co-chair of the IPBES assessment. It’s a consequence of the openness and connectedness of marine systems, she says.
In 2004, conservation biologist Joe Roman coined the term “invasivorism” to describe the idea of eating invasive species to help control their populations. Since then, a growing movement across North America is attempting to transform ecological menaces into culinary commodities, from Florida to Hawai’i, British Columbia, Maine, and the Mississippi River basin. That movement is still expanding: in 2025, for example, 70 restaurants and fish markets across the U.S. participated in Green Crab Week, a national campaign encouraging diners to eat the invasive European green crab.
The goal, says Isabelle Côté, a marine ecologist at Simon Fraser University, is often “functional eradication”: reducing an invasive population to a level where its ecological impacts are considered acceptable. That’s where our dinner tables can help, by turning the removal of the species into an economic opportunity.
David Standridge’s philosophy is all about harvesting what’s plentiful and turning it into something delicious. Since 2022, the James Beard Award-winning executive chef of The Shipwright’s Daughter in Mystic, Conn., has processed more than 10,000 lbs of green crab, making it a menu mainstay.
Commonly considered one of the world’s worst invasive species, the green crab has successfully invaded every continent except Antarctica. The species, native to Western Europe and Africa, has few predators, aggressively hunts its prey, and can consume a wide variety of shellfish, including oysters, clams, mussels, lobsters, and other crabs. One crab can eat more than 40 juvenile soft-shell clams in a day, while also destroying seagrass habitats. And a single green crab can produce up to 185,000 eggs per year, while its larval life stage allows young crabs to drift considerable distances in ocean currents, spreading from one invaded area to another.
Rather than a nuisance, Standridge describes the green crab as tremendously flavorful, producing a beautiful stock that can be used across dishes. “We use them not to eliminate green crab, but to take some pressure off the ecosystem,” he says. Getting green crab onto the menu, however, wasn’t so straightforward.
When Standridge first tried to source the species in 2020, he discovered that Connecticut, like many states, classified green crab as bait and technically couldn’t be sold for human consumption. He finally found a supplier to help in 2021, and then in 2025, a change to a single line of state code allowed green crab and other species on the bait list to be harvested and sold as food. Parks says the market is beginning to take shape. Suppliers across New England now regularly carry green crab alongside other seafood, making it more accessible to chefs.
The green crab’s global spread is only expected to increase with climate change, says Mary Parks, executive director of GreenCrab.org, a nonprofit organization building culinary markets for the invasive species while raising awareness of its impact. “We used to have these really cold winters and those helped keep green crab populations in check,” says Parks. “But with winters getting warmer and warmer, that population control got taken out of the picture.”
On the other side of the continent, in 2020, the first green crabs were detected on Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the coast of British Columbia. To slow the species’ establishment, the Council of the Haida Nation launched a full-scale trapping and mitigation program. Over five years, 36 crews removed nearly 2 million crabs, including more than 1.3 million from the Honna and Tarundl estuaries alone. The scale of the invasion has made control difficult, and harvester and marine economic development coordinator Eli Gladstone hopes a viable market for the crabs could help reduce their numbers. But he cautions that commercial demand alone won’t be enough: trapping will also need to become more efficient, and some continued public investment may be necessary.
Communities across the U.S. have been grappling with the ecological and economic impacts of introduced species for decades.
In the 1950s, bluestripe snapper, also known in Hawai’i by its Tahitian name, ta’ape, was introduced to O’ahu, when roughly 3,000 fish were released to bolster fishing opportunities and establish a new food source. But ta’ape, native to the South Pacific, never became a sustained part of Hawai’i’s seafood market. By the 1980s, the overabundant fish was largely considered a “trash fish,” prompting the state’s Department of Aquatic Resources to launch a market-development project in 1985 that used consumer education and supermarket promotions to try to build demand. The effort failed to gain lasting traction: supply was inconsistent, and demand tapered off after the project ended.
Freediver and spearfisher Kimi Werner has seen firsthand just how dramatically the ta’ape has come to dominate the reefs. Where schools of snappers in their native ecosystems might number just a handful, she says Hawai’i’s ta’ape, with its electric-blue stripes and lemon-yellow skin, can blanket the seafloor. “You can see the power of numbers taking over these habitats where native fish belong,” she says.
Since 2019, Conservation International Hawai’i, in partnership with local businesses and organizations including the nonprofit Chef Hui, has been trying to turn that abundance into an opportunity: promoting ta’ape as a food source to reduce its numbers while supporting local fishers and food security. The approach is starting to resonate across Hawai’i’s tourism industry, says Jhana Young, sustainable seafood senior manager with Conservation International Hawai’i. Hotels now serve the fish to staff and guests; Hilton Hawaiian Village alone purchases about 500 lbs a month. In 2025, an average of 27 commercial fishers sold approximately 42,000 lbs of ta’ape statewide, 47% more than in 2018. And a March 2026 “Eat the Invaders” tournament removed more than 1,200 lbs of invasive reef fish from Maunalua Bay in a single weekend, nearly 90% of it ta’ape. Where fishers once received an average of just $0.65 per lb. for ta’ape in the 1980s (about $2.63 today), says Young, today some O’ahu fishers receive as much as $6 per lb.
“When we started, ta’ape was a fish people threw back or used for bait,” says Amanda Corby Noguchi, co-founder of Chef Hui. “Now we regularly get organizations, schools, and hotel properties reaching out to us wanting to be part of it, not the other way around.”
But creating a market for an invasive species also raises the question of whether it can genuinely serve conservation goals—or simply become another fishery. Young argues that it can redirect existing fishing pressure toward a species whose removal benefits the ecosystem. “Fishers are always going to fish. By helping create markets for a species that didn’t exist before, it helps point fishers in the direction of a choice that is ultimately better for nature’s long-term balance.”
More than 4,000 miles away, in the lower Mississippi River basin, Asian carp populations have proliferated since the species was imported to the U.S. from China in the 1970s. They were brought in to control nuisance algae in wastewater-treatment plants and aquaculture ponds, as well as for human consumption. Within a decade, they had escaped confinement and spread into the Mississippi River basin and its major tributaries, including the Illinois and Missouri rivers, disrupting aquatic food webs, harming native fish communities, and interfering with commercial and recreational fishing. The invasive Asian carp is one of the most urgent, far-reaching, and complex environmental challenges facing the U.S., according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS). And experts now worry about their potential to reach the Great Lakes.
For Angie Yu, founder of Two Rivers Fisheries in Wickliffe, Ky., the potential of invasive carp was obvious. Yu grew up in China, where carp is a dietary staple—so commonplace, she says, that it is eaten “just like chicken.” When she first read about the Asian carp problem in 2010, she saw an opportunity others in the U.S. had largely overlooked: a fish considered “trash” by many Americans but which had an established market in Asia. She began connecting the fish with Asian markets, eventually exporting to 12 countries. Before the pandemic, nearly 90% of the company’s products were destined for overseas markets. But then shipping disruptions, rising fuel costs, and steep international tariffs made exporting increasingly difficult, prompting Yu to turn her attention to building a domestic market. She has since developed a use-everything model for the fish, making meatballs, patties, dumplings, along with pet food, as well as fish meal and fertilizer from the trimmings, guts, and other waste, while finding uses for the skin and bones. Her carp is now sold in Asian supermarkets across the U.S., and her processing plant can handle up to 40,000 lbs of carp a day. “The fish is not trash,” she says, “it’s a treasure.”
The question now is whether commercial demand for invasive Asian carp can grow large enough to meaningfully reduce their populations. For Peter Stoett, a professor at Ontario Tech University and co-chair of the IPBES Assessment on Invasive Alien Species and Their Control, the key is to “measure the population, not the market.” A growing commercial fishery, more restaurants serving an invasive species, or thousands of pounds harvested may signal that a market is working—but not necessarily that the ecosystem is recovering. Reductions in an invasive species’ numbers or biomass, he says, are the clearest indicators of whether management is working. But measuring that requires sustained monitoring: “Money must be spent monitoring these populations or we won’t know if targets are being met.”
Stoett argues that if a market is used to encourage removal, the commercial activity should exist because the species needs to be reduced, contained, or eradicated—not because the goal is to establish a sustainable fishery for that species. In other words, the conservation objective has to come first, with the market serving as a tool rather than becoming the goal itself. As populations decline, he says, there needs to be ongoing dialogue among scientists, industry, local communities, and government about whether incentives should continue, change, or eventually end.
In Kentucky, there is some evidence that removal efforts are having an effect. The Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources has increased its fishing incentive to $0.15 per lb. for invasive carp harvested from Kentucky Lake and Barkley Lake, citing evidence that management efforts are reducing populations in both lakes. Most of the carp processed by Yu comes from those same two lakes. Meanwhile, according to a USFWS spokesperson, around 30 million lbs of invasive carp are removed from Midwestern waters each year.
The idea of harvesting and eating invasive species can sound like an elegant solution: turn an ecological problem into dinner and let appetite do the work. But Roy cautions against treating consumption as a panacea for control. The ecological payoff from harvesting is rarely proportional to the share of a population removed. Taking half of a population, for example, does not necessarily mean halving its impact on the ecosystem.
That does not make the markets emerging around lionfish, green crab, ta’ape, and carp meaningless. They can provide food and income, engage communities and, in some cases, redirect fishing pressure toward invasive or overabundant species whose removal can benefit ecosystems. But Roy stresses that these benefits must be considered separately from the ecological damage caused by an invasion: “There’s no simple sum here.”
Creating demand could theoretically give people an incentive to keep an invasive species abundant, although Côté says she is not aware of evidence that this has happened. And while “nothing beats prevention,” says Stoett, once an aquatic or marine invasion is established and containment is the only realistic option, a market for their safe consumption could provide another tool—one whose economic benefits can be weighed against the ecological impacts of the invasion. The goal, ultimately, is not to eat our way out of an ecological disaster. It is to make sure that, when we eat an ecological problem, we are actually helping to reduce it.
In front of foraging chef Robin Kort’s home on Galiano Island in British Columbia’s Salish Sea, is a sea urchin barren—an underwater desert where kelp once swayed but has since been devoured by the urchins that cover the seafloor like a spikey carpet. Unlike lionfish or Asian carp, red and green sea urchins are native to the region. But when their populations become too abundant, they can have invasive-like effects.
Urchins are remarkably effective grazers. Marine ecologist Anne Salomon, a professor of applied marine ecology and social-ecological system science at Simon Fraser University, says urchins and kelp can coexist when food is plentiful. But when food becomes scarce, urchins form what she calls “active feeding fronts,” stripping away vegetation that provides food, shelter, and habitat for a wide range of marine life. Selective harvesting can help restore kelp forests, Salomon says, but doing so effectively requires sustained effort.
“We have this commercial fishery around sea urchin, and we have, in Vancouver, a huge population that likes eating them,” says Kort, who calls uni “the parmesan of the sea,” describing it as cheesy, creamy, and versatile enough for both sweet and savory dishes. Last year, Kort helped launch an Eat the Invaders event, bringing chefs together to channel people’s appetite for delicious food by cooking with invasive and overabundant species. Part of her effort is to incentivize more harvesting of the older, less desirable but more destructive urchins. “Humans’ greatest power is the amount of stuff we can eat, basically, if we want to,” she says. “So can we use that superpower for good?”

On the Decline in Reading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Sasha Quinton speaks about the decline of reading, lessons in leadership and female leaders, taking calculated risks, and her vision for the future of the publishing industry
I am deeply passionate about this topic, and firmly believe that reading engagement should be a central focus for all of us.
We know reading proficiency has declined significantly. While the pandemic accelerated the trend, the decline began even before that. There are now countless articles discussing a post-literate America and concerns about students reaching college without strong reading skills. It’s alarming.
The encouraging news is that reading proficiency is finally beginning to improve. Our schools, educators, and communities have invested tremendous resources into addressing the problem, and we’re starting to see those efforts make a difference.
What concerns me even more, however, is reading engagement.
We measure how often children choose to read for pleasure on their own. According to the Scholastic Kids & Family Reading Report™, the number of kids who identify as frequent readers has dropped over the past 15 years from 37% in 2010 to 28% in 2022. Furthermore, as kids age, that number of frequent readers drops dramatically as well, from 46% of 6–8-year-olds to 15% of 15–17-year-olds. As we call it, the decline by nine.
That matters because it shows that reading is not only about skill. It’s about desire.
What is one calculated risk you want the publishing industry to take?
I would like to see us make a real commitment to changing access and engagement.
This is a highly solvable problem, and together we can make sure every child born in America has books. I talked before about reading engagement and creating a desire for reading among kids. That begins with access. We need to make sure all kids have the opportunity to love reading.
How do we stay open to the unexpected?
That’s one of the things that makes publishing so exciting: finding something new and fresh. The question is, how do we leave room for that?
I was just talking with Jackie DeLeo, our publisher, about this. You can build an extraordinarily successful list based purely on data: you can identify a category, a price point, a cover style, and create something that performs very well.
But you also have to leave room for genius.
I remember Jackie saying to me, “Nobody would have predicted that a book about a very hungry caterpillar would become a classic.” And she’s exactly right.
The challenge is making space for what is deeply human: creativity, imagination, and the spark that talented teams bring. Whether it’s 10%, 20%, or 30% of your list, some portion should be dedicated to exploration, experimentation, and imagination.
What is one leadership lesson you had to learn the hard way?
Allowing yourself to fail. Part of being deeply human is failure. You learn so much more from failure than you do from success.
I would also say: fail fast, fail often, and build that mindset into your culture. Create an environment where people feel comfortable taking risks because that’s where you ultimately find the greatest rewards.
On women in leadership
Some of our greatest female leaders have demonstrated exactly the traits I emphasized before: exploration, experimentation, and imagination.
I also think progress is cyclical, like the tides. We are beginning to see more women in leadership positions, and that momentum matters.
I believe it was Adam Grant who spoke about how meaningful change happens when representation reaches critical mass. One woman in the room is not enough. But when there are two, three, or more, the dynamic begins to shift and doors start to open.
I’m inspired to be sitting alongside these extraordinary women today. As more women take seats on stages, in boardrooms, and in leadership roles, more will follow. We have so many examples of strong, successful, effective female leadership, and I believe we’ll continue to see that number grow.
What would the publishing industry look like if we had a “Year of Yes”?
One of the things I’ve always admired about Dominique [Raccah, Publisher & CEO of Sourcebooks] is her ability to dream bigger than everyone else in the room.
I first knew her as a customer when she would visit us at Readerlink. She would come in with an idea, and my immediate reaction was often, “That’s impossible. There’s no way we can do that.”
Yet somehow, she would see a path forward, and the impossible would become possible.
Because of that, our leadership team within Scholastic’s Children’s Book Group has adopted a phrase: “It’s impossible unless…” Whenever someone says, “We can’t do that,” the follow-up question becomes, “Unless?” And people almost always know the answer. “Unless we open another warehouse.” “Unless we bring in a freelance design team.” “Unless we change the process.”
That simple shift in thinking opens doors and creates pathways you may never have considered otherwise.
On September 30, 2026, Sasha Quinton, Scholastic EVP and president of the company’s Children’s Book Group, spoke on the She Who Leads panel, part of the Association of American Literary Agents’ annual People of Publishing conference in New York City. This article provides the main takeaways (edited for clarity) from her speech. Alongside Mary McAveny, president & CEO of Abrams, Dominique Raccah, publisher & CEO of Sourcebooks, and moderator Regina Brooks, president of the Association of American Literary Agents,

Apple iPhone Duo Review: Is It Worth It?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Polished hardware with a graceful hinge. Nanotexture finish cleverly hides the crease. Makes multitasking easy. Fun camera features to make use of the multiple screens. Reliable battery life.
TIRED
Heavy. Some multitasking elements are too rigid. Lots of apps aren’t optimized (yet).
It’s a little hard to review the iPhone Duo. I’ve been toting Apple’s first folding smartphone for the past week, and several apps I’ve tried to open on the sprawling 7.6-inch screen look awful. Thick, black bars on the sides, with a phone-sized app in the middle of this tablet-like display. But you likely won’t encounter this problem once the Duo is in your hands.
In the past day, a handful of apps I use regularly updated to add full support for the iPhone Duo’s screen sizes and vertical user interface elements. Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.
Developers need to target the iOS 27.1 software development kit (SDK) for full Duo compatibility. That will take some time. But it is a little maddening that some app developers, who for years have never seemed to care about optimizing their app for Android folding phones, are so quick to embrace Apple’s fold. Slack, for example, never offered the two-pane view of its desktop app in the Android version, but it’s on the Duo. C’est la vie. Hopefully, Apple’s entry into foldables will result in a “rising tide lifts all boats” situation and Android fold lovers will get to enjoy those optimizations.
In Duo Time
The iPhone Duo’s Standby mode turns on when the phone is propped up via a kickstand.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
The iPhone Duo arrives seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold. In Apple tradition, its first entry into an existing category feels fully mature; the Duo has significantly less jank than the first few generations of its Android counterparts. The infamous crease—where the phone folds—is hardly visible thanks to Apple’s display stack and clever use of a matte-finish nanotexture screen. The phone is IP68 dust- and water-resistant (though avoid taking the Duo to the beach, as sand is notoriously detrimental to phone hinges). The software experience, barring the unoptimized apps, feels carefully considered.
Apple has also landed on the right shape, months after Samsung realized it following seven years of narrow, somewhat awkward book-like folds. The wider, shorter “passport” design feels better than what’s come before in this category. The 5.4-inch outer screen is still big enough to be useful, and the hinge glides open gracefully and stays put at various angles. The hardware feels polished.
That’s not to say Apple has completely trounced the competition. I still appreciate that Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Fold8 is super lightweight at 201 grams, as the iPhone Duo’s hefty 254 grams (heavier than an iPhone 18 Pro Max) can get tiring after extended doomscrolling. I don’t love the fact that, when closed, one side of the Duo has angled corners and the other is curved—the Fold8 looks better in that regard. Touch ID also takes a little getting used to after years of relying on Face ID, mostly when you’re holding the Duo with your left hand and you suddenly have to authenticate an app or purchase with your right hand. (It can mercifully auto-unlock if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.)
Apple also tightly controls the multitasking experience. If you have two apps split-screen on the Duo, Apple won’t let you resize one app to be slightly bigger than the other like you can on Android. Here, a 50-50 split is always enforced. You can’t add a floating third app when in split-screen either, even though Apple has offered a similar capability on iPads for years. (The exception is video apps—you can have them float in picture-in-picture mode.) In portrait orientation, you can split-screen only with a video app; Apple won’t let you stack two apps, something Android has enabled for years.
That rigid software philosophy extends to basic input handling, too. I am typing this review on the iPhone Duo using a compact folding keyboard with a tiny attached trackpad. The trackpad works OK, but I could only get it to work after turning on AssistiveTouch in iOS’ accessibility settings. If the Duo is the iPhone that lets you do more, Apple should natively enable cursor support just like it does on iPads.
Then there are the physical quirks. The Duo supports MagSafe, so you can magnetically stick the phone to MagSafe tripods, mounts, and the like. (When it’s open, the Duo’s weight makes the phone sag to one side.) But what about MagSafe wallets? They’ll work, but Apple’s official wallet sticks out past the phone’s lower edge—not what you’d expect from a company that pores over every detail. Apple doesn’t have an official solution, so you’ll have to rely on a third-party accessory (and I suspect there will be many Duo accessories).
The iPhone maker follows the industry standard with a dual rear-camera system, lacking the third zoom camera from its Pro iPhones, which I sorely miss. At least the selfie cameras—the one on the outer screen and the “hidden” under-display inner camera seem to produce good results. On a Zoom call, my editor remarked that the video quality looked “really good” with both selfie shooters. (Zoom, by the way, wasn’t optimized.)
Dynamic Duo
When an app is properly optimized, the experience is chef’s kiss. Multi-pane views let you see a lot more in an app than candy-bar phones, a boost to productivity. Split-screening two optimized apps looks excellent, with plenty of room for each app to breathe and let you multitask. I haven’t found myself putting the Duo in angled positions much, mostly because I’ve really enjoyed using it with Apple’s Folio With Kickstand case, so much so that I wish the kickstand were integrated into the phone itself; I strongly recommend investing in an accessory to prop the Duo up.
Battery life has been pretty great. With average use, I’ve ended most days with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Right now, with over six hours of screen-on time because I’ve been working off the Duo for most of the workday, it’s almost 6 pm, and I’m at 45 percent. Impressive.
As for performance, the only thing I've noticed is the Duo can get toasty. This isn't necessarily tied to a demanding task, though. Half an hour in Battlefleet Duo or Pokémon Go didn't make the phone feel much warmer (though 15 minutes in Ungodly did), but at random moments, the right half of the Duo heated up quickly. It's something to keep an eye on.
Duo Preview lets the photo subject see themselves in the frame.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
The dual rear cameras are reliable, too. You don’t get the fun variable-aperture wizardry of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera, but after comparing photos I’ve captured on both devices, the results aren’t drastically different. That brings us to the features I think will help bring folding phones into mainstream appeal—Smart Take and Duo Preview.
The latter is a staple of folding phones, letting you show the camera’s viewfinder to the photo subject—good news for anyone who has ever complained about their Instagram husband. Now you can make sure they’re angling the camera just right before hitting the shutter button. You can also take better-quality selfies with the rear camera yourself— open the camera app on the larger screen and flip the phone; you’ll get an option to view the camera controls on the outer screen, letting you see a live preview while snapping with the superior 48-megapixel cameras.
Smart Take is similar to Google’s Magic Capture. Set the phone down in a partially folded shape (so it looks like a tiny laptop) and tap the shutter button. The camera will then wait for you to get into position and snap a series of photos when it thinks you’re posing. You can forget about asking someone to take a picture for you. It’s not as smart as the Pixel feature—I ended up deleting a bunch of awkward Smart Take photos—but it’s convenient.
I’m sure Kids Cue will be popular too. I don’t have a kid, so I couldn’t vet how well it works, but it loops cute Snoopy animations on the outer display to capture a child’s attention and make them smile. Google and Samsung have similar versions on their folding phones, but neither has Snoopy—a big win for Apple.
The nanotexture finish on the inner screen is the star of the show. The matte surface reduces the crease’s visibility, while also minimizing glare and reflections. It also feels like e-paper, which I imagine will be very welcome when Apple Pencil support is added later this year (via a software update). Writing on a screen always feels better when the screen isn’t entirely smooth.
You don’t get the crisp video quality, deep blacks, and sharp contrast of the iPhone 18 Pro when watching movies and shows on apps like Netflix on the nanotexture panel. However, colors are still just as vibrant, and the experience is very similar. I didn’t have any issues with screen brightness—the Duo gets up to 3,000 nits at peak outdoor brightness—even with the textured finish, though off-axis viewing isn’t great in direct sunlight.
Much of my time this past week has been thinking about wasted space. Sometimes I questioned Apple’s decision to move all the navigation elements of iOS to the right rail—there’s so much wasted space in some apps! Then I use an app that uses all that space, and I’m content. That’s probably my takeaway. If you want to try Apple’s first folding phone, wait a few months for developers to optimize their apps. (It might actually help that the phone is backordered until January.) Waiting might help in other ways too—Apple plans to add Reachability later this year for the Duo, letting folks with small hands more easily access the left or right edges of the screen with a tap.
You’ll likely spend most of your time on the outer screen of the Duo.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
This is often the case with first-generation products, but it may be prudent to wait for the Duo 2—not because there are glaring issues but because I suspect Apple may tackle the weight problem with the next version, just as Samsung did on its latest iteration.
Folding phones will never be for everyone. Some people do not care for the bigger screen. Others have durability concerns, and a device with more moving parts will never be as repairable or robust as its single-slab counterpart. Price is a barrier for others—but, on that note, the Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors (though still expensive).
But the folding category is here to stay. I know people who swear by the fold and won’t buy anything else. I’m starting to convert, especially with the newer passport-style shape. Now if only someone could figure out how to put a real zoom camera on there.
Julian Chokkattu is Senior Editor, Gear at WIRED, overseeing personal technology, gadgets, and gizmos. He has been reviewing consumer products for a decade, specializing in mobile—from smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches to smart glasses and virtual reality. This is his sixth year at WIRED. Sudan conflict: Peace efforts resume to end ‘drone war’ fuelling humanitarian crisis

Unknown Publisher

Sudan conflict: Peace efforts resume to end ‘drone war’ fuelling humanitarian crisis
Talks to halt the fighting in Sudan and alleviate the humanitarian crisis there continued in Geneva on Wednesday, where nearly two dozen countries convened to discuss a pathway to a ceasefire and transition to peaceful governance that represents all Sudanese people.
“Our first session, devoted to de-escalation, will offer an opportunity to explore practical ways forward,” said Pekka Haavisto, Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan, in a call to delegates to identify measures and use their “respective channels of engagement [to] build confidence and help create conditions conducive to a comprehensive ceasefire”.
Now in its fourth year, the conflict began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) – former allies who had jointly seized power in a 2021 coup.
Deadly drone attacks against civilians and public infrastructure have been a feature of the war and frequently condemned by humanitarian and human rights officials.
“The war in Sudan has become a drone war; it kills mostly civilians,” said Alexandre Fasel, State Secretary of Switzerland, which is co-hosting the meeting with the UN. “Famine-like conditions persist in Darfur, the Kordofan state and elsewhere in the country; it is the war that drives this hunger.”
Highlighting the protections offered to non-combatants by international law, Mr. Fasel insisted that the Geneva Conventions “are very clear: the protection of civilians and humanitarian access must not wait for a ceasefire and a political solution. Civilians are suffering and dying today.”
Millions in need
Across Sudan today, almost 34 million people need humanitarian support, according to the UN aid coordination office, OCHA, Mr. Fasel noted. He also cited UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) alerts that eight million Sudanese children are out of school today.
“This is not only a violation to the right of education but an immense risk factor for a future stable Sudan. Conflict-related sexual violence has re-emerged as a tactic to terrorise and humiliate the civilian population, often targeted along ethnicity or perceived affiliations,” he insisted.
In addition to discussing efforts towards a ceasefire, delegates are expected to consider a Sudanese-led “transitional political phase that reflects the aspirations” of the country’s people, by means of “an inclusive and credible dialogue”, the UN chief’s Personal Envoy, Mr. Havisto, said, insisting that “our role is to support the Sudanese in shaping their country’s shared future, with due regard for the diversity of their voices and experiences”.
Latest round of talks
The talks, known officially as Consultative Meetings on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives and Efforts in Sudan, have previously taken place in Cairo twice (June 2024 and January 2026) and in Djibouti (July 2024), Nouakchott (December 2024) and Brussels (June 2025) and Cairo (January 2026).
Neither the Sudanese Government nor the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are represented at the meeting in Geneva, as the mechanism was established for mediators to coordinate their actions.
On the margins of Wednesday’s meeting in Geneva, the UN Personal Envoy was also expected to engage with key regional and international partners from the so-called “Quad” mechanism” – involving the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt – and the “Quintet” mechanism of the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the UN, the European Union and the League of Arab States.
The current talks followed a day of humanitarian-focused discussions also at UN Geneva that involved delegations, senior UN officials and international non-governmental organizations operating in Sudan including the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the Sudan INGO Forum.

Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:59:14 UTC
20:59:14 KST

Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- Northwestern University
- Summary:
- A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.
- Share:
A journey to Mars may be less challenging for the human heart than scientists once feared. A new study suggests that astronauts can adapt remarkably well to months of weightlessness, offering encouraging evidence that humans could endure the long trip to the Red Planet and function under its weaker gravity.
Researchers from Northwestern Medicine, UT Southwestern, and UT Houston monitored the hearts of 13 astronauts who spent approximately six months aboard the International Space Station. Their findings showed that although spaceflight initially affected heart performance, the astronauts gradually adapted, with intensive daily exercise playing an important role in maintaining their cardiovascular health.
One of NASA's major concerns about sending humans to Mars is how astronauts' hearts and circulatory systems will respond when they leave the weightless conditions of spaceflight (known as microgravity) and encounter Martian gravity, which is only about one-third as strong as Earth's.
Encouragingly, the researchers found that the astronauts showed no significant signs of cardiovascular strain when exposed to simulated Martian gravity after returning to Earth.
"With our findings, there is now reason to think that we would be able to traverse to Mars, get there and actually work on the surface of Mars," said study senior author Dr. James Thomas, professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
The study, published last month in the journal Circulation, is the first to investigate how the heart responds to simulated Martian gravity following an extended period in space.
How Daily Exercise Protects Astronauts' Hearts in Space
Living without gravity creates unusual challenges for the human body. On Earth, the heart constantly works against gravity to circulate blood, while muscles must support the body's weight. In space, those demands decrease substantially, allowing muscles and even the heart itself to shrink over time.
Returning to a gravitational environment can also be difficult. Astronauts on previous missions have frequently experienced dizziness or lightheadedness when standing after landing. This happens because gravity pulls blood toward the lower body, sometimes causing blood pressure to drop suddenly. The condition is called orthostatic hypotension. (If you've seen Sandra Bullock crawling after returning to Earth in "Gravity," you get the idea.)
However, the astronauts involved in the new study generally handled this transition well, potentially because they had maintained demanding exercise schedules throughout their missions.
As part of NASA's Exercise Countermeasures program, astronauts exercised for up to two hours each day. Their routines included 30 to 45 minutes of endurance training, which strengthens the cardiovascular system, along with 60 to 75 minutes of resistance training to help preserve muscle mass and strength.
"You lose muscle mass and cardiac mass when you're in a weightless environment because you are working less up there," explained Thomas, who also is a Northwestern Medicine cardiologist. "You're floating around in the air, and you give a little tap with your foot, and you can sail over to say hello to your buddy."
"To counter that, exercise is crucial when you're in space," Thomas added.
Heart Scans Reveal How the Body Adapts to Weightlessness
To understand what happens to the heart during prolonged spaceflight, the researchers collected echocardiograms before, during, and after each astronaut's mission. These ultrasound scans use sound waves to produce moving images of the heart, allowing doctors to examine its structure and measure how effectively it pumps blood.
While aboard the International Space Station, astronauts were trained to perform these scans on one another every few weeks. The recordings were transmitted to Earth, where researchers could monitor changes in heart function throughout the missions.
Thomas worked alongside Dr. Benjamin Levine of UT Southwestern Medical Center and Dr. Michael Bungo of the McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.
"It would be typically about 3 a.m. for me because the space station runs on Greenwich Mean Time," Thomas said. "I would watch the recordings come in live and coach the astronauts in real time to improve the images."
The scans revealed that the astronauts' hearts initially struggled to adjust to their new environment. During the first two weeks in space, researchers observed declines in cardiac filling, stroke volume, and several other measures of cardiovascular performance.
Cardiac filling refers to how much blood enters the heart between beats, while stroke volume describes the amount of blood pumped out with each contraction. Both measurements decreased early in the missions, indicating that the astronauts' hearts were temporarily moving less blood with each beat.
But the changes did not persist.
As the astronauts spent more time in space, their cardiovascular systems adapted. Cardiac filling and stroke volume gradually improved, approaching the levels recorded before launch.
These results suggest that the heart can adjust to prolonged weightlessness more effectively than early measurements might indicate, particularly when astronauts maintain regular physical activity.
Astronauts' Hearts Pass a Simulated Mars Gravity Test
The researchers also wanted to answer a particularly important question for future Mars missions: What happens when an astronaut who has spent months in weightlessness suddenly encounters gravity again?
Mars has roughly 38% of Earth's surface gravity. Although this is considerably weaker than what people experience on Earth, it would still force astronauts' hearts to work differently after months of floating in space.
To reproduce some of these effects, the researchers conducted a simulated Martian gravity test after the astronauts returned to Earth.
Each astronaut was tilted upward by 22 degrees from a lying position. This posture caused blood to shift toward the lower body, approximating the circulatory effects of Martian gravity.
The results were encouraging. After spending about six months in space, the astronauts' hearts performed just as well under simulated Martian gravity as they had when standing upright on Earth before their missions.
This suggests that astronauts who maintain their cardiovascular fitness during spaceflight may be capable of transitioning to the weaker gravity of Mars without experiencing major cardiovascular difficulties.
Although the findings come from a relatively small group of astronauts and a simulation rather than an actual Mars landing, they provide valuable evidence for planning future missions.
Combined with the benefits of daily exercise, the heart's ability to adapt to weightlessness and respond well to simulated Martian gravity offers another reason to be optimistic about sending humans to the Red Planet.
The study is titled "Impact of Prolonged Spaceflight on Cardiac Structure and Function: An Exploratory Longitudinal Observational Study." Funding was provided by the National Space Biomedical Research Institute (grant NCC9-58), NASA (grant NNJ04HH01A), the IDP Foundation, Sandra Helton, and the National Heart Foundation of Australia.

EU Seeks More Ukraine Aid From Canada, UK as Kyiv Faces €70 Billion Funding Gap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:58:32 UTC
20:58:32 KST

Ukraine faces a €70 billion ($77 billion) funding shortfall next year, prompting the EU to seek greater financial commitments from countries outside the bloc as it struggles to cover Kyiv’s growing needs.
The issue is expected to feature in upcoming EU summits with Canada on Oct. 29-30 and the UK on Nov. 20. According to POLITICO, citing EU officials and diplomats, Brussels wants to use the meetings to encourage both countries to increase their contributions to Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The effort comes as the EU tries to secure long-term financing for Ukraine’s defense and state operations while Russia continues its war and the future of US support remains uncertain.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last week that the EU and its member states provide 80% of Ukraine’s external aid.
“We urgently need other partners to step up,” she said.
The funding challenge follows the EU’s commitment to a €90 billion loan ($101 billion) for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027. The package is expected to meet roughly two-thirds of Kyiv’s financial requirements, leaving a substantial amount to be secured elsewhere.
Brussels had expected non-EU partners, including Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Norway, to contribute another €45 billion ($50 billion). But some of the anticipated funding has yet to be finalized or disbursed, POLITICO reported.
Putin Orders US Teacher’s Release as Witkoff Arrives for Talks
The European Commission has also been tasked with exploring ways to bridge the financing gap.
Allies face growing pressure to contribute
The EU is seeking broader international support rather than relying increasingly on European taxpayers to cover Ukraine’s needs.
European Council President António Costa told the European Parliament on Wednesday, Oct. 21 that international partners must intensify their financial support for Kyiv.
European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis also raised the issue during last week’s meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok, saying Ukraine’s 2027 financing needs were a prominent topic.
He called for “broad burden sharing” among international partners as Ukraine continues to resist Russian aggression.
EU officials stressed that the initiative was not intended as criticism of Canada or the UK, both longstanding supporters of Ukraine. They said the country’s financial requirements had grown and more partners would need to help cover them.
The UK says it has committed £25 billion ($33 billion) in support for Ukraine, according to its official government figures.
Canada has pledged the equivalent of €5.4 billion ($6 billion) in military assistance and €8.2 billion ($9 billion) in direct financial support, according to the Canadian government’s Ukraine assistance overview.
The EU and its member states say they have contributed more than €231 billion ($259 billion) since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
That total includes military aid, budget support, guarantees, assistance for Ukrainians living in the bloc, and proceeds from immobilized Russian assets.
Funding push coincides with wider EU negotiations
The upcoming summits will also address broader economic and defense ties, giving Brussels an opportunity to discuss Ukraine alongside other priorities.
Von der Leyen has proposed making Canada the EU’s first “associate member.” Ottawa is also set to participate in the bloc’s SAFE defense procurement program, which finances joint weapons purchases and opens eligible contracts to Canadian companies.
Canada says it has committed nearly C$26 billion ($18 billion) in military, financial, development, and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine. Its support includes a military aid package worth $900 million, announced in July.
“Canada continues to stand by Ukraine and remains engaged with international partners on Ukraine’s needs,” Privy Council Office spokesperson Kathryn Serieux told POLITICO.
The Nov. 20 EU-UK summit is expected to advance British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s efforts to reset relations with the bloc.
London also wants British companies to qualify as European under the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which would favor European-made goods in public procurement and industrial support.
British officials told POLITICO they were unaware of any request to link those benefits to increased aid for Ukraine.
An EU official said Ukraine was expected to feature in the summit’s joint declaration, but characterized it as recognition of both sides’ support for Kyiv rather than a demand for additional funding.
Brussels is also seeking greater contributions from Japan. One EU official described Tokyo’s 2026 support as lagging, although a person familiar with the Japanese government’s position disputed that assessment, citing around $20 billion already provided to Ukraine and saying further assistance could be considered if Kyiv requested it.
Australia said it had not received a request for additional funding for Ukraine in 2027. An Australian official suggested Canberra might be a lower priority after its leaders announced additional funding and a security agreement with Kyiv last month.
European support faces political uncertainty
The push for more international funding comes as support for Ukraine could face renewed political pressure in elections across Europe next year.
In France, Marine Le Pen has vowed to end aid to Ukraine if elected president in 2027. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces a challenge from Russia-friendly politician Roberto Vannacci ahead of next year’s election.
Combined with uncertainty over Washington’s future commitments, those political risks are encouraging European officials to look beyond their own budgets.
The Commission is also urging Ukraine to seek more contributions directly from non-EU partners.

Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for Ukraine war talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

Breadcrumb
Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for talks on Ukraine war
Russia's Vladimir Putin began talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff on ending the Ukraine war in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday, with the American official saying he had brought "ideas" for a possible peace deal.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Norway, where he met Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in talks Washington described as "positive."
The meeting is taking place as the United States pushes an end to Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with Russia pounding Ukrainian cities ahead of winter and amid a bitter feud between Donald Trump and Zelensky.
As Witkoff touched down in Putin's home city, Russia announced it would soon begin shipments of diesel to the United States under a deal with Trump, and that it had freed a US citizen—Stephen Hubbard—held by Moscow since the start of the war on allegations of fighting as a "mercenary" for Ukraine.
"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff—Trump's business partner and envoy—told Putin in Saint Petersburg's Konstantinovsky Palace.
Putin thanked Trump for his efforts to resolve the war and said he was eager to be informed about the US meeting with Zelensky.
The longtime Russian leader has repeatedly refused to hold face-to-face talks with Zelensky and said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Witkoff told Putin he hoped trilateral talks can resume.
"I'm hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process so we can begin to have technical teams discussing what are those next steps," he told the Russian leader.
Putin thanked Trump for his "attention" to the conflict and said the US leader had "insisted that it was necessary to end this conflict" in their last phone call.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of troops on both sides as well as thousands of civilians.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Moscow's strikes killed at least four people —including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
'Momentum' in talks
Meeting Putin, Witkoff described his talks with Zelensky as "productive."
"I think there's some degree of momentum and I hope that today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict," he said.
Zelensky on Tuesday thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting in Norway followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, with Zelensky urging the US not to side with Russia and Trump calling for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is also due to participate in Wednesday's talks with Putin remotely.
US-led talks on the conflict have so far not led to a breakthrough and Moscow insists it intends to press on with its offensive.
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a diesel deal—met with astonishment in Kyiv and across Europe—that saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of testing midterm elections in the US next month.
Washington was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
"We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a "mercenary" fighting for Ukraine.
Witkoff hailed the move and called Putin a "humanitarian".
Trump later said that Hubbard was on his way to the Unites States and that the release had not been part of a swap deal.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has indicated that Russia is testing NATO’s collective defense by carrying out attacks that come very close to triggering the Alliance’s Article 5.
Sinkevičius noted that the phrase that Russia is testing boundaries appears with increasing frequency in political discussions—and this does not concern only Lithuania, Latvia, or other countries on the eastern flank. Russia is testing how far it can go without crossing the threshold that would necessitate the activation of NATO’s collective defense.
Referring to recent events in Europe, Sinkevičius pointed out that these pose serious challenges for the Alliance regarding the appropriate response. These are not classic, conventional attacks, nor are they direct and unambiguous border violations. Often, such acts are carried out by individuals hired specifically for the purpose, and investigations reveal that the party behind them is to be found in the East.
Sinkevičius stated that he will continue close cooperation with his Polish counterparts to accelerate response times and improve communication in the event of future incidents.
The most significant agreement reached is an arrangement for the heads of government to communicate directly with one another. He and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk have exchanged private contact details, ensuring that in the event of incidents or the receipt of critical information—including intelligence—they can communicate immediately, rather than waiting for the offices of the prime ministers to make contact.

Ukraine plans to test the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026 - Zelenskyy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:55:38 EEST
20:55:38 KST

Ukraine plans to test the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026 - Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine and its European partners plan to test the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on the initial results of the development and Norway’s active participation in the project.
Ukraine, together with its European partners, plans to conduct the first tests of the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026. As President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported, developers have already achieved the first results in creating individual components of the system, while Norway is actively involved in implementing the project, UNN writes.
Details
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on a new stage in the implementation of the pan-European FREYJA anti-ballistic shield project following a meeting with Norway’s Minister of Defence Tore Sandvik, Kongsberg CEO Eirik Lie, and representatives of the corporation. According to the head of state, Norway is playing an active role in creating the future missile defence system.
Norway is also actively participating in our European FREYJA anti-ballistic programme. There are already initial results in creating individual elements of the system. Today, we determined where we can and must accelerate in order to begin testing by the end of this year. We also discussed in detail the launch of work on new satellite communications capabilities for our soldiers. We will involve partners that have the capabilities to provide support
Zelenskyy separately highlighted the contribution of Norwegian company Kongsberg, which manufactures NASAMS air defence systems. These systems protect Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks every day. The head of state also expressed hope that partners would provide additional packages of defence assistance next month.
Ukraine has already completed its part of the work on FREYJA
Earlier, Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Ukraine had completed its part of the work on the FREYJA anti-ballistic project. At the same time, European partners continue to carry out their own tasks.
The President of Ukraine stressed that creating anti-ballistic systems is an extremely complex technological process that usually takes decades. However, due to the ongoing threat of Russian ballistic strikes, Ukraine seeks to significantly shorten the development timeline.
Background
FREYJA is a Ukraine-initiated pan-European anti-ballistic shield project intended to protect Ukrainian cities from Russian ballistic missiles. To implement it, Ukraine and its European partners established the Anti-Ballistic Coalition, which brought together 10 countries and leading defence companies. The joint efforts are aimed at developing indigenous missile defence technologies and establishing their mass production.
The foundation of the future system is the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile, being developed by Ukrainian defence company Fire Point. The project envisages integrating the Ukrainian missile with European technologies, including German radar systems and Norwegian guidance technologies.
As UNN previously reported, Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh said that development of FREYJA had already moved to the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem—radars, the launcher, data transmission channels, and the command centre. According to her, technical tests of individual components are conducted up to twice a week.

Russia is losing almost US$2.5bn a month due to Ukrainian port blockade – Russian newspaper
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:55:00 EEST
20:55:00 KST

Russia is losing almost US$2.5bn a month due to Ukrainian port blockade – Russian newspaper
Operations have virtually ground to a halt at Russian ports on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov due to drone and uncrewed surface vessel (USV) attacks, with industry players estimating that government budgets and businesses are losing out on more than RUB 200 billion (about US$2.43 billion) a month.
Source: the Russian newspaper Kommersant, citing sources, including OTEKO, which operates terminals in Taman
Details: Cargo handling at terminals in Russia's southern ports fell by 95-100% in September, and passenger traffic dropped by 85%. Cargo flows have been redirected to ports in northwestern Russia or overland routes.
Russian agricultural exports have also been affected. In July and August, 3.8 million tonnes of agricultural cargo passed through ports in Krasnodar Krai, compared with 7.9 million tonnes during the same period in 2025.
Kommersant reported that Russia's largest southern ports, including Novorossiysk, Taman and Tuapse, have begun cutting staff, with some employees forced to take unpaid leave or accept shorter working weeks.
Against this backdrop, Krasnodar Krai governor Veniamin Kondratyev has proposed that Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev consider providing state subsidies to the region's ports along the same lines as those granted to airports in the region that have been closed.
Possible measures include subsidising employees' wages and the costs of maintaining and servicing equipment, silos, warehouses and berthing infrastructure, as well as covering electricity and utility bills.
The authorities are also considering reimbursing part of the interest on loans and borrowings intended to keep terminals ready to resume operations. On 6 October, Patrushev instructed the relevant ministries to consider the proposals.
Russia's Association of Commercial Sea Ports has also asked for government support, addressing its request to Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak.
The association has called for a deferral of taxes and lease payments on federal property, wage subsidies equivalent to one month's minimum wage per employee, and more favourable terms for war risk insurance.
Russia's southern ports employ around 20,000-25,000 people. Experts estimate that providing support equivalent to one month's minimum wage per employee would cost Russia RUB 550-670 million per month (US$6.67 million-US$8.13 million), or RUB 6.6-8 billion per year (US$80.0 million-US$97.0 million).
Background:
- Ukrainian agricultural producers managed to increase exports in September compared with August, although Russia's continuing blockade of Ukrainian seaports remains one of the main economic risks for the agricultural sector.
- In August, it was reported that Russian grain exports, which bring around US$15 billion into the Russian economy annually, had been almost completely paralysed by Ukrainian strikes on ports in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. The Yastreb mobile system for detecting and neutralizing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has been showcased at the Security Space exhibition in Moscow, a spokesman for K-Avia told TASS.
"Upon entering the operational range of a particular sensor, an enemy aerial vehicle is detected and identified. The crew comprises two people: a detection operator and a UAV interceptor operator. The detection operator spots and identifies the target, determines whether to engage it, and issues a command to the UAV interceptor operator. The UAV interceptor operator presses a button, the launch box opens, and our missile comes out <...> to pursue and hit the enemy drone. <...> The combat ammunition load comprises nine rounds. Speaking at a discussion at the Berlin Global Dialogue conference, Merz said Europe is supporting Ukraine to end the war, not prolong it.
“We are not supporting Ukraine in order to continue this war. We are doing this to end it as soon as possible,” he said, adding that there has been “some progress” in the Oslo talks without elaboration, as reported by Ukrainian state media Ukrinform.
The Kremlin has long accused Kyiv’s allies of prolonging the war by supporting Ukraine, while they argue they are supporting Kyiv’s right to defend itself from Moscow’s invasion.
Merz added that Ukraine’s surrender would mean “the capitulation of all of us,” adding that supporting Ukraine is “entirely in our own interests.”

Air Raid Alerts Stall Ukraine-Poland Border Crossings
Merz said Russia’s invasion represents an attack on “the entire political order that we have achieved since 1990.”
“This is not just a war in Ukraine,” he said, echoing European intelligence reports that Russia has stepped up hybrid attacks on Europe, with tactics ranging from drone incidents to assassinations against arms executives.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reiterated Moscow’s rejection of Europe’s stance on Wednesday, arguing that, from Moscow’s perspective, the new proposals are “unlikely to be a constructive contribution to a settlement.”
The developments came as the US stepped up pressure on Kyiv toward a peace settlement after pursuing a diesel deal with Moscow, with Europe pushing back against the deal and Washington’s subsequent pressure on Kyiv.
Peace on whose terms?
While all parties – including the US and Europe – have called for peace in Ukraine, the terms have been polarizing.
Europe has sided with Kyiv, arguing that Russia is responsible for the invasion and that any peace should be just and lasting, rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Russia has long cast its own Ukraine invasion as a war against NATO, initially demanding that Ukraine be demilitarized and barred from joining the alliance, and recently reiterated demands for Kyiv to voluntarily withdraw from eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, to which Moscow has laid claims via unrecognized referendums.
Kyiv, meanwhile, called for a freeze along the contact lines, arguing that ceding the Donbas region could weaken its own security and allow Russia to recuperate for another invasion against the rest of Ukraine; Ukraine’s recent Operation Vivaldi also reversed much of Russia’s gains in the region throughout 2026.
While the previous US administration backed Ukraine’s sovereignty, the current administration has pursued economic incentives to bring Moscow to the negotiating table, with President Volodymyr Zelensky saying in March that Washington had pressured Kyiv to give up the Donbas in exchange for security guarantees.

SUVA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Fiji is bracing for worsening water shortages as a strengthening El Nino is expected to bring drier conditions in the coming months, the Fiji Meteorological Service has warned.
Shweta Shiwangni, a scientific officer at the service, told local media on Wednesday that the El Nino event had become established in the tropical Pacific and was expected to intensify, increasing the risk of prolonged dry conditions as Fiji enters the 2026-2027 tropical cyclone season, which runs from November to April.
Rainfall toward the end of November could ease dry conditions in the Western Division, but significant rainfall remains uncertain and may depend on the development of a low-pressure system or tropical disturbance near Fiji, she said.
Shiwangni urged communities already facing water shortages to seek water deliveries through relevant authorities and collect rainwater wherever possible.
Meanwhile, Fiji could be affected by two to three tropical cyclones during the upcoming season, with one or two potentially reaching Category Three or higher, according to the Meteorological Service.
The Northern and Eastern divisions have historically experienced greater cyclone impacts during El Nino conditions, Shiwangni said, while warning that all parts of the country could face destructive winds, heavy rainfall and flooding.
Authorities have urged residents to secure their homes, clear gutters and drains, prepare emergency supplies and identify evacuation centers.
Farmers have been advised to move livestock to higher ground when flooding threatens, while businesses in flood-prone areas should take steps to protect infrastructure. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Australian Capital Territory (ACT) Legislative Assembly passed new planning reforms to speed up housing approvals and increase housing supply in Canberra, the territory government announced on Wednesday.
The changes will simplify planning and leasing processes for smaller-scale housing developments, including townhouses, duplexes, terraces and secondary residences.
Under the reforms, assessment and approval timeframes for smaller-scale subdivisions and land consolidations will be reduced from 60 days to 30-45 working days.
Homeowners will also be automatically entitled to build secondary residences, such as granny flats, without requiring a Crown lease variation.
Minor lease variations, including changes to permitted dwelling numbers, will be processed through a streamlined pathway, reducing assessment times to 10 days.
ACT Minister for Planning and Sustainable Development Chris Steel said the reforms would make the planning process simpler and help deliver more housing choices for Canberra residents.
The reforms form part of the ACT government's broader housing strategy, which aims to enable the construction of 30,000 new homes by 2030. ■

The platform has maintained effective operations over the years through regular meetings, case referrals and other forms of cooperation, making itself an important channel for people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait to lodge complaints, seek advice and assistance, and protect their legitimate rights and interests, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news briefing.
Since the beginning of this year, the Taiwan Work Office of the CPC Central Committee and the KMT have held multiple consultations to improve the platform's operations and effectiveness, and they have reached a consensus on further cooperation, she said.
The two sides will maintain regular communication and provide timely feedback, and the platform will offer Taiwan residents professional legal services, Zhang said.
They will also work to enhance assistance for Taiwan residents facing temporary difficulties, help people search for missing relatives and provide humanitarian care, she added.
The two sides of the Strait established an investment dispute settlement mechanism in 2012 under a cross-Strait investment protection agreement reached on a common political foundation of the 1992 Consensus.
However, the mechanism was suspended in May 2016 because Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities refused to recognize the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, Zhang said.
The mainland is willing to engage in dialogue on resuming the mechanism's operations, provided that the DPP authorities recognize the 1992 Consensus, Zhang said.
The Taiwan question stems from a civil war fought between the forces led by the CPC and the KMT about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, while the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. ■

Israeli patient receives new non-invasive treatment for epilepsy in first outside Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:52:46 UTC
20:52:46 KST

An Israeli patient received a non-invasive epilepsy treatment at Clalit-Beilinson Hospital, making her the first outside of Europe to use the technology.
The EASEE brain stimulation system, first developed in Germany by PRECISIS, is designed to treat epilepsy without opening the skull or inserting electrodes into the brain.
"This is the first time we can treat patients with epilepsy without penetrating the brain or inserting an electrode into it, while potentially achieving a significant reduction in the number of seizures," Dr. Idit Tamir, Director of the Functional Neurosurgery Unit at Clalit-Beilinson, said.
"The technology has demonstrated results comparable to the improvements seen with invasive neurostimulation devices. In appropriately selected patients, it offers a genuine alternative to these treatments."
Approximately one-third of the 100,000 people in Israel living with epilepsy do not achieve adequate seizure control through medication.
Israeli patient did not respond to medication for epilepsy
The first Israeli patient to undergo the treatment, 42-year-old Olga Moisa, has lived with epilepsy for 15 years and did not respond fully to medication.
"Some patients do not respond to medication. We sometimes try one drug after another, but none succeeds in controlling the seizures," Professor Felix Benninger, Director of the hospital’s Epilepsy Treatment Unit, explained.
On August 31, Moisa received treatment through the EASEE system, which electrically stimulates the seizure focus in the brain from outside the skull. Since then, she has not experienced any seizures, but it is still too early to fully determine its effectiveness.
"At the moment, the device is operating at a low stimulation level, allowing her body to gradually adjust to the stimulation. We still do not know what the outcome will be. We will only know in a few months," her son, Sasha, said. "Even if there is something that can reduce the seizures by 50%, that is already better."
