Representatives of Ukraine, NATO and partner countries discussed in Vilnius the modernization of military rehabilitation centers, provision of modern equipment and training of Ukrainian specialists, the NATO Representation in Ukraine said.
A meeting of representatives of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, NATO and partner countries on developing the system of physical and psychological rehabilitation for wounded Ukrainian servicemen under the RENOVATOR project was held in Vilnius on October 14, the representation said. Participants from Ukraine, Lithuania, Britain, Norway, Sweden and Latvia discussed the priority needs of Ukrainian rehabilitation centers, supplying them with modern medical equipment, raising specialists' qualifications and continuity of medical care during the full-scale war.
RENOVATOR is aimed at strengthening the capacity of Ukraine's military rehabilitation system, it said. It provides for modernizing rehabilitation infrastructure, supplying the necessary equipment and professional development of medical workers who help Ukrainian defenders recover from injuries.
"The main measure of our cooperation is not the number of events held but a tangible result for the serviceman. Every wounded defender should receive proper help on time, reach the fullest possible functional recovery and have a clear and understandable further rehabilitation route. RENOVATOR can become a practical basis for this through common standards, capacity development and scaling up proven best practices," Medical Forces Commander Colonel Kostiantyn Humeniuk said.
The team of NATO's Comprehensive Assistance Package for Ukraine (CAP) stressed the importance of coordinating the efforts of Ukraine, Lithuania and other lead countries of the project, the representation said. This cooperation makes it possible to align support with the current needs of Ukrainian troops, develop rehabilitation infrastructure and strengthen the professional capacity of Ukrainian specialists.
CAP team head Iryna Novakova said the aim is to provide infrastructure, equipment and training to strengthen rehabilitation capacity for Ukrainian defenders and for NATO allies.
"We work together, learn and improve, supporting Ukraine and at the same time building our own collective defense capabilities," she said.
RENOVATOR is one of the key projects under the Comprehensive Assistance Package for Ukraine. Its implementation involves coordinating the efforts of NATO, Ukrainian defense institutions and partner countries to create a sustainable rehabilitation system that can meet the needs of Ukrainian defenders both during the war and in the long term. The NATO Representation in Ukraine works with Ukrainian partners at all stages of the project, from identifying needs to delivering equipment. NATO continues

Reform Party leader: 20 seats in parliament enough to be a political player
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:47:00 UTC
19:47:00 KST

Reform Party leader: 20 seats in parliament enough to be a political player
The Reform Party is aiming for 20 seats after the March elections for a strong team with which to defend the liberal worldview, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.
The Reform Party held a party council meeting over the weekend, setting a goal of winning 20 seats in parliament in next spring's Riigikogu elections. Host Arp Müller noted in his question that 20 seats would not be enough to win an election.
"You can get a strong team into parliament. I remember speaking with Siim Kallas a little while ago and his message was that even when times are difficult, populism is on the rise and the media often criticizes those in power rather indiscriminately, you still have to hold your head high and make sure there is a strong team in the next parliament. And a strong team means that our goal is to win 20 seats, which would give us a foundation to work from, remain a force in Estonian politics and defend what we believe in," Michal replied.
"Because the thing is, Social Democrats are not liberals, conservatives are neither Social Democrats nor liberals and liberals are neither Social Democrats nor conservatives. We are clearly a strong liberal party that stands for individual freedoms, economic freedoms and many other things and you can't get that anywhere else," he added.
'Scope for lowering income tax'
Asked whether the Reform Party plans to cut income tax during the next parliamentary term, Michal said there was scope to do so.
"We have already reduced the tax burden. Last year it was 36.2 percent and next year it will be 35.2 percent, so the tax burden is declining. We have cut income tax and we are cutting it this year. And I think it will be possible to do so in the next term as well, if we review how we do things. We will need to find ways to pay for it because my recommendation is to prioritize several things. First, defense spending must remain at 5 percent. Second, when it comes to the budget, we need to continue what we have been doing — reducing the deficit by half a percentage point a year. That will bring borrowing under control and should eventually start reducing it. At the same time, we can review public services or find other ways for the state to generate revenue, including through new technologies, whether by cutting costs or generating revenue from them. That would also create room to cut income tax," Michal said.
The prime minister declined to specify how large an income tax cut would realistically be possible.
"You'll have to wait a little longer and enjoy the suspense. It will take some time before the election platforms are unveiled, but perhaps I'll talk about it on the next show or the one after that," he said.
'Possibility to cancel next year's fuel excise hike'
Regarding a possible increase in fuel excise duty next May, Michal said it was important to consider developments in the global market more broadly.
"We don't know what fuel excise duties or fuel prices will be next spring. I've said this several times at government press conferences, but we're monitoring the situation quite regularly. At our last couple of Cabinet meetings, we've met with representatives of the Bank of Estonia, the Estonian Stockpiling Agency and the Ministry of Finance. Market participants, including Neste and Alexela, have also attended and shared their assessments of the situation. We're keeping a very close eye on the fuel market," Michal said.
"There are several factors we're monitoring. The first, and the state's main concern and responsibility, is ensuring that reserves are sufficient and security of supply is guaranteed. That means making sure there is enough fuel of every type, which is the responsibility of the Estonian Stockpiling Agency. Based on assurances from the agency's head, Ando Leppiman, I would say that our current reserves are sufficient to see us through," he noted.
"Why is this important? Because if we look at the current risks, the rise in fuel prices originated in the Strait of Hormuz, but now, according to market participants and experts, the bottleneck has shifted to refineries, which are unable to supply enough fuel to the market. We certainly need to ensure that any new disruptions do not lead to shortages of physical fuel supplies. Fortunately, at the moment, there appear to be no such shortages in any fuel category. The second thing we're monitoring is, of course, prices. When it comes to prices, we're looking at the potential risk of losing tax revenue to Latvia, for example. Latvia has repeatedly taken various measures concerning fuel and if we look at average pump prices, we're at virtually the same level. Generally, prices are higher in Latvia on one day, while occasionally it's the other way around and so on. We're fairly evenly matched. But if Latvia takes further steps next year, we'll certainly have to monitor the situation and make decisions about our own fuel excise duty rates accordingly. That's something we're assessing on an ongoing basis," Michal said.
Michal acknowledged that if the government planned to cancel next year's excise duty increase, it would have to take that into account when preparing the budget.
"But we certainly won't make that decision before next year because we don't currently know what fuel prices will be next year. How will the U.S. midterm elections turn out? What will happen next in the Strait of Hormuz? There is an enormous amount of uncertainty. What happens after that? Will fuel supplies recover? Will refineries be able to meet demand? Which direction will things go? We simply don't know yet. So we'll make our decisions accordingly. And I would remind you that this year when it became necessary and we in the government considered it appropriate to cancel the excise duty increases, we made that decision. We can do the same next year," Michal said.
Estonia's Rail Baltica cost sharing component could go up
Michal has previously said that delaying the Rail Baltica construction deadline would make the project cheaper for Estonia.
"When the infrastructure construction market isn't so overheated and overstretched, the cost per unit doesn't rise as much. If you inject a very large amount of money into a single market very quickly, each unit becomes more expensive. That's the first point. Second, from the Estonian state's financial perspective, if you can use more EU funding and other external financing for the project from the next budget period, which you otherwise wouldn't be able to use, you don't have to borrow money on behalf of taxpayers and pay interest on it later. So it's cheaper financially and cheaper in terms of construction costs — cheaper in both respects," Michal said.
However, Estonia's share of the project's costs could rise to 25 percent, with European Union funding covering the remaining 75 percent.
"Yes, the original plan, or the original approach, was an 85-15 split. The idea is that the European Union covers most of Rail Baltica's construction costs. I think the current split for Estonia is probably closer to 80-20, roughly speaking. And the European Commission's new proposal has been to reduce the EU co-financing rate to 75 percent. That would mean a ratio of about 75-25. That's what the debate is about," Michal said.
According to Michal, Estonia would still come out ahead even if it received less funding from the European Union.
"The benefit for us becomes clear when you compare it with completing construction by 2030. During the gap years in EU funding, we would have to contribute more of our own money. That would mean a substantial increase in Estonia's share of the costs, requiring us to borrow money and repay it with interest. On top of that, because we would be pouring so much money into the infrastructure construction market all at once, the cost per unit would also be higher. So spreading construction over a longer period means we can make greater use of EU funds, regardless of whether the co-financing rate is 75 or 80 percent at the time," Michal said.
"Even if it's 75 percent, that still brings money into Estonia's budget in any case," he added.
Passport functionality more important than color
Speaking about the Ministry of the Interior's plan to change the color of Estonian passports back to blue, Michal said he would discuss the matter with Taro on Thursday.
"That's a good question. We can certainly give it plenty of thought. There's a certain nostalgic appeal to blue and we've had blue passports before. But when you travel elsewhere in the world, border guards recognize the burgundy color as indicating an EU passport. In my view, what's far more important than either color is that, regardless of the color of the passport cover, it allows you to pass through all checkpoints electronically as quickly as possible. But to add a little good-natured discussion to the debate, why should it be blue? It might as well be blue, black and white, like the Estonian flag," Michal said.

Britain’s cargo drone becomes a low-cost drone interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:46:59 UTC
19:46:59 KST

- A BAE Systems TRV-150 drone armed with a three-pod APKWS launcher intercepted several attack drones during a Pentagon experiment at Eglin Air Force Base.
- The adapted Malloy T-150 fired laser-guided rockets at multiple targets in one flight without landing to reload.
A heavy-lift cargo drone built by BAE Systems subsidiary Malloy Aeronautics has shot down several one-way attack drones with laser-guided rockets during a Pentagon experiment in Florida, firing one rocket after another without having to land and reload.
The modified aircraft, known as the TRV-150, carried a three-pod launcher loaded with BAE Systems’ APKWS rockets during the Joint Readiness Experimentation exercise run by the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering at Eglin Air Force Base from Sept. 21 to 25, BAE Systems said in a statement on Oct. 21.
The TRV-150 is a version of Malloy’s T-150 quadcopter, a British-built electric drone designed to carry cargo, which Maryland-based SURVICE Engineering adapted to meet U.S. Army requirements while BAE Systems’ FalconWorks division developed the APKWS kit and integrated it on the aircraft. BAE Systems says the trials show that low-cost precision weapons can be fitted to uncrewed platforms to counter drone threats on the battlefield, and the company now wants to take the same setup to sea to protect ships from similar attacks.
“Our customers are facing drone threats right now, so we’ve worked at pace with our partners to move from concept to a proven system, which can engage multiple targets in a single mission,” said Thomas Lancashire, head of UAS business development at BAE Systems FalconWorks.
APKWS, short for Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, turns an ordinary unguided 70 mm (2.75-inch) Hydra rocket into a precision weapon by fitting a laser-guidance section between the warhead and the motor, which makes it far cheaper than the air-to-air missiles traditionally used to shoot down drones. The rocket has become one of the U.S. military’s main low-cost answers to cheap attack drones, and in May the U.S. Navy awarded L3Harris a contract worth up to $98.4 million for proximity fuzes that make APKWS more effective against drones, while BAE Systems test-fired the rocket from a Royal Air Force Typhoon in March as it adds counter-drone rockets to the fighter.
The Eglin trials build on the first firing of a precision munition from an adapted T-150 in July 2025, when the drone launched a single APKWS rocket, and this time the team used a production-ready three-pod launcher to engage targets in the air. The ability to fire several shots in one sortie matters against attack drones, which often arrive in groups and leave little time for a launcher to land, reload and take off again.
“Supporting the warfighter has been at the core of SURVICE’s mission since its founding over 45 years ago. Bringing the TRV-150 to the US warfighter and now adding APKWS as a proven, precise, and cost-effective capability to our TRV-150 UAS platform is exactly the type of innovation SURVICE was designed to deliver,” said Gregory Thompson, president of SURVICE Engineering.
BAE Systems bought Malloy Aeronautics in 2024, and the T-150 is already in service with British forces as a logistics drone. During the Royal Navy Carrier Strike Group’s eight-month deployment to the Indo-Pacific last year, the drone carried supplies between ships throughout the voyage, and SURVICE is one of several partners BAE Systems is working with around the world to turn the aircraft into a multi-role counter-drone system.
BAE Systems has not said when an armed TRV-150 could enter service, but the company’s next step is to adapt the rocket-armed version for maritime use, where it would help defend ships against the kind of drone attacks that have hit vessels in the Red Sea and the Black Sea.

FAO to strengthen pest management, protect production in Kerman date palm groves

FAO to strengthen pest management, protect production in Kerman date palm groves
TEHRAN – A delegation from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has visited date palm groves in Kerman Province to strengthen the management of pests and diseases through technical cooperation, field-based interventions and engagement with national and provincial stakeholders.
From 11 to 14 October, the delegation led by FAO Representative to Iran Farrukh Toirov visited project sites in Jiroft, Anbarabad, Bam and Narmashir to review progress on integrated Pest Management (IPM) in date palm groves.
The mission assessed the application of project-supported interventions, examined the use of equipment provided to pilot sites and engaged with farmers, researchers, plant protection specialists, agricultural authorities and private-sector stakeholders across the date value chain.
The project addresses key threats to date production, including the red palm weevil, palm borers, Dubas bug and Date Palm Fruit Bunch Wilting Disorder. During field visits, the team observed pest management interventions in both modern, large-scale orchards using drip irrigation and traditional orchards employing flood irrigation.
The delegation also examined orchards affected by pest infestations and visited date sorting, packaging and processing facilities serving domestic and export markets.
The mission also provided an opportunity to discuss current pest control practices and explore potential approaches to improving the effectiveness and sustainability of interventions.
Discussions with stakeholders highlighted the red palm weevil as one of the most significant challenges facing date production in the province. Meetings held at the South Kerman Agricultural Jihad Organization and the Bam County Governor’s Office brought together local governors, agricultural authorities, researchers, farmers and private-sector representatives to discuss pest management, production challenges and constraints affecting the date value chain, including the control measures and access to export markets.
The FAO Representative welcomed the strong engagement and shared commitment demonstrated by stakeholders in Kerman, noting that their collaboration provides a favourable foundation for expanding technical cooperation.
Through this project, FAO continues to work with national and provincial counterparts to strengthen technical capacities and promote more effective management of date palm pests and diseases. The project’s field-based approach supports the assessment of practical interventions under local production conditions and helps identify opportunities to protect date palm groves, reduce pest-related losses and strengthen the sustainability of date production in Iran.

“Go woke, go broke” was a culture war rallying cry of the Biden years, with American conservatives waging battles against any corporate entity that dared to pay lip service to diversity or LGBTQ rights.
But customers of one successful anti-woke alternative brand later found their own wallets a bit lighter—with nothing to show for it.
In April 2023, at the height of a right-wing freakout over a sponsored Instagram post in which transgender actress and singer Dylan Mulvaney showed off a can of Bud Light with her face on it, a Georgia man named Seth Weathers smelled an opportunity to cash in. Conservatives were vowing to ditch the Budweiser brand and take their business elsewhere. (A tearful Kid Rock even filmed himself shooting up a few cases with a semiautomatic rifle.) It was an angry political demographic in need of a new low-ABV lager.
Weathers, a political consultant who briefly served as Georgia state director for Donald Trump’s presidential campaign in 2015 and went on to work with a county commissioner known for racist Facebook posts, swooped in to pitch a replacement beverage. Under his social brand “Conservative Dad,” he marketed a brew called Ultra Right Beer to the MAGA voters making a stink about trans inclusivity.
“America’s been drinking beer from a company that doesn’t even know what restroom to use,” Weathers said in a YouTube ad that included a clip of Mulvaney sipping Bud Light. “That’s why I created Conservative Dad’s Ultra Right 100 percent woke-free beer.” The commercial shows Weathers teeing up a can of Bud Light and walloping it with a baseball bat. “Stop giving money to woke corporations that hate our values,” he said, warning such companies to “stay the fuck away from our kids.”
The concept made a splash in right-wing media, which sent droves of readers and viewers to the Ultra Right Beer website to place orders—even though Weathers had yet to find a brewery to make the stuff. (He was also facing logistical hurdles to shipping the hypothetical beer, a process subject to heavy regulations that vary from one state to the next.) Within two weeks, Weathers had partnered with Big Kettle Brewing in Lawrenceville, Georgia, to produce the beer, and claimed he was closing in on $1 million in sales of six-packs priced at $19.99 apiece.
But while Fox News and similar outlets continued to tout Ultra Right as a stunning victory over Budweiser’s brewer, Anheuser-Busch, deliveries were slow to materialize. Weathers’ company, Ultra Right Beer LLC, would eventually receive an “F” rating from the Better Business Bureau, which notes that it has failed to respond to nearly 200 complaints over missing six-packs and virtually nonexistent customer service. The author of a one-star review of Ultra Right on the BBB website griped that its special edition “Revenge” cans of beer with Trump’s mugshot on them took a year and a half to arrive, while a “Fight”-themed six-pack (styled with the image of Trump raising his fist after surviving an assassination attempt at a July 2024 campaign rally) never arrived at all.
Weathers claimed in August 2024 that sales of the special edition Fight beer had reached the $1 million mark. It’s not clear how many orders of Fight beer ultimately shipped. On eBay, resellers have listed empty six-packs for as much as $115.
Two years later, around 400 people are members of a Facebook group called “People Still Waiting for Ultra Right Fight Beer,” with many claiming that they have received neither the limited-edition beer nor a refund after placing orders in 2024. “I no longer want the beer … just my money back!” reads a recent post on the page.
Enough of these customers have contacted Georgia attorney general Chris Carr to report on Ultra Right Beer LLC that the office has opened an investigation into the company, which has been unresponsive to compliance orders, according to court filings. Ironshield Brewing, the company that operated Big Kettle Brewing as a contract brewer, announced that it was shutting down in December 2023. Weathers did not respond to a request for comment and hasn’t posted to his Facebook or Instagram pages since late last year.
Many of the comments on Weathers’ dormant social media pages are from people demanding refunds or updates on beer orders. In response to a Facebook commenter who wrote that Weathers’ announcement of an Ultra Right restock in November was “plain bullshit” and called him a “thief,” Weathers wrote, “We do not want you as a customer,” adding that he had refunded the person’s order. “I cannot imagine how miserable someone must be to reach your age in life, to spend your time harassing small businesses who have made mistakes but is [sic] out here fighting for the causes you supposedly believe in,” he wrote.
Rich Alan, a police officer in New Jersey who spent more than $60 on two sixers of Fight beer that he says he never got, claims Weathers is a “fraud” and “scammer” who took advantage of Trump supporters. As his Conservative Dad character, Alan says, Weathers was “ stealing the hearts of these patriots and making you think that you're like you're one of them, basically. Like, ‘Hey, I'm just like you, I'm standing up to woke Bud Light.’ And then just taking their money and running with it.”
Paul Roberts, an employee of the Oregon department of transportation who shared a September 2024 receipt for three six-packs of Ultra Right Fight beer totaling $91.36, says he has tried in vain to get an update on the order. “Sent many emails, replies to texts, and on their Facebook page,” he says, and called a listed number as well. “No response.”
Both Roberts and Alan tell WIRED they only purchased the beers as collectible items and had no plans to actually drink them. They also say that their orders were not motivated by the Bud Light boycott. “I don't care what people drink,” Alan says. “You drink Bud Light, you drink Bud Light.” Roberts had previously bought the Revenge beer with Trump’s mugshot on it, which did arrive, although he says delivery was slow. “The mugshot had been used in a negative light, so I thought it was cool and collectible that they placed it on a beer can.”
Alan notes that as Weathers began running into difficulties with catching up on orders, he blamed these on legal wrangling with Anheuser-Busch. The company filed trademark opposition against Ultra Right Beer LLC in 2024, citing similarities to its own Michelob Ultra beer. Weathers called it an attempt at “corporate intimidation.” That litigation remains ongoing.
While Alan and Roberts have given up hope of getting their money back, they’d like to see justice served in some way or another. “I would like the state to enforce whatever laws apply to a business that takes your money and doesn't provide the product or service,” Roberts says. Alan adds that in his experience as a law enforcement officer, he’s used to seeing people get away with petty scams. “Accountability would be nice, whether it's seizing assets or seizing everything he has, some jail time,” he says.
“I'd like to cross paths with him one day,” Alan says of Weathers. “I'm sure a lot of people would.”

Families in Gaza fear return to hunger as WFP slashes food aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:44:10 UTC
19:44:10 KST

Breadcrumb
Families in Gaza fear return to hunger as WFP slashes food assistance
Safiya Abu Sabha, a displaced Palestinian woman from Gaza City, questions how she will be able to feed her four children if the food aid her family depends on vanishes.
Since the Israeli army killed her husband in an attack and she fled the Shuja'iyya neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City, the 40-year-old has been raising her children alone, struggling to cope with soaring living costs without an income.
Her concerns have deepened following the World Food Programme's (WFP) announcement of cuts to its assistance in Gaza amid funding shortages.
On Monday, the WFP announced a one-third reduction in its food assistance in Gaza due to funding shortages, affecting approximately 500,000 people.
Around 1.1 million vulnerable Palestinians will receive food or cash assistance, down from approximately 1.6 million the previous month, the WFP said in a press statement.
Food rations will be halved, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, while wheat flour distributions will also be reduced, it added.
The number of hot meals provided daily will fall from 250,000 to 150,000, and cash assistance for 75,000 households will be reduced, it explained. In hard-to-reach areas, including those near the so-called "Yellow Line", hot meals will be distributed every other day instead of daily.
For Safiya, who lives in a worn-out tent at a shelter in western Gaza City, the prospect of receiving less assistance threatens the limited support she relies on to feed her children.
"What scares me most today is that the aid might be cut back even further. I have no income with which to buy food for my children. I don't know how I will manage to feed them if we lose this support," she told The New Arab.
"The aid we receive isn't enough to cover everything my children need, and I can't always provide the most suitable food for them, but at least it helps me ensure they have something to eat. Something is better than nothing," she said.
Although the assistance does not meet all her family's nutritional needs, it helps Safiya put food on the table when buying groceries is beyond her means.
Losing a lifeline
Safiya's concerns are shared by Samir Abu Hasira, who lives with his wife and three children in a tent near Gaza's beach.
The Israeli army destroyed his house during the genocidal war, leaving his family without shelter or a livelihood.
His situation worsened when Israeli forces shot him as he tried to reach food aid trucks during the famine, costing him a leg and leaving him unable to work. He has since become increasingly dependent on humanitarian assistance to feed his wife and three children.
"I used to regularly receive a sack of flour and a carton of canned goods, which helped me provide food for my wife and children," he told TNA.
The supplies helped cover part of the family's needs, but further reductions could leave Samir struggling to compensate for the shortfall. With no income and no alternative means of support, buying food from local markets is difficult.
"The war has turned our lives upside down. I lost my home, and after losing my leg, I lost my ability to work. My family now depends on aid to survive," he said. "I never imagined reaching a point where I couldn't provide food for my own children. What frightens me most is not knowing what tomorrow will bring for them."
His experience highlights the vulnerability of families that have lost their livelihoods, particularly those caring for people whose injuries or disabilities prevent them from working.
For such households, reduced assistance means more than smaller food rations; it threatens their ability to meet basic needs.
Despite the cuts, the WFP intends to continue supporting bakeries that meet around one-third of Gaza's bread requirements, providing food assistance to approximately 300,000 women and children and nutritious snacks to 200,000 schoolchildren.
However, the funding crisis threatens the programme's ability to maintain assistance at a time when many families have few alternatives. For households such as Safiya and Samir's, the prospect of receiving less food aid adds to the uncertainty of living without stable shelter or income.
Hunger, with psychological and social pressures
The WFP estimates that approximately 1.4 million people, or 67 per cent of Gaza's population, face acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. Only one in five children has access to a sufficiently diverse diet.
According to the programme, with unemployment exceeding 80 per cent, many families cannot afford fresh produce and protein-rich foods, even when these are available in local markets. Food assistance has served as a lifeline for up to 90 per cent of households in Gaza over the past three years.
Since the ceasefire began in October 2025, the WFP has reached approximately 1.6 million people each month through food parcels, flour, bread, hot meals, nutrition programmes and cash assistance.
However, funding received for its operations in Palestine in 2026 amounted to no more than half of what it had received in previous years. The programme urgently needs US$450 million to sustain its operations in Gaza and the West Bank from October 2026 through March 2027.
Beyond its physical consequences, food insecurity is taking a psychological toll on families, particularly mothers struggling to provide for their children amid displacement, poverty and the loss of their homes.
Mustafa Ayesh, a social expert from Gaza City, told TNA that food shortages affect mental health and family relationships.
"When a mother cannot provide food for her children or fears she will not be able to feed them the next day, she faces intense psychological pressure and a sense of helplessness," Ayesh said.
He added that cuts to aid increase families' anxiety about the future, while children may feel more fearful and insecure as tensions rise at home.
Ayesh warned that continued shortages could force families to eat whatever food they can find, increasing the risk of malnutrition, particularly among children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers.
"For many families, food assistance is a basic safeguard against hunger when they have no income or other support. Any reduction adds to the pressure on people already struggling to survive," he said.
For Safiya, food aid cannot restore her home or bring back her husband, but it helps her feed her children.
For her and Samir, the assistance they receive remains essential despite falling short of their needs. As funding shortages threaten further cuts, both families face growing uncertainty about how they will secure their next meal.

Reform UK claims undercover racism exposé has left some of its members 'psychologically damaged' as it reports ITV to police
Reform UK says it has reported “multiple” ITV journalists, and the company’s board of directors, to the police on the grounds that their undercover reporters working on the exposé of racism in the party broke the law. The party says it will also be suing them for damages.
Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, posted this on social media summarising his party’s allegations.
Reform UK has reported ITV, its board, and its undercover reporters to the police.
Some of the crimes carry up to 10 years in prison.
They forged a passport.
They directly interfered in elections and almost certainly altered the results. Being paid to “canvass” for Reform in crucial wards we lost by a few dozen votes.
They lied to a veteran about their service and left him “violated”.
This is unprecedented.
The police are now involved.
Scrutiny of political parties is one thing.
But anyone breaking the law to try and ruin the lives of Reform’s staff, members or volunteers will be reported to the police and pursued relentlessly in the courts.
In a video setting out his case against ITV at greater length, Yusuf claimed ITV “psychologically damaged innocent and decent Reform staff and members who were not featured in any documentary”.
As an example of this, Yusuf said that one of the undercover reporters met a Reform UK member in Portsmouth who had served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He said:
One of the undercover reporters told him that they shared the same military background. That was a lie. The marine, believing him, took him for a drink. They spent hours talking about their service, and the marine shared deeply personal stories from the front line because he believed he was talking to a friend and a fellow soldier. He has told us he feels violated.
Yusuf also explained why he was alleging electoral interference. In Portsmouth two undercover reporters were tasked with delivering leaflets in one ward where Reform UK lost in the local elections by 24 votes, and in another ward where Reform UK lost by just 85 votes. Yusuf said these margins were smaller than the number of leaflets the undercover reporters were supposed to deliver.
But he did not assert in the video that they failed to deliver the leaflets, and he offered no evidence that they had done anything to suppress the Reform UK vote at the time.
Asked about the legal threats, an ITV spokesperson said:
ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest. All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch we would fully cooperate.
People tend to assume that a public interest defence will protect journalists from allegations of minor law-breaking if they are investigating wrongdoing. In fact, the law is more complicated than that, a public interest defence applies in some instances and not in others, and there are probably enough allegations in the Yusuf video to keep a media lawyer busy for days assessing the evidence.
But, in practice, it is rare for the criminal law to be used successfully against legitimate journalists. When the Crown Prosecution Service prosecuted police officers who had taken bribes, and the journalists who had paid them, under Operation Elveden, the officers were largely convicted but the journalists were largely acquitted. Juries seemed to accept they were operating in the public interest.
In the ITV case, the public interest case for the programme is particularly strong. Reform UK has accepted that some of the people exposed making racist comments should not be in the party – although it has also claimed they were not representative of the membership as a whole.
NEU says robust action on antisemitism in schools needed, but rejects reports call for teacher impartiality rules to be tightened
Richard Adams
Richard Adams is the Guardian’s education editor.
The review of antisemitism in England’s schools and colleges by Sir David Bell has now been published, with the Department for Education saying it will adopt its recommendations including antisemitism training for education leaders, strengthened safeguarding guidance and improved reporting and investigation of antisemitic incidents.
Bell’s full report goes into detail about the challenges that Jewish students and institutions face directly from antisemitism, as well as ways to tackle antisemitism in schools across the country.
The review also talks about the external pressures that schools face from parents and other community members, noting:
Schools and colleges should make decisions based on safeguarding, professional conduct, employment law and evidence, not on who can generate the strongest public pressure campaign or out of fear of stoking community tensions.
Presenting the review to parliament, education secretary Lucy Powell said:
We have a duty to teach this generation and the next what antisemitism is, why it’s wrong and what happens when it takes hold. That goes for every school and college, whether or not they have Jewish staff and students.
Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union, said:
Robust action to challenge antisemitism is certainly needed because young people are exposed to antisemitic ideas and tropes, including on social media, and to influencers and figures who espouse violence. Educational experiences that empower young people to develop positive attitudes and respect for each other are critical.
But Kebede rejected the need for schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism or new rules on political impartiality, saying they would make it harder for schools to discuss complex world events. He said:
This report will not tackle antisemitism. It wrongly calls into question the professionalism of teachers. The existing rules on impartiality in the classroom are very clear and teachers take that responsibility very seriously.
For three years, teachers have been responding to concerned pupils’ questions about this conflict. These classroom discussions are familiar territory, not uncharted ground.
The recommendations in the report include one saying the DfE “should strengthen guidance for schools on political impartiality” and another saying school leaders should “consider the appropriateness of political expression and identifiers in their respective settings”.

Judging by the latest post on Truth Social, it looks as thought the Jackdaw announcement may have made Fox News in the US this morning. This is from Donald Trump.
That felt like quite a routine PMQs, but it was one that went quite well for Andy Burnham. It was not so much that he won; it was more that he emerged completely unscathed because none of Kemi Badenoch’s attack lines landed. It is always hard for an opposition leader to criticise a decision they agree with (Jackdaw), and so she tried the argument that Labour was to blame for rerunning the application process instead of fighting the legal challenge against the original decision all the way to the supreme court (where it may have lost anyway). Burnham’s response, that the Tories were to blame for mucking it up in the first place, was more convincing. After that Badenoch trotted through some very familiar lines on welfare and debt. It was hard to see what “story” she was trying to land, and it felt a bit as if she was not trying too hard. Maybe she is saving up her ammunition for her budget response next week.
Burnham also successfully seized the initiative with an announcement, about standing charges on gas bills. These are only worth about £100 a year, and presumably the money would be recouped from consumers in some other forms. Still, it’s news.
But what made Burnham’s performance quite strong today was not so much his standing charge teaser (which sounded like a hint for what might be in the budget) as his overall tone. One of the big complaints about PMQs is that MPs treat it as just a game. Badenoch herself is quite open about this, and she has said that she only started to do it well when she decided to view it like a panto. Burnham, though, can speak in the Commons with a degree of conviction and moral force that marks him out. We saw it today when he was talking about Aberfan, or social care, or Covid, or the importance of big decisions. This does not make him unique, and of course he is a professional politician, and he can equivocate as much as the rest of them. But at other moments he can convey seriousness and sincerity, rooted in lived experience, better than others. By comparison, Badenoch sounds glib.

Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states held an extraordinary meeting in Riyadh on Wednesday to discuss strengthening cooperation and coordination among their armed forces amid continued Houthi militia attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The meeting was convened by the GCC Armed Forces Operations and Training Committee at the headquarters of the GCC General Secretariat, according to the UAE defence ministry.
The ministry said discussions focused on strengthening joint military cooperation in operations and training, as well as developing coordination and integration mechanisms among Gulf armed forces.
The talks also aimed to support joint Gulf defence efforts and improve military readiness and efficiency, the ministry said, without disclosing the participants or any decisions reached.
The GCC comprises Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman.
Calls for action against Houthis
The meeting comes amid escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and regional and international efforts to halt them.
Although the GCC has not issued a statement on Wednesday’s meeting, Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi called on Sunday for “effective” international action against the Houthis following a ministerial meeting in Manama.
Yemen has seen renewed fighting since July between government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthi militia, following a period of relative calm under a truce that began in April 2022.
The conflict started in September 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and several other provinces.

Nigeria reports Ebola case, fourth African country affected by outbreak
- Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case in more than a decade. The patient is a Ugandan woman who arrived in Abuja on 5 October and was confirmed positive on 20 October.
- Health officials have traced 44 contacts, mostly healthcare workers, and the woman is in isolation receiving treatment. Nigeria says it has the systems to respond, after containing Ebola in 2014.
- The outbreak has spread to four African countries and killed 4,646 people since May in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Officials warn that misinformation and funding gaps could help it spread further.
AI generated
ABUJA - Nigeria reported its first Ebola case in more than a decade on Oct 20, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that health officials have described as the fastest-spreading on record.
The Ebola species behind the outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
Since the first cases were confirmed in Democratic Republic of Congo in May, the disease has killed 4,646 people.
Health officials fear misinformation and funding shortfalls could fuel further spread within the region and across borders.
“Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa. The situation demands urgent action and political leadership at the highest level,” Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director General Jean Kaseya said on X on Oct 21.
The Nigerian case involves a Ugandan woman who arrived in Nigeria’s capital Abuja via Addis Ababa on Oct 5, Odianosen Ehiakhamen of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control told Arise TV on Oct 20.
She began feeling unwell two days later and sought treatment at a private hospital in Abuja on Oct 11 with malaria-like symptoms, but her condition did not improve, Ehiakhamen said.
After health officials learned she had recently travelled to Uganda, one of the countries affected by the current outbreak, they tested her for Ebola on Oct 19.
The positive result was confirmed on Oct 20.
Authorities have identified 44 contacts, most of them healthcare workers.
They included the patient’s husband, a Swiss national who lives with her in Abuja.
Officials are also tracing passengers who travelled with her but do not believe she was symptomatic during the flight.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told public broadcaster NTA that the woman was in isolation and receiving treatment.
Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases
Uganda’s health ministry said the woman had travelled to Congo, where more than 9,500 Ebola cases have been recorded across eight provinces.
It was not immediately clear where she had been in Congo.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here,” Uganda’s health ministry said, adding that the country has no active Ebola cases.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organisation declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Earlier in October, Kenya reported its first Ebola case, involving a traveller who arrived from Congo via Uganda.
The country has since reported nine cases, all linked to the same patient.
The spread of Ebola to Kenya raised questions about the effectiveness of border screening systems designed to prevent cross-border transmission.
Pate, Nigeria’s health minister, said the country had successfully contained Ebola in 2014 during the West African epidemic, the largest outbreak on record.
He said Nigeria had the systems in place to respond to the new case. REUTERS

A majority of Arab Israeli young adults are open to voting for non-Arab parties in the upcoming Knesset elections, according to Arab-Jewish Center for Empowerment, Equality, and Cooperation – Negev Institute for Strategies of Peace and Economic Development (AJEEC-NISPED), citing a recent survey conducted by Dialog, an Israeli consulting firm.
AJEEC-NISPED, per the organization's website, is made up of a joint team of Arabs and Jews who work to create a society in which Arabs and Jews can coexist while preserving their identity and culture.
The poll, conducted in August, collected data from 257 Arab Israelis aged 18-26.
Sixty percent of respondents said they would consider voting for a non-Arab party if it presented a clear plan to address issues important to them.
Only 48% of respondents said they were loyal exclusively to Arab parties. About 20% said they had no preference regarding party identity, and 9% preferred an Arab party but were also willing to consider other parties.
What issues matter most to the younger generation in Arab society?
Violence and crime were the top concerns among young Arab Israelis, with 55% of respondents identifying them as a key priority when choosing whom to vote for. Employment and income opportunities followed at 22%, while 20% prioritized investment in education and higher education, and 19% cited housing solutions.
The surge in crime and violence across Arab towns and cities, with armed gangs controlling public space, has left many Arab Israeli citizens feeling helpless and under constant anxiety, several members of the Arab community in Israel told The Jerusalem Post in January.
The poll also found that 70% of respondents believe that political parties in Israel do not listen sufficiently to young people in Arab society.
"This survey should be a wake-up call for the entire political establishment," said Suleiman al-Amour, CEO of AJEEC. "Young Arabs in Israel are not asking for much...They want to know who intends to address the crime and violence threatening their personal safety...They are yearning for practical plans, with goals, budgets, and accountability for implementation."
"It is time for the political establishment to stop talking about Arab society and start talking with its young people and its leadership, and above all, to offer them a future," he concluded.
Dana Ben Shimon contributed to this report.

Iran’s greatest vulnerability

Swiss government wants CO2 levy on cement imports
The governing Federal Council wants to ensure a level playing field between Swiss cement and cement from abroad. To this end, a CO₂ compensation levy is to be imposed on cement imports above a certain quantity.
A CO₂ border adjustment mechanism is intended to offset differences in the CO₂ costs of cement production between Switzerland and third countries with less ambitious climate policies, the Federal Council announced on Wednesday. It recommends that parliament approve a corresponding bill from the National Council’s Environment Committee.
In Switzerland, cement production is integrated into an emissions trading scheme (ETS). The ETS sets a price on CO2 emissions, thereby creating an incentive to reduce CO2.

As Serbia votes, students emerge as greatest threat to Vucic’s long rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:36:31 UTC
19:36:31 KST

As Serbia votes, students emerge as greatest threat to Vucic’s long rule
BELGRADE, Oct 21 - Aleksa Simic, a political science student at Belgrade University, did not hesitate when he learned that the collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad had killed 16 people in November 2024.
Demanding justice for the dead, and an end to the kind of corruption that many believed led to the station's shoddy construction, he and other students blockaded the political science faculty in protest. As Serbia mourned, sympathetic residents brought them homemade meals, mattresses and pillows. Many stopped by to discuss the students' demands.
"For the first time, I had a sense of belonging to a community. I realised that my voice mattered," Simic said.
Two years on, as Serbia prepares for elections on October 25, the student protest movement has ballooned to become one of the most powerful political forces in the country and poses the greatest threat yet to the rule of Aleksandar Vucic, who has dominated Serbian politics first as prime minister, then president, since 2014.
With protests raging in cities across Europe, fuelled by the high cost of living, a shortage of jobs and poor education standards, the Serbian students have shown what a force younger generations can be when they harness widespread discontent.
In interviews with Reuters, a dozen students and teachers described how a methodical countrywide door-knocking campaign, peaceful marches, a tightly controlled media message and a constant rotation of leaders to protect individuals from government smear campaigns have helped maintain momentum in Serbia.
Now, they have their own "Students Win" list of 250 candidates for Sunday's election, which includes university professors, actors, farmers and even a popular rapper.
The only poll published this month, by New Serbian Political Thought (NSPM) on October 20, showed the students' list of candidates edging ahead of Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with 44.5% of the vote to 42.7%, although betting odds favour Vucic.
"The protests changed the society. It showed people they are not alone," said Florian Bieber, professor of Southeast European history and politics at the University of Graz.
UNKNOWNS SURROUND STUDENT MOVEMENT
The big question is how the students would govern should they win on Sunday.
Vucic is a significant international figure, managing a delicate balancing act that seeks closer ties with China, a major investor, and Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, while leaving the door open to joining the European Union even with the accession process stalled.
The students' list is headed by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although they have said this does not mean he would become prime minister should they win.
Some political analysts wonder how the country would fare on the international stage with an unknown at the helm, while there are scant details about how the students will set about fulfilling their pledges to fight corruption, promote transparency, create greater media freedom and enact education reform at home.
Critics also point to their silence on joining the EU and relations with the former province of Kosovo. Pro-European opponents of Vucic's government criticise them for saying that they would not introduce sanctions on Russia.
"A (student-led) government would pursue broad reforms to tackle corruption, overhaul key public institutions and companies, and dismantle patronage networks," consultancy Teneo said in an analyst note on Tuesday. "However, strong bureaucratic resistance could generate short-term institutional instability."
GROWING DISCONTENT WITH VUCIC RULE
Vucic, 56, stepped down as president in September to run again for prime minister in the snap election.
While he has overseen a period of strong economic growth and a fall in unemployment, critics blame him for democratic backsliding, the silencing of critics and the media, and hampering Serbia's EU accession by not undertaking necessary reforms. Police have beaten protesters and threatened people who voice opposition online, rights groups, activists and students told Reuters.
Simmering anger towards the government boiled over with the collapse of the station roof in Novi Sad. Vucic has sought to discredit the student movement, saying it is trying to destroy Serbia and accusing foreign agents from Croatia and Montenegro of financing it, but that has not dented their support.
Government representatives did not respond to a request for comment. Vucic and the authorities have repeatedly denied the allegations of corruption and violence and attempts to discredit the opposition. The students dismiss claims that they are being organised from abroad.
HOW A SMALL MOVEMENT GREW
The student protests were small to begin with: days after the canopy collapse, a few dozen people blocked traffic in Novi Sad and Belgrade for one minute for each person who was killed.
Less than three months later, in late January 2025, then prime minister and close Vucic ally Milos Vucevic resigned a day after tens of thousands of people blocked one of Belgrade's main junctions, joined by farmers in their tractors.
In March that year, the students led hundreds of thousands of people through Belgrade, the biggest anti-government march in a generation. By then, the movement had a symbol: a red handprint, representing the blood that the protesters say is on the government's hands.
"We felt we had importance and that we had a greater responsibility," Simic said.
University faculties across the country held plenums and working groups focused on media and social media strategies, and organising marches.
On the first anniversary of the roof collapse, the students walked from Belgrade to Novi Sad. People in small villages offered fruit. An image of a man with a traditional Serbian hat hugging a Muslim student in a headscarf flooded social media - which supporters hailed as an emblem of a young, progressive Serbia after the devastating Balkan wars of the 1990s.
Ahead of Sunday's vote, student groups have undergone training on election fraud and say teams plan to be present at polling stations.
Gavrilo Andric was a software engineer for a big company when the protests began. An amateur photographer, he watched the movement grow, eventually leaving his job to become its unofficial documenter.
"I finally realised that in our society we have a group of people who see things can be improved and want to work on it together with other people," he told Reuters. REUTERS

Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:35:34 UTC
19:35:34 KST

Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?
For students, the slogan has come to represent a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement.
As violent protests roil France, bringing together students demanding better educational conditions and groups rejecting the high cost of living, one chant has become an improbable rallying cry: “Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres”.
The unofficial slogan does not mean much taken literally, but students have channelled a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement into this nonsensical expression. It is meant to mock racial stereotyping by the police.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets nationwide over the weekend, in the largest mobilisation since protests over education reforms and rising prices began last month. The protest movement has been triggered by grievances ranging from overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages to systemic inequality and lack of opportunity.
Police conduct has also come under scrutiny. France’s police inspectorate, the IGPN, has opened dozens of investigations into alleged police violence since protests began.
What does the slogan mean?
“Bismillah” is Arabic for “in the name of God”, an expression used by Muslims before beginning an activity. In French slang, it has lost some of its original meaning, becoming more akin to “let’s do it”.
“C’est les ténèbres” literally translates as “it’s the darkness”, which alludes to a situation that is bleak and hopeless.
The slogan therefore translates as “In the name of God, it’s the darkness”, which does not convey a clear message in and of itself.
Where did the slogan come from?
Students say the phrase is a mockery of the police force, which tried to infiltrate social media chats used by protesters to coordinate.
The screenshot of a Snapchat conversation featuring the expression began circulating in early October. In it, a user named Mamadou requests to be added to a group, saying: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?”
The message also featured emojis with Algerian flags.
Students say the message was sent by undercover police officers attempting to infiltrate their chats by using an unconvincing mix of Arabic and slang. The claim has not been verified and French authorities have not issued any statement.
Youssef El Chazli, associate professor in Arab and Mediterranean sociology at Paris 8 University Vincennes – Saint-Denis, said the phrase “reinforces an image of out-of-touch policemen filled with stereotypes”.
“Such stereotypes appear to disproportionately aim at youths from Arab and African descent,” El Chazli told Al Jazeera. “This appears as one more example of how out-of-touch state agencies seem to be with the current movement.”
What does the slogan tell us about the protest movement?
The slogan has appeared on cardboard placards as a mockery of racial stereotypes and as a symbol of how authorities are out of touch with the realities of young people.
The slogan has spread as far as Italy and Belgium, where similar protests over the high cost of living and poor education also took place over the weekend.
El Chazli said satirical memes and internet trends have become tools to express political grievances during protests, which have traditionally been “inventive and creative”. “With youth mobilisations, protest creativity will draw heavily on youths’ subcultures,” he said.
Discussions around Islamophobia have also taken a front seat in public debate. French authorities have been reluctant to comment publicly on a significant spike in Islamophobic acts in France. One report cited by the Reuters news agency last year showed a 72 percent increase in such incidents during the January-March quarter of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.
The French far right quickly resorted to racist language to blame Muslim youths for the violence, while United States President Donald Trump also chimed in, claiming that this is about “Islam wanting to take over”.
“What used to be a nonsubject 20 years ago is now a debated point,” El Chazli said. “For younger generations, Arab and African influences have been steadily mainstreaming in youth subcultures, owing to sports and arts figures, as well as new radio shows or social media content.”

Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:35:00 UTC
19:35:00 KST

Does Pakistan-Taliban conflict create a strategic opening for India?
October 21, 2026
Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between the two nations.
The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan's defense minister said the country was at "open war" with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban's "terrorist hubs" reported earlier in October.
At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan's accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.
Where does India come into play?
As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict "presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India," Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
D'Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan's traditional influence in Afghanistan and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.
"India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups," she said.
However, D'Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.
"There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban," she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.
India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan's influence, she notes. "The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched."
Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan's expense.
"The issues have very little to do with India," Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan's military actions for Afghan civilians.
"Yet the rupture has made Kabul's search for alternative partners more pressing," he added.
For India, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.
The cost of closer ties
Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
"The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India," Mukhopadhyaya told DW. He warned, however, that New Delhi's own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.
He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.
"For all practical purposes, India's security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and 'terrorists' by default," he said.
Former Afghan partners had been left "disappointed, even bitter," Mukhopadhyaya added. "A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation."
Trade cannot overcome geography
India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in northwestern India in December 2025.
Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million (€807 million) in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.
On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d'affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul's interest in expanding economic cooperation.
But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.
New Delhi has sought to use Iran's Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.
D'Souza cautioned that "the ongoing conflict in Iran" limits India's ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.
Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.
"In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul's efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts," Sachdeva told DW.
"Afghanistan's potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured," he added.
Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan's wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.
Islamabad's security fears
Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India's growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.
"Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan," Ajmal said.
The allegation reflects Islamabad's position and has not been established as fact.
Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.
India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan's position.
"India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence," she told DW.
Siddiqa added that Pakistan's establishment continues to view the crisis through "a singular security lens."
"Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides," she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create "a dangerous two-front security trap" for Pakistan.
India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi's basket.

"I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck. MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.," the president said in a post on Truth Social.
Data centers have become a hot-button issue ahead of the midterm elections in November. Public opposition to the buildout of the facilities and their environmental impact has been growing, with multiple states considering moratoriums.
AI infrastructure company Nebius is "100% in principle" having discussions about investing in communities, the company's Chief Revenue Officer Marc Boroditsky told CNBC when asked about Trump's suggestion of a dividend.
There could be "some sort of way where the rewards are actually funneled back to the community," Boroditsky told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of Nvidia's GTC Berlin conference.
"We see it today in terms of the tax revenue that are arriving. I could see something like a benefit of some sort that's more direct economic opportunity for the community as well," he said.
Boroditsky added: "A dividend is being paid in different forms — investing in education, job development, overall economic development. The concept that the president identified... it's not crazy to consider something like that."
Data center stocks have also come under pressure this week amid growing concerns about the financial health of the sector. As the AI infrastructure buildout grows more costly, companies are increasingly turning to debt markets to finance deals.
When it comes to investing in infrastructure underpinning the technology, HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery advised discernment over an all-in approach.
"One has to be selective," Elhedery told CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."
Power constraints
Much of the concern centers around water usage, power consumption, electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. Access to power is a major constraint on the sector, as power grids in the U.S. and Europe become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers.
"Energy is always a bottleneck, and trying to find powered land and areas that we can build large-scale AI factories is a big focus for us," Chase Lochmiller, CEO of compute infrastructure firm Crusoe, told CNBC Wednesday in Berlin.
"Increasingly there's a lot of policy permitting and just working through local communities to make sure that everything can come online effectively," he said.
Trump, a long-time supporter of data centers, said Wednesday that he has been watching them "very closely" and has now come to a "very strong conclusion."
"New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data enters are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease," Trump said, in a post around 1.37 a.m. ET.
In some cases, data centers can operate as flexible loads, adjusting their electricity use to help stabilize the grid.
Hyperscalers have secured deals where they agree to help finance badly needed updates to local power grids. However, some experts have warned that the AI boom will ultimately result in higher electricity prices.

Russia wants AI to help design its next aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:32:23 UTC
19:32:23 KST

- Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said it is evaluating new software, including artificial intelligence, to speed up the design of future aircraft and modifications.
- UAC is already running a pilot project with Sberbank’s GigaChat AI for generative design at the early stage of a new aircraft.
Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation is looking at artificial intelligence and other new software to speed up the design of future aircraft and cut the cost of developing new versions of existing ones, the state-owned planemaker said in a statement on its social media.
UAC, which builds nearly all of Russia’s military and civil aircraft, from Su-57 and Su-35 fighters to the MC-21 airliner, said its engineers are evaluating new software products, including AI technologies, as the company moves its design work onto digital models.
The company said digital models let its engineers analyze far larger volumes of data and test many more aircraft layouts before choosing the best one, which makes developing new modifications faster and cheaper over an aircraft’s life cycle. UAC added that it is taking a measured approach to AI and will only use the new tools where they make sense and help solve specific engineering problems.
“Digital technology makes it possible to take a larger sample and understand a problem more deeply. Over the life cycle, this will be faster and cheaper when creating the next modifications,” UAC specialists said.
The statement follows remarks by UAC general designer Sergey Korotkov, who said on Oct. 13 that there is no reason not to use AI in aircraft design as long as it helps with the task at hand and is applied thoughtfully. UAC has already been testing the idea, and in May its chief executive, Vadim Badekha, said the company was running a pilot project with Sberbank to use the bank’s GigaChat AI model for generative design of a new aircraft at the early design stage, with plans to extend it later to strength and aerodynamic calculations.
The shift to domestic digital tools has been driven largely by sanctions, since Western design software vendors such as Dassault Systèmes, Siemens and Autodesk pulled out of Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and left the country’s aerospace industry without the programs it had relied on for decades. UAC says it has since replaced software at its design bureaus with Russian products, equipping about 4,000 engineering workstations and swapping out nine key product lifecycle management modules, and on Oct. 16 it said digital design had cut some aircraft system calculations, such as cabin heat balance and hydraulic networks, from months to days.
Those efforts come as UAC struggles with delays on its most important civil programs, which have had to replace Western parts and systems with Russian-made equivalents. President Vladimir Putin said in June that the MC-21 had been set back by almost two years, partly because of problems with the wing, and First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said certification of the version built entirely with Russian components is now planned for the end of 2027.

Giant tunnel proposed to tackle Windermere sewage discharges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:32:12 UTC
19:32:12 KST

Plans are under way for a new giant tunnel to transport sewage away from Windermere, England’s largest lake.
Windermere, in the Lake District, has suffered from widespread raw sewage and bacterial pollution driven by discharges from United Utilities. Campaigners say this pollution has caused more frequent toxic blue-green algal blooms, with the public advised to avoid swimming in the lake.
Modelling indicates the climate crisis will exacerbate these challenges, with the catchment expected to experience more intense rainfall over the coming years, placing further pressure on the wastewater infrastructure.
A new project, backed by United Utilities, the Environment Agency and local campaigners, has set out a vision to end sewage discharges into the lake by building an 12-mile (19km) tunnel to transport sewage away from the lake.
The water company said the use of tunnelling techniques would minimise the disruption to local communities.
Windermere is at the heart of the Lake District Unesco world heritage site and has been the inspiration for poets, storytellers and lyricists for generations, with an estimated 17.7 million people visiting every year.
The treated effluent would then be discharged into either the River Leven or the Irish Sea at Ulverston. It is estimated the project will cost £3.6bn, with United Utilities to seek permission from the government to raise customer bills to pay for it. It said the programme could add up to £3.17 a month to water bills in 2035.
The project will now enter the detailed design phase during which specialised engineers will work out the technicalities of the build, which is expected to take two years.
If granted permission to raise bills to pay for the project, United Utilities said the project could be complete within seven years and would provide a “one and done” solution with an immediate impact.
Matt Staniek, a campaigner at Save Windermere, which is a partner on the project, said creating the feasibility report had involved weekly meetings over 15 months.
Staniek, who has been calling for the end of sewage discharges into the lake for more than five years, said he was concerned at first about partnering with the company causing the pollution, but said they were the only people who could actually fix it. “This has demonstrated that it is possible not to dump sewage in Lake Windermere,” he said.
In planning for the project, the team considered the transformation of Lake Annecy in France, which is widely recognised as one of the cleanest lakes in Europe. In the 1950s, Annecy faced similar pollution problems, but the authorities invested in long-term infrastructural improvements to eliminate the sewage discharges.
“This is up to the government now. The plan is there, it’s in place, we’re not going to stop until Andy Burnham is on the shores of Lake Windermere with a spade announcing that the construction has begun on this project,” Staniek said.
