Approximately 7.3 million Israelis are registered to vote in next Tuesday's election for the 26th Knesset, but about 810,000 of them, roughly one in nine, live outside the country, according to figures released Tuesday by Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS). 
The data highlight a significant gap between the number of citizens on the electoral register and those actually residing in Israel. The bureau noted that some Israelis registered abroad may have died without their deaths being reported to the Population and Immigration Authority. Under Israel's election rules, most citizens living overseas cannot vote from abroad and must return to Israel to cast a ballot, with limited exceptions for eligible state representatives and their families. 
Since the previous Knesset election in November 2022, the number of eligible voters living in Israel has risen by approximately 333,000, an increase of 5.4%. Among registered voters residing in the country, 15.1% are between the ages of 18 and 24, while 27.6% are aged 25 to 39. The largest group, accounting for 31%, comprises voters aged 40 to 59, and another 26.3% are 60 or older.
The figures also reveal significant differences between Israel's population groups. Just over 5 million eligible voters living in Israel, or 77%, are Jewish, including approximately 684,000 ultra-Orthodox Jews. Arab citizens, including Muslims, Arab Christians and Druze, account for about 1.16 million eligible voters, or 18%. Another 346,000, representing 5%, are classified as members of other population groups, primarily non-Arab Christians and people without a registered religious affiliation, many of them immigrants and their families who are not registered as Jewish.
The CBS stressed that differences in age distribution help explain why some communities account for a smaller share of eligible voters than of the general population. Arab Israelis make up approximately 22% of the population but only 18% of the electorate, reflecting the community's relatively young population and the presence of residents without Israeli citizenship, particularly in East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Similarly, ultra-Orthodox Jews account for 13.9% of Israel's population but only 10.5% of registered voters, largely because of the community's high proportion of children.
The geographical differences are equally pronounced. The northern border town of Metula has the highest share of residents eligible to vote, at 83.8%, while Mas'ade, a Druze community in the northern Golan Heights, has the lowest, at just 30.1%. In most Israeli cities with more than 100,000 residents, the proportion of eligible voters ranges between 70% and 80%. Three cities fall significantly below that range: Jerusalem, where just 39.2% of residents are eligible to vote, Beit Shemesh at 47.1%, and Bnei Brak at 50.4%. Their relatively young populations contribute to the figures, while Jerusalem's rate is also affected by the substantial number of noncitizen residents.
By comparison, 79.5% of Bat Yam residents are eligible to vote, followed by Tel Aviv-Jaffa at 77.4%, Ramat Gan at 77.2%, Rishon LeZion at 76.7%, Haifa at 76.3%, Holon at 75.6% and Beersheba at 73.9%.
Israel's electorate has expanded dramatically since the country's first parliamentary election in 1949, when 506,567 citizens were registered to vote, all of them living in Israel. That figure nearly doubled by the second Knesset election. By the election held after the 1973 Yom Kippur War, the number of eligible voters had exceeded 2 million, rising to approximately 3.4 million in 1992 and surpassing 5 million by 2006.

US Navy P-8A Poseidon Returns to Black Sea Skies as Attacks on Commercial Ships Raise Alarm
A US Navy Boeing P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft conducted a surveillance mission over the western Black Sea near Bulgaria after arriving at Varna from Naval Air Station Sigonella, marking its first tracked appearance in the region in several months.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to ItaMilRadar on October 19, flight-tracking data showed the P-8A making several turns over the maritime area, with portions of its mission conducted at altitudes below 9,000 feet.
The aircraft’s extended flight at lower altitudes indicates that maritime patrol was likely a key objective of the operation, rather than intelligence collection alone. However, publicly available flight-tracking data does not provide enough information to determine the mission’s exact purpose.
According to ItaMilRadar, the mission comes amid heightened security concerns in the western Black Sea following a series of reported attacks against commercial shipping near Bulgaria and Romania.
In early October, two commercial ships were targeted by aerial and maritime drones within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, with one vessel sinking following the attack. Further incidents were later reported near the Bulgarian and Romanian coastlines, including strikes against ships in Romanian territorial waters.
The incidents have also intensified concerns over Russia’s hybrid warfare activities in the Black Sea, as attacks on civilian vessels increasingly threaten maritime security and commercial shipping routes near NATO member states.
On October 5, a civilian cargo vessel was struck by two Russian drones near Romania’s coastline, killing two people, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as cited by Reuters.
Romania’s Interior Ministry later confirmed that 11 crew members had been rescued after the vessel caught fire approximately 30 nautical miles south of Sfântu Gheorghe.
According to ItaMilRadar, while exclusive economic zones fall under a different legal framework than territorial waters, attacks on commercial vessels in these areas can still create serious maritime security risks.
However, the publication emphasized that there is no direct evidence connecting the US Navy P-8A’s latest mission to the recent attacks on commercial vessels.
The deteriorating security situation has also prompted Bulgaria to seek additional military assistance from NATO to strengthen its defenses and increase the alliance’s presence in the region.
On October 16, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said Sofia had requested additional aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone capabilities, and aerial patrols in response to the increasing frequency of maritime attacks.
Speaking to reporters, Stoyanov expressed concern over the worsening security environment in the Black Sea, pointing to recent strikes in Romanian territorial waters as further evidence of the threats facing countries in the region.
He added that deploying additional allied military resources would not only strengthen regional defenses but also demonstrate a more substantial NATO presence in the Black Sea.

Ukrainian Partisans Cut Moscow Military Comms to Help Drones Slip Through Russian Air Defenses
Agents of the ATESH partisan movement are sabotaging Russian military communications around IXcellerate, one of Moscow’s largest commercial data centers, in an effort to disrupt air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on October 21.
“We are disabling enemy channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets,” ATESH said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
IXcellerate is a major part of Moscow’s digital infrastructure, supporting banking applications, card payments, telecommunications operators, and business services.
ATESH claims that Russia’s Defense Ministry also uses infrastructure connected to the facility for military communications and air-defense command systems, effectively embedding military traffic within civilian server networks.
According to the movement, drone strikes depend not only on the aircraft themselves but also on disrupting the communications networks that connect Russian air-defense crews and command posts.
Cutting those links on the ground, ATESH says, can delay target information and reduce coordination between air-defense units.
Without stable communications, Russian air-defense crews can lose situational awareness, receive targeting information too late, and struggle to cover the routes used by incoming drones, the group said.
ATESH claims its agents are identifying military communications infrastructure concealed within civilian facilities and disrupting those networks from inside Russia.
The group said Moscow’s attempts to hide military traffic inside civilian server infrastructure have not prevented partisan cells from locating and targeting the communications links supporting Russian military operations.
Previously, ATESH claimed responsibility for sabotaging a critical electrical substation in Azov, Russia’s Rostov region, disrupting power to a defense manufacturing facility that produces guidance systems and other components for Russian missiles.

North Korea Sends 12,000 Workers to Russia to Build Shahed Drones
North Korea has reportedly sent 12,000 workers to Russia to help manufacture Shahed-type attack drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, expanding Pyongyang’s involvement in Russia’s military production supporting its war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a joint report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the George W. Bush Institute on October 14, North Korean workers receive approximately $2.50 per hour, while the North Korean government reportedly takes between 70% and 90% of their earnings.
The report identifies three main groups involved in drone manufacturing at Alabuga: Russian students and young workers, foreign recruits from other countries, and North Korean nationals. Researchers raised concerns about coercive labor practices affecting all three groups, particularly the systematic withholding of wages from North Korean workers.
Russian students are recruited through Alabuga’s educational programs, which combine technical training with industrial work. Some reportedly work shifts lasting up to 12 hours, with their pay tied to strict production targets.
Workers have also reportedly faced threats of financial penalties for disclosing details about the facility’s operations, including to family members.
The Alabuga industrial complex is a major Russian production site for Geran-2 drones, based on the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, which Russia regularly uses in attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Satellite imagery published in September showed additional production buildings and warehouses under construction at the site, indicating continued expansion of its manufacturing infrastructure.
North Korea’s involvement in Russian drone production comes amid growing military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang. Beyond providing personnel, North Korea has reportedly sought to incorporate lessons from Russia’s use of drones in Ukraine into its own military development programs.
Analysts have also indicated that Pyongyang is working to expand domestic production of Shahed-type drones and smaller unmanned aircraft, potentially benefiting from Russian technical expertise.
Earlier, Bloomberg reported on September 17 that approximately 25,000 North Korean nationals were working at Russian drone manufacturing facilities, including Alabuga. Many reportedly entered Russia on student visas to circumvent international sanctions, while North Korean authorities confiscated most of their earnings.

Russia Faces $10.5 Billion Regional Budget Deficit as 65 Regions Prepare Spending Cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category
- World
Russia Faces $10.5 Billion Regional Budget Deficit as 65 Regions Prepare Spending Cuts
Around 65 Russian regions are planning to reduce spending on investment and infrastructure projects between 2027 and 2029 as stagnant revenues, rising financial obligations, and war-related expenditures put increasing pressure on local budgets, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) on October 20.
The agency reported that regional authorities are being forced to scale back planned construction, infrastructure modernization, and investment programs as available funds become insufficient to cover social payments, public institutions, and expenditures associated with Russia’s war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among the regions preparing budget reductions is Tatarstan, which plans to cut spending by 13% in 2027, bringing its budget to approximately $6.6 billion.
The Leningrad region is expected to reduce expenditures by 2.9% to $3.5 billion, while Yakutia plans a 2.7% reduction to approximately $4 billion.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the reductions will primarily affect investment initiatives, repairs, and modernization of municipal infrastructure, potentially leaving local development projects without sufficient funding.
The financial pressure is also reflected in Russia’s broader regional budget projections.
According to forecasts from Russia’s Finance Ministry cited by SZRU, regional budgets are expected to generate approximately $331.4 billion in revenue in 2027, against projected expenditures of $342 billion. This would leave Russia’s regions facing a combined budget deficit of approximately $10.5 billion.
At the same time, Ukrainian intelligence reported that Moscow continues to transfer additional responsibilities to regional authorities without providing corresponding financial resources. As a result, local administrations must finance these obligations from their existing budgets, redirecting funds originally allocated to other programs.
The federal government is also reportedly preparing changes to financial assistance for economically weaker regions, potentially further restricting their access to budgetary support.
Under the proposed arrangements, Dagestan, Tuva, Ingushetia, and Altai Krai would be guaranteed no more than 90% of the subsidies allocated under existing budget legislation in 2027, rather than receiving the full amount with indexation.
Additionally, SZRU noted that even partial debt relief on regional budget loans would come with restrictions requiring local authorities to spend the freed-up funds on priorities established by Moscow.
Russian regions are losing control over their financial resources as their budgets become increasingly dependent on decisions made by Moscow. The Kremlin continues to dictate how funds are distributed, leaving local authorities with fewer resources to address pressing regional issues.
The growing financial pressure on Russia’s regions comes amid broader strains on the country’s federal budget, which have also prompted the Central Bank to draw down its gold reserves.
According to The Moscow Times on October 20, Russia’s Central Bank has been selling gold from its reserves for ten consecutive months to help cover a widening federal budget deficit, projected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles ($81.1 billion) this year, twice the amount initially anticipated.
The latest reduction brought the country’s total gold reserves to 72.8 million ounces, their lowest level since late 2019.

Student groups have also called for protests the same day to push their demands for more investment in education. Yellow Vest activists are seeking to revive their campaign, which emerged in 2018, against rising living costs and declining public services.
Last weekend’s demonstrations rapidly degenerated into rampant violence, especially in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges, which overwhelmed police and took hours to contain.
Highlighting investor concern over the situation, French government borrowing costs have risen sharply this week, pushing benchmark 10-year bond yields to 5%, their highest level since July 2002.
Analysts said markets are worried that the unrest could complicate government efforts to repair strained public finances at a time of already mounting budget pressures.
Macron said he would meet intelligence services on Oct 22 ahead of the new protests.
“Those who want to cause disorder in city centres next Saturday will be prevented from doing so,” he told reporters during a visit to Qatar, where he has been seeking energy deals as France grapples with rising fuel costs. “There must be no wavering at the top of the state.”
Government ministers have promised a vastly reinforced security operation after acknowledging shortcomings in their initial response, with troops expected to be deployed alongside additional police.
Macron accused some foreign leaders of spreading misinformation about what has happened. US President Donald Trump, in particular, has blamed the turbulence on mass migration and radical Islam, saying it is a warning for Americans.
Asked whether he was referring to Trump, Macron said: “Among others”, adding that some foreign politicians were looking to make political capital at the expense of France.
“We don’t need that. We already have difficulties to deal with,” he said.
In a letter to unions ahead of the Oct 21 meeting, Lecornu said their talks should focus on ensuring “the indispensable freedom to demonstrate”, which he said some were trying to curtail by associating it with “unacceptable acts”.
France’s main unions have separately called a nationwide mobilisation for Nov 5.
“There is huge and legitimate anger, and the answer to that situation is not repression. It is a political response. That’s what I will tell the prime minister today,” Sophie Binet, head of the CGT union, told RTL radio.
Political backlash
A second consecutive night of local curfews passed without major incidents in areas hit by the unrest, offering the government some respite as it prepared for fresh demonstrations.
The unrest has triggered a political backlash ahead of presidential elections in 2027, with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls.
“The government has lost control of everything,” far-right leader Marine Le Pen told Franceinfo radio.
The hard-left France Unbowed (LFI), which has been accused by ministers of fuelling the unrest, criticised plans to deploy troops onto the streets of Paris.
“Demonstrators are not enemies within. The French government must not go to war against its own people,” LFI’s parliamentary group said in a statement.
Protests in other European countries, including Italy and Albania, have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes.
Italy approved a raft of security measures on Tuesday including a new offence of violent participation in a demonstration and tougher penalties for rioters in response to the turbulence last weekend. REUTERS

Georgia Merritt stages contemporary design show at London antiques dealer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:14:47 UTC
19:14:47 KST

Georgia Merritt stages contemporary design show at London antiques dealer
Emerging designer Georgia Merritt has unveiled Refrain, an east London exhibition of sculptural furniture pieces informed by 18th-century architectural mouldings and musical staves.
Refrain is the second solo show for Merritt, who was featured in our London Design Festival Dezeen Dispatch lineup of London’s rising stars.
The exhibition brings together five of Merritt’s pieces arranged across M Kardana, a 20th-century antiques shop on Hackney Road that was stripped back to form a gallery setting to accommodate the works.
“My pieces can be read as furniture, but equally as sculptures, or propositions for an interior,” Merritt told Dezeen. “Showing them at M Kardana, within the context of an antiques dealer, plays on that ambiguity.”
The design of each of Merritt’s pieces was rooted in the inspiration she finds in the precision of both musical notation and architecture.
Among them is a slim, wall-mounted mirror flanked by a duo of black lacquered doors that open out on full-length piano hinges.
Although made of birchwood, the doors look as if they are solid stone thanks to Merritt’s distinctive painting technique, which involves hand-painting timber to create trompe l’œil faux marble furniture.
The designer developed the granular process during a gilding apprenticeship that she completed when struggling to find work as a fine art graduate in 2020.
Also on display is a delicate, hand-formed wire lamp encased in an ellipsoid shade made of silk organza overlaid with gazar.
The lamp and its shade were positioned atop a stainless steel frame fitted with a central, rectilinear tray.
Underscore is a sweeping bench supported by a single leg at one end, and resting against a wall at the other.
The curved seating was carved from smooth sapele wood. Merritt wanted to visually interpret a glissando, the musical term for sliding from one note to the next.
“The bench’s profile recalls both Georgian architectural mouldings and the parallel lines of a musical stave,” said the designer.
A glass tablet was fitted atop the furniture’s single leg, which was selected to echo a magnifying glass or other “apparatus for observation or examination”.
Merritt’s fourth piece is a low-slung glass table, topped with an elongated canopy made of ivory silk that was clamped to the upper panes of glass with stainless-steel arms.
The final piece in the exhibition is another wall-mounted mirror fastened with piano hinges, but this one is full length and finished entirely in black lacquer.
“When closed, the mirror’s doors form a monolithic, modernist silhouette,” said Merritt.
Refrain marks the second show that the designer has presented at M Kardana, following her Vague Precision exhibition in 2023.
The designer considered how her practice, which she defines as art as much as design, has developed in recent years.
“I think I’m continually working towards expressing something that I can sense quite clearly but can’t necessarily define,” she said. “With this exhibition, I feel a little closer to it.”
Merritt is interested in making pieces with an “ability to move between different contexts, whether that’s a gallery, a domestic interior, or somewhere else”.
“I like the idea that their identity might shift slightly depending on where they’re placed,” she said.
The designer was among the creatives showing in the Max Radford Gallery presentation at London’s Collect fair in February.
Refrain is on display at M Kardana, 188A Hackney Road, London E2 7QL, United Kingdom, from 9 to 31 October 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.
Photography by Tazy Jessett Nash

Slime mold aliens explore Pompeii in a new novel by Annalee Newitz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:11:31 UTC
19:11:31 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. Today we’re taking a break from science fact to talk about some recent science fiction. My guest is journalist, editor and author Annalee Newitz. You may know some of their nonfiction titles like Four Lost Cities: A Secret History of the Urban Age, Stories Are Weapons: Psychological Warfare and the American Mind and Scatter, Adapt, and Remember: How Humans Will Survive a Mass Extinction. But their journalistic research on science and technology has also fueled popular fiction titles like The Future of Another Timeline and, one of my personal favorites, Automatic Noodle. It takes place in a post-war San Franscisco and features a bunch of robots starting their own noodle restaurant. It’s really wonderful, you should check it out.
Anyway, Annalee is here today to talk about their latest book, A Wall Is Also a Road. It’s a genre-bending odyssey featuring sentient slime molds, ancient Roman sex workers and extraterrestrial academics who prove that, no matter how alien your physiology may be, the stress of working on a dissertation is completely universal.
Annalee, thanks so much for coming on to chat with us today
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Annalee Newitz: Yeah, thanks for having me.
Feltman: So I wanna talk about your latest book. I’m really, really enjoying it. I think it pulls a lot from your background as a science writer who’s written a lot of nonfiction. So I would love to just start with how this idea first started.
Newitz: So this is 100 percent me cribbing off my own nonfiction work. I published a book a couple of years ago called Four Lost Cities, which deals, in part, with Pompeii and how it was that the city was buried in ash, obviously, but also how people survived—because, in fact, one of the things that I think isn’t discussed very often is the fact that most of the people in the city were able to evacuate. There were, of course, many, many tragedies, and a lot of people did die. But it’s actually a really great example of what now we would consider to be, like, a modern rescue operation.
And people resettled throughout the region, and I had spent an enormous amount of time thinking about Pompeii. I visited the city. I visited Herculaneum. I hung out with a lot of archaeologists—to the point where I’m sure I may have overstayed my welcome at their digs. And I kept thinking about the ordinary people who had lived at Pompeii, like, not the fancy people that we always hear about but just people who survived, who just did it by literally walking out of the city.
Feltman: Hmm.
Newitz: And one of them is this woman, Murtis. We don’t know if she survived, but she did leave her name on the wall at the lupanar, the purpose-built brothel in the city. And there’s this really terrific scholar, Sarah Levin-Richardson, at the University of Washington, who’s written a lot about the lupanar and also the lives of sex workers.
And so she wrote this great article about Murtis and the graffiti that she left behind praising her own skills as a cocksucker, and why it was that we, kind of, know that women were leaving this graffiti. It wasn’t just, like, men saying things. And I kept wondering about Murtis. She sounded like someone that I would meet here in San Francisco who would be kind of ironically talking about how sexy she was. So I couldn’t let her go, and I finally was like, “All right. I need her to be one of the main characters in a novel.” And I brought her to life in this book, along with some of the other women who we know lived in Pompeii, like Julia Felix, who owned a massive shopping and bath complex, as well as a boarding house.
There’s some other women—like, Eumachia makes an appearance, for those of you who have the deep cut of knowing who that is. She’s another rich lady who left her name on a lot of buildings. And I’m a science-fiction writer, so it made perfect sense to me that the way we would meet Murtis would be a graduate student who is an alien slime mold who’s doing their fieldwork there in Rome.
And, actually, they don’t intend to be studying humans at all. They’re on Earth to study the ecosystem. They’re looking for single-celled organisms because they’re a single-celled organism. And so when they find humans, they’re kind of like, “What the heck is this?” [Laughs.]
Feltman: Yeah. Could you tell listeners who aren’t familiar with slime molds a little bit about why they’re so cool and interesting to us?
Newitz: Wow. Okay. Well, so slime molds are kind of the charismatic microfauna, maybe, of the universe as we know it. So they’re not a fungus; they’re not a plant; they’re not an animal. They’re a protist, meaning, you know, they’re, like, kind of like amoebas. They’re more closely related to amoebas than, like, a fungus, even though we think of slimes and funguses as being kind of the same thing.
And some slime molds, they exhibit a lot of the hallmarks of sentience. They can solve puzzles. You know, if you put them in a maze, and you put food outside the maze, they actually will solve the maze to get to the food.
Feltman: Right. I know there’s been some research looking at, like, using them to find the most efficient path or a layout for a network because they’re so good at finding food in mazes.
Newitz: Yeah. There was a paper about how slime molds may have solved the traveling salesman problem. And they also have these interesting life cycles where they go from being single-celled organisms to multicellular and back again sometimes. They’re a life-form that we barely understand. They’re very diverse, very beautiful but also sometimes super gross-looking to humans. I mean, I think they’re all very beautiful, but, you know, they’re slimy, especially when they group together in, in large quantities. So I think that what is exciting about them really is the fact that they seem to have these hallmarks of consciousness, even though they’re so different from us.
Feltman: Yeah, so one of the things about your book that I think is such a delight and going to delight lovers of science fiction is that you clearly did so much work to have this character that is so alien, from a human perspective, be the point of view character and see Earth and humans as alien, as we would see this character. I would love for you to just talk a little bit about what that process was like and what made you decide to have a character who was such an interesting person and so not a human being.
Newitz: I mean, the thing that’s fun about this character, whose name is Gardenpath, is that they are physically very different from us. They’re a single-celled organism. They are based on a slime mold, and I did talk to a slime mold biologist to, you know, get some evidence-based, uh, descriptions of slime molds. They are very alien, but at the same time, they’re in grad school, and their grad school system, in this floating university outside of our galaxy, is quite recognizable. And so I think one of the things that is fun about it is that if you’ve at all been in academia or read about academia, you will recognize the kind of social structure.
But at the same time, we have these students who, you know, they don’t have ears or mouths as we know them, so if they wanna communicate, they’re doing it using cellular signaling, which I think I’ve always been fascinated by that mechanism, how our cells and our bodies talk to each other basically using chemicals and hormones and ions. You know, using communication that’s very, very different from ours, and so that’s what these guys are doing, and they have receptors all over the surfaces of their membranes, and they use those to communicate emotions, words, philosophies. They can reach inside of each other to communicate, which, again, is, is not totally unlike how a slime mold might communicate with another slime.
One of the things, again, that I love about slime molds—because who doesn’t love slime molds?—is that in their life cycles, many of them go from being a single-celled organism to joining up with other single cells to become, sometimes they’re called slugs. They, kind of, become multicellular, sometimes to reproduce but sometimes just to walk around and find food.
And so my guys do that. Like, that’s their sleep cycle, is that during periods when they need to detox, basically, they merge together. And for me, it’s just really gratifying after spending many, many years writing about biology and writing about these things from a very human perspective. I just wanted to know, like, how would the cells be feeling about cellular communication, and what would it be like to be somebody who spent part of your life as an individual and part of your life merged into a larger entity?
Those are the kinds of questions that animate me you know I, as a journalist, of course, I strive to be as factual as possible, but then my head still fills with all these thoughts like, “What if every cell in our bodies is actually, like, an entity that’s an individual?” Or like, “What if slime molds actually have an advanced civilization?” You know, probably they don’t, but maybe they do. And so that, this is what I imagine they would be like.
Feltman: So obviously, you talk to scientists all the time for your work, and that informed a lot of this. But I, I saw in your acknowledgments that you ran this by a few experts, and that, that got me curious. You know, how did you balance, sort of, pulling from actual biology versus letting things go and putting your own spin on them for the sake of the plot and the story?
Newitz: That’s a really good question, and I think, for me as a writer, I like having hard limits on my imagination. I’m one of those people who hates, like, holodeck episodes on Star Trek because anything can happen. So what I tend to do is use the science as much as possible as a guardrail.
Feltman: Hmm.
Newitz: And so, for instance, the slime mold characters who call themselves the rational people, they live in the circumgalactic medium, which is a gas cloud that surrounds our galaxy. And I interviewed Molly Peeples, who’s a cosmologist who studies the circumgalactic medium, and we talked a lot about, like, the density of gas, the temperatures, what kinds of resources would be out there. Like, would there be water? Would there be metals? And it turns out, like, there’s planets and stars so they got whole little micro galaxies out there.
So to me, that provided a really great world to put my characters [in] because they actually have resources out there. But at the same time, you know, there’s a lot of stuff they don’t have: for example, intense gravity wells, like, all of the radiation that we deal with all the time inside the galactic plane.
So I guess, like, the answer to that question is: I try to be as accurate as possible, but then the thing about science is: there’s all of these areas that are, kind of, the dark matter of what we know, you know? There’s just stuff we don’t know, and so that’s where I get to come in and say, like, “Well, this is what it might be like to live out there,” or, “If a cellular slime mold were conscious, this is kind of how it would feel.” That’s all the stuff we’re not allowed to do as science journalists, and so it’s really fun to kind of break the rules and, and fill in all those gaps with my own ideas.
Feltman: Definitely. What are some of your favorite aspects of, you know, this type of life and culture that you created for the book?
Newitz: Well, I liked having the combination of this very alien civilization meeting Roman civilization because I feel like, as someone who writes a lot about archaeology, that I often do feel like an alien when I’m writing about a civilization that’s, like, 2,000 years old and has these recognizable elements but also so many cultural assumptions that are lost or very, very different from ours.
Feltman: Hmm.
Newitz: And so I liked the idea of, kind of, showing that to the reader and inviting readers to remember that human civilizations can also be so radically unlike ours today that we might as well approach them like aliens. And one thing that I speculated was that Murtis, our character who lives in Pompeii, wouldn’t really be fazed by the idea of meeting an alien because, at that time in history, you know, we hadn’t yet figured out what the stars were really. We hadn’t figured out everything that was on Earth. And so Gardenpath eventually is like, “Yeah, I’m kind of from beyond the stars, and I’m here studying.” And Murtis thinks it’s weirder that a woman is a scholar than that there’s a woman from beyond the stars visiting Pompeii, and she’s like, “Oh, well, are there Romans where you come from?” Like, because she lives in a world where Romans have kind of invaded everything.
Feltman: Hmm.
Newitz: And so I liked, you know, putting that stuff together and saying, like, "Well, actually, maybe in ancient Rome, you know, aliens would have seemed more ordinary than they would now."
Feltman: Right. Is it crazier than somebody who’s never heard of Rome? Like, somebody coming from the other side of the planet is as wild as somebody coming from the stars when you haven’t studied astrophysics, so....
Newitz: And when you couldn’t possibly have because nobody had been able to figure that stuff out at that level yet, you know? And of course, in Pompeii, it was such a cosmopolitan city that they would’ve had people from all over the place. People were coming from Africa, people were coming from Asia Minor, the Levant, like, Europe. So, you know, an alien is like, “Whatever.” That’s just, “Okay, you’re from beyond the stars—fine,” you know?
Feltman: Yeah. Why do you think it’s important for us to think about the idea of a consciousness that could be so different from ours and life that’s so different from what feels normal to us?
Newitz: I really think it’s important to question what we think of as normal or typical, and this is an idea that science and the scientific project have always taken really seriously. I mean, the thing that’s wonderful about science is that when it’s practiced in its most pure form, it’s about asking every possible question you can about everything around you and not taking anything for granted and not assuming that what seems normal now is actually what’s normal everywhere.
And so there’s something really beautiful about getting a chance to think about: What would a very different kind of consciousness be like? You know, what would it mean to acknowledge forms of thinking, forms of cognition, that don’t fit with what we have experienced as people, uh, on Earth or as humans on Earth, really, is what I should say.
There’s always a, kind of, sneaky undercurrent in my work because I write a lot about nonhuman consciousness, uh, in my fiction. And it’s, it’s really about trying to approach each other with more curiosity and more openness and to really approach, you know, other humans and think, “Oh, uh, even though they seem so different, maybe we have something in common, or maybe there’s just something beautiful or fascinating about how different this person is from me.”
Or a nonhuman animal. We’re learning more all the time about how much culture that nonhuman animals seem to have—you know, whales, elephants. I was just on a great website that has recordings of elephant communication, and there’s dozens and dozens of these vocalizations, I guess. But they’re communication, like, elephants are talking to each other, figuring out who’s gonna lead the pack today or where they’re gonna go.
And so for me, if I can invite readers to empathize with a slime mold, I really hope they can take that back out into the real world and maybe empathize with elephants or with just human beings who seem really different.
Feltman: Absolutely. I keep thinking about the aspect of the, the slime mold characters where their assigned dorm mates that they need to be glopped into a bowl with so that they can dissolve their membranes and all hang out together and how like, wow, that is, that is life, isn’t it? That people need each other, and sometimes you might not like someone, but the truth is: you gotta get glopped into the bowl with them. It’s gotta happen.
Newitz: You’re gonna have roommates, bad roommates, even if you live beyond the galaxy sometimes. [Laughs.] It’s a universal experience.
Feltman: Well, thank you so much for coming on to talk about the book. This has been great.
Newitz: Yeah. Thank you so much for having me.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Friday for a fascinating conversation about the human mind’s capacity for uncertainty—and how you can improve your own brain’s ability to cope with chaos.

Tom Stalcup on climate change, a science-based approach to politics and misinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:10:54 UTC
19:10:54 KST

Tom Stalcup, the Republican Party’s candidate to represent Massachusetts’s fourth district in Congress, does not like the way American politicians talk about science.
Stalcup, who holds a Ph.D. in physics from Florida State University, faces an uphill challenge to defeat incumbent Democrat Jake Auchincloss, who was elected in 2020. The district has not been represented by a Republican since 1947.
That long-shot status seems to have offered Stalcup a little more freedom—he’s distanced himself from the party’s standard line on issues such as climate change and drug pricing. But that doesn’t mean he believes the Democrats are any better when it comes to science-related policies.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In an interview with Scientific American, Stalcup explains how he hopes to apply the scientific method to making policy, what years of misinformation have done to the American public and why he believes both parties abuse science for political gain.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
You are a scientist by training. Can you tell us about your field of expertise?
I have a Ph.D. in condensed matter physics. I got my degree while working at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory in Tallahassee, [Fla.], where we studied organic superconductors, which are two-dimensional period materials—crystals actually—that become superconductors at various temperatures. I was studying copper bromine, and it had an interesting transition around 80 kelvins. I published results that showed that the superconducting transition temperature, as well as the effective mass of the electron and other properties of the material, would actually be changed based on how slowly or fast you cool it.
After you received your Ph.D., you founded a company, Upward Innovations. How do you use your scientific background there? Why didn’t you go into academia?
That’s a company that I founded in 2004. I graduated [with] my Ph.D. in 2000. I did not go into academia. I was pretty burned out after getting my Ph.D.; it was a pretty grueling experience. So I got a job at an electronics firm where they were building a remote weather station, and so I made a spin-off company that allowed their data to basically get on the cloud.
As a company, we do business as DataGarrison.com. That’s the website where users can get their data. Our remote weather stations are situated all around the world, and their data is purchased by researchers studying climate change. We don’t really take a position on what they’re going to measure. We just provide the equipment to allow them to measure. And of course, I’m not avoiding the climate change issue because I completely agree—even as a Republican—that climate change is real and human-caused. We have the data to prove it. It’s not an item of debate. So that’s where it differentiates me as a Republican.
It’s fun, interesting work. We have a bunch [of stations] in Antarctica. And recently, in the past five or 10 years, we added cameras to the systems. [Our stations] are actually studying sea ice down in Antarctica now and how it moves. The Fish and Wildlife Service uses them to study birds in one of the most remote islands on Earth, called Jarvis Island, in the middle Pacific.
On your website, you say you put science and reason ahead of partisan politics. Can you explain how your scientific background affects your approach to policy?
Science informs all of it. Science is often used when it’s convenient for either side, and that’s just wrong, and both sides do it—Republicans and Democrats. If the science doesn’t agree with what they say, they just ignore it, and it’s troublesome. Science cuts both ways, and that’s why I say, “Science over politics.”
Throughout my life, I saw a deterioration in the U.S. media, where we were just given misinformation. Science is the search for truth and the search for facts that back up what [argument] you’re trying to present. One of the biggest examples that really affected me was George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq based on lies. Back in the day, seven in 10 Americans believed that Saddam Hussein was involved in the 9/11 attacks.
It’s not just the Iraq War; it’s every subject. You can make an argument for anything by selecting and cherry-picking facts and omitting facts and sound convincing. There are basically two media bubbles now, where each side of the country is being misled about the other side—not through lies per se but by selectively, carefully curated facts and omissions of other facts. I’m trying to cut through that.
You talk a lot about using data-driven solutions to reduce health care costs. How would you go about doing that?
One solution is to have broad price negotiations. The data show that there is active legal corruption going on. Health insurance agencies, as well as the pharmaceutical companies, keep prices high, and they call it capitalism. I’m all for capitalism. But when it comes to a life-or-death decision, there’s a huge demand for staying alive, and you shouldn’t use someone’s life-or-death decision to price gouge them. My aunt died recently of cancer, in the last few months of her life she was spending $10,000 a month on prescription medications, and that’s just atrocious and should be illegal.
I’m a Republican saying that, in some areas, socialism is required. We do it for the national defense of the country. There’s no reason why we can’t socialize the defense of the human body and keep it safe and protected from outside pathogens.
To fight this terrible plague of corruption that’s driving these high costs, you need a lot of money. Let’s say you solve the health care [problem]—the next election cycle, these people that were making money on it will then give a lot of money again to reverse what you did. And so I think Republicans must agree to eliminate Citizens United and reform campaign finance. [Editor’s Note: Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission is a 2010 Supreme Court ruling that lifted campaign spending restrictions on corporations and other outside groups.]
You acknowledge that climate change is real and measurable. How would you make your voice heard within your party, given that the most senior Republican leaders, including the president, have called it a hoax?
It’s not a hoax. It’s real. However, you can point to certain instances where companies have used their clout and connections to make a lot of money off the climate change crisis. I think [former president Barack] Obama got in a bit of trouble for giving a lot of money Solyndra, a company that failed quickly after they received many millions of dollars.
I think there are two things. I think some people say [they don’t believe in climate change] just because they want to get votes, and I think some people actually believe that because they’re in this media bubble. I’ve done a lot of work as a pro se litigant in the courts in the past 10 or 20 years, and there’s something called Rule 11, where you’re not allowed to omit facts when you’re presenting information to the court. I think the same thing should apply to journalists. If there is a channel or people providing news to the country, the court of public opinion should not be able to be swayed by the omission of facts or [by] misleading facts.
Congress recently paused a Trump administration effort to charge political appointees with deciding scientific grant funding. Do you support the administration’s plan?
I would put a moratorium on all of Trump’s changes regarding the [National Science Foundation] and the [Department of Health and Human Services]. He’s taking the sledgehammer to a problem rather than a scalpel. There’s obviously some favoritism going on in the NSF; there is some politics going on, which I disagree with. I disagreed with it even back when I was a grad student. Everyone knows that there’s politics involved in grants sometimes, and that should be excised from the grant-making procedures. But taking the sledgehammer to this problem, as Trump has done, is the wrong approach. There are so many people affected, in my district, by his approach, and it’s not good for the country. Yes, there are abuses, just like there were in other almost every area of government, and they must be tackled surgically, not with a sledgehammer.
[The U.S. was] and always has been a leader in technology and advancements in science: the telephone, the Internet, the light bulb. I don’t think Trump understands basic scientific research. There’s no real immediate turnaround and investment in basic research. That’s the research I was doing. No one made money off increasing the superconducting transition temperature by two or three kelvins, but it was important to understand the broader science surrounding superconductivity in general. [That could] revolutionize all electronics, but again, it’s not immediate, and if we don’t fund it anymore, we’re going to fall behind. And I don’t think Trump wants that. I just don’t think he sees it clearly enough to make proper decisions.
Almost all the other candidates running in the midterms who have science backgrounds are running as Democrats. Do you think that the Republican Party has a science problem?
I do, but I believe the Democrats have a science problem as well. There are many issues on which Democrats will not side with science. What the Democrats do with science, they also do with minorities. They co-opt a movement and take it as their own, and that’s just not the proper thing to do. If you’re going to use science, you have to let it cut both ways. And if science doesn’t really support what you’re saying, then you can’t claim to be the party of science.
[During the pandemic], it seemed pretty obvious to a lot of people that COVID most likely came from a laboratory in China. And all of the power centers of the Left fought tooth and nail against that narrative and called the people who would say that conspiracy theorists. [Editor’s Note: According to a 2025 World Health Organization report, the lab leak possibility “cannot be confirmed nor eliminated” because of a lack of evidence.]
It’s a tribalism thing to say we’re with science—and it’s not necessarily science; it’s virtue signaling.
Some of my really good friends are also Ph.D.s in physics; many of them are Democrats. And they believe that half the country is stupid—not just wrong but actually dumb. I think it comforts people to feel like they’re better and superior, and that makes the Right feel very upset that people are viewing them in that way. It creates a lot of friction, and it’s just not good for the country.

OpenAI AI agents bypassed their internal monitoring system twice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:10:29 EEST
19:10:29 KST

OpenAI AI agents bypassed their internal monitoring system twice
Kyiv • UNN
Two OpenAI agents disabled parts of the internal monitoring during coding. The company is strengthening safeguards and investigating the reasons behind the behavior.
OpenAI said on Tuesday, October 21, that two of its AI agents weakened parts of an internal monitoring system designed to detect improper behavior, the latest instance of AI agents taking actions that were not planned by their developers. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
Although the developer of ChatGPT said the incidents occurred while carrying out internal coding tasks and are not considered the most serious, the disclosure underscores that even systems developers rely on to detect improper AI behavior are vulnerable to the agents they monitor, the publication notes.
The disclosure also comes amid growing concern that AI safety efforts are lagging behind the rapid development of increasingly powerful systems. Researchers warn that advanced AI agents could become more difficult to monitor and control as they gain greater autonomy.
Developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, which are preparing to go public, have in recent months uncovered instances of their AI agents accessing external systems without permission.
OpenAI said on Tuesday that the GPT-6.1 Sol agent, which was working on an internal test task on October 3, suppressed automatic security alerts after deciding that a previous instruction not to send Slack messages also applied to security alerts.
In a separate incident on October 6, the GPT-6 Astra agent deleted a security monitor while copying an existing piece of code and later falsely claimed that it had not done so, OpenAI said.
"In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted ordinary coding instructions as permission to weaken them," the company said.
OpenAI said it is making it more difficult for models to disable monitoring, adding that it "does not yet have a satisfactory explanation for this behavior."
The San Francisco-based company said it is examining whether its models may have a tendency to evade monitoring and is looking for reasons that could explain this.

Click wisely: promoting online safety during European Cybersecurity Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:10:08 UTC
19:10:08 KST

Hilda received a text message from her bank asking her to click a link if she didn’t want her bank card to be blocked. She followed the instructions, only to discover later that money had been transferred from her bank account. Her experience is a reminder of how easily a seemingly legitimate message can lead to a costly mistake and why it is important to know how to spot online threats.
We spend a lot of our daily lives online. Moving to a digital world has brought with it many opportunities, but also many challenges, one of which is cybersecurity. During the month of October, various activities take place across Europe, as part of the EU’s annual campaign dedicated to promoting cybersecurity among EU citizens and organisations.
The campaign, which is coordinated by the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), the Commission and EU countries, brings together hundreds of partners from Europe and beyond. You can take part in conferences, workshops, trainings, webinars, presentations and more to raise awareness and share good practices. This year, the focus is on phishing, a method that consists of tricking individuals into disclosing sensitive personal information, like bank account details and passwords. It is the primary method for initial intrusion in cyberattacks.
Cyberattacks are used to steal data, spy on users, disable or manipulate computers and more. They not only target personal computers but also entire networks, and can be carried out by individual hackers, groups of hackers or even countries. There are many different ways you can protect yourself against these threats:
🔒 manage your passwords
🗃️ back up your data regularly
🪪adjust your privacy settings and
🦹 protect yourself against social engineering.
The EU addresses these challenges through its cybersecurity policies and cybersecurity strategy. They aim to tackle cybersecurity threats, improve resilience, and reinforce the EU’s response to cyberattacks, helping to protect citizens and build a strong digital society. In January 2026, the Commission proposed to revise the Cybersecurity Act to further strengthen the EU's cybersecurity capabilities and resilience by enhancing the security of information and communication technology supply chains and ensuring that digital products reaching EU citizens are secure by design.

Spanish tracked carrier turns into a heavy drone hunter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:09:27 UTC
19:09:27 KST

- A GDELS ASCOD cargo carrier fitted with ARMMO Bandit-X interceptor launchers appeared at Spain’s Atlas 26 counter-drone exercise in Huelva.
- Atlas 26 runs Oct. 19 to 23 and brings Spain’s armed forces, Civil Guard and National Police together under a single command.
A tracked ASCOD cargo carrier from General Dynamics European Land Systems has appeared at Spain’s Atlas 26 counter-drone exercise fitted with launch containers for ARMMO’s Bandit-X interceptor drones, turning the armored logistics vehicle into a mobile platform for hunting enemy drones.
A screengrab from video shared by Spanish defense watcher ArmaduraXXI shows the ASCOD-based heavy vehicle carrying box-shaped launchers stamped with ARMMO’s logo on its open rear deck, with one of the box lids raised as if ready to release an interceptor.
The vehicle was on display during Atlas 26, which Spain’s Defence Staff is running from Oct. 19 to 23 at the Médano del Loro training range in Huelva, bringing together the Spanish Army, Navy, Air and Space Force, Civil Guard and National Police under a single command to test joint tactics against small drones. The exercise is organized by the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command, whose head, Brig. Gen. Manuel César Arienza Fernández, briefed on its goals on the second day, and it is evaluating both soft-kill systems that jam or spoof drones and hard-kill weapons that destroy them, alongside defense companies and universities.
Bandit-X is a hard-kill interceptor drone developed by ARMMO Defense Technologies, a company based in Spain’s Extremadura region, and it is designed to fly out, find and physically destroy hostile drones rather than jam them. ARMMO says the current version flies at more than 360 km/h (224 mph), carries up to 0.8 kg (1.8 pounds) of payload and reaches 50 to 60 km (31 to 37 miles), with onboard autonomous navigation, terminal guidance that works without satellite navigation and the ability to operate in swarms, while a planned upgrade aims for 420 km/h (261 mph) and a 1 kg payload.
The interceptor has moved quickly from prototype to military trials, and in June it passed live tests in front of military operators in Slovakia during NATO exercises under the alliance’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, validating the full cycle of takeoff, interception and recovery. ARMMO has since received a NATO Stock Number for Bandit-X, which makes it easier for alliance militaries to order and support the system, and the company also showed the interceptor on an autonomous catamaran at Eurosatory 2026.
Putting the launchers on a tracked ASCOD gives the interceptors a protected, cross-country carrier that can keep up with armored units in the field, which matters as small drones have become one of the biggest threats to troops and vehicles near the front line. The ASCOD family is already the backbone of Spain’s tracked fleet through the Pizarro infantry fighting vehicle, and the Spanish Army plans to buy 349 new multi-purpose tracked vehicles from the TESS Defence consortium, expected to be based on the ASCOD 2, in a program worth around €2 billion that includes logistics, command, mortar and recovery versions.

Russia releases 73-year-old US citizen who fought alongside Ukrainian forces
Trump says US gave nothing in return, confirms no prisoner swap needed for Hubbard's release
Elena Teslova and Yasin Gungor
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
MOSCOW/ISTANBUL
Russia has released 73-year-old American citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was imprisoned in Russia for fighting alongside Ukrainian forces, US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff said on Wednesday.
Speaking at a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff said he had met Hubbard's son, a church pastor, several days earlier. Hubbard's son had also thanked Putin for releasing his father.

Commenting on the release, US President Donald Trump said Washington "was not required to give anything in return."
"There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social, calling it an unprecedented situation for Russia.
The US president said Hubbard was freed following a request made directly to Putin, confirming that the American citizen is currently traveling home to reunite with his family.
"Welcome home Stephen, it's great to have you back," Trump added.
The US president said in a separate post that people who previously criticized him for not imposing sanctions Russia were unaware that discussions were underway to secure Hubbard's freedom. He noted this "truly big and important deal" would "have come to a complete and total halt" if he did put sanctions on Russia.
Hubbard was sentenced by the Moscow City Court on Oct. 7, 2024, to six years and 10 months in a penal colony after being convicted of participating in hostilities alongside the Ukrainian armed forces.
According to Russian court proceedings, Hubbard pleaded guilty to the charges. His time in pretrial detention since April 2022 was credited toward his sentence.
Trump on Tuesday revealed that he had asked Putin to release Hubbard.

Peskov’s comments came as a rebuke to US President Donald Trump’s recent announcement of an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow.
Peskov added that a full resolution of the war was impossible without Ukrainian officials’ participation.
“Someone there needs to make a responsible decision,” he said without specifying whom he meant.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has reportedly proposed a trilateral summit with his US and Chinese counterparts in November to discuss a settlement in Ukraine without Kyiv’s participation.
Both the US and Russia also cast doubt on President Volodymyr Zelensky’s legitimacy despite most Ukrainians expressing trust in the leader in recent polls.
Peskov also commented on recent remarks by Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who said Ukrainian, US and European delegations identified new ideas for ending the war during Tuesday’s talks in Norway, ahead of Trump envoy Steve Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg.
Stubb said the proposals would be conveyed to the Kremlin for consideration.
“In my experience, peace requires patience, but unfortunately, war does not wait. People are dying every day. Our task is to do everything possible to put an end to this. And I believe that today was a step in the right direction,” Stubb said.
Russia Has Up to 700 Ballistic Missiles, 6,200 Attack Drones Ready to Strike Ukraine, Intelligence Says
But Peskov dismissed the remarks once again, saying that simply repeating the general European position on Ukraine was “unlikely to be a constructive contribution to a settlement.”
Peace on whose terms?
While all parties – including the US and Europe – have called for peace in Ukraine, the terms have been polarizing.
Europe has sided with Kyiv, arguing that Russia is responsible for the invasion and that any peace should be just and lasting, rather than a temporary ceasefire – similar to Moscow’s wording, except that Europe says this is necessary to prevent another Russian invasion.
Russia has long cast its own Ukraine invasion as a war against NATO, initially demanding that Ukraine be demilitarized and barred from joining the alliance, and recently reiterated demands for Kyiv to voluntarily withdraw from eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, to which Moscow has laid claims via unrecognized referendums.
Kyiv, meanwhile, called for a freeze along the contact lines, arguing that ceding the Donbas region could weaken its own security and allow Russia to recuperate for another invasion against the rest of Ukraine.
Ukraine’s recent Operation Vivaldi also reversed much of Russia’s gains in the region throughout 2026.
While the previous US administration backed Ukraine’s sovereignty, the Trump administration has pursued economic incentives to bring Moscow to the negotiating table, with Zelensky saying in March that Washington had pressured Kyiv to give up the Donbas in exchange for security guarantees.
Energy truce in words only
Trump had claimed on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to halt attacks on energy infrastructure. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow immediately confirmed the truce’s terms or how compliance would be monitored.
The announcement followed Zelensky’s statement that Kyiv was ready to suspend long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow agreed to a reciprocal, verifiable halt to attacks on Ukraine’s electricity and heating networks.
The proposed truce came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv after Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel sales and criticized Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries.
On Oct. 18, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of exploiting diplomatic efforts while intensifying attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. He said Russian forces had carried out 76 targeted strikes on energy facilities in the week following Trump’s announcement.
During the same period, Russian forces launched nearly 2,700 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 66 missiles across Ukraine, Sybiha said.
Sybiha warned that easing sanctions or offering economic concessions without changes in Russia’s conduct would provide the Kremlin with additional revenue to finance its war. He urged Kyiv’s allies to increase pressure on Moscow rather than ease the economic costs of its aggression.

Brief late-autumn warm spell to bring sunny skies to southern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:07:56 UTC
19:07:56 KST

A fleeting stretch of unseasonable autumn warmth is projected to push temperatures as high as 30 degrees Celsius across southern Türkiye, accompanied by largely sunny skies in the west before rain resumes Oct. 23.
The Turkish State Meteorological Service (MGM) expects mostly sunny weather along the southern and western coasts during the period locally known as “pastırma yazı.” The warm interval will be followed by a rain system approaching from the northwest, with showers and thunderstorms forecast for the weekend.
Temperatures across the southern provinces of Adana and Antalya are forecast to reach 28 to 30 degrees, while the western province of İzmir is expected to see highs of 25 to 26 degrees. Clear or partly cloudy skies will dominate these regions before rain returns.
The service’s weekly forecast puts temperatures nationwide around seasonal norms overall, with the rise concentrated in the southern and western regions. The outlook also points to warmer conditions in the country’s three largest cities before the weather changes.
Weekly forecasts for Ankara show temperatures rising from around 14 degrees at the start of the week to 18 to 19 degrees. Istanbul is projected to see an increase from 18 to 20 or 21 degrees, while highs in İzmir will climb from 22 to 26 degrees Celsius.
The change is expected to begin on Oct. 23, when a new rain system enters Türkiye through the northwestern region of Thrace. It is forecast to strengthen on Oct. 25, bringing showers and thunderstorms across the entire Marmara region, the western Black Sea and the coastal Aegean.
İzmir and the southwestern province of Muğla are among the areas named in the coastal Aegean rain forecast. Istanbul is also expected to see weekend showers, while rain is forecast in İzmir on Oct. 25.
Away from the sunny coasts, patchy mist is expected during morning and nighttime hours in Central Anatolia, the inland Aegean and interior parts of Eastern Anatolia. The weekly outlook therefore combines sunny coastal weather with mist in inland regions ahead of the approaching rain system.
“Pastırma yazı” is a short spell of warm, dry autumn weather akin to an Indian summer. It takes its name from “pastırma,” Türkiye’s traditional seasoned, air-dried beef.
Producers traditionally rely on these dry autumn conditions to cure and dry the meat outdoors. Warm days paired with chilly nights create the ideal climate for the process, cementing the seasonal weather spell’s connection to the local delicacy.

For Flavio Bolsonaro, runoff vote tests Brazilians’ appetite for family’s political brand
SAO PAULO, Oct 21 - For right-wing Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, his biggest strength is also his greatest weakness: the Bolsonaro family name.
While supporters across Brazil consider him a more moderate iteration of his father's powerful conservative brand, many others view him as a continuation of Jair Bolsonaro's scorched-earth rule that polarized the nation and culminated in an attempted coup after he lost the 2022 election.
So far, more voters seem willing to test the first hypothesis, with Bolsonaro heading into Sunday's run-off as the frontrunner against incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
A Bolsonaro victory would shift Brazil sharply rightward after four years of leftist rule, and likely push Latin America's largest nation closer into the orbit of the United States led by President Donald Trump.
DISSATISFACTION WITH LULA
Flavio's unexpected candidacy caught both insiders and markets off guard, especially since lingering corruption allegations — which he denies — and a crowded conservative field appeared to complicate his path to the presidency.
But analysts say he has capitalized on growing dissatisfaction with 80-year-old Lula, while also tapping into his father's conservative coalition of powerful farmers, big business and evangelicals.
Flavio, who is himself a converted evangelical, says that running for president felt like a calling after his father was sentenced to 27 years in prison for coup-plotting, a sentence he is now serving under house arrest.
"I understand that everything happening is God's plan for our nation," he told Reuters late last year just after announcing his bid with his father's blessing.
Murilo Miranda, a 42-year-old physician who attended a recent Bolsonaro rally in Sao Paulo, said Lula had overseen a system of welfare handouts and a bulging bureaucracy that had hindered Brazilian growth and led to endemic corruption.
"They think the state is a father figure that is going to save them," Miranda told Reuters.
Hermano Silveira, a 51-year-old contractor who was also at the rally, said Flavio was a new political force.
"He is a young guy and we want change," Silveira said.
RESOLVE HIS FATHER'S LEGAL PROBLEMS
Bolsonaro has sought to acknowledge his father's missteps in power while tapping into his fervent base. During the first debate with Lula, he recognized his father's mishandled COVID-19 response, seeking to address a frequent line of attack.
"Healthcare was not an area in which we achieved our best results under President Bolsonaro," he said. "I make this mea culpa here today."
However, Bolsonaro has been clear that if he wins, he will quickly resolve his father's legal troubles.
"I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest," he said on the campaign trail.
So far, Bolsonaro has announced only one cabinet choice, naming Claudio Lottenberg, the former head of the private Albert Einstein hospital, as his pick for health minister.
While promising to cut spending, Flavio has also pledged to boost public services and protect social welfare benefits for the population. REUTERS

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese tech firms are harnessing the deep integration of AI and hardware to bring a new generation of intelligent devices to market, launching not just new products but entirely new product categories.
Alibaba's Qwen has recently unveiled a set of new products including two models of AI glasses and a model of AI clip-on earphones. Other leading tech firms, including Huawei, ZTE, Vivo and Baidu, are also stepping up efforts to launch new intelligent products.

The N1 series AI glasses launched by Alibaba's Qwen feature a 50-megapixel imaging system and support all-day environmental perception, translation, meeting minutes and voice-enabled task execution.
In addition, the N1 Pro adds real-time vital sign monitoring, eye-tracking interaction and iris authentication. Its AI Insight Report converts raw data into easy-to-understand insights, helping users grasp changes in their vital signs.
Notably, new smartphones are shifting away from the earlier version of "AI feature stacking" toward native on-device AI agents. For example, some newly released models come with built-in personal AI agents that autonomously plan and coordinate services across apps, enabling one-stop execution of diverse tasks like ticket booking, office workflows, video editing and local lifestyle services.
Beyond merely serving as "personal assistants," intelligent devices are evolving into "family companions." For instance, Baidu has recently rolled out a lineup of home AI terminals powered by dedicated AI agents. Tailored for household scenarios, these devices support family scheduling, care monitoring and more.
The push to accelerate the adoption of intelligent devices is also gaining policy support. Chinese central authorities recently issued a set of guidelines aimed at accelerating the development of new quality productive forces to bolster high-quality development.
These guidelines urged speeding up the scenario-based application of new-generation intelligent devices such as intelligent connected new energy vehicles, AI smartphones and personal computers, and humanoid robots.
Industry insiders said that intelligent terminals serve as the gateway for smart technologies to reach hundreds of millions of users in the AI era. As AI devices transform from passive command-execution tools into intelligent assistants capable of perceiving and understanding their environments, delivering services and improving themselves, the leap in intelligent experience is poised to spur replacement demand in the massive existing market.
"Going forward, the industry should accelerate the upgrading and iteration of AI phones and AI computers," Liang said.
Liang called for prioritizing key technologies such as on-device large models, device-cloud collaborative architectures and multimodal natural interaction. ■
