Across China: Three years after UNESCO listing, Jingmai's tea community balances tradition and innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:05:36 CST
19:05:36 KST

KUNMING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Driving up Jingmai Mountain is both a pleasure and a challenge. Towering trees rising above rugged valleys and mountains make for a fine view, but halfway up the slopes, smooth asphalt gives way to bumpy stone road.
The rough surface is intentional. Villagers endure the bumpy ride to protect their ancient tea trees, as asphalt at high temperatures can release chemicals that may seep into the soil and contaminate the trees.
Located in Lancang Lahu Autonomous County, Pu'er City, in southwest China's Yunnan Province, Jingmai Mountain is home primarily to the Blang and Dai ethnic groups. On Sept. 17, 2023, the Cultural Landscape of Old Tea Forests of Jingmai Mountain in Pu'er was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, making it China's 57th World Heritage Site and the world's first tea culture UNESCO heritage site.
Since the UNESCO inscription, the average annual income of residents engaged in the tea industry has increased from 15,400 yuan (about 2,291 U.S. dollars) to 26,000 yuan, demonstrating how merging cultural heritage with traditional industry is proving a winning formula for many rural regions.
Tea production and sales have long been the main source of income for local residents.
Around 2008, rising tea prices prompted some villages elsewhere to replace ancient tea trees with densely planted bushes arranged in terraces to boost yields. Jingmai's villagers resisted the trend, said Li Ping, a Hani ethnic official and deputy head of Huimin Township, which administers Jingmai Mountain.
The centuries-old practice here, known as forest-based tea cultivation, allows tea trees to grow naturally beneath tall forest trees, with ground vegetation helping protect the soil. The trees are scattered rather than planted in neat, dense rows. A mu (about 667 square meters) produces just over 30 kilograms of dried tea, far less than a terraced plantation.
Following the UNESCO inscription, environmental regulations have become stricter. Farmers who need chemical fertilizers for rice cultivation must report the types and quantities to their villages. Fertilizers brought up the mountain along its only access road are inspected at a checkpoint, and unregistered or excessive quantities are not allowed through.
While preserving tradition, residents are also finding new ways to share their culture with visitors.
San Wen, a Blang tea-roasting craftsman recognized as a municipal-level inheritor of intangible cultural heritage, has turned his tea garden into an interactive experience site. Visitors can pick fresh leaves, roast them and press them into tea cakes to take home.
The activity is particularly popular with families. By taking part in the labor involved in making tea, children gain a better understanding of how much hard work goes into the products they see every day, and come to appreciate both food and nature more.
Jingmai Mountain also offers something increasingly rare for urban visitors: quiet. At night, people can gather around a fire to brew tea beneath the moon and stars.
"This would not have been possible without the government's efforts to improve road access and secure World Heritage status for Jingmai Mountain," San said.
Tourism has also brought older residents new income and a new rhythm of life. Some who once had little to do now sell locally made roasted milk tea from stalls outside their homes, while others simply enjoy chatting with passing tourists -- that's what San's 85-year-old grandmother likes doing at her courtyard gate.
Official figures reflect the transformation. In 2025, Lancang County received 694,300 tourist visits, up 56.27 percent year on year, with cultural and tourism revenue reaching 563 million yuan.
The tourism boom has also drawn young people back to the mountain. Xian Jin, a young Dai woman born in the 2000s, was among the first villagers to sell tea through livestreaming.
"After the county organized e-commerce training and Jingmai Mountain gained World Heritage status, my livestream audience has grown from just a handful of people to tens of thousands," she said.
She also introduced Pu'er tea ice cream to the mountain. In 2025, while staying in Pu'er during her pregnancy, she craved ice cream from KFC. Her husband then experimented with tea from their own garden to create a Pu'er tea-flavored version. After two months of testing, they launched the product during the May Day holiday, selling 680 cones at 10 yuan each on the first day.
Its strong tea flavor and grainy texture from tea powder quickly made it a local hit. Xian shared the recipe and introduced the equipment to other villagers. Now the annual ice cream sales across the village are estimated at around 1 million yuan.
Young returnees and newcomers settling in the area have also introduced walking tours, travel photography, bakeries and coffee shops, allowing visitors to enjoy mountain life without giving up familiar urban comforts.
Local authorities, however, are mindful of the risk that fluctuating tea prices pose to local incomes, given that tea production remains the main pillar of the local economy. Pu'er City issued a 2025-2027 action plan to strengthen the Jingmai Mountain tea brand and cushion farmers against the effects of tea price fluctuations.
The plan calls for assessing the output and quality of tea trees across the mountain and standardizing tea-roasting and processing practices to ensure consistent product quality. Each tree in the ancient tea gardens now has an identification plate and number. In the future, products will carry QR codes enabling consumers to trace their origins and helping keep unverified tea out of the market.
"The goal is to strengthen the value and credibility of the Pu'er Jingmai Mountain tea brand, help tea farmers increase their incomes steadily and improve the industry's quality and efficiency," Li said, adding that the aim is to ensure the fragrance of Jingmai's 1,000-year-old tea tradition reaches an ever-wider audience, while building a stronger foundation for the industry. ■

24% of Ukrainian readers quit Russian books - survey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:04:56 EEST
19:04:56 KST

After the start of the full-scale invasion, 24% of Ukrainian readers stopped reading books in Russian altogether, and another 25% began reading them much less often, according to a study by Gradus Research commissioned by the Ministry of Culture.
Respondents were asked in which languages they had read or listened to books over the past 12 months. Some 87% said Ukrainian, 42% Russian, 8% English and 1% other languages, and 1% found it hard to answer.
Asked whether their attitude to reading books in Russian had changed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, 24% said they had stopped reading books in Russian altogether, 25% said they now read in Russian much less often, 22% said their attitude had changed but this had not affected the language they read in, 16% said their attitude had not changed, 8% said they had not read books in Russian either before or after the full-scale invasion, and 5% found it hard to answer.
The comprehensive study "Reading in Ukraine: Behavior, Motivation and Engagement Tools" was carried out by Gradus Research with the support of the Believe in Yourself Foundation. It included 41 in-depth interviews (March-May 2026) and a survey of 2,200 respondents aged 14 and older (August 17-25, 2026). The survey did not cover temporarily occupied territories or areas of active combat.
The Ministry of Culture initiated a national reading study in spring 2026. The first insights from the qualitative research were presented on May 30 at Book Arsenal.
The quantitative study, published on October 20, showed that 59% of Ukrainians read or listened to books at least a few times a month over the past year, 22% do so a few times a year or less, and 13% had not done so once in the past 12 months. Almost 50% of Ukrainian readers had not bought books in the past three months, and 34% bought only print books. Print books remain the most common reading format: 58% of respondents said they choose print, 44% electronic books and 35% audiobooks. Only 34% of Ukrainians think their locality has enough bookstores, 22% say there are too few, and 21% say there are none at all.

‘Then, you are not Gen Z?’ Delhi High Court’s light-hearted exchange with CJP leaders; Dipke reacts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:04:45 UTC
19:04:45 KST

NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court had a light-hearted exchange during a hearing on Wednesday involving Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, with Justice Subramonium Prasad remarking that the two were not part of Generation Z after being told their ages.During the hearing, Justice Prasad asked advocate Abhik Chimni, appearing for the petitioners, how old the two leaders were. Chimni told the court that Das was 27 and Ranka was 32.“Then you are not Gen Z. What is Gen Z?” the court asked.
After being informed that Generation Z generally refers to people born after 1997, the court reiterated, “Then you are not Gen Z.”The exchange took place while the high court was hearing the leaders’ challenge to an October 19 order by a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) extending their judicial custody until October 21.The exchange also drew a reaction on social media, with CJP leader Abhijit Dipke posting an image of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and writing, “The only person who qualifies as GenZ.”
Court questions choice of legal remedy
During the hearing, the court questioned why the petitioners had approached it under Article 226 of the Constitution when an alternative remedy of revision could be available to challenge the magistrate’s order.“Your second incident. You are a person who has actually broken a bond.
Your remedy actually lies in revision,” the court observed.The bench also questioned whether the authorities could insist on stricter surety conditions following an alleged second breach of a peace bond.“Once you have broken peace for the second time, are the authorities not entitled to insist upon everything?” the court asked.The court further noted that a challenge to the denotification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site was pending before the Supreme Court and that the notification had not been stayed. It questioned the petitioners’ decision to return to the site in those circumstances.The bench also expressed concern that breaking barricades could encourage others to violate prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).“The two petitioners here are at the forefront. When you go and break a barricade, the chances of 10 or 20 more people in violation of 163 are very high,” the court observed.
Petition withdrawn
Advocate Chimni argued that the SEM's October 19 order extending the petitioners' custody was legally unsustainable. He contended that the magistrate lacked jurisdiction to extend their custody and alleged that preventive proceedings were being used arbitrarily.He also questioned the rejection of the sureties, arguing that two additional sureties were available but had not been called for consideration.
According to his submissions, the magistrate's order referred to discrepancies in photographs and difficulties in verifying details relating to one of the petitioners.The court suggested that the petitioners await the outcome of proceedings before the SEM, which was scheduled to reconsider their sureties at 2 pm on Wednesday. Chimni, however, expressed apprehension that the sureties could again be rejected on fresh grounds, requiring the petitioners to approach the High Court again.The petitioners subsequently withdrew their plea. Justice Prasad permitted the withdrawal, and the High Court clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case.Additional solicitor general Chetan Sharma, along with advocate Ashish Dixit, appeared for the Delhi Police, while Chimni represented Das, Ranka and the other petitioners.

Houthis claims attack on Saudi position in Aden while clashes flare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:04:00 UTC
19:04:00 KST

Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on a Saudi target in Aden Wednesday, with smoke reportedly rising near the airport, marking the third strike in a week against the seat of the Riyadh-backed government.
"Our armed forces were able to target the Saudi enemy's operations room in the Badr camp in Aden with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement.
A police official in Aden earlier said there had been a blast "caused by a Houthi missile," speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
Two other security sources in the city told Agence France-Presse (AFP) the attack targeted a site near the airport that belonged to forces from the Saudi-led military coalition that has been battling the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognized Yemeni government have recently come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Earlier Friday, two missiles landed within the perimeter of the airport, with the Houthis claiming the attack.
A day earlier, the Houthis launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, hitting command centers located inside the al-Maashiq presidential compound, which is used by government forces and the Saudi-led coalition.
Al-Jumhuriya TV, meanwhile, reported renewed heavy clashes between Yemeni armed forces and Houthi fighters at the old airport and around Mount Han, west of Taiz city.
The developments come amid the internationally recognized government's ongoing military offensive against the Houthis in southwestern Yemen.
On Tuesday, the Yemeni army said it had carried out 744 attacks against the group over 24 hours, neutralizing around 200 of its members and destroying or damaging 90 vehicles and other military assets.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh's control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing government-held territory in Yemen along the Red Sea coastline in a lightning campaign.
In response, the Saudi air force has been regularly targeting the Houthis in support of the Yemeni government.

Murder arrest over British tourist's Greece death
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:03:56 BST
19:03:56 KST

Murder arrest over British tourist's Greece death
- Published
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murdering a British woman who died in Greece earlier this year, an inquest opening has heard.
Jacqueline Causton was found unresponsive at her villa on the island of Zakynthos on 14 May, Doncaster Coroner's Court heard.
She was taken to a local hospital on the island, also known as Zante, but later pronounced dead and her body was subsequently repatriated.
Det Con Mike Tilley, of South Yorkshire Police, told the court a man had been arrested on 12 June on suspicion of murder, before being bailed and then re-arrested last weekend when "fresh evidence" emerged.
After the hearing, the force said the suspect was aged 69 and had been arrested in Worcestershire.
The officer said the police's probe into the case was "complex" as investigation material uncovered by the Greek authorities was "still held" in the country and that some potential witnesses were foreign nationals.
He said there was "likely to be some further pathological work" required and that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) was yet to decide whether or not Greek or British authorities would lead the investigation.
The hearing was not told how the 66-year-old, from Bawtry in South Yorkshire, may have died.
Offering her condolences to the family, area coroner Louise Slater said the case would return to court in February 2027 for an update.
In June, Doncaster Mind paid tribute, describing Jacqueline as a "much-loved supporter" of the mental health charity.
It said she and her late husband had "brought so much joy to our community by transforming their home in Bawtry into a magical Christmas wonderland each year".
A spokesperson for the charity added: "Their kindness, generosity and community spirit touched countless lives, and we will always be grateful for everything they did to help us continue our work."

Indian startup shows first look at new jet-powered drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:02:51 UTC
19:02:51 KST

- Indian startup Apollyon Dynamics released the first photos of its Nightshade Mk-2, a jet-powered drone following the Nightshade ADX-1 unveiled in August.
- The company plans pilot deliveries of the Nightshade target-drone version to the Indian Army by December.
Indian defense startup Apollyon Dynamics has released the first photos of its Nightshade Mk-2, a new jet-powered drone that the Hyderabad-based company is developing as a successor to the Nightshade it unveiled earlier this year.
Co-founder and CEO Jayant Khatri shared an image of the aircraft lying on a hangar floor next to a team member for scale, while the company’s official account posted darker teaser shots under the caption “Nightshade Mk-2 SOON!”
The photo shows a compact jet autonomous aircraft with a pointed nose, a slender fuselage, sharply swept wings with control surfaces along the trailing edges, and a small turbojet engine mounted in a pod on top of the rear fuselage above a pair of swept tailplanes.
Apollyon Dynamics has not yet published performance figures for the Mk-2, but its predecessor gives an idea of where the design is heading. The company unveiled the Nightshade ADX-1 in August as a jet-powered combat drone that it says cruises and attacks at 600 to 700 km/h (370 to 435 mph), carries up to 5 kg (11 pounds) of explosives, weighs up to 70 kg (154 pounds) at takeoff and can strike targets more than 100 km (62 miles) inside hostile territory, with future versions expected to reach beyond 150 km (93 miles).
The company says the Nightshade uses inertial navigation with terrain-following so it can keep flying accurately when GPS signals are jammed or spoofed, and it has test-launched the drone from the roof of a moving vehicle, which it describes as a first for a jet-powered system in India. Apollyon is offering the Nightshade in several configurations, including a target drone for air defense training, a decoy and a loitering munition, and it plans to deliver pilot batches of the target-drone version to the Indian Army by December, with trials of the loitering munition expected next year.
Apollyon Dynamics grew out of a student project at the BITS Pilani campus in Hyderabad and was founded in May 2025 by Khatri and Sourya Choudhury, who quickly drew attention when Indian Army units in Jammu, Chandimandir, Panagarh and Arunachal Pradesh began using the startup’s high-speed kamikaze drones, which the company says can fly at more than 300 km/h (186 mph). The company raised a $480,000 pre-seed round led by Naandi Ventures, employs about 20 people across two manufacturing labs in Hyderabad and is aiming to raise $5 million in a seed round within six months.
The Mk-2 is part of a wider shift at the company, which has stopped building conventional quadcopter-style drones to focus on faster systems, including the jet-powered Nightshade family, an interceptor called Ahuti Mk II with a reported top speed of 498 km/h (309 mph) and a maritime uncrewed system known as Project Piranha. Apollyon has given no date for the Mk-2’s first flight or public debut beyond its promise that the aircraft is coming soon.

Iran strikes Iranian opposition group Kurdistan Freedom Party in latest attack

10:02:12 UTC
19:02:12 KST

Iran carried out attacks targeting Kurdish Iranian opposition groups on Wednesday. Reports said that the Islamic Republic targeted a site linked to the Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK) in the Balisan Valley. This area is northeast of Erbil.
This latest strike follows a set of attacks in which Iran targeted the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (PDKI), Komala, and the Khabat Organization in recent weeks. Iran is also pressing Iraq to expel Kurdish Iranian opposition groups.
Rebaz Sharifi, a PAK spokesperson, told Rudaw that “between two and four projectiles targeted the group’s positions at around 9:30 a.m. near the village of Hasanawa in the Balisan mountains.”
Sharifi told Rudaw that there were no casualties. Another security source also confirmed the attack. The source believed Iran used two Hadid-110 drones in the attack. It is unclear whether this is accurate.
“At least one strike hit the western side of Bani Harir mountain 70 km northeast of Erbil, according to a resident of a nearby village,” Rudaw reported.
Iran’s Ambassador to Iraq Mohammad Kazem Al-Sadegh wrote on social media on Tuesday that Iran and Iraq had agreed that Iraq would expel the Kurdish opposition groups.
The groups have rejected this. Meanwhile, Iraq’s National Security Council did not mention it in recent meetings. Iran appears to be signaling that it wants Iraq to act.
PAK fighting against Iran for Kurdish self-determination
PAK is an Iranian Kurdish opposition group that has operated for decades from Iraq’s Kurdistan Region. The group advocates Kurdish self-determination and has maintained an armed fighting force. Its fighters gained fame during the war against ISIS in Iraq, when they fought alongside Kurdish Peshmerga forces in some of the most exposed front lines.
In February 2026, PAK joined four other Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in announcing a new coalition. The new coalition includes the PDKI, the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), the Khabat Organization of Iranian Kurdistan, and a branch of Komala. Later, a second Komala branch joined.
Iran has carried out more than 1,000 attacks on the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq since February. Reports in March indicated the US might support a Kurdish uprising or transfer arms via Kurds to resistance groups in Iran.
Meanwhile, other Iranian opposition groups have slammed Kurdish groups as “separatists.” Many Kurdish groups have exercised caution regarding an uprising.
In recent weeks, Tehran has launched increased operations against PJAK in Iran, targeting the Shaho mountains and areas near the border.
The Islamic Republic has also continued targeting Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in northern Iraq with drones and missiles. On Saturday, October 17, two drones launched from Iran struck a Komala base in the Balisan area of the Erbil Governorate, according to Rudaw. One drone hit the base, and another struck a guard post. Buildings were damaged, but no casualties were reported.
On Monday, October 12, the PDKI said an Iranian drone targeted its Azadi Camp near Koya, where families of party members live. The group said this was the third attack on the camp in two weeks.
On Thursday, October 8, a drone also targeted a residential complex in the Khabat District north of Erbil, with no casualties reported. Khabat here refers to the district, not necessarily the Kurdish opposition organization.
Iraq, Kurdistan Regional Government reach new agreement
There are other developments. Iraq and the autonomous Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) have reached a new agreement.
“The Ministry of Martyrs and Anfal Affairs in the KRG announced on Tuesday that it has reached understandings with the federal government to unify financial entitlements for the families of martyrs and for political prisoners in the Kurdistan Region. These entitlements are to be included in the federal general budget bill for 2027,” Iraq’s state-led Iraqi News Agency (INA) said.
Rudaw, reporting on what is said a monitor had told the news agency, noted that “the Kurdistan Region’s internal political rivalries and institutional paralysis have weakened its bargaining position with Baghdad and accelerated the erosion of its federal powers.”
Meanwhile, a KDPI official told Rudaw that “the party would not lay down its weapons or abandon its struggle for Kurdish rights.”
The source added that the party had rejected “Tehran’s demands the same day after Iran claimed Baghdad had agreed to expel Iranian Kurdish opposition groups or hand them over to the Islamic Republic.”
An Iraqi source has denied any agreement to expel the groups.
In Turkey, Nationalist Movement Party leader Devlet Bahceli mentioned the PJAK group, Rudaw said in a report.
He said that it was important to create a “terror-free” region. The PJAK is linked to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). Turkey and the PKK have a new peace process. The PJAK is not involved in this process, which concerns Turkey.

IDF was not planning to strike Iran on Oct. 10 despite reports of attack blocked by Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:01:56 UTC
19:01:56 KST

Despite a Financial Times report, the IDF was not planning a strike on Iran on October 10, The Jerusalem Post learned on Wednesday.
It is true that over the last several months since the April 7 Israel-Iran ceasefire, the IDF has been on a war footing a few times, should the Iranians seem to be about to launch an attack or should US President Donald Trump decide on a renewed joint US-Israel operation against the Islamic Republic.
One of those times was in the days surrounding October 7, as there was high concern in the IDF that Tehran would choose to initiate a new conflict with Israel around that anniversary date.
But neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor Defense Minister Israel Katz, nor any other government official, had told the IDF to prepare to attack in the way that such orders were handed down leading up to the June 2025 and early 2026 conflicts with Iran.
In that sense, sources have told the Post that the premise of the Financial Times report - that Trump blocked Israel from an attack on Iran which it was about to carry out - is wrong, because Israel was not about to carry out an attack.
Put simply, Trump could not block an attack that was not planned.
Sources have speculated that a leak of such a potential attack on Iran to the Financial Times could be designed to impact the Israeli election, with Netanyahu claiming that he was ready to attack Iran a third time, but was prevented by Trump.
Such a story might also assist Trump in the US midterm elections, as it would seem to present him as responsibly managing the conflict with Iran, which is extremely unpopular among both Democrats and Republicans.
The narrative that Netanyahu is seeking to attack is also easy to support, since the IDF has been on a war footing a few times recently, including in the days before and after October 7.
In other words, the narrative isn't true, but it's not far from the truth, according to sources.
More comprehensively, sources have told the Post and other Israeli and foreign media that the IDF has been prepared to take action against Iran for months in two main scenarios: 1) where the IDF would see that Iran is about to attack first; or 2) with a joint US-Israel resumption of hostilities.
Trump stated he backed out of attacking Iran in August
On August 2, Trump himself publicized that he backed down from an attack on Iran which could have eventually involved the IDF.
In recent days, Trump has heightened his public threats against Iran, including specifically against Pickaxe Mountain, and sources have confirmed that if Washington had gone forward with a strike, this could have made Israeli participation far more likely.
Another issue with the Financial Times report is the idea that a future attack by Israel and the US would be larger in scale than the early 2026 war, when Iran has not repaired enough of what was bombed then for a larger attack to take place.
Sources have noted that top Israeli officials have publicly called for targeting Iran's energy sector more robustly, something which was more limited in early 2026, but this by itself would not constitute a larger-scale attack after Israel and the Us dropped around 30,000 bombs.
In addition, sources said that it was strange that IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir was not invited to a meeting with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth at the Ovda IDF air force base this week.
Although US secretaries of defense usually meet with their Israeli counterparts and often with the prime minister, rare visits to Israel invariably involve the IDF chief because of his influence on war and peace matters.
Sources speculated that Netanyahu may have been influenced by political considerations about how to portray Hegseth's visit and what messages would be passed back and forth, in his decision to keep Zamir and the IDF out of the meeting.
Hegseth has held far fewer visits with Israel than his predecessor, and his visits, as well as Katz's, have at times been shortened or canceled.

Magasin data breach exposes customer details
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:01:45 UTC
19:01:45 KST

Unauthorized people have gained access to parts of the computer systems of the Danish department store chain.
Magasin reported the incident in an email to DR, the Danish public broadcaster.
Following the breach, Magasin warned members of its customer loyalty club, named Goodie, that their personal details may have been compromised. The exposed data includes names, addresses, and purchase history.
“We are working dedicatedly with external experts to handle the incident, including re-establishing our access to the systems. In addition, we have reported the incident to both the police and Datatilsynet,” Magasin stated in the email. Datatilsynet is the Danish Data Protection Agency, the national authority that oversees data privacy rules.
Magasin warned that the compromised details could be used to make phishing scams look more believable.
Phishing is a deceptive practice where scammers try to trick individuals into handing over personal information. This often happens through fake emails designed to steal login details for MitID, the official digital identification system used across Denmark for banking and public services.
Magasin stressed in its message to club members that the security breach did not include any credit card information.
“We want to emphasize that we are working to limit the scope of the breach and to ensure that something similar does not happen again,” the email said.
The incident follows a similar alert sent to shoppers a few weeks ago by the British online retailer Asos.
In that case, Asos stated that an unauthorized person managed to enter an employee account. The intruder used that account to pull information from external platforms that Asos works with.
That breach allowed the unauthorized user to access customer names and contact details.
Following the incident, Asos told its customers to be cautious of unexpected phone calls and messages from individuals pretending to work for the company. Asos also reported its security breach to the police.
Severed network cable disrupts departure screens and train information apps across Denmark
A severed network cable at Banedanmark disrupted departure and arrival information at many train stations across Denmark on Wednesday.
The problem also affected the MitTog app, while users experienced difficulties getting updated information on Rejseplanen, Denmark’s journey planning service.
Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, said information about train times was being provided through station loudspeakers wherever possible.
The disruption did not affect information screens for the S-trains, Copenhagen’s suburban rail network, according to railway operator DSB.
Shortly before 1 p.m. Wednesday, Banedanmark’s press office said the damaged cable had been restored.
The company expected information screens and apps to gradually return to normal operation.
New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.
Venstre and other opposition parties expect to be left out of Denmark’s 2027 budget deal
Venstre does not expect to be included in an agreement with the government on Denmark’s 2027 national budget, party chairman Troels Lund Poulsen said after an introductory meeting on Wednesday.
“There is no willingness to listen to our views. It is a budget that has been agreed upon in advance with the government’s support parties. And that is just how it is,” Lund Poulsen said, according to Danish public broadcaster DR.
The government’s support parties are Enhedslisten, the Red-Green Alliance, and Alternativet, a green political party. Both are expected to reach a budget agreement with the government, particularly as it is the first national budget deal since the general election earlier this year.
Lund Poulsen said Venstre would be willing to attend further negotiations if the government invited the party.
Other opposition parties also expressed doubts about their chances of joining the agreement after meeting with Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard, a member of the Social Democrats, on Wednesday.

The same applies to De Konservative, the Conservative People’s Party.
“That is what I think. Because regarding the wishes we have for the budget, we have not been accommodated,” party chairman Mona Juul said.

Danmarksdemokraterne, another opposition party, also attended negotiations on Wednesday.

The decision was welcomed by Pelle Dragsted, Enhedslisten’s political spokesperson.
“We are very happy about that. It was antisocial to cut the opportunities of worn-out workers to be able to retire,” he said on Tuesday.
Under its budget proposal, the government had planned to save 200 million kroner in 2028, 500 million kroner in 2029 and 800 million kroner in 2030 by tightening the requirements for senior pensions.
Enhedslisten and Alternativet held their budget negotiations with the government on Tuesday.

Foreign workers and older employees fuel Denmark’s job market growth
The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.
The payment company Nets has lost a court case against Konkurrencerådet, the Danish Competition Council, which serves as the public competition authority in Denmark.
The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.
The case involves the company Teller, which was a subsidiary under Nets during that period. Teller offered what were described as exclusivity discounts to a number of large customers. The competition authorities determined that this practice broke legal rules meant to secure free competition, and they made their official decision on the case back in 2018.
The legal process has taken several years. Alongside the civil lawsuit, police have also run an investigation into Nets. That investigation led to criminal charges against the company, with authorities seeking a fine. The criminal case was put on hold to wait for the result of the civil case, and it has not yet gone to trial.
The specific legal reasons behind the court decision are not yet known. In a brief summary published on its website, the Maritime and Commercial Court stated that the full ruling will be released within four weeks.
The court noted that the delay is needed because the text of the ruling may contain business secrets that cannot be made public.
Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.
Denmark warns travelers in France to avoid protests as curfews continue
Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has advised people in France to stay away from demonstrations and large gatherings because of the risk of violence.
In updated travel advice on its website, the ministry warns that unrest and clashes between protesters and police remain possible in major cities, including Paris.
It also warns that authorities may introduce curfews at short notice.
Curfews were imposed overnight into Tuesday in parts of Paris and the northern French cities of Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain.
According to AFP, French police said the Paris curfew began at 11 p.m. Monday. In the other cities, restrictions remain in place Tuesday from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday that the curfews had helped restore calm overnight, according to Reuters and AFP.
He added that local authorities could impose further restrictions if necessary.
“Tonight, new curfews will be introduced where the situation requires it. The decisions will be made locally by the prefects in cooperation with the mayors,” Lecornu wrote on X.
The measures follow a weekend of demonstrations that brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets across France.
Protesters are demonstrating against the high cost of living and what they see as a lack of economic opportunity and security.
The demonstrations were accompanied by reports of vandalism and looting.
According to the Paris Chamber of Commerce, between 300 and 400 shops were vandalized in the capital.
Nationwide, around 2,000 shops were affected, the French Chamber of Commerce told Reuters.
More than 1,800 people were arrested Saturday following demonstrations across the country.
Plans to tighten Denmark’s senior pension rules dropped after political opposition
The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.
This would have made qualifying for senior pension more difficult. In 2026, a single person receiving senior pension gets 22,053 DKK per month.
The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.
Four Danish opposition parties demand broader tax cuts in government plan
Denmark’s Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and Denmark’s Democrats say they will reject the government’s upcoming tax plan unless it includes cuts for people earning less than 58,000 DKK a month.
The four opposition parties will present their demands during tax negotiations with Minister for Taxation and Growth Jakob Engel-Schmidt later this week.
The government wants to remove the top-top tax and intermediate income tax, benefiting people earning more than approximately 58,000 DKK a month.
It also plans to reduce corporate tax by three percentage points starting in 2030.
The four parties argue that lower-income workers should also benefit.
“It is only fair and reasonable that the police officer, the shop assistant, the electrician, and everyone else with a salary below 58,000 kroner also get a tax cut,” Conservative leader Mona Juul said in a written statement.
Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen said his party supports reducing corporate and intermediate taxes but wants cuts for everyone in employment.
Liberal Alliance leader Alex Vanopslagh said “completely ordinary Danes must get more out of going to work”.
Denmark Democrats leader Inger Støjberg called for tax changes that would help families facing higher fuel, energy and food prices.
The government may need support from the four center-right parties to pass its plan.
Its usual parliamentary allies, The Red-Green Alliance, a left-wing party, and The Alternative, a green progressive party, are not expected to support several of the proposed measures.
Government plan would remove SU from 14,000 students living with parents
About 14,000 higher education students living with their parents would lose their entire state education grant under the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Another 8,000 students in the same group would receive lower payments, Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said in a parliamentary response.
Denmark’s state education grant is commonly known as SU.
An estimated 31,800 higher education students living at home received SU in 2025.
The government proposes ending payments for students whose parents have a combined annual income above 710,077 DKK. This corresponds to an average monthly income of 29,583 DKK for each parent in a two-parent household.
Payments would gradually decline for students whose parents earn between 419,589 and 710,077 DKK annually. The lowest monthly grant would be 500 DKK before disappearing entirely above the upper threshold.
The government initially estimated that 81,000 students living at home across different education programs would be affected. The later decision to reduce grants gradually for middle-income households means the final number could be higher.
Disability supplements and additional support for single parents would remain available regardless of parental income.
The Socialist People’s Party and Social Liberal Party have faced criticism for supporting the reductions.
SF leader Pia Olsen Dyhr acknowledged that her party had not proposed the measure but said it was part of the compromises required in government.
Minister calls for talks after report finds major employment losses due to stress
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”
Chief Economic Adviser Jakob Roland Munch said severe stress has long-lasting effects on people’s connection to the labor market.
However, the report found no evidence that the number of severe stress cases has increased during the past 15 to 20 years.
Dyhr said Denmark must place greater emphasis on preventing stress instead of responding only after people become ill.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget includes 50 million DKK for a prevention fund intended to help people remain healthy and employed.
Dyhr said the government wants stronger evidence about which preventive measures work before deciding how to prioritize future efforts.
The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.
Social Democrat warns foreign labor risks creating master-servant society
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek has warned that Denmark risks developing a society divided between those providing low-paid services and those becoming dependent on them.
“What do we become as human beings if we slowly let low-paid Africans and Asians do everything that is not immediately manageable?” Dybvad Bek said Monday during a budget debate in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
He questioned whether Danes lose practical skills and the ability to learn when they rely on foreign workers, delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for routine tasks.
Dybvad Bek referred to German philosopher Georg Hegel’s theory that a master becomes increasingly helpless as a servant performs more of the work.
He said individual consumers were not responsible for the development.
“It is up to us politicians to stop the flow of underpaid labor that forms the basis for these services,” he said.
Dybvad Bek argued that goods and services should be priced at a level that allows workers to earn a living wage.
He also warned that Denmark could create new parallel societies if foreign workers remain socially separated from the people they serve.
The comments came as Dybvad Bek presented a government proposal requiring employers to finance Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive.
He said companies should help pay for the integration of workers from whom they profit.
Lego named Denmark’s most valuable brand at 114 billion DKK
Lego has Denmark’s most valuable brand, with an estimated value of 114 billion DKK, according to a report by British consultancy Brand Finance.
The Danish toy company’s brand value increased by 54 percent from the previous year, business newspaper Børsen reported.
Nordea placed second with a brand value of 46.2 billion DKK, while shipping company Maersk ranked third.
“Lego is an exceptional brand, regardless of how you measure it,” Brand Finance Chief Operating Officer Mike Rocha told Børsen.
Brand Finance calculates how much a company would hypothetically have to pay to license its brand if it did not own it.
The consultancy said Lego’s financial performance contributed to the increase in value.
Lego recorded revenue of 83.5 billion DKK in 2025, an increase of 12 percent from the previous year and the highest annual total in the company’s history.
Growth accelerated during the first half of 2026, when Lego’s revenue rose by 21 percent compared with the same period in 2025.
Lego declined to comment to Børsen on the Brand Finance report.
MobilePay launches digital proof of age for use in Danish stores
MobilePay’s nearly 4.8 million Danish users will be able to document their age through the payment app when shopping in physical stores.
The feature will appear under the app’s “Wallet” menu in an update being gradually released from Tuesday, Vipps MobilePay said.
Users can add a passport-style photograph to the digital proof, which displays only their name, photo and age category.
Vipps MobilePay product manager Dennis Kvade said the need to confirm age and identity was increasing both online and in physical stores.
“It is not particularly practical to bring your passport on a night out,” he said, adding that existing age checks can also be vulnerable to fraud.
Supermarket chain Rema 1000 will accept MobilePay’s proof of age. Its employees will receive information about the feature.
However, the MobilePay document is not an official identification card and cannot replace a passport, health insurance card or driving licence.
It is intended for situations in stores and nightlife venues where young people must show they are old enough to purchase restricted products such as alcohol.
Individual businesses can decide whether to accept it, meaning users cannot assume it will be recognized everywhere.
Denmark’s Agency for Digital Government launched AltID earlier in 2026 as the country’s first official digital proof of age and identification app for both online and in-person use.
Pensioners occupy Aarhus rehabilitation center to protest closure
Between 10 and 12 pensioners occupied Rehabiliteringshøjskolen in Risskov on Tuesday and locked staff outside to protest its planned closure.
The demonstration began after the Aarhus City Council decided to close the residential rehabilitation center at the end of 2026, TV2 Østjylland reported.
“The folk high school cannot raise the dead, but it can keep them alive,” read one sign displayed in a window.
The center provides residential stays lasting two to five weeks, during which people receive support and guidance from a healthcare team.
Protester Torben Blom said the program had been crucial after both his legs were amputated.
“It has meant that I have become a human being again,” he said.
The center opened in 2018 but will close because Denmark’s healthcare reform requires Aarhus Municipality to transfer certain responsibilities and buildings to the regional authority.
Health and Care Alderman Metin Lindved Aydin of the Social Liberal Party said the municipality could not afford to build a similar facility during the next four years.
He said the reform required the municipality to save 185 million DKK.
Aydin said other rehabilitation services would remain available but acknowledged that they would differ from the existing program.
He described the occupation as a new form of senior activism and called it “refreshing” and “brave,” while saying he could not encourage illegal occupations.
Aydin said he would not call the police.
Danish home sales fall 12 percent as higher rates slow market
Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
Housing transactions during the first nine months of 2026 were three percent below the corresponding period in 2025.
Apartment sales have fallen most sharply. Eight percent fewer apartments have been sold nationwide this year, while Copenhagen has recorded a decline of 23 percent.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said rising mortgage rates could partly explain the slowdown.
Fixed-rate mortgages have recently fluctuated between four and five percent, compared with 3.5 percent at the beginning of the year.
Higher prices for gasoline, natural gas and electricity are also reducing the money households have available, he said.
However, strong employment and rising inflation-adjusted incomes continue to support the housing market.
Sales of houses and terraced homes are also below last year’s level. Holiday home sales, by contrast, have increased by 4.5 percent.
Boligsiden communications director Birgit Daetz said the increase indicates that many households remain financially secure because holiday homes are traditionally purchased during periods of economic strength.
Rising property values and the possibility of rental income may also make such purchases more affordable, she said.
Copenhagen mayor disputes Frederiksen’s claims about meat in nursing homes
Copenhagen Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of the Socialist People’s Party has accused Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of presenting an inaccurate picture of food policies in the city’s nursing homes.
Frederiksen wrote on Instagram that a Copenhagen proposal could prevent nursing home residents from receiving the meat they want.
“It is a lack of respect for the elderly person’s right to make decisions for themselves,” Frederiksen wrote. “Those people in nursing homes who have toiled and slaved for our country must of course be allowed to eat meat.”
Welling rejected the claim.
“The elderly must naturally have the food they know and like. For many of them, that involves meat,” she wrote.
Welling said individual nursing homes can decide how to plan menus and how much meat to serve. She said residents’ nutritional needs should take priority over climate concerns.
The dispute follows debate over Copenhagen’s food and meal strategy, which aims to make municipal meals more sustainable and reduce purchases of beef.
A consultancy analysis reported that some nursing homes had rejected residents’ birthday requests for beef because of carbon reduction targets.
The study surveyed 200 nursing home residents and 607 people receiving meals at home.
Between 58 and 60 percent were satisfied with the food, while 8 to 13 percent reported little or no satisfaction.
Several nursing home residents criticized meat quality and said beef rarely appeared on menus. The analysis also found that residents wanted greater influence over their meals.
More than half of surveyed Danish teachers feel stressed every week
More than half of teachers in a new union survey said they experience stress daily or weekly, with most attributing it to their working conditions.
The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.
Nine in 10 of those experiencing stress said workplace conditions were responsible.
“We are facing a working environment problem in the public schools, while at the same time many teachers choose to leave,” union chair Gordon Ørskov Madsen said.
More than one in three respondents said they had taken sick leave from teaching because of stress.
Teachers identified classroom disruption, insufficient preparation time, heavy workloads and difficulty obtaining help for pupils with special needs as major pressures.
Some also reported that parents expected them to resolve conflicts between pupils that occurred outside school.
Nana Vaaben, an associate professor at University College Copenhagen, said teachers can experience moral stress when they know pupils need help but lack the authority to provide it.
Respondents identified fewer teaching hours, more preparation time and better support for pupils with special needs as the measures most likely to reduce stress.
The union plans to raise those proposals in upcoming negotiations with the government and other labor market parties.

Denmark and Vietnam will establish a strategic partnership during Vietnamese President Tô Lâm’s state visit to Denmark this week.

Independent authority to investigate police strikes against photographers
The Independent Police Complaints Authority will investigate reports that police officers struck two press photographers with batons during demonstrations in Copenhagen on Saturday.
The photographers worked for Danish newspapers Politiken and Ekstra Bladet and were involved in separate incidents during demonstrations for and against remigration.
Copenhagen Police referred the cases to the independent authority, known as DUP, following criticism from both newspapers.
“The Copenhagen Police in no way wish to place obstacles in the way of the press carrying out their work,” police said.
Politiken reported that its photographer was struck several times, had his camera smashed and received treatment at an emergency room.
Ekstra Bladet’s photographer said he was struck on the arm with a baton despite carrying cameras and visible press credentials.
Politiken editor-in-chief Christian Jensen described the incident as a serious attack on press freedom.
“The police make the press their adversary by preventing us from doing our job, which is also about witnessing the police’s exercise of their power,” he wrote.
Ekstra Bladet editor-in-chief Knud Brix also called the reported incident “completely unacceptable.”
The Danish Union of Press Photographers and the Danish Union of Journalists have requested a meeting with the national police commissioner.
They want police leadership to explain how similar incidents will be prevented and how journalists will be protected while covering demonstrations.
Delayed UN climate reports could weaken action before COP33, Danish expert warns
Global climate efforts could face serious setbacks if the UN climate panel does not publish its next assessment reports before the COP33 summit in 2028, a Danish climate expert has warned.
“Without the reports, countries will stand on a basis that is less comprehensive. They will lack crucial knowledge,” said Adrian Lema, head of the National Centre for Climate Research at the Danish Meteorological Institute.
He said countries could spend time debating scientific facts instead of agreeing on action.
“The consequence may be that we set climate action back years, and that uncertainty is created about some of the progress we have achieved,” Lema said.
COP33 will include the next major review of countries’ progress under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A weeklong meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, known as the IPCC, ended Friday without agreement on a budget or timetable for the reports.
Lema attended as Denmark’s lead negotiator and wanted the reports published well before COP33.
Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran, India and China argued that publication before the summit was unnecessary, he said.
IPCC decisions require consensus rather than majority votes.
Lema said an agreement remained possible but had become more difficult.
“If we can get enough countries to say it loud and clear, then the few who disagree will be under a different pressure,” he said.
Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.
Government wants employers to fund Danish lessons for foreign workers
The Danish government wants employers to pay for Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive in Denmark.
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek announced the proposal Monday during the Folketing’s debate on the government’s 2027 budget bill.
“It provides a saving of 100 million DKK, but first and foremost it sends a clear signal that people who come to the country to work must speak Danish,” he said.
Dybvad Bek said the issue concerned Denmark’s understanding of itself as a society.
More foreign workers have entered the restaurant and service industries in recent years, particularly in Copenhagen. This has led to more customers being served in English rather than Danish, he said.
During the debate, Dybvad Bek also argued that Danes risk losing practical skills when they rely on food delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for manageable tasks.
He also referred to planned restrictions affecting what he called “underpaid African agricultural workers.”
Dybvad Bek further criticized Nepalese and Iranian nationals who, he said, use Denmark’s education system to enter the labor market while avoiding other requirements.
Regional trains suspended between Odense and Fredericia after cable damage
Regional train services between Odense and Fredericia have been suspended until at least 2 p.m. Monday because of a severed cable.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, has ordered rail replacement buses and updated its journey planner.
InterCity and express trains continue to operate on the route, although passengers may experience longer travel times.
“In Odense and Fredericia, there are staff in orange vests who can assist with guidance,” DSB said.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, is working to repair the damaged cable.
Train services on the route were expected to return to full capacity Monday after several days of disruptions. The cable damage means that this is no longer possible.
Passengers have experienced longer journeys and fewer trains between the two cities since a fire damaged a relay hut near Aarup in western Funen on October 9.
The hut contained electronic equipment used by the railway’s signaling system. The fire caused signal failures between Middelfart and Odense, disrupting services on Funen and across Denmark.
Even after more trains return, services will continue at reduced speeds near Aarup Station, where trains will temporarily be unable to stop.
Sunny Monday to give way to rainy and windy week in Denmark
Denmark can expect sunshine Monday before rain and stronger winds arrive during the rest of the week.
“On Monday, we have a beautiful autumn day in store,” Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Marie Timm said. “There will be some high-altitude clouds in the sky, but otherwise it is a beautiful day where there will be sun for everyone.”
After overnight temperatures fell close to freezing in some areas, daytime temperatures will rise to between 9 and 13 degrees Celsius.

One in three Danish teachers reports verbal abuse from pupils
One in three Danish public school teachers experienced rude or abusive language from pupils during the previous week, according to a new survey.
Four in 10 teachers said such incidents occurred daily or several times a week, education trade publication Folkeskolen reported.
The survey was completed by 1,901 teachers and kindergarten class leaders between August 26 and September 14, 2026.
Teachers reported comments including “You fucking bad teacher,” “You are a damn idiot” and “You don’t boss me around.”
Lars Peter Sønderbo Andersen, a senior researcher in occupational and environmental medicine at Regional Hospital Gødstrup, said the language damages teachers’ working environment and undermines their authority in classrooms.
He said the problem has worsened in recent years.
In a similar survey conducted almost 10 years ago, one in four teachers reported being called derogatory terms such as “bitch,” “idiot” or “whore” at least once a month.
Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, described the new findings as concerning.
“Some of these statements are quite severe, and we can hear from the inquiries we receive that it affects the teachers when they are spoken to like that,” union representative Thomas Andreasen said.
He called for schools to establish clear, shared rules for acceptable language. He also said having more permanent teachers in classrooms could help.

Denmark has contacted more than 25 European countries about potentially renting prison spaces as its correctional system faces record overcrowding.
“The Danish Prison and Probation Service is in a serious situation,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said. “We must do everything we can to resolve the capacity challenges in Danish prisons.”
Denmark already has an agreement to rent 300 prison spaces in Kosovo for foreign nationals sentenced to deportation. However, delays mean the renovated prison is not expected to begin accepting inmates until late 2027 or early 2028.
The original plan expected inmates to begin serving sentences there in early 2023.
Wammen called the Kosovo agreement important but said additional measures were needed to relieve Denmark’s prisons.
The Justice Ministry declined to identify the countries it contacted or disclose the correspondence. It said publication could risk damaging Denmark’s foreign policy interests.
