Becerra's time in Washington: Steady rise with a bumpy final ascent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Examining Becerra’s quarter of a century in Washington
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor, was part of a wave of young Latino lawmakers entering Congress in the 1990s and won a place on the influential Ways and Means Committee.
- He drew criticism on multiple fronts during his time as President Biden’s Health and Human Services secretary.
WASHINGTON — Xavier Becerra was dubbed a “rising star” before he even entered the halls of Congress.
His June 1992 Democratic primary victory over Los Angeles school board member Leticia Quezada in California’s 30th Congressional District earned the 34-year-old candidate that description in The Times.
When the boyish, affable congressman became the first Latino lawmaker appointed to the powerful House Ways and Means Committee in his second term, national outlets took notice.
Thirty years later, in the final weeks of his gubernatorial race with Republican Steve Hilton, Becerra now finds himself poised to lead the most populous state in the country.
An examination of Becerra’s more than 25 years in Washington shows a politician who was skilled at building important alliances and amassing power on Capitol Hill, but had some stumbles along the way and faced criticism for his performance in his highest profile role.
Becerra built his reputation as a diligent consensus-builder — a workhorse rather than a show horse, to use an analogy favored by political scientists — but also revealed himself to be an ambitious political operator in key moments.
“He’s an affable person who’s not afraid to pull out a knife in politics while smiling,” said Christian Grose, a political science professor at USC.
After months publicly absent from the campaign trail, Democrat Xavier Becerra has increased public appearances and begun airing television ads as mail ballots reach California voters.
Becerra’s campaign declined to comment on his time in Washington.
Becerra’s origin story traces back to his youth in Sacramento, and a moment when a high school friend was about to throw out a blank, unused application to Stanford University. The elite university was only 125 miles away, but it might as well have been across the ocean from the working-class world Becerra was raised in. Still, he applied.
Becerra — whose parents spent their early years in Mexico — became the first in his family to graduate from college when he earned a degree from Stanford in 1980.
He earned a law degree there four years later, and it was at Stanford that he met his wife, Carolyn Reyes, who became a physician.
After living in Boston while Reyes attended Harvard Medical School, Becerra moved to Los Angeles to work for state Sen. Art Torres. Within a few years he was tapped by Henry Lozano, then chief of staff to trailblazing Latino Rep. Edward Roybal, to run for state Assembly in 1990; and then, two years later, to succeed Roybal, who was retiring after 30 years in Congress.
Roybal endorsed Becerra, whose victory in the heavily Latino district that included Central and Eastside Los Angeles communities, was seen as a passing of the torch to the next generation.
Frank Villalobos, the founder and president of Barrio Architects, was among the leaders in East L.A. who encouraged Becerra to run for political office, and he said he was impressed early on by Becerra’s genuine commitment to the community and his ability to unite the area’s sometimes divided political factions.
“I thought if we kept this going, someday he’ll become the governor,” Villalobos said.
Becerra was part of a wave of young Latino lawmakers entering Congress, and his growing power within Democratic ranks helped him escape Roybal’s long shadow. Soon after Becerra’s barrier-breaking appointment to the Ways and Means Committee — which writes tax legislation — Becerra became chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, a position he held from 1997 to 1999.
An early test
He put his growing stature to the test a few years later when he decided to enter the L.A. mayor’s race in 2001.
It didn’t go well.
Former state Assembly Speaker Antonio Villaraigosa was also running, and Becerra — who had slept on Villaraigosa’s couch when he first ran for Congress — faced criticism for potentially splitting the Latino vote.
Becerra performed poorly, winning only 6% of the vote in the Democratic primary. His nice-guy reputation took a hit when his campaign was found to have been behind automated phone calls attacking Villaraigosa by a woman who falsely gave the impression that she was county Supervisor Gloria Molina, whose endorsement had been crucial in Becerra’s first run for Congress.
Becerra also faced criticism for his role in contacting White House staffers as part of an effort to push for the release of convicted L.A. cocaine dealer Carlos Vignali, whose father was a political contributor to Becerra. Vignali’s sentence was commuted by President Clinton on his last day in office; Becerra acknowledged calling the White House several times to discuss the possibility of Vignali’s release. Villaraigosa also wrote a letter on Vignali’s behalf.
Becerra told The Times in 2001 that he wasn’t lobbying for Vignali’s release, but merely asking White House officials to review the details of the conviction on behalf of the family.
“If I was going to try to put pressure on, I would have tried to call the president,” Becerra said at the time.
Villaraigosa fared better than Becerra but ultimately lost the 2001 election to City Atty. James Hahn, then rebounded to win the first of two terms as mayor in 2005.
Becerra got the better of Villaraigosa in their rematch this year in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, and won Villaraigosa’s support after.
“We’ve been friends a long time and, yes, we’ve been adversaries as well, but most of the time we’ve been friends,” Villaraigosa told The Times. “He’s got the experience and the wherewithal to lead this state.”
As for Becerra as a house guest during his first run for Congress?
“He makes his bed. He was neat,” said Villaraigosa. “He was pretty inconspicuous.”
Capitol Hill climbing
After his mayoral defeat, Becerra’s focus returned to Washington, where an alliance with another powerful Californian was a boon to his career on Capitol Hill.
Becerra was a close ally of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-San Francisco), serving as assistant to the speaker from 2007 to 2009.
John Lawrence, Pelosi’s former chief of staff, said that Becerra’s standing within the California delegation and particularly among Latino lawmakers was a big part of his appeal.
“Speaker Pelosi had set a goal of elevating minorities and women who had historically been excluded from leadership,” he said.
Their relationship took a hit after Becerra told progressive lawmakers in 2009 that he believed party leadership gave up too easily on including a public option in the Affordable Care Act, which was signed into law the following year.
“I understand I have tire tracks on my back because Xavier threw me under the bus,” Pelosi said during a Democratic Party leadership meeting in 2009, Politico reported.
And Pelosi would later question Becerra’s appointment in 2021 to be secretary of Health and Human Services. She has not endorsed Becerra in the gubernatorial race.
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing in the race for California governor. Here’s what you need to know about the candidates.
But any bad blood between the two didn’t stop Becerra from continuing to advance within the party ranks.
He became chair of the House Democratic Caucus in 2012, leading weekly meetings of all Democrats in the House and uniting the party’s members.
Former Wisconsin Democratic Rep. Ron Kind said Becerra was an excellent listener and skilled at building consensus.
“He could get in the room with anyone and find common ground,” Kind said.
Becerra joined several high-stakes negotiations, notably a 2013 bipartisan effort to pass comprehensive immigration reform, in the wake of the “Gang of Eight” deal struck in the Senate.
John Yarmuth, a Democratic congressman from Kentucky who was also part of the House negotiation, said Becerra was “an amazing positive force” in the process.
“I think he, more than anyone else, was focused on fixing the problem,” Yarmuth said.
The group was able to achieve a compromise, but it never saw the light of day.
Then-House Speaker John Boehner, an Ohio Republican, later blamed then-President Obama, whom he accused of “poisoning the well” on an immigration compromise. Yarmuth said Republicans were spooked about potential blowback.
Several potential off-ramps appeared during Becerra’s time in Washington. He was considered by Obama for U.S. trade representative in 2008, but Becerra declined the offer. After flirting with the idea of running for outgoing U.S. Sen. Barbara Boxer’s seat, Becerra declined to enter the race, ultimately won by then-California Atty. Gen. Kamala Harris. He was briefly floated as a potential running mate for Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential election, but that didn’t materialize either.
In late 2016, Becerra found himself at a crossroads.
After more than a decade on the Ways and Means Committee, he faced the possibility of becoming the top Democrat on the committee and had the endorsement of the outgoing top Democrat, Rep. Sander Levin of Michigan.
But Harris’ victory in the 2016 Senate race created a vacancy for state attorney general.
Becerra decided to return home to Sacramento to take the role and spent the next four years as the state’s top law enforcement official, serving as “defender-in-chief” of the state, as USC’s Grose put it, against the Trump administration.
Fraught second act in D.C.
Becerra returned to Washington in 2021 for a second act that would prove to be far more controversial than his first.
Despite having no background in healthcare, Becerra was nominated to be the secretary of Health and Human Services and confirmed, over significant opposition by Republicans.
He took the reins of the healthcare agency as the country was still grappling with the COVID-19 pandemic and struggled to establish a clear role for himself in a response effort that was centered in the White House.
In his first year in office, he was called out by reporters for failing to hold regular press briefings.
And he faced criticism when health officials under his purview offered contradictory information in late 2021 about reduced quarantine requirements for people testing positive for COVID-19.
He continued to face criticism for the disappearance of thousands of unaccompanied migrant children who were supposed to be monitored by the agency’s Office of Refugee Resettlement after entering the country.
And Becerra’s chief of staff at Health and Human Services and longtime advisor, Sean McCluskie, pleaded guilty last year to participating in a scheme to use campaign funds from a dormant Becerra state political committee to pay for McCluskie’s frequent travel between Washington and California.
Dana Williamson, a longtime political consultant for Becerra and former chief of staff to Gov. Gavin Newsom, pleaded guilty earlier this year for her role in the scheme. McCluskie and Williamson are scheduled to be sentenced in December. Neither Becerra nor Newsom were accused of wrongdoing.
Xavier Becerra says he is the best candidate for California governor because of his long experience in government. His critics say that same record shows poor leadership on his part.
Democratic operative Xochitl Hinojosa, who served as the spokesperson for the Department of Justice in the Biden administration, earlier this year offered a blunt assessment of Becerra’s performance.
“He was not effective in government, and I think that a lot of people in the Biden administration are talking about this because they realize that he was not an effective HHS secretary,” Hinojosa said on CNN in May.
While other members of the Biden administration have defended Becerra’s performance, his time at the helm highlighted an issue that even allies concede has bedeviled Becerra in the past, his tendency to sometimes recede into the background.
Loretta Sanchez, a former Democratic congresswoman from Orange County who credits Becerra with encouraging her to run for Congress, put it simply.
“Will Xavier be bold?” she said. “I hope he takes those bold moves, because California needs it.”

Photographs:Sidney Zag, Francesca Iovene, Yves Marchand & Romain Meffre
Text description provided by the architects. For twenty years, the former Nanterre School of Architecture was a ghost building, yet its spatial power never faded. Designed in 1971 by Jacques Kalisz and Roger Salem, it was the first public building of a vast social redevelopment project. It stands in the heart of the André-Malraux Park, conceived from the beginning as a true cultural city, surrounded by public buildings dedicated to culture such as the Théâtre Nanterre-Amandiers and the Paris Opera Ballet School. Abandoned since 2004, the site entered the Inventons la Métropole du Grand Paris 2 competition in 2018. The Campus du Parc project was born, curated by IT'S, in a shared path with Eiffage Immobilier, developer of the operation, and the De Vinci Higher Education group, which opened its new campus headquarters for 4,500 engineering, business, and digital students.

Young people feel no one listens says Draghi on rioting
Italy

Vision 2040 for a thriving fisheries and aquaculture sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:58:45 UTC
18:58:45 KST

Thanks to the EU’s fisheries and aquaculture strategy, we will receive safe, sustainably sourced and fully traceable fish, so we can enjoy good fish on our table every day. Fisheries and aquaculture form a vital part of Europe’s prosperity and food security, employing together more than 200 000 people. The European Commission has set out its vision for fisheries and aquaculture towards 2040 to support fishers, aquaculture producers and local communities.
The vision lays out several key priorities:
Energy transition
Until 2030 we will improve energy and resource efficiency and develop new technologies. From 2030 onwards, efforts will shift towards scaling up zero-emission technologies, supported by financing, infrastructure and fleet modernisation.
Securing Europe’s supply of aquatic food and encouraging consumers to choose EU-produced aquatic products
The Commission will support investment in vessels, innovation and income diversification.
To boost demand for EU aquatic food, the Commission will support diversification and help consumers make informed choices. It will also promote digital traceability for all products across the supply chain by 2029, helping strengthen transparency, trust and market value.
Creating the right conditions for success
To turn the Vision into reality, the Commission will launch targeted initiatives to:
- improve access to finance
- support small-scale fishers
- strengthen research and innovation to better anticipate future fish stock availability
- introduce harmonised training and certification standards
- launch a blue generational renewal strategy in 2027 to help attract younger generations to the sector.
Acting globally to protect sustainability and fairness
The vision promotes sustainable fisheries globally while helping secure a diversified and resilient supply of aquatic food in the EU by:
- stepping up the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing
- strengthening international fisheries rules
- developing a new generation of Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements
We will continue to uphold a level playing field and protect the European fisheries value chain from unfair global competition.
The vision was developed through an extensive participatory process including fishers, aquaculture producers, the fish processing industry, EU countries, NGOs, advisory councils, young people and citizens.

Survey finds 87% of Taiwan internet users have used AI customer service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:58:44 UTC
18:58:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A survey released Tuesday by the Market Intelligence and Consulting Institute found that 87% of internet users had used AI customer service.
Among AI customer service users, 55% had used it in financial services and insurance, followed by telecommunications at 38%, retail and e-commerce at 32%, food and beverage services at 26%, and technology and consumer electronics at 23%, per CNA. However, 59% used the technology infrequently, while 21% used it frequently.
MIC senior industry analyst Liu Yu-lin (柳育林) said global labor shortages were driving demand for AI customer service as businesses sought to improve efficiency, cut costs, and improve customer experiences.
Users aged 46 to 65 were more likely to have used the technology in financial services and insurance, while 53% of users aged 18 to 25 reported using it more frequently.
Respondents prioritized accurate and useful answers (67%), smooth communication (52%), and the ability to transfer to human agents (46%). Although 57% of users had successfully transferred an unresolved issue to a human agent, 36% had experienced an unsuccessful transfer.
Less sophisticated systems were the most widely used, with 66% of respondents having used rule-based systems, compared with 40% who had used systems capable of understanding and reasoning and 18% who had used human-like interactive systems.
Overall, 42% of users were satisfied with AI customer service, 23% were dissatisfied, and 35% were neutral. Meanwhile, 57% of respondents said systems should disclose that they were not human.
Nearly half of respondents said a very poor AI customer service experience would have a moderate or greater impact on their view of a company or brand. Only 11% said such an experience would have virtually no impact.
The online survey collected 1,068 valid responses in Q4 2025. MIC reported a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

Taiwan Water, Miaoli sign deal for NT$407 million water project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:58:39 UTC
18:58:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Water Corporation and Miaoli County Government signed a memorandum of understanding Wednesday for a NT$407 million (US$12.56 million) water treatment plant and pipeline network to improve water supplies in eastern Miaoli County.
Taiwan Water Chair Li Chia-jung (李嘉榮) and Miaoli County Magistrate Chung Tung-chin (鍾東錦) signed the agreement, which is scheduled to run from 2027 to 2030, per CNA. The system aims to improve water supply in mountainous areas where steep terrain and more frequent dry years pose challenges.
The plant will be built in the Longshan section of Tai’an Township and have a daily output of 5,000 metric tons. It will draw water from subsurface flows of the Wenshui River, while the downstream network will include about 23 kilometers of pipelines and five distribution reservoirs.
The project budget includes NT$112 million for the treatment plant and NT$295 million for the pipeline network, according to Taiwan Water. The plant is expected to be completed in 2028, with space reserved for future expansion.
Once operational, the system will supply residential and industrial users in Tai’an, Dahu, Shitan, and Gongguan townships. It is also expected to improve water access for Indigenous communities and Hakka villages, meet demand during peak tourist seasons at Jinshui Hot Springs, and support wildfire suppression in mountainous areas.
Taiwan Water and central government agencies will fund the project, while the county government will help secure land for the plant, reservoirs, and related facilities.

A minor student in the Belgian city of Liege has accused police officers of making racist remarks and physically assaulting her during student demonstrations against education austerity measures, public broadcaster RTBF reported on Wednesday.
The student, identified by the pseudonym Anais to protect her identity and that of her family, said she was verbally and physically abused by police officers during a demonstration in downtown Liege on Oct. 5.
Anais was among a group of students who organized a blockade outside their school to protest education cuts.
After taking part in a blockade with around 10 other students, Anais and her friends headed to the city center to join a larger demonstration.
According to her account, police officers surrounded the group after noticing their foreign backgrounds and subjected them to racist insults.
"They called us 'dirty Arabs' and hit us with batons," she told RTBF, adding that one officer also made a derogatory remark about her Asian heritage.
A spokesperson for the Liege police district, Jadranka Lozina, said she was unaware of the alleged remarks but stressed that any racist behavior by police officers would be unacceptable.
"Racist remarks have no place in a police intervention, regardless of the circumstances," Lozina said.
Anais said officers also described the protesters as "vandals" and "thugs" and told them "to return to their country."
"They are supposed to protect us, but in the end, it backfires on us," she said.
Anais said she had decided not to file a complaint, expressing doubts that legal action would lead to any meaningful outcome.
Despite the incident, she said she intended to continue participating in demonstrations.
According to figures released by the Liege municipality, 327 people were arrested following the student demonstrations and subsequent unrest in the city.

Unauthorized drones flew over several military sites in southern France, including the Toulon naval base, during a military exercise earlier this month, broadcaster ICI Provence reported Wednesday, citing maritime authorities.
The nighttime flights occurred between Oct. 9 and 13, over areas including the naval base, the Directorate General of Armaments’ premises in Toulon and the 54th Artillery Regiment in nearby Hyeres, according to the report.
The Maritime Prefecture confirmed that the aircraft were unrelated to drones deployed during Exercise Typhoon, which ran from Oct. 5 to 16.
The exercise included aerial maneuvers designed to train personnel to protect military installations in and around Toulon harbor, involving various aircraft, including drones.
The precise number and models of the unauthorized drones remain unknown. The broadcaster reported that authorities were unable to locate them despite deploying sophisticated electromagnetic jamming systems.
“There were several of them each time, and they were large aircraft,” a source told ICI Provence.
A judicial investigation has been opened under the authority of the Toulon public prosecutor’s office to establish who operated the drones and the motives behind the flights.
Flights over the designated “LF-P 62 Toulon” zone are prohibited by decree to protect sensitive military installations, with exceptions including emergency services, the report said.
The Maritime Prefecture said no sensitive infrastructure was threatened.

Who is Stephen Hubbard, the US citizen released by Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:56:36 UTC
18:56:36 KST

Who is Stephen Hubbard, the US citizen released by Russia?
Oct 21 - President Vladimir Putin announced the release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard from Russian detention on Wednesday, at the start of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff.
Here are details of Hubbard's case:WHO IS STEPHEN HUBBARD?
Hubbard, 74, a retired schoolteacher, grew up in Big Rapids, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force and National Guard, according to military records cited by the New York Times.
He earned a master’s degree in English and lived in Japan for 25 years where he taught English before moving to Cyprus and then, in 2014, to Izyum in eastern Ukraine with a Ukrainian partner, according to his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox.
Fox told Reuters in 2024 that Hubbard subsisted on a pension of about $300 a month and had few connections with local people. The siblings last spoke in September 2021.
HOW WAS HE CAPTURED?
Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 and captured Izyum two months later. Ukrainian forces retook the city in September 2022, but Hubbard was already in Russian custody by then.
Russian state media said Hubbard had been detained in April 2022 and alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Reuters could not independently establish the circumstances of his capture.
Fox said she recognised her brother in a YouTube video showing a man being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. Another video showed him with his hands bound, being struck with a sandal. Reuters could not verify when or where the videos were recorded.
WHY WAS HE IMPRISONED?
Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media said he had pleaded guilty to the charges he faced.
Fox questioned the reported confession, however, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms in his seventies.
Martin De Luca, his US-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. He cited Hubbard as telling him Russian soldiers had simply grabbed him from his house.
WHAT IS HUBBARD'S CURRENT STATUS?
In January 2025, Washington designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, enabling the US government to pursue negotiations for his release.
The State Department has said Russia refused to grant US officials consular access.
The New York Times reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been moved through at least five Russian detention centres before his trial.
His lawyer said Hubbard's legal team found out only in April 2025 that he was being held in a facility in the Mordovia region, east of Moscow. REUTERS

Ukraine wants F-16 repairs at more sites, tells Lockheed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:56:28 UTC
18:56:28 KST

- Ukraine’s defense minister and army chief met Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President Orlando Sanchez Jr. to discuss F-16 support and PAC-3 interceptor supplies.
- Kyiv wants to expand F-16 maintenance to more sites in Ukraine, including through localization, to keep as many jets flying as possible.
Ukraine’s Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi met a Lockheed Martin delegation led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, to press for steady weapons deliveries, more PAC-3 interceptors for Patriot and wider F-16 maintenance across Ukraine, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said.
The talks centered on the F-16, which the ministry described as one of the Ukrainian Air Force’s key tools against Russia’s new jet-powered attack drones, and on Kyiv’s push to service the jets at more locations inside the country, including through local production.
“The F-16 is part of Ukrainian aviation. Ukraine is committed to a long-term partnership with Lockheed Martin. It is important to increase weapons deliveries and do everything we can to ensure that as many F-16s as possible remain in service and operate in Ukrainian skies,” said Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara.
The meeting followed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s own talks with a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19, when he praised the F-16’s record against Shahed drones and said Ukraine is counting on the program continuing. Sources at Lockheed Martin have told The Defence Blog that the company is promoting the idea of a special F-16 version tailored to Ukraine, with longer range, a new AESA radar to spot low-flying drones and cruise missiles faster, and deeper integration of European weapons, although no formal talks on such a variant are underway.
Lockheed Martin systems already make up a large share of Ukraine’s long-range firepower and air defense, from the HIMARS rocket launchers that have struck Russian logistics hubs since 2022 to the F-16 fighters and the PAC-3 interceptors that Patriot batteries fire against Russian ballistic missiles. The F-16 has become the backbone of the Ukrainian Air Force since the first jets arrived in 2024, and the type now flies roughly 80 percent of all Ukrainian Air Force sorties, with one wing alone credited with downing more than 1,000 Russian drones and cruise missiles.
Keeping those aircraft flying is a growing challenge, since Ukraine’s F-16s are older airframes donated by European NATO members and fly near-daily combat missions, which wears down engines and structures far faster than peacetime training. Expanding maintenance to more sites inside Ukraine would cut the time jets spend out of action and reduce the risk of concentrating them at a few bases that Russian missiles and drones could target, while localization would give Ukrainian industry a direct role in sustaining the fleet.
The PAC-3 request reflects Ukraine’s most urgent air defense need, since Patriot is the main system in its inventory able to intercept Russian ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-M and the Kinzhal. Lockheed Martin is ramping up production of PAC-3 MSE interceptors, and Zelenskyy said after his own meeting that Kyiv hopes to buy part of the increased output to protect more cities from ballistic attacks.
The ministry said Ukraine is ready to share its combat experience with Lockheed Martin to make the company’s weapons more effective in modern warfare, and the talks come as Lockheed Martin offers Ukraine its own version of the F-16, a variant that sources at the company told The Defence Blog would bring longer range, a new AESA radar to detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles faster, and deeper integration of European guided bombs and cruise missiles.

Who's a vulture? Spain struggles to identify culprits in fury over evictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:56:23 UTC
18:56:23 KST

Who's a vulture? Spain struggles to identify culprits in fury over evictions
MADRID/LONDON, Oct 21 - As anger boiled over in Spain about the death of Maricarmen Abascal two weeks after the 87-year-old pensioner was evicted from her Madrid home, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had no doubt who was to blame for the mounting housing crisis.
Emergency housing legislation passed after he dissolved parliament and called a snap election for November 29 would "stand up to vulture funds," Sanchez said on October 6, adding that the measures would "target only those who regard housing as just another commodity to be speculated on."
With rents rising 44% and house prices 58% over five years, protesters clamoured for a halt to speculation by so-called "fondos buitre" (vulture funds) that many blame for a raft of evictions such as Abascal's.
But many in Spain are struggling to pin down exactly who these supposed predators are.
In the case of Abascal's eviction, her landlord was not a big name private equity firm but rather a small consultancy called Urbagestión. Owned by two brothers, it has eight staff, a net profit of 2,990 euros ($3,350) last year and two properties to its name, according to the Association of Spanish Registrars.
After buying Abascal's apartment eight years ago, Urbagestión increased her monthly rent to 1,650 euros from 570 euros, more than her monthly pension, according to the tenants' union that represented her. The company took Abascal to court after discovering that her regulated rent contract had expired, court documents show.
“Urbagestión may not have been a ‘fund,’ but it is a ‘vulture SME (Small and Medium-sized Enterprise),’” Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez said.
WIDENING THE NET
Vulture funds first entered the Spanish lexicon after the 2008-2014 financial crisis to describe private equity funds or investment banks that bought rent-controlled flats and jacked up rents.
But companies including investment funds account for just 8% of Spain's rental market, according to the Bank of Spain. The government has now widened the net to include anyone that makes a profit in the market, enmeshing small landlords who make up the majority of Spain's rental market, said Fernando Rodriguez de Acuña, general director of Madrid-based real estate analysis firm Acuña.
"It’s only natural that anyone should make a profit in the market. Otherwise, you wouldn’t get involved in the first place," he said.
The government first attempted to define and regulate vulture funds in a 2023 housing law that limited the activities of "large holders" – people or companies who own 10 or more properties.
In the decrees issued this month, the parameters were tweaked so that those who own five or more properties in areas deemed to have housing shortages must also be included. They are now banned from buying property for less than 70% of its market value.
The legislation goes further by banning owners of more than two properties from evicting tenants until 2030, while all landlords will be subject to automatic contract extensions and rent freezes.
EVICTION SURGE
The increasingly nebulous definition of a vulture fund last week ensnared Montse Minguez, a parliamentary spokesperson in the Socialist party, who stepped down after Spanish website Articulo 14 reported that her husband owned a property company that rented out 30 apartments and had evicted several tenants.
When Antena 3 asked her why Urbagestión was considered predatory and her husband's company was not, she said it was a family company that abided by the law and paid its taxes while vulture funds were "foreign money that buys up entire blocks of flats to drive people out of their neighbourhoods to turn them into holiday lets."
"All we’re saying is that you can’t go for the jugular, nor can you turn to speculation or vulture funds," she said.
Spain has seen a surge in evictions since March when a pandemic-era law to protect vulnerable tenants expired.
Orders for about 70,000 evictions were reinstated after the law was not extended, according to the Tenants Union.
Olga Matute took her own life on September 7 after she was evicted in April. Her case had been pending since 2020 after a bank sold her apartment to a fund which would not accept a reduced rent.
The new measures give protection to nearly 5 million people, including 122,683 at risk of eviction, social groups including the Tenants Union said in a statement.
SMALL INVESTORS UNSETTLED
The decrees "are still a long way from what is needed, but they represent victories in guaranteeing the right to housing,” said Enric Aragonès, a spokesperson for the Catalonia Tenants’ Union.
But the measures will only serve to exacerbate the shortage of rental homes in the long term, said Jorge Galindo, director of Esade Center for Economic Policy (EsadeEcPo). "These are policies that protect those who have a rental at the expense of those who don't yet have one," said Galindo.
The National Federation of Estate Agents' Associations (FAI) said some 600 estate agents had reported the withdrawal of some 2,067 properties for long-term let in the days after the decree. A further 1,523 letting agreements have been put on hold.
Nearly half of Spain's housing rental stock is owned by single-property landlords, while large landlords account for just 3.6% of the market in the hands of individuals, according to EsadeEcPo research.
Foreign private equity has been cutting its exposure to residential real estate in Spain for some time. Blackstone has reduced its portfolio of residential properties in Spain to 12,000 from a peak of 40,000 in 2017.
Funds are investing instead in projects such as student housing and shared, short-term rents often inclusive of amenities like gym membership known as flexible living, which are not governed by the same regulations.
More than 40% of the nearly 24,000 Spanish homes bought by investment firms over the past 12 months were student flats, according to MSCI data company.
CPP and Greystar, two of the top four cross-border investors in Spanish homes over the past two years, said their investments were entirely or mostly in student housing and flexible living.
"The fact is that the market isn’t controlled by large funds; it’s in the hands of small investors. So now it’s all the small investors who have to bear the entire burden," Rodriguez de Acuña said. ($1 = 0.8923 euros) REUTERS

2026-10-21

18:55:22 KST

Ukraine's national postal operator, JSC Ukrposhta, is launching the Ukrposhta Market marketplace in partnership with Kasta, offering access to more than 10 million products and free delivery to post offices throughout Ukraine.
"This is not just another marketplace, but a unique one with a specific positioning: to give people in every corner of Ukraine the opportunity to get everything they need, even when air raid sirens are sounding and nearby stores are not operating," Ukrposhta CEO Igor Smelyansky explained in a Telegram post on Wednesday.
According to him, to use Ukrposhta Market, customers need to download or update the Ukrposhta 2.0 app.
Smelyansky also said that the marketplace is not subsidized by the state and is a market-driven project.
The head of the national postal operator added that the service is aimed, in particular, at users who want to purchase essential goods without waiting until their order has accumulated enough items to qualify for free delivery.
"However, research shows that Generation Z, in particular, expects instant gratification. They do not want to wait until their shopping cart is full to receive free delivery. With this service, there is no need to wait," Smelyansky's statement said.
JSC Ukrposhta is Ukraine's national postal operator.
As reported, Ukrposhta increased its revenue by 4.2% in the first half of this year, to UAH 6 billion 776 million, and posted a net profit of UAH 92 million, compared with a net loss of UAH 312 million in the first half of last year.
The national postal operator has 7,200 customer service locations, including 2,000 mobile post offices serving 21,300 settlements. The average number of employees at the national postal operator in the second quarter of 2026 was 25,800, while the average salary was UAH 20,300.

While it used to be standard for state schools in England to have one-week half terms, some pupils and staff are being given a fortnight off.

Spain's Sanchez gives Milei ironic welcome as Argentine leader calls him 'unpresentable dictator'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:53:36 UTC
18:53:36 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez gave Argentine President Javier Milei an ironic welcome to Madrid on Wednesday, proudly embracing the term "leftie" that Milei frequently uses to insult his political opponents.
"Hello, Milei. The lefties welcome you to Spain, the fastest-growing country in Europe," read a large banner displayed outside the headquarters of Sanchez's Socialist Party in Madrid.
Sanchez also posted a video on US social media platform X responding to Milei's repeated use of the Spanish word "zurdo," or "leftie," as a derogatory term.
"There are those who think they insult us by calling us lefties," he added.
Sanchez added that if raising pensions, increasing the minimum wage yearly, giving parents more time with their children, defending abortion rights and opposing war made someone a leftie, he was proud to be one.
"So yes, I'm a leftie, and proud of it," he concluded.
Milei's visit comes amid longstanding tensions with Sanchez, whom the Argentine president has repeatedly criticized during trips to Spain.
Since taking office in December 2023, Milei has made several visits to Spain without holding official meetings with Sanchez, an unusual pattern that has contributed to diplomatic friction between the two governments.
The latest trip, his seventh to Spain since becoming president, comes ahead of the country's Nov. 29 general election.
The Argentine government has described the visit as part of the election campaign, with Milei seeking to support Spain's right-wing political parties.
However, Milei is not expected to meet far-right Vox leader Santiago Abascal, who is campaigning elsewhere in Spain. Instead, he is scheduled to meet the Vox secretary-general and the director of the party-linked Disenso Foundation.
A possible meeting with Madrid regional President Isabel Diaz Ayuso of the Popular Party, who he called a "friend" on Wednesday, has yet to be confirmed.
During the visit, Milei also renewed his criticism of Sanchez, calling the Spanish premier an "unpresentable dictator" during a business forum in Madrid on Wednesday.
“When I come to Spain, I'm not going to meet a criminal and a thief like Pedro Sanchez, because I'm not willing to have to sew my pockets shut to avoid being robbed," he added.
Speaking to reporters before the event, Milei also dismissed his critics as "stupid, incompetent, impoverishing lefties."

Zurich Airport reorganises management after rocky start in India

Unknown Publisher

18:53:00 KST

Zurich Airport reorganises management after rocky start in India
Zurich Airport is carrying out a partial reshuffle of its senior management. Chief Operating Officer Stefan Tschudin is leaving the company in mid-2027. Chief Commercial Officer Stefan Gross is moving to India, where he will take on a leading role at the new Noida Airport.
At the same time, the organisation at Zurich Airport is being restructured. The changes are due to be implemented in the course of 2027, as the airport operator announced on Wednesday.
Tschudin has worked for the airport since 2007 and has been a member of the executive board since 2017. It was stated that he is leaving the company by mutual agreement in light of new strategic priorities.
A rocky start in India
Gross, who has been in charge of the retail, catering and other services business at Zurich Airport since 2016, will become Chairman of the Board of Directors at Noida Airport near the Indian capital, New Delhi. This move underlines the Group’s commitment to its business with its Indian subsidiary.
The new airport there began operations in June. However, business is getting off to a slower start than originally expected. Zurich Airport still expects Noida to post an operating loss this year. The break-even point is expected to be reached in 2027. In the longer term, the group aims to significantly expand its international business.
Merger of divisions
At Zurich Airport itself, Lydia Naef, previously head of real estate, is taking on the role of new commercial director, assuming responsibility for all business outside of actual flight operations. This includes, amongst other things, the letting and management of property, retail outlets, restaurants and other services for passengers and visitors.
More
Construction of Zurich Airport began 80 years ago
In addition, the existing property division is being reorganised. A new department will in future be responsible for construction projects as well as the operation and maintenance of the buildings. This move is driven by the extensive construction and refurbishment work scheduled to take place at the airport in the coming years.
The search for new members of the Executive Board to head up flight operations and the new construction division will begin in the coming weeks, according to the press release. The number of members on the Group Executive Board is to remain unchanged.
Zurich Airport has recently benefited from a strong appetite for travel and achieved a record profit in the first half of 2026. However, the high costs associated with the new Noida Airport in India are weighing on the results, which is why the group expects a decline in profits for the year as a whole.

Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:52:11 UTC
18:52:11 KST

Andy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is, where does it come from?”
It was a nod towards several awkward energy facts. First, oil and gas provided 75% of the UK’s energy in 2025, government data shows. Second, even with the rollout of domestic renewables for generating electricity, about 43% of overall energy was imported last year.
Third, all credible paths to net zero emissions by 2050 involve using a lot of oil and gas on the way because we’re still in the foothills of electrification. Fewer than 2% of UK households have heat pumps, according to the lobby group Electrify Britain.
While sales of EVs are accelerating, nearly 95% of vehicles on the road run on petrol and diesel. Meanwhile, hydrogen and biomethane have barely taken off as alternatives to gas for those industrial processes that require higher temperatures than electricity can achieve – tricky for a government pursuing “reindustrialisation”.
Fourth – and this one must alarm Downing Street – the global energy market has simply become less reliable. The strait of Hormuz can close overnight. The US president can threaten to ban diesel exports. Russian ships prowl the North Sea. Even the nice Norwegians, with an eye on their own energy consumers, scrapped a planned electricity cable to Scotland in 2023.
It is no longer a world of always-available “just in time” supply. Thinking has shifted to “just in case” scenario-planning. And a truly scary scenario would be disruption to the 725-mile Langeled pipeline that is the primary route for gas supplies from Norway, 40% of the UK’s consumption last year. The pipeline is a security vulnerability if ever there was one (if you doubt it, watch Sky News’ recent report).
Now we have the start of an answer to Burnham’s “where should it come from?” question. The Jackdaw gasfield, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, has finally been approved to produce in time for winter. About time, too.
All the arguments from pragmatism were in the field’s favour. As this column has said in the past, less North Sea gas would inevitably mean more imported liquefied natural gas, with the extra carbon emissions created by chilling the fuel to -160C for shipment and then “regasifying” it at the other end.
Such cargos were 20% of UK gas imports last year, mostly from the US. It already feels absurd that the 24m UK households with a gas boiler burn any gas at all from the shale fields of Texas and Pennsylvania. Why increase the exposure if lower-polluting supplies are available off Aberdeen?
More UK North Sea gas production won’t lower the price for consumers much, if at all. But that was never the argument. It was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security that comes with having domestic volumes piped straight into the national gas network.
Jackdaw is not a gamechanger – it will be 6% of UK North Sea gas production at peak – but it’s definitely worth having while the UK is still using gas, which will be at least as long as the field’s 11-year life. The next question is whether other “tie-back” gasfields in already-explored areas, such as Tornado, west of the Shetlands, will follow. The line in the government’s announcement about “asking the regulator to consider urgent cases that could benefit from similar measures now” suggests so.
Rosebank, also near the Shetlands, is a trickier political proposition because it’s mostly oil, which is more polluting, and will be producing for longer. But the arguments aren’t wholly different. The common elements are still jobs, investment, taxes and the government’s ability to impose higher environmental standards during the production stage.
Meanwhile, the “it’s all exported” objection to Rosebank misses the fact that the UK oil industry operates within a European network. If the UK had more than four refineries (compared with nine at the turn of the century), a chunk of Rosebank’s output might be processed at home. As it is, some – perhaps the majority – will come back to the UK as petrol, diesel and jet fuel once it’s been refined in Rotterdam or elsewhere in north-west Europe.
Take a step back and the North Sea debate is really about how much oil and gas it is sensible for the UK to produce itself on the way to net zero. On the current trajectory, only about a third of consumption will come from domestic sources on a net basis. Even offshore lobbyists reckon a boost to North Sea production would only get the ratio up to about a half, albeit the figure would obviously increase if consumption of fossil fuels can be made to fall faster. Nobody is talking about the UK becoming a net exporter again.
Commitment to net zero by 2050 was intact, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted. We wait to see what the new “energy wealth fund”, which will reinvest oil and gas revenues into renewable and low-carbon projects, means in practice. But the financial logic is sound: recycle the receipts from the old system to quicken the transition. Electrification, enabling consumers to make use of lower-carbon energy, is still the main story.
The bizarreness in the government’s previous approach was that, even as it proclaimed the virtues of “clean homegrown energy” such as wind, solar and nuclear, it pursued an approach that maximised imports when it came to oil and gas. Many, including the general secretary of the GMB union, Gary Smith, pointed out the flaw: it was hard for the UK to claim real climate leadership if it was simply off-shoring emissions.
In a small way, Jackdaw addresses the UK’s extreme reliance on imports. It is a step towards a joined-up commonsense approach to energy security. The real transition test remains the pace at which the UK stops using fossil fuels.

Foreign Minister Tsahkna in call with Ukrainian Foreign Minister: Estonia is stepping up practical support for Ukraine ahead of a difficult winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:51:12 UTC
18:51:12 KST

Foreign Minister Tsahkna stressed that a just and lasting peace must be based on respect for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, and that no decisions concerning Ukraine’s or Europe’s security can be made without Ukraine and Europe being involved.
“Ukraine’s security is a matter of European security. We must not find ourselves in a situation where decisions are made behind our backs or where Russia gets at the negotiating table what it failed to achieve on the battlefield. Peace must be just and lasting, and must include credible and effective security guarantees for Ukraine,” Tsahkna said.
According to Tsahkna, the first step towards peace must be an end to Russia’s deliberate attacks. “Ukraine has repeatedly demonstrated its readiness for a ceasefire and agreed to halt deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure on the condition that Russia does the same. Putin, however, has chosen the opposite course and intensified the attacks further,” he noted.
“In recent weeks, drone and missile attacks, along with power cuts affecting hundreds of thousands of people, have become part of everyday life in Ukraine. The number of civilian casualties rose by 85% in September, and more than 2,000 energy infrastructure facilities have been attacked since July. The conditions for serious peace negotiations will not exist until Russia changes its behaviour,” Tsahkna said.
The Foreign Minister added that, as Russia continues to attack Ukraine’s civilian and energy infrastructure and winter approaches, Ukraine must receive even more extensive practical assistance. “Last week, we confirmed a plan to provide Ukraine with €10 million through NATO’s PURL initiative, bringing our total contribution to €30 million. As Russia has targeted critical infrastructure, including the transport network, and has already destroyed or damaged 340 railway carriages this year, we are working to send a substantial number of locomotives to Ukraine. This will help keep the country’s transport links operational even under the most difficult conditions,” Tsahkna said.
Discussing the Ukraine Recovery Conference to be held in Tallinn in January, both ministers confirmed that preparations were progressing in close cooperation. “Our aim is to mobilise the broadest possible international support for Ukraine and achieve as many substantive, practical outcomes as possible at the conference to help rebuild Ukraine and strengthen its resilience,” Tsahkna said.

Ukraine-proven Senator joins Canada’s capital police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:50:12 UTC
18:50:12 KST

- The Ottawa Police Service tactical unit has a new Roshel Senator armored vehicle fitted with Patriot3’s LIBERATOR elevated assault ramp.
- The ramp reaches full height in under 10 seconds and can be removed from the vehicle in 10 to 15 minutes.
The Ottawa Police Service’s tactical unit has added a Roshel Senator armored vehicle fitted with a hydraulic assault ramp that can lift officers to second-floor windows and rooftops in seconds, giving Canada’s capital the same Canadian-built armored vehicle that Ukraine has used in large numbers on the battlefield. U.S. manufacturer Patriot3 announced that its LIBERATOR Elevated Tactics System had been installed on the unit’s new Senator, a version Roshel calls the Senator ERV.
The LIBERATOR is a single-ramp system mounted on top of the vehicle that rises to its maximum height in under 10 seconds, according to Patriot3, so that tactical officers can make an elevated entry into a building, intervene during a barricade situation or rescue people from upper floors without exposing themselves on ladders. The company says the wide ramp leaves the vehicle’s roof hatch or turret accessible, and that the whole system can be removed in 10 to 15 minutes, which lets the police use the Senator in its standard configuration when the ramp is not needed.
Roshel founder and CEO Roman Shimonov said the company was proud to support the Ottawa Police Service in protecting the national capital and stressed that the vehicle is made at home.
“Built in Canada, by Canadians, for those who protect Canadians,” said Roman Shimonov, CEO and founder of Roshel.
Roshel builds the Senator in Ontario on a Ford F-550 heavy-duty chassis and offers it in configurations ranging from police and security vehicles to military armored personnel carriers. The Senator became widely known after Canada began sending it to Ukraine as military aid in 2022, and Roshel delivered its 1,000th Senator to the Ukrainian armed forces at the end of 2023. Ukraine has since received more than 2,200 of the vehicles, and earlier this year Mexico chose the Senator after trials by its armed forces and National Guard.
Patriot3, based in Fredericksburg, Virginia, has supplied its LIBERATOR systems to police tactical teams in the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia, including SWAT units in San Francisco and Glendale, Arizona, the Police Service of Northern Ireland and New South Wales Police, where the ramp is typically mounted on Lenco BearCat armored vehicles. The Ottawa installation pairs it with a Canadian-made vehicle instead, giving the city’s tactical unit an armored platform that can both carry a team into a high-risk area and put officers directly at a building’s upper windows.
Elevated entry systems let tactical teams reach second-floor windows, balconies and rooftops while staying behind armor for most of the approach, an option police forces have used in barricaded-suspect and hostage situations where ground-floor doors are covered by an armed suspect.

American Stephen Hubbard released by Russia, Trump confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:46:37 UTC
18:46:37 KST

U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard released by Russia after 4 years in jail, and Trump says "no 'swap'"
Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen who was jailed in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine, has been released from custody, President Trump confirmed Wednesday. The release was announced during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
President Trump said in social media posts that Putin agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said the American would not have been released had the White House not stopped new sanctions against Russia from taking effect last week.
The news came as Trump administration officials, including Witkoff, were in St. Petersburg for talks with Putin and other senior Russian officials focused on the Ukraine war.
Video of the meeting showed Witkoff thanking Putin for freeing the American — whom the U.S. government had declared wrongfully detained — and offering the Russian autocrat, who ordered the ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine almost five years ago, effusive praise, including calling him "a humanitarian."
"I wanted to thank you very much. The president sends his thanks. Our whole nation sends it's thanks," Witkoff said. "Because of you, he's going home to his family."
"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian, you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," Witkoff told Putin.
Russian state news agencies, citing Putin, said Hubbard was at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport.
Hubbard, a 74-year-old Michigan native, was the last American in Russia whom the State Department had formally declared wrongfully detained. As many as 10 other Americans, including dual nationals, remain in Russian custody.
Hubbard, who is in poor health, was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment at a military hospital.
In a statement posted on his Truth Social platform early Wednesday, Mr. Trump said Hubbard "was just released from prison, at the request of President Donald J. Trump, made directly to President Vladimir Putin in a telephone conversation last week."
Mr. Trump said in his post that Russia released Hubbard "out of respect for President Trump," and the U.S. "was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."
The American's release came five days after Mr. Trump announced that his administration would waive some sanctions on Russia just before they were due to take effect. That decision by the president was praised by Putin but criticized harshly by members of Congress, including some Republicans.
In a subsequent post on Truth, Mr. Trump did link Hubbard's release to the easing of U.S. sanctions on Russia, claiming "numerous people" who had called for the sanctions to take effect as previously planned had "called to apologize to President Trump in that they didn't know that he was negotiating the release of Stephen Hubbard, a truly big and important deal for the U.S. If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt."
A retired school teacher who served in the U.S. National Guard and Air Force, Hubbard was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022. Russian authorities accused him of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was sentenced in 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony.
Hubbard's family had little contact with him while he was detained, and they have maintained his innocence.
Hubbard's release follows the return of American Robert Gilman, who was freed from Russian custody in August after his health deteriorated to a life-threatening condition. A former Marine who spent more than four years imprisoned in Russia, Gilman was granted a humanitarian pardon following a direct appeal by Mr. Trump to Putin.
Early last year, Russia released American school teacher Marc Fogel, and in 2024 journalist Evan Gershkovich and Marine veteran Paul Whelan were among those released from Russian custody in a complicated multi-country prisoner swap.
The State Department maintains a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" advisory for Russia, warning U.S. nationals against all travel to the country due to the risk of wrongful detention, arbitrary enforcement of local laws and limited U.S. consular assistance.
The Trump administration last year established a new designation for countries that are deemed "state sponsors of wrongful detention," CBS News previously reported. The measure gives the State Department expanded authority to impose sanctions, export controls and travel restrictions on countries that use detained Americans as political leverage.
Despite its lengthy history of imprisoning Americans on questionable charges, Russia has not faced the designation, which was applied to Iran in February and Afghanistan in March.
Some Americans jailed in Russia have not been declared wrongfully detained by the U.S. government, including Aleksandr Antonov, who was arrested in Russia last year and sentenced to six years in prison.
His family argues that he was detained because he is a U.S. citizen, and they have urged the State Department to prioritize his case. CBS News reported earlier this year on an internal debate within the department over whether to designate him as wrongfully detained.

Libya's approval of maritime deal with Turkey rejected by Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:44:07 UTC
18:44:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Libya's approval of maritime deal with Turkey is rejected by Greece
Libya's parliament unanimously approved a contested maritime agreement with Turkey on Tuesday, reversing years of opposition and reviving a dispute with Egypt, Greece and Cyprus over rights in the eastern Mediterranean.
The House of Representatives, the eastern-based parliament aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar, voted to adopt the memorandum of understanding signed in 2019 by Turkey and Libya's then-government in Tripoli, the Government National Accord.
Greece's Foreign Ministry rejected the vote, saying in a statement that it "does not alter the illegal, invalid and groundless nature of the memorandum."
The ministry said Turkey and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coasts that could provide a legal basis for delimiting maritime zones. It said the agreement disregards the rights of Greek islands, which lie between the Turkish and Libyan coasts.
"Geography and the international Law of the Sea cannot be changed by unilateral, legally unfounded parliamentary decisions," the ministry said. It added that Greece had informed its partners and allies and "will take all appropriate measures to safeguard its sovereign rights."
Cyprus also condemned the vote, calling the memorandum "illegal, null, and void".
The Libyan-Turkey agreement defines maritime jurisdiction areas between the two countries in the Mediterranean, where major natural gas discoveries in recent years have fueled competing claims to offshore waters.
Lawmakers also repealed two resolutions passed in 2020, parliamentary spokesman Abdullah Bliheg said. One rejected agreements with Turkey, while the other cut political ties with Ankara. Parliament had opposed the accords at a time when Turkey was backing the Tripoli government against Haftar’s forces.
Officials in both camps welcomed Tuesday's vote. Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son, said in a statement that the decisions reflected "a move toward overcoming disputes of the past." He called the maritime agreement a tool to protect Libya’s economic interests in the Mediterranean and described Turkey as "a significant regional power."
The Foreign Ministry of the Tripoli-based government, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, called the vote "a positive development" for relations with Turkey. It said cooperation would proceed "in accordance with the relevant rules and principles of international law."
Dbeibah also met Tuesday in Tripoli with Turkey’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin. A government statement said they discussed security, regional developments, and migration.
The European Union has said the agreement violates the rights of third countries. Turkey is not a party to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Egypt, a longtime backer of Haftar and Libya's eastern parliament, also rejected the accord. In August 2020, Cairo and Athens signed their own maritime agreement in response. Greek officials have said it effectively nullifies the Turkish-Libyan deal.
Tuesday's vote means Egypt's main allies in Libya now endorse an agreement Cairo has opposed. Egypt's Foreign Minister, Badr Abdelatty, said he discussed the situation in Libya and the eastern Mediterranean in a phone call with his Greek counterpart on Tuesday, without directly mentionning the vote.
The vote follows a rapprochement in recent years between Turkey and eastern Libya.
Libya plunged into chaos after a NATO-backed uprising toppled and killed longtime ruler Moammar Gadhafi in 2011. The oil-rich country later split between rival governments in the east and west.
Dbeibah heads the internationally recognised government in Tripoli, in the west, while Prime Minister Ossama Hammad leads the eastern administration. Haftar, who commands the Libyan National Army, also holds power in the east.
The North African country is also a major transit point for migrants from Africa and the Middle East fleeing war and economic hardship and attempting dangerous sea crossings to Europe.

Revived Eilat-Ashkelon pipeline could introduce new dynamics in the politics of the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:43:51 UTC
18:43:51 KST

Israel has proposed reviving the Ashkelon-Eilat pipeline to divert oil cargo away from the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb in the Red Sea. The war between Saudi Arabia and the Ansar Allah Houthis continues to disrupt oil exports, particularly for Saudi Arabia, at the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Saudi Arabia has been using its Yanbu port, which has a long pipeline exporting its own oil. The plan proposes a new pipeline from Saudi Arabia that will join its Ashkelon-Eilat pipeline in the Red Sea via Jordan.
According to reports in Haaretz and other outlets, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu offered Israeli military assistance to help Saudi Arabia fight the Iran-backed Houthis, viewing it as a potential pathway toward normalisation. Fearing a backlash, Mohammed Bin Salman rejected the offer.
Israel is desperate to normalise relations with Saudi Arabia. Any formal partnership between Saudi Arabia and Israel could be seen as an act of capitulation by Bin Salman and an achievement for Israel, particularly for Benjamin Netanyahu. Notwithstanding Bin Salman’s rejection of Israeli advances, Netanyahu continues to court Saudi attention. Israel has pitched to the US and the Gulf nations the idea of using the Eilat-Ashkelon pipeline as a land bridge for Gulf oil exports. Netanyahu and his Energy Minister, Eli Cohen, are championing the plan to revive an old oil pipeline that runs from the port city of Eilat to Ashkelon.
The Eilat-Ashkelon pipeline was originally built in 1968 as a secret joint venture between Israel and Iran under the Shah. Following the 1979 Islamic Revolution, the two nations became bitter adversaries, and Iran canceled the project.
If this project succeeds, it could be a new lifeline and an alternative route for exporting oil from the region.
These plans come as Al Ansar Houthis continue to target strategic facilities in Saudi Arabia, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, which is fed by the Petroline pipeline. The Petroline pipeline is 1200 kilometers long, running from Abqaiq in eastern Saudi Arabia to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. Its maximum transport capacity is 7 million barrels of oil per day. The plan is to build a new inland pipeline from Saudi Arabia through Jordan to connect to existing infrastructure in Israel, enabling oil exports from the port of Ashkelon, a few kilometers north of Gaza, and reducing Gulf countries’ reliance on the Strait of Hormuz.
OPINION: Türkiye’s message to the Middle East: Security requires peace
The latest escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Al Ansar Houthis began when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa Airport, preventing a delegation of the Al Ansar Houthis returning from the funeral of Ayatollah Khamenei from landing in Sanaa. This was a miscalculation by Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and de facto leader, Mohammed bin Salman. Before the bombing, there was a truce between the Al Ansar Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis started in 2015, when Saudi Arabia lobbied the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to wage war against the Houthis to support the President of Yemen, Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi, the internationally recognized president of Yemen. In 2022, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis entered into a truce that saw attacks reduced from both parties. Large-scale attacks have decreased significantly since 2022; however, the two parties have never agreed to a permanent ceasefire.
The US, Pakistan, and other Saudi allies have been calculative in their efforts to assist Saudi Arabia. Islamabad maintains that its support is strictly defensive and limited to protecting Saudi territory. It has deployed several military personnel and assets to Saudi Arabia under the activated Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. According to CNN, the U.S. is helping Saudi Arabia against the Houthis by deploying 100 to 200 military advisers to provide intelligence and targeting support, supplying billions in weapons and missile defence systems (such as Patriot and THAAD batteries), and issuing regional security warnings. The Egyptian House of Representatives has delayed the vote authorizing the armed forces to assist Saudi Arabia until 26th October 2026. Reuters reports that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also asked Syrian President Ahmad Al Sharaa for assistance against Iran-backed Houthi rebels during an October 2026 meeting in Riyadh.
Israel is the only country that is open to offering blanket assistance that traditional allies of Saudi Arabia, including the US, have been reluctant to offer. Saudi Arabia, especially Bin Salman, is tempted. However, accepting offers from Israel could legitimise Israel, and entering into any sort of deal could draw condemnation, lead to the isolation of Saudi Arabia, and be the end of Saudi Arabia’s leadership of the Muslim world.
Importantly, it could provide Israel with resources and possible new leverage against the Gulf countries.
Significantly, as US funding of Israel increasingly comes under pressure, the proposed pipeline project could become an alternative financial source of funding for Israel. However, as existential pressures on Saudi Arabia and on Mohammad bin Salman personally increase, all cards are on the table.

Italy’s births set to sink to a record low in 2026
ROME - Italy is set to suffer a further drop in the number of births in 2026 to a historic low, aggravating the country’s demographic crisis, national statistics bureau ISTAT said on Oct 21.
Italy in 2025 recorded just 355,772 births, the lowest figure since Italian unification in 1861, and the 17th consecutive year in which the figure declined.
In the first seven months of 2026 the negative trend continued, with just under 197,000 newborns, down 1.1% from the same period of 2025, ISTAT said in a statement.
The fertility rate, measuring the average number of children born to each woman of child-bearing age, edged down in January-July to 1.13, from 2025’s record low of 1.14.
Italy’s long-declining birth rate is considered a national emergency.
Despite Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her predecessors’ pledges to confront the issue, no one has been able to halt the drop.
ISTAT reported that in 2025 the average age of women when they had their first child was 32, broadly in line with the year before.
In 2025, 44.1% of children were born to unmarried parents, up from 43.2% the year before.
The most common first names given to Italian children born last year were Sofia for girls and Leonardo for boys. REUTERS

Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard
Published October 21, 2026last updated October 21, 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.

Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard
Published October 21, 2026last updated October 21, 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.
Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024.
Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family."
US President Donald Trump later said he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week.
"The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."
However, in a follow-up post, Trump also claimed that "numerous people" had called him to apologize after they criticized him for suspending a new round of sanctions, which he said was a necessary concession.
"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump's post said.
Russia agrees to trilateral talks with Ukraine, US
The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administration as the two sides discuss a deal for peace between Russia and Ukraine.
"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin.
After the talks, the Kremlin said Witkoff's proposals "lacked substance" and would not be of real use for a potential peace settlement.
However, Putin agreed "in principle" to resume peace talks with Russian, Ukrainian and US delegates after November 10.
Such talks should focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends," Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said.
Putin also proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow.
Meanwhile, Putin appeared open to a potential trilateral meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.
"A possible first-ever meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the United States... is being prepared," Ushakov said.
The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin — came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway.
European leaders hope for productive negotiations
Zelenskyy on Wednesday called for freezing the front line as a first step toward ceasefire talks.
"Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire... freeze and stop," Zelenskyy said in an interview with "Fox & Friends."
The European Union, which was represented by delegates from several member states at the Oslo talks on Tuesday, said it expected to be debriefed by Washington after Wednesday's talks.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also said on Wednesday that Berlin was supporting Ukraine to end the war as quickly as possible, adding that any capitulation by Ukraine would be "a capitulation by all of us."
Witkoff to return to Oslo
The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations after his trip to St. Petersburg.
"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he told Norway's public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.

British Army’s next tank reaches seven test prototypes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:41:19 UTC
18:41:19 KST

- Britain has received seven Challenger 3 prototype tanks for demonstration trials, with an eighth in the final stages of build.
- The 148-tank program targets initial operating capability in 2027 and full operating capability by 2030.
Britain has now received seven Challenger 3 prototype tanks for trials, with an eighth in the final stages of build, as the British Army works to prove the design of its next main battle tank before full production begins, UK Defence Journal reported.
Defence minister Luke Pollard gave the figures in a written answer in Parliament to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who had asked how many Challenger 3 tanks have been delivered so far.
“Seven Challenger 3 prototype vehicles have been delivered to date for use in the Demonstration Phase trials programme, with an eighth prototype vehicle in the final stages of build. These vehicles are being used to demonstrate and assure the performance and safety of the Challenger 3 capability in preparation for manufacture,” said Luke Pollard, the UK Minister of State for Defence.
The eight prototypes are meant to run firing, mobility, electromagnetic and safety trials in parallel during the demonstration phase, when the design has to prove itself before the Ministry of Defence commits to building the rest of the fleet. Trials have been taking place at Bovington and with the Armoured Trials and Development Unit, and a Challenger 3 fired its main gun for the first time in 2024, the same year Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land rolled out the first prototype at its plant in Telford.
The Challenger 3 keeps the hull of the existing Challenger 2 but adds a completely new turret, a 120 mm smoothbore L55A1 gun that fires standard NATO tank ammunition, modular armor, an active protection system to defeat incoming missiles and rockets, and a new sighting and fire control system. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land is converting 148 tanks under the program, which will equip two armored regiments in the British Army’s 3rd (UK) Division.
The switch from a rifled gun to a smoothbore gun ends decades of British practice and was driven largely by ammunition supply. The Challenger 2’s rifled 120 mm gun fires rounds that no other NATO army uses, and the industrial base that produced them had shrunk to almost nothing, so moving to the same ammunition as allies such as Germany and the United States lets British tank crews draw on shared stockpiles in a long war.
The Ministry of Defence has tied the start of series production to the results of the trials rather than to a fixed date, with Pollard telling Parliament last year that manufacturing would begin once the tank’s performance has been validated, we reported in December. The British Army is still planning for an initial operating capability in 2027 and full operating capability by 2030, which leaves Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land about three years to convert the remaining 140 tanks once the design is cleared.
The 148-tank fleet will be considerably smaller than the force Britain fielded at the turn of the century, when the British Army operated nearly 400 Challenger 2 tanks, and the conversion program covers fewer than half that number, with the eighth prototype the last vehicle needed before the trials program can run at full strength.

IMC is an integrated group of companies operating in the Sumy, Poltava and Chernihiv regions of northern and central Ukraine, with activities in crop production, grain elevators and storage facilities.
