Ebola outbreak spreads to Nigeria as Kenya reports ninth case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:29:49 UTC
17:29:49 KST

Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in the latest outbreak, while Kenya reported its ninth infection, raising concerns about the spread of the deadly disease across Africa.
Nigeria’s case involves a woman who travelled from Uganda to the capital, Abuja, and was diagnosed after receiving treatment at a private hospital for several days, Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said on Tuesday. She is in isolation and receiving medical care, while authorities have identified 44 close contacts for monitoring.
Kenya’s latest case is a 24-year-old man who tested positive while in quarantine after developing symptoms. He is a close relative of the first confirmed patient, who died in Nairobi on October 5, the Health Ministry said.
Kenya has recorded nine cases, including one death. Authorities said all infections remain within a single cluster, with no evidence of transmission beyond it. They have traced and quarantined 134 of 135 identified contacts and said eight surviving patients were responding positively to treatment.
The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, now affects four countries — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria — and has so far infected about 9,400 people and killing at least 4,500, according to figures cited in reports.
‘Most geographically widespread outbreak’
Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), warned that the outbreak had become the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history, affecting multiple countries across three African regions.
“With mortality approaching 50% in DRC, we face an extremely serious threat,” Kaseya said on X, urging the international community to provide funding, medical supplies and health workers.
There is no approved vaccine or drug for the current strain, and the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that the outbreak continues to outpace efforts to track and contain it.
The first clinical trial of a potential vaccine is expected to begin by the end of October, according to WHO.
Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will undergo a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
Two vaccines specifically for Bundibugyo are also being developed, one by the University of Oxford and another by the US-based Moderna group. They are currently in the early stages of testing in smaller-scale clinical trials.
Capobianco, director of global health security at Gavi, told RFI they have the potential to save lives in this and future Ebola outbreaks.
Psychological toll on communities
Beyond the immediate health risks, the outbreak is worsening the hardships faced by communities in eastern DRC, where conflict, crisis and severe malnutrition have already left many people vulnerable.
Mirella Riccardi, a mental health specialist with Doctors Without Borders, said Ebola had compounded the psychological distress of people living in areas already devastated by conflict and deprivation.
A Congolese teacher whose family experienced suspected Ebola symptoms recalled feeling abandoned as neighbours kept their distance until responders took sick relatives to a clinic and disinfected their home.
“It felt as though we were living all alone because of the illness,” she said. “It has caused severe trauma within our family.”
The psychological effects of Ebola outbreaks can persist long after the immediate crisis, according to the WHO, with survivors and affected families experiencing anxiety and mood disorders.

Europe's growing rebellion against the ICC could change the game for Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:26:12 UTC
17:26:12 KST

On October 9, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sweeping, full-blocking financial sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC). It was an unprecedented escalation in the clash between sovereign states and international institutions, and a direct challenge to the Hague-based tribunal.
The decision came amid a turbulent October. Demonstrations and riots were intensifying in major cities, instability was widespread, and conventional diplomacy was under strain. The sanctions risk dismantling the postwar architecture of international justice.
Washington calls the sanctions a defense of national sovereignty against what it sees as the Court’s political overreach. The dispute, however, goes back years. The US has long objected to ICC investigations involving American personnel and the actions of close allies, particularly Israel. Now the breach between Washington and the Court has widened, giving fresh momentum to critics in Europe.
Their objections go beyond US policy. They question the neutrality, selectivity, and professionalism of the Court’s personnel. Critics argue that an institution founded to judge the gravest international crimes has become a vehicle for political agendas. Much of their attention has centered on Luis Moreno Ocampo, the ICC’s first prosecutor, who served from 2003 to 2012.
Ocampo’s activities since leaving office have fueled allegations of commercialization and political activism. Between 2023 and 2026, he became a vocal critic of Israeli military operations in Gaza, describing them as a "risk of genocide" and suggesting that arms supplies from allied states could constitute complicity.
Ocampo maintains his independence. His critics say that such statements, coming from a former head of ICC prosecution, objectively intensify political pressure on Israel and undermine the perceived neutrality of the Court’s former leadership.
In April 2026, Newsweek România reported on recordings purportedly featuring Ocampo and his son discussing private funding, ways to influence the European Parliament, and efforts to pressure European Commission leaders over EU policy toward Azerbaijan and Armenia.
Whatever the eventual legal assessment, critics see a former chief prosecutor using his reputation and connections in ways incompatible with the independence expected of international justice.
The concerns are not new. In 2017, a joint investigation by major European news organizations revealed Ocampo’s use of offshore structures and a multimillion-dollar consulting contract with a Libyan businessman linked to the Gaddafi regime. To those who regard the ICC as an instrument of geopolitical interests, a former chief prosecutor becoming what they call a "legal gun for hire" is not an isolated professional lapse.
Signs of systemic institutional degradation
It is a sign of systemic institutional degradation. Calls for a full review of former ICC prosecutors’ financial and lobbying activities have become central to the debate.
The Court has also faced questions about its own leadership. In May 2024, allegations of sexual misconduct involving a female ICC staff member were referred to the Court. The initial process ended when the complainant declined to participate, but a second referral followed in October.
The United Nations Office of Internal Oversight Services investigated the matter from November 2024 to December 2025 and reviewed thousands of pages of evidence and testimony. The allegations concerned the Court’s then-chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. On July 24, 2026, the Assembly of States Parties removed him from office after finding serious misconduct and a serious breach of duty. Khan denies the allegations.
This criticism now has a prominent voice in the European Parliament. Harald Vilimsky, head of the Austrian Freedom Party (FPÖ) delegation and vice chair of the Patriots for Europe group, wants the EU to follow Washington’s lead. After the U.S. sanctions announcement, his party called for a "decisive shift in thinking" and urged the EU to impose sanctions on the ICC.
Vilimsky points to the Court’s actions against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, beginning with a 2024 arrest warrant request, as evidence of what he sees as political motivation.
"International institutions have clearly defined tasks to fulfill and must not elevate themselves to the status of political actors who disregard the sovereignty of states and interfere in their affairs," he said in his October 12 German-language statement. In his view, the ICC increasingly acts as a "self-appointed moral and political authority," making unconditional European support untenable.
Vilimsky has influence in certain political circles, but the EU remains divided. Senior EU officials reaffirmed their commitment to the Court as a cornerstone of the rules-based international order at the October 15 and 16 summit. That official position has not silenced Vilimsky and others who challenge it. Their pressure suggests that the consensus behind the ICC is fracturing.
His intervention carries particular weight in Israel. Vilimsky has been warmly received there, and ministers Amichai Chikli and Miri Regev have publicly welcomed the political rapprochement he helped advance. That has raised his standing as a European voice on Israel and the ICC. The debate over the Court is not simply legal. It is also about alliances, sovereignty, and competing views of accountability.
Together, US-led sanctions, scrutiny of past institutional conduct, and political opposition in Europe have placed the ICC in an existential crisis. The current unrest, marked by street riots and a pervasive sense of instability, reflects a broader climate of uncertainty in which confidence in international institutions is increasingly being questioned. It remains unclear whether this is a temporary setback or the permanent dismantling of the existing order.
The court faces a stark choice. It can continue its current course, risking further isolation and the loss of support from major global powers. Or it can undertake a profound, transparent review of its governance, the conduct of former officials, and its operational mandate. Without that transformation, the ICC risks being seen permanently not as an independent court but as a political instrument. That would signal the end of an era of international accountability that began at the turn of the century. The future of international justice itself is at stake.
Dr. Philip Levy is a member of the International Dialogue Circle, a forum focused on international affairs, geopolitical engagement, and collaborative initiatives.

Drone attack in disputed Sudan-South Sudan border region kills at least 153
South Sudan authorities say Sudan’s army launched a drone attack on a market, as MSF says it is treating 20 wounded people, some with severe burns.
A drone attack on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by South Sudan and Sudan, has killed at least 153 people, according to a South Sudanese official.
The Abyei administration’s caretaker minister of information on Tuesday blamed the attack, which took place a day earlier on Amiet Market, north of Abyei town, on Sudan’s military.
Yohanna Akol Ngor said fires continued to burn at the site and that the death toll was likely to rise.
He told the news agency Reuters that the “situation is terrible”, adding that some bodies had been burned to ashes.
Blaming the Sudanese military for the attack, South Sudan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said drones hit several locations in the market. It said it has summoned Sudan’s ambassador and called for its northern neighbour to “refrain” from acts that endanger civilian lives and property.
There was no immediate comment from Sudan’s armed forces.
A senior Sudanese officer, who spoke anonymously to The Associated Press news agency, said the army struck fuel tankers coming from South Sudan that were headed to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
He added that those killed in the attack were RSF members and fuel smugglers, saying the military does not “target civilians”.
Unnamed diplomats told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market the RSF has used in the past to supply its fighters.
There was no immediate comment on the attack from the RSF.
In a statement on Tuesday, the United Nations secretary-general’s spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, condemned drone attacks near Amiet Market and Todach, saying dozens of civilians, including women and children, had been killed and many others injured. The statement did not identify who carried out the attacks.
The UN said many people remained missing and the death toll was likely to rise as the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) continued verifying casualties.
Medical charity Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said it was treating more than 20 wounded people, some with severe burns.
The war between Sudan’s army and the RSF, which began in April 2023, has ignited a devastating humanitarian crisis in the country.
South Sudan says it has not taken sides, but diplomats say Abyei has become a key route for RSF fuel supplies.
Abyei is claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan, which became independent in 2011, and is jointly administered. The oil-rich region borders Sudan’s Kordofan area, which has become a major centre of fighting in the war.

Researchers identify new subtype of depression linked to body clock
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:25:39 CST
17:25:39 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have identified a subtype of depression linked to disruptions in the body's internal 24-hour clock that regulates the sleep-wake cycle, potentially paving the way for more targeted behavioral and medical treatments.
The study analyzed clinical and genetic data from more than 10,000 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, identifying nearly a quarter of participants as having what researchers termed "circadian depression," according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Sydney.
The subtype is characterized by symptoms including seasonal patterns of illness, longer sleep when depressed, waking feeling exhausted, and being a night owl, according to the study published in the British Journal of Psychiatry.
People with circadian depression were more likely to develop the illness earlier in life and had more severe symptoms, including higher levels of suicidal thoughts. They also had higher genetic risks for inflammatory and cardiovascular conditions and major neurodevelopmental disorders, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, the study showed.
Researchers said the subtype is more resistant to treatment by common serotonin-based antidepressants, but is more responsive to behavioral and medical therapies targeting the body clock's unique brain circuits, such as melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants and light therapy.
The researchers warned that not recognizing circadian depression in young people often led to early treatment failures and more side effects. ■

====================================================================================================

World Insights: Cost-of-living protests highlight mounting economic, social pressures across Europe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:25:25 CST
17:25:25 KST

FRANKFURT, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Recent protests across Europe have brought social and economic strains into sharper focus, reflecting concerns that extend beyond prices to housing, incomes, public services and economic security. Governments face growing pressure to respond, but high debt, tight budgets and long-standing structural problems leave few quick or easy solutions.
DEMONSTRATIONS ACROSS EUROPE
Holding a cardboard sign reading "I am 81 and being evicted," retiree Maria Teresa Faleiro joined crowds in Lisbon protesting against soaring living costs and a deepening housing crisis.
Despite never missing a payment on the 724-euro (813-U.S. dollar) monthly rent for the home she has lived in for 22 years, Faleiro faced eviction after her landlords refused to renew her lease. With nowhere else to go, she plans to appeal the court-ordered eviction, she said.
Faleiro's struggle highlights the growing plight many pensioners in Portugal face in securing affordable housing. It also reflects a broader cost-of-living squeeze across Europe, where thousands have taken to the streets to protest rising housing, food, fuel and energy costs, even as headline inflation has eased.
In France, protests that began with students demanding better school conditions and more teaching staff broadened into nationwide demonstrations over rising living costs and wider social grievances. Violence soon erupted on the sidelines of some rallies, with clashes, looting and arson reported in several cities. The historic city hall in Limoges was largely destroyed by fire.
In Spain, more than 50 protests took place in Madrid and dozens of other Spanish cities on Oct. 3, demanding action on soaring rents, evictions and housing affordability after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.
Elsewhere, protests in Italy and Belgium have reflected a broader mix of concerns over wages, prices, public services and fiscal tightening. In Milan, hundreds of black-clad demonstrators besieged Piazza del Duomo on Saturday, throwing firecrackers and bottles at police. At least four officers and 20 protesters were injured, while about 50 demonstrators were detained, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
ECONOMIC SECURITY UNDER STRAIN
Beyond higher daily expenses, mounting financial pressures are fueling a broader sense of economic insecurity across the continent. Although inflation has eased from its peak, households continue to feel the cumulative impact of earlier price increases.
The European Central Bank said food prices across euro-area countries were already 20 percent to 57 percent higher in August 2025 than at the end of 2019. Renewed energy pressures have added to the squeeze, with euro-area consumer energy inflation reaching 18.9 percent in September 2026, according to Eurostat.
Housing pressures are particularly acute among young Europeans. Data released by Eurostat showed that in 2025, 26.9 percent of young people aged 15 to 29 in the European Union (EU) lived in overcrowded households. And 9.1 percent of them lived in households spending at least 40 percent of their disposable income on housing, way above the 7.7 percent recorded for the total population.
Similar pressures are visible beyond the EU. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, property prices have risen by about 70 percent over the past five years, real estate agent Haris Kadic told the Federation News Agency (FENA).
Local media also reported that some residents are borrowing money or relying on help from children and friends to cover basic expenses as housing and fuel costs rise.
Emmanuel Conte, Milan's city councilor responsible for housing, told Italian daily la Repubblica this month that when people who keep a city running can no longer afford to live there, housing is no longer just a social and economic issue but a political one.
Similarly, Jean Faniel, director general of Belgium's Centre for Socio-Political Research and Information, told Belgian media outlet BRUZZ that violence accompanying recent protests should be understood in the context of mounting social frustration.
Faniel said peaceful demonstrations and violent confrontations are potentially interconnected rather than entirely separate phenomena, noting that successive austerity measures have placed mounting pressure on people's living conditions, generating frustration and resentment.
STRUGGLE TO BALANCE FISCAL, SOCIAL NEEDS
European governments have introduced housing, energy and income support, but high debt, aging populations and competing demands for defense and investment are narrowing their room for further action.
As the European Commission expects France's deficit to reach 5.1 percent of GDP in 2026 and public debt to reach 118.1 percent, Oliver Nachtwey, a sociologist at the University of Basel, said the country's efforts to contain public debt through spending cuts leave governments with less room to invest in schools, teachers and other public services.
Experts said the challenge is to reconcile fiscal discipline with social stability. Thomas Decreus, a scholar at the Department of Philosophy at Tilburg University, warned that weakening basic social protections could undermine social peace. "A budget must be sound, but social investments are also necessary," he said.
Former Croatian Economy minister Ljubo Jurcic told Xinhua that price freezes can help contain immediate pressures, but governments must consider who ultimately bears the cost. In the longer run, stronger productivity and a better economic structure offer more sustainable protection for households, he said.
While subsidies and price controls can provide relatively quick relief, expanding housing supply, improving public services and raising productivity can take years, analysts said.
The challenge lies in how governments should respond to demands for immediate results while pursuing reforms that may take much longer to deliver tangible benefits, they said. ■

China Focus: One keystroke, a new career: AI reshapes China's film and TV industry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:25:22 CST
17:25:22 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- At a film and television industry park in Suzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, Qin Wenshan sits glued to his computer screen, watching as visuals, sound effects, subtitles and special effects fall into place on a video timeline.
With a single press of the Enter key, a team of AI agents springs into action, analyzing the script, designing characters and building scenes frame by frame.
Qin entered the field in late 2023, after stumbling across AI-generated content (AIGC), leading him to experiment with AI video production in his spare time. Before that, he had worked as a safety management officer in the local rail transit sector.
After his short-video series racked up hundreds of millions of views, Qin turned his hobby into a business, putting together a team focused on AI-powered content production.
His journey offers a glimpse into a broader transformation sweeping China's film and TV industry, where advances in AIGC video technology are changing not only how content is made, but also who can make it and at what cost.
PRODUCTION GETS A RESHUFFLE
Making a film or TV series used to require large teams of screenwriters, directors, cinematographers, production designers, editors, and visual effects artists, with all hands on deck. A crew could range from a few dozen people to several hundred and beyond.
The bigger the spectacle, the higher the bill. Productions involving animation, sci-fi or fantasy often come with high costs, particularly when they feature complex settings and elaborate visual effects.
AI is changing the math.
Qin's team put AI to work on "PandaPawz," a sci-fi animated short featuring futuristic settings and intense fight scenes, completing the film in just 28 days at a cost of around 30,000 yuan (about 4,464 U.S. dollars).
Industry data shows that AI can dramatically shorten production schedules, cutting timelines that once stretched over months or even years to just days. Some short-form drama episodes can now be produced in just hours, while efficiency in visual effects and previsualization has increased threefold to tenfold.
Yet AI's role goes far beyond generating images. Li Nan, a creator of AI-generated animated dramas, said the process begins with refining the story outline and developing detailed storyboards. AI tools then generate frames with consistent visual styles and character designs, which are turned into videos and combined with AI voice-overs and automated editing to create finished episodes.
This streamlined workflow enables small teams to handle work that once required extensive collaboration. In April, Li formed a two-person team dedicated to AI-generated animated dramas. Since then, its account has amassed more than 140,000 followers.
"Film and TV production used to be a massive team effort. Now, one person can do the work of an entire department, with AI as the backbone," Qin said.
GROWING DEMAND
The rapid expansion of AI-generated dramas is evident in both output figures and market projections. Official data released in September showed that 430,000 micro-dramas had been released nationwide in the first eight months of this year -- 13 times the total for all of 2025 -- with AI-made productions accounting for more than 90 percent.
The country now has more than 800 million viewers of micro-dramas -- series whose episodes run for less than 20 minutes. The market was worth more than 100 billion yuan in 2025.
The demand is expected to grow further. According to a report by DataEye, an industry data platform, China's AI-generated drama and animation market alone is projected to reach 40 billion yuan in 2026, a year-on-year increase of 138 percent.
The boom, however, also raises questions about content quality and the protection of rights and interests. The National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA) has acknowledged that AI is creating new opportunities for creative expression and more cost-efficient micro-drama production, while also highlighting the challenges the technology poses.
"Our position is clear: live-action dramas are the mainstay of quality productions and should receive strong support," said Wang Xiaoliang, an official with the NRTA, at a September news conference on the development of radio, television, and the online audio and video sector over the next five years.
At the same time, the administration said it will guide and regulate the innovative use of AI across the entire production process of audiovisual content in the coming years.
For industry leaders, the future may lie not in choosing between AI and traditional filmmaking, but in combining the two. Gong Yu, founder and CEO of iQIYI, a leading online entertainment platform, believes the use of AI in film and drama production will be common in the future, and that a hybrid approach combining live-action filming with AI may be the way forward.
The Chinese company is already exploring the potential of AI in longer productions. In July, it premiered "Mystic Tales: The Spider Lady's Vendetta," an AIGC internet feature film running over 60 minutes, which brings Chinese supernatural folklore to life, on both its domestic and international platforms.
Recently, it unveiled a trailer for "Immortals Over Mortal Love," its first full-length, multi-season drama combining AI filmmaking with live-action performances by professional actors. The first season of the series is produced on NadouPro, the company's film and TV production platform empowered by large models.
The move toward AI-generated long-form dramas signals a new stage in the technology's development, industry insider Hu Jie said, adding that these productions may face a tougher test of their storytelling, visual quality and ability to strike an emotional chord with audiences. ■

Around 950,000 displaced people in the Gaza Strip are living in areas at medium to high risk of flooding, including more than 400,000 facing a high risk, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said “Available supplies could partially assist only 18 per cent of the 294,250 families requiring shelter assistance for the rainy season.”
On 17 August, the Gaza government media office said 2.15 million displaced Palestinians, representing 509,393 families, are living in “dire” humanitarian conditions. More than 800,000 of them are staying in tents unfit for “human habitation”, it added.

In September, the office warned that conditions for hundreds of thousands of displaced people in Gaza are deteriorating as winter approached, saying more than 60 per cent of their tents are worn out and need immediate replacement.
Palestinian and UN human rights officials have previously warned that winter storms and rainwater flooding have destroyed or damaged thousands of tents and temporary shelters, forcing displaced people to endure cold, damp and unsafe living conditions.

Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:18:53 BST
17:18:53 KST

Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia
- Published
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Russia to meet President Vladimir Putin after Ukraine's leader said American intelligence sharing about deadly Russian strikes "works now".
Kyiv had accused the US of recently withholding such intelligence, causing Ukrainians to lose their lives - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by Washington.
Volodymyr Zelensky was speaking after meeting Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday for talks later described as "constructive" by a US official.
The Ukrainian president and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday to discuss measures to end the war.
Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said the Kremlin will listen to what Witkoff offers while ruling out "any political concessions".
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks in Oslo alongside the Norwegian prime minister, said "genuine progress" had been made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details, and warned that patience would be needed.
Witkoff was not present at their joint press conference with Zelensky after the talks, nor was President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner who had attended via video link.
A US official later said the meeting had been "very productive and constructive" and that there was a "strong alignment at the working level" between the US, Ukraine and Europe on "next steps".
Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that President Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
Speaking after the news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal".
He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
Russian drone attacks have continued this week. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed on Tuesday - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.
Another attack overnight on Wednesday killed two more people near Kharkiv, the country's second-largest city.
- Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism 
  - Published20 hours ago
Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now".
"Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," he said.
Zelensky also said he hoped for a good result on Starlink, after Ukraine's military had reported speed restrictions on drones using its internet network to conduct strikes against Russia.
A bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into the restrictions last week.
The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine had also been discussed, as well as energy ceasefire proposals, and restated that Kyiv was "ready for negotiations" to end the conflict.
"Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre meanwhile stressed that Europe needed "to be at the table" during any discussions about how to bring the fighting to an end.
Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine, but stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.
European leaders have meanwhile expressed concern about recent US statements towards Russia.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war on Monday, and said that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".
"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.
Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".
"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs after car attack as suspect appears in court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs after car attack
Published October 19, 2026last updated October 21, 2026
Helen Haines, an Australian lawmaker struck by a car in an apparently deliberate attack on Monday, has lost both of her legs, her husband said on Wednesday.
Counterterrorism investigators have joined a police probe into the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.
A 43-year-old suspect, Brendan N. from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Haines loses both legs after apparent attack
The independent MP underwent surgery on Monday night after suffering what were described as critical injuries in the incident, with national broadcaster ABC and the daily Sydney Morning Herald reporting on Tuesday that her left leg had been amputated.
Doctors then proceeded to amputate her right leg on Wednesday after having tried to save it.
"The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family," Phil Haines told reporters in Melbourne.
"We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape," he said.
What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?
Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, which police said was a white Toyota, outside her office. She suffered serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.
ABC cited witnesses as saying they heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars. Later reports from witnesses said that after first pinning Haines against her own car, the driver reversed and rammed into her a second time.
The driver was arrested shortly after, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
Albanese said early investigations suggested the driver made a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading items at the trunk of her car.
"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC.
The suspect's lawyer, Chirag Patel, told Magistrate Allison Vaughan on Wednesday that his client suffers from a rare neurological condition, as well as an undiagnosed mental health condition. He also said the defendant was suffering from a concussion.
Local barber ran to assist
Local barber Ricky Jeffries, whose shop is next to Haines' office, has been widely hailed as a hero after he ran to pull the driver out of the car and restrained him until police arrived.
Jeffries downplayed his role, despite having intervened in what could have been a highly dangerous situation, as the man had a knife in the car.
"He [the driver] did have a knife. He didn't pull it out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.
Jefferies said he then held the man down until police arrived.
"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.
Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "My wife would be disappointed if I'm injured."
"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me ... they deserve the credit," he added.
Political violence on the rise: PM Albanese
Albanese said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.
"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."
Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."
At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."
Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.
Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.

Taiwan outlines limits on Philippine use of donated patrol vessel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:13:30 UTC
17:13:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The patrol vessel donated to the Philippines cannot be used to enforce laws against Taiwanese fishers under the donation agreement, Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling (管碧玲) said Tuesday.
The Coast Guard Administration’s retired 500-tonne-class vessel Kinmen was transferred through the Philippine nonprofit We Protect Our Seas, which donated it to the Philippine Coast Guard on Sept. 21. It entered service on Oct. 2 as BRP Sarangani.
Speaking at the Legislative Yuan, Kuan said the agreement explicitly prohibits such enforcement to protect Taiwanese fishers’ rights and interests, per CNA.
Taiwan and the Philippines have established mechanisms for fisheries law enforcement cooperation and emergency notifications while deepening cooperation on maritime humanitarian assistance, she said. Donating decommissioned vessels to strengthen diplomatic ties and humanitarian cooperation has precedents, she added.
Kuan said the two countries already have a solid foundation for resolving fisheries disputes. Established communication and real-time coordination mechanisms help safeguard their fishers at sea, she said.
The CGA has also stationed a liaison officer at Taiwan’s representative office in Manila to maintain communication with Philippine counterparts, the minister said.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said the Philippines had promised to limit the vessel’s operating areas and enforcement targets so its duties would not involve waters or fishers connected with Taiwan.
Cho said past incidents had provided important lessons. Greater goodwill, exchanges, and cooperation between the two countries and other parties could prevent unnecessary misunderstandings, he said.
Cho described the Kinmen donation as both a gesture of solidarity with democratic partners and an act of humanitarian cooperation.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former TPP Chair Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) commented on co-defendants entering guilty pleas in the Core Pacific City development and campaign finance cases, describing their decisions as admitting defeat rather than guilt.
The Taipei District Prosecutors Office accused Ko of accepting NT$15 million (US$470,000) in bribes and NT$2.1 million in political donations in exchange for granting a floor area ratio bonus to a Core Pacific City development project, per Tai Sounds. Ko was also accused of embezzling NT$62.3 million in presidential campaign contributions through Muko Public Relations Co. and misappropriating funds from the Chung Wang Foundation (眾望基金會).
The trial court found that the NT$2.1 million constituted bribes but found insufficient evidence to establish the NT$15 million allegation. Ko received a combined 17-year prison sentence in March for bribery, embezzlement, and breach of trust. The cases are now before the Taiwan High Court on appeal.
Muko Public Relations Co. Chair Li Wen-chuan (李文娟), a co-defendant in the campaign finance case, pleaded guilty to embezzling campaign donations alongside her brother, Li Wen-tsung (李文宗), and Ko, per SETN. Notably, Li Wen-chuan also pleaded guilty to a charge on which the lower court had acquitted her, involving the use of NT$1 million in donations for a media venture with producer Chiu Fu-sheng (邱復生).
Li Wen-chuan asked the presiding judge to temporarily lift her travel ban so she could take her 90-year-old mother on a cruise, per Liberty Times. She pledged to comply with surveillance and other restrictions upon returning to Taiwan.
Li Wen-tsung, Ko’s presidential campaign chief financial officer and then-chair of the Chung Wang Foundation, pleaded guilty to allocating roughly NT$8.27 million from the foundation but pleaded not guilty to the campaign donation embezzlement allegation, per UP Media.
When asked what he wanted to say after entering his plea, Li Wen-tsung said, “There’s not much to say since it can’t be helped,” per Liberty Times. Asked whether his plea could lead to Ko being imprisoned, he said, “I did nothing with that possibility in mind. Since the witnesses are telling some truths, the correlation between my plea and that outcome seems low.”
Ko commented on his co-defendants’ guilty pleas at a news conference, saying the legal proceedings had imposed an immense financial burden on Li Wen-chuan over the past two years, per CNA.
Ko cited the case of former Core Pacific Group legal affairs manager Chen Chun-yuan (陳俊源), who pleaded guilty to bribery during questioning before changing his position in court. Ko said Chen had explained that although he did not believe the funds provided to the TPP constituted bribes, the time and financial burden of legal proceedings had pushed him to plead guilty.
Ko further noted that Li Wen-tsung had been detained for 11 months in connection with the Core Pacific City development case before eventually receiving a not-guilty ruling. Ko claimed that prosecutors had failed to “fabricate sufficient evidence to convict Li,” per UDN.
Ko stressed that the judicial system should not be used as a political tool, adding that judicial reform would be next on Taiwan’s agenda. He said he would never surrender to pressure and argued that his co-defendants were under pressure because of their association with him.

Pakistan’s army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir reiterated his call for Iran to persuade Yemen’s Houthi group to halt attacks on Saudi Arabia during his latest meetings with Iranian leaders in Tehran, Pakistani government sources told Anadolu on Wednesday.
“The field marshal’s latest meetings with the Iranian leadership were more focused on the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia during his latest visit, in addition to Islamabad’s continued efforts for the resumption of US-Iran talks,” a source familiar with the developments said.
“He (Munir) once again urged the Iranian leadership to use its influence to bring a halt to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, explaining Pakistan’s commitment to defend the kingdom under the Mecca defense pact,” the source added.
Munir arrived in Tehran on Tuesday, accompanied by a delegation of officials, including Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who has played an active role in the mediation process.
The visit comes amid continued tensions between Iran and the US, with diplomatic efforts aimed at resolving their differences remaining stalled.
Iran, in return, reiterated its offer to mediate between the Houthis and Riyadh, insisting that it “doesn’t want the Middle East conflict to further widen,” the sources said.
The sources, however, did not provide further details about Tehran’s response to Munir’s request regarding Houthi attacks.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have signed two defense agreements aimed at collective deterrence -- the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement and the Mecca Joint Defense Alliance, which also includes Türkiye.
The Mecca agreement, signed Aug. 7, allows signatories to treat an attack against one member as an attack against all three.
Pakistan army spokesman Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said in an interview last week that Islamabad was providing Saudi Arabia with “whatever support is needed” to defend the kingdom amid attacks by the Houthi group.
He, however, did not elaborate on the details of the support.
 
Resumption of talks
Munir, according to the sources, discussed “different ways” with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Bagher Ghalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, a representative of Iran’s supreme leader and secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, to resume the long-stalled direct talks with the US.
Iranian leaders, however, did not offer “anything new in this regard,” insisting that Washington had to return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding before any talks could resume to end the conflict, the sources added.
Iranian leaders told Munir that Washington must take the first steps to rebuild trust and that acceptance of Tehran’s seven-point proposal could provide a starting point for renewed negotiations, the sources said.
President Pezeshkian, for his part, told Munir that the US must end pressure and threats and lift sanctions before any negotiations.
The two sides, however, agreed to continue ongoing indirect messaging between Washington and Tehran through mediators, the sources said.
The sources said they were unaware whether Munir had taken any new proposals to Tehran for the resumption of stalled talks with the US.
Pakistan has played a mediating role in efforts to reduce tensions between Washington and Tehran amid the war launched by the US and Israel on Feb. 28.
Washington and Tehran signed the memorandum on June 17, agreeing to advance negotiations toward a permanent settlement on several contentious issues, including Iran’s nuclear program, within 60 days.
However, hostilities that began in July have cast uncertainty over the future of the agreement.

Taiwan’s electricity business indicator stays red for 18th straight month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:12:52 UTC
17:12:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s electricity business climate indicator remained red, signaling brisk economic activity, for the 18th consecutive month in September as semiconductor power consumption reached a record high, the Taiwan Research Institute said Wednesday.
Semiconductor electricity consumption topped 4.5 billion kilowatt-hours in September, up 11.55% from a year earlier amid strong AI demand, per CNA. The institute expects the industry’s annual power consumption to exceed 50 billion kWh.
Electricity consumption among industrial users supplied at high voltage or above rose 1.76% year-on-year in September, while manufacturing consumption in the same category increased 1.96%. The institute estimated economic growth of 12.6% for September, supported by high-tech production, exports, and business investment, per Liberty Times.
Demand for AI, high-performance computing, and data centers kept production brisk across semiconductor, electronic component, and server supply chains, the institute said. AI-related opportunities in servers, equipment, materials, and key components also boosted investment and production in related industries.
However, electricity consumption in the chemical materials and textile industries remained below year-earlier levels. Chemical materials manufacturers faced global oversupply and a slow recovery in demand, while textile makers struggled with weak international demand and price competition. Both sectors’ electricity business indicators remained blue, signaling contraction.

Italian Cheeses in Japan: ICE and Assolatte Revive Promotional Efforts
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:12:07 CEST
17:12:07 KST

Original recipes, training, and tastings to introduce Italian cheeses to Japanese dietary habits. This is the program promoted in Japan by ICE-Agenzia in collaboration with Assolatte, the Italian Dairy Association, as part of a partnership launched in 2019 that has so far included trade show appearances, business meetings, and promotions on cooking websites and digital channels.
                                    
The initiative involves the development of ten recipes that pair typical ingredients of Japanese cuisine with ten cheeses selected by Assolatte. The recipes for restaurants are curated by Chisako Hori, executive director of the historic Kikunoi restaurant in Kyoto, while those for home cooking are created by Megumi Fujii, a culinary expert. The dishes will be published on the “Orangepage net” portal and shared through its digital channels. The project consists of three training sessions in Osaka, Tokyo, and Fukuoka, featuring Hori, Fujii, and Miyuki Ikeda, a master cheese taster certified by the National Organization of Cheese Tasters (Onaf). Tastings are also scheduled for November 7 at Hills Marché, located at Ark Hills in Roppongi, in central Tokyo, and on November 14 during an event dedicated to content creators. 
   “Japan offers significant opportunities for Italian cheeses, which stand out for their variety and their connection to their regions of origin,” says Gianpaolo Bruno, director of the ICE office in Tokyo. “The inclusion of Italian cuisine on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity highlights the heritage of knowledge of which our cheese-making tradition is an integral part. Together with Assolatte, we aim to raise awareness of these products and integrate them into Japanese dietary habits.” Market trends confirm the interest in Italian products. In 2025, Japanese cheese imports reached approximately 201 billion yen, equivalent to 1.13 billion euros, a 2.7% increase compared to 2024, while volumes fell from 260,238 to 251,841 metric tons. 
   Italy is the fourth-largest supplier after New Zealand, Australia, and the United States, and the leading EU country, with a 9.4% share by value. Imports from Italy rose to approximately 18.9 billion yen (+7.6%), while volumes remained essentially stable at 12,237 metric tons: growth in value exceeded that of the overall market. Performance was strong in certain segments. In fresh cheeses and curd, Italy ranks second, with 17.4%, behind Australia (42.9%). In blue cheeses, it ranks first, with a share of approximately 65%, ahead of Denmark (17.7%).

Poll shows Swiss voters are undecided on arms exports
Whilst the initiatives on fireworks and tax fairness are enjoying broad support and the proposal to fund the 13th pension payments is likely to be rejected, the outcome of the vote on the War Materiel Act remains to be seen. These are the findings of the YouGov poll.
According to the first opinion poll by the Yougov research institute, published on Wednesday, the proposal to fund the 13th pension payment through VAT would be clearly rejected on November 29. With 51% voting “no” and 39% voting “yes” it is unlikely to stand a chance. Crucially, it would not be accepted in any canton, when a double majority of votes and cantons is required.
More
The Swiss voted for a pension hike. Now they must decide how to pay for it
This proposal highlights a generational divide. It is supported by 46% of those aged over 60, whilst only 30% of those under 45 would vote “yes”.
The outlook appears more favourable for the Centre Party’s tax initiative for married couples. It is expected to pass with 51% in favour and 29% against, according to YouGov.
More
Why is Switzerland voting again on the ‘marriage tax penalty’?
The outlook is also positive for the initiative calling for the ban on fireworks. It has 62% in favour, compared with 33% against and 6% undecided, according to the polling organisation.
More
Nuisance or festive tradition? Swiss vote on fireworks ban
Military equipment wide open
The outcome is much more uncertain when it comes to the law on military equipment. Thirty-eight per cent of those surveyed are in favour of relaxing export rules, whilst 33% are against, according to YouGov.
This proposal reveals a clear gender divide. Half of men are in favour, compared with just 28%, who are also significantly more likely to be undecided.
More
Swiss to vote on loosening arms-export restrictions
According to Yougov, 42% of those surveyed found the War Materiel Act complex. An equally large proportion of respondents felt they were not well informed. This is a key factor explaining the high proportion of undecided voters, with nearly three in ten voters yet to make up their minds.
Yougov Switzerland surveyed 2,949 voters from its panel between 7 and 19 October 2026. The margin of error is plus or minus 1.8 percentage points.
A previous poll, published just over a week ago by the Leewas institute, showed that only the initiative “to restrict fireworks” was likely to pass, with 65% voting “yes”. The other three proposals were expected to be rejected.

Expenditures by ministries and government agencies in the Ukrainian draft 2027 state budget can be reduced by UAH 161.5 billion, with the funds redirected to defense needs.
"This is the next set of our amendments to bill No. 16000," Nina Yuzhanina, a member of parliament from the European Solidarity faction, wrote on Facebook.
The proposal concerns two types of expenditures: consumption expenditures (excluding utilities), which are to be reviewed based on the actual 2026 baseline and the relevant growth indices; and development expenditures, or capital expenditures, which are to be reduced under designated budget programs.
"And here I want to draw attention to a fundamental point. We are not proposing to halt the operations of government agencies or leave them without the funding they need. But how can we continue to accept increases in expenditures amounting to billions of hryvnias across the judicial system, the prosecutor's office, the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Verkhovna Rada?" Yuzhanina said.
As is known, European Solidarity is demanding that all populist and corrupt expenditure items be removed from the draft 2027 state budget. Instead, the released funds should be allocated exclusively to defense and strengthening the Armed Forces of Ukraine. According to party leader Petro Poroshenko, reallocating non-targeted expenditures would make it possible to direct at least an additional half a trillion hryvnias to the military.
"Our demands are specific: at least UAH 500 billion in additional funding for the military to purchase weapons and defense technologies; 30% of the military personal income tax revenue to go directly to brigades; indexation of military pay; protection of the energy sector and the economy; cancellation of non-priority and propaganda-related expenditures; fulfillment of European commitments and restoration of our allies' trust," Poroshenko said.

Prince Harry on family rift: ‘Some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:06:19 UTC
17:06:19 KST

Prince Harry has once again expressed his desire to repair his fractured relationship with his older brother, Prince William, and their father, King Charles III. But his latest comments have already prompted controversy, with the Duke of Sussex's spokesperson forced to clarify that a remark about people who do not want reconciliation was not intended as criticism of any member of the royal family.
In an interview with Zach Baron for GQ, published Tuesday, October 20, Harry, 42, discussed the painful family divisions that have dominated headlines for years. Asked whether he grieves his complicated relationships with William and Charles, the prince acknowledged that he does, describing family estrangement as something many people can identify with. He said disagreements between siblings and broken relationships between parents and children frequently arise in conversations with members of the public.
Harry suggested that the intense interest in his family's troubles reflects how common such experiences are, and that people might learn something from seeing how he handles his own situation. But one comment immediately attracted attention: "And some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to work out." When Baron pressed him on whether he genuinely wanted reconciliation, Harry insisted that repairing relationships was his priority, saying that with everything happening around the world, "the most important thing is to reconcile."
The remark about people supposedly resisting reconciliation was widely interpreted as a possible reference to William, who has remained estranged from his younger brother. Shortly after the interview was published, however, Harry's spokesperson rejected that interpretation. In a statement reported by People, the spokesperson said the comment was "absolutely not intended as a swipe at his brother or any other member of his family." The spokesperson stressed that Harry was making a general observation rather than accusing his relatives of blocking reconciliation.
The relationship between the two princes began deteriorating around 2018, and tensions intensified after Harry and Meghan Markle stepped back from royal duties in 2020 and moved to California. Their subsequent interviews, Netflix documentary series and Harry's memoir Spare, published in January 2023, exposed deeply personal grievances about the royal family. In the book, Harry described an alleged physical confrontation with William, further damaging a relationship that had once been presented as exceptionally close.
Now, after six years in the United States, Harry and Meghan have returned to Britain with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. The family moved back in late August, and Harry told GQ that providing the children with a British education and allowing them to experience the country where he grew up were important factors in the decision. He also expressed hope that old disputes involving his family and the British press could eventually be left behind.
Harry appeared particularly determined to move beyond the bitterness of recent years. Asked whether the wounds within his family could be repaired, he acknowledged that "scars stick around forever" but emphasized the importance of letting go of past grievances. The interview, conducted in New York in late September, also explored his lifelong struggle with grief following the death of his mother, Princess Diana, and the ways that loss has shaped his relationships and approach to parenting.
There are signs that Harry's relationship with King Charles is improving. According to People, a source close to the prince described their relationship as better than it had been. Charles reunited with Harry, Meghan and their children in July, and father and son have spoken at least once since the Sussexes returned to Britain on August 26. However, those developments have not translated into progress with William, with a source close to Harry telling the magazine that the brothers remain out of contact.
Sources close to William and Kate Middleton, the Princess of Wales, say the emotional wounds behind the estrangement have not healed. One palace source recently told People that the fallout had been extremely difficult for the couple and that William's reluctance to reconnect was understandable. The assessment suggests that even if Charles is prepared to rebuild his relationship with his younger son, the Prince of Wales remains far less willing to do the same.
Royal author Russell Myers, whose book William and Catherine examines the couple's relationship and public roles, offered an even more pessimistic outlook. Speaking to People, Myers said William considers his father's relationship with Harry to be entirely Charles' decision. But Myers believes the future king has no intention of restoring ties with Harry and Meghan, whether officially or privately, describing the possibility of a relationship "in a working or private capacity whatsoever" as effectively closed.
Harry's latest interview therefore highlights the distance between his public desire for reconciliation and the reality of his relationship with William. While his return to Britain and improving ties with Charles may represent meaningful changes, the brothers' estrangement appears no closer to being resolved. For now, Harry says he wants to move forward, but there is little indication that William is prepared to join him.

Europe is in trouble, and it is blaming Muslims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:02:49 UTC
17:02:49 KST

Europe is in trouble, and it is blaming Muslims
A recent European Parliament resolution shows the European mainstream is fully embracing an Islamophobic agenda.
As protests in France turned violent late last week, the French far right quickly resorted to racist language to blame the Muslim youth for the violence. Weeks earlier, when thousands of migrants tried to enter the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco, the Spanish far right spoke of an organised “invasion” by Moroccans.
United States President Donald Trump has also chimed in, claiming that this is about “Islam wanting to take over”.
While the far right’s readiness to exploit crises to fuel Islamophobia is to be expected, the idea that Islam and Muslims are to blame for Europe’s growing woes is no longer reserved for that extreme of the European political spectrum.
Last week, while student protests were heating up in France, the European Parliament quietly passed a resolution “on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network”. The text was tabled by the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), the largest group in the parliament, which European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hails from.
It passed with 381 votes in favour, 167 against and 15 abstentions. Four other groups backed the EPP almost unanimously: the far-right Patriots for Europe and Europe of Sovereign Nations, the liberal Renew Europe, and the European Conservatives and Reformists.
The Social Democrats, the Left and the Greens mostly voted against but could not stop it.
The resolution, which draws on a highly problematic report by the French government on “political Islamism”, makes a number of flawed claims that have wide-ranging implications for Muslim communities.
It defines “Islamist entryism” as “a political strategy of influence, progressive structuring, institutional penetration and ideological legitimisation”. It claims that “Islamist influence operates through a broad and fragmented ecosystem of associations, foundations and cultural, educational, religious, charitable, university, youth, anti-discrimination or social action structures”.
More specifically, it says that “diversity, equity, inclusion and anti-discrimination frameworks may be diverted as vectors of institutional legitimisation, by integrating a politicised religious identity into legitimate causes for the protection of minorities”. In other words, networks like the Muslim Brotherhood “infiltrate” European societies through anti-Islamophobia initiatives.
The resolution is not binding and European Union member states do not have to implement it. Its call to put the Muslim Brotherhood and affiliated individuals and entities on a terror list is unlikely to be implemented across Europe, given the movement’s renunciation of violence as a political tool.
However, the resolution still gives legitimacy to an ideological framework that can have grave implications for Muslim communities.
It puts under suspicion Muslim institutions and organisations that operate independently of the state and presents the inclusion of Muslim civil society in public activity as a form of infiltration.
The resolution names several organisations, including the Brussels-based European Network Against Racism (ENAR), as espousing this type of “Islamist” behaviour, and calls for blocking access to EU funding and restricting any EU-funded entity from working with them. The vague notion of a “Muslim Brotherhood network” can make guilt by association possible for almost anyone.
This can easily be weaponised by outside actors and already has been. The United Arab Emirates, for example, has funded a wide-ranging campaign in Europe and elsewhere to smear individuals and organisations as Muslim Brotherhood affiliates. Interestingly, a few months before the resolution was tabled, an Emirati ambassador participated in a conference titled “Muslim Brotherhood: A real threat to Europe” held at the European Parliament. While Emirati influence is there, the resolution itself problematises “foreign funding” that allegedly supports “Islamist entryism” from Qatar or Turkiye, another indication of the geopolitics behind the scenes.
Most importantly, the resolution frames defending Muslims against racism as part of an Islamist infiltration plot. This can directly impact initiatives and public debates that seek to address Islamophobia in European societies.
Symbolically, the resolution is a major victory for Europe’s right-wing anti-Muslim forces. It shows that the European Parliament has started abandoning any firewall against the far right as the centre right draws closer and closer to the far right. The EPP appears to have almost completely absorbed the far-right agenda but seeks to cushion it in the language of national security.
The resolution also demonstrates how European Islamophobia has evolved. The fear is no longer of the immigrants as strangers who fail to “integrate” but of the Muslims who are able to speak for themselves and defend their civil liberties.
For the centre right, this Islamophobic framework comes with political perks. Not only is it able to benefit electorally from anti-Muslim fearmongering, but it is also able to strike at those on the left who choose to reject racism and stand up for Muslim communities.
It is no surprise that the idea of “Islamo-leftism” – Islamo-gauchisme in French – is being promoted on the political scene in France. Jean-Luc Melenchon of the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) is particularly popular among marginalised communities and a strong contender for the presidency. He is now being accused of encouraging the “rioters”, who – it is implied – are Muslim.
This dual attack on the left and on Muslims mirrors the old Judeo-Bolshevik conspiracy theory that blamed Jews for the spread of communism with the aim of destroying Western civilisation.
Today, “Islamo-leftism” serves conservatives, liberals and the far right alike as a scapegoat in their effort to complete a counter-revolution against the modest progress the West has made on tackling racism and inequality since the 1960s. Their project appears to be a fortress Europe without Muslims.
However flimsy the basis of the “Islamist entryism” resolution is, we should expect further legally dubious moves by conservative alliances in individual member states to curb Muslim agency outside state control, especially when it defends Muslim civil liberties. Meanwhile, fearmongers will keep blaming Islam for social ills and for legitimate protests against austerity, and politicians will keep directing public anger at Muslim communities to distract from their own governance failures.
What is needed now is a strong response to this conservative counter-revolution through a firm defence of civil liberties for everyone.

Seven Challenger 3 tank prototypes delivered for trials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:00:23 BST
17:00:23 KST

Seven Challenger 3 prototype vehicles have been delivered for the Demonstration Phase trials programme, with an eighth in the final stages of build, and the vehicles are being used to demonstrate and assure the performance and safety of the tank in preparation for manufacture, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Correction 21/10/1990: this article originally said Challenger 3 was moving from a smoothbore gun to a rifled barrel. It is the other way round. Challenger 2 has the rifled gun and Challenger 3 has the smoothbore. The two were simply mixed up, and the text has been corrected. Thanks to the reader who pointed it out.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked how many Challenger 3 tanks have been delivered to date, following an answer given on 8 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Seven Challenger 3 prototype vehicles have been delivered to date for use in the Demonstration Phase trials programme, with an eighth prototype vehicle in the final stages of build. These vehicles are being used to demonstrate and assure the performance and safety of the Challenger 3 capability in preparation for manufacture.”
Challenger 3 takes the hull of the existing Challenger 2 and gives it a new turret, a smoothbore gun firing NATO standard ammunition, modular armour, an active protection system and a new sighting and fire control fit. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land is building the vehicles at Telford under a contract covering one hundred and forty eight tanks, and the first prototype rolled off the production line in 2024.
The Demonstration Phase is where the design is proved before the department commits to building the rest, and the programme needs eight prototypes to run the firing, mobility, electromagnetic and safety trials in parallel.
The move from a rifled gun to a smoothbore reverses decades of British practice and was driven by ammunition supply, since the rifled 120mm round Challenger 2 fires is made for no other army in NATO and the industrial base behind it had shrunk to almost nothing. Common ammunition means Challenger 3 can draw from allied stockpiles, which matters more now than it did when the choice was first debated.
Delivery of the full fleet runs towards the end of the decade, with an initial operating capability planned for 2027 and full operating capability by 2030, and the one hundred and forty eight tanks will equip two armoured regiments inside 3rd (UK) Division.
Britain operated nearly four hundred Challenger 2 at the start of the century, and the conversion programme covers fewer than half that number.

Apple showcases upcycled found furniture and banana palm-paper lantern at Designers of Tomorrow show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Apple showcases upcycled found furniture and banana palm-paper lantern at Designers of Tomorrow show
Designers Parafernalia, Yoonjeong Lee, Salem S Charabi and Isabel Rower will celebrate “the art in the making” at technology brand Apple‘s Designers of Tomorrow exhibition at Design Miami.Paris.
The emerging designers, who have all designed furniture or lighting, were chosen by exhibition curator Rodman Primack, together with a jury that included Design Miami president Jennifer Roberts and designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
For its latest edition of the exhibition, which opens today, Apple wanted to showcase how its products are used by emerging designers in the process of creating their pieces.
“Designers of Tomorrow celebrates the process – the art in the making,” Apple said in a statement.
“Each of the designers use Apple products in a variety of ways within their creative processes, from early ideation to creation,” the company continued.
“Apple has long believed that the full potential of their products is only fully realised when put in the hands of the world’s most talented creatives.”
Among the works on show will be Egyptian-Danish designer Charabi‘s delicate lamp, made from date palm from Saqqara, limestone from the Galala Mountains and paper made from banana palms in the Nile Delta.
The theme of the exhibition this year was Design for Presence, which Charabi took into consideration by pondering “what is present?”
“A structure inspired by the date palm-cleaving methods of the qafassin, makers of boxes and trays used in the country’s souks and bakeries,” the designer said.
“A skin created by multiple layerings of banana stems, found in Beheira, in the Nile Delta of Egypt,” he continued. “A mass carved from limestone from the Galala Mountains, carrying the trace of its making through repetitive patterns.”
Seoul-based artist Lee, meanwhile, explored how objects can change their functions by using a pencil to nail paper to a surface, before taking the idea further by creating a lamp.
“For this project, I took that approach further, using wood to build a table that holds the pencil nail and paper, completing the piece as a three-dimensional lamp,” Lee explained.
“To make the table, I repeatedly stacked thin sheets of veneer to build a new, solid piece of wood – approximately 5,000 layers, perhaps more.”
Designer Rower used upcycled furniture for her piece, which she then decorated with ceramic beads.
“The chair was made using found furniture left on the curb near my studio in Brooklyn, reconstituted into a wooden armature onto which I built up layers of papier-mâché and a pulp composite containing wood glue, sawdust, and paper pulp made from shredded waste paper,” Rower said.
After spraying the surface of the chair with black paint, she glued 1,500 handmade ceramic beads to it.
The final designers taking part, Sebastián Zorrilla and Genki Matsumura of studio Parafernalia, created their design, MonoAmbiente 1, as a “landscape”.
“Its acid-etched stainless steel surfaces invite closer observation as light reveals and conceals details across them,” the designers said.
“As it unfolds, the landscape unfolds with it: rocks become stools and a table, turning a distant scene into a place for two to converse, play, or share a drink,” the designers continued.
Apple first launched Designers of Tomorrow at Design Miami.Paris last year, when it showed pieces including a table designed to look like butter.
Designers of Tomorrow takes place at Design Miami.Paris 2026 from 21 to 25 October 2026 at L’hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris, France. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

Belgium’s police oversight body, Committee P, has received 26 complaints concerning police conduct during recent youth protests in Brussels, following two weeks of unrest that resulted in more than 250 arrests, news portal Bruzz reported Wednesday.
The complaints relate to alleged police misconduct during demonstrations on Oct. 9 and Oct. 17, according to Committee P.

Police arrested 152 people, including 19 in judicial arrests.

‘It’s hard for us’: Paris small businesses bear brunt of protest violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:56:14 UTC
16:56:14 KST

‘It’s hard for us’: Paris small businesses bear brunt of protest violence
Shopkeepers – including those from immigrant backgrounds – count losses from violence last weekend.
Paris, France – Jagged shards of glass frame the hole kicked through the window of Hassan Rashdul’s mobile phone shop near Place de la Republique, the epicentre of looting and rioting that swept this part of Paris on Saturday.
“I was crying,” Rashdul says, as he watches a CCTV livestream on his phone.
The glass countertop is shattered, the floor carpeted with broken glass. The display cases that were full of new and reconditioned mobile phones, iPads, and computers are empty. The walls where headphones, cables, phone cases and other accessories hung have been stripped bare.
“It’s really terrible,” the 32-year-old Rashdul says. “It was very, very hard for us… It’s already hard for small business owners like us. We’re not operating to keep the business going, but just to survive, really.”
Rashdul says he’s lost at least 70,000-euros ($78,600) worth of stock. His insurance won’t cover it, because loss from theft wasn’t included in his policy, though Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said the government will cover employee salaries of about 3,000 businesses across France affected by the rioting.
There will also be a “dedicated support fund” to help businesses restock, the French government has announced. Lecornu has ordered more than 200 investigators to work on catching the perpetrators of the riots and looting.
But the rioters are moving quickly: Some businesses say they found their stock being sold online within hours of being looted.
“Stolen items from this weekend are being offered for sale on certain platforms,” digital minister Anne Le Henanff said on X. “We expect these platforms to remove the listings in question without delay.”
She held a meeting with representatives of six platforms in the presence of Interior and Justice Ministry officials. According to the French commerce ministry, representatives of Vinted, Amazon, eBay, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok, as well as French online retail association Fevad, were invited.
“They will also be required to cooperate closely with state authorities so that those reselling stolen goods can be prosecuted,” Le Henanff added.
Around Rashdul’s shop, there are mini-markets, opticians, phone stores and cafes that bear testimony to the violence last weekend.
Some are boarded up. Others, where there’s nothing left to steal, have been left open and exposed to the damp October weather by their owners.
But amid his suffering, Rashdul spots a glimmer of hope.
“There’s another side to it,” he says, “a positive – local customers, people from the neighbourhood.”
These people have set up appeals on social media to secure help for shopkeepers, he says.
“They really make you want to try again,” says Rashdul. “People are helping us to rebuild our shop, to get back to work and serve this neighbourhood once again.”
But it will not be easy. It took Rashdul, who immigrated to France from Bangladesh, 10 years to build his business. He now calls himself a proud French citizen – respectful of the right to protest but also worried about the impact of violence on businesses like his, and on France as a whole.
“Even though I want to rebuild, next Saturday they’ve announced another protest,” he says. “I know we’re in a democracy and there’s a right to protest, but if that ends up in more looting, then that’s hard on France and damaging for its international reputation.”
