Al Ain provided similar information, noting that the court had revisited the case of the perpetrator’s fiancée as well as of a person who had arranged accommodation for the perpetrator and communicated with him.
Based on this report, the Tunisian National Guard member had killed his colleague “before heading toward the vicinity of the Ghriba temple and opening fire, in an incident that resulted in deaths and injuries.”
The incident “brought back to the forefront the issue of securing sensitive sites during religious and tourist visits,” Tunisie Telegraph noted.
Further, several security forces were wounded in the attack. “The attack also killed two visitors and injured others,” the news source said.
Reversal of previous decision to not hear defendant's case
The “new appellate rulings are of particular importance” because they reversed a previous decision not to hear part of one defendant’s case, the report pointed out.
“These rulings remain part of the judicial process related to determining responsibilities in the case, while the perpetrator of the attack who opened fire should not be confused with the rest of the defendants to whom the judicial authorities are responsible for the actions attributed to them,” Tunisie Telegraph reported.
It noted that the attack on the historic synagogue took place during an annual Jewish pilgrimage season. The perpetrator, it said, shot his colleague and then stole his ammunition. He then attacked the synagogue, killing three other security officers and two Jewish visitors.
The Jews who were killed included a local Tunisian and a relative visiting from France, the report added. The same site was attacked in 2002 by terrorists using a truck bombing. The attack killed 21 people and was believed to be carried out by al-Qaeda.
In May, the Associated Press noted that “the annual Jewish pilgrimage to the 26-century-old El-Ghriba Synagogue in Tunisia drew a modest but notable return of international visitors this year, worshipping together under tight security after a deadly 2023 attack disrupted the festival.”

====================================================================================================

Beneath a German lake, above a Nazi bunker: Israeli artist explores buried memory - feature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:30:32 UTC
16:30:32 KST

Clay mines inscribed with Hebrew letters and submerged in a German lake above a Nazi-era bunker are at the center of Israeli artist Yehudit Sasportas's video installation Lake of Void, which opened at Jerusalem's Tower of David Museum on October 12.
The exhibition, hosted as part of the Jerusalem Biennale, one of the world's largest platforms for contemporary Jewish and Israeli art, is expected to remain on display until the end of November.
At the opening, Sasportas, Tower of David Museum director Eilat Lieber, and exhibition curator Hillie Wurtman Moyal addressed a small audience atop the citadel's tower, discussing the significance of presenting the installation in Jerusalem, the motivations behind Sasportas's work, and the relationship between archaeology and contemporary art.
The exhibition is housed within Jerusalem's ancient citadel, home to the Tower of David Museum, which preserves and presents the stories of the people and cultures that have shaped the city.
For Lieber, hosting contemporary art in the historic structure offers a chance to add another dimension to Jerusalem's history.
"Alongside being a historical museum, we also want to host art exhibitions here, because it's another layer [of the city's history]," Lieber told The Jerusalem Post.
"It's a layer of our generation that gives more perspective and meaning to the story of Jerusalem, especially Israeli art at its best, dealing with memory."
Memory beneath the surface
Sasportas, who represented Israel at the 2007 Venice Biennale, approaches the preservation of memory differently from traditional archaeologists, Lieber explained.
"Unlike archaeologists, [...] she's creating the remains. She's connecting the memories, sounds, and she creates artifacts, trying to be the archaeologists of the future," Lieber said.
Presenting the installation inside a hall dating back approximately 800 years, to the Crusader or Ayyubid period, creates a dialogue between the ancient structure and Sasportas's exploration of memory.
"To be able to host [the exhibition] inside the original... hall... and contemporary art that thinks about memories, the past and their meaning, is important for us," Lieber said.
Rather than uncovering objects left behind by previous generations, Sasportas creates artifacts intended to preserve traces of the present for those who come after.
In Lake of Void, that idea takes the form of clay sculptures resembling land mines, each containing a concealed message.
From Germany's Black Forest to a submerged Nazi bunker
The installation draws on Sasportas's earlier work in Germany's Black Forest, where she produced hand-drawn seismographic lines inspired by recordings taken from inside more than 138 trees.
The recordings were made near the cabin of German philosopher Martin Heidegger and the approximate location of his historically charged 1967 encounter with Romanian-born poet Paul Celan.
For Sasportas, the trees became "a living archive," their sounds translated into marks made by needles and pencils on drawing paper.
The resulting drawings were rolled, sealed inside black metal boxes, and placed within the clay mines, turning recordings of the natural world into physical repositories of memory.
The mines were subsequently submerged in Lake Bant in Wilhelmshaven, Germany, a lake beneath which lies a bunker constructed during the Nazi era.
Sasportas documented their descent with underwater footage and sound recordings, making the submerging of the sculptures part of the artwork itself.
Lake of Void is set "in a place that was [formerly] a lake, but underneath that lake there was a bunker that was created during the Nazi regime," Moyal explained.
The location reflects the exhibition's broader exploration of what remains hidden beneath seemingly ordinary landscapes.
Moyal described the work as examining the "underlying layers of the unseen reality – all the stories and memories and traumas and conflicts that are beneath the ground."
By bringing these buried histories to light, Sasportas confronts the legacy of places marked by historical violence.
"She deals with traumas under the ground, but through art revealing those stories," Moyal said.
"In her work, she [Sasportas] works through art to kind of change these charged memories and create something [..] to heal these charged places."
In Mine Sentence 3/6, an underwater camera focuses on the Hebrew letters inscribed on the clay sculptures. Their combinations form words, verses, and sentences carrying "intention and meaning," according to a Tower of David Museum press release.
The work forms part of Sasportas's ongoing The Liquid Desert Project, which began in 2013.
Sending a letter to the past
Sasportas's practice frequently takes her to locations across Europe and Israel where traumatic histories have been buried, forgotten, or denied.
According to the museum, her work seeks to bring those histories back into view, using art to connect different periods.
The discovery of the bunker beneath the Banter See was particularly significant to Sasportas, who recalled being struck by the contrast between the lake's peaceful appearance and the history concealed below.
When she "realized that there is an actual underground architecture like this bunker" beneath a lake that appeared "too beautiful," she wanted to "send a letter to the past" and "be able to correspond with the collective subconscious."
Although Sasportas acknowledged that the idea might sound "very abstract" and "very poetical," she described art as a way to communicate across time.
"Through a drawing, through a sculpture, through a mute image, you’re able to correspond with different times, and I think that this defines the quality of art as a timeless thing," she said.
The sculptures remain at the bottom of the lake, forming a permanent underwater installation above the submerged bunker.
According to the museum, the work is the third of six Mine Sentence installations submerged across Europe and Israel between 2020 and 2025.
From 'ani' to 'ayin': Finding meaning in nothingness
Beyond the physical landscape, Sasportas draws on the Hebrew language to explore the relationship between identity, absence, and creation.
Central to the exhibition is the connection between ani, meaning "I," and ayin, meaning "nothingness."
In Hebrew, the two words contain the same three letters, rearranged to produce different meanings.
For Sasportas, that transformation represents an opportunity to move beyond the self and into a space of creative possibility.
"You can also move the letters for a certain... artistic practice, creative practice, spiritual practice," she said.
"The transformation from 'ani' to 'ayin' inspires me a lot, and this is the lake of void, the lake of an ayin."
Sasportas also explored another meaning of ayin through the opening of Psalm 121, Me'ayin yavo ezri, traditionally translated as "From where will my help come?"
While the verse is commonly understood as a question about the source of assistance, Sasportas also interprets it as suggesting that help can emerge from nothingness itself.
"Ayin can be like nothing, nothingness, but ayin is also a space," she said.
She explained that the distinction depends on the viewer's state of consciousness and the meanings they bring to the work.
"I'm very inspired by artistic actions that can activate within themselves those different levels of consciousness," she said.
Sasportas also connected her artistic practice to the Hebrew expression Hashem hakol bizman, which she invoked to describe trust in divine timing.
Working "from a certain space-time," she explained, allows an artist to "open up other dimensions."
For Sasportas, the ability to hold seemingly contradictory states together, the concrete and the abstract, the visible and the hidden, is central to the power of art.
"If an artwork can embrace two states, like a very concrete, recognizable one, and start losing the face slowly into more abstract, but in the same body," she said, it can "activate all dimensions simultaneously."

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said on Wednesday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in court.
Doctors amputated Haines' left leg after the alleged attacker struck her twice with his car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said. They worked for days to save her right leg but were ultimately unsuccessful, he told a press conference in Melbourne.
"The good news in all this is Helen is alive, and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said.
Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines' electorate, was charged with three offenses: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official.
Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against Nugent, court filings showed.
The suspect was restrained by members of the public at the scene before being arrested.
Haines in critical condition after rare attack on Australian official
Haines, an independent lawmaker who has championed causes including climate change and regional housing, remains in critical condition.
Police are still investigating the motive for the rare attack on an elected official.
During a brief court appearance on Wednesday, the accused's lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. His lawyer told the magistrate his client had some mental health concerns and that it was his first time in custody.
There was no application for bail, and the case was deferred until February 4.
Anti-terrorism police are among the agencies investigating the incident. While police allege the attack was "targeted," they believe it was an isolated incident.
No intelligence suggested any threat to Haines, and the Australian Federal Police received no warning of imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.
"What I can say is we didn't have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon," she said.
Victoria police investigating motive for attack on Haines
Victoria state police said they could not find any direct past contact between Haines and the accused, with the motive still unknown.
"Motivation is one of these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centerpiece of the investigation," Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said.
Bush declined to comment on the man's mental health, saying the matter was before the court.
Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery, and academia before being elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in both 2022 and 2025.
Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders, and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee, or attending community events with relatively little security.
However, concerns about politicians' safety have grown in recent years amid rising political polarization, online abuse, and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterized Australian politics.

Impermanence by Design: An Architectural History of Antarctica
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

"Antarctica is known through narratives," states Victoria Nuviala Antelo during the lecture on Inhabiting the Extreme: An Architectural Biography of Antarctica, presented at the Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial. Indeed, throughout architectural history, numerous stories, experiences, ways of inhabiting, and building practices have often been excluded from official narratives. Buried beneath thick layers of ice, the history of Antarctic architecture tells a story of impermanence. The ice surrounding the continent expands and contracts each year, doubling its surface area, while the species that inhabit it migrate and return according to their life cycles. Ice covers structures as katabatic winds erase the traces of more than 200 years of human presence. Explorations, settlements, architectural interventions, and ways of inhabiting remain concealed within one of the most extreme landscapes on the planet.
As a geologically complex territory characterized by mountainous landscapes and a constant interplay of extremes, Antarctica is home to more than 16,500 marine species and approximately 1,890 recorded species in its ice-free terrestrial areas. Among the latter are approximately 200 species of lichens, more than 50 bryophytes, over 700 algae species, and two vascular plant species. Among its most recognizable inhabitants, Antarctica's coasts and surrounding waters are home to millions of penguins and hundreds of thousands of whales, including approximately 500,000 minke whales and more than 2,000 Antarctic blue whales.
 Antarctica is, traditionally, impossible to write. This idea is sustained by the powerful metaphor of the continent as a canvas, the 'vast white page.' -- Leane, 2012. Antarctica in Fiction: Imaginative Narratives of the Far South.
As described by Encyclopaedia Britannica, Antarctica is the world's fifth-largest continent by land area, covering approximately 14 million square kilometers. Winter temperatures range from −89.2°C (−128.6°F), the lowest temperature ever recorded, in 1983, to around −50°C (−58°F) in areas near sea level. During the summer, temperatures on the Antarctic Peninsula can reach up to 15°C (59°F), although they generally remain lower across the rest of the continent, averaging around 0°C (32°F) along the coast and ranging from −20°C to −35°C (−4°F to −31°F) in the interior. Under such extreme conditions, how can architecture be conceived and constructed? How can we inhabit, protect, and preserve such fragile ecosystems with responsibility and environmental awareness?
Antarctic architecture is part of architectural modernity, engaging with the principles of the Modern Movement, postwar technological utopias, the radical experiments of the 1960s and 1970s, postmodernism, and the contemporary challenges of building and inhabiting environments under increasingly extreme conditions. Indeed, India's Bharati Research Station reinterprets Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye, Buckminster Fuller's ideas and geodesic structures take physical form in the South Pole Dome, and Archigram's Walking City concepts come to life in the United Kingdom's Halley VI Research Station.
Inhabiting the Extreme: An Architectural Biography of Antarctica reveals the history of a territory shaped by more than two centuries of construction, where prototypes of minimal living environments coexist with radical reinterpretations of the International Style, transformations of Soviet Brutalism, and the materialization of some of the great architectural utopias and dystopias of the postwar era. The 6044 SUR collective, formed by Victoria Nuviala Antelo, Violeta Nuviala Antelo, Ximena Senatore Connolly, Lucia Roitman, Lucila Salvo, Guadalupe Tagliabue, Paz Fodde, Melina Lotarynski, Sol Lavintman, Emilia Oszlak, Mariana Gigliotti, Nerina Estelrich, and Bautista Marull, was established to recover and document 200 years of human occupation in Antarctica, tracing an architectural biography that brings together successive layers of history.
 The history of Antarctic architecture is not separate from the history of global architecture. -- Violeta Nuviala Antelo, Director of SUR, Virtual Archive of Architecture and Habitat in Antarctica
The Search for Shelter: Exploring Antarctica (1800–1930)
Driven by exploration and exploitation, the earliest encounters with Antarctica were initially shaped by commercial and scientific interests. Among its first temporary inhabitants, sealers and whalers approached the continent's shores in search of marine mammals, constructing temporary settlements using locally available resources. Small stone shelters, covered with sealskins and furnished with materials derived from the animals themselves, such as whale vertebrae, were generally located near marine mammal colonies and occupied for short periods according to hunting seasons.
Scientific habitats, however, followed a more deliberate approach to planning and construction. Given the limited knowledge of Antarctic conditions, the earliest structures were designed in advance and, in many cases, prefabricated based on experiences in Arctic regions. Through compact layouts organized around shared spaces, these structures sought to optimize spatial efficiency, minimize surfaces exposed to the exterior, and consolidate the activities essential to survival and scientific research. Scientific expeditions also relied on complementary architectural solutions to explore the territory, combining prefabricated huts serving as base camps, pyramidal tents, and vessels that enabled movement inland and along the coast.
These different approaches to exploration reflected distinct relationships with the material world. While the earliest expeditions were ephemeral, flexible, and opportunistic, relying on architectural solutions shaped by locally available resources, these practices coexisted in the early 20th century with geographical and scientific exploration, which introduced planning and architectural design conceived from afar.
 "Despite their differences, these various ways of inhabiting the continent shared a common condition: inhabiting without remaining." -- Ximena Senatore Connolly
Building Permanence: How to Inhabit Antarctica (1940–1980)
As Antarctica shifted from a territory of commercial exploitation to an international domain dedicated to peace and science, the continent underwent a transformation. Following World War II, several countries renewed their focus on Antarctica, and its architectural landscape began to expand and take shape. Nations such as Argentina, Australia, Chile, and the United Kingdom developed strategies for exploration and long-term occupation alongside new architectural experiments. Some established small research stations at strategic locations, while others pursued approaches based on stations that gradually expanded their footprint across the landscape. By 1957–1958, the architectural landscape had grown increasingly diverse and complex, encompassing designs ranging from timber and metal structures to concrete buildings and even constructions made from plastic materials.
In 1959, with the signing of the Antarctic Treaty, twelve nations agreed to preserve the continent for peaceful purposes and scientific research. In the following decades, the Antarctic Treaty System expanded, incorporating additional nations and new legal instruments to protect the Antarctic environment. Over time, it established a framework for international cooperation and territorial governance, reflecting a model of coexistence and collaboration among dozens of countries, including Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Chile, China, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Russia, South Africa, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Uruguay, among others.
 Between polar Brutalism, minimal demountable structures, large elevated installations, geodesic domes, and underground stations, the Antarctic continent becomes a unique landscape of architectural modernity and postmodernity. -- Victoria Nuviala Antelo, Director of SUR, Virtual Archive of Architecture and Habitat in Antarctica
An Architectural Laboratory: Designing in Antarctica (1990–2026)
Antarctica emerged as a field for architectural experimentation; a territory for visionary possibilities and future scenarios. By the 1990s, the continent had become subject to the Environmental Protocol, marking a new phase in its protection. At the same time, its architectural landscape began to undergo a process of modernization, as countries upgraded their research stations and infrastructure to reduce their environmental footprint and minimize the impact of human activities on the continent. Architectural experimentation continued to evolve, with competitions becoming more frequent and new perspectives emerging on how to inhabit this extreme environment. These projects introduced new material, morphological, and siting strategies, establishing different forms of dialogue with the natural landscape, each nation's cultural heritage, and the temporal conditions and life cycles characteristic of Antarctica.
Architecture has also evolved into an environmental apparatus, integrating elevated volumes, elongated horizontal profiles, and sophisticated energy systems. The architectural landscape has come to embody modernity's futuristic vision. Yet as new research stations occupy the territory, older facilities must be removed, erasing traces of previous human occupation. Although Antarctica has no unified building codes or urban planning regulations, the protection of its nonhuman species remains a fundamental priority. Under the Environmental Protocol, obsolete structures and materials must be removed to prevent further environmental damage.
Antarctica thus emerges as a radical laboratory for technical, political, and environmental experimentation, where architecture operates simultaneously as shelter, infrastructure, and a geopolitical instrument. Inhabiting the Extreme: An Architectural Biography of Antarctica is a research project presented at the Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial. Seventy institutions contributed materials to the exhibition, which seeked to recover forgotten histories and invites visitors to consider Antarctica as a testing ground for possible futures of inhabiting extreme and uncertain environments.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Jio Platforms initial public offering (IPO), valued at $3.2 billion, was fully subscribed within two hours of opening Wednesday, marking the country’s largest-ever share sale.
The 302.13 billion-rupee ($3.2 billion) offering was subscribed 1.15 times by 10.45 am local time (0515GMT), with bids for 227.1 million shares against 197.5 million available, Indian financial news outlet Moneycontrol reported.

Musk backs SpaceX-Tesla merger as SpaceX reports $4.4B profit

Unknown Publisher

07:24:06 UTC
16:24:06 KST

Elon Musk said on Tuesday he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms.
Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield," but that a combination would be "a good idea."
Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly five percent in after-hours trading following the comments.
Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders.
He added that he could not take part in their talks because he has a conflict of interest.
Musk is chief executive of both companies, and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX.
He owned 48.4 percent of SpaceX as of June 30, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82 percent of its voting power through super-voting shares.
He holds about 20 percent of Tesla.
The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating it to treat a merger as a certainty.
Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle."
He said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.
His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier.
Revenue jumped 161 percent to $14.6 billion. The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street.
SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on June 12 after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion.
Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion and a net loss of $541 million.
The AI division, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI.
The unit's revenue rose more than nine times from a year earlier to $7.6 billion, overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales.
Cloud computing
SpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding startup.
SpaceX’s cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centres.
Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million a month from October through June 2029.
The AI unit turned an operating profit of $431 million, compared with a loss of $1.7 billion a year earlier.
As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy.
SpaceX invested $19.6 billion in the quarter, $16.4 billion of it in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion.
Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier.
Musk said he was "fairly confident" SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027.
That would come on top of the roughly 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year.
He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were "somewhat of a limiting factor."
Revenue at the Starlink satellite internet unit grew 69 percent to $5.2 billion, and consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million.
Average monthly revenue per consumer, however, fell to $69 from $83 a year earlier.
SpaceX also completed the first revenue-generating flight of Starship, the giant rocket central to Musk's Mars ambitions and to deploying satellites at scale.
The flight carried 26 next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit.

US officials familiar with the situation told the Journal that Musk capped the speeds of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine, rendering some of its military drones virtually useless.

But Trump told reporters Monday that he did not know who was responsible for the Starlink slowdown, adding: "but I would like to find out."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday that "we haven't pulled anything back," but "Starlink has the option to make decisions concerning its terms of service."
 
Without US assistance, 'there would be no Ukraine': Rubio
Responding to a reporter’s question on whether US national security advisor “should have been given a heads up on before” since it “is vital national security infrastructure for Ukraine,” Rubio said: “I'm not going to comment on what we knew that they might or might not do.”
“Suffice it to say that the reporting out there was that somehow the United States government was denying them something they needed in order to defend their country. That's not true. That's not accurate.”
“And for leaders in Ukraine to continue to represent that is also not accurate,” he added.
“There was no foreknowledge" and the US President Donald Trump "hasn't had nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," he added.
He, however, warned the Trump administration was “no longer going to be defensive about this topic.”
“Because… if it were not for the assistance of the United States, including under the Trump administration, there would be no Ukraine right now. Ukraine as a sovereign state would not exist.”
Rubio also clarified that the US military has a contract with SpaceX for Star Shield and “that's a different matter because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use.”

France loses a Mirage 2000D fighter in night crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:20:05 UTC
16:20:05 KST

- A French Mirage 2000D from Air Base 133 Nancy-Ochey crashed near Rogéville late on Oct. 20 while returning from a mission.
- One crew member’s body has been found and is awaiting identification, while the search for the second crew member continues.
A French Mirage 2000D ground-attack jet crashed late on Oct. 20 near the village of Rogéville in Meurthe-et-Moselle, in eastern France, as it was returning from a mission, killing at least one of its two crew members, while rescuers continue searching for the second. The French Air and Space Force said the accident happened at around 10:40 p.m., and the Ministry of the Armed Forces said in a statement on Oct. 21 that a body had been recovered and is awaiting identification.
The two-seat jet belonged to Fighter Squadron 2/3 “Champagne” at Air Base 133 Nancy-Ochey, the home of France’s Mirage 2000D fleet, and carried a fighter pilot and a weapon systems officer, known in the French Air and Space Force as a NOSA. Air force spokesman Col. David Pappalardo told French media that the crew consisted of a young pilot in training and an experienced weapon systems officer with many flight hours, that at least one of them was unable to eject, and that it is far too early to draw any conclusions about the cause.
Residents of Rogéville heard an explosion shortly before 11 p.m., and a drone located the wreckage at around 4 a.m. in fields and woodland between Rogéville, Tremblecourt and Domèvre-en-Haye, roughly midway between Toul and Pont-à-Mousson. Firefighters, gendarmes, teams from Air Base 133 and a rescue helicopter with thermal imaging have been searching an area of about 15 km (9 miles) around Pont-à-Mousson for the second crew member, with a command post set up in Rogéville.
Separate safety and judicial investigations have been opened to determine what caused the crash, the ministry said. The aircraft was not carrying weapons, according to French media, and officials have not said what kind of mission the crew had flown before heading back to Nancy-Ochey.
The Mirage 2000D is a two-seat strike aircraft built by Dassault Aviation to fly ground-attack missions by day and night in complex environments, and it has been one of France’s main combat jets in every major French air campaign of the past two decades, from Afghanistan and Libya to Mali and the fight against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. France received 86 of the jets, the last in 2001, and 55 are going through a mid-life upgrade worth about €532.5 million that adds new avionics, MICA air-to-air missiles, a gun pod and new guided bombs, with the first modernized aircraft accepted in April 2025 and the type expected to serve until at least 2035.
The crash is the deadliest accident for the Nancy-based Mirage 2000D fleet since January 2019, when a jet from the same base went down during a low-level training flight over the Jura mountains, killing Capt. Baptiste Chirié and Lt. Audrey Michelon. In August 2024, two Rafale fighters collided over Meurthe-et-Moselle near Colombey-les-Belles, about 20 km from the latest crash site, killing two crew members while a third ejected.
The search for the second crew member was still underway on Oct. 21, and the ministry has not released the names of the two airmen.

21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday urged operators of large artificial intelligence data centers to strike financial agreements with local communities and pay them dividends to ease public backlash over rising energy costs.
"If companies want to make their data centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a 'dividend,'" Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social, arguing that projects facing fierce local opposition quickly gain acceptance once direct economic pacts are reached.
Trump said facilities must produce their own power rather than draining public utilities. He maintained that new and large data centers are required to "make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid," asserting that such measures would prevent utility inflation and potentially yield "a substantial decrease" in electricity rates.
The US has more than 5,000 data centers, with facilities projected to expand roughly 9% annually through 2030, according to the US Department of Commerce.
The directive comes amid escalating friction over power consumption driven by the artificial intelligence boom ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Public surveys show strong bipartisan opposition, with a Gallup poll finding 71% of Americans resisting local developments over concerns that facilities will inflate residential utility bills.
The policy builds upon Trump's voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge established in March, which called on technology firms to cover all power generation and transmission costs.

07:16:23 UTC

Turkish space technology company Fergani has successfully deployed its sixth test satellite into orbit as part of SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 mission, manufacturer Baykar announced.
The FRG-100D4 satellite was launched from Florida and separated from the launch vehicle about 63 minutes after liftoff, reaching its target orbit at an altitude of 590 kilometres at 3.07 pm Turkish time (1207 GMT).
Fergani Space Technologies was founded by Baykar Chairman and Technology Leader Selcuk Bayraktar and developed the satellite using domestic engineering capabilities.
The company said FRG-100D4 incorporates several technological improvements over its predecessors.
Its domestically developed components include a reaction wheel, magnetic torque rod, magnetometer, inertial measurement unit, Global Navigation Satellite System receiver, steerable solar panels, battery pack, regenerative modem and phased-array antenna.
The satellite also carries an AI-powered computer designed to support more advanced missions.

IDF soldiers begin voting in Israel's election as 850 military polling stations open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:13:50 UTC
16:13:50 KST

Israeli soldiers began casting their ballots in early voting for the country's 26th Knesset election on Wednesday, with 850 military polling stations deployed across IDF bases and operational sectors ahead of the nationwide vote on October 27. The IDF said approximately a quarter of the polling stations are mobile, allowing troops stationed in remote locations and combat zones to exercise their voting rights. Military voting will continue until polling stations close on election day.
Col. Vered Ben Yehuda, the IDF's chief elections officer, said the military was committed to ensuring that every service member could vote, including soldiers engaged in combat operations beyond Israel's borders. "Our mission is to enable all IDF service members to exercise their democratic right to vote by secret ballot, even during operational activity and combat beyond the border," she said. "The IDF is a national army that will do everything necessary to ensure the elections are conducted properly."
Under the military's voting procedures, soldiers may cast their ballots at a civilian polling station corresponding to their registered address at the Interior Ministry or at any military polling station, provided they vote only once. The military system is designed to accommodate soldiers whose operational assignments prevent them from reaching their regular polling locations.
Voting at military polling stations uses a double-envelope system to preserve ballot secrecy and prevent duplicate voting. Soldiers place their chosen party's ballot slip inside a blue envelope behind a voting screen. That envelope is then inserted into a white outer envelope bearing the service member's identifying information.
Once voting concludes, the sealed military ballot boxes are transferred to the Central Elections Committee at the Knesset in Jerusalem for counting. Specially trained regional military elections officers are responsible for collecting the locked ballot boxes and maintaining supervision until they are formally handed over to election officials.
During the counting process, the blue envelope containing the vote is separated for counting, while the white envelope bearing the soldier's personal information is destroyed. The entire process of opening ballot boxes and counting votes is conducted by the Central Elections Committee, without IDF involvement, ensuring that military personnel can exercise their democratic rights while maintaining the secrecy and independence of the electoral process.

Emergency authorities ordered residents within a 1.6-kilometer (1-mile) radius of an industrial area in the US city of Toledo, Ohio, to evacuate late Tuesday following an active hazardous materials leak.

Lockheed Martin offers Ukraine its own version of the F-16
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:11:52 UTC
16:11:52 KST

- Lockheed Martin is promoting a Ukraine-specific F-16 version with longer range and a new AESA radar, sources at the company told The Defence Blog.
- Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19, praising the F-16’s role against Shahed drones and calling for the program to continue.
Lockheed Martin is promoting the idea of a special version of the F-16 fighter built around Ukraine’s needs, with longer range, a new AESA radar and stronger air defense capabilities, sources at the company told The Defence Blog.
The idea is being floated as the U.S. defense giant expands its work with Kyiv, and it surfaced days after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19 to discuss F-16 support and pilot training, the President’s Office said.
According to the sources, one option under consideration is a new F-16 variant with extended range and an AESA radar that would let pilots detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles earlier and faster than the radars on Ukraine’s current jets allow. The company is also looking at deeper integration of European weapons on the aircraft, including guided bombs and cruise missiles, which would give Ukraine more options than the mix of Western munitions its F-16s carry today.
No concrete negotiations on a new version are underway, the sources said, but the Ukrainian side has shown interest in an affordable, versatile fighter that its pilots have already mastered in combat. Lockheed Martin is counting on numerous joint projects with Ukraine, the sources added, and Zelenskyy said after the meeting that Kyiv wants the F-16 program to continue.
“It has been working from the first day the F-16 was used and still is today. Especially ahead of a difficult winter, during massive attacks with Shaheds, the F-16s destroy them. And we have a very good rate of destroying Shaheds. That is why we are very proud that we have this capability. Thank you very much. We are counting on the program continuing,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The F-16 has become the backbone of Ukraine’s air force since the first jets arrived in 2024, and the type now flies roughly 80 percent of all Ukrainian Air Force sorties, as we reported last year. One Ukrainian F-16 wing alone has been credited with downing more than 1,000 Russian Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles, and its vice commander told a U.S. audience that what Ukraine needed most was newer Block 70 jets and more missiles.
That request goes to the heart of the radar issue, since the F-16s that Ukraine received from European NATO members are older airframes upgraded under the Mid-Life Update program, which still rely on a mechanically scanned radar. Newer Block 70 aircraft use an AESA radar that can track more targets at longer range and is better at picking out small, low-flying objects such as drones and cruise missiles against the ground, which is the main threat Ukrainian pilots face during Russia’s mass overnight attacks.
At the Oct. 19 meeting, Zelenskyy also discussed work to let Ukraine service and repair its F-16s on its own territory, as well as larger deliveries of the anti-ballistic interceptors that Lockheed Martin builds for the Patriot air defense system, which the company is ramping up and part of which Kyiv hopes to buy. A Ukraine-specific F-16 would sit alongside the country’s other fighter plans, which include 16 Gripen E jets ordered from Sweden in June with deliveries from 2029 and a separate donation of Gripen C/D fighters, we reported at the time.
The sources did not say how much a dedicated Ukrainian variant would cost, how many aircraft could be involved, or which European weapons Lockheed Martin would prioritize for integration, and any such program would need approval from Washington before talks could move beyond the idea stage.

Life before Barents: Russian scientists reiterate Spitsbergen discovery discussion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:07:21 UTC
16:07:21 KST

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS Correspondents Maria Kartuz, Konstantin Malykh/. TASS correspondents visited the archipelago and gathered opinions about its discoverers. Why the discussion about the Pomors' early sites on Spitsbergen has faded away and how it may return to the scientific sphere - read about it in this material by TASS.
The archipelago discovery's stories vary. One of them, the most well-known and document-proven, is that the first discoverer was Dutch navigator Willem Barents in 1596. It is believed that he gave the name to the archipelago - Spitsbergen (Sharp mountains). Another story is related to Soviet archaeologist Vadim Starkov, who claimed that Russian hunters and fishers had known the land under the name of Grumant at least half a century before Barents. He proved the claim by results of own dendro-chronology analysis of wooden buildings' remains.
Scandinavian scientists insist the Vikings discovered the islands back in the 12th century, but any evidence is hidden in the depths of centuries and waters. Their claim is based on a single source - the Icelandic Chronicles of 1194, where the archipelago (Svalbard, or Cold Shores) was mentioned for the first time. This is exactly the name Norway uses for the archipelago nowadays. However, no traces of the Vikings have been found there, thus this story may be put aside for now.
As for the first two versions, historians are sure it is quite unreasonable that from the discussion stage they have moved into the stage of categorical claims. While Western critics used to study Starkov's conclusions, argued, offered reasons, nowadays the discussion has been artificially stopped, and the Norwegian museum ultimately presents the period of Grumant's Pomors as the term between 1700 and 1850.
"Nor should we take a hard line claiming the Pomors definitely were there in the middle of the 16th century. On the other hand, it is impossible to turn one version into an ultimate claim. There exist Starkov's conclusions, as well as a number of indirect arguments in favor of the Pomors' early presence on Spitsbergen, and there is also criticism of these data. We need to remain at the level of scientific discussion: double-checking arguments, searching for documents, and discussing methods," leader of the Russian Geographical Society's expedition to Spitsbergen Pavel Filin said.
The last great discovery
The discovery of Severnaya Zemlya in 1913 is commonly considered to be the last great geographical discovery on the planet. But the North's historical map still remains being incomplete. It contains territories of well-known routes, settlements, and even names of participants in events, but their sequence is not clear, and Spitsbergen is not an exception.
We talked with Pavel Filin at the Barentsburg Museum. The scientists have arrived in the archipelago on an expedition of the Russian Geographical Society to map the Russian cultural heritage on Spitsbergen. Collected artifacts are very numerous here. For example, a fragment of the Pomors vessel's hull - thick planks are connected by flexible bundles of steamed roots. The planks keep holes through which the "thread" passed, as well as the darkened surface, and traces of repair. Other museum showcases present fishing devices, household items, fragments of crosses. A map on the wall shows old settlements' locations.
Vadim Starkov's Spitsbergen expedition worked on the archipelago since the 1970s. The researchers managed to identify many monuments associated with Russian fishers and hunters, and the archeologist dated some of them to the middle of the 16th century. As for technical reasons of those who criticize Starkov - they may be shared or waived, but as for the logics - the story seems quite clear.
The Pomors' culture on the White Sea formed in the 15th-16th centuries, or even earlier. It was based on fishing, hunting sea animals, shipping, and seasonal sea navigation. The fishermen and hunters, guided by the approach "the sea is our field", traveled following the resources and developed fresh marine areas similar to the ways agricultural communities do.
The Pomors were sailing further on towards Spitsbergen to hunt walruses, arctic foxes, and to fish. People traveled and worked in teams, and brought supplies with them - they transported dismantled houses, bricks, and sometimes firewood. They used fins as fuel, but it was impossible to rely on them alone in the treeless archipelago. "Wintering is a specific technology," the scientist said. "They were to know how not to die there. Of course, many did die. But the Pomors had the experience of survival gained in the White Sea, on the Kola Peninsula, and Novaya Zemlya."
In the 17th century, Spitsbergen was a place of intensive European whaling. British, Dutch, French and German vessels entered the archipelago's waters in the summer, hunted whales, butchered the carcasses on the shore and left before the ice settled. Competition for fishing and hunting areas sometimes led to armed clashes. Noteworthy, European whalers did not practice wintering - only a few such cases are known, and those cases used to end tragically.
The Pomors' presence was different. For Russian hunters and fishermen, Spitsbergen was part of the northern economic area that required a long year-round stay. They were preparing for winter, hunted arctic foxes, repaired rigging and ships, and organizing life on the shore. The camps and settlements became a material trace of this approach.
There are many traces of the Pomors in the archipelago - settlements and camps, remains of crosses, burials, fragments of ships. Archaeologists have discovered about 70 camps, which is a significant number for the high-latitude territory. At the same time, the early period's documentary history remains fragmentary. According to the scientist, the earliest Russian document directly related to Spitsbergen, that he knows, dates back to 1710.
"This does not mean that Russians had not been there earlier. Documents from the early 18th century describe sailing to Grumant like a fully formed practice. Perhaps Russian documents from an earlier period are still to be found in archives. Besides, the Pomors' navigation is a traditional culture that has long existed in the oral form. People could understand from experience the winds, currents, prominent capes and landmarks. They could have not recorded such voyages in written sources," he explained.
The political formula
The dispute about who was the first acquired special importance back in the early 20th century. Norway gained independence in 1905, and in 1920 was signed the Treaty of Spitsbergen, which stipulated Norway's sovereignty over the archipelago with a special international regime of economic activity. In such a situation, the dispute about the discoverers reached an ideological level. Historical arguments have become part of discussions about cultural memory and national presence in the Arctic.
The expert believes that the history of Spitsbergen demonstrates most clearly how a research discussion may acquire a political sounding. "The historical science turns very easily into politics," he said. "The researchers, who argued with Starkov, presented counterarguments, and questioned the methods - this is a regular scientific process. But further on, the complex and interesting dispute has turned into a short museum formula."
What is permitted when nothing is permitted
Work with Spitsbergen's archaeological heritage continues under a strict regime of monument protection. Excavations, sampling, and removal of objects are significantly limited by the Norwegian legislation. Therefore, to re-test earlier stories, specialists need archives, museum collections, field reports, non-invasive examination methods and detailed fixation of objects on the ground. This is exactly the kind of data map that the Russian Geographical Society's expedition has been developing.
In the expedition, cartographer Alevtina Paramonova is responsible for the creation of the map's thematic basis. At first, she said, it is necessary to collect and compare various sources - archival plans, old maps, photographs, publications, field survey materials, and stories by local residents. "We have been working on maps of cultural and natural heritage. It's a special genre. We need to build a foundation, show periods, types of objects, and connections between them. The map must accumulate knowledge about the territory."
The map will present the archipelago's heritage as a linked system, said Egor Shevyakov of the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of Archaeology. "The map is needed to systematize knowledge: when Russia appeared on the archipelago, what types of activities it conducted there, and what objects have been preserved. This is the basis for conservation projects, educational programs, tourist routes, and for further research," he added.
The Pomors' wintering grounds on Spitsbergen will become the earliest and, perhaps, the most disputable layer of the future map. Anyway, the truth often lies somewhere inside layers of the kind.
The Russian Geographical Society has organized a comprehensive expedition to Spitsbergen to create a map of the archipelago's Russian historical and cultural heritage. The expedition participants are recording objects related to the Pomors ' culture, scientific expeditions, coal mining, and the history of Russian villages. They are working with archives and talk to local residents. The Russian Geographical Society has organized a press tour for Russian reporters to cover the expedition's work.

The right to enforce civil rights is under attack in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:06:41 UTC
16:06:41 KST

The right to enforce civil rights is under attack in the US
The Trump administration and conservative courts are restricting the ability of individuals and advocacy groups to challenge rights violations.
This autumn, the Supreme Court will consider a question with potentially far-reaching consequences for civil rights in the United States: Who gets to enforce them? On November 30, the justices will hear a case over whether employees of federally funded universities can sue under Title IX over alleged workplace sex discrimination. The Trump administration has urged the court to rule that they cannot, arguing that Congress never gave university employees a private right to bring such claims.
The dispute is the latest front in a broader legal push to restrict the ability of individuals and advocacy groups to take rights violations to court themselves. In June, the Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to a federal appeals court ruling that barred Arkansas United, an immigrant advocacy organisation, from suing to enforce protections for voters who need assistance at the polls. Across a growing number of cases, Republican-led states and the Trump administration are advancing the same basic principle: Unless Congress has clearly authorised private citizens to sue, enforcement should largely be left to the government.
That may sound like an arcane legal argument, but its implications are anything but. If individuals and civil rights groups cannot go to court when laws protecting them are violated, the power to decide which rights are actually enforced increasingly rests with the very government that may be violating, ignoring or choosing not to enforce them.
A private right of action allows individuals, or groups acting on their behalf, to file lawsuits to enforce rights protected by law. These lawsuits can seek compliance with the law or compensation for past violations. Private rights of action are not automatic under US federal and state law. Congress and state legislatures sometimes explicitly authorise private lawsuits. Where they have not, courts have had to determine whether a law implicitly allows individuals or groups to sue, or whether enforcement rests solely with government authorities.
In practice, private litigation has been an essential part of enforcing rights throughout much of US history. As University of Virginia School of Law Professor George Rutherglen writes in a 2015 law review article (PDF):
“The long history of civil rights, dating back to Reconstruction, makes them quintessentially private rights, whose exercise and enforcement should depend primarily on the initiative of the individuals who bear those rights. Public enforcement no doubt remains necessary, and it has an equally long and distinguished pedigree in civil rights law, but it cannot entirely displace individual control over individual rights.”
Proponents of private rights of action, such as AARP, consider them an effective tool for vulnerable individuals and groups to protect their rights when government agencies are unwilling or unable to act. Critics, such as the US Chamber of Commerce Institute for Legal Reform, however, argue that private lawsuits can encourage frivolous litigation.
These critics, often from the political right, have attempted to restrict private litigation through legal arguments against private causes of action. An example is the 2001 Alexander v Sandoval decision, in which a Supreme Court majority led by Justice Antonin Scalia ruled that Title VI did not provide a private right of action to enforce regulations prohibiting policies or practices with a disparate impact on protected groups – discrimination that can occur without clear evidence of intent.
The legal push against private rights of action has intensified in recent years. Republican-led states have increasingly challenged the doctrine of implied private rights of action, arguing that courts should reject private suits to enforce various types of rights. The Trump administration has also adopted this stance. When the court decided a 2021 voting rights case, Justice Neil Gorsuch submitted a one-paragraph concurrence, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, questioning whether “the Voting Rights Act of 1965 furnishes an implied cause of action,” despite that issue not being raised in the case itself.
The conservative push to restrict private rights of action has extended to a variety of areas. In June, the Supreme Court ruled against Falun Gong practitioners who accused Cisco Systems of helping the Chinese government develop surveillance technology used to facilitate their persecution, concluding that they could not pursue those aiding-and-abetting claims under the federal laws they had invoked.
One of the most consequential implications of restricting private rights of action is the threat to voting rights. In the Arkansas United case, the Eighth Circuit ruled that the immigrant advocacy organisation did not have the right to sue on behalf of non-native English speakers over the right to have language assistance in the voting booth. The ruling concerned Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But it extended a much broader argument already adopted by the Eighth Circuit: that private individuals and advocacy organisations cannot sue to enforce key provisions of the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court’s refusal in June to hear Arkansas United left that ruling in place.
This argument has also been pushed by Republican-led governments in two redistricting and vote-dilution cases: Board of Election Commissioners v NAACP in Mississippi and Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians v Howe in North Dakota. In May, the Supreme Court vacated judgments in both cases and sent them back for reconsideration in light of its ruling in Louisiana v Callais, without resolving the private-enforcement question. That decision sharply raised the bar for some racial vote-dilution claims, endangering the voting power of Black, Hispanic and Native American communities across the US. At the same time, conservative-controlled governments are attempting to deny members and advocates for these communities the right to even bring some of these cases before the courts, arguing that only the Department of Justice can initiate action over such voting rights violations.
The broader danger is that, as private rights of action are curtailed, enforcement of federal law increasingly depends on decisions made by the executive branch.
The Trump administration is now pursuing a different means of restricting private enforcement. The Clean Air Act explicitly gives private citizens the right to bring certain lawsuits, yet the Justice Department has sought to intervene and dismiss a case brought against xAI over allegations that gas turbines at its power facility in Southaven, Mississippi, are violating federal environmental law and polluting surrounding communities. The facility powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data centre in nearby Memphis. In September, the Justice Department appealed to the Fifth Circuit and sought to halt the case. The department has argued that allowing the suit to proceed would threaten national security and the US pursuit of global leadership in AI. Here, the issue is not whether Congress created a private right to sue – it did – but whether the executive branch can nevertheless step in to stop such a case when it conflicts with its priorities.
Relying solely on the Justice Department to pursue such cases at the federal level is a particularly dubious proposition under the current administration. The department has also been weaponised to target political foes of President Trump. Its Civil Rights Division has been steered away from defending the rights of racial and ethnic minorities and refocused on cases brought by white plaintiffs alleging so-called “reverse discrimination”.
The Justice Department’s current politicisation may be reversed under a future administration. But even then, the erosion of private rights of action would leave the enforcement of civil and political rights increasingly dependent on a federal agency with limited resources and subject to political direction. For example, as Democracy Docket noted in 2024, of the 216 active voting rights and redistricting cases it was tracking at the time, only five were cases brought by the Justice Department. As Professor Rutherglen noted in his article, to rely primarily on government actors to enforce rights “is to transform the nature of those rights: from private to public, from individuals to groups, from legal control by plaintiffs to political control by administrators.”
Private rights of action are now being eroded, case by case. Politicians, civil liberties advocates and organisations must challenge this trend before more avenues for enforcement are closed off. Otherwise, protections won over decades may become increasingly dependent on the willingness of government authorities to uphold them, leaving those whose rights are violated with fewer ways to seek redress.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Reporting on Gaza is our duty, but who protects us?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:04:07 UTC
16:04:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Reporting on Gaza is our duty, but who protects us?
It is that time of year when we Palestinians seem relevant again.
My inbox is flooded with interview requests about 7 October. Media outlets are interested in hearing my thoughts on the anniversary, and journalists want to know whether I condemn Hamas or not.
But what difference does it make?
Growing up, I dreamed of the day I would wear the press vest and helmet and tell the stories of Gaza to the world through my own eyes. I wanted to tell stories about how Palestinians love life, how they try to create something out of nothing, and how they try to bounce back after Israeli aggression and continue. I wanted to tell the stories of the Gaza I know, instead of the Gaza the media focuses on only when there is Israeli aggression or genocide.
But shortly after I graduated, it was 7 October.
In no time, wearing press gear became risky. Instead of protecting journalists and media workers, it made them a target.
Since the genocide began, over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including over 21,000 children, and this only accounts for the official numbers. Nearly 2 million people have been displaced, and 80% of the infrastructure in the Gaza Strip has been destroyed. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, 247 journalists have been killed, 174 injured, and 118 imprisoned.
Staying alive
For the first 45 days of the genocide, I was on the ground reporting closely with two colleagues, Hatem Rawagh and Mohammed Abu Safia. They were both fathers, carrying the responsibility of staying strong and, most importantly, alive for their children. They held on to the hope of watching them grow up, giving them a future, and seeing them live in a better world than the one they were reporting on.
I still remember how Nour, Mohammed’s youngest daughter, would call him while we were out in the field reporting. She would tell him “bahebak” (I love you) in her soft voice, still learning how to pronounce the word. I could see how those words affected him each time he heard them.
His family has always been his reason for living, but Mohammed’s desire to tell the world the truth in hopes that this carnage could end forced him to stay away from them. Every day, he wondered whether it was safe to visit his family, or whether going would put them at more risk of being targeted.
His biggest fear was that Israel would kill them because of his profession, and that he’d remain alive to bear that agony.
He thought a lot about what Wael Dahdouh endured. After learning that his family had been killed by an Israeli airstrike, the Al Jazeera journalist had to report on the tragedy.
This was not the only loss we shared.
Belal Jadallah, the founder of Press House Palestine, who was a father figure to all journalists in Gaza, was also targeted and killed by Israel. He trained so many of us, including how to stay safe and how to be careful with our language and terminology because of the weight they carried for the wider world.
I was with Hatem when he told us the news: “Belal got targeted with an Israeli tank shell, or an airstrike hit his car.”
If the person who taught us how to protect ourselves could not be protected, then the vest and helmet were certainly never going to be enough.
It always felt like the only certainty in Gaza was uncertainty.
We had watched Israel kill our colleagues one after the other. Many others had also been injured or imprisoned. Each time, we’d wonder who would be next as it became harder to escape.
We were surviving one day at a time, never knowing when our turn might come.
Duty
Hatem and Mohammed are still in Gaza, still reporting. They explain: “It’s our duty.”
Part of them still wants to believe that if the world learned more about what is happening in Gaza, the genocide would stop. But now, three years into it, we know it’s not enough. Knowledge without accountability and justice means nothing.
As journalists, our responsibility is to bear witness and tell the truth, and in Gaza, we risk our lives to do it. But the responsibility cannot rest on our shoulders alone. The rest of the world must also be willing to carry that truth forward, to turn what it knows into action.
I used to dream of telling the world how Palestinians love life, how they build something out of barely anything and keep going. Instead, I have spent the last three years telling the world how they are being killed.
Whenever I see the number of journalists killed on the news, I think of the families they left behind, and of the people who are still waiting for a call that will never come. Whenever I watch the news from far away, I imagine the journalists behind the footage, standing in the same streets in the same vests, wondering if today is their turn.
Now, three years into a genocide, there is less and less coverage coming out of Gaza, and it is because journalism itself has become a target.
Despite our colleagues around the world watching so many being killed in Gaza, which sets a dangerous precedent for the future of their own work, too many are contributing to the injustice through the so-called measured language they choose, the realities they obscure, and the violence they help justify and normalise.
So every year around this time, when those press requests come flooding in, I think about the journalists who are still in Gaza, still on the ground reporting, and who will never get an email asking for their expert opinion, their experiences of tragedy and destruction.
Hatem and Mohammed say it is their duty, but it should not be theirs alone.
Plestia Alaqad is an award-winning journalist and author who has emerged as a powerful voice in digital media. She gained international recognition for her heartfelt, on-the-ground reporting during the genocide on Gaza, where her raw, personal storytelling brought global attention to the human impact of the violence. She recently published her book The Eyes of Gaza, that became an instant New York Times, Indie, San Francisco, and Boston Global Bestseller.

Aussie mothers with postpartum psychosis 'falling through the cracks'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:03:35 UTC
16:03:35 KST

Report finds women with postpartum psychosis contact health services repeatedly
In short:
Many Australian women with postpartum psychosis actively seek help despite not understanding what is wrong with them, new research has found.
The rare mental health condition affects one to two in 1,000 new mothers and is considered a psychiatric emergency.
What's next?
The women interviewed by Flinders University researchers said healthcare staff needed more awareness of postpartum psychosis to identify it quickly.
Australian women with postpartum psychosis are "falling through the cracks", with some contacting health services dozens of times before getting care.
A new report by researchers at Flinders University found women were seeking help an average of seven times before receiving it.
The peer-reviewed report, published today in the Australian Journal of Advanced Nursing, interviewed 15 women diagnosed with postpartum psychosis.
The condition, which affects one to two in 1,000 mothers, is considered a psychiatric emergency, developing suddenly in the days or weeks after birth.
But many of the women interviewed said their symptoms were not met with urgent concern, lead author and provisional psychologist Donna McMahon said.
"One of the stand-out findings of the research for me was that all the women we interviewed recognised something felt wrong to them," she told the ABC.
"They all describe having this feeling soon after childbirth, but before other and more overt psychotic symptoms developed.
"None of the women thought to be disingenuous or hide their symptoms, they were actively seeking help.
"[But] they described feeling like their symptoms were going unheard and minimised when they were asking for help."
Women report a sense 'something was not right'
More than half of the 15 women interviewed by researchers had never been diagnosed with a mental health condition prior to developing postpartum psychosis.
The lowest number of contacts with the Australian healthcare system when seeking help was four times.
The highest number was 27.
Women often had recognised a "vague, yet persistent sense that something was not right soon after childbirth", the report said.
Many said they had requested to be taken to the hospital, identifying they needed "urgent" support.
"I can remember thinking I've got to get to the bottom of this," one woman told researchers.
"Like … I'm going to get everyone together. I need my doctor. I need my psychiatrist. I need to … work out what's going on."
But the process of getting help, according to the report, was "fragmented".
Many women found the healthcare professionals they spoke to were unfamiliar with postpartum psychosis, often underestimating or overlooking symptoms.
They found their symptoms were "invisible" until they deteriorated further.
"It was sort of determined that it was probably a bit of baby blues," one woman said.
"I had lost touch with reality in that next 24 hours."
More follow-up needed from healthcare staff
The report identified a "critical period" for detecting postpartum psychosis early in its onset.
Failure to get help when they first noticed something was not right, according to the women interviewed, left many of them experiencing worsened outcomes.
"We are very lucky to have a health system like we do in Australia … but just like any system there is room for improvements," Ms McMahon said.
"From our research, one of those areas is [that] we need to actively and carefully listen to women and families when they are presenting time and again, saying something isn't right.
"We found the women felt that healthcare professionals weren't asking enough follow-up questions or probing questions that could help [the women] articulate what this feeling was.
"One way that the system can improve on their detection of this disorder is by improving the awareness and knowledge of what postpartum psychosis is, how it may present."
The report noted some limitations, including that its small sample size had been recruited via social media support groups.
This, according to the report, may mean the women were "more engaged with services and willing to share their experiences".
"However the sample reflects the target population relevant to the study and provides a realistic snapshot of the help-seeking experiences of women within the Australian healthcare system," the report said.
The localised sample size also meant the findings were more specific to Australia, and should not be used to draw global conclusions.
Concerns among women put down as 'part of new motherhood'
Asked about the report, psychologist Ariane Beeston said having localised research was vital.
Ms Beeston was diagnosed with postpartum psychosis after the birth of her son, Henry, in 2011.
She has since written a book about her experience and now works for the Centre of Perinatal Excellence (COPE), Australia's peak perinatal mental health body.
"[Postpartum psychosis] has definitely been an under-researched area, so while the findings aren't surprising, it's so important ot have them documented," she said.
"One thing that stood out to me was just the fact [that] when we're at our most vulnerable, we're left navigating this really confusing, fragmented system that's often ill-equipped to meet our needs.
"The other thing [was] concerns being dismissed and minimised, or put down as simply being part of new motherhood."
She said the number of women in the report who had actively sought help had surprised her.
"[I] and other women found it really difficult to speak up and ask for help, and certainly were fighting [or] downplaying symptoms,"
she said.
"I think while there are women who are very proactive and presenting to health professionals … there's still a lot of stigma and shame around this condition.
"It's not the case that everyone feels comfortable enough to seek help."

Pollard gives figure for Albion class write-down
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:00:51 BST
16:00:51 KST

The remaining economic value written down when the Royal Navy’s two landing platform docks left service was about £195 million for HMS Albion and £233 million for HMS Bulwark, a combined figure of roughly £428 million, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for a breakdown of the remaining economic value of each Albion class vessel at the time of the write-down recorded on page 139 of the department’s Annual Report and Accounts for 2024-25, published on 4 November 2025.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The remaining economic value written down was approximately £195.3 million for HMS Albion and £233.2 million for HMS Bulwark. The hon. Gentleman will know that this is the write down value and not a cost or payment made from the Defence budget.”
A write-down is the accounting recognition that an asset the department still carried on its books no longer has the service life it was assumed to have, and no money moves when it happens. The figure measures what the Treasury’s accounts said the ships were still worth on the day the decision was taken to stop using them.
Bulwark carrying a higher residual value than Albion follows from her refit history, since she had been in extended readiness and had received investment that Albion’s longer operational run had already consumed. Both ships were commissioned in the early 2000s, Albion in 2003 and Bulwark in 2005, and both were designed for a service life running towards 2033 and 2034.
The withdrawal came in the fleet decisions announced in late 2024, when the department confirmed that the two assault ships would go alongside a frigate and other units, and this publication reported at the time that the Albion class assault ships and a frigate were to be scrapped. The crews were reassigned across the fleet in the months that followed.
