Liverpool fought back from two goals down to claim a dramatic 4-3 victory over Villarreal on Tuesday, while Phil Foden scored his first UEFA Champions League hat trick as Manchester City defeated AEK Athens 5-1 on Matchday 3.
The Spanish visitors stunned Liverpool at Anfield in the fourth minute when Georges Mikautadze capitalized on Virgil van Dijk's misplaced header and finished past Alisson Becker.
Villarreal doubled their advantage in the 29th minute as Nicolas Saliba's through ball caught Liverpool's defense out of position, allowing Sergi Cardona to slot the ball into the bottom left corner.
However, Liverpool began their comeback seven minutes later through Alexis Mac Allister, who headed home Kostas Tsimikas' cross following a corner.
The Reds completed their first-half recovery in stoppage time when Rio Ngumoha delivered a cross to the far post, where Ronald Araujo headed home to make it 2-2.
Liverpool took the lead for the first time in the 65th minute as Ngumoha beat Cardona on the right flank and cut the ball back to Mac Allister, whose first-time finish struck the crossbar before finding the net.
Just three minutes later, Florian Wirtz extended the hosts' advantage, converting Cody Gakpo's pass with a low shot through Renato Veiga's legs.
Villarreal refused to surrender, with Tani Oluwaseyi pulling a goal back in the 87th minute after meeting Ayoze Perez's cross at the far post.
However, Liverpool held on to complete their comeback and secure a thrilling 4-3 victory. 
Foden hat trick powers Manchester City past AEK
Manchester City cruised to a 5-1 victory over AEK Athens at the Etihad Stadium, with Phil Foden scoring three times.
City opened the scoring in the 12th minute through Elliot Anderson, who netted his first goal for the club after Enzo Fernandez's free kick struck the crossbar, leaving him to finish the rebound into an empty net.
Foden doubled the hosts' advantage in the 34th minute, firing into the roof of the net after exchanging passes with Rico Lewis following a move initiated by Rayan Cherki.
City took a 2-0 lead into halftime, but AEK pulled a goal back seven minutes after the restart through Stavros Pilios, who finished into the bottom right corner after being played through by Zine.
The hosts responded five minutes later as Cherki cut inside from the edge of the box and beat Brignoli to restore their two-goal advantage.
Foden added his second goal in the 65th minute, meeting Lewis' pass with a first-time strike into the top corner following a diagonal ball from Cherki.
The England international completed his first Champions League hat trick in the 76th minute, converting Ryan McAidoo's low cross from close range to seal City's 5-1 victory.

UN experts call on India to stop using ‘excessive force’ against protesters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
01:43:38 UTC
10:43:38 KST

UN experts call on India to stop using ‘excessive force’ against protesters
UN experts have called on the Indian government to stop the use of “excessive force” in the wake of the crackdown on opposition and student protests in India.
In a statement on Tuesday, the two dozen independent experts pressed for an impartial investigation into Indian authorities’ conduct, saying that demonstrators had sustained injuries and some reported being subjected to ill-treatment.
“Protesters have sustained injuries, with some reporting being subjected to ill-treatment. The experts expressed particular concern about reports of sexual violence and other forms of gender-based abuse in the protests and related detentions,” according to the statement.
UN experts are appointed by the UN Human Rights Council to monitor and document specific human rights crises but are independent of the organisation itself.
India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), along with other opposition parties and student organisations, has led protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, after 130 million names were removed from voter lists.
The protesting groups said the removal disproportionately affected poor and homeless people as well as ethnic minorities including Muslims, who are unlikely to vote for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The BJP and India’s Election Commission deny the accusations. The Election Commission said it was removing duplicate, deceased, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters and that anyone excluded in error can pursue appeals.
‘Deployed force’
“Despite the non-violent nature of the assemblies, law enforcement agencies have reportedly deployed force against unarmed students including by means of police so-called lathi charges, and have prevented thousands from joining the protests,” the UN experts said.
Lathi charges are coordinated movements by a policing force using sticks to disperse crowds.
“We call on the authorities to immediately cease the use of excessive force, rescind blanket assembly bans, and refrain from the misuse of digital surveillance, including through biometrics, and internet disruptions,” they added.
India has repeatedly dismissed such criticism and cast it as interference in the country’s internal affairs, including when the UN human rights office earlier this month expressed concerns over mass detentions in relation to the latest protests.

Diyar Güldoğan
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied any change in Washington’s policy toward Ukraine, saying the Pentagon had not issued directives to restrict satellite communications services and was seeking to ensure that US forces have sufficient supplies of Patriot missile interceptors.
“There’s a lot of things that have been said in the press that are not true about the Department of War,” Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, when asked about reports that the Pentagon was delaying transfers of Patriot interceptors from allied countries to Ukraine.
“We haven’t changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians, but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well,” he said.
Hegseth added that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was aware of the situation.
Asked whether his assertion that US policy toward Ukraine remained unchanged also applied to coverage provided by the Starshield satellite network, he said Washington had not withdrawn any support.
“We haven’t pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied with, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” he said.
“But nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that,” Hegseth added.
His remarks came amid reports questioning the Trump administration’s handling of military assistance to Kyiv and the status of satellite communications services used by Ukrainian forces.

U.S. Army to take over training of Ukrainian troops in Germany

2026-10-21

U.S. Army to take over training of Ukrainian troops in Germany
Ukrinform reports this, citing the U.S. military outlet Stars and Stripes.
“The colors casing for Joint Multinational Training Group-Ukraine marks a shift for how we will support training requirements for our Ukrainian partners on a more permanent and sustainable path,” Col. Michael Weisman, a senior spokesman for the Army in Europe, said in a statement Monday.
He stressed that the reorganization did not mean a reduction in U.S. support for Ukraine or in the United States’ commitment to meeting Ukraine’s defense needs.
Weisman said the U.S. Army would continue coordinating support for Ukraine’s Defense Forces through U.S. European Command and NATO’s Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine (NSATU) mission, in line with U.S. policy.
A ceremony marking the end of the Vermont Army National Guard’s 86th Infantry Brigade Combat Team (Mountain) mission was held at the Grafenwoehr military base in Bavaria on October 15, according to Stars and Stripes. The brigade had led the Joint Multinational Training Group–Ukraine (JMTG-U).
The training will now be conducted by regular U.S. Army units under U.S. Army Europe and Africa and the 7th Army Training Command, which are already stationed in Germany. Training will continue at facilities in Bavaria, including Grafenwoehr, home to one of Europe’s largest military training complexes.
The JMTG-U mission began in 2015 at the Yavoriv training center in Ukraine. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, it was relocated to Germany.
Over the past decade, approximately 150 U.S. National Guard personnel have supported the mission, deploying to Europe on nine-month rotations. They trained Ukrainian troops in combined-arms warfare and coordination among different military branches.
The Vermont Army National Guard’s unit was the 18th and final rotation under this arrangement.
According to U.S. officials, American instructors have trained more than 24,000 Ukrainian service members since the mission was relocated to Germany in 2022. The training covered 50 weapons systems, types of equipment, and specialized training areas, with approximately 300 courses conducted.
As reported, in August, The U.S. Secretary of War directed U.S. European Command (USEUCOM) to oversee the reorganization of Security Assistance Group-Ukraine (SAG-U) and realignment of roles and responsibilities across components, and NATO Security Assistance and Training-Ukraine (NSATU).

Heading to France? Amid recent unrest, here’s what to know

Heading to France? Amid recent unrest, here’s what to know
Ceylan Yeginsu and Tariro Mzezewa
- Anti-government protests in France have turned violent, with more than 2,000 arrests and nearly 1,000 police officers injured, according to the French Interior Ministry.
- Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities have seen clashes, fires and damage to public buildings, while curfews and gathering bans have been imposed in some areas.
- Tourist sites stay mostly open, but the Louvre closed after protesters blocked it, and travellers are told to avoid protest areas, check updates and expect transport disruption.
AI generated
PARIS - Anti-government demonstrations across France escalated into widespread violence over the weekend, as thousands of protesters clashed with the police, set municipal buildings and cars on fire, and ransacked storefronts.
The unrest, which began in September as largely peaceful, student-led protests over the quality of the public education system, spiralled into the country’s worst rioting in decades, with more than 2,000 arrests and nearly 1,000 police officers injured, according to the French Interior Ministry.
To reassert control, the authorities issued curfews in parts of several cities on Oct 19, including Paris, Nice and Lille.
More demonstrations have been planned over the next two weeks. Here is what you need to know if you plan to travel to France soon.
What parts of France have been affected?
Paris became the epicentre of demonstrations over the weekend, with major clashes and rioting at Place de la Republique and surrounding avenues. Many of the shops across Les Halles were looted and vandalised, while the Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde became flash points for stand-offs between the police and protesters.
Marseille, France’s second-largest city and a popular tourist destination, also saw significant unrest, with protesters breaking into City Hall and ransacking the building, leaving graffiti and knocking over the bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic. In response, the authorities banned public gatherings in the city between noon and 8pm.
In Lyon, tens of thousands of protesters marched through the city on Oct 17, and some set fire to the city’s tourism office. Other major cities – including Bordeaux, Lille, Calais and Limoges – also experienced violence and damage to public buildings.
Is it safe to visit Paris?
While Paris is generally considered safe, government travel advisories, including those from the US State Department, urge citizens to avoid protest areas and exercise increased caution because of civil unrest. Travellers have also been advised to follow local media outlets for updates on planned demonstrations.
The next major protests are scheduled for Oct 24, Oct 31 and Nov 5, with the Yellow Vests, a populist protest movement, calling for gatherings at Place de la Bastille and Place de la Republique. But times and routes have not been finalised and are awaiting police approval.
By Oct 20, major streets in central Paris had been cleaned up and Parisians had returned to work, although many storefront windows remained broken, and burnt cars and bikes littered the streets.
Parks, including Luxembourg Gardens, Tuileries Garden and Parc Monceau, were calm. At cafes, people sat on patios with coffee and wine, and tourists and tour guides went about their days as planned.
Sophie Gacheny, an independent tour guide based in the city, urged visitors to stay on the Left Bank, or the southern bank of the River Seine, which is typically quieter during protests. Like other guides, Gacheny is planning her tours around the protests and will not run any on the days when demonstrations are scheduled.
Kiana Tiese, who offers private tours of Paris, said she took a group of visitors out for a tour on Oct 18, a day after the protests, and said everything went well.
How are tourist attractions affected?
While most major Paris landmarks including the Eiffel Tower and Arc de Triomphe remain open, local authorities can close them on short notice if large-scale protests pass through them.
On Oct 19, the Louvre was forced to shut down after protesters blocked the entrance, causing anger among tourists who had paid for their tickets. The museum has not announced when it will reopen.
The tourism board, Paris Je T’Aime, advises travellers to monitor live updates through its website and dedicated city pass app, which provide real-time updates on operating hours for major landmarks and venues.
Municipal buildings, shops and outdoor monuments have been damaged across other major cities too, creating road closures and areas with restricted access. Be sure to check the status of a landmark and surrounding areas before travelling there.
How is local transportation affected?
French unions have called for a nationwide general strike on Nov 5, which could affect the national rail, public transit networks and roads. Under French law, transportation workers must file notice of a strike at least 48 hours before the planned action.
On demonstration days, the police shut down metro stations and roads along protest routes, and bus and tram schedules are reduced.
Are there curfews?
French authorities imposed curfews on Oct 19 across parts of several major cities, including Paris, Lille, Lyon and Nice.
In Paris, the authorities enacted strict curfews in areas where demonstrations turned violent, such as Place de la Republique and the Les Halles commercial district.
The authorities banned public gatherings in those areas between 8pm and 6am, and prohibited people from being in public outdoor spaces across dozens of districts between 11pm on Oct 19 and 6am on Oct 20.
The police set up checkpoints around the perimeter of the curfew zones to verify the identities of residents and exempt emergency workers. It was unclear how long the curfews would last.
At the five-star Hotel Lancaster Paris, steps from the Champs-Elysees, hotel guests sipped drinks and ate French tapas on the night of Oct 19 in the lobby’s plush Copperbay cocktail bar.
The rest of the neighbourhood was equally tranquil, with no police or sirens in sight. Along the tree-shaded grand boulevard, international crowds strolled under the wrought-iron streetlamps, window-shopping at big global stores including Sephora and Zara.
Lauren Bell, 38, who was visiting the city with her sister from Madrid over the weekend, said that while the city felt calm on Oct 20, people also seemed to be preparing for the next wave.
“We were shocked to see how quickly and badly the situation got violent and out of control,” she said. “It feels like it’s not over.”
Will my travel insurance pay if I decide to cancel?
Whether your travel insurance will cover trip cancellation depends on your policy. Most standard policies do not cover civil unrest, but if you purchased a “cancel for any reason” policy and meet the conditions, you may get reimbursed for your trip. NYTIMES

The top three eligible National Olympic Committees (NOCs) in the team final earn quota places for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games, with each qualifying team entitled to send five gymnasts.

Led by Olympic all-around champions Daiki Hashimoto and Shinnosuke Oka, Japan secured its eighth world men's team title and second in succession, adding to its team gold at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games.
Hashimoto scored 14.866 on the high bar in the final rotation, while Fusuke Maeda contributed 14.333 to help Japan seal victory.
Britain led after four rotations but dropped out of the medal places after errors on parallel bars and the high bar, finishing fourth with 247.395.
Switzerland placed fifth with 246.497, followed by the United States with 245.161, the Netherlands with 241.294 and Colombia with 240.093.
The women's team final is scheduled for Wednesday, followed by the men's and women's all-around finals on Thursday and Friday, respectively. The apparatus finals will be held on Saturday and Sunday. ■

BERLIN, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Paris Saint-Germain beat Barcelona 4-2 in the UEFA Champions League on Tuesday, with Vitinha and Fabian Ruiz scoring late to settle a contest in which the visitors twice equalized.
The defending champion started aggressively, forcing Barcelona into mistakes near its own penalty area. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia struck the post after two minutes, while Ousmane Dembele and Desire Doue also threatened early on.
Barcelona gradually created opportunities of its own, but PSG goalkeeper Matvei Safonov denied Raphinha and Gordon in quick succession. Both sides suffered first-half injuries, with Dembele and Dani Olmo forced off.
PSG regained control and broke through in the 38th minute. Barcelona failed to close down Doue outside the area, allowing the forward to score from distance. Safonov then kept out Fermin's effort as the visitors sought an immediate response.
Barcelona improved after halftime and drew level in the 55th minute when Fermin released Xavi Espart, who finished for his first Champions League goal.
The hosts restored their advantage after Ferran Torres struck the post. Lucas Hernandez rose above Gordon to head in from the resulting corner in the 72nd minute.

The victory kept PSG top of the league-phase standings with nine points from three matches. Barcelona remained on six points in fifth place after suffering its first defeat of the season.

S. Korea's September producer prices rise on holiday demand, utility hikes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:30:10 CST
10:30:10 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Prices for goods and services among South Korean suppliers rose for the second straight month, fueled by holiday-driven agricultural costs and higher utility bills, central bank data showed Wednesday.
The producer price index increased 0.2 percent in September from a month earlier, after ticking up 0.1 percent in the previous month, according to the Bank of Korea.
The growth was led by higher farm goods prices ahead of the late September traditional Chuseok holiday, alongside higher residential electricity rates after the summer progressive billing discount came to an end.
Producer prices for agricultural, livestock and fishery products advanced 2.6 percent month-on-month in September.
Prices for electricity, gas, water and waste among suppliers rose 1.3 percent, propelled by a 13.4 percent surge in residential electricity rates.
Prices for industrial products, including oil products, remained flat as higher chemical product prices offset a decline in prices for computer, electronic and optical devices.
Service prices were down 0.1 percent, affected by lower room rates for hotels and tourist lodging facilities. ■

Speaking earlier on Wednesday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio that police have not yet determined a motive for the attack.
The 43-year-old man appeared at Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday morning and did not apply for bail. ■

Burnham’s Britain can learn from Trump in engaging with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
01:30:05 UTC
10:30:05 KST

Burnham’s Britain can learn from Trump in engaging with China
While an IPAC report accurately notes that Britain is woefully unprepared to get relations with China right, the audit’s ideological framing is unhelpful
Getting relations with China right is widely seen as Britain’s epoch-defining challenge. It is also one it is woefully unprepared to face.
So concluded a recent audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), which highlighted that top negotiators lacked basic Chinese language skills. More critically, it exposed a deeper deficit: a poor grasp of China spanning political elites and the public alike. This is rooted in a desk-bound classroom sinology rather than a nuanced appreciation and lived immersion.
Yet IPAC’s audit will do little to fix this deficit. Indeed, its ideological framing will deepen it.
The report depicts China as a neo-totalitarian state seeking to engineer the souls of its citizens. It alleges that this coercive ambition extends globally, that Beijing seeks to upend the liberal world order to usher in an era favourable to authoritarian imperialism.

France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots and what to learn from them
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
02:22:51 BST
10:22:51 KST

Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them
- Published
"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"
Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.
I'd stopped Elisabeth and her friend to ask their thoughts on what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.
"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."
But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.
Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.
The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.
French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.
French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black, folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.
A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left.
It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. LFI denies this.
The mass looting of what is said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?
Emmanuel Macron, who is on his way out as president and viewed by many in France as a lame duck, and his government are accused of dropping the ball and failing to keep the country safe on Saturday.
Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.
Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts have led former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.
Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's interior minister, Bernard Quintin, warned of the "TikTokisation" of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liège on "known far-left groups".
In France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire", said Nuñez. On Tuesday Lecornu spoke of "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".
Previously he had accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.
It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.
Mélenchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.
What do the students say?
In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students had organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians.
"Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.
But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."
France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.
The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.
Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist prime minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy."
Mélenchon went on to apparently imply Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances".
France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.
As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's interior minister admitted there were not enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance.
Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.
Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration National Rally party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.
She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said.
She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness".
She ended her video by reminding French voters they would have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in six months' time.
Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed-border message and, like US President Donald Trump and US Vice President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday. French authorities have not implicated migrants in the violence.
One teacher called Mar complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services", she said.
"Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."
Public frustration with politicians
But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system".
That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium.
These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives.
What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask.
Voters increasingly say they are losing faith in traditional or governing political parties to listen to concerns and address them. The young look at climate change, social inequality, impossible housing prices and AI potentially threatening their place in the job market.
According to opinion polls conducted by this year by Pew, 69% of people in France are dissatisfied with democracy. In Spain, it's 68% and in Italy, 62%. The US is experiencing similar disillusionment with 69% saying they are dissatisfied with how democracy is working.
So many people I've spoken to in France since Saturday's riots emphasise the importance in making a clear distinction between angry but peaceful protesters, and those intent on wreaking violent havoc.
Politics aside, is what we're now seeing in Europe's protest wave perhaps a powerful cocktail of a bubbling over of frustration, cries for help for the authorities to listen but also, for some, a dark sense there's little left to lose?

US jails Guatemalan man for 30 years over deadly smuggling operation

01:01:25 UTC

US jails Guatemalan man for 30 years over deadly smuggling operation
The 2022 incident resulted in the deaths of 53 immigrants trapped inside a tractor-trailer in dangerously high heat.
A Guatemalan man has been sentenced to 30 years in a United States prison for his role in a human-smuggling operation that killed 53 migrants trapped in a truck – a disaster that had been described as one of the deadliest such incidents along the US-Mexico border in recent history.
US District Judge Orlando Garcia handed 39-year-old Rigoberto Ramon Miranda-Orozco a 30-year prison term on Tuesday, more than a year after his extradition from Guatemala in March 2025.
He was first arrested in Guatemala in August 2024, as part of a cross-border effort to dismantle the human-smuggling network.
The charges stem from a fatal incident on June 27, 2022. According to the US Department of Justice, emergency crews discovered dozens of people trapped inside an abandoned truck in a remote area on the southern outskirts of San Antonio, Texas.
A total of 64 migrants had endured a lengthy journey that began in Guatemala and continued through Mexico across the border into the US.
By the time the truck was driving from Laredo, Texas, to San Antonio – a distance of 250km (155 miles) – prosecutors say the air conditioning had stopped functioning. When the truck was discovered, temperatures were approaching 32C (90F).
Forty-eight people were pronounced dead on the scene, and five more died while receiving emergency medical treatment for heat-related illness and dehydration.
Among the dead were six children and a pregnant woman. Of those killed, 21 were Guatemalan nationals.
Miranda-Orozco has admitted to arranging travel and accommodation for two of the migrants who died in the truck and another who survived but suffered grave injuries.
He pleaded guilty in July to conspiring to bring a migrant into the US resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting the unlawful entry of migrants resulting in death and serious bodily injury.
According to The Associated Press news agency, Miranda-Orozco is among a group of nearly 20 people sentenced in the US and Guatemala in connection with the tragedy.
Felipe Orduna-Torres, identified as the leader of the operation in the US, was sentenced to life in prison in a federal court in San Antonio in June 2025.
Armando Gonzales-Ortega, described by prosecutors as Orduna-Torres’s top assistant, received an 83-year sentence.
Further proceedings remain pending, including in the case against the truck driver.
According to prosecutors, investigators found signs of passengers’ desperate attempts to escape the abandoned truck. Some had reportedly removed clothing. Scratch marks on the trailer’s interior, meanwhile, suggested that some people had clawed at the walls in a futile bid to escape.
The prosecutors said the passengers had paid as much as $15,000 for passage across the border.
“It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” US Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a Tuesday news conference following the sentencing.
The I-35 highway near where the truck was found runs through San Antonio from the Mexican border.
It is considered a popular smuggling corridor because of the large volume of truck traffic, Jack Staton, a former senior official with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), told the Reuters news agency at the time.
The administration of President Donald Trump has cited the need to end human trafficking as a rationale for his crackdown on irregular immigration across the southern border.
But critics have argued that hardline enforcement tactics may drive immigrants to pursue more dangerous methods for crossing the border irregularly.

RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' as next decision looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
01:01:00 UTC
10:01:00 KST

RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' ahead of November meeting
In short:
The RBA deputy governor says there are signs some people do not expect inflation to come back to the RBA's target, which is "central banker's nightmare".
Markets are putting the chance of a November rate hike at more than 50 per cent.
What's next?
The RBA's rate-setting board will next meet at the beginning of November, with a decision handed down on Melbourne Cup day.
Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the inflation outlook is "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike as soon as November.
Just under a fortnight out from the next interest rate decision, Mr Hauser warned high inflation was becoming entrenched in the Australian economy.
"We are beginning to see some signs that some people in the community are not sure if we're going to bring inflation back into target at all, or certainly not for an extended period," Mr Hauser told the Citi Investment Conference in Sydney.
The RBA targets headline inflation between 2 and 3 per cent on average over time.
Inflation currently sits at 4 per cent, according to the August consumer price index.
Mr Hauser said the central bank's liaison program and surveys showed there was "an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that, maybe, sort of 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent [inflation] is the new normal".
"Look, that is the central banker's nightmare.
"We can't allow expectations to shift away from target."
Market pricing now puts the chance of an interest rate hike in November at 51 per cent, based on Bloomberg data.
The odds of a hike next month had dipped below 20 per cent last week, after the unemployment rate reached a five-year high in September.
UBS chief economist George Tharenou described Mr Hauser's remarks as "hawkish" and said the investment bank was forecasting a November rate hike.
"Hauser's comments today are consistent with our view of the likelihood the RBA staff provide an explicit recommendation at the November meeting to raise the cash rate," Mr Tharenou said.
The RBA will release its quarterly forecasts in its Statement on Monetary Policy on November 3, the same day the interest-rate-setting board next hands down a decision.
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese agreed that the RBA official was setting the stage for a Melbourne Cup day hike.
"Despite the steadfast claims that the Reserve Bank is no longer in the business of offering forward guidance, its signals to the market in recent weeks have rarely been clearer," Mr Bassanese said.
"In short, the RBA seems increasingly prepared to risk a recession to get inflation down – given it has been above target for an extended period and it is sensing evidence of rising inflation expectations within the community."
"It remains possible the RBA board vote will be split, and the external members have a majority to hold rates, and hence effectively 'outvote' Bullock and Hauser," Mr Tharenou said.
However, even if the RBA holds rates in November, he still would expect "a 'hawkish hold', with the RBA retaining a tightening bias … and also setting up a hike at the subsequent meeting in December".
'Laying shorter-term pain on top of pain'
Mr Hauser reiterated the "hard choices" facing the RBA as it balanced the pressures on prices from the Middle East crisis, the AI and technology boom and weak productivity growth.
Asked about the pain of higher interest rates hitting many households, on top of cost-of-living pressure, the deputy governor said: "It's a continuous challenge to explain this."
"The reason is that, even though we are laying shorter-term pain on top of pain, it's to prevent a longer and potentially far worse pain down the track if inflation expectations get locked in," Mr Hauser said, echoing comments RBA governor Michele Bullock has made as the central bank has lifted rates.
Mr Hauser downplayed concerns about the state of the jobs markets, saying there was potentially "noise" in the numbers, after the unemployment rate rose to 4.7 per cent in September.
"That said, it clearly was a little weaker than we and others have been expecting," he said.
"I stress the 'little'. These unemployment numbers in Australia are still right at the bottom or very near the bottom of G20 out-turns on labour markets."
He said "no lost job is one to celebrate" but the labour market needed to soften.
"We need to see some easing in the economy, whether [the unemployment rate] goes to 5 [per cent], whether it goes to some other number," Mr Hauser said.
"That's a debate we're having in the context of our forecast at the moment, and you'll see our answers to that in a week or two."

From ideas to impact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
01:00:11 UTC
10:00:11 KST

From ideas to impact
- From university entrepreneurship to community trials and industry partnerships, Sino Group is helping promising technologies move beyond the development stage and into wider use.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
The HKUST-SINO One Million Dollar Entrepreneurship Competition and Impactathon take different approaches to helping promising ideas move from early concepts to practical applications in businesses and communities.
Across these initiatives, Sino aims to connect innovators with communities, universities and businesses at critical stages when feedback, practical experience and industry connections can help their ideas gain momentum.
Supporting ideas at an earlier stage
Launched in 2011, the HKUST-SINO One Million Dollar Entrepreneurship Competition gives aspiring entrepreneurs access to training, mentorship, investors and industry contacts as they develop technologies and business models.
Support after the competition continues through HKUST InnoBay 1M PLUS, which gives promising teams access to real-world application scenarios, industry networking, partnership matching and proof-of-concept opportunities as they progress from technology validation towards market adoption. Smart City will be its first theme.
According to David Ng, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of Sino Group, this initiative seeks to connect young ventures with partners across government, industry, academia and the community, as well as businesses and investors that can help promising ideas progress towards application.
“Through the HKUST InnoBay 1M PLUS programme, we hope to connect promising teams with start-ups, industry partners and investors, opening up more opportunities for collaboration, application and commercialisation,” he said.
Partners include Samsung Electronics, Cyberport, Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation and the Smart City Consortium. Companies from the competition’s mainland regional contests will also gain access to Hong Kong’s industry, investment and business networks.
The finalists this year showed why young companies can require different kinds of support.
For Waveity, the immediate challenge is putting the technology into a full-scale operating environment.
“Our first priority is full-scale deployment because we still need to validate the idea under real-world conditions,” the team said after the competition. “After that, we can potentially look at Hong Kong infrastructure and try to implement the technology here.”
Prof Carrie Ling, Director of the HKUST Entrepreneurship Centre, said early-stage companies often need time to establish customers, refine products and produce evidence that investors can assess.
The need for support does not end once a technology leaves the university or competition setting. The next challenge is often seeing whether it works for the people it was designed to serve.
Impactathon addresses that stage by matching start-ups with community organisations in the Northern Metropolis, enabling them to test their solutions with residents and refine them through direct feedback.
More than 50 partners participated in the five-month programme, including the Northern Metropolis Co-ordination Office (NMCO), Social Ventures Hong Kong (SVhk), over 10 start-ups and six local universities. More than 1,000 residents and stakeholders were engaged, while seven community partners helped identify local needs before start-ups worked directly with the people their technologies were intended to serve.
Hong Kong healthtech start-up GOFA had developed a solution using AI to screen older people for fall risk and provide exercise training, intervention and ongoing monitoring. What the team had lacked was direct access to its intended users.
Through Impactathon, GOFA was paired with the Chinese YMCA of Hong Kong and invited 28 older people to try its solution.
After refining the solution through the community trial, GOFA received both the Grand Prize and Most Innovative Award at Impactathon.
For start-ups such as GOFA, direct user feedback can reveal design and usability issues that are difficult to identify during development alone.
Melanie Kwok, Deputy General Manager for Sustainability and Innovation at Sino Group, said: “What is most important is that the business sector can provide an application setting.” She added that feedback gathered from operating properties or customers can help start-ups refine their products, while industry connections may open doors to more opportunities.
Beyond community-based trials, Sino’s property portfolio has also served as a testing ground for emerging technologies, while Sino Inno Lab provides a platform for proof-of-concept development and pilot projects.
Established in 2018, Sino Inno Lab has engaged more than 800 innovators and supported more than 140 technology solutions.
As a start-up matures, it may need university guidance, industry contacts, community trials and investment at different stages. Access to these networks, user feedback and real-world testing can help promising technologies progress towards wider adoption.

Musk ordered cuts to Ukraine's Starshield services, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:56:29 UTC
09:56:29 KST

SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukrainian forces, sparking panic in Kiev and causing confusion within the Trump administration, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal (WSJ).
US officials familiar with the situation told the WSJ that Musk capped the speeds of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine, rendering some of its military drones virtually useless.
Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision before and after the slowdown became public last week, according to sources cited in the report, while the president made clear that he had not ordered it.
Musk posted on X hours after the slowdown became public that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the acronym for the President of the United States.
However, Trump told reporters on Monday that he didn't know who was responsible for the Starlink slowdown, adding, "but I would like to find out."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday that "we haven't pulled anything back," but "Starlink has the option to make decisions concerning its terms of service."
"We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth added.
Starlink makes the call as a private company
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also denied any US government involvement in the reported Starlink slowdown on Wednesday.
“Starlink is a private company. They have a contract. They have contractual terms upon how that technology can be used. The important point is we cannot direct a private company as to the decisions they make or not make,” Rubio told reporters in India’s financial capital Mumbai.
“What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States, nor anyone in our system, ever requested that any changes to that system be made, and that's what we said repeatedly,” Rubio said.
“There was no foreknowledge" and the US President Donald Trump "hasn't had nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio added.
‘No longer defensive’
He, however, warned the Trump administration is “no longer going to be defensive about this topic.”
“Because… if it were not for the assistance of the United States, including under the Trump administration, there would be no Ukraine right now. Ukraine as a sovereign state would not exist.”
Rubio also clarified that the US military has a contract with SpaceX for Starshield and “that's a different matter because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use.”
"Musk acted unilaterally”
After the Starlink slowdown was carried out, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that "Ukrainians could die if the unrestrictive service wasn't restored."
Some US officials told The Wall Street Journal that "Musk acted unilaterally and that Trump didn't specifically order any retribution against Ukraine."
Ukraine uses Starshield, Starlink's military-grade satellite service, for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes, and its interceptor drones. It also uses SpaceX's parallel Starlink civilian satellite system.
Relations between Washington and Kiev have been increasingly tense in recent days, with Trump calling for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced after he slammed a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

Brazil's cellphone theft crisis takes center stage in presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:47:42 UTC
09:47:42 KST

Brazilian content creator Tabata Lenk had just lost her job in São Paulo and was sitting in traffic when two assailants on a motorcycle smashed her car window and snatched her new cellphone from the dashboard. Footage of the robbery, which took place in late August and was captured by her dashboard camera, quickly went viral.
The reactions underscored how an urban nuisance has become one of the defining issues in this year's presidential election, which culminates in a runoff Sunday. Although cellphone thefts in Brazil have been declining since 2023, approximately 830,000 cases were still reported last year, according to the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.
While Brazil's homicide rate has fallen 40% over the past decade, reaching 15.4 per 100,000 people in 2025, cellphone thefts remain a reminder of how far the country still has to go to make its more than 210 million residents feel safe. A survey conducted in March found that cellphone theft ranked as Brazilians' fourth-biggest public safety concern, ahead of stray gunfire and home burglaries.
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, who will face off in a closely contested presidential runoff Sunday, are both seeking to demonstrate a tough stance against cellphone thieves. Earlier this year, incumbent President Lula signed a law increasing penalties for the theft of electronic devices to up to 10 years in prison and launched a platform for registering devices and reporting thefts. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, is proposing a minimum sentence of eight years in prison for any cellphone theft.
Lenk says the robbery left her feeling so unsafe that she did not resume driving alone until she had her car windows tinted. "No one should be afraid to leave their house, walk in the street, or use their own cellphone," she says. "So, I believe choosing politicians committed to public safety is essential."
Brazil is one of the world's most digitally connected countries, with social media and digital payments playing a central role in daily life. In this environment, cellphones have become virtually indispensable. Natasha Bachini, a researcher at the University of São Paulo's Center for the Study of Violence, says the prevalence of cellphone theft helps explain its political impact.
"It's far more common for someone to know of, or have been exposed to, a case of cellphone theft than a car theft, a homicide, or a kidnapping," she says.
Cellphones are expensive in Brazil, and replacing a stolen device can be a major financial burden. A Deutsche Bank study found that tariffs, taxes and the weakness of the local currency make Brazil the world's second-most expensive country in which to buy an iPhone 17 Pro. A new device costs about $2,260, compared with $1,181 in the United States.
Even more modest devices represent a major expense for many Brazilians. The average price of a cellphone in 2025 was approximately 2,310 reais ($456.83), equivalent to about two-thirds of the country's average monthly income.
Thieves are often just as interested in gaining access to victims' online bank accounts as they are in the devices themselves. With the rapid expansion of digital financial services in Brazil, led by the central bank's Pix payment system, fraud cases involving stolen devices more than quadrupled between 2024 and 2025.
Lenk experienced this firsthand. After stealing her phone, the criminals withdrew 2,000 reais from her bank account using Pix.
"It's terrible to experience the violence of having your cellphone stolen, but realizing that someone invaded your privacy and managed to steal money from your account is downright agonizing," she says.
As Brazil's most populous state, São Paulo accounts for nearly one-third of all cellphone thefts nationwide, with 268,184 devices stolen there last year. Only a small fraction of stolen phones are eventually returned to their rightful owners.
Between June 2025 and September 23, 2026, São Paulo state police located 38,028 cellphones and returned 11,445 devices to theft victims.
One of the lucky ones was 17-year-old student Natalia Eduarda Benvindo, who could hardly believe it when police recovered her stolen phone.
"I asked, 'are you joking?'" Benevindo recalls. "I couldn't even believe it at the time, wow! I was really happy."
Her experience, however, is rare. Whichever candidate, Lula or Bolsonaro, can convince voters that he will keep their phones safe from now on could pick up a handful of crucial votes.
In a race in which polls show Bolsonaro leading Lula by just a few tenths of a percentage point, those votes could make all the difference.

PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:42:08 UTC
09:42:08 KST

The PNG Chiefs have unveiled the club's logo and a supporters' jersey.
The logo was designed by a team of graphic artists in PNG and brings together elements representative of the country.
What's next?
The Chiefs will enter the NRL in the 2028 season.
The PNG Chiefs have unveiled the club's inaugural logo and jersey ahead of its debut NRL season in 2028.
Revealed at a breakfast rich with singing, dancing and performance, the designs reflect Papua New Guinea's diverse cultures, according to the franchise.
Fashion designer Tabu Pelei, the artist behind the jersey, said finding a motif that could unite a country with over 800 different tribes was a challenge.
"I thought what better way than a kundu [drum], which is a cultural item that is found in every part of Papua New Guinea," she told the ABC.
A kundu drum is a musical instrument made from wood and animal skin that is often used in traditional performances.
Pelei said she also drew inspiration from the country's natural landscape and a tattoo from her own tribe, which represents sweat and tears.
"I needed to include that in the design because of the process that it took to get the country through to the NRL," she said.
It is also a theme that will resonate with foundation Chiefs like Jerome Luai, Alex Johnston and Brian To'o.
"These are sporting icons for … not PNG alone but all over the Pacific and Australia. They'll be wearing one of my designs, [I'm] so extremely proud and excited," Pelei said.
With several marquee signings already announced, PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson hinted at more to come.
"November 1 is looming so you will see lots of things happen in the next couple of weeks but I can't reveal any of those secrets at this point," she told the ABC.
There has been speculation the Chiefs are looking to recruit star half back and Penrith Panthers player Nathan Cleary, who is free to begin contract negotiations next month.
But for now, McPherson is focused on the branding reveal, which she described as a defining moment for the new club in a nation obsessed with rugby league.
She said the unveiling of the logo marked "one of the most significant milestones in the journey of the PNG Chiefs".
"This is the first time that our club has its true, complete identity — a logo and jersey that our players, partners and fans can hold to as their own," McPherson said.
"The logo of the PNG Chiefs tells a story about Papua New Guinea — our people, what makes us strong and what makes us unique.
"The jersey of the PNG Chiefs is more than what players wear when they take to the field; it is a symbol of belonging, unity and the opportunity to represent millions of Papua New Guineans on the national stage.
"We know the responsibility that comes with establishing this club and we are incredibly proud to show our club to the world today.
"We strive for the PNG Chiefs to be something our country is proud of in every way — not because of the success that we will achieve on the field, but for the opportunities and legacy we will create for our country."
Elements of the PNG Chiefs logo
As per the PNG Chiefs media release
The feather headpiece: Inspired by Papua New Guinea's ceremonial plumes, the five feathers represent strength, beauty, chiefly status and national pride, with the Southern Cross connecting the club to the nation's flag.
The cassowary bone: Inspired by warrior traditions, the cassowary bone symbolises chiefly status, courage, power and the fighting spirit of the team.
The face: The chief's face represents the shape of Papua New Guinea, with ceremonial red paint showing a nation united through one warrior, one team and one purpose.
The kina shells: Representing traditional wealth, trade and prestige across Papua New Guinea's coastal, island and highland communities, the kina symbolises the value, legacy and future the club is building for the nation.

Rights advocates say the government has deployed national security reasons to target critics and used isolated cases of fraud to broadly target immigrant communities such as the Somali American community in Minnesota.
While Trump campaigned in 2024 on stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult, for example by imposing expensive fees for certain work visas.

Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX network, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:35:05 UTC
09:35:05 KST

Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX satellite network, sources say
A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.
The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week.
Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.
It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X.
Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown.
"I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service.
"We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success."
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday there were still limits on Ukraine's Starshield service.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink.
The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close.
What happened in Ukraine?
Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones.
The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things."
Zelenskyy has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored."
The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week.
"There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend.
Why have Trump and Zelenskyy clashed?
Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S., and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down.
A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.
Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.
In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.

NASA advances lunar rover development for future Moon Base
China
Unknown Publisher

08:34:50 CST
09:34:50 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- NASA on Tuesday provided an update on the development of crewed and robotic lunar rovers to support its planned Moon Base initiative, highlighting efforts to develop the surface mobility capabilities needed for future exploration and sustained human operations on the Moon.
NASA's Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover is scheduled to embark on a mission to the lunar South Pole region in 2027 to explore permanently shadowed craters in search of water and other potentially valuable resources that could support sustainable lunar exploration.
The rover will be delivered to the lunar surface by Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 1 lander and is expected to travel more than 30 kilometers, collecting data on local temperatures, lighting conditions and terrain.
NASA said the data could help scientists better understand the origin and distribution of water on the Moon and assess how lunar resources might be used to support future exploration.
Meanwhile, NASA has awarded task orders to Astrolab and Lunar Outpost to build the first phase of Moon Base rovers capable of carrying crew, called lunar terrain vehicles (LTVs), which are intended to reach the Moon ahead of crewed Artemis missions.
Blue Origin has been tasked with delivering the rovers to the lunar South Pole region by 2028 through NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative.
The LTVs will allow astronauts to explore geologically diverse areas near the lunar South Pole, collect samples and transport equipment. They will also be remotely operated from Earth to map the lunar surface before astronauts arrive, NASA said.
According to NASA, the LTVs are designed to travel up to 10 kilometers on a single battery charge, support up to three moonwalks per Artemis mission, and carry up to 80 kilograms of lunar samples and tools.
"Lunar rovers are central to our surface mobility strategy," said Robert Pickle, director of NASA's Surface Mobility Office within the Moon Base Program.
Their performance will help lay the groundwork for the mobility systems needed to build, operate and expand infrastructure for long-duration lunar exploration, he said. ■

Germany’s most popular party targeted by unknown hackers

2026-10-21
00:33:14 UTC
09:33:14 KST

Hackers target Germany’s most popular party
Germany’s most popular party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), has suffered a massive cyberattack, with unknown hackers reportedly stealing and publishing hundreds of thousands of internal emails, while the country’s political establishment seeks grounds to outlaw the opposition party.
The breach, which was first reported by Bild on Tuesday, reportedly exposed 421,179 emails totaling 281 gigabytes, including correspondence involving AfD co-chair Alice Weidel, honorary chairman Alexander Gauland, and other senior party figures.
The leaked material reportedly includes photographs of identity documents, bank statements, invoices, membership applications, and internal party lists. Bild said it examined a small sample of the files, including an identity card belonging to Markus Frohnmaier, the deputy leader of the AfD parliamentary group in the Bundestag.
The identities and motives of the hackers are unknown, and the authenticity of the published material has not been independently established.
The AfD confirmed that a hosting provider working with the party was hacked in September, but disputed suggestions that its current communications systems was compromised.
“Only a few email inboxes were unlawfully copied, most of which had not been used for years,” a party spokesman told Bild, adding that current federal party email accounts were unaffected.
The AfD condemned the breach as an “attack on the German party system and therefore on democracy” and said it reported the cyberattack to the security authorities.
No statement from investigators or condemnation of the breach by senior government officials has emerged as of early Wednesday.
The leaked correspondence has already drawn scrutiny from activists seeking to outlaw the party. Valentina Chiofalo, a representative of the German civil liberties organization Gesellschaft fuer Freiheitsrechte, told taz that the stolen emails could help strengthen the case for banning the AfD, while their publication and journalistic scrutiny could also shape public opinion against the party.
The attack comes amid an escalating campaign by Germany’s established political parties to isolate and potentially ban the AfD. The Euroskeptic party, which advocates stricter immigration controls and opposes Berlin’s military support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia, has surged to 30% support in the latest INSA poll for Bild, opening a 12-point lead over Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU/CSU bloc, which has slumped to 18%.
Earlier this month, the AfD secured the presidency of Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament for the first time, breaking through the political ‘firewall’ maintained by establishment parties. Its rise prompted Social Democratic parliamentary leaders to demand the creation of a federal-state working group to examine a possible ban, accusing the AfD of threatening democracy from within and promoting extremism.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has also sought to classify the party as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization, but a Cologne court blocked the designation in February pending further legal proceedings.
The AfD has rejected the accusations, portraying the proposed ban as an attempt to overturn the will of millions of voters and eliminate political competition.

Why former FDLR fighters are returning to Rwanda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:25:43 UTC
09:25:43 KST

Why former FDLR fighters are returning to Rwanda
From the forest to Mutobo, former fighters face the challenge of rebuilding their lives after leaving the armed group.
Musanze, Rwanda – Jean Claude Hategekimana feared that returning to Rwanda could cost him his life. After years with the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), he decided to leave the armed group and return home. At Rwanda’s Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre, he began preparing for civilian life.
Born in 1996 in Rutsiro District, in western Rwanda, Hategekimana moved to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) with his parents and grew up in an area controlled by the FDLR. He joined the group in 2018, underwent military training and eventually reached the rank of captain.
“I arrived at the Mutobo Centre after fighting to defend Goma. Following our defeat, I fled to Masisi. After realising that I was fighting for nothing, I decided to return to Rwanda. I came back on February 24,” he told Al Jazeera.
Hategekimana said FDLR members had been taught that anyone who returned to Rwanda would be killed.
“Upon arriving in Rwanda, I realised that the FDLR had been lying to us. For me, returning home felt like embarking on a suicide mission,” he said.
His experience illustrates the challenge of reintegrating former fighters whose beliefs and fears have been shaped by years in an armed group.
Rebuilding civilian life
Francis Musoni, secretary-general of the Rwanda Demobilisation and Reintegration Commission, said the Mutobo centre, located in Musanze in Rwanda’s Northern Province, was established in 2001 to receive members of the FDLR and other Rwandan armed groups returning from the DRC.
The FDLR emerged in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsis. After the genocide, members of the former Rwandan armed forces and militia groups fled to what was then Zaire, now the DRC. The Rwandan government accuses the FDLR of carrying out attacks against Rwanda and contributing to cross-border insecurity.
At Mutobo, the rehabilitation programme includes medical care, psychosocial support, civic education and assistance with reconnecting with families. Returnees can also contact relatives and friends through a telephone service, Musoni said.
“We help them to build confidence among themselves, build trust, and empower them to go back into the community and contribute to the development of the country together with their families,” he said.
The centre also allows visitors and media representatives to meet returnees. Musoni said those undergoing rehabilitation can visit their communities for short periods to help rebuild their confidence in returning home.
“They can travel to their communities [during rehabilitation]. They are given written permission for a week or two, and we even facilitate transport,” he said.
Different journeys home
For the former commanders interviewed by Al Jazeera at Mutobo, the decision to leave the FDLR was shaped by family ties, disillusionment and concerns about personal safety.
Major-General Anastase Munyaneza served in the former Rwandan armed forces in Kigali’s Kicukiro District during the 1994 genocide. He said he left Rwanda after the genocide and later joined the FDLR, eventually commanding its South Kivu sector.
Although he had come to accept the group’s beliefs, Munyaneza remained in contact with his family in Rwanda. News of their lives made him question his own circumstances.
“I was the only one who had fled to the DRC. I regularly received news about them. I knew they were still alive, attending school, working for the government and improving their lives. I began asking myself what I was doing in the forest,” he said.
He added that seeing other members return safely encouraged him to consider going home.
Munyaneza said he contacted personnel from the United Nations Organisation Stabilisation Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), who transported him from South Kivu to Bukavu and then to the Congolese-Rwandan border. He subsequently proceeded to Mutobo.
Lieutenant-Colonel Idrissa Bizimana, who was responsible for ideology, propaganda and recruitment within the FDLR, said his decision to return followed a change in his convictions.
“I no longer believed in the ideology I had been promoting. After receiving verified information about what was happening in Rwanda, I decided to return home,” he said.
Bizimana said he had been in contact with a MONUSCO general who had offered to help him return. Using a satellite phone equipped with GPS, he sent his location and the date. A helicopter was then dispatched to retrieve him, he said.
Lieutenant-Colonel Emilien Mpakaniye, who joined the FDLR in 1998 and was responsible for economic affairs at its headquarters, said he began questioning the organisation after becoming disillusioned with what he described as its lies.
Colonel Augustin Nshimiyimana, a former FDLR intelligence commander, returned to Rwanda in 2022 and underwent rehabilitation at Mutobo. He said he decided to leave after another commander accused him of working with Rwanda following a disagreement over a mission in Bujumbura.
Nshimiyimana said the accusation made him fear for his life.
“When they accuse you of working with Rwanda, it means they consider you a Tutsi, and the next step is to kill you,” he said.
Preparing for a new life
At Mutobo, former fighters receive education and practical support to prepare for life after discharge.
Febronie Mukankiko, a teacher at the centre, said teaching people who grew up in the forest required a different approach.
“Our students are different from ordinary students. They are adults who grew up in the forest, so teaching them requires special skills. We undergo additional training to ensure that we can teach them effectively,” she said.
She added that completing their studies could be a significant achievement for those with limited access to formal education.
“When they graduate and receive their certificates, they are very happy,” she said.
Musoni said the average stay at the centre was five months, after which returnees completed a formal discharge process. He said assistance could include financial support, vocational training, formal education and help establishing income-generating activities. The commission also follows up with former residents to assess how they are adjusting to life in their communities.
For those who have spent years away from Rwanda, leaving Mutobo marks the start of another transition: finding work, reconnecting with family and adjusting to civilian society.
For Mpakaniye, disillusionment came partly from the contrast between the lives of senior commanders’ families and those of ordinary fighters.
“First, their family members live in Rwanda and in Europe, while ours are in the forest,” he said.
