What's behind the pile-on for 'Oscar contender' and stinging satire, Digger?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

What's behind the pile-on for 'Oscar contender' and stinging satire, Digger?
Imagine being at the top of your game in Hollywood after a lifetime of hard work and using that privilege to create one of the most daringly original art-house satires since Dr. Strangelove.
Then imagine being in an era of online film criticism when reviewers can appear eager to take the wind from the sails of a high-stakes project the moment it's launched.
Digger director Alejandro González Iñárritu and the film's star, Tom Cruise, must feel stuck in the doldrums.
With accusations of "auteurist grandstanding", being an "insufferable slog", and an obsession with opening weekend box office takings, words such as "flop" have been bandied about as if Digger was a terrible "misfire".
What it is, however, is a brilliantly executed modern take on the satire that will almost certainly be nominated for several Oscars, and one with a sharp sting that will ache long after you've left the cinema.
That's my subjective view, of course, and Digger is not without flaws. But I wonder if some critics unable to objectively credit the craftsmanship at work here — whether they liked the film or not — had something else on the mind.
Indeed, a large divide has already appeared between published reviews and audience feedback. Aggregator sites such as Metacritic and Rotten Tomatoes are giving the film audiences score of 7.2 and 76 per cent, respectively, compared to aggregated critic scores of 46pc and 53pc.
There has also been a surge in passionate defenders of Digger on social media as people encourage others to ignore the commentary and see it themselves — a request Warner Bros (in damage control) has also adopted while urging viewers to "decide for yourself".
"There definitely seems to be a push for the film to fail, with reports immediately surfacing about much the film is losing after a less than stellar opening weekend," Adelaide University's Peter C Pugsley said.
The School of Communication, Media and Journalism associate professor said "attention-seeking headlines throw around figures like a '$250-million loss' without indicating the film's important messages about the excesses of corporate greed, political corruption, and our willingness to stand by as environmental devastation occurs".
"Some critics write at length how 'awful' the film is, but then engage in some serious fence-sitting about how it might be a worthy Oscar contender."
Ben Affleck has likened the phenomenon of the pile-on to "high school bullying" and "cultural schadenfreude" or, in regular speak, tall poppy syndrome and taking pleasure in seeing prominent figures fall.
So what is going on?
A 'sport' in trashing big budget films
Melbourne Cinematheque president and RMIT University Associate Professor Adrian Danks said the film's trailer may have contributed to animosity because it was largely seen as being misleading.
He also said it was becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish between professional reviews and "the much wider ecology of film reviewing and commentary".
"That said, there is a trend to treat some large budget Hollywood films in this fashion," Dr Danks said.
"There is a tendency to be critical of high-budget, seemingly somewhat personal films that might seem something of an overstretch, and in this case starring an actor hardly beyond criticism … in the social media age, once this process starts, it's hard to stop."
He said it was not uncommon for the public to occasionally round on Cruise, usually for his wider public profile rather than his acting.
"This is also something of a sport," Dr Danks said.
"Think of the many films that have suffered this fate, for one reason or another, dating back to at least the 1960s and including films like Paint Your Wagon, Heaven's Gate, which is probably the closest parallel, Waterworld, etc."
Dr Pugsley said prosthetics made Cruise mostly unrecognisable in Digger but, because his role was necessarily "over the top", some critics might have seen it as "blatant Oscar-bait appeal for him to finally win Best Actor".
"Or is it a case of rewriting Iñárritu's legacy of films like The Revenant and Birdman, the latter described disparagingly by one critic as a film defined by its 'splashy theatrics'?" he said.
"Quite the accusation. Has that critic seen Barbie, perchance?"
There have been plenty of highly favourable reviews published about Digger, of course, and they continue to emerge. But for now, at least, they remain outnumbered.
Is it groupthink?
Dr Danks said the early negatively that emerged was unlikely to be a case of groupthink, but rather a matter of needing to get a review or opinion "out there as fast as possible".
"We are a long way from an era where longer-form criticism — say, the writing of Pauline Kael — could make a significant difference, as a film was released in stages," he said.
"But there is also some glee in playing the game that the major studios play, where a film is made or broken on its first weekend."
Dr Danks also pointed out that there were "far fewer paid reviewers" today, and that the modern mode of criticism was often dependent on "less measured reviews".
"Most reviewers are required to give a star-rating and, I imagine, encouraged to be a bit more polarising, in keeping with the wider culture," he said.
It's worth pointing out that another satire that took aim at political failures and corruption regarding climate change mitigation, 2021's Don't Look up, was also panned by critics on its release.
Like Digger, it shares a disparity between critic responses and audiences': 49pc and 6.6 respectively on Metacritic, and 56pc and 78pc on Rotten Tomatoes.
On that occasion, however, there was a sense some media agencies didn't like how the film held a somewhat unflattering mirror to their faces.
Newsrooms are packed with big egos, after all, and having their image bruised by a film like Digger, in which Cruise's character sinks a cowboy boot into society's hypocrisy over its demand for fossil fuels, is unlikely to win it friends — even if it's true.
"The negative reviews all seem to touch on the same 'problems' with the film, including that it is too 'heavy-handed' in its critiques of capitalism," Dr Pugsley said.
"To take a more conspiratorial stance, one could argue that the owners of the mass media are increasingly willing to take the sides of the mega-rich and the fossil fuel industries, adding pressure on critics or editors to downplay such a revolutionary film as Digger."
As well as Affleck, a growing list of celebrities and artists including Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Neil Young, Tom Waits, Guillermo del Toro, Ron Howard and Alfonso Cuarón have come out publicly to defend the film.
They've warned that when daring, big-budget films such as Digger are rejected, it results in less risk-taking by studios and more homogenised films (think Marvel and tired superhero franchises).
"I think a stand is also being made here, by people like Affleck and Young, that we do need to support films like this emerging from the mainstream, films that are outside the norm, ambitious and socially critical," Dr Danks said.
He said many films suffering the fate of Digger found supporters and were often reassessed at a later date.
"I would say it's generally true that we don't really know the true value of a film until much later," Dr Danks said.
"Many of the films we celebrate now, particularly from Hollywood, were much less successful, financially and critically, when first released."
This includes classics like Blade Runner, John Carpenter's The Thing, Fight Club, The Shining, Vertigo and Metropolis.
Regardless of your tastes, a cultural phenomenon is underway in our cinemas.
For me, Digger is a level-four — sorry, four-star — film at least, and I'll probably see it again, if I can convince someone to join me.

NEW DELHI: Three sites from India have been added to the tentative list of United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization's World Heritage Convention, the Permanent Delegation of India to UNESCO announced on Tuesday.The three sites are the Karst-mud-volcano Complex of Baratang and Andaman Subduction Volcanoes in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and the Sirpur Cultural and Archaeological Landscape in Chhattisgarh.In a press release dated October 20, the Permanent Delegation of India to Unesco, based in Paris, announced the additions to India's Tentative List under the UNESCO World Heritage Convention.Inclusion on the tentative list is a prerequisite for any property to be considered for nomination to the World Heritage List. India ranks sixth globally and second in the Asia-Pacific region.
The five countries with the highest numbers are Italy with 62 sites, China with 61, France with 56, Germany with 55 and Spain with 50.India’s first four sites were inscribed in 1983: the Ajanta Caves and Ellora Caves in Maharashtra, and Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal in Uttar Pradesh. These were all cultural sites recognised for their historical, architectural and artistic significance.

Mother of all bombs or father of all missiles?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:28:22 UTC
03:28:22 KST

Mother of all bombs or father of all missiles?
In a note, Etemad examined US rhetoric about using the “Mother of All Bombs” and Iran’s response that it could employ the “Father of All Missiles.” The paper argued that Iran’s statements do not necessarily mean such bombs would be ineffective, nor that Tehran has publicly revealed the nature or scope of any potential response. Political declarations, deterrent warnings, and military operational plans are three distinct matters.
The verbal clash between the “Mother of All Bombs and the Father of All Missiles” reflects a battle of narratives more than a definitive answer to a military question. Washington seeks to intimidate through displays of destructive power, while Tehran emphasizes its retaliatory capabilities and the costs of any attack. Ultimately, the impact of either narrative will depend not on the names of bombs and missiles but on real military capabilities, political decisions, and the consequences of any confrontation.
Khorasan: Iran has achieved many of its war objectives
Khorasan argued that Iran has already achieved many of its goals in the conflict. According to the paper, many of the developments currently unfolding in Europe are a result of Iran’s actions. While Western governments had intended to dedicate significant financial resources to supporting their populations, they have instead been forced to return to older policies to manage the economic consequences of the war. This has led to growing public dissatisfaction and notable social reactions. The newspaper claimed that Iran has already attained a large portion of its objectives: it succeeded in limiting the conflict from a national to a regional level, forcing its foes to operate under those constraints. It also asserted that Iran overcame infrastructure-focused warfare, severely suppressed enemy agents within the country, and maintained overall domestic stability by preventing major shortages and deep economic stagnation.
Ettelaat: Which side will compromise, Iran or the US?
Ettelaat discussed the lack of progress in ongoing negotiations between Iran and the United States, citing former Minister of Culture and Islamic Guidance Ali Jannati. He argued that diplomacy has not failed, because opportunities for negotiation remain available even under the most difficult circumstances. Over the past month, Qatari mediators have reportedly conveyed Iranian proposals to the United States and delivered Washington’s responses back to Tehran. According to Jannati, the talks have stalled because Iran proposed seven principles as the basis for negotiations and the United States broadly accepted the framework but strongly disagreed over the sequence in which the provisions should be implemented. Washington wants the nuclear issue to be addressed first, whereas Tehran views it as the final matter for discussion. He suggested that both sides continue to insist on their positions and that little progress is likely unless one party shows flexibility and makes concessions. Otherwise, he warned, the possibility of renewed war remains.
Vatan-e-Emrooz: France bowed to Hormuz
Vatan-e-Emrooz analyzed protests in France and comments made by President Macron. According to the paper, Macron acknowledged in a televised address that French citizens had reason to be upset about rising fuel prices linked to developments in the Persian Gulf. The newspaper noted that Macron had previously stated that France was living with the consequences of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. It linked current economic pressures to events eight months earlier, when US and Israeli attacks on Iran led to the closure of the strategic waterway. The paper argued that the disruption of oil shipments through Hormuz triggered increases in fuel costs, inflation, and living expenses worldwide. It contended that these economic effects have fueled ongoing protests in France, which began in mid-September over shortages of teachers and inadequate school facilities but have continued for more than a month due to broader concerns about the cost of living.
Shargh: Repeated US threats aim to weaken social resilience
In an interview with Shargh, Seyed Jalil Mirmohammadi Meybodi, a member of the Iranian Parliament’s Industries and Mines Committee, discussed the main source of “psychological warfare” against Iran by the Trump administration. He argued that it originates from US policy and Washington’s extensive media capabilities. Psychological warfare is one of America’s principal tools in its confrontation with Iran, and Tehran faces an enemy that controls powerful global media networks. He claimed that the United States has failed to achieve its objectives and has therefore resorted to new threats and attempts to project victory. He said that Donald Trump continually seeks to portray himself as victorious and might use a major military action, such as a large-scale bombing campaign, to claim success. Meybodi also argued that any new military action against Iran would be met with a reciprocal response. In his view, frequent public discussion of war often makes actual conflict less likely, and recurring threats may be intended more to influence Iran’s political and psychological calculations than to signal an imminent military operation.

Starlink problems could be resolved within two days: Zelenskyy reveals the results of talks with the United States
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy said that Starlink would be restored in Ukraine within two days. The United States and Ukraine have also resumed exchanging intelligence.
Starlink operations in Ukraine are planned to resume within 48 hours. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this on October 20 after talks with U.S. presidential special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, UNN reports.
The exchange of intelligence between the United States and Ukraine has already resumed. In particular, regarding ballistic missile launches. Starlink operations will also be restored within 48 hours
Details
According to Zelenskyy, during the meeting with the American side, the issue of restoring the full operation of the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems used by the Ukrainian military was discussed quite actively.
The president also expressed hope that the relevant restrictions could be removed within two days, that is, approximately by October 22.
In addition, during the talks in Oslo, the Ukrainian and American sides raised the issue of supplying Patriot air defense systems, military assistance, and security guarantees for Ukraine.
Context
On October 14, the Ukrainian military encountered restrictions on the operation of Starlink and Starshield. In particular, satellite terminals lost connection while moving at speeds of more than 160 km/h. This created problems for the use of Ukrainian drones, including interceptor drones used to destroy Russian jet-powered "Shahed" drones.
Against this backdrop, Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that, due to restrictions on the speed of satellite communications, Ukrainian forces were unable to effectively use some of the means to counter Russian air attacks.
It should also be noted that on October 20, the President of Ukraine held a telephone conversation with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The restoration of Starlink/Starshield operations, the supply of means to counter ballistic missiles, and the exchange of intelligence data regarding Russian attacks ran as a common thread through the key topics discussed.
We remind you
Earlier, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine had not received early warning of the first wave of the Russian Federation's ballistic attack. He also accused the United States of failing to explain the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield.

Zelensky on meeting with Witkoff: There are proposals on ceasefire, NATO-like security guarantees
According to Ukrinform, the head of state made the remarks at a press conference in Oslo following talks with U.S. President Donald Trump's Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, which were attended by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere and Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
"We are ready for negotiations, and it is important for us to demonstrate any signs of de-escalation. That is why there are certain proposals for different ceasefire formats," Zelensky said.
He also noted that a wide range of issues had been discussed during today's talks.
"We talked about security guarantees, as well as various sensitive issues. As for territories, everyone understands that such issues must be discussed at the highest level," Zelensky said, once again expressing his readiness for a trilateral meeting with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Zelensky clarified that security guarantees for Ukraine had been discussed with the U.S.
"I am grateful to the American side for reiterating that these guarantees will be reliable. We have various proposals. We discussed NATO, Article 5, in particular, as well as the option of 'Article 5 light,'" he said.
Zelensky added that the document Witkoff would deliver to the Russian side contained various types of security guarantees, and said Ukraine would receive a response within a day.
He stressed that no issues concerning Ukraine could be discussed without Ukraine's participation.
"I do not know what is involved in the trilateral meeting between the United States, China and Russia. That is their business. But, of course, when it comes to Ukraine and its future, it is absolutely clear that any such discussions can be acceptable only if we participate in the negotiations. And, as I said, this morning began with positive signals from the American side. Following our phone call with the Secretary of State [Marco Rubio], we are continuing a very constructive dialogue," Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, the Oslo talks also addressed Ukraine's post-war reconstruction.
"We also discussed very important issues, including what will happen after this war ends. Of course, we want to do everything possible to bring it to an end as soon as possible. After the war, the focus will be on rebuilding our country and many other issues," he said.
As previously reported, Trump said on October 11 that an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine had supposedly taken effect, urging both sides not to violate it.
Zelensky said he had been unaware of such an arrangement but confirmed Ukraine's readiness for a ceasefire provided that Russia also stopped attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
However, during the night and morning of October 17 alone, Russian forces attacked energy infrastructure in the Vinnytsia, Volyn, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Zhytomyr, Odesa, Rivne, Ternopil, Khmelnytskyi and Kharkiv regions.

A supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, the Navy of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Tuesday.
In a statement carried by state broadcaster IRIB, the navy said the vessel was committing violations and that it had switched off all its radar and navigation systems.

Iran’s security chief rejects moving enriched uranium out of country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:24:42 UTC
03:24:42 KST

Iran’s security chief rejects moving enriched uranium out of country
- Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir that “not even a tiny bit of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran”, calling it a national asset.
- Rezaei and speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said there will be no talks until the US builds trust and meets Iran’s “seven conditions”, including a ceasefire, frozen assets and oil sanctions relief.
- The nuclear talks remain stalled after US and Israeli attacks in February, a short-lived June deal, and failed UN talks, while Iran rejects claims it seeks nuclear weapons.
AI generated
TEHRAN - Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Oct 20 told the visiting Pakistani army chief Asim Munir that Tehran would not allow nuclear material to leave the country, according to state TV.
“Not even a tiny bit of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran; such materials constitute a major asset and national wealth for the Iranian people, intended for use within the country,” said Rezaei, Iran’s secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.
“There will be no negotiations until America takes steps to build trust – a process that must begin with the fulfilment of Iran’s conditions,” he added.
Iran’s chief negotiator and Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf made similar remarks to Munir, who is in Tehran as part of a renewed push to mediate a peace deal between the Islamic republic and the United States.
“We have nothing new to say; America cannot gain Iran’s trust unless it fulfils the seven conditions,” said Ghalibaf, noting that “threats and military manoeuvres cannot influence Iran’s strategic decisions”.
Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad and the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector.
The Middle East war was sparked in late February by the United States and Israel when they launched a wave of surprise attacks on Iran, while Washington and Tehran were in the midst of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The warring parties agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that was expected to create a framework for a permanent resolution to the conflict, but the deal did not last long.
Negotiations have effectively been at an impasse since then, and recent indirect talks between the US and Iran on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly failed to produce a breakthrough.
Tehran had previously maintained it would not hand over its nuclear materials – enriched to 60%, close to the atomic bomb threshold of 90% – to any country but had hinted at the possibility of diluting them within Iran’s borders.
Washington and its allies have imposed waves of sanctions on Iran, accusing it of seeking to build nuclear weapons, a charge Tehran has long denied. AFP

What Chair Yoga Can Do for Your Body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:22:16 UTC
03:22:16 KST

At first glance, chair yoga might seem like a workout just for older adults with mobility issues. The gentle, accessible workout offers a modified take on the ancient movement and meditation practice, usually from a seated position. No one’s asked to climb down onto the floor or independently hold themselves upright in tricky standing postures—which makes it ideal for those with limited strength or balance.
But experts say chair yoga shouldn’t be pigeonholed, because anyone can benefit. “It is a practice that meets you where you are,” says Divya Balakrishnan, a yoga instructor in New York City. “You’re still using your strength and flexibility, just in other ways.”
What is chair yoga?
A yoga teacher named Lakshmi Voelker first began adapting some yoga poses to a chair in 1982 to make the practice more accessible for a student with arthritis. Since then, numerous instructors have found ways to use a chair for adapted versions of a surprising number of traditional yoga movements, like lunging warrior poses and standing-to-lying sun salutations.
While students typically crouch, sit, and lie down on a mat in traditional yoga classes, the chair, in a way, brings the floor closer. Some chair yoga classes are done entirely seated, moving through modified variations of classic yoga sequences without ever asking participants to get up. Other classes transition between sitting and standing while holding onto the back for a little extra help with balance, or doing poses like downward dog with hands on the seat instead of reaching to the floor.
In a sense, the chair is simply another prop. “Just like you would use a strap or blocks to increase the accessible range of motion or bring different awareness to the body, the chair can be used in a similar way,” says Jessica Pate, a Boston-based yoga teacher.
Experienced yogis also use a chair for athletic feats that wouldn’t be possible on a mat alone. In particular, the Iyengar style of yoga uses a yoga chair (designed with an open back and a completely flat seat) for advanced postures like an upside-down inversion where the yogi’s shoulders rest on two chairs while their head hangs in between.
“There's an infinite number of ways that you can use the chair,” says Jules Mitchell, a Las Vegas–based yoga educator.
The health benefits of chair yoga
Research on the physical benefits of seated chair yoga has found that practitioners tend to improve their functional fitness and experience a decrease in how much pain interferes with their daily life. Much of that research has focused on older adults, who generally have a lower baseline of fitness than younger, healthy adults. It’s unlikely that people who are in peak shape would see as much benefit.
“You're not challenging your muscles or your balance as much as traditional yoga,” says Justin Smith, an assistant professor at Wichita State University who recently co-authored a case series on the benefits of chair yoga.
But that doesn’t mean it’s a waste of time for more athletic folks.
For experienced yogis, doing yoga from a chair can offer new ways to explore familiar movements, says Pate, who incorporates a chair into many of her regular yoga classes. By sitting, the body’s weight gets distributed differently, which makes the muscles engage in new ways and can bring a fresh awareness to the body. “For example, with Warrior 2, having the chair underneath [my] pelvis, I'm able to feel where my sit bones are,” she says. This can help people better recognize if their hips are twisted or tilted.
Although most people assume that sitting makes everything easier, that isn’t always the case. Sometimes the challenge just changes: Pate says she actually feels her outer hips working harder in Warrior 2 on a chair than they do when she’s standing in the pose because she’s forced into a more neutral alignment, and bigger muscles can’t take over.
Sitting on a chair can also sometimes help people go deeper into poses. Say you’re trying to target your glutes with a Figure 4 pose, where one ankle rests on the opposite knee as you bend forward. When you’re seated, you’re able to focus more on the stretch because you’re not struggling to balance, Balakrishnan says. “If I was doing a standing Figure 4, half of my attention is going to be on the standing foot and keeping myself upright, so I may not sit as deep,” she says.
The same is true for breathing. Pate says that the extra support of the chair makes it easier to focus on breathing deeply and intentionally—something that many students forget to do once poses get challenging.
One group that might particularly benefit from chair yoga is people who are stuck sitting in front of a computer all day. “For anyone who works at a desk, it is a lifesaver,” Balakrishnan says. A simple seated yoga routine can relieve tight, achy joints, and multiple studies have found that chair yoga can significantly reduce stress. Balakrishnan regularly takes yoga breaks right from her chair, doing neck rolls, spinal twists, or anything else her body is craving to bring some movement and mindfulness back to her day—without feeling like she has to stop what she’s doing and carve out time for a full yoga session. “You don't have that mental barrier of, ‘Okay, let me get out of my chair, go roll out my yoga mat, go get my blocks,’” she says. “It requires less of you to begin the practice.”
There’s also a simpler reason to do seated chair yoga: It just feels good. The low-key movement can help stretch out tense muscles and get some blood flowing without feeling like you have to do a workout that impresses anyone. Smith says that all the participants in his case series were incredibly enthusiastic about their routine. “You can tell that they really just love chair yoga,” he says.
Seated chair yoga may not build Olympic athlete–level strength and agility. But experts agree it still has plenty to offer, no matter your age or fitness level. “We all can benefit from calming down, observing our sensations in our body, and getting in a little bit of stretching,” Mitchell says.

Pakistan to continue mediation between Iran and US, Dar says
TEHRAN– Pakistan will continue its diplomatic efforts to facilitate engagement between Iran and the United States, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar said on Tuesday, reaffirming Islamabad’s support for dialogue and a peaceful resolution of regional disputes.
Speaking at the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Dushanbe, the Tajik capital, Dar said dialogue and diplomacy remained the most effective means of addressing regional tensions.
Pakistan’s efforts to facilitate engagement and reduce tensions in West Asia and the Persian Gulf, he added, reflected Islamabad’s commitment to constructive diplomacy.
Dar said his country would maintain its mediation efforts between Tehran and Washington and support initiatives aimed at promoting dialogue, resolving disputes peacefully and achieving lasting peace and stability.
He also emphasized that regional challenges required collective, cooperative and sustainable solutions, underscoring the importance of multilateral diplomacy in addressing complex security and political issues.
Pakistan’s renewed commitment to mediation comes as diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States remain a significant issue for regional stability. Islamabad has sought to facilitate engagement between the two sides, while emphasizing diplomacy as an alternative to further escalation.
Dar’s remarks at the SCO meeting also highlighted the importance Islamabad attaches to regional cooperation and multilateral approaches to resolving disputes. The organization provides a forum for its member states to discuss political, economic, and security issues and coordinate their positions on shared challenges.
His statement reaffirmed Pakistan’s intention to remain engaged in efforts to bring Tehran and Washington toward dialogue, although he did not provide further details about the timing or format of any potential diplomatic contacts.

Six Palestinians, including two children and a married couple, were killed and eleven injured in Israeli attacks in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, in the latest violations of an effective ceasefire.
A Palestinian was killed and another injured in an Israeli strike near al-Sawarha cemetery, west of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, medical sources told Anadolu Agency.
One Palestinian was seriously injured in an Israeli drone strike on the al-Qasasib area of the Jabalia refugee camp in the north, according to medical sources.
Another Palestinian was killed in an Israeli strike in the Zeitoun neighborhood southeast of Gaza City, medical sources told Anadolu.
A Palestinian child was also killed by Israeli army fire in the Wadi Gaza area in the central Gaza Strip, the sources said.
A medical source at Al-Shifa Hospital told Anadolu that the bodies of a married couple were brought to the hospital along with four injured Palestinians, including three women, following an Israeli airstrike on a home in western Gaza City.
Witnesses said an Israeli helicopter fired at least one missile at the family home near Al-Shifa Hospital, killing the couple and injuring others.
The strike sparked a fire in the house, which civil defense crews later extinguished, the witnesses added.
In southern Gaza, a Palestinian child was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Qizan Abu Rashwan area south of Khan Younis.

Five other Palestinians, including a woman and two children, were injured by Israeli army fire in Hamad City north of Khan Younis and areas south of the city.
In eastern Gaza City, the Israeli army carried out artillery shelling and opened heavy fire from military vehicles and quadcopter drones toward Palestinian homes and tents sheltering displaced people in the Tuffah neighborhood.
The shelling and gunfire continued throughout the night, while several explosions were heard as the Israeli army demolished homes and civilian structures inside areas under its control, witnesses said.
Israeli warships also fired bullets and shells toward the northern coast of Gaza City, while military vehicles opened heavy fire toward the Sudaniya area in the northwestern Gaza Strip.
Witnesses said Israeli tanks opened heavy fire toward homes and tents sheltering displaced people in several areas of central, southern and northern Khan Younis.
The army also carried out extensive demolitions inside areas under its control east of the city, they added.
Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement had killed 1,522 Palestinians and injured 5,421 others since Oct. 10, 2025, according to the latest figures from Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others during its war on Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Tuesday that Iranian leaders wanted him to suffer setbacks in next week's Knesset election and were trying to interfere in the election.
In an interview with Army Radio, the prime minister said, "This is the truth; it isn't spin. This is intelligence information that Iran and its proxies want to try to influence the elections because they know we have changed the equation, that we are stronger than ever."
Asked if Iran was "on its way to a surprise attack," he replied: "We are preparing for that possibility."
Also Tuesday, Defense Minister Israel Katz warned Hezbollah against joining any Iranian attack on Israel, writing on X that the IDF was prepared to seize additional territory in the Nabatieh and Litani areas of southern Lebanon.

On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump said that he had spent more than $300 million on the Republicans’ election campaign. At the same time, The New York Times reported that former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg was allocating $80 million to support Democrats ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The media note that these financial injections are being made at a time when Democrats are attempting to regain control of Congress, where 470 seats in chambers currently controlled by Republicans are at stake.
"By Election Day, I will spend—or am already spending—more than $400 million. More than $300 million has already gone toward advertising, direct and indirect voter engagement, rallies, renting venues for them, televised rallies, programs to mobilize citizens to vote, election integrity, and so on," Trump wrote on social media.
Bloomberg’s team told The New York Times that he would give Democrats approximately $80 million in September and October.
Bloomberg’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to The New York Times, at least $50 million of Bloomberg’s funds was directed toward House of Representatives races. In particular, $24 million went to the organization "Everytown for Gun Safety," which Bloomberg co-founded. He also gave $16 million to the political action committee "House Majority PAC," which supports Democrats in the House of Representatives.
Reuters did not independently verify the data on Trump’s or Bloomberg’s spending.

Seven West Media had 'diabolical' culture, secret review hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:18:16 UTC
03:18:16 KST

Seven West Media sexism and bullying allegations detailed in secret 2024 review into company culture
In short:
A 2024 review found allegations of sexism, bullying and a toxic culture at Seven West Media.
The review was commissioned after court claims the company reimbursed Bruce Lehrmann for drugs and sex workers to secure an interview.
What's next?
The company's new owner says it has since had a "cultural reset".
A bombshell review of Seven West Media in 2024 has been told of a "diabolical" corporate culture, with allegations that sexism, bullying and harassment were rife and "sacred cow" executives favoured by then-chairman Kerry Stokes were protected amid a ratings obsession.
The ABC has seen a copy of the 65-page review, conducted by independent consultancy Interchange.
It was concluded in July 2024 and has never been made public.
The review was commissioned by the former Seven West board in May that year in the wake of Federal Court claims by former Spotlight producer Taylor Auerbach that the network had reimbursed ex-Liberal staffer Bruce Lehrmann for drugs and sex workers in order to secure an interview with him.
Mr Auerbach acknowledged he had never seen an invoice for this and Seven vehemently denied the claims, saying it was "appalled" by them.
Former Seven chief executive James Warburton resigned in April 2024 following those claims as well as the network's on-air misidentification of the Bondi stabber, and was replaced by Jeff Howard.
Mr Warburton had previously announced his intention to step down in June.
Mr Lehrmann was ultimately found by the Federal Court, on the balance of probabilities, to have raped colleague Brittany Higgins in a federal Parliament House office in 2019.
That finding was made as part of a defamation trial and remains untested in a criminal court. Mr Lehrmann has denied the rape allegation.
The Interchange review into the network's corporate culture interviewed Kerry Stokes and the rest of the board, as well as half a dozen advertising clients and agencies, and did 127 interviews or small focus groups with Seven employees across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth.
Interchange also drew on more than 800 responses to a company survey.
The report does not suggest that Mr Stokes, Mr Warburton or other senior management were aware of or involved in the alleged incidents discussed by staff.
Mr Stokes declined to comment for this story.
"Immoral, unethical and illegal behaviour has been prevalent for a very long time," one anonymised NSW Seven West leader told the review.
Another interviewee said: "There are people in this office every day crying and there is nothing I can do about it."
"The culture here is abhorrent … I know the stuff they have been exposed to. Some of them have been touched up; the less pretty ones get verbally abused. Pick your poison. It's not just the girls either, but they cop it the worst."
"We've had some diabolical situations culturally, but they've been allowed to keep going," another said.
"Certain people in power who have continually abused their position time and time again; nothing happens because they are a protected species."
Interviewees told Interchange that they immediately believed the Lehrmann allegations "because of other misconduct they witnessed".
Other testimonies in the final report include:
- "The news guys are ruthless and get away with really bad behaviour because of their legacy and results. People are scared to cross them because they're sacred cows."
- A senior leader in NSW said: "I think decisions made in the past indicate that people are protected by the Stokes'."
- One executive said: "The way to leave Seven with very heavy pockets is to behave appallingly".
- A Queensland leader said: "The ambulance was called due to someone who 'mentally snapped' after an incident of bullying at the office — it included seven senior males piling onto a female".
- A Victorian leader said: "We are a man's world in media. It is a big swinging dick culture, unfortunately. It's got better than it used to be, but everyone's having affairs, and people are getting ahead because of those things."
- A Victorian team member said a manager once threw a chair at a colleague. "It didn't hit him, but it didn't miss by much either. I noticed him crying a bit later at his desk, but he was embarrassed when I went over, so I left him to it."
- A WA team member said their manager was "a chronic gaslighter … I saw a psychologist for a while because I started having panic attacks at work".
- A WA leader said: "It's relationship and loyalty to Kerry over all else — and the people that play that game play it very well".
The company-wide survey found 63 per cent of respondents did not know what Seven West Media's organisational purpose was, 59 per cent were not clear on its future strategy, and 48 per cent said "yes" there were psychosocial hazards in the workplace.
Ratings dips had to be justified to Stokes, review told
The review also painted a picture of an organisation with "low commercial acumen", fixated on Channel Nine and divided into "territorial tribes" with the executive committee "Kings and Queens of the drama cyclone".
"We make drama, but internally, if you want drama, you can set the clock for 8:58 every morning when the ratings come out," one executive said.
The consultants noted the influence of proprietor Kerry Stokes on Seven West Media in contrast to Channel Nine, which is controlled by a board representing institutional investors.
"Numerous interviewees mentioned phone calls or emails from the chairman that required them or their direct reports to justify a dip in ratings," the review wrote.
"If you lose the ratings, you've got Kerry on your doorstep," said one team member in NSW. "That's what we're worried about."
The review found Seven West Media was operating "more like a not-for-profit, in service of society, yet is unwilling to part with the glamorous side of what traditional media offered when the money flowed".
Even board members joined the criticism, telling Interchange the company "generates a billion dollars of revenue but also a billion of costs," and there were "so many people on old media salaries that just don't add up anymore".
Southern Cross buys up Seven
The review also found Seven "didn't pivot fast enough" after the arrival in Australia of streaming services such as Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon, and digital advertising platforms such as Google and Meta, resulting in "anxiety, denial and outlets of bad behaviour" in the company.
The Interchange review was conducted as the ABC's Four Corners program was investigating the culture at Channel Seven — an episode which subsequently went to air in August 2024.
Since the review, Seven West Media was bought for $385 million by Southern Cross Media in a deal completed in January.
The Stokes family emerged with a 20 per cent stake in the combined company, and through the course of the year crept up to 23 per cent — enough for Kerry Stokes's son Ryan to be appointed as chairman.
Earlier this year, a longtime Stokes lieutenant, Bruce McWilliam, acquired an additional 9 per cent of Southern Cross Media — funded by rival mining billionaire Gina Rinehart — however, he did not secure a seat on the board.
A Southern Cross Media spokesperson told the ABC everyone in its business "should feel safe, respected and supported".
"Measuring workplace culture and acting on employee feedback are essential responsibilities of any contemporary business,"
they said.
"Seven West Media commissioned Interchange more than two years ago to give employees an anonymous, independent platform to speak up and identify where workplace culture needed to improve.
"As you would expect, the organisation has fundamentally changed over the past two years. There has been a merger and a cultural reset, with a new board, a new CEO and a new executive team.
"That work is supported by ongoing employee feedback and rigorous measures to track progress, and we are immensely proud of the business and culture we are building."
In its most recent annual report for 2025–26, Southern Cross's accounts showed its audio business, which includes the Triple-M and Hit networks, was the division with the highest profit margin and the only division to report growth in revenues and earnings before interest, tax and depreciation (EBITDA).
The television division, including the Seven network, recorded a 32 per cent drop in EBITDA, while the publishing division, including the West Australian newspaper, recorded a 2 per cent drop.
Former NRMA, Seven West and Foxtel executive Rohan Lund took over as chief executive in May.
Southern Cross will hold its annual meeting in Sydney on November 5, at which all seven non-executive directors will face election, including recently appointed former WA Premier Mark McGowan and former Twitter Australia boss Karen Stocks.

The mathematical impossibility of making a perfect world map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:15:46 UTC
03:15:46 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly newsletter that explores the joys and peculiarities of math. Sign up today for a weekly math essay and puzzle in your email inbox.
On September 4, 2026, the United Nations adopted a resolution to promote a new map of the world. The resolution encourages governments, schools and organizations to replace the much-criticized Mercator projection, which significantly overestimates the size of countries and continents near the poles, with the area-preserving Equal Earth projection developed in 2018.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The move sparked a lot of chatter. Some called the decision a step to dismantle “cartographic colonialism,” others a “radical ideological project.” In total, 164 nations voted in favor of the proposal, six abstained, and the U.S. was the only country to vote against. The resolution is not legally binding, but it sends a clear signal to use a fairer (and more accurate) representation of our world in the future.
Creating a suitable map of Earth might not sound too difficult at first. But mathematics makes it an unsolvable problem: a sphere cannot be mapped onto a flat plane. Try to wrap a spherical object in gift paper, for instance, and you will inevitably crease the paper. Cartographers have been aware of this challenge for centuries. It is impossible to design a world map that accurately depicts both the precise shape of the continents and countries and their area simultaneously. Compromises—and heated debates—are unavoidable.
A Solution for Seafarers
In 1569 scholar Gerardus Mercator developed a projection, now named after him, that accurately depicts angles on a sphere. With this approach, all continents and countries retain their shape, which is particularly advantageous for seafarers. Using a Mercator projection, a compass course corresponds to a straight line on the map. For centuries, this world map was the standard.
To obtain the Mercator projection, a cylindrical map is placed around Earth so that it touches the globe along the equator. Then every point on Earth is projected onto the cylinder from Earth’s center. The result is that countries near the poles are enlarged such that Greenland (836,330 square miles) and Africa (11.7 million square miles) appear roughly the same size on this map—even though Africa is 14 times as large.
In the 20th century, German historian Arno Peters objected to the Eurocentric worldview and the ways this map contributed to it. He called for a new representation and, in 1973, designed an equal-area projection. Technically cartographer James Gall developed a similar world map a century earlier, but it received little attention at the time.
To obtain this Gall–Peters projection, a cylindrical map is used, similar to the Mercator projection. In this case, however, the points of the globe are not projected onto the map from Earth’s center but along horizontal lines. The result is an equal-area representation: the sizes of the countries on the globe correspond to those on the map.
But critics raised several objections to this map, including the significant distortions to the shapes of countries and continents. Countries in low latitudes become especially warped in this presentation.
An Aesthetic Option
In March 2017 the Boston public school system announced its intention to replace its Mercator projection maps with the Gall-Peters projection. In response, software developer Bojan Šavrič of the Californian company Esri and cartographers Tom Patterson of the U.S. National Park Service and Bernhard Jenny of Monash University in Australia began searching for more suitable equal-area projections. And when they could not find an option that met all of their aesthetic criteria, they decided to develop something new that they called Equal Earth.
The researchers based their work on the Robinson projection, developed in the early 1960s. This is a variant of the world map that is neither area-preserving nor angle-preserving. Unlike the previously mentioned examples, it does not correspond to a mathematical projection, meaning it has no underlying formulas that generate it. Instead it is constructed using a table of empirically determined reference points. The points in between these reference points are determined by interpolation. While this may seem unscientific, the result appears natural: the Robinson map only shows significant deviations in angle and area in the polar regions.
Šavrič, Patterson and Jenny aimed to create a similarly natural effect but wanted to preserve the area of various landmasses. In 2018 they published their Equal Earth map in the International Journal of Geographical Information Science. It is a pseudocylindrical projection: Latitude lines are represented as straight lines, as in ordinary cylindrical projections, but longitude lines are not (except for the prime meridian).
They determined the details of the new world map in two steps: First, the researchers combined two existing projections using custom-developed graphics software. This visual approach allowed them to create a subjectively appealing appearance for the coordinate grid and the continental landmasses. The second step involved calculating the corresponding projection equations.
“Generally speaking, there are no truly ‘perfect’ maps,” cartographer Lorenz Hurni of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich told Swiss broadcaster SRF. “This map seeks a compromise to minimize the distortion of the shapes of countries and continents.” That’s why many countries—including members of the African Union—consider it the best possible representation of a world map. The state of Togo therefore introduced the new resolution at the United Nations, entitled “Correct the Map,” on its behalf in an aim to establish the Equal Earth map as the standard.
Although the U.N. flag uses a completely different representation of the world (an equidistant azimuthal projection that has been artistically corrected along the lines of latitude), many hope that the U.N. resolution will gradually be implemented throughout the world, updating the way we look at it.
This article originally appeared in Spektrum der Wissenschaft and was reproduced with permission. It was translated from the original German version with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by our editors.

Brother Munir! The Ball Is in the US Court
Pakistan's army chief came to Tehran to break the deadlock, but the US has repeatedly derailed mediation with fantasies like Iran's surrender
TEHRAN – Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, arrived in Tehran on Tuesday for consultations with Iranian officials. It is General Munir's fifth visit to Tehran since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28.
In continuation of the Pakistani government's sincere mediation, the country's army chief arrived in Tehran yesterday and held talks with senior Iranian officials. Islamabad's efforts come as Iran has always given credibility to mediators, but in recent years it is the US that has consistently neutralized those efforts and discredited them. Iran gave the four European countries the opportunity in the JCPOA to appear as international actors, but when Trump withdrew from the JCPOA in his first term, those countries failed to honor their commitments to Iran and even aligned themselves with the US policies and anti-Iran actions. After that, Iran engaged with Oman, and Muscat also sincerely tried to untie the knot between Washington and Tehran, but in the end Trump even threatened to bomb Oman, leaving observers stunned.
Pakistan's sustained efforts in the ongoing war also led to the Islamabad MoU and placed Pakistan in the position of a major international actor, but once again it was the US that destroyed it only weeks later with adventurism in the Strait of Hormuz and violation of the memorandum's provisions.
Tehran was the first country to recognize Pakistan's independence and has always had warm and close relations with Islamabad. Islamabad knows well that the Islamic Republic of Iran is a strong barrier against the sinister intentions of the Israeli regime, and if Tel Aviv's malign actions are not contained, they know no limits. Tehran and Islamabad have many common interests, and Pakistan's role and efforts in resolving the ongoing conflict are welcomed by Tehran. But has the US had, and does it have, the same view of mediators?
Pezeshkian: Iran does not trust the US
President Masoud Pezeshkian, in his meeting with the Pakistani army chief, recalling the record of US bad faith and breach of promises – attacking our country in the middle of negotiations and martyring the Supreme Leader of the Revolution, scientists and innocent schoolchildren without any legal justification – said: All the problems created in the region, from escalation of tension and conflict to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, all stem from the warmongering nature of the US. All their claims against our country lack legitimacy, because we had proven our goodwill both with regard to negotiations and inspections in the nuclear file within the framework of international laws and regulations.
Emphasizing that the US must first show it will lift threats and sanctions so that conditions for dialogue can be met, Pezeshkian stated: You cannot increase sanctions and pressure day by day and close routes and roads to our country, and then claim you seek dialogue and negotiation. What kind of dialogue is this?
Noting that we know war benefits neither us, nor the region and the world, nor even the US, the President added: It is the US that must answer why it started the war in the first place, entangling itself and the world in problems and difficulties?
Pezeshkian noted: We have been and are ready for dialogue, but the US must first remove threats and sanctions and then we will talk, because if they are truly seeking dialogue and agreement, such behavior is completely in contradiction with their claim and is not logical.
The President, further pointing out that they imposed all these criminal acts on our country and our region under the false claim of nuclear weapons, while they martyred our Leader who had repeatedly stressed the prohibition of nuclear weapons, and drove the region into deadlock, said: They will certainly not achieve their objectives through war and will only bring destruction and damage, not only for Iran but for the entire region; something we do not want to happen.
Stressing that they must prove to our nation that this time they do not want to lie to us, Pezeshkian said: Our nation today does not trust the US and believes that if we negotiate, they will attack us again.
The President added: They constantly propagate in the media that they want to attack our country to frighten our people, while our nation has no fear of martyrdom. You, as our Muslim brothers, must make them understand that this is not how one treats Muslims. We do not want to impose our will on anyone, but we will not submit to coercion.
Field Marshal Asim Munir, in the meeting expressed pleasure at meeting Pezeshkian, presented a report on diplomatic actions and efforts to reduce tensions, and while expressing concern over a renewed outbreak of war, stressed the importance of resolving issues through diplomatic solutions and Pakistan's readiness to help settle matters in this regard.
He, while regretting the non-implementation of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, said: Negotiation never means weakness and acceptance of submission to the US, because the Iranian nation has repeatedly shown its dignity, authority and power to the world; rather it is an opportunity to resolve issues through a path other than war, conflict and insecurity.
Iran will not take out its uranium
General Munir also met in Tehran with the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Major General Mohsen Rezaei stated: All the Iranian people and officials have unanimously and with one voice concluded that until confidence-building is done by the US, there will be no negotiation, and the start of this confidence-building is the fulfillment of Iran's conditions. He also stressed the fraternity of the Iranian and Pakistani nations.
Asim Munir, emphasizing the reopening of the border between Iran and Pakistan, said the Iran-Pakistan border problem has been resolved and the border has been reopened as of Tuesday.
Referring to the courageous defense and resistance of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the 40-day war, he stressed regional cooperation between the two countries without the presence of foreigners.
US threats have no effect on our decisions
The Pakistani army chief also met with Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Speaker of Parliament, in Tehran. In the meeting, Ghalibaf, while appreciating the support of the Pakistani government and nation for Iran in conditions of war and negotiation, stressed the fraternal relations of the two countries. Asim Munir also announced the reopening of the two countries' border as of today and described border issues as temporary and technical.
Referring to Iran's deep distrust of the US and the Trump administration's violation of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, Ghalibaf stressed that the US can win Iran's trust only by implementing Iran's seven conditions presented in New York.
He also said that Iran is not warmongering but is fully prepared to defend the homeland and national dignity, stressing that threats and military moves cannot change the strategic decisions of the Islamic Republic, and that it is the US that must act to get out of the quagmire of war.
A deadlock that is not easy to break
General Munir's visit to Tehran took place while negotiations between Iran and the US have reached a deadlock, and Tehran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could not untie this knot either. The deep divide between the two sides' views of the balance of conflict and tension is one of the main reasons mediation efforts have failed. Iran, by tightening control over the Strait of Hormuz and dealing with violating vessels seeking to pass through the strait without permission, has increased pressure on the US, and oil prices have even exceeded 110 dollars. From the 5,000-dollar promise to every US adult and personal appearances at campaign rallies in various states, telling people to imagine they are going to the ballot box to vote for him, all show how vital this election is for him.

Iran is ready for the next round of war

In the event of any renewed miscalculation by the enemy, we will neutralize the effect of the enemy's expensive and advanced equipment with a wide range of cheap but effective equipment, and this will be painful, worrying and costly for the enemy.
It seems Trump is seeking even a temporary achievement to pass easily and triumphantly through the upcoming elections, but whether he loses or wins this election, it is unlikely to fundamentally affect his strategy toward the war with Iran. Trump is not after a deal
While some unofficial sources in the region have said Pakistan and Qatar have prepared a proposal covering part of both sides' demands that could be agreed by Tehran and Washington, evidence shows that from Tehran's perspective, Trump is merely seeking to pass through the difficult strait of the midterm elections, not to end an unjustified and costly war whose declared objectives have changed repeatedly.
Tehran has no doubt about Islamabad's sincerity in resolving the current situation, but the point is that the ball is in Washington's court, not Tehran's. Until the US government abandons the illusion of forcing Iran to surrender and imposing its unilateral conditions – whether through negotiation or military aggression – this conflict and tension will not end.

pieni III: kenko’s ultra-tiny camera captures lo-fi photos without a screen

pieni III: kenko’s ultra-tiny camera captures lo-fi photos without a screen
with its miniature film-camera styling and unpredictable framing, kenko's latest release makes taking pictures a little more spontaneous.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
kenko’s tiny pieni III camera captures lo-fi photos without a screen
Japanese photography brand Kenko Tokina has released the Pieni III, a tiny digital camera that weighs just 18 grams and hangs around the neck like a pendant. Measuring 53 millimeters (2 inches) wide, the working camera is small enough to fit between two fingers, with a familiar silver top and circular lens that recall the proportions of an old film camera. It arrives in four colors, including pastel pink Strawberry and pale blue Soda, alongside Milk and Black.
The Pieni III also has a curious omission. There is no screen or viewfinder, and thus leaves photographers to point the lens toward a subject and press the shutter without seeing exactly what they’re capturing. The images remain a mystery until they’re transferred to another device. A subject might drift toward the edge of the frame, or an unexpected detail could make its way into the shot. Part of the fun is eventually discovering what the little camera has actually seen.
a miniature camera with a taste for imperfect photographs
Kenko keeps the controls simple, with just two buttons handling power, shutter release, and the switch between photography and video. A small indicator light on the back glows red for still images and blue for video. The camera also captures footage with sound, at a resolution of 720 × 480 pixels and 30 frames per second. Despite its miniature dimensions, the Pieni III functions as a standalone digital camera.
Its photographs have a peculiar character of their own. Inside is a tiny 1/10-inch CMOS sensor with just 0.32 megapixels of effective resolution. Still images are saved as 1440 × 960-pixel JPEGs through digital interpolation, so the files contain far less detail than their dimensions might suggest.
In Kenko’s sample photographs, flowers become fuzzy patches of vivid color while foliage softens into something approaching watercolor. The coarse edges and unpredictable exposure give the images the familiar appearance of early digital photography, with their imperfections coming directly from the camera’s hardware.
a magnetic back and USB-C connectivity
The camera’s small body holds another useful detail: a built-in magnet on its back. This allows the Pieni III to attach to compatible metal surfaces, including a refrigerator or a railing, for hands-free recording. A neck strap is included for carrying it around, making the miniature camera easy to keep within reach whenever something catches your eye.
Photographs and videos are stored on a removable microSDHC card, supporting capacities between 4GB and 32GB. The card is sold separately. For this third-generation model, Kenko has introduced USB-C connectivity, allowing files to be transferred directly to compatible smartphones with the included cable. The same connection handles charging, so the entire process remains fairly straightforward once the photographs are ready to be viewed.

Trump sued over 50% tariffs on Canada in latest trade challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:06:13 UTC
03:06:13 KST

A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.
Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.
"Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says.
The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.
Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.
The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.
The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs.
"This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.
Trump on July 20 signed three presidential proclamations targeting different sets of Canadian imports with the Section 338 tariffs in response to alleged unfair treatment in the U.S. motor vehicle, alcohol and dairy sectors.
The tariffs took effect Aug. 22, after last-ditch trade talks with Canadian officials in Washington fell apart. Canada later retaliated with "dollar for dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods.
Tuesday's lawsuit argues that even if the 1930 tariff law is upheld, the Trump administration did not meet the legislation's requirements when it imposed the duties on Canada.
It says that the law permits tariff action "only upon finding 'as a fact'" that a foreign country is unequally imposing unreasonable charges or trade limitations on U.S. products, or that its customs rules otherwise unfairly disadvantage the U.S.
"Even then, the President may impose only such duties 'as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage,'" the lawsuit states.
But the Canadian actions cited in Trump's proclamations "do not discriminate against the United States," it says.
Two of those actions are "Canada's responses to the President's own tariffs, including tariffs the Supreme Court has held unlawful, and retaliation is not discrimination," the lawsuit contends.
Another centers on dairy quota terms that were negotiated in USMCA, the U.S.'s trilateral trade deal with Canada and Mexico. Those terms "give American cheese better access to Canada than the cheese of most of the world receives," the suit states.
The suit says Gellert Global boasts more than $1.7 billion in annual revenue. In 2025, the company imported $71 million worth of Canadian cheese — including sheep's and goat's milk cheese, mascarpone, brie, camembert and the hybrid cheese borgonzola, the complaint says.
Gellert says it paid no tariffs on its imports of Canadian cheese under USMCA. The Trump administration said in July that it would not renew that trade pact for another 16-year term.
Under the Section 338 tariffs, "Gellert now pays a 50 percent duty on the entered value of its Canadian cheese, an estimated $40 million per year," according to the suit.
While it plans to absorb the costs through the end of the year, the situation is "not sustainable long term," the company says.
"If the tariffs continue, Gellert will be forced to raise the prices on its products, resulting in lost or reduced sales, decreased customer loyalty, risk of losing product placements due to higher costs, and supply chain interruptions as producers scale down or go out of business due to increased costs," the suit says.

More than 210,000 tourists used the services of Join UP! Ukraine during the summer 2026 season, from May through September inclusive, while the average price of an international package tour increased by 8.6% to EUR 620, the tour operator's press service told Interfax-Ukraine.
"This summer, much depended on our ability to adapt quickly. Airfares increased, prompting tourists to wait for discounts and book at the last minute. There were risks of missing flights because of train delays, which increased demand for our bus transfers and bus tours in general. We adjusted our programs to meet these needs throughout the season," said Iryna Mosulezna, director of Join UP! Ukraine.
As reported, nearly 415,000 Ukrainians used Join UP! Ukraine's services last year.
July was the busiest month of this summer in terms of tourist numbers, with more than 50,000 Ukrainians going on vacation.
Türkiye ranked first in the number of bookings with Join UP! Ukraine, overtaking Egypt, which topped the ranking last year. Other popular destinations included Greece, Bulgaria, Spain, Montenegro, Tunisia, Cyprus, and Albania. In 2025, the top five destinations were Egypt, Türkiye, Greece, Bulgaria, and Montenegro. This year, Spain replaced Montenegro among the five most popular destinations.
The average price of an international package tour in the 2026 season was UAH 29,800 (EUR 620) per tourist, an increase of 8.6% in euro terms compared with the previous year.
The lowest starting prices per tourist, based on double occupancy, were in Türkiye, starting at UAH 14,750. Tours to Egypt started at UAH 19,950, Greece at UAH 20,120, Montenegro at UAH 21,400, and Spain at UAH 34,450.
Regarding travel logistics, Chisinau Airport remains a key hub for Ukrainian tourists. The Moldovan capital's airport accounted for 58.1% of departures, compared with 55% in 2025. The popularity of Polish airports declined noticeably this season compared with last year. While Rzeszow accounted for 12% of departures last year, its share fell to just 6.7% this year. Warsaw's share also declined, to 2.3% from 5%.
Mass train delays caused by security risks were the main logistical challenge at the end of the summer. The situation worsened in August, substantially increasing the risk of missing flights. As a result, demand for organized bus transfers surged toward the end of the season, both through Join UP! Ukraine and across the market as a whole. More than 26,000 tourists used the tour operator's bus tours. The main departure cities for bus services were Kyiv, Lviv, Zaporizhia, Kharkiv, and Uzhgorod.
As for domestic tourism, western regions of Ukraine remained the clear leaders due to the security situation. Most trips during the season lasted two to three days, except for stays at health and wellness resorts, which lasted from seven to 14 days. The average price of a tour per person during this year's summer season was approximately UAH 14,000. The main criterion when choosing a hotel was the availability of as many services as possible in one location. Tourists sought resorts offering spas, swimming pools, meals, and children's entertainment programs so they would not have to spend time organizing leisure activities. The number of bookings at pet-friendly hotels also increased noticeably.
Egypt remains the leading destination for the upcoming winter season, accounting for the largest share of current bookings. Interest is also growing in trips to exotic destinations, particularly Vietnam and Zanzibar.
The company said it had already opened early bookings for the summer 2027 season. Croatia is among the new destinations being prepared.
Join UP! LLC was established in 2013. Its ultimate beneficial owners are Yuriy and Oleksandr Alba. The company's authorized capital amounts to UAH 72.671 million.
The company currently operates in Poland, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Moldova. Since its launch, the brand has served more than 8 million tourists across all its markets and expanded its partner network to nearly 10,000 travel agencies, according to internal company data.
