New study suggests touch is a key ingredient in dogs’ stress-buffering power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:00:24 UTC
03:00:24 KST

Stroking a pet dog may not immediately erase the physical toll of a stressful experience, but it appears to prepare the body to handle the next challenge more calmly. A new study published in Biological Psychology indicates that dog owners who physically petted their companions after a high-pressure mental test showed gentler brain and heart responses when facing a second round of stress shortly afterward. Simply sitting near the dog, making eye contact, and talking to it without physical contact did not provide the same protective effect.
Psychologists use the term stress buffering to describe how supportive social contact softens a person’s physical and emotional reaction to difficult situations. In human relationships, affectionate touch is a primary driver of this protection. In one frequently cited experiment, women who received a brief neck and shoulder massage from their partner before giving a speech showed smaller rises in heart rate and the stress hormone cortisol than women whose partners offered only verbal support.
Because many people treat their dogs as family members, scientists have examined whether companion animals offer similar biological protection. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in August 2025 found that people accompanied by their dogs during a laboratory stress test had smaller spikes in the stress hormone cortisol and a more balanced nervous system reaction than those tested alone.
Isolating physical touch as the specific mechanism behind these benefits has been difficult, because owners typically pet, look at, and talk to their animals all at once. In a 2019 randomized controlled trial of university students, spending 10 minutes petting cats and dogs lowered salivary stress hormone levels more than sitting nearby and watching others pet the animals. However, trials testing whether animal touch calms people down during an active stressor have yielded mixed results. For example, a 2021 laboratory study of adolescents found that touching an unfamiliar therapy dog during a stressful evaluation did not reduce anxiety or physical arousal any more than talking to the dog without touching it.
Other evidence suggests that animal contact might instead act as a preventative shield before a challenge arrives. In a 2017 experiment with undergraduate students, interacting with a therapy dog beforehand muted the physical sweat-gland response when students later tackled a fast-paced math test. Building on this work, study authors Vanessa Kaufmann and Annett Schirmer of the Department of Psychology at the University of Innsbruck and Schirmer’s Brain and Behavior Lab, along with their colleague Xiaoqin Cheng, designed an experiment to isolate physical touch with one’s own dog from other forms of interaction, tracking both immediate stress recovery and resilience to a subsequent stressor.
“Interactions with pets have a long history as therapeutic interventions and a lot of research suggests that they can indeed be good for us,” Kaufmann and Schirmer told PsyPost. “However, little work has been done to uncover potential factors or mechanisms that make human-animal interactions beneficial. Hence, we were interested in the ‘how,’ i.e., what is it about these interactions that might actually produce positive outcomes for the human?”
“Touch seemed like a particularly interesting candidate because physical contact emerges very naturally between people and their pets, and research on human touch has already shown that touch can buffer stress,” the researchers explained. “Therefore, we wanted to examine whether touch with a pet could have a similar effect.”
The researchers recruited 66 dog owners and their pets to visit a university laboratory in Austria. After excluding one person who stopped early and another who had excessive noise in their brain recordings, the final sample included 64 White European adults (51 women and 13 men) with an average age of 34 years. All of the dogs were healthy, over two years old, and comfortable in unfamiliar rooms.
Each participant completed two experimental blocks that followed the same five-step sequence: a five-minute resting baseline, a 10-minute stress test, a one-minute post-stress rest, a five-minute recovery period with their dog, and a five-minute post-recovery rest. During the 10-minute stress test, participants answered rapid-fire general knowledge questions within five seconds and counted backward in fixed steps to the beat of a flashing red dot. To induce social-evaluative stress, which is the anxiety of being negatively judged by others, participants were told their performance was being recorded for later analysis and were monitored over a video call by a staff member who gave only critical feedback.
The two blocks differed only during the five-minute recovery phase in a separate room. In the touch block, the dog roamed freely so the owner could spontaneously pet or hold it. In the no-touch block, the dog was kept on a short leash out of reach, preventing physical contact while still allowing the owner to talk to and make eye contact with their pet. Thirty-one participants completed the touch block first, while 33 completed the no-touch block first.
During the resting and stress phases, the researchers recorded brain activity using a cap with 64 sensors, a method called electroencephalography. They tracked alpha waves, which are slower electrical rhythms in the back of the head that accompany a relaxed mind and drop during stress, and beta waves, which are faster rhythms across the front and sides of the head tied to alertness and mental strain. Forearm sensors measured heart rate and heart rate variability, which tracks tiny beat-to-beat timing fluctuations driven by the calming parasympathetic branch of the nervous system, while self-report scales and video cameras captured participants’ mood and recovery behaviors.
Across both blocks, the mental test reliably triggered stress across multiple bodily systems. Compared to baseline rest, the stress task caused a drop in calming alpha brainwaves, a surge in alert beta brainwaves, a faster heart rate, and lower heart rate variability, with the rise in beta brainwaves lingering into the one-minute rest after the task ended. During the stress test, these physical responses synchronized with one another: stronger rises in beta brainwaves corresponded with faster heart rates, which in turn paired with lower heart rate variability.
By contrast, although participants reported feeling more negative, more tense, and less in control after the stress test, these conscious mood ratings showed almost no statistical connection to the size of their brain or heart changes. Only a small link emerged between higher heart rate variability and feeling calmer. The authors suggest this gap is consistent with research indicating that people’s reports of how stressed they feel may be tied more to context and expectations than to what is happening in their bodies.
When allowed to touch their dogs during the five-minute recovery break, owners spent about 64 percent of the time (roughly three minutes and 12 seconds) in physical contact, primarily stroking the animal’s fur. When the leash prevented touch, owners compensated by spending over 53 additional seconds making direct eye contact with their pets during the five-minute period compared to the touch condition.
“One notable aspect of the study is that participants were not instructed to touch their dogs,” Kaufmann and Schirmer noted. “When physical contact was possible, it emerged naturally, and participants spent about two thirds of the recovery period touching their pet. This highlights how central touch is to the way people naturally interact with their dogs.”
“Touch was very prominent in all the human-pet interactions we recorded, sometimes even when the pet wasn’t really into it,” the researchers added. “It seemed participants had a strong need to be in physical contact. Moreover, when this contact was not possible or allowed in the experiment, participants increased gazing at the dog, possibly as another way to connect.”
Contrary to the researchers’ initial prediction, touching the dog did not speed up immediate recovery: by the post-recovery rest, brainwaves, heart rates, and mood had returned toward baseline at similar rates whether the owner had petted the dog or not. The authors suggest the recovery setup may help explain why an immediate effect did not appear. Reaching out to stroke a moving dog involves physical activity that can mildly raise heart rate, and the extra eye contact in the no-touch condition may have offered its own calming effect by prompting the release of bonding hormones like oxytocin.
Instead, the benefits of touch emerged later, acting as a protective buffer when participants faced the second stress test. Participants who petted their dogs during the first recovery break showed a dampened biological reaction during the second stress test compared to their first stress test. Specifically, after recovering with touch, this group showed less suppression of calming alpha brainwaves throughout the second session, including during the stress test, along with a slower heart rate and higher heart rate variability during the second challenge itself, while also reporting a greater sense of control. Among participants who touched their dog first, the second-session differences had standardized effect sizes of about 0.36 for alpha, 0.40 for heart rate variability, and 0.72 for heart rate.
Participants prevented from touching their dogs during the first recovery break did not show these protective biological shifts during the second stress test; the differences in their alpha waves, heart rate, and heart rate variability between the two stress sessions were not statistically significant. Although this group reported feeling less tense after the second test, their beta brainwaves pointed to elevated tension during the second baseline period. Self-reported feelings showed an inconsistent pattern across the two groups and did not line up well with the physiological measures. Additional statistical models confirmed that the physiological results were not altered by the dog’s fur length, how much the dog whined or barked, or how worried owners felt about their pets.
“Our findings suggest that physical contact with a pet may reduce how strongly the body reacts to a subsequent stressful situation,” Kaufmann and Schirmer said. “Interestingly, there was no difference in how stressed participants reported feeling, suggesting that physiological buffering can occur without us necessarily being consciously aware of it.”
“While the effects were moderate in magnitude, we saw a consistent pattern across several physiological measures,” the researchers pointed out. “Brain activity, heart rate, and heart-rate variability all pointed toward a less pronounced physiological response to the subsequent stressor after participants had touched their dog. However, it remains unclear how effects observed in such a controlled laboratory setting translate to stressful situations in everyday life.”
The brainwave findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which similarly found that hands-on activities with dogs boosted relaxing alpha wave activity, though that earlier study measured immediate brain activity during calm interactions rather than buffering against a laboratory stressor. The authors speculate that stroking a dog’s coat stimulates specialized nerve fibers in human skin that respond to gentle, slow touch and send soothing signals to the brain. While these nerve fibers are scarce on the hairless palms of the hands, video recordings showed that owners mostly ran their fingers through their dogs’ fur, stimulating the sides and backs of the fingers where these receptors are present.
As with all research, there are some caveats to keep in mind. The study’s preregistered prediction, that touch would speed recovery right after the first stress test, was not supported. The protective effect on the second test came from an exploratory analysis, so it will need to be confirmed in a study designed to test it directly. In addition, the researchers cannot entirely rule out the possibility that touching the dog changed how much mental effort participants put into the second test, which could also lower physiological responses.
Participants also spoke out loud during the stress test but sat silently during rest. Because speaking changes breathing patterns, which directly influence heart rhythms, some cardiac changes during the stress test could reflect speaking or task effort rather than pure emotional stress, especially since a secondary, respiration-linked measure of heart rate variability did not replicate the main touch effect.
“Our findings provide causal evidence for a stress-buffering effect of touch under controlled laboratory conditions and as such support prior correlational observations that pet owners who engage in more physical contact with their pets report greater wellbeing,” Kaufmann and Schirmer told PsyPost. “However, real-life stress is varied and complex and it remains unclear whether different types of stress may differently benefit from touch. We also studied people interacting with their own dogs, so we cannot assume that the same effects would occur when interacting with an unfamiliar animal.”
The team also emphasized that the comfort of the animal is just as important as the comfort of the human. “Lastly, we would like to highlight the wellbeing of the animal who may or may not seek touch,” the researchers said. “Physical contact with another being should always be mutually wanted and positive.”
Sample makeup is another consideration, as around 80 percent of the participants were women and all were White Europeans. Future studies will need to test whether the findings hold across more diverse samples, examine other everyday stressors, and compare interacting with one’s own pet at home against interacting with an unfamiliar animal.
“A next step is to understand more precisely what it is about physical contact with an animal that produces these effects,” Kaufmann and Schirmer explained. “We are interested in both bottom-up mechanisms, such as how different characteristics of touch and the resulting sensory signals contribute to stress regulation, and top-down mechanisms, such as the relationship with the animal, expectations, or the meaning of the interaction.”
“One approach to tackle bottom-up mechanisms involves a closer look at how people touch,” the researchers continued. “Here we found that they primarily use their fingers relative to other body parts including the palm. Moreover, preliminary data suggests that contact with the fingers is particularly pleasurable, possibly because they are densely innervated by mechanoreceptors.”
The study, “Pet-induced stress buffering depends on touch: Evidence from brain and cardiac measures,” was authored by Vanessa Kaufmann, Xiaoqin Cheng, and Annett Schirmer.

Firm linked to suspected investment scam investigated, $138m feared lost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Australian firm investigated over fears investors may have lost up to $138 million
In short:
Australian investors lost millions to a licensed investment scheme they allege was an international scam with possible terrorism links.
They are now asking how it went undetected by authorities and its financial licensor.
What's next?
ASIC is investigating the Sydney company that authorised the alleged scammers to have a financial services licence, but the firm denies due diligence failures.
An Australian company that extended its financial licence to a group of suspected scammers is under investigation over fears that its failures cost investors $138 million.
More than a dozen Australians claim they were duped by a sophisticated investment scheme called Main Group FX, which appeared legitimate because it had a financial licence.
An ABC investigation into the alleged scam found ghost addresses leading to Caribbean headquarters, a famous Australian cricketer acting as ambassador, and an enigmatic chief executive listed as having alleged connections to terrorism.
The corporate regulator is now investigating the Australian Financial Services Licence (AFSL) provider company that gave the alleged scam legitimacy by making it an authorised representative.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) regulates financial services providers through a licensing scheme, but these companies can also act as licensors — supplying an effective sub-licence to others who become their authorised representatives.
Sydney-based company MGF Capital holds an AFSL, and its sole director is Matthew Starkey, a former Goldman Sachs trader.
Corporate records show Main Group FX was an authorised representative of the parent licensor MGF Capital between February and December 2023.
It is understood Australians may have lost as much as $138 million from financial products they believed were being offered by multiple authorised representatives under the umbrella of MGF Capital, including at least $2 million from Main Group FX.
It has sparked fears the alleged criminals behind Main Group FX were effectively given a licence to scam.
ASIC told the ABC it was "actively investigating" whether there were "oversight, due diligence and compliance failures" related to MGF Capital's corporate authorised representatives.
"ASIC is concerned many investors may have been exposed to significant financial losses,"
a spokesperson said.
MGF Capital's Matthew Starkey declined an interview and referred the ABC to a lawyer and crisis PR manager, who denied any due diligence failures had occurred, but would not say what checks had been carried out to allow Main Group to be its licensee.
Monthly dividends arrive late, then not at all
Candice Driver is among 13 investors the ABC knows of who have collectively lost more than $2 million to Main Group FX.
The Sydney marketing executive said she was glad ASIC was investigating, but she had "no trust whatsoever" in the system that allowed the alleged fraudsters to have a financial licence.
The reason she invested with Main Group was because their financial services licence meant they were regulated by ASIC.
"Which, as Australians, we're told to trust,"
she said.
Ms Driver poured tens of thousands into Main Group FX in 2023 believing she was investing in commodities on a trading platform.
By year's end, the company was unravelling, with her monthly dividends arriving late and then not at all.
She could not withdraw her cash and felt staff were "making excuses", with two separate workers claiming they had been slow to respond because their fathers were in hospital.
Another financial authority called in
Ms Driver reported Main Group's licence provider, MGF Capital, to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).
The complaints body acts as an ombudsman for external dispute resolution between financial institutions and customers.
Within days of the complaint, MGF Capital's director, Mr Starkey, contacted her urging her to withdraw her complaint.
"If you could make contact with them [AFCA] and explain you are in the process of resolving the matter that would be great," Mr Starkey said in an email.
Main Group's CEO Karim Farag also called her, saying her complaint was blocking company funds.
That was the last she ever heard from Mr Farag, who has since been accused of having alleged links to a terrorist organisation.
Main Group's investment portal shut down, emails bounced and staff became uncontactable. It was eventually deregistered.
Mr Starkey said in a statement that his firm "had no contact with any of the perpetrators of the [alleged] scam", but could not explain how Main Group staff knew about Ms Driver's AFCA complaint.
Complaint still with AFCA
Years later, Ms Driver and Mr Starkey are still locked in a long-running AFCA dispute.
Ms Driver questions what due diligence MGF Capital did on Main Group, with serious questions about the veracity of at least one of its company directors.
An international student called Junru Sun was Main Group's first director in February 2023, at the time it became an authorised representative of MGF Capital.
"She was a 21-year-old who was the director on ASIC paperwork for one month only," Ms Driver said.
Junru Sun is listed as a director of several other companies — Highstone Capital, which was also an authorised representative of MGF Capital, and a ceiling business in Western Australia.
Ms Sun told the ABC she had no idea how her name ended up on these documents.
In his statement to the ABC, Mr Starkey claimed Ms Sun "met the relevant regulatory requirements" to direct an authorised representative.
The directorship then switched to Australian-Lebanese woman Robin Mahfouz, who is now based in Lebanon and has refused to speak to the ABC.
MGF Capital said it "did not learn of the change in directorship" until afterwards.
Company cancels itself out of regulation
Despite the devastation facing investors, MGF Capital has been able to escape future AFCA compensation claims by essentially checking itself out of oversight.
By January 2024, MGF Capital had cancelled its AFCA membership — stripping the financial authority of the power to order compensation in any future claims.
Being an AFCA member is optional if licensees are only dealing with "wholesale" clients, meaning sophisticated investors or big companies, rather than "retail" investors or "mum-and-dad" types.
MGF Capital's representatives were only authorised to provide wholesale advice.
Ms Driver said this seemed to be a "huge and unbelievable loophole".
"I was completely gobsmacked."
AFCA said its membership "is dependent on the financial services a firm is licensed to provide".
"Where a firm is not legally required to be an AFCA member, AFCA cannot compel the firm to become a member," it said.
AFCA powerless to help other victims
Other investors missed out on the chance to pursue MGF Capital through the financial ombudsman.
Adelaide man Lewis Murray lost $390,000 to the alleged criminals behind Main Group FX and tried to lodge a complaint in early 2024, but MGF Capital had already withdrawn its membership.
Perth retiree Jean Giles had to sell her home after losing $176,000 to Main Group FX.
She was also too late reporting to AFCA.
They are among a small group of investors considering a class action against MGF Capital, in lieu of them not being able to lodge their own complaints with AFCA.
AFCA and ASIC both declined to comment on Main Group investors' allegations of regulatory failure.
More than just résumé checking needed: expert
Sean Graham, of compliance advisory business Assured Support, said this case raised important due diligence questions.
He said AFSL providers were obliged to ensure their representatives were competent and complied with the law on an "ongoing basis".
Companies could not simply appoint a representative and think of it as "game over".
"As a licensee, your obligation doesn't end the moment I check your résumé,"
Mr Graham said.
He likened some AFSL providers to "franchise models", whereby they appointed representatives en masse — such as Lanterne Fund Services, which ASIC shut down in 2024 for running a "licensee for hire" business model.
Not the first alleged due diligence failure
In 2022, a company Mr Starkey co-directed — now-defunct cryptocurrency exchange Mine Digital — landed in the Victorian Supreme Court for allegedly allowing scammers onto its platform.
A self-managed super fund sued Mine Digital after losing $1.6 million to a UK-based investment firm, which turned out to be "not a legitimate one", the court heard.
The super fund alleged the scam company used the cryptocurrency exchange as an Australian "intermediary" to facilitate money transfers.
The super fund claimed Mine Digital should have done more to vet the fake investment company before allowing it to use their services.
Mine Digital went into liquidation owing $16 million to creditors, effectively ending the lawsuit.
MGF Capital still operating
MGF Capital is now called Trade Prime and continues to authorise licensees, one as recently as last month.
Since MGF Capital's inception in 2017, it has authorised 136 representatives, though many are no longer active.
Mr Starkey claimed it was "critical to distinguish" between the Main Group his firm authorised and a separate group of scammers that impersonated the company.
The ABC has not encountered any evidence suggesting there were two separate groups, and Mr Starkey did not provide further information when asked.
Mr Starkey said Main Group FX was only authorised to provide financial advice to "wholesale" clients, while the alleged victims would be considered "retail" clients under the law.
MGF Capital "is appalled by, and deplores, the [alleged] scam", his statement said.

Australia could collect extra $45b a year through better resource taxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Australia could collect an extra $45b a year if it taxed surging resource profits better
Does the mineral wealth in our soil and beneath our ocean belong to Australians or to mining companies and their shareholders?
Prosper Australia, a tax reform think tank, says this country has a resource tax and royalty problem.
It estimates Australia is losing $45 billion a year in potential revenue because it is failing to collect more from the extractive mining and gas industries when commodity prices boom and profits surge.
It says we need to fix our tax system's "boom sensitivity" so public revenue rises automatically when public resources generate windfall gains.
"Once coal, iron ore, or gas is extracted and sold, it is gone," the organisation says.
"Companies invest capital, technology, and expertise to extract these resources, and they should earn a commercial return.
"But they do not create the underlying resource, so when resource prices and profits surge, the public should share properly in the upside.
"There is a clear public demand for Australia to rapidly modernise its public-capture mechanisms before more finite public wealth is extracted without a fair public return."
Australia's resource wealth giveaway
The organisation released a report last week, Australia's resource wealth giveaway: How weak public capture leaves billions in revenue on the table.
The report's author was Richard Wielga, a former economist with Victoria's Department of Treasury and Finance.
It compares Australia's resource tax and royalty system against selected resource-rich peers, including Norway, Alaska, Chile, Peru, Québec, and Queensland's coal sector specifically, given Queensland's recent tax changes.
It asks three questions about Australia's resource tax regime:
- Is the system designed to collect more when prices and profits surge?
- What level of revenue does the public actually collect?
- Does stronger public capture automatically drive investment away?
It says if Australia's system had better boom sensitivity, it would collect about $45 billion more every year across state and Commonwealth revenue streams as it rode the global commodity price cycle.
It estimates Australia would collect an extra $28 billion a year from "mining" activity (coal, iron ore, gold, copper, lithium and other miners), and $16—$18 billion from the "petroleum" sector (oil, gas and LNG).
See the graphic below:
International comparisons
The report asks: For every dollar of value created by the resource sector, how much was collected by the public?
It then compares Australia's "public-capture ratio" with some of its global peers.
It shows that Australia's public-capture ratio for petroleum is very weak compared to Norway and Alaska.
It makes the point that Norway's mixed state-participation model is very different to Australia's private-operator model, so to make Norway's public-capture ratio more comparable with Australia's, it removes state-participation activity from Norway's numbers (it makes other adjustments for Alaska).
It shows Australia's mining result is stronger relative to peers, but it could be much stronger, as Queensland coal shows.
"Australia's mining-only public-capture result is stronger than might have been expected," the report says.
"It is higher than the observed ratios for all three selected international mining peers: Quebec, Chile, and Peru.
"That is surprising because Australia's mining design relies heavily on low and flat royalties, while those peers have more boom-sensitive mining regimes.
"[But] this result does not mean Australia's mining royalty design is optimal or that the status quo should remain."
The report says several factors may help to explain the result.
"Actual collection depends on commodity mix, price cycles, project maturity, and cost structures," it says.
"Australia's mining sector includes large, mature, high-volume iron ore and coal production. Quebec, Chile, and Peru have different commodity mixes and cost structures.
"Differences in tax administration and compliance may also affect observed collections."
How different designs respond to a boom differently
The report says not all royalties or taxes respond to resource booms in the same way, and some tax designs can appear good on paper but perform badly.
For example, it says Australia's Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT) was designed to tax super-profits from offshore petroleum projects, so its boom sensitivity design is high.
But it has failed to produce strong and timely revenues, and current forecasts show no sustained improvement.
"Australia's experience of the PRRT does not mean super-profit taxes cannot work," the report says.
"But it does show that design rules matter and if these are too generous or complex, a resource rent tax can look strong on paper while collecting much less in practice."
Queensland coal is the proof point
The report says recent tax changes in Queensland show that much stronger boom-sensitive public-capture is possible in Australia.
Since July 1, 2022, Queensland's coal royalty scheme has had highly progressive price bands.
Its coal royalty rate rises in several steps with price: from 7 per cent at lower coal prices, to 40 per cent once coal prices exceed $300 a tonne:
- 7 per cent on the first $100/t
- 12.5 per cent on the portion from $100-$150/t
- 15 per cent on the portion from $150-$175/t
- 20 per cent on the portion from $175-$225/t
- 30 per cent on the portion from $225-$300/t
- 40 per cent on the portion above $300/t
Prosper Australia says that kind of royalty schedule is much more "boom-sensitive" than a flat royalty.
Prior to July 1, 2022, the highest Queensland coal rate was 15 per cent on the portion above $150 a tonne.
What happened when the new tax schedule was introduced?
In three years since July 2022, the number of active coal mines in Queensland increased from 53 in 2021–22 to 60 in 2024–25.
The state's coal employment remained around 26,000 workers on a four-quarter average basis, and its saleable coal was "particularly stable", the report says.
Prosper Australia says that evidence is important.
It says arguments have recently been mounting against Queensland's royalty regime, particularly since some mine operators in Queensland began cutting jobs in 2025 and reducing production, blaming higher royalties, alongside falling coal prices and rising costs.
But it says even under a well-designed, boom-sensitive royalty regime, some mines will become uneconomic when global prices fall, costs rise, or deposits mature.
The latest Queensland government figures showed there were 58 active coal mines in Queensland in 2025–26.
Low royalties are a policy choice
Overall, the report makes two suggestions.
It says Australia should modernise its royalties system and address its petroleum under-capture, while allowing viable resource projects to earn a commercial return.
It says governments should adopt market-linked royalties that rise when commodity prices exceed long-run norms.
Or, as an alternative to a purely market-linked royalty, it says states could combine a minimum royalty floor with a second boom-sensitive component linked to prices, profits or profit margins.
"This helps ensure a minimum public return while production continues, and allows the public share to rise when market conditions are strong," it says.
And the same principle should apply when trying to fix Australia's petroleum under-capture, it says.
"This report does not design a new Commonwealth petroleum tax, but future reforms should be judged against the same principle: public returns should rise when prices and profits surge," it says.

Europe remembers its murdered Jews, but does it listen to living ones? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

The gates are gone. So are most of the people who once passed through them. On a quiet street in Kaunas, Lithuania, a small memorial marks the entrance to the Jewish ghetto established here in 1941.
Behind it stands a residential building, its walls covered in colorful geometric patterns. Someone has left a few stones at the foot of the memorial. People live here now. They come home from work, carry their shopping upstairs, and go about their lives. I wonder how often they stop to think about what happened on this street.
Before the Holocaust, Kaunas was home to some 37,000 Jews. By August 1941, nearly 30,000 had been forced into the ghetto. Most were murdered by the Nazis and their Lithuanian collaborators. Only a few thousand survived.
Later this month, Kaunas will mark 85 years since the Great Action of October 28-29, 1941, when some 9,200 Jews, including 4,273 children, were selected and then murdered at the Ninth Fort.
I have visited many Holocaust memorials over the years. Yet standing before this modest marker, I found myself thinking less about the past than about the present.
Europe has invested enormous effort in remembering its murdered Jews. Museums, memorials, and Holocaust education have become part of European public life. All of this matters deeply. But why does a continent so committed to remembering dead Jews sometimes struggle to listen to living ones?
The dead make no political demands. They do not criticize European governments or challenge European Union (EU) institutions. Living Jews do. So do Israelis, whose relationship with Europe has always involved disagreement, disappointment, and sometimes genuine affection.
European Jews and Israelis are not the same community. European Jews should never have to defend an Israeli government or answer for its decisions. Yet both encounter, in different ways, a Europe that sometimes seems more comfortable with Jewish history than with Jewish voices today.
For European Jews, this is painfully real. A 2024 survey by the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights found that, at least occasionally, 76% of Jewish respondents concealed their Jewish identity, while 75% felt that people in their country blamed them for the Israeli government’s actions because they were Jewish. The survey was conducted before October 7, 2023.
Think about what those numbers mean. Everyday choices become questions of personal safety. These concerns accompanied me to the annual conference of the European Association of Israel Studies, held in Kaunas this month.
The conference offered something increasingly precious: people willing to listen to arguments they might strongly oppose. Scholars discussed Israeli democracy, Palestine, antisemitism, Holocaust memory, and Israel’s relationship with Europe.
Arab citizens of Israel were among the presenters. A researcher from the University of Haifa examined restrictions on spatial planning in Israel following October 7. Others addressed Jewish-Arab relations, academic boycotts, and the challenges of teaching Israel in European classrooms.
I did not agree with everything I heard. But agreement was never the point.
Yet elsewhere in Europe, the channels for such exchanges are narrowing. In June 2025, Erasmus University Rotterdam froze institutional cooperation with Bar-Ilan University, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and the University of Haifa after an independent committee warned of risks of complicity in human rights violations. Student exchanges were suspended, and new institutional research collaborations halted.
Universities have a responsibility to examine their partnerships, particularly during a war that has caused such terrible suffering in Gaza. Those moral questions are real and cannot simply be brushed aside. But making academic contact harder does not make difficult political questions easier to answer.
The University of Haifa is among the institutions affected by Rotterdam’s decision. One of its researchers, an Arab citizen of Israel, could still present his work in Kaunas. But what of the students who might have studied abroad, the young researchers who could have worked together, and the conversations lost when institutional connections are severed?
Some of those missing conversations might have challenged Israeli government policies more forcefully than anything said from a distance.
Blaming European Jews for Israel’s actions and questioning partnerships with Israeli universities are not the same thing. But neither should mean treating people as proxies for a government. Europe does not become more principled by narrowing academic exchange. It becomes less equipped to understand a society whose decisions affect Israelis, Palestinians, and Europeans alike.
Another encounter in Kaunas captured the complexity of Europe’s relationship with its Jews. Lea Goldberg, one of the great poets of modern Hebrew literature, looks down from a mural. She grew up in Kaunas before immigrating to Palestine in 1935.
Beside her portrait appears her poem “Pine,” in Hebrew and Lithuanian. It speaks of two landscapes, two places that feel like home, and the difficulty of belonging entirely to either.
Goldberg’s memories of Lithuania were complicated. In 1919, as her family returned from wartime displacement, her father was detained and severely mistreated. He never fully recovered.
I was glad Kaunas remembered her. But I wondered how she might have felt about being celebrated in a place that had given her both a childhood and painful memories.
The ghetto memorial and Goldberg’s portrait tell different stories. One recalls a Jewish world that was destroyed. The other reminds us that Jewish life continued elsewhere, including in Israel. Neither story is simple. Neither should be.
Civil discussions with people of different views
Our hosts at Vytautas Magnus University welcomed us warmly. We could criticize Israeli government policies, discuss Palestinian suffering, disagree about history, and still sit together over coffee. Nobody needed to pretend our disagreements were small.
After years of attending academic conferences, I never expected to feel grateful simply because people with different views could sit in the same room and talk. In Kaunas, I did.
At the ghetto memorial, I thought again about the families who once lived in these streets. They were Europeans. They went to school, fell in love, and made plans for the future. Some probably wanted to leave. Others could not imagine living anywhere else. They did not know they would one day be remembered primarily for how they died.
Jewish life in Europe was never only a story of loss, and it is not one today. Israel cannot replace the Jewish Europe that disappeared. Nor should European Jews be treated as representatives of Israel. Both deserve to be encountered as people, not as symbols in arguments others have already settled.
I am grateful for Europe’s memorials, museums, and ceremonies. I want future generations to visit them – and to understand that the people we remember were once living Europeans, with opinions, fears, ambitions, and disagreements of their own.
The stones at the Kaunas memorial honor people who can no longer speak. Listening to those who can would be another way of honoring their memory.
The writer is a senior fellow at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev at the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) and a professor of European studies and international relations in the Department of Politics and Government at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev.

UK police suspect Iranian intelligence role in plot targeting US air base, rearrest 2

British counterterrorism police on Tuesday rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence in connection with an alleged plot targeting RAF Fairford, a British air base used by the U.S. military to launch strikes against Iran earlier this year.
The suspects, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, were detained under the National Security Act as investigators intensified their examination of possible Iranian state involvement in the September 27 incident.
The 24-year-old was among five men initially arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, while the 25-year-old was arrested several days later in central London. Both had previously been released on bail.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Britain's National Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators increasingly suspected a connection to Tehran.
"This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," Taylor said.
"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it," he added.
The investigation stems from a major security incident near RAF Fairford on September 27, when five men were arrested after suspicious activity was reported close to the installation. Two additional suspects were detained in the following days, bringing the total number of arrests to seven. The five men not rearrested Tuesday remain on bail. No charges have been filed.
The initial incident prompted a large-scale security operation involving armed police, military bomb disposal teams and the evacuation of dozens of nearby residents. Investigators discovered three suspicious vans containing gasoline, which police described as an accelerant, but found no explosives.
Early reports had suggested the vehicles contained explosive materials, raising fears of an imminent attack. Police subsequently clarified that no explosive devices had been recovered.
RAF Fairford has played a significant role in American military operations against Iran. U.S. B-1 bombers stationed at the base were used in strikes against Iranian targets during this year's conflict, making the installation a potential target amid escalating tensions between Tehran and Washington.
Following the September incident, the United States withdrew its B-1 bombers from the base amid security concerns.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that the suspected activity at RAF Fairford was likely coordinated from Iran, an allegation rejected by the Iranian ambassador to Britain.
Tehran had previously denied any connection to the suspected plot. In a statement following the initial arrests, the Iranian Embassy in London condemned what it called "malicious and baseless speculation," accusing those linking Iran to the incident of fueling anti-Iranian sentiment in Britain.
The arrests followed an unusual encounter involving a local farmer who reported seeing three vans blocking a rural road near the base shortly after midnight on September 27.
According to earlier British media reports, the woman was returning from a party when she noticed the vehicles and several masked men acting suspiciously near the installation. After turning her car around, she saw men scattering into nearby fields and trees, including in the direction of the air base.
She immediately contacted emergency services and warned other residents through a local WhatsApp group. Police arrived within minutes and detained the five initial suspects.
"It looks like by doing that I basically disrupted whatever they were planning," the woman told British media.
The farmer later said the vans appeared to display suspicious business markings and telephone numbers. Fuel2U, a British fuel delivery company whose name reportedly appeared on the vehicles, denied any connection to them.
Her account raised questions about whether the suspected plot had been uncovered through intelligence gathering or an unexpected encounter with a civilian.
U.S. President Donald Trump subsequently praised the arrests, saying British and American authorities had worked together to apprehend the suspects. He claimed the men had been under joint surveillance for an extended period and had intended to cause serious damage to the installation.
However, British media reported that local police had responded to information from residents rather than a preplanned intelligence operation.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting praised the farmer's actions but suggested that her account did not reflect the full extent of the authorities' knowledge. "She did exactly what we would hope someone in such an unusual situation would do, and I am genuinely grateful to her," Streeting said at the time, adding that she had only a "partial picture" of events.
The woman later criticized the response, saying investigators had not contacted her for a follow-up interview despite her role in reporting the suspicious activity.
The investigation has taken on added significance because of Iran's previous warnings that military installations used to conduct American strikes against Iranian territory could become targets. Tehran threatened in July to target bases such as RAF Fairford if U.S. aircraft continued using them for operations against Iran.
The latest arrests mark a significant development in the investigation, with police now explicitly identifying Iran as the foreign state suspected of involvement and examining whether individuals in Britain were acting on behalf of its intelligence services.
Taylor emphasized that investigators were pursuing multiple lines of inquiry in what he described as a highly complex case. "We know the public have unanswered questions," he said. "I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will."

Tap water no longer drinkable near South Africa’s capital

Tap water no longer drinkable near South Africa’s capital
PRETORIA - Residents of neighbourhoods in South Africa’s Tshwane municipality, which includes the capital Pretoria, have been told to stop drinking tap water after waterborne pathogens led hundreds of people to seek medical treatment, the city said Oct 20.
Africa’s most industrialised economy is grappling with chronic water woes as decades of infrastructure decay and poor maintenance push the system to the brink, making water a hot-button issue ahead of local government elections in November.
Tests found high levels of E. coli bacteria in water from the Bronkhorstspruit water treatment plant supplying the affected areas, the city said.
Stool samples from patients also contained norovirus, campylobacter and shigella, which can cause stomach cramps and diarrhoea.
E. coli lives in the intestines of humans and animals, and its presence in drinking water can signal contamination by sewage or other waste.
The water could only be used to flush the toilet, the city of Tshwane said.
The Bronkhorstspruit plant went without chlorination for three weeks because of problems with its chlorine supplier, the government said.
Between Oct 7 and 18, more than 400 people had been taken ill, most of them children under four.
No deaths have been reported while new cases peaked at 72 on Oct 13, according to government records.
“No cholera bacteria were found in the sampled stools,” the health department said in a statement on Oct 19.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Oct 20 the national government had intervened and hoped to resolve the crisis within days.
“We are very sorry that it has resulted in the challenge of gastroenteritis,” he said, adding: “We cannot afford a situation where our people are drawn to illness because of our inability to treat water properly.”
In 2023, the same region was hit with a cholera outbreak that claimed some 30 lives. AFP

AI Adoption: Are Air Force and Space Force Ready and Willing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:57:10 UTC
02:57:10 KST

Air Force and Space Force leaders are calling for Airmen and Guardians to enthusiastically embrace artificial intelligence and apply emerging tools to their work. In September, Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe even went so far as to say those who don’t embrace AI “will end up in someone else’s rearview mirror.”
Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink opened AFA’s annual Air, Space, and Cyber Conference Sept. 14 with the comments of a true believer, saying the department is “putting more than 300 AI tools into the hands of our people.”
“I use them every day,” Meink said. “This includes tools that streamline work for nearly 150,000 Airmen, and for our Guardians, data fusion tools that turn millions of data points into actual information.” He praised the maturing self-driving technology available in his personal automobile, and hinted that he was hard pressed to find a more complex problem for AI to solve than driving in downtown Washington D.C.
In June, following a “Corona” meeting of Air Force’s top three- and four-stars generals, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach announced forthcoming guidance for AI.
New Chief of Space Operations, Gen. Douglas A. Schiess noted even before he became Chief in September that his service was “not doing enough” to leverage AI. He stressed scaling AI across the force as a route to ensuring decision advantage. 
Yet despite leadership’s exhortations to embrace AI for automating burdensome admin tasks and accelerate decision-making, some experts see risk. “DOD’s approach to AI has been very interesting,” said Leah Siskind, an AI research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracy in October. “They’ve taken a lot of bold moves in kind of lowering the hurdles in procurement for AI tools… I think it was a really great approach. That being said, I think the intense cultural pressure coming from the top down, of use AI and we’re, you know, putting out AI slop posts that say, ‘We’re an AI-first workforce’ is a lot because leading technical transformation in government, it’s often largely a cultural process. You have to get people to trust the tools that they’re using, and you have to get them comfortable with this.”
But without a structured approach to vetting what AI tools Airmen are using for what tasks, risks abound. “My biggest concern with the kind of pace we’re adopting AI is it’s actually going to expedite bad processes,” Siskind said.
Keeping a Close Watch
Retired USAF Lt. Gen. William Bender, former Air Force CIO, told Air & Space Forces Magazine he thinks the Department of the Air Force has good intentions, but he questions their ability to manage AI use at an enterprise level.
“Two things can be true at once: we’re measuring it, we’re watching it, and setting objectives and … it’s completely out of control,” Bender said.
Bender, who advises Kosmoy, a company that builds enterprise AI infrastructure and governance platforms, said that institutions should have governance controls in place before they push widespread use of AI tools. With any new technology, users may be inclined to find and adopt their own solutions rather than wait for the institution to certify specific solutions.
The result is what IT professionals call “shadow IT,” which are IT processes that the IT leaders can’t track or protect. He’d like to see the department adopt an enterprise tool to manage and track AI usage.
“Otherwise, it’s a formula for disaster if you don’t really know how it’s being managed,” Bender said.
Shadow IT or shadow AI use poses more than just risk. It carries costs that disappear in operational budgets but add up across the enterprise. “The Air Force has so much IT that was never headquartered-sanctioned, and yet it’s still costing the Air Force,” he said. “So, it’s one of the biggest problems in managing a finite IT budget, because you don’t know where most of it is. And there’s heavy reliance on some of the shadow stuff that was never sanctioned in the first place.” While Bender sees value in bottom-up innovation where Airmen use AI tools to solve real operational problems, the management challenge is to provide a top-down approach to control and protect data and networks.
“I would be looking for efficiencies and productivity by enabling AI to automate and drive an enablement of changed business practices and workflows inside of a constrained environment,” Bender said.
Both Bender and George Dougherty, a retired Air Force colonel and the author of “Beast in the Machine: How Robotics and AI Will Transform Warfare and the Future of Human Conflict,” see risk in unbounded use of the tools.
Army Acting CIO Gabe Chiulli announced in May “unlimited” AI access for Sage AI, a Defense Department platform for accessing various AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini. But usage far outstripped the budget. By mid-June, the Army had burned through its 100 million-token allotment for the year.
Constraints can be helpful to make people thing about efficient and effective use of resources.
DAF Chief Information Officer Ashely Devoto told Air & Space Forces Magazine in October that the department is already working on this.
For example, she said, running basic cybersecurity vulnerability checks might not require the top-of-the-line AI model, and instead could be accomplished with existing, non-AI tools.
“Start with your baseline scanner so that you’re not burning all the tokens identifying what a vulnerability scanner could have already identified,” Devoto said. “We’re trying to be thoughtful about the usage of these models that are going to get expensive very quickly.”
The department is working through usage questions for using AI tools and calculating compute requirements as DAF looks at how AI use will fit into its mid- and long-term budget planning.
Using Gemini, Grok, or ChatGPT for every search is “kind of like driving your Bentley everywhere,” Dougherty said. “If you were just going to go to the 7-Eleven and get a Slurpee, it doesn’t really make sense to take the Bentley there if you’ve got your Honda Civic.”
Usage and Tracking
The Department of the Air Force embraced DOD’s GenAI.mil platform earlier this year for unclassified and sensitive back-office tasks, such as budget planning. The platform provides access to Google Gemini, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and xAI’s Grok.
To date, more than half the 3.3 million uniformed and civilian DOD personnel with access have used the platform, according to the Pentagon.
DAF Chief Data and Artificial Intelligence Officer Susan Davenport is responsible for AI strategy, policy, governance, oversight, and acceleration of AI capabilities within the department.
The department tracks “relevant use cases and capabilities” through a central inventory dubbed CLARA, an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“These use cases are at different stages of maturity, ranging from evaluation and pilot efforts to more established operational applications,” the spokesperson said. “Access and use depend on mission need, security requirements, applicable approvals, and the sponsoring organization.”
The department’s goal is “pervasive, enterprise-wide adoption, supported by the DAF AI Strategy and the DAF AI Hiring & Talent Development Plan, which establishes the DAF as an AI-first force and mandates baseline AI literacy for all personnel.”
Wolfe, USAF’s top enlisted Airman, is doing his part to lead the charge. He established an AI Action Team, a widespread confederation of about 165 Airmen and Air Force civilians who meet virtually to identify “promising grassroots” AI projects for potential enterprise-level “visibility, support and adoption” for the broader Air Force, a lead member of the CMSAF’s AI Action Team told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email response.
Wolfe’s staff did not disclose the names of any of the action team members. But speaking to Airmen at the conference in September, he invited them to bring their ideas and challenges to him and promised to connect them with task force members to help.
Among the more than 50 projects the team has brought to Wolfe’s attention so far are AI training for the 300-, 500-, and 700-level Air Force Foundation Course, beta testing for emerging DOD AI products, and building AI tools to streamline headquarters processes, the lead member wrote.
CMSAF and the team measure the utility of the tools by evaluating “project delivery, adoption, time and cost savings, process improvement, and the ability to scale successful solutions across the force,” the member wrote.
While Davenport’s CDAO office tracks the use cases and capabilities, responsibility for managing the development, authorization, and delivery of AI tools resides with the mission owners, the spokesperson wrote.
“A use case’s inclusion in the enterprise inventory does not itself constitute authorization for Department-wide use,” the spokesperson wrote.
The CDAO and DAF Data and AI Council provide oversight.
DAF evaluates whether AI tools being used for various missions support those mission outcomes via its AI Strategy.
Learning and Risks
Even when Airmen or Guardians use AI for routine office tasks or promotion board reviews, Bender said, unintentional risks remain.
Users could expose private information unwittingly through an errant prompt, he said. Or a user may ask the AI tool to perform a task, but the prompt may be interpreted differently than intended.
“Exposure to the internet is exposure to the world,” Bender said. “That also opens up-doors into your own networks that would otherwise have been potentially constrained.”
Air Force Maj. Megan Hainline, chief of air superiority programs in the International Affairs Weapons Division on the Air Staff and a visiting fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracy, said in a panel discussion in October that AI adoption will ultimately come Airman by Airman and unit by unit.
“There’s a lot of resources out there, but actually trickling that into the unit level and having somebody walk you through it” takes time, she said. People are busy, and may not be inclined to adopt tasks without a push, Hainline added: “It’s hard to take a step back and get to learn about these new technologies until it is kind of forced upon you.”
She advocates for squadron-level units to designate unit experts who can take the lead, updating and advising colleagues on tools specific to their jobs and duties and courses or videos for training.
“Give them a foothold, because it is overwhelming,” she said. “If you’re like, ‘I want to learn about AI,’ you have no idea where to start.”

Reported by
After months of public unrest and more than a week of escalating anti-government protests, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has called demonstrators to the negotiating table, setting up chairs labeled "DIALOGUE" at the bottom of the stairs leading into the government building.
"Now, whoever wants unconditional dialogue, wherever they want, whenever they want, even here if they want, I am available along with the Government," Rama said in a video posted to Facebook on Tuesday. "The only ones who are not welcome are those who commit violence and those who do not distance themselves from violence."
The overture comes as student-led demonstrations enter their eighth day, with crowds demanding Rama's resignation over allegations of widespread corruption. Authorities said masked suspects attacked officers and police vehicles with hard objects and set fire to road signs, injuring seven officers.
Police emphasized that over the past seven days, 271 individuals have been arrested. Authorities highlighted that 51 of those detained have prior criminal records involving serious offenses such as murder, drug production, extortion, prostitution, and illegal weapons possession, reinforcing the prime minister's claims of outside agitation.
The heavy-handed police response has sparked severe human rights concerns. In a preliminary report released Tuesday, the People’s Advocate (Ombudsman) detailed numerous violations during the detention of protesters.
Commissioner Ahmet Prençi reported that at Police Station No. 1, five out of eight detained minors alleged physical and verbal abuse by police, with two showing visible signs of physical injury. The Ombudsman’s monitors also documented that authorities conducted baseless cell phone searches without judicial orders, escorted bystanders without cause, and failed to wear identification numbers.
Furthermore, the report highlighted severe overcrowding at the Security Block, which was holding 109 arrested individuals without adequate beds, water, heating, or medical care. The Ombudsman has demanded an immediate reduction in overcrowding, an absolute halt to illegal phone searches, and mandatory visible identification for all officers on duty as its administrative investigation continues.

Polish lawmakers vote to ease abortion ban, but face likely presidential veto
WARSAW, Oct 20 - Poland's lower house of parliament on Tuesday voted to allow abortion in case of foetal abnormalities and to decriminalise providing help in getting an abortion, as lawmakers seek to reverse a near-total abortion ban introduced by the previous government.
The legislation, however, is almost certain to be vetoed by the nationalist president.
Poland, a predominantly Catholic country, introduced a near-total abortion ban in 2021 after the constitutional court ruled that terminations due to foetal abnormalities were unconstitutional. The abortion ban led to widespread protests.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-European coalition won the 2023 election partly on a pledge to ease abortion restrictions. President Karol Nawrocki has signalled he would block any liberalisation of the law.
"The reality is that these pieces of legislation represent very limited small-scale reform and would not improve the situation for most women in Poland who need abortion care," Leah Hoctor, Vice President for Europe at the Center for Reproductive Rights, told Reuters.
Separate draft legislation that would legalise abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy is under consideration in parliamentary committees.
Tusk's government had earlier taken steps to expand access to abortions under existing regulations which allow abortion on mental health grounds.
Under the current law, abortion is only legal in cases involving rape or incest, or when a woman's health or life is at risk. REUTERS

US judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:50:59 UTC
02:50:59 KST

Rabia İclal Turan
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
A US federal judge has dismissed a civil lawsuit filed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s sister accusing him of repeated sexual abuse more than two decades ago, an accusation he denies.
US District Judge Zachary Bluestone of the Eastern District of Missouri dismissed Ann Altman’s claims with prejudice Monday, meaning they cannot be refiled.
“Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice,” wrote Bluestone.
The judge said she failed to appear for a court-ordered independent medical examination “on three separate occasions,” despite accommodations including “the presence of a female nurse, the option of traveling to Boston instead of St. Louis, and ensuring she could knit.”
“The Court has repeatedly warned Annie that her failure to appear for a court-ordered IME (independent medical examiner) would result in the dismissal of her case with prejudice,” said the order.
Bluestone found that her conduct amounted to “a pattern of intentional delay” and that her “explanations or excuses” were not credible.
The court also granted Sam Altman’s request to dismiss his counterclaims without prejudice. It denied his request for attorneys’ fees, saying the dismissal “is a sufficient sanction.”

With further U.S. support for Ukraine in doubt as relations between Zelenskyy and Trump sour again, the Ukrainian leader said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is on a trip to Asia.
That conversation came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down... support for us."
Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy also said he sought Rubio's help to ensure that the United States continues to share vital intelligence with Ukraine after Kyiv received no or belated warnings about Russian missile attacks in recent days.
The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.
Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.
"Nothing has changed," he told reporters.
The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.
With the Russian army held up on the front line, Putin is trying to bomb Ukraine into submission while robbing it of vital U.S. support, Western leaders and analysts say.
European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.
European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.
"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for ... one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.
Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.
Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.
On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said.
National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks.
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa.
Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

Russian attacks on vessels, multimillion-dollar losses, and a threat to global grain prices: the European Parliament explained how the Black Sea will be protected
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:48:06 EEST
02:48:06 KST

Russian attacks on vessels, multimillion-dollar losses, and a threat to global grain prices: the European Parliament explained how the Black Sea will be protected
Kyiv • UNN
The European Parliament discussed protecting shipping after six attacks by allegedly Russian drones in ten days. The EU will strengthen monitoring and pressure.
On October 20, the European Parliament held a debate in Strasbourg on the escalation of attacks on merchant vessels in the Black Sea. The EU is considering strengthening maritime surveillance, counter-drone measures, and diplomatic pressure on russia.
UNN reports in more detail on how the European Union proposes to protect the Black Sea from the lawlessness of the russian federation.
Why Black Sea security is being discussed in the European Parliament
The debate was prompted by a series of strikes on civilian vessels near Romania and Bulgaria, which are members of the EU and NATO. According to European diplomatic chief Kaja Kallas, six attacks, allegedly involving russian drones, occurred in the region over ten days.
"The risks are already extending beyond Ukrainian ports: the lives of sailors, trade routes, and the security of neighboring states are under threat. The EU must respond with economic, security, and diplomatic measures," the European diplomatic chief emphasized.
Attacks on merchant vessels in the Black Sea: what you need to know about the main incidents
On October 15, Reuters reported that two tankers had been hit near the Romanian coast. The San Marino-flagged vessel Wine Trader was attacked near the entrance to the Sulina Channel, outside Romania's territorial waters. Five of the 12 sailors were rescued, while seven others were being searched for by rescuers. The Comoros-flagged tanker Yara J was hit in Romanian waters. A fire broke out on board, but the crew was unharmed.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan, for his part, confirmed the drone strikes but did not identify their origin. A Reuters source in NATO called the drones russian. On October 17, Romanian F-16s shot down two more drones over the country's territorial waters. Romania's Ministry of Defense suggested they were Geran-4 drones.
The consequences of russia's aggression in the Black Sea for Ukraine's maritime exports
According to an estimate cited by Kallas, Ukraine is losing approximately €60 million in revenue every day due to strikes on export routes. Since mid-July, russia has intensified attacks on agricultural infrastructure, Black Sea and Danube ports, grain storage facilities, vessels, and logistics hubs.
This is occurring as maritime transport remains the backbone of grain exports. Around 90% of Ukraine's key agricultural export commodities pass through the Black Sea corridor. Threats to vessels increase insurance and delivery costs, disrupt sailing schedules, and reduce exporters' revenues.
Why global food security has come under threat
Ukraine remains a major food supplier. In her October 20 speech, the European diplomatic chief cited the following shares of our country in global exports:
-  15% of corn;  
-  10% of wheat;  
-  15–20% of barley;  
-  about 50% of sunflower oil.  
"Therefore, the strikes (by the russian armed forces, — ed.) also affect importing countries," the diplomat concluded.
The markets of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East are particularly vulnerable to the threat of a food crisis.
"Global grain prices have reached their highest level since February 2023. Droughts and difficulties with fertilizer supplies are aggravating the situation. Disruptions in the Black Sea compound these risks and could further affect prices for consumers," Kaja Kallas explained.
How the EU plans to protect shipping in the Black Sea waters
Kallas outlined the need for early threat detection and rapid data exchange.
"In particular, EU member states can use the MARSUR network to exchange maritime surveillance information. Romania and Bulgaria, with the support of the European Union, are establishing a joint maritime security center in the Black Sea," she said.
Other areas include joint procurement of systems to combat aerial and maritime drones, strengthened surveillance on the eastern flank, and mine-countermeasures capabilities. The European Parliament was also presented with an emergency protocol for consideration, intended to accelerate consultations among EU countries and coordination with NATO during major hybrid crises.
Separately, the European People's Party group called for an EU naval operation to protect merchant vessels near Bulgaria, Romania and the Danube Delta. ANSA reported this, citing MEP Andriy Novakov. However, no decision to launch such a mission has been made so far.
Can alternative routes replace the sea for exporters?
The EU supports exports through the so-called "solidarity lanes," which combine rail, road, river and European port routes. According to Kallas, grain shipments along these routes have increased by nearly 2 million tonnes since July. However, there are many nuances and "sticking points" here.
First, overland logistics have limited capacity, require the transshipment of goods and are usually more expensive for large consignments of grain. Second, Russia is also attacking border infrastructure near Moldova, Romania and Poland. Therefore, alternative routes help reduce dependence on seaports, but do not provide an equivalent replacement for the Black Sea corridor.
The Kremlin's aggression in the Black Sea: what is the world's response and what diplomatic steps are being proposed
The European Council condemned attacks on civilian and merchant vessels, including in the exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania. EU leaders called them serious violations of international and maritime law, including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and called for the safe passage of vessels to be restored.
And today, October 20. Kaja Kallas said that the EU had been in contact with Turkey, India and the countries of the Global South regarding an agreement on freedom of navigation. According to her, Ukraine proposed such a mechanism, but Russia rejected it.
What to expect next
On October 22, the European Parliament is scheduled to vote on a resolution concerning the escalation of Russian strikes and the security of the Black Sea. The document will set out the political position of MEPs. However, it is important to understand that it will not automatically create a European naval mission capable of countering Russia's aggressive actions in the Black Sea region.
Therefore, the further situation will depend on the ability of the countries in the region to protect vessels and ports, establish the exchange of intelligence and maintain alternative routes. For Ukraine, uninterrupted access to maritime exports remains crucial for now.
Recall
Somewhat earlier, Turkey warned that the Black Sea must not become a new front in the Russian-Ukrainian war. Official Ankara also said that attacks on civilian vessels were increasing, along with risks to shipping and food security.

French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:41:58 UTC
02:41:58 KST

TikTok and eBay were among six online platforms summoned by the French government this week, as authorities sought to contain widespread rioting and looting and prevent the resale of stolen goods.
Anne Le Hananff, France’s minister of digital affairs, convened representatives from social media firms on Tuesday for an emergency meeting, after their platforms were blamed for fanning the flames of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years. The goal of the meeting was to remind platforms that they need to moderate content on their sites, including livestream video, to avoid violent content or anything that could encourage people to break the imposed curfew, according to French TV station BFM.
A review by WIRED of TikTok found that the search term “blocus”—meaning blockade in French— showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, including viral images of a protester in a Pink Panther costume. The search term is also being used to promote “Act II” of the protests for October 24. The platform issued an “evolving situation” tag on the search term that said: “This situation is developing rapidly. Information available now may be unverified, incomplete, inaccurate, or subject to change. Take care when viewing this content, and report anything that may violate our Community Guidelines.”
A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.
Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.
French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.
The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
