Russia builds long-range radar in Kaliningrad: Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:41:00 UTC
02:41:00 KST

Russia has constructed a powerful radar facility in its Baltic Sea exclave of Kaliningrad capable of tracking aircraft, missiles and ships as far as 3,200 kilometers (2,000 miles) away, British media reported.
The system could expand Moscow’s surveillance capabilities in northern and western Europe, including the U.K., The Times newspaper reported Monday, citing satellite imagery.
Located near the town of Gvardeysk, the installation is in Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory bordering NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
The facility features three radiating arms of antenna masts, each 500 meters (1,640 feet) long, according to the report.
The configuration suggests the installation could be an over-the-horizon (OTH) radar – technology designed to detect targets beyond the line of sight of conventional radar systems.
OTH radars use high-frequency radio waves that can reflect off the ionosphere, allowing them to detect potential targets over much greater distances than conventional systems.
The radar’s reported range is estimated at between 885 and 3,200 kilometers (550 to 2,000 miles), potentially enabling Russia to monitor military activity across large parts of Europe.
Kaliningrad is strategically important to Moscow because of its position on the Baltic Sea, between Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members.

After quiet night, France imposes nightly curfews ‘for as long as necessary’ in Paris, big cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:34:18 UTC
02:34:18 KST

Fresh curfews were being imposed across the city centers of Paris and Lyon on Tuesday after the first quiet night since France’s most destructive rioting in years, as Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said a “massive” security operation was planned for new protests Saturday.
Paris police said the curfew in two designated zones — around Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district — had restored “public peace” overnight and would remain in place “for as long as necessary.” The curfew zones leave out other areas hit on Saturday, including the Champs-Elysées and the area around the Saint-Lazare train station and parts of the Rue de Turbigo in central Paris, where protesters set up barricades and lit fires.
In Lyon, one of France’s largest cities, authorities also renewed a curfew in the city center from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., saying no disturbances had been recorded overnight.
Marseille, France’s second-largest city, imposed a curfew for unaccompanied minors starting Tuesday night. Lecornu said the targeted curfews “helped keep last night calm.”
Student unions and groups from the “ yellow vest ” movement, whose protests over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, have called for another day of protests Saturday.
Soldiers from Sentinelle, the anti-terrorism operation that has patrolled French cities since the 2015 Islamic State group attacks, will take over guarding sensitive sites to free up more police officers and gendarmes for crowd control, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers Tuesday.
“The deployment (of police forces) for next Saturday will be massive,” Lecornu told the National Assembly, France’s lower house of parliament, without giving figures.
Suspect held over Limoges city hall fire
Police on Tuesday arrested a suspect in the arson attack that charred the historic city hall in Limoges, in central France, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, adding that the person was being held in police custody and may not have acted alone.
French media reported that the suspect was close to radical environmentalist movements and was on a watchlist of people considered potential threats to national security. Darmanin declined to comment on the suspect’s profile, but said far-left groups appeared to have organized to attack symbols of the state throughout France.
Footage of the 143-year-old building in flames, its bell tower collapsing, spread widely online over the weekend. U.S. Vice President JD Vance shared it on X, blaming the unrest on immigration and writing, “I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn.” President Donald Trump, who also relayed the video, said migrants had “taken over France.”
French officials have instead blamed the violence on far-left groups and opportunistic looters. At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire and stormed public buildings, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.
In Paris on Monday night, a police helicopter circled over Place de la République overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the curfew was being respected. Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument.
Louise Belanger, a volunteer who came to help with the cleanup, said she still could not apprehend the level of violence. “Normally when you are 20 you should be optimistic, you should be starting to build something (...) If you are only anger and violence, what are you going to do? This is sad for everybody in society,” she said.
Courts promise ‘extremely firm’ response
Speaking in Lille, northern France, Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,400 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.
In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the October 17 protests, the city prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Darmanin said he had asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. “People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of,” he said, arguing that the French justice system will be “extremely firm.”
In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and jailed immediately for looting a video game store in the city’s old town.
The National Assembly is launching an inquiry into the October 17 violence and the authorities’ policing strategy, its speaker, Yaël Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected “by the end of the year.”
Protests continued Tuesday on a smaller scale. Some 400 people, mostly high school and university students, marched in the western city of Rennes, and about 750 in Lyon, under pouring rain.

The IDF on Tuesday showed footage of Hezbollah using a truck to move weapons from one location to another. These weapons, the IDF said, were supposed to have been seized by the Lebanese army.
The footage then shows the IDF striking the truck as it pulled away from its original location. The IDF said this was one of many examples that demonstrated that the Lebanese army lied about having dealt with Hezbollah’s weapons.
On Tuesday, the IDF declined to reveal when the strike in question took place. However, given when the rest of the narrative was publicized, it likely took place around or after mid-2026.
According to the IDF, in December 2025, a military asset in the Kfarra area of southern Lebanon, which Hezbollah had used to store weapons, was referred to the Lebanese army for handling through the US-led monitoring mechanism.
The Lebanese army subsequently stated that the asset had been addressed, the IDF said.
IDF: Hezbollah continued operating after the Lebanese Army declared control
Several months after this statement, the IDF asserted that it discovered that Hezbollah had continued operating at the site.
Several months after the Lebanese army had declared that it had addressed the asset, Hezbollah was still able to use it for its own purposes, the IDF claimed.
Furthermore, the IDF stated that “the accompanying footage shows Hezbollah operatives loading weapons stored at the site onto a truck in an attempt to remove them and preserve them as part of the terrorist organization’s capabilities.”
“After the activity was identified, IDF troops struck the truck carrying the weapons removed from the site. The footage indicates that, after the site was reported as having been addressed, Hezbollah activity was identified there in an attempt to remove and preserve weapons and military equipment,” said the IDF.
Lebanese Army coordinated with Hezbollah, IDF says
Next, the IDF stated: “The Intelligence Directorate has identified instances in which elements within the Lebanese army coordinated with Hezbollah regarding enforcement activities.”
“This coordination assisted efforts to prevent, delay, or thwart enforcement operations, and enabled Hezbollah to prepare in advance to remove and transfer weapons from the area,” said the IDF.
Tuesday was not the first time the IDF had presented evidence of this nature. In the past, the IDF presented extensive evidence that showed certain senior Lebanese army officials cooperating with Hezbollah in 2024-2025.
In response to the IDF’s evidence, the US said it raised the issue with the Lebanese army. IDF officials have commended the US for its efforts, but claimed that the Lebanese army continues to fall short when it comes to clearing southern Lebanon of Hezbollah.
IDF expects the Lebanese Army to act 'more effectively' against Hezbollah
According to the IDF, “the Lebanese army is responsible for ensuring the full and thorough implementation of all tasks assigned to it.”
“The IDF emphasizes that it expects the Lebanese army to act more decisively and effectively to fulfill its responsibilities and prevent the presence of weapons and military infrastructure belonging to the Hezbollah terrorist organization in southern Lebanon,” said the IDF.
Next, the IDF said that both itself and “the Intelligence Directorate continue to monitor Hezbollah’s attempts to rebuild and strengthen its capabilities, and will not allow any violation that poses a threat to the State of Israel and its civilians.”
Moreover, the IDF said that Hezbollah “dragged Lebanon and its residents into a war in service of Iran during Operation Roaring Lion, launching thousands of rockets, including from areas south of the Litani River, where no armed elements, assets, or weapons belonging to anyone other than the Lebanese government or UNIFIL should be present.”
Officials from the US MARCENT military command, which supervises US-Israeli-Lebanese army relations, had not responded to an inquiry about the issue by press time.
Substantial disparity between Lebanese statements and reality on the ground
The IDF added: “Under the 2024 understandings, which guided Israeli and Lebanese actions until Operation Roaring Lion, the Lebanese army was responsible for acting against the presence of weapons and military infrastructure belonging to the Hezbollah terrorist organization in southern Lebanon.”
“However, this responsibility was not fulfilled as required, allowing Hezbollah to continue entrenching itself, arming itself, and building military infrastructure in the area,” said the IDF.
In early 2025, IDF sources told The Jerusalem Post that the Lebanese army had drastically improved its enforcement against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon, though it still fell substantially short of full enforcement.
In its statement on Tuesday, the IDF said, “Even during the Lebanese army’s 2025 Operation Homeland Shield, a significant gap remained between statements and the reality on the ground, and the operation did not dismantle the terrorist organization’s military capabilities or prevent it from continuing its activities and buildup.”
Israeli, Lebanese military delegations meet in US
Lebanese and Israeli military delegations are set to meet in Tampa, Florida, for another round of US-led negotiations. This follows several rounds of earlier negotiations, which began the process for Israel’s partial withdrawal from southern Lebanon. However, these talks were stalled by Israel accusing the Lebanese army of not doing enough to get rid of Hezbollah.
The renewed negotiations will take place at the headquarters of US Central Command (CENTCOM) and are projected to continue through Wednesday.
If further IDF withdrawals were to occur, they would likely be coordinated by US Lt.-Gen. Clearfield. He was the main coordinator for Lebanon-Israel issues from Fall 2024 until the early 2026 war.
IDF sources said in July that Clearfield properly understands the Lebanese army’s weaknesses. However, they said they could not vouch for other American officials, whose timeline differs from Israel’s and may lead to clashes with Israel’s security needs regarding Lebanon.
In the past, MARCENT officials refused to confirm any progress made in Lebanon.
The Post understands that Clearfield met with IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir on July 1 and secretly visited Lebanon on July 2.

Brandeis Center files complaint alleging antisemitic harassment at Montgomery high school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:33:49 UTC
02:33:49 KST

The Louis D. Brandeis Center for Human Rights Under Law has filed a federal Title VI complaint on Monday against Montgomery County Public Schools (MCPS) in Maryland, alleging that the district failed to protect a visibly Jewish student from severe antisemitic harassment, online targeting, and death threats at Montgomery Blair High School.
The filing follows the US Supreme Court's agreement to hear a separate legal case involving the Maryland school district's magnet middle school admissions policies. That Supreme Court case centers on a challenge to a lottery-based admissions system implemented to boost racial diversity, which critics argue unlawfully discriminates against Asian American applicants.
The Brandeis Center’s complaint outlines an escalating pattern of hostility directed at an Orthodox Jewish senior. Before transferring to Montgomery Blair High School, the student attended Northwood High School, another MCPS facility, where he faced severe antisemitic abuse, including teammates throwing coins at him while telling him to "pick it up, Jew," students making Hitler salutes, and an online message calling him a "Jewish freak" and telling him to kill himself.
After transferring to Blair, he continued to face continuous intimidation. Early on in his time there, he encountered isolated hostility, such as being told to "go back to 1935" by classmates.
'You’re a stupid f***ing Zionist Jew'
The hostility intensified significantly in April this year. While participating in a student-organized game known as "Senior Assassin," he received an anonymous phone call stating, "You’re a stupid f***ing Zionist Jew, and we are going to bomb you." Immediately following the call, fireworks were set off outside his home from a passing car, terrifying the student and his siblings.
Later that month, a student-run Instagram account publicizing post-graduation plans announced that the student intended to study in Israel before attending Yeshiva University. The post drew an influx of Palestinian flags and online accusations accusing him of involvement in "genocide." Rumors then spread through the student body that he was joining the IDF, heightening his safety concerns.
In-person interactions grew similarly hostile. In May, classmates intervened when a friend asked to look at a yearbook, telling the friend, "wait, take it back, he’s a Zionist," and demanding that the friend sever ties and declare support for Palestine. Witnesses reported that students frequently deployed "Zionist" and "Zio" as pejoratives to socially isolate and shun Jewish students.
According to the complaint, school administrators repeatedly minimized the severity of the incidents. The principal allegedly dismissed the social media targeting as "just a flag" and questioned why being called a Zionist was problematic. Although the school implemented minor safety measures, the cumulative intimidation forced the student to reduce his attendance and leave early during his final weeks before graduating in June 2026.
The filing highlights that this case reflects a broader climate of concern across the district. In September, more than 40 local rabbis and cantors issued a public letter warning that MCPS’s inadequate response to antisemitic incidents had normalized hostility and driven Jewish families to withdraw their children.
"School administrators have no justification for failing to respond effectively to antisemitic harassment under their watch. An explicit anti-Jewish bomb threat should leave no doubt about the seriousness of the danger or the urgent need for an effective response from school leadership," said Hon. Kenneth L. Marcus, Chairman and CEO of the Brandeis Center and the former US Assistant Secretary of Education who ran the Office for Civil Rights during two administrations.
"A Jewish student was threatened with life-threatening violence, accused of genocide, ostracized by his classmates, and ultimately became afraid to attend school, while administrators allegedly treated his harassment as a political disagreement. It is both unfortunate and grimly ironic to see such incidents in a county that has such a robust Jewish community. Montgomery County school officials have an obligation to respond promptly and effectively to antisemitic incidents, just as they must respond to other forms of hate or bias."
"It is deeply concerning that this school district is facing multiple serious civil rights allegations, from racial discrimination in admissions to antisemitic harassment," Marcus added. "It is no coincidence that Montgomery County is attracting national attention for multiple alleged failures to protect different minority groups from discrimination. We welcome the Supreme Court’s decision to review the admissions case and hope it brings greater attention to the district’s responsibility to protect the rights of all students."
Brandeis Center pushes for investigation, sweeping corrective actions
The Brandeis Center is asking the US Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights (OCR) to investigate the district and mandate sweeping corrective actions. Requested remedies include the formal adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, mandatory staff and student training, policy revisions to account for cumulative harassment, and the appointment of an independent outside monitor for five years.
This legal action forms part of a broader nationwide push by the Brandeis Center to address anti-Jewish discrimination across primary and secondary educational institutions. Previous interventions include launching a lawsuit against California’s public school apparatus over widespread student harassment, pursuing litigation against Virginia’s Nysmith School following the purported expulsion of Jewish siblings who flagged bullying, and filing federal civil rights complaints against Georgia’s Fulton County School District.
Additionally, the organization partnered earlier this year with the Anti-Defamation League and Mayer Brown to secure a federal settlement that bolsters anti-discrimination protocols in Massachusetts’ Concord-Carlisle Regional School District.
JCRC: Dozens of children experience 'school-based antisemitism' every year
Guila Franklin Siegel, chief operating officer of the Jewish Community Relations Council (JCRC) of Greater Washington said in a statement, “While the JCRC is not a party to this action, we worked closely with the affected child and family during the time period in question, urging MCPS to take stronger steps to ensure the student’s safety in the face of relentless antisemitic bullying.”
Siegel added, “Every year, the JCRC supports dozens of Jewish families throughout the DMV whose children experience school-based antisemitism, advocating on their behalf with school officials and partnering with educators to implement responsive anti-bias education. This case was one of the more difficult we have encountered. As always, we thank our colleagues at the Brandeis Center for ensuring that Jewish families can seek legal relief to compel school districts to respond forcefully to the hatred taking place in their schools.”
“The complaint filed last week speaks to the devastating and long-term consequences of antisemitism on children and families - and the considerable work that remains for MCPS to properly address it. Whatever the outcome of this particular matter, the JCRC will continue to urge MCPS to take immediate and proactive steps, including better teacher and staff training, additional Holocaust and Jewish peer education programs, and stronger enforcement of social media guidelines to ensure that every Jewish child feels safe and protected at school,” Siegel said.

Benny Gantz's exit from Knesset race could help Ofer Winter cross electoral threshold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:33:31 UTC
02:33:31 KST

Benny Gantz's withdrawal from the Knesset race could provide Ofer Winter with the additional votes he needs to cross the electoral threshold, according to an internal poll conducted in recent days for one of the coalition parties.
The vote also found that 24.2% of Blue and White voters would switch to Winter's People of Israel party if Gantz's party did not run in the election.
The finding is particularly significant amid growing pressure from the Right on Winter to withdraw from the race over concerns that votes cast for his party could be wasted.
The poll was conducted among 800 respondents from Israel's Jewish population. Blue and White received 1.2% of the vote, equivalent to approximately one Knesset seat, or around 40,000 voters.
According to respondents' answers, nearly a quarter of Gantz's voters could move to Winter after his withdrawal, potentially adding about 10,000 votes to Winter's total.
Could Gantz's withdrawal from Knesset elections push Winter over the electoral threshold?
For Winter, those additional votes could prove decisive. Recent polls have placed his party anywhere between four and five Knesset seats, putting it near or below the electoral threshold. In such a close race, even a few thousand additional votes could determine whether the party enters the Knesset.
Based on the estimate of approximately 40,000 votes per Knesset seat, the potential gain for Winter from Gantz's supporters amounts to roughly a quarter of a seat. While relatively small in parliamentary terms, it could carry considerable weight for a party fighting to enter the Knesset.
The poll also found that 31.1% of Blue and White voters do not know which party they would support following its withdrawal. Another 17.6% said they would switch to Gadi Eisenkot's party, 9.4% to the Reservists-Economic Party led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, 9% to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, and 8.7% to the Democrats led by Yair Golan.
Winter holds a substantial lead over each of the other parties among Gantz voters who identified an alternative choice. His share in the poll exceeds that of Eisenkot, even though the latter has been considered one of the main potential beneficiaries of his former political partner's withdrawal.
Nearly a third of Blue and White voters surveyed have not yet chosen another party, so the vote distribution after Gantz's withdrawal remains uncertain. In the remaining days before the election, parties are expected to compete for these voters as well, a group that could influence the prospects of electoral lists polling near the threshold.
How will Blue and White supporters vote now?
The breakdown of responses indicates that Gantz's voters are not necessarily moving as a unified bloc toward parties in the anti-Netanyahu camp. Some favor Winter, others Likud, while others prefer Eisenkot, Hendel, or Golan. Blue and White's withdrawal could therefore affect more than one political camp, depending on where its supporters ultimately cast their ballots.
Gantz announced his withdrawal from the race following a prolonged period in which Blue and White struggled to cross the electoral threshold. He announced it on the eve of voting among IDF soldiers, and figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc presented it as a move to prevent wasted votes.
In discussions preceding the decision, Gantz maintained that he still believed Blue and White's standing could be improved through its election campaign. The decision to withdraw was ultimately made when it became clear that the party had not recovered sufficiently in the polls, against the backdrop of the start of early voting. Once voting began, it would no longer be possible to prevent votes from being lost if they were cast for a party that failed to cross the electoral threshold.
Figures on the Right quickly seized on Gantz's withdrawal to intensify pressure on Winter. Ministers Gideon Sa'ar and Shlomo Karhi urged parties that failed to cross the electoral threshold to draw similar conclusions.
In recent days, figures close to Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also pressured members of Winter's party, and one of its candidates, Davidi Ben-Zion, has already announced his withdrawal.
Against the backdrop of Likud's ongoing campaign against People of Israel, the internal poll raises the possibility that Gantz's withdrawal could instead strengthen Winter and improve his chances of entering the Knesset, even as figures on the Right attempt to persuade him to withdraw.
That possibility could also affect Likud's campaign calculations. If Winter gains support after Gantz withdraws and moves closer to comfortably crossing the electoral threshold, the argument that voting for him would necessarily waste a vote becomes harder to sustain.

Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who travelled from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
The case in the West African country comes amid an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and some cases in Kenya, raising concerns about a spread across the continent.
According to Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the woman began showing symptoms on October 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on October 11, before being diagnosed with Ebola.
Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun trying to trace 44 people who came into contact with the patient.
“We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.
New case in Kenya
Earlier on Tuesday, Kenya confirmed its ninth case of Ebola.
A 24-year-old man, who was already being held in quarantine, is the latest to test positive, Kenya’s Ministry of Health said in a statement on Tuesday.
“He was isolated at the first sign of illness, tested and started on treatment immediately upon confirmation of his positive test result,” it said, adding he “was already in quarantine when he fell ill”.
The man was a close family member of Kenya’s first Ebola patient, who had travelled from the DRC, through Uganda and before arriving in Kenya and dying at a Nairobi hospital on October 5.
“All nine cases belong to one cluster, and as of today there is no evidence of transmission outside this group,” Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said in a statement on Tuesday.
“Eight patients are stable and responding well to treatment, while 134 of 135 contacts have been traced and quarantined,” Amoth said.
Amoth said a milestone was in sight for the majority of the contacts in quarantine as they had remained well for the 21-day monitoring period and could return home from October 25.
It appealed to communities to welcome them back, saying they “pose no risk of infection”.
The ministry said no infections had occurred within quarantine facilities and that it was continuously monitoring infection-prevention measures to protect health workers.
Despite the nine infections, Kenya has not imposed restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, with authorities saying the country remains open for business.
In the DRC, there have been more than 9,000 Ebola cases and 4,000 deaths since May.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says it’s the second-largest epidemic on record.
It has been difficult to contain because there is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of the virus.
Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but was later declared free of the virus.

Turkey submits Saudi-Pakistan defence pact to Parliament for ratification, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:31:11 UTC
02:31:11 KST

Turkey submits Saudi-Pakistan defence pact to Parliament for ratification, sources say
ANKARA, Oct 20 - Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to Parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The agreement's first article says the parties shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.
"In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them," Article 2 of the agreement says.
The provision, similar to NATO's Article 5, refers to Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers the individual or collective right of states to self-defence against armed attack.
The three countries "will decide on the scope and nature of the support to be provided following an objective assessment of the assistance required" and will cooperate within their available resources, including military capabilities and resources, the same article says.
At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Turkey, which has a robust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh's military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
The agreement also envisages close cooperation on defence industry, intelligence sharing, logistical support and the fight against "all means of terrorism," including at the operational level.
Parliamentary ratification is required for Turkey to formally approve the agreement.
AIM TO "STRENGTHEN COLLECTIVE DETERRENCE"
Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, will refer the agreement to parliament's foreign affairs commission upon his return, two of the sources said. The contents and details of the agreement are expected to become public once it is submitted to the commission.
The commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday, another source said.
President Tayyip Erdogan's communications director, Burhanettin Duran, said that Turkey's recent step marked an important milestone towards the institutionalisation of strategic cooperation between the three nations.
"This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to strengthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region," Duran said in a post on X.
A Turkish official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Turkey's own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far.
Asked how Turkey could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Houthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Mecca Agreement was not an "offensive agreement," adding that Turkey would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory.
Turkey's constitution requires separate permission from parliament to deploy troops abroad regardless of any international agreement. REUTERS

Bangladesh’s Vital Garment Industry Struggles Amid Global Energy Crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:29:13 UTC
02:29:13 KST

It’s 11 a.m. at Ha-Meem Group’s Ashulia garment factory north of Dhaka and every floor is a whirlwind of feverish labor. Industrial jigsaws slice stacks of denim into precise panels, which nearby seamsters then stitch into jeans, skirts, and jackets.
Next comes washing, ironing, and affixing buttons and zips before the brand labels are attached—Gap, American Eagle, and JCPenney are major clients—and the finished garments are stacked into boxes by some of the group’s 90,000 staff, who together produce 9.3 million apparel items every month.
But suddenly the lights flicker, the workshop dims for a moment, and then full illumination returns accompanied by four cacophonic British-made diesel generators, which automatically splutter into life whenever the gas supply weakens.
“In Bangladesh, the grid electricity is bad, there are frequent interruptions,” says Tanul Chakraborty, head of power, energy and environmental sustainability for Ha-Meem Group. “After gas the most reliable energy in Bangladesh is diesel. Grid electricity is third. Almost the entire economy moves on diesel.”
It’s a startling admission given that Bangladesh’s economy is worth $510 billion, South Asia’s second-largest after India. But the nation is in the grip of a severe power crunch, as wars in Ukraine and Iran expose the fragility of its growing dependence on imported fuel. Since Russia’s invasion, industrial gas prices have risen by 150%, and diesel by about 70%. Since the Iran war began, the cost of spot liquefied natural gas (LNG) has nearly tripled.
That’s bad news for a garment industry that is the country’s largest source of formal employment, directly providing 4 million jobs and supporting countless more livelihoods, while generating $38.7 billion last year—over 80% of export earnings. (Ha Meem alone accounted for $1 billion of exports.)
But the strain extends across the Global South, where developing nations struggle with a prolonged energy crisis that disproportionately squeezes the planet’s most deprived. In the Philippines, heavy dependence on imported Gulf oil has forced emergency conservation measures, including four-day working weeks, restrictions on official travel, and flight cancellations. Diesel prices have risen 86% in Nigeria and more than 50% in Tanzania and Ethiopia, driving up the cost of farming, trucking, and electricity from generators—and, in turn, the price of staples such as rice and corn.
“The poorest people, who spend the highest share of their income on food and fuels, will be hit the hardest,” Indermit Gill, World Bank Chief Economist, warned in April.
In Dhaka, a sprawling megacity of almost 40 million that is usually defined by relentless momentum, the nights have grown eerily dark. With the national power shortfall exceeding 3,000 megawatts, the government has imposed sweeping cuts, exempting only essential services such as hospitals and pharmacies. Illuminated billboards along busy commercial corridors now dim soon after sunset, while shops close an hour early. The burden is even heavier in rural villages, where residents have recently endured blackouts lasting as long as 16 hours a day.
For ordinary citizens, daily life has become a relentless calculus: Residents are forced to rise before dawn in the hope that their stove's gas pressure might be strong enough to cook. Other quandaries include how long they can run a fan against the suffocating humidity, and how far the queues will stretch at the gas station. As businesses flounder, a secondary crisis looms: global malnutrition monitors warn that 18.1 million Bangladeshis may soon face food insecurity.
Internal missteps have only tightened external bottlenecks. The country of 175 million drastically underinvested in both transmission infrastructure and domestic gas fields, meaning today it relies on imports from the Middle East for almost half of its energy. But between July and August, imports of LNG plummeted 83% largely owing to disruption around the blockaded Strait of Hormuz as well as a blaze that temporarily disabled one of its two floating regasification terminals.
Last month, thousands of opposition supporters staged a long march to pressure Prime Minister Tarique Rahman—who only took office in February, just weeks before the Iran war broke out—to do more to tackle soaring fuel costs. “Energy is the biggest test for the new government and has become a galvanizing point for the opposition,” says Michael Kugelman, resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council.
While the global energy crisis is tied to geopolitics, Bangladesh’s woes are uniquely entwined. Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party took power following the popular ouster in 2024 of autocratic former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whom India granted sanctuary, deepening the rift between the neighbors.
Bangladesh imports roughly one-sixth of its electricity from India, which hasn’t been shy in wielding that strategic vulnerability as diplomatic leverage. Compounding the disruption, many of the key architects of national energy policy over Hasina’s 15-year reign have been placed on special duties ostensibly due to their ties to her Awami League party.
Bangladesh also finds itself hostage to shifting Great Power rivalry beyond its neighborhood. Dhaka invested $12.65 billion—chiefly via Moscow-backed loans—in its first nuclear power station in the town of Rooppur built by Russian energy giant Rosatom. The plant was supposed to begin operations in July 2024 but faced repeated delays due partly to the Ukraine war, which complicated payments to Russian banks and blocked the arrival of air and maritime cargo. After finally completing its first controlled nuclear reaction on Oct. 11, it is now expected to go into service in December, although months of staged testing will be required before it reaches a touted output of 1,200 MW.
Complicating matters, the U.S. Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act comes into force on Oct. 18, with provisions including sanctions on senior Russian officials and businesses supporting Russia’s energy sectors. This could mean Dhaka has to secure specific U.S. Treasury waivers or approved payment channels to service its plant debt and buy nuclear fuel.
Meanwhile, Washington is dangling its own alternatives. On Sept. 25, Bangladesh and the U.S. signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on strategic civil nuclear cooperation that focuses on small modular reactors. That comes on top of an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade inked in February that committed Dhaka to massive purchases of U.S. commodities, including $15 billion worth of U.S. energy products over a 15-year period.
But Bangladesh is also looking to Washington’s superpower rival. Rahman’s first overseas trip in June was to Malaysia and China. In Beijing, the two nations signed 17 agreements and other instruments to mark a “new era” of bilateral relations, with one explicitly covering renewable energy cooperation. But two of the agreements involved corporate groups subject to U.S. sanctions, and the growing ties between Dhaka and Beijing have caused consternation in Washington, State Department sources tell TIME. Bangladesh is also in advanced negotiations with a Chinese state-owned firm to build a third floating LNG terminal.
Seemingly pulled in every direction, Dhaka is desperate to instill more energy independence. The government recently launched a special incentive package for rooftop solar, slashing import duties on solar equipment from 17% to 1%, while particularly encouraging systems paired with battery storage. Bangladesh added some 200 MW of solar capacity to the national grid over the first half-year, according to government figures. However, that rate must be ramped up sixfold to have any hope of achieving ambitious five-year targets.
“We are actually looking into diversification, new areas where we can source energy from,” Shama Obaed Islam, State Minister for Foreign Affairs, told TIME as part of a panel at the 2026 Bay of Bengal Conversation last week. “We have [also] been looking into solar energy [and] making every citizen self-sufficient in energy.”
But while rooftop solar may work well for homes, it is far less useful for energy-intensive factories. Ha-Meem has 29.2 MW installed on its roofs—one of the largest private solar installations nationwide—though Chakraborty says it is only helpful for perhaps four hours per day when the sun is highest at a factory complex that operates around the clock.
Paradoxically, Ha-Meem has seen demand increase since the energy crisis. It has absorbed orders from some of the more than 400 smaller factories forced out of business in the three years till June (as well as from customers shifting production out of China to skirt Trumpian tariffs.) But with Ha-Meem’s energy bills rising from roughly $200,000 to $300,000 every day, and clients refusing to budge on prices, there is a relentless drive to boost efficiency.
In the office of Ha-Meem Senior Executive Director Brig-Gen (Ret.) Mohammad Abdul Moeen, a computer spreadsheet maps every employee against hourly targets. Workers who fall behind are counseled by managers—“maybe she had some problem with the machine,” says Moeen. “She may have just been tired”—and offered additional support and training. Those who consistently fall short are replaced by some of the dozens of applicants clutching résumés who queue up at the factory gate each morning.
“We may be facing some kind of energy crisis but that’s more reason why we cannot compromise with productivity,” says Moeen.
Moeen’s relentless focus on efficiency is easy to fathom. The garment industry is ruthlessly competitive and manufacturers fear that any rise in costs or supply disruption could see orders shift to rival Vietnam, Cambodia, or Pakistan. However, simply securing energy is not alone sufficient; with many Western brands making ambitious sustainability commitments that rely on shifting away from fossil fuels, how power is generated is also a key concern.
And if preserving Bangladesh’s dominant role in global garment production is precarious, diversifying the economy is harder still. The nation has ambitious goals of ramping up existing pharmaceutical and leather industries, and even moving into autos, medical devices, and semiconductors. But competition is tough, and few serious investors are charmed by candlelight meetings.
Last month, Bangladesh unveiled a new energy roadmap that aims to add 12,940 MW of generation capacity via new solar installations and coal-fired projects, alongside modernization of grid distribution networks and a total of 300 new exploration wells to firm up domestic gas supplies (31 have already been drilled.)
“We are satisfied with that plan,” says Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association, which represents over 2,500 garment factories. “Within three or four years, maybe there will be no more electricity crisis.”
For now, however, Bangladesh’s garment workers—and billions across the Global South—have little choice but to endure given scant signs of relief in oil markets. In recent days, Yemen’s Houthis have intensified missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, cities, and oil infrastructure, killing civilians in Riyadh, disrupting flights, and provoking Saudi-led strikes that have stoked fears of a wider regional war.
“It’s a difficult situation for the present government,” says Fazlee Shamim Ehsan, managing director of Fatullah Apparels Ltd., which produces 22,000 finished garments per day. “It would be much better if there was no war in the Middle East.”
—With reporting by Zia Chowdhury/Dhaka

Ukrainian government expands measures to address aftermath of emergency affecting heating, water and internet
Ukraine's Cabinet of Ministers has extended a decision containing measures designed to address the energy sector emergency so that it also covers the heating and water supply, transport infrastructure, communication networks and data centres.
Source: Resolution No. 1292 of the Cabinet of Ministers dated 16 October
Details: The decision previously applied to electricity systems. It now also covers heating, water supply, wastewater disposal, engineering and transport infrastructure, electronic communications networks, broadband internet infrastructure and data centres.
The minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport will lead efforts to deal with the consequences of the emergency with respect to utility systems and transport infrastructure. Update at 20:45: The headline and opening paragraphs of the article have been revised in light of a clarification from the Cabinet of Ministers: the decision concerns coordination of efforts to repair critical infrastructure following Russian attacks and does not introduce an emergency situation or impose any new restrictions on the public.
"Responsibility for dealing with the aftermath of attacks on the energy, heating and water supply sectors, as well as telecommunications, has now been assigned to specific ministers. Their joint efforts will subsequently be coordinated by a joint headquarters," the Cabinet of Ministers said.
The headline has been amended to be more accurate. It previously read: "Ukraine declares emergency situation in several key sectors". The editorial team apologises for the misinterpretation.

As Macron visits Gulf, can France forge its own energy-for-security future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:22:05 UTC
02:22:05 KST

As Macron visits Gulf, can France forge its own energy-for-security future?
President Macron’s Gulf visit aims to address rising energy prices and strengthen ties amid regional security concerns.
President Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Bahrain during his tour of the Gulf region, as France continues to reel from a wave of violent protests.
The French leader is hoping to strengthen defence ties and secure oil and gas supplies amid major disruption to global fuel shipments arising from the US-Israel war on Iran. He has already visited Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as part of his three-day trip. His next stop is Qatar.
On the first day of Macron’s trip, France and Kuwait signed eight agreements and cooperation documents covering defence, artificial intelligence, investment and more.
Macron then met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi on Monday. The two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to advancing cooperation in energy, advanced technology and artificial intelligence (AI).
According to the French Foreign Ministry, the UAE is France’s biggest importer in the Gulf, with bilateral trade standing at 10.8 billion euros ($12.1bn) in 2025. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) [PDF], France supplied 18 percent of the UAE’s arms and defence imports in 2025 – the second highest after the United States, at 42 percent.
But this isn’t all about simple trade.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at King’s College London’s School of Security Studies, explained that Macron’s visit to the region is “symptomatic of a much larger geopolitical transformation”.
“We are witnessing the gradual emergence of a post-American Middle East in which Washington remains militarily powerful but increasingly struggles to exercise the political leadership it once enjoyed,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.
“Europe and the Gulf now face a remarkably similar strategic challenge. Both have become excessively dependent on American security decisions, and both are discovering that this dependence carries substantial economic and political costs.”
An urgent need for energy
Most pressing for Macron is finding solutions for strife at home.
France has been engulfed in protests and violence over a proposed government budget seeking tens of millions of euros in savings to public spending. Protesters angry about the crumbling state of French schools and planned pay freezes for public-sector workers have taken to the streets in increasingly violent protests, and authorities have imposed curfews in some cities.
More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday as protesters demanded better education infrastructure and government steps to address the cost-of-living crisis. During weeks of protests, more than 2,500 people have been arrested, and demonstrations have descended into looting and arson in numerous locations.
A major issue is the spike in energy prices affecting all of Europe – much of it as a result of the Iran war – which has also fuelled growing public anger in France. Disruptions to the supply of refined oil products such as petrol and diesel caused by the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz have caused up to 20 percent of French petrol stations to run out of both at various times since the conflict began.
Macron’s visit to the Gulf, accompanied by senior executives from France’s two biggest energy groups, TotalEnergies and Engie, comes as oil prices hover above $100 a barrel.
What France needs most urgently, therefore, is new suppliers. Those look to have been secured.
On Tuesday, the UAE committed to supplying 100,000 tonnes (746,000 barrels) of diesel per month to France for an unspecified duration, according to Bloomberg.
Bahrain has agreed to supply 100,000 tonnes of diesel per month for an unspecified duration, while Saudi Arabia will provide 95,000 tonnes in each of October and November, via TotalEnergies.
Cooperating on Gulf defence
Besides securing oil imports, however, France is also looking to boost its own exports, particularly of its defence equipment to the Gulf region, as the country suffers from record national debt – the highest level since the immediate aftermath of World War II, analysts say.
France has already strengthened its military partnership with Saudi Arabia, which has been battling the Iran-backed Houthi group from Yemen.
Last month, Macron said France would send troops and defence systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which is crucial for energy transport. Oil installations and airports in Saudi Arabia have come under attack from the Houthi group.
In late September, Macron said France would deploy what he termed “military means” to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Yanbu Red Sea oil terminal. Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, which carries oil from its eastern oilfields across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea, has come under attack during the Iran conflict. It is the country’s main means of continuing to export oil while the critical Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted. But Yemen’s Houthis have also been attacking Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
Macron stated in a TV interview that “soldiers, radars, defence systems” would be sent.
While he did not give specifics about volumes, it was a move described by French newspaper Le Monde as marking “a geopolitical shift”, as defence cooperation between the two countries has previously been “discreet, ambiguous and marked by extreme caution when it came to defining it”, the newspaper noted.
Last week, France’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Pascal Confavreux, said again that “operational elements” to defend Saudi oil facilities had been put into action, without specifying which “military means” had been sent.
Meanwhile, on Monday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot met with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, to review bilateral relations and discuss regional developments. Barrot also reaffirmed France’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks.
Krieg assesses that France can offer Gulf states generally something that has become “increasingly valuable”: military capabilities not entirely dependent on the US.
“France can offer defence industrial cooperation, technology transfers, joint production, training and greater operational autonomy,” he said. “For countries such as the UAE and Qatar, this means progressively reducing their dependence on American weapons systems, spare parts, intelligence and political permissions.”
Involved – but not too involved
However, Krieg cautioned that the “central strategic dilemma” for France is likely to be whether increasing its involvement in the region could draw it into the ongoing conflict.
“Consider the protection of Saudi energy infrastructure against Houthi attacks,” he said. “French air defence systems intercepting missiles would directly undermine the Houthis’ military strategy. If French forces are subsequently targeted, Paris could face pressure to retaliate. What begins as a defensive deployment could gradually become an operational commitment with much wider implications.”
Krieg explained that the same is likely to apply to naval deployments around the Strait of Hormuz, adding that “escalation in one theatre can rapidly affect another”.
France’s ties with Iran have already been strained over tit-for-tat diplomatic expulsions and political rhetoric against each other.
In July and August, France strongly condemned Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
In July, two French Embassy staff members were detained in Tehran and then declared personae non gratae. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said the diplomats had “interfered in Iran’s internal affairs under the pretext of engaging with civil society”.
In August, French Foreign Minister Barrot expelled two Iranian diplomats in retaliation.
A new regional security architecture
Speaking at the Global Security Forum in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Tuesday, US Envoy Tom Barrack said that Washington is moving away from its traditional security-for-oil relationship with the Middle East and no longer seeks to dominate the region.
“The US no longer wants to own,” said Barrack, who serves as US ambassador to Turkiye and special envoy for Syria. “The bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We’re not leaving.”
Barrack acknowledged that, following months of Iranian strikes on their infrastructure, regional partners are increasingly recognising the limits of US involvement.
Across the Middle East itself, defence partnerships have grown. In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed a trilateral security pact, also known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The pact has been activated amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
But there may now be an opening for other external actors – such as France – to find more of a role.
Krieg said Gulf states do not believe France will replace the US, whose military and intelligence infrastructure remains “unmatched”. Rather, they want a “diversified network of security partnerships”.
“France is particularly attractive because it possesses genuine expeditionary capabilities and has demonstrated a willingness to defend Gulf partners without joining Washington’s offensive campaign against Iran,” he said. “Its military presence has consequently acquired greater political significance.”

Round-the-clock Russian terror: how much longer will the enemy be able to attack Ukraine continuously
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:22:03 EEST
02:22:03 KST

Round-the-clock Russian terror: how much longer will the enemy be able to attack Ukraine continuously
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has intensified its drone attacks, seeking to exhaust air defenses and pressure Ukraine. Stronger defense and strikes against Russia's military-industrial complex could reduce the attacks.
Russia continues its massive drone attacks on Ukraine and is attempting to cover as large an area as possible with its strikes. Military expert Oleh Zhdanov told a UNN journalist more about why the Russian Federation is relying on massive air attacks, how they are connected to political pressure on Ukraine, and what could force Russia to reduce the intensity of its strikes.
Details
Russian drone attacks are taking place virtually around the clock, but the nature of the air strikes changed at the end of October. According to the military expert, whereas reactive drones predominated earlier, Russia is now once again actively using conventional attack drones. In addition, the enemy is attempting to simultaneously cover as much of Ukrainian territory as possible with its attacks.
It is very strange that now "our old song is starting again—we are starting it all over again." In the sense that they are now going to attack 24/7. And what have they been doing all this time? Even now, if you look out the window, air raid alerts are in effect 24/7 across most of Ukraine. And we made it through the whole of September like that
Russia plans to increase drone production: Politico learned the details21.09.26, 10:29 • 5874 views
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov noted that at the end of September, short intervals began to appear between drone raids. In particular, in Kyiv and other cities, there was sometimes approximately an hour between successive attacks, but at the end of October, Russia once again intensified its attacks.
The difference at the end of October is that they began trying to cover all of Ukraine. They have returned again: whereas in September they were mostly reactive, now they have once again added conventional "Shaheds" and "Geran-2" drones. And their number is greater—more than half of the drones in these continuous raids at present
Ballistic missiles also remain a separate threat; their launches, Oleh Zhdanov emphasizes, are more difficult to predict. He explains that recently Russia has used them at intervals of approximately once every 7–10 days. Moreover, the intensity of such strikes may vary, so Ukraine must also be prepared for combined attacks.
Will Russia have enough resources for continuous attacks
The expert notes that Russia is using the means of destruction at its disposal, while the scale of drone use depends, in particular, on production capabilities.
They can provide a large number of drones—and they do. Note that in September they were stockpiling conventional "Geran-2" drones. In fact, they used very few of them for a month, and then in the first ten days of October they carried out two powerful strikes, when the number of conventional drones exceeded 500 units. And now they are launching them within the limits produced by their enterprises
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov believes that Russia has limited capacity to accumulate large stockpiles of weapons, so it is forced to constantly replenish the resources it has used. However, this does not mean that the intensity of the attacks will necessarily decrease in the near future.
They are essentially operating straight from the production line; there are very few stockpiles at present. And I say again, we have two options: the first is to destroy their production facilities, but we cannot reach them, plus they have now begun burying the same "Geran" drones in the ground. So the second option is to build an air defense system in a new, modern sense, rather than according to the old approaches of the Soviet Union or the Second World War
Why Russia is relying on drones
Massive drone attacks allow Russia to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses over a prolonged period and create a constant threat to the civilian population and infrastructure. In the expert's view, the Kremlin seeks to use these strikes as an instrument of pressure on Ukrainians in order to secure concessions on its own terms.
The objective is one and only one—to break public opinion so that people agree to capitulate on the terms of the Russian Federation. And now, by the way, negotiations are underway in Norway, and it is the same old song: "Surrender, and everything will be fine for you. If you do not surrender to us, we will continue the shelling." That's all
The expert also links the intensity of Russian attacks, in particular, to the upcoming midterm elections in the United States and negotiations on ending the war, in order to increase pressure on Ukraine precisely during periods of important international events.
Absolutely. putin always ties powerful shelling of Ukraine and massive combined strikes to political events. Today, the midterm elections in the United States are at the top of our agenda. And in fact, in my view, both Trump and putin have simultaneously gone all in. They are applying pressure in every way they can, - with all available forces and means
What could force Russia to reduce the number of strikes
The expert identifies strengthening Ukraine’s air defense as one of the key areas for countering Russian attacks. In his opinion, it is necessary to improve the ability to intercept targets at short and medium ranges, as well as to develop weapons capable of destroying threats before they are used. In addition, strikes against Russia’s military-industrial enterprises also play an important role.
Sanctions are a long song. And the most effective sanctions are our missiles and our drones. Unfortunately, our strikes against military-industrial complex enterprises are not as powerful as one would like, because even a drone carrying 100 kilograms of explosives is not a missile carrying 300 or 500 kilograms of explosives
Oleh Zhdanov also drew attention to the importance of ballistic weapons, which, according to him, could enhance Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian launchers and other military targets. At the same time, the effectiveness of countermeasures depends not only on the availability of such weapons, but also on the ability to detect targets in a timely manner and strike them. The expert believes that the development of indigenous missile technologies could become one of the factors deterring Russian attacks.
If we had ballistic missiles, we would take out the launchers or at least drive them away from the border so that they could not reach our territory. There is very little time to hit a launcher at its launch position or in the loading area. That is why Russia is very afraid of Ukraine acquiring ballistic weapons

'Unsettled' MPs say security measures meant to protect them are lacking
In short:
Federal MPs have told the ABC they are afraid for their safety after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines.
MPs said some of the security measures available to them were infrequent or "lacklustre", while others, like threat assessments for their homes, had not been offered.
What's next?
The Australian Federal Police Association has called for privately contracted security assessments of MP homes to be brought under the AFP.
Federal MPs have described deep fears for their safety in the wake of the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, with some describing a mixed experience of the security services made available to them.
The Australian Federal Police Association says police protection for MPs and the threat assessments conducted for them must be reviewed, and has called for privately contracted home security inspections to be taken over by the AFP.
While ministers and high-profile individuals receive regular protection and threat assessments, other MPs have described infrequent or "tokenistic" threat assessments. In some cases, MPs said they had never been offered risk assessments for their home security.
The attack on Ms Haines outside her Wangaratta electorate office in regional Victoria has shaken federal politicians, particularly because Ms Haines is considered well-liked and less at risk than higher-profile or more controversial MPs.
Australian Federal Police Association president Alex Caruana said the number of MPs expressing safety fears was increasing.
"Certainly the experience I have had is MPs ringing me and saying they are feeling unsafe," Mr Caruana said.
"We need to make sure that not just that particular person is safe but their entire family. And the number of politicians and the number of MPs that have rung me to say, 'Hey, I feel safe but my family don't feel safe,' … has increased significantly."
National security agencies have repeatedly warned of the growing threat of politically motivated violence.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said security agencies identified more than 1,000 threats to federal politicians in the most recent financial year, and every federal MP that the ABC spoke to described receiving death threats, with some also describing court action resulting from threats made to them, particularly online.
MPs, who the ABC has not named in order to protect their security arrangements, have described feeling exposed after an attack on a "delightful" regional MP with "non-aggressive politics", who would have been categorised as being at lower risk.
"I feel unsettled, that's how I feel. Unsettled and grieving," one MP said.
Another said: "As a woman in politics, I feel pretty nervous at the moment."
"I am certainly not instilled with confidence they are doing all they can."
Minister for Women Katy Gallagher said colleagues had expressed fears for their safety to her.
"Yes, they are [afraid] and I don't think we should pretend otherwise," Senator Gallagher told ABC Afternoon Briefing yesterday.
AFP protection levels must be reassessed: police union
The AFP provides "close personal protection" to high-profile politicians, including MPs deemed to be at higher risk, though for many MPs that service is only periodic or in response to a specific threat.
Mr Caruana said two years ago there were far many more operational hours required than there were sworn officers to meet it, something that had since been assessed and rebalanced.
But he said staffing levels would have to be revisited in the wake of the attack against Ms Haines.
"I think it is very pertinent now that we look at what is the risk assessment, the real risk assessment, and what is the risk appetite of the people we are serving," Mr Caruana said.
"My gut feeling is we may have prioritised costs over safety in some of those instances."
The AFP received a little over half a billion dollars in the 2024-25 financial year to protect politicians and sensitive facilities, funding which the home affairs minister said received "a major increase" at the last budget.
At the 2025 federal election, more than 600 AFP personnel worked more than 45,000 operational hours to provide protective security to politicians and candidates campaigning across the country.
Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson said the attack would change the way politicians managed their safety and it would be "prudent" to have a security review.
He acknowledged it would not be practical to provide full-time protection for every member of parliament but said change was needed.
"Our electorate offices are the places where we're most identifiable and where Helen was when this attack occurred," Senator Paterson said.
"They are not well protected in my view. They are exposed and that's not just a risk to us, that's a risk to our staff, to our family members and to our constituents who are visiting."
An AFP spokesperson said it did not comment on the specific protective security arrangements for MPs or its capabilities.
MPs have told the ABC the frequency of engagement with the AFP could vary, and that changes in roles or circumstances did not always prompt a fresh threat assessment.
One MP said they were caught off guard after changing roles and attending an event with their children, who were "terrified" when it was crashed by violent protesters.
A 24-hour contact point is available for MPs to report safety concerns, with a dedicated team resourced to investigate threats.
Senior Home Affairs, AFP and ASIO officers will update MPs today on the current threat environment, and will also encourage MPs to share their diaries in order to more proactively manage risks to their safety.
An AFP spokesperson said the agency had delivered six multi-agency briefings for MPs just this year, including security awareness resources, engagement and reporting pathways.
But MPs say for some safety tasks they have been left to themselves and have received "lacklustre" advice such as to vet constituents before meeting them or to not share in advance that they will attend an event.
"That's just not practical for most members of parliament because they need to be able to tell their constituents where they are so they can be accessible to their constituents," Senator Paterson said.
Community Strong MP Allegra Spender said she feared politicians would pull back from the very sort of "active, available and very locally engaged" politics that Ms Haines embodied.
"Security services will only get us so far. I think the bigger issue is culturally," Ms Spender said.
"I think a lot of us thought that something like this could easily happen, truthfully, because of the level of aggression you see online, but also that you sometimes see on the streets."
Mixed experiences with home security for MPs
The AFP conducts individualised threat assessments for the highest-risk politicians, such as ministers on the National Security Committee of cabinet, or MPs with Jewish or Arabic backgrounds, but for those deemed to face the lowest risk, threat assessments by the AFP are conducted at a group level.
Further assessments can be conducted in response to an incident or concern, either by the AFP or privately contracted firms.
For many MPs, residential assessments are also contracted to private security firms, which politicians have told the ABC has been a mixed experience.
At least two MPs said they had never received an offer for their home security to be assessed, and that changes in roles or taking on more senior positions did not prompt new threat assessments.
Another said they felt that residential assessment had been "tokenistic", and they had to self-fund some security measures.
Mr Caruana said those residential assessments should be brought under the AFP.
"We need to ensure we have got some consistency across the board … the AFP does their own risk assessments for residentials for some of our own high-profile members … so we have the capability already, we have the training," he said.

2 men rearrested on suspicion of spying for Iran over suspected plot at U.S.-run air base in England
British police said Tuesday they have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service over the suspected plot at a U.S.-run air base in England last month.
Counter Terrorism Policing said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.
The men were earlier arrested but had been bailed pending more investigation.
Police are investigating a suspected terror plot on Sept. 27 against the U.S.-run base at RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year's war.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford.
Five other men who were also arrested earlier remain on bail. No one has yet been charged.
Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K., said detectives are looking at "many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation."
"This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," he said in a statement.
"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it," he added.
Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. But the Iranian Embassy in London said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Air Force removed all of its bombers from the air base following the security incident.

Russian satellite dangerously nears European spacecraft supporting Ukraine’s military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:10:25 UTC
02:10:25 KST

Russian satellite dangerously nears European spacecraft supporting Ukraine’s military
- A Russian military satellite, Cosmos-2612, came within 100m of the ICEYE-X36 spacecraft on Oct 18, raising fears it was meant to inspect or interfere with the satellite.
- ICEYE says it is “tracking it closely”, while experts say the manoeuvre was worrying because it deliberately matched the satellite’s orbit and supports Ukraine’s military.
- The US Space Force says Russia has made similar “fuel-intensive” moves before, and analysts warn more close approaches could happen in the coming weeks.
AI generated
PARIS - A Russian satellite moved within just 100m of a European commercial spacecraft that supports Ukraine’s military at the weekend, orbital tracking data showed, raising concerns about Moscow’s activities in space.
Russia launched the Cosmos-2612 military satellite into low Earth orbit in April.
It began changing course in late September and eventually moved into the same orbit as ICEYE-X36, a satellite operated by Finland’s ICEYE under contract with the United States.
The two spacecraft came within 100m of each other on Oct 18, according to orbital tracking data analysed by AFP.
“There is no reason it would have needed to manoeuvre the way it did... and into such close proximity to the ICEYE satellite for a benign reason,” Clayton Swope, a space security specialist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, told AFP.
The incident has drawn attention from space experts, who say such close approaches can be used to inspect, monitor or interfere with other satellites.
While Russian satellites have passed near foreign spacecraft before, experts said several factors of this case stood out.
“It was a combination of factors that made this event so concerning”, Swope said.
The Russian satellite not only approached the Finnish spacecraft but deliberately adjusted its orbit to closely match it, he explained.
ICEYE’s satellite constellation also provides imagery and space-tracking data that supports Ukraine in its war with Russia.
‘Tracking it closely’
An ICEYE spokesperson told AFP the company was aware of the incident and “tracking it closely”.
The US Space Force accused Russia of unusually “fuel-intensive” manoeuvres in May to move four military satellites close to a Western commercial satellite used by Ukraine.
ICEYE’s satellites use radar technology that can capture images of the Earth’s surface at night and through cloud cover, making them particularly valuable for military intelligence.
The satellite approached by Cosmos-2612 uses the same tech as another ICEYE spacecraft involved in the May incident.
The US Space Force says Russia has launched several satellites in recent years to test technologies that could be used to intercept or disrupt other spacecraft.
Swope stressed, however, it was impossible to confirm whether Cosmos-2612 carried a weapon.
In a published note, he said the incident should be viewed in the broader context of Russia’s efforts to challenge Western space capabilities.
Since the start of its Ukraine invasion, Moscow has argued that Western commercial satellites supporting Kyiv are indirectly taking part in the conflict.
A Russian foreign ministry official in 2022 warned at the UN that such “quasi-civilian infrastructure” could become a legitimate target for retaliation.
By the morning of Oct 19, Cosmos-2612 was moving away from ICEYE-X36 and the two satellites were again separated by several kilometres.
Analysts at the US-based ISR Institute last week predicted that another close approach involving Russian satellites and an ICEYE spacecraft could take place in the coming weeks. AFP

IDF strike kills Hamas terrorist linked to Shani Louk’s abduction
The IDF and Shin Bet say the man participated in the October 7 attack and later worked to rebuild Hamas’s military capabilities and prepare new attacks
An Israeli airstrike in northern Gaza has killed a Hamas operative who took part in the abduction of Shani Louk during the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, according to a joint statement from the Israeli military and the Shin Bet security agency.
The statement identified the man as Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of Hamas’s military wing, and said he was killed Monday in the Jabalia area.
Israeli authorities said he had crossed into Israel during the Hamas-led assault and participated in Louk’s abduction.
Louk, a German-Israeli tattoo artist, had attended the Nova music festival. Israeli authorities later determined that she was killed while fleeing the attack and that her body was taken into Gaza.
Footage showing her body in a pickup truck circulated internationally, drawing widespread attention to her fate. Israeli forces recovered her remains in May 2024.
The military and Shin Bet said Al-Zabaq had continued planning attacks against Israeli troops and civilians during the war, including recently, and had worked to rebuild Hamas’s military capabilities. They described those activities as violations of the ceasefire and said the strike was intended to remove the threat he posed.
The statement did not detail the evidence linking Al-Zabaq to Louk’s abduction or identify the recent attacks he was accused of preparing.
Israeli authorities said precision munitions and aerial surveillance were used to reduce the risk of civilian harm.
