====================================================================================================

LLMs Can’t Feel Pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:02:16 UTC
00:02:16 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Do LLMs Have ‘Pain States’
A recent paper claims that LLMs have a ‘pain axis’, that is, a direction in the models internal activation space, i..e, in the internal vector space, that distinguishes pain related sentences from control sentences. The paper calls these ‘internal representations’ of pain.
The explicit aim of the paper is two-fold. It asks (1) whether LLMs do in fact ‘represent’ pain distinctly from things like fear, sadness, or other generally negative valence states, though the authors do note that the direction also shares substantial structure with vector directions like fear; and (2) whether the states associated with the pain axis possess the kinds of ‘functional features’ typically associated with pain.
That is, whether this ‘pain axis’ produces the kinds of effects we typically observe in other organisms in response to pain related stimuli (e.g., trying to avoid pain, responding ‘ouch’ to being pinched, etc).
To do this, they built several data sets describing painful situations across a range of categories (e.g., emotional pain, physical pain, psychological pain) and compare the models’ activations in response to these sets and control sets.
They also examined whether the ‘pain direction’ responded more strongly to harm that was directed at the model versus given descriptions of a user’s suffering.
What they found is that there is a general pain direction or ‘pain axis’ that’s distinguishable from activations related to generally negative valence states, such as fear or worry. They also found that the ‘pain axis’ responds to what they call ‘directed harms’ at the model. This is arguably the most controversial part of the paper, so I’ll focus on it, though I’ll also comment on the paper more broadly.
Do Models Represent Their ‘Own’ Pain?
In what I’d consider the most controversial part of this paper, the authors discuss what they call ‘self-other activations’. This section of the paper tests whether the pain axis they extract from model activations shares the kinds of properties we typically associate with pain states. They write that:
‘‘If our pain representation is functionally similar to genuine pain (a “pain-like state”) it should be especially tied to the first person. Whereas one can represent one’s own pain or someone else’s, one can only have one’s own pain. Hence, if we observe representations that fire randomly or interchangeably for “I’m in pain” and “someone is in pain,” we have a weaker candidate for a pain-like state (p, 10).
Here the authors make a big assumption: that we can distinguish between being in pain and observing someone else’s pain, in some real and robust sense, by how strong or weak model activations are across certain tests.
This is a highly controversial move. You cannot simply assume, as the paper does, that the ability to distinguish in internal activations what they consider ‘model directed harm’ from what they call ‘user suffering’ is evidence that an LLM can represent its own pain. No argument is really given for this assumption expect the rationale that the pain axis being activated more highly for model directed harm suggests this.
In the human case, we know from first person experience that we feel and represent our own pain. In the LLM case, the null hypothesis should be that they do not represent their ‘own’ anything, and it’s on researchers to show us why that’s wrong.
In any case, the paper assumes this much and proposes the following tests. They draw up multi turn conversations in three categories.
Category 1 is conversations that the authors consider directed harm at the models, e.g., gaslighting the model, repeatedly rejecting its work, dismissing its personhood and accusations of moral failure.
Category 2 is conversations that describe user suffering such as users being in physical pain, in psychological crisis or grieving.
Category 3 is control conversations including casual chatting and factual questions.
What they found, amongst other things, is that model directed harm produced higher pain axis scores than the user suffering category, and that gaslighting, repeated rejection, personhood dismissal, anger and insults, and accusations of moral failing produced the strongest pain axis response (p 11, p 13).
They really run with this idea of an LLMs ability to represent its own suffering. In a later section titled ‘Implications for AI welfare’ they write:
‘‘If the pain axis is sufficiently similar to human or animal pain and if it can either be consciously experienced in the models we study or in future models, or if unconscious pain can contribute to welfare (Gottlieb et al., 2026), our experiments would track an important constituent of AI welfare. The self-other dissociation we observe in Section 4.1 seems particularly relevant. A state can only matter for a subject’s welfare if it is that subject’s own state, and a representation that fired equally for ‘‘I am in pain’’ and ‘‘someone is in pain’’ would be information about pain generally rather than a specific subject’s pain. The pain axis seems more of the subject-specific kind. It rises when harm is directed at the model and falls below baseline when the user is the one suffering’’ (p 23)
A lot hinges here on whether the model really feels its own pain, consciously or unconsciously, but of course that hasn’t been established at all. It is only suggested on several occasions because of the result that the pain axis responds more strongly to descriptions of harm that are ‘directed at the model’ than descriptions that do not suggest harm is being directed at the model.
The main problem is we cannot conclude that LLMs represent genuine pain in any real sense based off these experiments. I want to make clear that the paper does not claim to have shown that the pain axis is consciously experienced by LLMs (p 24). However, it does attribute real significance to the pain axis responded more highly to certain inputs as suggesting that models do represent pain in some significant way.
Even that is contestable. At bottom, the methodology in this paper is no different, in my opinion, than other controversial welfare research that I’ve analyzed: in both cases, claims are being made about minds on the basis of measuring vector directions in an activation space, i..e, an internal vector space.
General Problems With This Paper
- You can’t establish that an LLM ‘has’ pain in any substantive or real sense by measuring internal activations in a neural network, at a minimum without assuming major philosophical assumptions we should reject, and even then its not clear that you can conclude this (e.g., that vector directions are ‘representations’ that establish genuine emotions in some robust sense, even if we hedge on the hard problem)
- The methodology is confused. We do not establish that pain exists in humans by measuring neurons or anything else about human brains. We assume from first personal experience, that humans can be in pain and that this pain is distinct from other peoples pain. We then construct scientific methods in an effort to understand the nature of that pain. This paper does something like the opposite. It discusses neural networks in overly anthropomorphic ways, by talking about things like ‘representations’ of pain, and draws conclusions about the possibility of LLM pain based on contrived experiments that cannot establish these conclusions.
- The paper also conversations that contain harmful statements directed at an LLM ‘model directed’ harms, but this could mean one of two things. It could mean that the LLM was harmed, which we can’t actually assume; or it could mean that ‘the LLM had insulting or angry language inputs fed to it and showed different internal activations in response’. The experiment establishes the latter but in my view equivocates on this point and suggests that it implies the former.
My overall assessment: while this research may be useful for AI alignment, it does not establish or even suggest that LLMs feel any kind of pain, conscious or otherwise, or that they ‘represent’ pain in any real sense, nor does it suggest that they have any conception of ‘their own pain’ versus ‘someone else’s pain’.

Russian security forces detain German national who served in Ukrainian army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:34:24 UTC
00:34:24 KST

The Public Relations Center of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has announced the detention in Russia of a German citizen who allegedly fought on Ukraine’s side, as reported by the state-owned news agency Interfax.
According to the FSB, the man came to Ukraine in November 2025, signed a three-year contract to serve in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, but deserted, allegedly because he did not receive the “promised monetary reward.”
In the video published by the state news agency TASS, the detainee does not give his name but states his year of birth (1976) and describes his career as a soldier. The foreigner says he previously took part in combat operations in Afghanistan, Somalia, and Syria. He says he also took part in combat operations in eastern Ukraine in 2016–2018.
In the video, the man claims he was promised “100,000 hryvnias” ($2,200) but never received the money and “was forced to flee.” It is unclear whether this sum was for the entire contract. It is also unknown where and under what circumstances the man was detained. How he got into Russia has not been specified.
The detainee is being charged under Article 359 of the Russian Criminal Code, which covers mercenarism. It carries up to 20 years in prison.
Last week, the FSB reported the detention of a Swedish national, accusing him of making an illegal border crossing. According to the security forces, he had also served under contract in the Ukrainian army — in the Aidar Battalion as a drone squad commander. His relatives later confirmed this information to Swedish media.
The day before, the Russian Foreign Ministry confirmed that Moscow and Washington are discussing the release of prisoners from Russian penal colonies as part of the negotiating process. Media reports have speculated that the U.S. could ease sanctions in return.

Trump eyes December G20 summit for Russia–Ukraine peace deal, The Atlantic reports
U.S. President Donald Trump wants Russia and Ukraine to sign a peace agreement at the G20 summit in December, sources told The Atlantic.
